Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī
Composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrīmad Abhinavagupta,
by the command of the illustrious Harisiṃhajī Bahādur, the King of Kings, the Great Emperor, the Sovereign of Kaśmīra.
After the completion of the editing and other refinements by Paṇḍita Madhusūdana Kaula Śāstrī, Director of the Research Institute, with the assistance of other scholars employed at the institute.
Having been completed and printed at the Nirṇayasāgara Press in Mumbai, it has been brought into publication.
(Third Part) Saṃvat 2000. Śrīnagara, Kashmir. Christian Era 1943.
(The rights of printing and publication of this work belong to the aforementioned noble Maharajas.)
[These] have been brought under one's own control.
[This is from] the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*,
composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the Great Mahāmaheśvara.
The Section on Ritual Action.
Now begins the first inquiry:
[I salute] Śiva, whose body is nectar, who partakes of the third portion of the fourfold digits of nectar.
I bow to Him who illumines manifold sequential order even within that which is devoid of sequence.

Having thus expanded upon and determined the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), the section on action (*kriyā-adhikāra*) is now commenced so that the essential nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) may likewise be determined. In this regard, by means of eight verses, it is said: "For this very reason... [and so forth].
With these words,

ending with "thus the distinction between the knower and the knowable is manifested," [it is shown that] although action is in reality non-successive in the Blessed Lord, for the bound subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*)...
It is established that there is succession because of the connection with manifestation. For instance: by one [verse], the previously stated prima facie position is refuted;
by one, the distinction between succession and non-succession is made; by three, the nature of succession is explained;
and by two, the division of the objects of succession and non-succession is shown. Even regarding this division of objects—
The meaning of this section is that, in reality, the rest of both [powers] lies in one and the same place—this is stated by the verse;

however, it is now examined according to each individual aphorism. Furthermore, by means of the logic applicable to the determination of the principle of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), another subject of inquiry under discussion is also established in the manner of a "conclusion by implication" (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*).
Thus, by this very [sūtra], that which was stated—"Action is not successive for a single [entity];
it is one," and so forth—is refuted, because that [single entity] has been established. (1)
(Page 2) Cognitions alone, existing as a continuous stream in the form of experience and conceptualization, are what manifest;
there is no substratum for them whatsoever. Furthermore, memory is established solely through mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). And cognition...

If it were insentient (*jaḍa*), to whom would there be the manifestation of objects? If it is non-insentient (*ajaḍa*), then since it is not subject to distinctions arising from connection with space and time, how could that [object] be other than the Self (*ātman*)? Thus much has been set forth as the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Regarding that, the following was offered as the reply: "Diverse cognitions do not constitute the basis for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); nor..."

Memory and cognition arise from mere mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); and cognition is the very same undifferentiated consciousness appearing in a contracted form through its own power by being colored by the object of knowledge—this [power] is called both "capacity" (*śakti*) and "attribute" (*dharma*).
For this very reason, even that which pertains to action has been presented as a counter-argument based on this collection of reasons.
This is rejected. The word "also" (*api*) implies that the refutation applies not only to the object of cognition. For it has been objected:

"How can an action be both unitary and successive? And if the substratum is conjoined with it, how can it maintain a single nature? Furthermore, how can a relation—which by its very form resides in two [relata]—be one?"

In this regard, the summary is as follows: how could one thing possess a manifold nature? In that context, just as in the case of a mirror, the diversity of manifold appearances does not bring about contradiction, as it does not subvert their unity; thus, the statement remains unrefuted.

An object, whose unitary nature is established by the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), has as its essence a manifestation (*ābhāsa*); thus, while assuming within itself those very same contradictory forms, it forcibly manifests those successive differences of manifestation within its own undivided self, and is therefore the substratum of action.

This is indeed appropriate. This very same method of proof applies to the relationship (*sambandha*) and so forth as well. Thus, by establishing a single substratum (*āśraya*), the objections regarding the causal capacity of the logical reason (*hetu*) are also resolved; such is the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*). "Everywhere" means both externally and internally. "They maintain" refers to the followers of Kaṇāda and others. But here...

In the doctrine that the essence of things consists in their appearance (*ābhāsa*), if an entity has cognition as its essence, then how could it be established as distinct from that cognition even by means of oaths? This is the intended meaning. (1)

(Page 3) But surely, sequentiality is the very lifeblood of action; and how could sequence exist in the Blessed Lord, who is unconditioned by time? He provides the resolution for this in the aphorism:
The succession of worldly activity is possible through the power of time, but it is not so for that which is eternal, such as the sovereignty of the Lord. || 2 ||

"It raises and lowers" refers to the hand; those moments of the hand that occur in the east and north are indeed successive. Among these, for some, those very moments constitute a single action that serves as the cause of disjunction and conjunction; for others, they bring about a specific transformation of the form residing in that hand.

Even though [the Lord] is eternally inferable, He is inferred as being sequential precisely by virtue of His sequential effects; thus, it is logical that action—which rests in worldly differentiation—is sequential, being caused by the power of Time characterized by the Lord’s sovereignty, which brings about the interruption of manifestations. But for the Lord...

Because it is not limited by time, that action which [belongs to the Lord] is also indeed not limited by time; for it is eternal, like the Lord Himself. This is what is meant: the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) of the Lord is the capacity to manifest the knower and the known, which is the root of the worldly transaction of cognition. In that very [context]:

In reality, action is nothing other than the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), whose nature is the independence [of consciousness] regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth. And this has been stated:
"And action consists of the activity of the supreme speech (*paravāk*)," and so on.

In such passages as these, the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) is as follows: although that [consciousness] is in reality devoid of succession, it appears as if possessing succession because it accepts limitations due to the infusion of the shadow of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), despite its own transparency; this is clear in the commentary (*vṛtti*) and the sub-commentary (*vivṛti*). Furthermore, "even from the swallowing of time" means that it is indeed without succession precisely because it is not limited by time.

"It remains exactly as it is. What is said here? Even when the multitude of objects of cognition has opened up, the Blessed One, while occupying the state of the subject under the influence of *māyā*, [perceives] the entire collection of objects—both external and internal—within his own self.
The repose of light within itself. (Āgamaprāmāṇya 22) (page 4)
By the principle stated in [Aparokṣānubhūtiprakaraṇasiddhi] 15, "This" (*idam*)— referring to this fragmented reflective awareness (*vicchinnavimarśa*)—
swallows and brings to rest; for as long as that is so, even the sequence of manifestation is grounded in that [consciousness].

It is indeed "seized"—that is, that activity characterized by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the specific final stage, which culminates in the withdrawal of the manifestation of all phenomena variegated by the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, such as the notion of "I" (*aham*); that [activity] is indeed the emergence. || 2 ||

Now, what is this "time" that is said to be the delimiter of entities? For how can that which is accepted by some as being of the nature of a specific eternal substance—being unitary—be the cause of cognitions of diverse forms such as "slow," "quick," and so forth, through its particular conjunctions? If it is argued that such designations occur by the power of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then those adjuncts alone [should be the cause].

"Let there be limiting adjuncts (upādhi); what of it? For that which is unconnected with those [adjuncts], such as qualities (guṇa) and actions (karman), there would be no delimitation by time. Anticipating this objection, [the author replies: "The power of Time is none other than the power of the Lord Himself, manifesting succession. And that which is manifested by it is attached to the subject (pramātṛ) of Māyā."
To demonstrate that time is precisely this sequence— which, as the primary factor, consists in the state of being the object of these [perceptions]— the aphorism states:
"Time is the movement of the sun and so forth, or the birth of various flowers and such."
Whether it be cold or heat, that very sequence is indeed its true nature.

Gold is measured by a counterweight (*prativartaka*) and the like, which have a fixed measure; yet in this case, there is neither an infinite regress nor mutual dependence. Similarly, Caitra’s journey is [measured] by means of an action whose duration is well known—namely, that consisting of the rising and setting of the sun. Thus it is said: "Caitra travels for a day."
When even the activity of the sun is to be measured, it is then measured by means of well-known measures of time such as the *nālikā*—

namely, that the sun is visible for thirty *nālikās*. Therefore, whenever and wherever a group of appearances is determined by its specific measure— such as the moon, the sun, cold, heat, the cuckoo, or a gathering [of people]— [it is so established].

Of that [time], at that place, then, it is that very time. Therefore, the fixed differentiation of intrinsic nature belonging to the sun and so forth is "sequence" (*krama*); that alone is [the sequence].
(page 5)

Time. By it, through the movement of the sun and other such means, another entity is perceived which possesses the property of flowing (pravahaṇadharman), which gives rise to the unmixed states of newness and antiquity, priority and posteriority, their various manifestations, and their abundance; and which brings forth [concepts] such as simultaneity, succession, slowness, and swiftness. It is the Vaiśeṣika... [entity].

For the followers of Kaṇāda, it is of the nature of substance (*dravya*); for the followers of Kapila, it is of the nature of *rajas*, because its essence is to set things in motion; for the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), it is of the nature of an eternal, independent activity;
and for the Buddhists (*saugatas*), it is the ultimate reality consisting of a continuous stream of states (*bhāva*). Yet even that, in reality...

Since it does not transcend the nature of succession, succession itself is what is conventionally designated as "external time. Within the manifold of appearances belonging to consciousness—which is largely like a dream, a mental construction, an illusion, or a magical trick—there is a fixed limit to the extent of succession, just as there is a fixed sequence in the story of Hariścandra’s night. Thus, in this regard:
It is the power of consciousness alone that shines forth, because the variety of appearances is created by it,
and because succession depends upon it; even where a cause called "time" is mentioned—
such as when one says "born in the day" or "born at midday"— there too, what is perceived as the cause is simply the succession of the sun's movement.

This is established, but not for anything whose nature is an eternal substance (*nityadravya*) of a perfectly fixed form (*pariniṣṭhitarūpa*). If it is argued that even that substance possesses the property of flowing (*pravahaṇadharmaka*), and that it is precisely this [flowing] which gives rise to the diversity consisting of newness and antiquity, as well as priority and posteriority, then once again—

Its nature as sequence alone is established in accordance with experience, and not any other form; thus it is proven that time is precisely this sequence, whose essence consists in its penetration into manifestation.
"From what will be stated" [refers to the following].
[This is seen] in such sūtras as "The sequence is [due to] difference... (2.1.4). The term "nālikā, etc. includes everything from a muhūrta up to the end of a kalpa.
Now, one might object: that by which one calculates, casts away, or delimits is time (*kāla*). Yet, it is action (*kriyā*) that is to be delimited.

In that case, how is that [time] time? To this he says: "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*). By characterizing [time] through its being well-known by way of its measure (*iyattā*), he states that even when that [measure] itself is intended to be measured, another action—such as the flow of a water-clock (*nālikā*) and so forth—is indeed time. And [the charge of] infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and the like is [resolved] by the analogy of the case of gold and its mold.
This has already been resolved.
Furthermore, time is conventionally employed by depending upon the difference between established and hypothetical fixed points (*dhruvaka*) that were previously determined.

For every worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) proceeds solely by depending upon forms already established beforehand; even the attainment of satisfaction occurs only through connection with satisfaction previously established. Therefore, it is said that [the Self] consists of consciousness alone (*cinmaya*). This has already been demonstrated: all transactions belong to Him alone, since there is no dispute regarding His primordiality and prior establishment.

For it is consciousness alone that, through the activity of vitalizing, brings forth the prior time; and even when Brahman is sleeping during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the conventional usage of time occurs through the activities of its inhalation and exhalation, as well as through the activities residing in the subsequent group of causal deities beginning with Viṣṇu and Rudra. But in the case of the Blessed Lord, this is not so.

There is a certain conventional usage regarding time. However, when the power of *māyā* prevails and a distinction of appearances (*ābhāsa-bheda*) arises, then time, which consists of succession, also unfolds. Now, if [time] is indicated by its movement, such as the milking of cows, and not accepted through the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), then [it must be so] in the Sūtra.
For what purpose is this? It is said: "The inclusion of another" (*anyagraha*) means the acceptance of another planet (*graha*) besides the moon and so forth.
And this is appropriate: if the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) were intended to include the milking of cows and similar acts, one would have said "wandering and so forth" (*sañcārādi*).
"All that" refers to what has been mentioned as implied (*upalakṣita*), as well as what is included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the Sūtra. That [is it].

In the *Saṃkṣepavṛtti*, it is explained by means of repetition (*vīpsā*). However, three *vā* particles need not be employed to express the property of being alternately conceptualized as it applies to each [object], since the state of being conceptually constructed is expressed in a single instance alone by the inherent power of its own nature.
Because it is perceived that [the action] culminates after many undertakings, how then can there be two *vā* (or) words in the Sūtra?
Do not say so. The first *vā* word, by expressing the state of being an alternative between two positions, indicates that their circumstances are equal. And thus:
The first two positions are established with the intention that time is that which is employed in the act of delimitation;
the third, however, is based on the intention expressed by the phrase "the name 'time' [is applied] to the cause. And therein, regarding the cause...
(page 7)

In the case of time, it is precisely its status as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) that is functional. And since the nature of succession (*kramarūpatā*) necessarily follows from being a delimiting factor, the word "or" (*vā*) is used to express this. Thus, whether time be of the nature of a non-cause or of the nature of a cause, the conclusion remains the same: it results in these two alternative positions.
It is appropriate to employ only two instances of the word "vā" (or). This is stated by the phrase "not merely," and so forth.
[The object] has a perfected form consisting of action; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is also included.
"All this" refers to the aforementioned. Now, even one's own will (*svecchā*) proceeds without depending on established convention (*prasiddhi*), acting as a delimiting factor—
"For the sake of conceptualization. True. However, common usage (*prasiddhi*) is not monolithic; thus he says, "and because of common usage.

Purifying the position that "time is coldness and so forth," he explains the meaning of the sūtra—"the designation 'time' applies to the cause"—in the form already stated, beginning with "of coldness and so forth. Of coldness and so forth...

Limitation (*avacchedakatā*) alone is what constitutes temporality, and that occurs precisely through the penetration of the nature of succession within the flow [of consciousness]. Thus, it is stated that time is simply the succession residing therein. And this "this" refers to limitation. By all of this, which was stated in the aphorism—

Whatever imagined delimiting factor is being perceived is known as having a stable form by those engaged in worldly discourse because of its uniform nature; and since such stability belongs to succession everywhere—
because there is no distinction in the mark of time (*kāla-liṅga*) which possesses the property of flowing— therefore, that which is one,

That indeed is time. And it delimits the cognition of objects, which are the things to be known (*prameya*). For an object of knowledge, while being known, does not exist otherwise than as "it was," "it is," or "it will be"—unless it is sustained by this sequential nature. Therefore...
It is thus stated that time is the delimiter of all actions by means of cognition;

or, the entire phrase may be "the entity whose nature is stable. Regarding the words "precisely sequence": for it is precisely sequence, when qualified, which demonstrates the state of being old or new, characterized as priority and posteriority.

Through the two [qualities] of priority and posteriority existing in a continuum, there is the conventional usage of "long" and, conversely, the conventional usage of "short," as well as the sequential persistence of its own nature.

Time is said to be that which, by depending on other entities and by delimiting various entities, establishes simultaneity among them— this being conflated with priority and posteriority through the forms of distance and proximity caused by spatial configuration. And in that very context:

The intention is this: if, according to the principle already stated, permanence and unity are treated as such, and substantiality (*dravyatva*) is attributed through the superimposition of independence, then there is no harm whatsoever to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine either, provided one accepts taking refuge in our own [Advaita] philosophy. Now, [one might object]: "But what about spring and so forth?"
Time is well-known; how, then, can it have the nature of succession? To this he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

The activity of the sun, such as its rising and so forth, which occurs due to its movement through the signs of Pisces and Aries, is experienced as "spring" while it is currently taking place. Now, one might object: that time, spring, is merely the sequential form of the sun.
Anticipating the objection, "How can there be a time for the blossoming of the mango tree?", he says: "by that very [time].

By the word "or" (vā), he indicates the firmness of this very position. Just as the very form of gold itself, when delimited, is called a *māṣaka*, whereas the [impurity] residing therein is the *prativartaka*...
This is merely an illustration; it is not that something belonging elsewhere actually migrates to another place.

In the same way, the very sequence inherent in the appearances of the mango tree—possessing the variety of its buds, flower-buds, blossoming, and so forth, which are internal, graspable, and external—is itself "spring. And that [sequence]...
The rising of the sun is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that; this should be understood to apply everywhere. Now, it might be objected:

from words such as "spring" (*vasanta*), a thing already established in its accomplished form (*siddharūpa*) enters the path of cognition, not the sequence itself. To this it is replied: "Spring, etc. And this—

This has been explained in detail under the rule *tiṅvācyakarmavat* (Pāṇini 1.4.51). For just as the action (*kriyā*) is understood from the verbal form alone and not from anything else, so too time—which has entered into the very heart of the nature of the action—is understood from that [verbal form] alone. Thus, [in the case of] *abhūt* ("it was"):
The activity of becoming (*bhavana-kriyā*) of the manifestation of an entity appears as being conjoined with a sequence of its manifestation being clear or unclear.
However, terms such as "will be" (*bhaviṣyat*) and so forth denote an object exactly like a jar or similar things; for that very reason, it is called "future."
In such cases as "it was," "this is the present day," and so forth, there is no confusion whatsoever regarding time.
(Page 9)

For this reason, time is not [the cause] here, because it emerges [only] as the present and future meanings of words; since its essential nature consists solely in resting upon specific days as qualifiers of established entities (*siddha-rūpa*), it is incapable of delimiting action (*kriyā*). This will be elaborated upon later—let it suffice for now. Because [time] enters into the interior of the body of action...
Time is indeed the sequence [of events] whose body is manifested through [the power of] *vaśa*; "that" means for this reason it remains thus:

that which is called time is, in its ultimate sense, nothing other than the sequence of the sixfold transformation of entities (*bhāvavikāra*). There is no action whatsoever that exists apart from the transformations of entities. As the venerable [author] has said:
"The six modifications, beginning with birth, are the sources of the differentiation of existence" (Vākyapadīya 1.3). || 3 ||
But surely, let it be that time is simply the very nature (*svabhāva*) of entities; in that case,
what other thing is there called the "power of time" (*kāla-śakti*), by virtue of which it was stated [in 2.1.2] that they possess succession?
Regarding this [objection], namely "due to the power of time," he provides the following resolution by means of the aphorism:
"Sequence depends upon difference; difference, too, exists due to the presence or absence of manifestation.
The presence or absence of manifestation, however, is brought about by the Lord through His variegated manifestations. (Kārikā 4)

If time were merely a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then even fingers would possess temporal differentiation. Therefore, the sequence that constitutes the essence of time is caused by a distinction characterized by manifestation and non-manifestation; it is not caused by mere difference.

Furthermore, the existence and non-existence of appearances in their various forms occur only from the presence of the Sovereign Lord, whose power to bring about sequential emergence has been observed in cases such as dreams and mental constructions.
As it was said by that venerable one:
"But that power belongs to the One alone, by which it manifests in this way" (Vākya-pada 2.22);
likewise, elsewhere also,
they call Him the stage-manager of this worldly machine.
By means of prohibition and permission, the universe is divided by him.
(10) If [the moments] were not held back, and if one did not release [the next] because of being held back,
then the states would be intermingled, devoid of priority and posteriority.
Thus, by stating that He possesses the sovereignty of both manifesting and non-manifesting, His divine power (*aiśvarya*) is declared.

For that Blessed Lord manifests appearances in manifold ways; for example, He manifests the appearance of a firm, red, and elevated jar through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and He manifests the appearances of a jar and a cloth simultaneously and separately.
By its own manifestation, which is of a single flavor within itself, and by the mutual non-manifestation, which is also of a single flavor— up to this point,
there is no succession whatsoever. But when it causes the manifestation of spring to be manifested as empty by the manifestation of summer, then [there is] succession.

The power of time (*kāla-śakti*) is precisely that capacity of the Lord alone to manifest both appearance and non-appearance, which is termed "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*). Therefore, the meaning of the aphorism is that time is the succession (*krama*) which, as it comes into being, serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for entities. He introduces this [point] with the word "succession," [explaining it] by means of "investigation" (*paryālocanayā*).

The intention is that the sequence [of manifestation] is established through the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*). "Variegated" (*vicitra*) means having produced the manifestation of jars, cloths, and so forth, by way of both manifesting and non-manifesting appearances.
This alone is the creative act (*kalanakriyā*) of the Lord as the agent; and this very thing belongs to Him who possesses the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of objective existence.
The capacity for manifestation belongs to time, whose nature is sequential, as it is being manifested.

In this sentence beginning with "ityādau" (in such passages), that fragment starting with "yat avabhāsa" (that which is manifestation) is the agent; it refers to that which was stated at the beginning of the commentary, namely "tat" (that), which functions here as the object—this is the connection. [The word] "asya" (of this).

Regarding the Sautrāntika [position]: because a single substratum is untenable; this refers to the two factors that sequentially trigger [the manifestation], so he considers. Otherwise, the jar would not appear, yet it does appear—so why would a single substratum not be tenable?
And by [the phrase] "as the cause of the distinction between these two," meaning as the cause for the distinction between those two sequential triggers. "Because of the material cause" (upādānāt).
In the Sūtra: "The state of being distinct" is useful with respect to the sequence—this is the sense. "For this very reason" means because in this [context]...
(page 11)

In the present context, two things are relevant. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the use of the terms "distinct appearance" (*bhinnāvabhāsa*) and "variety" (*vaicitrya*)—with the neuter singular remainder (*napuṃsakaikaśeṣa*)—demonstrates the relevance of these two.

Regarding the term "variegatedness" (*citratvam*): it refers to variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) which is of the nature of consciousness (*bodhātman*). And thus, it refers to the unity of variegated cognition (*citrabodhaikatva*).

Regarding the contradiction between difference and unity, he places the burden of proof upon the words of the Noble One (Ārya): for what was stated here in the first three quarters [of the verse] is one thing, while the other is stated by the fourth quarter. He explains this statement in brief with the words "of blue and so forth," and by the words "consciousness" (*bodha*) and so on, the fourth quarter is explained.

The remainder [of the definition] is: "Because of being delimited by mutual non-abandonment"—by this [it is meant that the universal] does not belong to anything else; it is impossible to perceive [as existing apart from its particulars]. (Pāṇini-vārttika 3.2.20)

The reality of the object (*arthatattva*) which is the opposite of this consequence and is [here] intended has been explained. By those very ones— namely, by those who speak in such a manner, whether they be proponents of blue and so forth or proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādin*)— even the syllable-less (*anakṣara*) reality of Brahman is accepted as being variegated (*citra*).

It occurs as follows: because the omniscient consciousness— which consists of a manifold appearance of existence and non-existence throughout all times and places— is itself admitted to be of the nature of awareness and thus unconditioned by space and time,
that which those who desire to refute [it] intend to invalidate is, for them alone, the ripening of their skill in the reflective awareness of consciousness (*saṃvit*).

The word "eva" (only/just) indicates that [the manifestation] flashes forth precisely because of the attainment of pure intuition (*pratibhā*) arising from the grace of the propitious Maheśvara. Having created the manifold universe, the Lord’s abiding as the soul of all (*viśvātmabhāvena*) is itself the cause for the expansion of time. Now, one might ask: what other entities exist apart from the nature of manifestation?
Regarding that which was stated as "in entities," he says there: "it is illusion. "Even in both forms" means this:

in both the Sūtra and the Vṛtti, this sequence of space and time is taught even in its dual form, by virtue of being the basis for the differentiation of entities produced through appearance and non-appearance, as stated in another Sūtra.

And it will be analyzed [later]. However, by me, the author of the commentary (*vivṛtikṛt*), the investigation into the power of time—which arises as a necessary consequence of the discussion on action—has been presented with the intention of following the temporal sequence; thus, the Sūtra and its Commentary have been interpreted according to the order of time. || 4 ||
(Page 12) He demonstrates the capacity to produce variegated appearances with a verse: "Due to the diversity of forms, this [consciousness] manifests a spatial succession."
Due to the manifestation of the variety of actions, the Lord [also manifests] the succession of time. || 5 ||

Because there is a diversity among manifested forms— that is, among entities that are objects of perception— distinguished by such differences as house, courtyard, marketplace, temple, garden, forest, and so forth, the Supreme Lord, manifesting that very diversity, makes manifest the spatial extension consisting of the expansion and non-expansion [of time].
However, by the power of a single recognition (*ekapratyabhijñā*), that which is non-different in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), such as the hand and so forth— as he will later state:
"because of the unity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), its nature as a non-different substance remains unobscured"—
its existence in various locations and its possession of various attributes does not contradict its oneness of essential nature.
Because of the manifestation of such a variety of actions— as in "Caitra goes" or "the fruit ripens"—

the Lord, by virtue of his sovereignty, manifests both contradiction and non-contradiction; thus, he manifests the sequence known as time, wherein even that which is improper for a single entity to possess contradictory forms is made possible.

"It illuminates"—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. Spatial sequence occurs in multiple objects, as in the case of a house and its courtyard; temporal sequence occurs as in the case of the mango, jasmine, and so forth. However, in a single [object], there is no spatial sequence because of the absence of distance and the like. There is also an extension of parts within that very one. Thus, it is in one place...

The intended meaning of the verse is that time functions exactly like a mango fruit ripening in its due course. Temporal duration resides only in the object of cognition (vedya), not in consciousness (saṃvit). Even within knowledge, time pertains only to the objective aspect, not to the aspect of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana); nor does it apply to the aspect of the reflective awareness (vimarśa) consisting of words—thus he connects [the points].

By the words "mere essential nature" (*svarūpamātra*) and so forth: [it refers] to that which belongs to space— that is, to the aspect of knowledge (*jñānabhāga*) in the form of the subject (*grāhaka*), which flashes forth as "I" within the space of the heart (*hṛdayagagana*), in the sky [of consciousness], being stirred by mere will and effort (*icchā-prayatna*) alone, independent of the impulsion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of differentiation" (*bhedābhāvāt*) in the context of that which consists of the apprehension "this is manifesting as such" within the *paśyantī* and *madhyamā* stages by means of the self:
the meaning is "because it is not an object of cognition" (*avedyatvāt*). As the venerable [author] has said:
"The unmanifest word, which possesses sequence, is that which is uttered in a whisper."
"But the non-sequential [utterance] is that wherein the intellect, having expanded [the sound], comes to rest" (Vākyapadīya 2.19).
[The phrase] "of the aerial and so forth" refers to [sounds] such as "jar," which have attained the status of *vaikharī*.

The distinction of distance and so forth indeed occurs for sounds of the same class (sajātīya) relative to those of different classes (vijātīya)— such as the whistling of birds like parrots, the crackling of fire, the splashing of water, and the clattering of earthy objects. However, they are not [produced] by being opened (*vivṛta*).

The intention here is that "form" (*mūrti*) refers either to the dimension of a non-pervasive substance or to solidity. In this regard, someone—unable to accept the materiality (*mūrtatva*) of sound and yet being mindful of its spatial succession—raises an objection (*pūrva-pakṣa*) with the words "But surely... (*nanu*), arguing that "materiality is not what accounts for spatial succession. [This is followed by the word] "effect" (*kārya*).

"Śuka-śukādi" [refers to the sounds "parrot-parrot," etc.]. Regarding the term "cause": even the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) is indeed a cause of air. For air enters [the body] as that which is born from sound and touch; thus, the meaning is that this [air] is not merely air itself, by virtue of which it would be material (*mūrta*). [Objection: But is this not its quality (*dharma*)? [Response: True, it is a quality, but it is not sound alone.

Wind. External wind is distinct from [the wind] whose quality is touch and so forth. This is shown by the phrase "even while entering. "Of that" means of the aerial [wind]; "of another" means of the fiery and so forth.
If spatial sequence were based on corporeality, then it would not belong to sound; yet it does belong to it. Thus.

"And it shows [them] simultaneously. By this, it is demonstrated that what is clearly perceived as being far or near in relation to things of the same class is not produced by limiting conditions such as causes;
rather, in this manner, from the perspective of ultimate reality, sound resides in space alone, and not in air or other elements. By which...

Since that [substratum] is corporeal, the sound, being perceived as non-different from its property, would also be corporeal. For, according to the principle that "the qualified is [perceived] through the qualifier," it is perceived in air and so forth;
and since air and such are corporeal while space is not, corporeality is defined as the dimension of a non-pervasive substance.

When questioned by one who has approached [the discussion], he replies: "Let it be so. Let there be the conventional usage of the term "incorporeal" (*amūrta*) for sound in common worldly parlance or in other treatises; for the world considers that which is corporeal (*mūrta*) to be suitable for activities such as grasping, holding, and giving, but not sound. It is precisely in accordance with that [worldly convention] that it is defined as "not all-pervading" (*asarvagata*).
And in the rule *mūrtau ghanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.77), "solidity" (*kāṭhinya*) is stated to be *mūrti*; he shows that this [solidity] is not the type [of *mūrti*] intended here.
"Manifesting a distinction here" means "devoid of action. This implies that there is no sequence of spatial location here, nor is action required.

Whether such action exists or not, the meaning is that the very nature of the object of knowledge (*vedyasvarūpa*) is what is relied upon to facilitate the sequence of distinctions between forms and locations. By this word "of the manifold" (*anekasya*),...

The "form" (mūrti) is manifested as the nature of the object to be known. Regarding the term "in the definition" (lakṣaṇe), the third case ending is used in the sense of a "characteristic" (itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa); or, when there is an intention to express the cause by means of a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of the indicator, it is used in the sense of a "cause" (hetu). Nor is this merely his own invention; thus he says "the venerable one" (tatrabhavat), implying that others also accept it—hence the word "desiring" (icchan).

The meaning is that one accepts what is expressed by such concluding Vedic statements as, "The manifestation of form and action is merely the operation of the power of ignorance. Now, [an objection may be raised]:
since cognition and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) are also not devoid of their own nature, would there not also be a spatial sequence (*deśakrama*) in them, just as in the case of form?

[Objection: It is logical. [Response: Not so; for "form" (*mūrti*) is not merely the essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather that which is being manifested while maintaining a status equal to another object of knowledge (*vedya*). However, this is not the case with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), for those two are colored by consciousness (*vidyoparakta*), not by the object of knowledge. This is what he says with the words beginning "knowledge," etc. Or else, [the term] "immaterial" (*amūrta*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
Furthermore, for that sound as well, the substrata are indeed corporeal entities such as air; and a quality resides in the locus of its possessor.

Therefore, whatever spatial distinction exists in the corporeal air or other substrata which possess that quality, it is perceived there [in the sound] through the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), but it is not ultimately real. Thus, the sequence of space belongs only to corporeal things.

Thus, even when adopting the perspective of other treatises regarding the nature [of the self], nothing has been undermined. Having explained the first half of the verse, he begins to explain the second half with the words "Because of cognition—mind alone," and so forth. The reason for the statement that agency is secondary is given as "because of the metaphorical attribution of agency."

On page 15: [This occurs] through metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*), based on the superimposition of agency (*kartṛtva*) upon the object of cognition because it is manifested internally by the act of cognition itself.
He states the reason for the sublation of the primary meaning with the words "of that which is of the nature of consciousness itself.
The phrase "even of those possessing form" means even of those things that do not have the nature of consciousness, because they are objects of cognition.
Having thus established their secondary status according to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he speaks in accordance with common usage as follows:

"Whether it be the primary perception (pratīti) or [the secondary]," "even the difference in time"—this "even" (api) implies multiplicity; for it is not only spatial difference that belongs to the manifold, but this temporal one as well. The temporal sequence of a single [entity] will be explained later, starting with the words "of a single [entity] again. He divides that time:

"By means of the conjunction of appearance and non-appearance, and thus [it is said]: 'of whom' refers to the knower; 'of which' refers to the object; 'of him' refers to the knower; 'that' refers to the object; the connection is that 'the present [object] shines.
In another sentence, one must establish the connection by carrying over the phrase 'of whom,' which refers to the object."

The logical connection is this: when an object that does not manifest to the perceiver is conceived as having a manifestation of existence in the present—by means of the manifestation of its cause together with the manifestation of the destruction of that present, perceptible manifestation of the cause—that object shines for the perceiver. This is the coherence [of the argument].
Since the past and the present are well-established, no example was stated for them; however, regarding the future,

because of the principle that "there will be [no proof] due to the absence of means of valid cognition," he states another example with the words "just as" (*yathā*), being hesitant regarding an example of the future such as the accounts of Karkī, Viṣṇu, and others.

For he demonstrates that, for a master whose will is unimpeded, the two modifications of being— existence and non-existence— are subsumed by the two alone: appearance and non-appearance, just as the duties intended for today and those to be performed today are both included within the single category of "what is to be done today."

Now, one might ask: what is the need here for a cognizer (pramātṛ) or for manifestation, since the establishment of the sequence of a single time is achieved through the power of the activity consisting in the variety of the modifications of existence, such as birth and so forth? Why, then, is there mention of a "cognizer" or "it appears"? This was shown in the *Vivṛti*, though it was not touched upon in the *Vṛtti*; [the answer is] "by way of action."
Such is the [objector's] position. He refutes this with the word "unfailing" (*askhalita*). For this is an investigation into the actual state of things;
however, in common usage, the cause [of the term 'eternal'] is in relation to worms, omniscient beings, and so forth, because for them it is eternal.

The connection with consciousness (*citsambandha*). This very point is indicated by the particle *eva*. It will be explained in the section on the investigation of the reality of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatattvavimarśaprakaraṇa*) [in the verse]:
"Due to the differentiation of manifestations, [there is] unity in one place... (2.4.19).

In such a sūtra as this, the diversity of time resulting from the diversity of actions of many [entities] possessing diverse forms has been set forth and explained. Now he explains that operation— beginning with the words "of one"— which constitutes the diversity of time even for a single entity that lacks such diversity, as indicated by the word "api" (even/also).
Furthermore, by the phrase "of one," the commentator demonstrates the absence of spatial succession.

Even that extension which exists within a house does not create a spatial distinction for the house itself, but rather for the parts of the house. These parts are indeed distinct. For this very reason, the whole (avayavin) is not spatially distinct.

Because of their oneness, the injunction regarding being in that location or not being in that location is entirely outside of experience in that context. For the cognition "cloth" refers to something of a fixed dimension; yet extension (*vaitatya*) is not the dimension itself.
Extension is indeed conjunction with many locations. The multiplicity of locations arises from difference.
And its differentiation arises from the differentiation of its substrates (*ādheya*). The substrate, namely the whole (*avayavin*), is one and not many;

multiplicity, however, belongs to the threads. Their very extension is merely a spatial succession. Furthermore, the cloth does not manifest in the cognition of the threads, nor do the threads manifest in the cognition of the cloth; for a real entity consists essentially in its manifestation.

For a certain cognizer shines forth within a certain manifestation; therefore, the parts and the whole exist precisely without confusion—let this suffice for now. By the word "only" (*mātra*), he excludes spatial succession, and by the particle "only" (*eva*), he excludes difference in essential nature. And the phrase "of those very [parts]" refers to those things possessing succession. Even there, there is succession.

Even a single moment, which consists of a prior, middle, and posterior part, is subject to conventional designation (*vyavahārya*) and not something absolute (*śuddha*); thus, even there, there is indeed a sequential nature. As the venerable one [said]:
Established in its sequence by preceding and succeeding moments (or parts),
that single entity is nevertheless designated by the names [of those parts] through superimposition upon it.
(Vākyapadīya 3.8.11).
Thus, he explains transformation as occurring even in insentient things by means of the example "in fruits such as the pomegranate.
The meaning is that this transformation is called "ripening" (*pāka*). The word "arising" (*udbhavantī*) implies continuity.

By demonstrating that [the object] is uncontradicted, the Buddhist must indeed accept the determination of a continuum (*santāna*), even while desiring to refute it with hundreds of contradictory arguments regarding its nature as a subverting factor; for contradiction and non-contradiction depend solely upon whether the appearance of the reality of action is present, and not through mere dry finger-squeezing.
It has been established that the two *ṭaṅkita* [stamps] effect the realization of the object—by virtue of having a single substratum (*ekāśrayatvena*).

Since this realization occurs through the unity of recognition and reflective awareness (*pratyabhijñā-pratyavamarśa*) even within a single [substratum], it is therefore distinct from that which exists in multiple locations due to spatial succession; here, there is no spatial succession.

It is to be considered as such—this is the sense. However, it is not merely the state of having a single substratum that serves as the cause for temporal sequence, since such a sequence is observed even when that [single substratum] is absent in cases such as spring and summer.
Now, let it be that time has the nature of sequence; but how does it have the nature of the present and so forth? To this he says: "In this way... and so on.

By the words "bathing" (*snāna*) and so forth: that manifestation (*ābhāsa*) whose nature consists of clarity and the rest is called "present" according to the principle to be stated in the subsequent sūtra. And what is such [a manifestation]?
It is that which manifests together with the Māyic body and so forth, which constitute the manifestation of the subject (*grāhakābhāsa*).

If it is argued that they exist simultaneously, he says: "internally. When that appearance as the subject exists, there is no appearance of its object; and when that appearance as the object exists, there is no appearance of its subject—such is the appearance of their mutual non-existence.

It was previously stated that "the being of appearance" (*ābhāsasattva*) is thus [defined]; based on that absence of mediation, that which is called "simultaneous manifestation" (*sahaprathā*) is referred to—this is what is known as "co-existence" (*sahabhāva*). This is explained by the following verse:

"It is clearly corroborated" means: [the author] raises the objection, "But if there is an interval of non-existence, then since the absence of presentness is equal in both cases, how can there be a distinction between 'future' and 'past'? Anticipating this, he establishes that distinction by stating "non-existence," showing what is excluded by the particle *eva* while establishing the past time.

By the words "the child" (*bāla*) and so forth: even though it possesses the nature of becoming (*bhavana-dharma*), the meaning is that even now, the external form—which has thus manifested as childhood—still exists internally as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). "Of the manifestation" (*avabhāsasya*) means of that which has the form of externality. Now, of this...

Since the sequence of time is established for all the world and is self-evident, it is impossible to deny it; therefore, its justification within the framework of external objects through the perception of duality is in no way tenable.
Since this must necessarily be justified, one has no recourse other than the theory that appearances themselves are the reality (*ābhāsa-vastu-vāda*). It is not [the theory of external objects].

Showing that this is the doctrine of the outsiders (*bāhyavāda*), he demonstrates the utility of this section on time for the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). By the aforementioned method, since this temporal convention has been stated as the cause for the entry into existence and non-existence, for that very reason, those two [exist and do not exist] for a single [subject].
These two [alternatives], being contradictory, give rise to a contradiction even regarding the sequence called "time" which is caused by them.

Thus, it is contradictory. It might be argued: "There is no temporal sequence whatsoever for a single entity; rather, that very thing, having existed, ceases to exist, and having not existed, comes into existence. And this alone is the ultimate reality."
It is conventionally expressed through conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) concerning the past, the future, and the present. To this, he says "of that which exists" (*sataḥ*).
Here, it should be understood that there is no arising of that which is non-existent (*asat*). And as for that which is non-existent, it is simply non-existent—(2.4.3).

This will be explained hereafter. But when, in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as an "object" at all, then to whom can an inquiry regarding contradiction be directed? For what constitutes its reality is that it is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) and autonomous;
so what inquiry can there even be regarding that? Thus, by way of this incidental discussion, [it is shown that] manifestation is the very essence.
(Page 19) Having discussed entities, he shows that what is relevant must now be examined, by saying "But for yogins" (*yogināṃ tu*).
The word "but" (*tu*) indicates this doubt: if it is only the state of appearing clearly...

If that were the case, then regarding the yogin’s cognition which directly perceives past and future objects, there would first of all be a clarity of those two—the past and the future—because direct perception otherwise could not occur; and consequently, it would follow that those two possess the status of being present. Here, the reason for the refutation is "mutually" (*anyonya*).

This is what is meant: for the yogin who has at all times abandoned the state of being a subject characterized by *māyā*, what indeed could be the distinction between past and so forth? That [distinction] would exist only for one who has not yet abandoned it, as a mere residual impression (*saṃskāra*).
And when that is not abandoned, [the distinction] exists together with the appearance of the body occurring during the time of meditative absorption.

Since, according to the stated position, both manifestation and non-manifestation are possible for that which appears as an object of perception, how could there be "presentness"? For it has been stated that presentness is not merely clarity, nor is it existence itself.
The mention of the past is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of the future. || 5 ||

Now, according to the principle stated, spatial and temporal succession would pertain only to appearances, not to the subject (*pramātṛ*), for that [subject] is indeed devoid of appearance (*nirābhāsa*). For everything appears to him, but he does not appear to anyone. Furthermore, he never fails to appear; and those two [successions] were said to have their cause in the entry into non-appearance.

How could those two [non-existence and existence] exist in that which has the nature of constant luminosity? For, since no cause for them is perceived, their non-existence alone is logical. Yet these two are observed: "I was," "I am," "I shall be";
and "I stand in a house," "in a village," "in a forest"; and "from the palace, I am on a couch."

Since the [distinctions of] "being" and "non-being" would be impossible for the categories such as the elements (bhūta) and for "distance" and so forth, unless they reside in the cognizer, it follows from an examination of cognition that these two are determined in relation to the cognizer alone; therefore, how could they exist even in the case of objects? Where, then, are these two firmly established?
Whoever might be confused is instructed by two sūtras. Among these, the sequence of time is first established by the first sūtra (p.
Even the differentiation of appearances everywhere would be characterized by a sequence of time;
for the appearance of the void and so forth is fragmented, whereas that of the manifesting subject is not simultaneous.

The word "api" (also/even) includes the object of cognition (*prameya*). Regarding all entities—whether singular or multiple—that temporal sequence which has been described, its source (*ākara*), which serves as the cause for the initial emergence of manifestation, is the differentiation of appearance (*ābhāsa*) consisting in the variety of existence and non-existence; that [source] is the void (*śūnya*), the intellect (*dhī*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the body (*deha*).

It is possible that [the object] becomes the object of the cognizer when it possesses characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), because its light is severed [from consciousness]. For its manifestation is not its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), since, like blue and so forth, it is insentient (*jaḍa*).
Indeed, its manifestation is nothing other than the pulsation of consciousness (*saṃvitsphuraṇa*); for when consciousness does not exist as its very self, [it cannot manifest].

When [the Self] manifests, then its manifestation does not exist, as in a state of swoon. Therefore, due to the impossibility of its non-manifestation, it possesses the nature of being real (*bhūta*) and so forth, and by comparison with that, so too do all entities. That which is "shining forth once and for all" (*sakṛdvibhātaḥ*)—by this mode of expression used by the knowers of Brahman, it is characterized by a perpetually uninterrupted luminosity.

The ultimate subject (*paramārthapramātā*) has been described as not having a manifold nature; for him, there is never the presence or absence of manifestation. Therefore, there is no connection with time in his case, nor, in relation to him, does it exist even among [manifested] entities—this is the meaning of the aphorism. That which is immovable in an entity is not dependent on anything else, unlike blueness; and...

"This is immovable"—thus, since mobility, which is incompatible with immobility (the pervader), is perceived as being dependent on something else (the pervaded), it negates independence; thus, he establishes mobility. To explain: "of those past" and "of those future"—it is indeed thus.

The omniscient ones—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others—as well as the lords of mantras (mantreśvaras) and so forth, engage in worldly discourse. The current worldly discourse is capable of manifesting as something yet to come for those such as Rāma, and as something already past for those headed by Karki and Viṣṇu; thus, when it is said "when that" (yadā tadā), it means "therefore" (tasmāt).

The word *vivṛtam* (explained) uses the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). Having introduced into the commentary (*vṛtti*) a topical term (*arthapada*) not explicitly contained in the aphorism (*sūtra*), the meaning of the aphorism has been explained. The phrase "that explanation is from that very [source]" refers to the aforementioned form of the meaning. For it is said: "sa hi" (for he...).

(Page 21) "The time prior to the appearance of the empty body and so forth" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. "In memory" means that it appears solely within memory. "Without distinction" means [it appears] either as the portion belonging to the subject (*pramātṛ*) or as the portion belonging to the object (*artha*).

The meaning is that this is not taught here. He confirms the absence of appearance regarding the body and so forth by saying "of the body etc. It will be stated that just as the appearance of a state is severed, so too is the essential nature of the one who abides in those states.

"In that state of abiding in just that [much], the state of deep sleep (sauṣupta), which is like cosmic dissolution (pralaya), is said to exist" (3.2.15)—this is what is stated here. The word "tathā" (thus) means that manifestation is its very nature (*svabhāva*). By the inclusion of the particle "vā" (or), he indicates that although there is a difference in the phrasing (*bhaṅgībheda*) between these two ways of speaking at first glance, they are equal in their result. Now, one might object:
Regarding the objection that since the word *eka* (one) signifies a single rotation (*āvarta*), how can a suffix denoting frequency (*kṛtvas-artha*) be applied to it—

the author dispels this doubt with the words beginning "of one" (*ekasyāḥ*). Here, the state of remaining itself (*sthiti*) is figuratively treated as a repetition (*āvṛtti*), and the cause for this [figurative usage] lies in the fact that there is a second, third, and so forth, instance of that state.

When there is a state of repetition in an action that has come to rest in a single entity, that is called "concomitance" (sāhacarya). For as long as one intends to express that first state in order to negate a second or subsequent state, that first state is [conceptually] conjoined with those second and subsequent states which are intended to be negated.

It flashes forth. And the purpose [of using figurative expression] is the comprehension of repetition (*āvṛtti*). For when it is said, "one state is repetition," it is conceived that the second [state] also exists as having the nature of repetition. And this alone must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, the well-known worldly convention would be subverted—thus he demonstrates.

Otherwise—that is, if figurative usage (*upacāra*) were not accepted—the two states would not be expressed by the word "āvṛtti" ending in the dual number as "āvṛttī. For the first state is indeed a state (*sthiti*), not a repetition (*āvṛtti*); the second is a state, being one repetition; and the third is a state, being the second repetition—thus [the expression] "he eats twice" (*dvir bhuṅkte*).

Three states of sustenance (*bhojana-sthiti*) should be understood. Thus it says: "Because it is commenced by one," for two states [of sustenance] are [accomplished] by means of one repetition in the form of the second state.

In the case of an undertaking, there are not two repetitions; and thus, by the word "once" (*sakṛt*), two states would be expressed. Nor is this the conventional meaning of words; in this way, this passage has been harmonized by the venerable Guru. If [the words] "two" (*dve*) and "of two" (*dvayoḥ*) were clearly intended as objects of repetition...
If it is explained according to the path [of the commentary], then what inconsistency is there in two repetitions regarding the three states?

Therefore, the interpretation as previously stated is the correct one. The intention is that, by the aforementioned reasoning (*nyāya*), the meaning of the word "once" (*sakṛt*) is established in common worldly usage through a figurative application (*aupacārikavṛtti*). As for the phrase "yadi nāma": [it means] even if...
In the state of the Lord Śrī Sadāśiva. || 6 ||
The same principle applies to spatial succession as well; this is stated in the Sūtra:
"Spatial succession also appears among entities for the Mother [the limited subject] whose self is contracted;
however, for the Unmeasured [the infinite subject], entities appear as full within His own Self by means of His own Self. (7)

"Of one who has measured himself" (*mitātmanaḥ*) is the reason (*hetu*), and this is a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). However, by means of repetition (*āvṛtti*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) as being used when there is an elision of a verbal suffix ending in *-lyap* (*lyablope*); it is not the fifth case itself.
For if the genitive were established in that context, there would be a contradiction with the initial grammatical framework (*prakrama*), and the word *tu* (but/however) would be incoherent.

There is affliction in applying the genitive case in reference to one's own self. Since all things appear to the immeasurable subject as full of their own self, because they are of the nature of pure light, they therefore appear within the self as being equal to one's own self, as immeasurable, and as entirely devoid of spatial succession. Thus it is said.

With respect to its own pure self, the Lord has no spatial succession; nor, with respect to the Lord, do entities possess spatial succession. For an object such as a jar, its own form is its "space," and the same applies to the body, vital breath, the void, and so forth; therefore, they exist through the mutual exclusion of their respective spaces.

Regarding "abiding" (*avasthāna*): that cognizer, such as the body and so forth, perceives the category of objects—such as a jar and so forth—as distinct both from itself and from one another in terms of space. He demonstrates this very distinction of space in various ways through the words "in front" (*puraḥ*) and so on. Its configuration (*saṃsthāna*), consisting of curved forms and the like, manifests; and that...
Of what nature is it? He says: it is the specific sequence [of moments] that is extended by direction—such as east, west, and so forth—and by location, such as the pervasive and so on.
(page 23)

Its manifestation—this very thing is the form of the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) such as squareness; likewise, that which appears as an equal extension of space in the four directions is precisely what constitutes squareness. The same applies to other [configurations]. Well then, what is the cause of that sequence of directions and spaces? He says:

By the power of consciousness (*saṃvit-śakti*), characterized as the capacity to produce variegated appearances and possessing the aforementioned nature, there are simultaneously and at one and the same time established the existence and non-existence of whatever appearance—such as blue—and so forth;
the difference or otherness (*anyatva*) brought about by those two is as follows: "Blue appears" and "it does not appear."
This [state] is characterized by that very cause; for this reason alone it has been praised by me:

"The state in which there is the simultaneous abandonment of sequence—the state of appearance and its manifestation, and their absence, which are variegated in nature and possess a self-form that shines through freedom."

I perpetually praise that form, eternally arisen, which consists of the manifestation of all states of being and bears the splendor of the shimmering crescent moon within the ocean of its own self-awareness.
Thus, this is the interpretation of the sentence from the *Vṛtti*:
"This Self is manifested once and for all; for this which is full, there is no possibility of non-manifestation anywhere."

Thus, with the intention that "the meaning of a portion of the *Sārasvatasangrahasūtra* becomes indeed stated when sound is mentioned as the cause by means of the perspective of superimposition (*adhyāsa-dṛṣṭi*),

and it is thereby made known that this is traditional scripture (*āgama*) and not one's own invention," the ablative case is employed after the imitation [of the word] and is stated in the commentary as the cause.

Thus: the construction is as follows—either with the intention that, by the partial statement "in the case of the option (*vibhāṣā*) 'na vā', the mention of the object (*artha*) [is understood]," the negative particle (*nañ*) will be established as functioning through exclusion (*paryudāsa*) even in a compound analyzed with the fifth case (*pañcamī-vigraha*); or else, because that which is non-manifest is impossible. Although density (*ghanatā*) is indeed hardness (*kāṭhinya*).
Although it is stated that [the term] "solid" (*ghana*) refers to a physical form (*mūrti*), nevertheless, by means of that term— which is impossible in this context—
there is indicated the absence of any intervention from heterogeneous elements associated with itself.
The universe is a solid mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*), full of the Self.
Thus indeed is the Sūtra. "Because of being the agent" means because of the autonomy [of consciousness] in manifesting as existence (*bhāvatayā*).
(Page 24) It nourishes and sustains this objective aspect (*idambhāga*); this is to be connected with what precedes. This follows from the context of action (*kriyāprasaṅgāt*).

While the power of time (*kāla-śakti*) was to be discussed, the sequence of space (*deśa-krama*) was mentioned first as its illustrative example in the verse beginning with *mūrtivaicitryata...* (2.1.5). However, the sequence of time (*kāla-krama*) is mentioned last, because the illustration [of space] was presented first.

Because it must be stated; however, here in the concluding verse, the sequence of time previously mentioned is the subject at hand. Now, one might raise the objection that, in this way, it follows that there is no action whatsoever in the Blessed Lord, due to the absence of connection with the sequence of time which pervades the very nature of action. Dispelling this doubt, [the author] states that both of these...

And demonstrating that the nature of succession is merely the unfolding of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), he shows through a sūtra the utility of this section on time for the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "But that power of creation also belongs to the Lord who knows [reality] in such a way."
In the same way, the distinction between the knower and the knowable is that which appears. || 9 ||
This is not the entirety of the reality of the sequence of space and time; rather, there is something else that must be stated here.

That is expressed as "thus" (*tathā*): from that very [reality], the entire range of subjects and objects, possessing the sequence of space and time, is manifested. This manifestation is the creative power (*nirmāṇa-śakti*) of the Lord alone.

The word *martyam* means the form of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). And "it is thus" (*evam*) refers to those who know that differentiation—that is, for one whose nature consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), and for that very reason, for one endowed with the power of will (*icchāśakti*). This is the literal meaning of the words.
What is meant is this: here, the will itself is the action of the Lord, as will be concluded later.
"Thus, desire itself is causality, agency, and action" (2.4.21).
For Caitra as well, that very desire expressed as "I am cooking" persists even amidst a thousand movements such as placing the pot on the fire;
though non-sequential in its own nature, it appears as if colored by the manifestation of sequential existence and non-existence.

In the very same way, let the sequence of knower and known also manifest for the Supreme Lord; thus, that ultimate reality which is the will within His own self— expressed as "I shine," "I reflect," "I revolve," and so forth— is itself without succession, yet [appears as such] due to the coloring of the distinction between subject and object.

(Page 25) It appears as having succession, like the surface of a mirror; yet, although it is without succession, it is colored by the appearance of thousands of lightnings arising and passing away through the sequence of a vast river that flows eternally and continuously.
Therefore, this very activity, though inherently without succession (*akrama*) everywhere, attains succession through its own limitation (*uparāga*);

thus, its pure form of succession is not its pervader (*vyāpaka*), such that it could be negated in the Lord by the non-perception of its pervader—this is the meaning of the aphorism. This very [point is as follows]:
The nature of consciousness (*saṃvedana*) is its sovereignty in manifesting in such a manner;
as it has been said: "the state of being a limited manifestation" (Bo. Paṃ. v. 8).

And so forth. With this intention, he introduces [the passage] with "tadatra" (therein), explaining that what was stated here is now being further elaborated by the words "kintu" (but). He explains the phrase "evam viduṣaḥ" (of one who knows thus) up until the end of the section with the words "sthitaiva" (it remains indeed).
For the state beginning with Śrī Sadāśiva is of the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). In that regard, the word "tu" (but) refers to the state of fullness (*pūrṇatā*).

The sense is that otherwise, that fullness would exist as a mere name. The phrase "this power is the state of supreme lordship (parameśvaratā) characterized by wonder through its overflowing fullness" is the construction of the section of the commentary within the middle of the sentence. He explains the word *mahat* with the words "wherein," and by the word *api*, others [are included].

There are millions of creations and dissolutions. But surely, dissolution has entered into creation—what kind of statement is this, given the contradiction? He says, "Even in dissolution," to show that there is no such contradiction. "In the form of a seed" means by way of being a residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). But if this is so, what is the purpose of dissolution? He says: "Only..."
Thus, this distinction in worldly convention pertains to the joining and non-joining of appearances;

that is to say, regarding this great power of emanation (*sṛṣṭiśakti*), there is a differentiation according to the forms of Brahmā and others among the knowers— ranging from the lords of creatures (*prajāpati*) down to stationary beings— who are composed of the qualities (*guṇa*).

And regarding objects of cognition such as jars, pleasure, and so forth—which consist of the *guṇas* and are being created in various ways—even when they constitute a single, solid creation, this [power] is the power of creation, this is the power of maintenance, and this is the power of withdrawal; thus it is combined. That...

It is produced by the power of *māyā*. For in that state of *māyā*, the Lord (*īśvara*) himself abides in the form of Brahmā and others. By this, [it is shown] that even in his capacity as the agent of the great creation, the Supreme Lord...
The complete agency of all things has been established by virtue of performing creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
and through its continuous manifestation in nine forms— as Brahman, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara— along with the recurrence of returning with the seed remaining, there exists an intermediate variety.

From the *mātrā*, there is that which is designated by the terms "creation, maintenance, and withdrawal"; and by the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that [the *mātrā*] is also, in its pure form, that which is designated by the term "great creation" (*mahāsṛṣṭi*). This so-called "creation" consists precisely of the manifestation of the aforementioned division between the knower and the known. That very [manifestation] is the internal [reality] of the great creation.

He explains that the triad beginning with *sṛṣṭi* (emanation) is of the nature of *bhūta* (the real), by means of the distinction "of such [things]" (*tādṛśāṃ ca*), referring to those things manifested as separate. By this method, that limited emanation (*mitasṛṣṭi*) has been explained;
this is done with the intention that there be no tautology. Thus, it is said "in three forms."

"By means of the triad beginning with emanation (sṛṣṭi), which is appropriate to the forms of Brahmā and the others. Now, if the triad of deities is thus ever-present, then the withdrawal (saṃhāra) proclaimed by the venerable Rudra would be the opposite of both [emanation and maintenance]; consequently, emanation and maintenance would not be perceived. To this it is replied: "In that [triad]"—that is, within the midst of the triad of deities.

This is what is meant: in the doctrine that appearances are the ultimate reality (*ābhāsa-paramārtha-vastu-vāda*), for whichever cognizer (*pramātṛ*) there is the conventional usage "these appear to me in such a way," for him they appear in that way. However, it has been stated that in some cases, regarding the aspect of appearance, their conjunction occurs through the will of the Lord (*bhagavat*). And thus, in the primordial state (*ādyatve*)...

With respect to the cognizer who is Lord Rudra; with respect to the cognizer who is a yogin established in the stage of deep sleep characterized by supreme cessation; with respect to the cognizers who are *pralayākala* and *vijñānākala*;
and with respect to living beings who have entered into profound deep sleep—in all these cases, objects appear only as seeds.

For they are merged there in that manifestation; and in relation to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Bhaṭṭāraka, as well as in relation to the worldly subjects who move through the states of waking and dreaming, both novelty and continuity appear here because they are mutually merged. Now, by this—

Fearing that—because only division (vibhāga) itself appears through the determination of division—the non-division from light (*prakāśa*) would be severed, and thus entities (*bhāva*) would lack the state of being manifest; [the author] addresses that [objection] with the commentary beginning with "And not... (*na ca*).

(Page 27) He explains [the phrase] "of Maheśvara" as follows: it refers to that which, while existing in its true nature as the one who effects the division of the fivefold principles beginning with *vidyā* and ending with *śiva* by way of the forms of Brahmā and the others, is nevertheless capable of being designated through differentiation.

Furthermore, they appear as being concealed within one's own self through the state of "I-ness" (*ahantā*), up to the point of attaining a state of complete fusion through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); and they shine forth for those who have reached the fourth state (*turya*) and the state beyond it (*turyātīta*), which is characterized by such meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), due to the intensification of their agency (*kartṛtā*).

The primacy of agency [is established] because of what will be stated in the passage beginning with *mukhyatvaṃ kartṛtāyāḥ* (3.2.12). By this commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with *na ca*, the contradiction is resolved. What is that [commentary]? It is the one in the preceding commentary (*vṛtti*) which provides an explanation of the word *api* found in the sūtra.
By the word *api*, that which is suspected is stated as being merely possible. Of what is this contradiction?

It is of the division into knower and so forth, which was mentioned as a subordinate [distinction], and which is also applicable here because it was introduced as the meaning of the preceding sūtra. But [one might ask]: "The Blessed One..."

That manifestation of existence which, in relation to everything from Śiva down to the Vidyās, is designated by the term "Great Emanation" (mahāsṛṣṭi)—why should that not also be a withdrawal (saṃhāra)? He says: let it be so, for this is withdrawal; just as returning to the state of the seed is withdrawal, so too is immersion within the I-consciousness (ahantā). However, in the state of Śiva-ness...

Even the name of entities does not exist; however, this does not mean that there is no creation or dissolution. For that very reason, it is called "Sadāśiva. The term "utterance" (ukti) refers here to the single reality itself through the linguistic conventions of creation and dissolution.
Now, [one might ask: was it the nature of creation in the prior state, or the nature of [dissolution] in the subsequent state?
[The question is: "How is it that the reality (*vastu*) here is not divided? To this, he says: "But not...

For here, in the sequence of prior and posterior, there is nothing that possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*). Furthermore, such a manifestation is grace (*anugraha*), and dissolution is merely a subordinate form of maintenance and emanation. Thus, [the Lord] is essentially the power that unfolds the fivefold set of cosmic functions (*kṛtyapañcaka*).
The intended meaning is "the Blessed One. May there be auspiciousness! || 9 ||

Thus ends the first reflection on the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) in the *Kriyādhikāra* of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*, composed by the venerable Great Māheśvara, the illustrious teacher Abhinavagupta. 1.
(Page 28) Now begins the second inquiry:
[an investigation] into the awakening of all entities, which is characterized by the fourth digit (*kalā*) of the life-sustaining power (*saṃjīvana*).
I pay homage to that auspicious one, who is like a breath of nectar for those shattered by the poison of refutation.
Now,
[the section] beginning with "The connection with action... and so forth.

With these seven verses ending with "therefore such an error does not exist," the unimpeded sovereignty of the Lord, which consists of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), is established, [refuting] the categories of entities such as the connection of action that have been criticized by others.
