Reflecting that what is untenable in the externalist (Bāhyavāda) doctrine is perfectly tenable here in this system, one must necessarily establish— even though it has been refuted by others on account of the imposition of contradictory properties— that action and so forth possess both a unitary and a manifold nature; thus, there is this single sūtra which grasps the entirety of what is to be stated.

The *kalpa* consists of verses; among them, one indicates the logical justification and the proof [of the thesis], one indicates the meaning that although this collection of objects is cognizable through non-conceptual experience, it appears in a distinct form only at the occasion of conceptualization,
and two define the distinction between the domains of unity and plurality— these being those indicated in the first aphorism.
The sixth [chapter] explains the essential nature of relations, such as the state of action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*), which are accepted [as real];

in the seventh, he considers their utility for purposeful action (*arthakriyopayoga*)—this is the meaning of the section; however, the meaning of each individual aphorism is now being investigated. The manifestation of that which is being created by the power of emanation (*nirmāṇaśakti*) is itself [the reality].

It has been stated that it is an emanation (*nirmāṇa*) and nothing else. And since that [emanation] is indistinguishable from a double moon, blue, pleasure, and so forth, as well as from their substrates—such as action, generality (*sāmānya*), and the like—how can there be a conventional usage based on the distinction between "unreal," "real," and "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛtisatya*)? [The answer is: It is true.

Conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is not "nothing at all," because universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth do possess truth; however, it is false in cases such as a double moon. For this is the logical justification here, which he states by means of the aphorism:
"The cognitions of action, relation, universal, substance, direction, and time..."
The real [categories] are considered to have single or multiple substrata, according to their stability and utility. (1)
(Page 29) Any cognition of action other than the reality of consciousness (*saṃvit-tattva*), which is the appearance of action— whether of a single or manifold form—
has as its object the reality of action (*kriyā-tattva*) differentiated by the power of *māyā*. That [cognition] is truly dependent upon that [reality of action] as its locus.

For this reason, it is stable because its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is not uprooted by any subverting factor, and it is possessed of correspondence (*saṃvādavat*), being thus useful for the intended action characterized by the attainment of the village. Indeed, an entity (*bhāva*), while performing a causal function (*arthakriyā*), accepts both difference and non-difference, and is possessed of correspondence. In that regard, what [is the case]...

Its very nature, which is never subject to deviation, is that form (mūrti); that power by whose influence even what is not its own nature becomes its own nature, as if fixed within the form, is action (kriyā).
For instance, the bodies of Caitra and Maitra, though differentiated by various places, times, and shapes, are indeed this very same [consciousness]—this is the meaning.
It appears precisely as that which has not abandoned its unity; this very thing is "action," as in "Caitra goes.

In such a state, the continuous reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is never uprooted, and according to that determination, the attainment of the village by Caitra is indeed an unbroken causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
In the case of the perception of two moons, however, the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that seeks to follow [the object] is indeed uprooted;

and although they may serve as causes for pleasure or agitation, because they belong to the same class as a single moon, they are unreal as objects due to their deficiency in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), such as the removal of excessive darkness. Thus...

The meaning of the sūtra is that [the categories] beginning with "relation" (sambandha) and ending with "time" (kāla) are to be applied according to the subsequent sūtras. With the intention that by the very explanation of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), external action itself is also explained, the word "action" (kriyā) from the sūtra is used here in the commentary as an illustration.

The dual designation has been explained in this manner. By the phrase "of all that is useful," stability is expressed; by the phrase "by way of being purposeful," the utility for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is indicated. Introducing the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*), he connects the preceding section with the subsequent section by means of the words "tadevam" and so forth. [This concludes] the action.

He indicates that this is presented here as an illustration by means of the words "yathā" and "tathā. He states, "Therefore, [it is] one God," and so forth, to show that this is logically consistent only within our own philosophical system. Furthermore, with the intention that it is not proper to remain indifferent because of an inability to refute this, he establishes its stability through the term "constantly uncontradicted" (*satatāvigīta*).

By the words "one" (*eka*) and so forth, he establishes the essential nature; by the words "maintained" (*nirvāhita*) and so forth, he explains its utility, characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyāvattva*); and by the words "revealed" (*prakāśita*) and so forth, he indicates its utility for the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
For it has been said:
"There must be attentiveness toward the relationship [between the words]" (Vi.bhai. 106).

Thus: the very nature of entities is their appearing-as-such, and not their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); yet this [appearing-as-such] belongs to them. Having grasped this in his heart, [the author] examines their capacity for causal efficiency with an extensive textual passage beginning with "here" (*iha*) and ending with "will be stated" (*vakṣyate*). In that regard, regarding the capacity for causal efficiency—

He reflects: "Are you the essence (*svarūpa*), the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), or a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*)—the latter by virtue of existing in proximity to the definition—of the sentient being (*sattva*), either as an infallible property due to identity with it, or as a fallible property? In this regard, he states that its status as the essence is merely figurative, saying "by way of metaphor" (*upacārāt*).
For instance, "possessing branches and so forth" is the very nature of a tree; this is merely a single exclusion (*ekavyāvṛtti*) because it is synonymous (*paryāya*).

It is not so with the statement "the non-existent does not perform a causal function," because in common worldly usage this is not known to be a synonym. Furthermore, he shows that it is not a definition (*lakṣaṇatva*) by saying "and it is characterized" (*lakṣyate ca*), [indicating] that the state of being a definition is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the word *hetumatī*.

The reason [for their identity] is their mutual non-deviation; for otherwise, there would be under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*atibyāpti*), as has been shown. Although "direct perception" (*sākṣātkārijñāna*), "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāśūnya*), and "cognition" (*vedana*) are not synonyms—since they are established by the exclusion of different [concepts]—nevertheless...

Because they do not deviate from one another, these two stand in the relationship of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). "Of others" refers to other objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

By this he says the following: that which is of the nature of the direct realization and experience of a particular object of knowledge belongs to that very [subject]; therefore, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is itself directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), and not—

Regarding the word "artha" (object/purpose): however, this principle does not apply here because of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Thus he says, "But that," referring to what is intended as the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). And "therefore" means because of the non-occurrence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a contradiction; for it is indeed contradictory to say that there is a definiendum (*lakṣya*) in the absence of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, possession of activity (*kriyāvattva*) is not the definition of a substance (*dravya*). If being a definition were based merely on the fact of not occurring elsewhere, then even the connection with "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) would be its definition. Moreover, the essential nature of a definition is not merely the quality of distinguishing [the object] from others; rather, it is that by which something is defined.
(The page 31) Its entire nature is thus determined. And this is not possible for that which possesses non-pervasion (*avyāpti*).
Therefore, possession of action (*kriyāvattva*) is a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), whereas independence (*svātantrya*), being the characterized, is its definition.
[The opponent] suggests that it is merely indicative by saying "Now" (*atha*). [The author] refutes this with "Even so" (*tathāpi*);

the meaning is that even what was stated in this sentence is not obtained at all. Therefore, because it is not perceived apart from its own nature (*svarūpa*), its capacity exists only in being characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

"It may be that perception is merely an indirect indication (upalakṣaṇa)"; this is suggested by the phrase "if at best. Expressing his lack of approval, he says this: even at the time of bathing, drinking, and so forth, water is not perceived as having a form exceeding its nature as water; rather, it is only when its effects are observed that the cognizer [recognizes] it as "this is the instrument [of cognition]."

"One engages in conventional usage while conceptualizing that 'this is capable. Now, the opponent, setting aside the [logical] pervasion (*vyāpti*), revives the status of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatā*): "Indeed, 'in the end' means in the absence of another cognizer. "'Characterized by that' means defined by that. This too results in the fallacy of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

"He vitiates it there as well" means that "knowability" (jñeyatva) is merely to be postulated by the force of knowability itself. And therefore, the production of cognition brought about by the force of knowability exists even in cases such as two moons, hair, or flies—which are admitted to be non-existent—thus making [the definition] over-extensive (ativyāpaka). Now, one might object: "But no..."

The object’s status as a producer of cognition does not arise by the mere force of its being an object of knowledge; rather, it consists in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that cognition occurs when the object exists and precedes it, and the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that it does not occur when the object is absent—it is through these two that the object is to be designated in conventional practice. Even this [position] is not tenable.

By the passage beginning with "it is seen that there is knowability," [the author] shows the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of "from knowledge," which is intended as the effect. Now, one might object: when someone, having inferred fire from smoke while stationed at the foot of a mountain, ascends to the peak and sees that [fire], then—

Therefore, because fire is already established prior to that perception, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established. He shows that this is not universal by saying "for it is not," [just as] the soft touch on a *kapittha* fruit is not dependent on the same causal complex as its blue color. Now, as for the cognition of blue...

(Page 32) Since [the effect] occurs only occasionally even when the eyes and other [causes] are present, it must therefore have another cause. Thus, the absence of the effect when that [other cause] is absent— which would otherwise follow— is established.

"Existence (*bhāva*); therefore, by way of the reversal of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*), there exists a previously established reason (*hetu*)—namely, that existence consists in being a producer of cognition. Having raised this objection, he refutes it with the words beginning 'kārye'. The particle *tu* is displaced in the sequence. "If, however" (*yadi tu*) means if, on the other hand, it is argued thus: [regarding] the exclusion of the effect (*kārya-vyatireka*)...
If it is argued that there is an inference [of the object], even then it does not support its own purpose,

because such an inference would pertain only to something other than the blue object appearing at the same time as the manifestation— namely, to a mere cause. "Of that very [object]" means of the one being manifested.
Furthermore, the inquiry at hand is this: what could be the existence of blue and so forth at the very same time as its manifestation?

For that alone is what must be investigated, and not anything else, which would be like a man's horn. Therefore, once it is established that what is manifesting is not a different entity from the manifestation itself, the Proponent of Cognition (Vijñānavādin) considers his task accomplished.
As for what was said:

"Therefore, even regarding an external object, there is a distinction between the appearing object and the knower of that object," and so forth; in that context, by virtue of producing that cognition, some cause possesses causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*).
It is established that [the object] is the *sattva* (the existent); however, it is not the blue object which appears simultaneously with its cognition.
Now, one might argue: "Let there be causality even for that which is simultaneous with its appearance. To this, the following must first be stated:
that there can be a relationship of cause and effect between two things existing at the same time—but this has not been asserted.
"To connect it with another object of cognition" is another refutation. To this, he says "equal":

for at that time, the very fact of appearing is the cause for the conventional usage [of causality], and that is no different even in the case of the double moon; such is the meaning. Now, as for the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) which exist only when...

That which is appearing is simultaneous with its manifestation; that alone is the cause of cognition. Those two [factors] exist in the case of the blue object, whereas that [blue object] existed only prior to the consciousness, unlike the case of a double moon. This is what is meant by the word "tathā" (thus).
Now, as for that thing characterized as blue which exists at a time prior to its manifestation—
That cognition characterized by manifestation, which follows positive and negative concomitance, is not itself the manifesting moment.

And consequently, that same aforementioned fault would apply, as well as the [fault that] causal efficiency belongs to that very [entity], and so forth. He refutes this with the words "and not" (*na ca*). First of all, this fault does not arise in your own system;
thus, let the view that "existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency" be accepted by you without obstacle. Therefore...
In your own position, that which is the cause of cognition is precisely what appears; thus, there is no contradiction at all.

For in this way, according to you, time—characterized by limitation—is a property of the cognizable object, and the cognizable is indeed the act of cognition itself, yet there is no contact with time therein; moreover, the very nature [of cognition] is the moment.
What connection does that definition have with other actions such as the closing of the eyes, and what, then, is momentariness? Indeed,
you who are now acting like a celebrant, like a poor man,
have perhaps fulfilled the expectations of others' views, but your own vision remains unfulfilled.

And it is fulfilled—thus he says, "even in the case of momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇabhaṅge’pi*). Although this matter is quite well-established on the basis of the intention that the continuum (*santāna*) is itself the preceding and succeeding form due to such a misconception, nevertheless, what is the use of such effort? For the preceding moment [produces] the succeeding moment, and that too...

With the passage beginning with "immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*), the opponent has established his own position, arguing that existence (*sattva*) is indeed established by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). [The author] refutes this here [with the word] "in this regard" (*atra*):
the manifest cause of cognition is supported by positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
When "blue" is being expressed, why is it that a double moon is not likewise [perceived as] such? It is not determined [as blue].
For there is no distinction whatsoever between the prior characteristic of blue and the characteristic of a double moon, provided they do not manifest.
Here, another objection is raised: "[It is] the cognition of blue. "Another" refers to [causes] such as cataracts (timira) and so forth. "It does not exist"—[meaning the double moon does not exist].

One considers that the ascertainment [of the truth] regarding Vedic statements and the like occurs in the same manner. "In the same manner" means appearing as it did previously while manifesting now. "Nothing else" refers to the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth. Now, if even the double moon were present in the preceding moment just as it is in the moment of its manifestation, then it would have to persist even after that.

But this is not the case, because when the visual impairment has ceased, that [object] is no longer seen at that very moment. To this he replies: "In the same way," because even for things like a flame—which are subject to destruction without a trace—it is possible [for them to appear], and thus objects such as a jar could likewise exist [in that state] as something standing in the place of [its subsequent parts, such as] shards.

And this is because it is easily conceivable that any effect whatsoever— even something like a mere mass of dust and wind, or a single lump formed by joining two moons— could have two moons as its material cause.

As for what was also stated— that [existence] is due to being the cause of subsequent moments within its own continuum— that too is refuted by this very [argument], namely "in that same way. By the mere fact that the final moment of a flame does not produce any subsequent moment of its own kind, that which was asserted— namely, that existence consists in being a cause of purposeful action (*arthakriyākāraṇa*)— is overturned.

This is indeed refuted. Now, with the desire to offer further refutation, he turns back that [position] with the words "But even so" (*athāpi*) and so forth. As for what was said—"Even if there is deviation, as in the case of the crow," etc.—that "the very form [is existence]," meaning that existence is simply the possession of its own nature (*sasvarūpatā*), is correct; and that has been followed accordingly.

The word "eva" (only) is used in the sense of "it exists. Now, if that [existence] is merely a specific nature (*svarūpa-viśe�ca*), then for what purpose is causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) made its defining characteristic? It is said: "that alone. [The term] "to be distinguished" (*vivecanīyam*) is used in the sense of being possible or fit. "It is determined" (*niścīyate*) by means of the division between existence and non-existence. "Some" (*kecit*)...

Those who have practiced worldly transactions since childhood and are endowed with eloquence and other such qualities—this he addresses with the words "here too. He uses the word "gem" (*maṇi*) as a point of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*);
for a gem is distinguished by its specific whiteness, shape, size, color, luster, touch, and sound.
The distinction between birth and non-birth is logical, and that is so because it is taught thus to another.

However, no diversity is perceived in the nature, characteristic, or intrinsic being of a hair, even by those who are discerning. Even a discerning person, when their vision is clouded by a cataract, [perceives] a hair...

One perceives exactly that which belongs to the same class as the hairs [seen in the sky]. Even when one experiences through the visual disorder (*timira*) that "this is mine," one does not fail to see them for that reason;

rather, this perception is produced by another cause, but it is not the case that they are not hairs. If you argue that such is the nature of that cognition, then this cannot be easily refuted even in the case of the blue [object]. Indeed, he [the subject] at least...

With the intention that for one who has attained proficiency (*vyutpanna*), the hair appears as something entirely different from what is tangible, he says: "Or let it be so. "That" refers to the variety of its own nature (*svarūpa-vaicitrya*). It is "technical" (*pāribhāṣikī*) because variety exists only when there is a specific nature, and since existence (*sattā*) is nothing other than this very nature, it is logical that existence consists precisely in that particular variety.
"Not elsewhere" is merely a conventional restriction (*samayamātra*).

He establishes this very point with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*), because [the particle] *na* is used here as a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), which results in sheer emptiness (*tucchatā*).

It is understood [by implication], just as in the expression "one who does not see the sun" (*asūryampaśya*). For here, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is precisely the absence of vision regarding visible objects; or rather, it is a similarity to that [absence] by way of excluding what was suspected, as in the expression "an oblation offered by a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇena hutaṃ*). For here, there is the understanding of a Kṣatriya. This occurs when a figurative contradiction (*lākṣaṇikavirodha*) is possible.

In accordance with the principle that, when one wishes to establish the intrinsic nature of a thing, it is logical to have a cognition of another thing characterized by a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or merely its having a different form— as is the case everywhere in inference and so forth— [the following applies].

By the passage beginning with "What is existence? he demonstrates that even in the conceptualization of two groups—such as blue and non-blue, fire and non-fire, Brahmin and non-Brahmin—non-existence is not tenable. The passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth is the refutation of a third possibility. The phrase "even if indeed" (*yadi nāma*) indicates that this is merely an admission (*abhyupagama*).

[The author] shows [the answer]: "Now, let it be so in the case of what is perceptible; but what is the situation regarding that which is conceptualized? To this he says: "Even that which... This has been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda: "In that case, non-difference is an error," and "it is a formless thing. What is meant is this: first of all, a lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvarūpatā) is not tenable here, as in the case of a mass of hair or a yellow conch-shell.

Because there would be the undesirable consequence of non-difference between the perceptions of a sky-flower, a moving tree, a wheel of fire, and so forth, on the grounds that they are all like a state of fainting. If it is argued that they possess their own specific nature through difference, then this very [nature] is indeed their non-temporal existence (*asāmayikī sadrūpatā*);
thus it is established that "existence is nothing other than the state of being manifest. This is the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
He withdraws [the manifestation] and applies it to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) by means of the passage beginning with "this," and so forth. Now, one might object:

by this much, the existence of the appearance of a jar and the like—which are objects of conceptual construction, such as the hair-visions of one suffering from ophthalmia—has been shown to be exactly the same as that of activity, connection, and so on. And this is not something denied by the opponent. Nor is it [resolved] by this much alone.

It is logical that [the object] should be subject to investigation. This cuts through the doubt that "worldly people, seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), investigate real entities (*vastu*), and investigators intent on teaching them do likewise. [The author replies: "[Because of its] utility" means "it certainly would be so. Consequently, the remaining objection is that even things such as a double moon would then be fit for instruction.
The causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) that is observed from one moon is not doubled by that same [efficacy] from a double moon; therefore,
it is of the same class as another moon.

A second moon does not exist, nor does the hair perceived by one with ophthalmia exist as something other than the location of that hair; this is because of the presence or absence of another appearance, and not because of the appearance of hair itself. Furthermore, it is not manifested there in the form of hair or the like—that which is to be manifested—and thus it is erroneous and unreal. Therefore...

When there is one appearance of hair that is mixed with another desired appearance of hair, the notion of unreality regarding that [first] appearance of hair is what is meant. Thus it says, "they have been stated. Regarding the phrase "appearances of reality" (*satyābhāsāḥ*) in the commentary, he first explains it according to the *karmadhāraya* analysis by saying, "because their essence is appearance" (*ābhāsasāratvāt*). Now, one might object:

Relations and so forth possess a nature that is both one and many, but they are not the objects [of those cognitions]. True; however, that external relation and so forth, which possesses a form that is both one and many, is the object of the appearances in the intellect; therefore, having metaphorically attributed the property of the subject to the objects, this was stated in such a manner. The purpose for this metaphorical usage—

"Do not [think] that the essence is appearance. When such a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) exists, he demonstrates what has become established by means of the passage beginning with "the connection" (*sambandha*), etc. "In front" (*agre*) refers to the distinct manifestation (*viviktābhāsa*) resting within one's own self. (2.2.4)

In such sūtras as these, [the author] shows what is excluded by the term *satya* (real) with the words "precisely because they are appearing" (*ābhāsamānatvād eva*). Now, one might object: "Reality (*satyatva*) must be predicated of the objects (*viṣaya*), not of the appearances which are the subjects (*viṣayin*);
therefore, how can there be a *karmadhāraya* compound? It cannot be a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) meaning 'appearances of the real'."

The term *māsa* (measure) is appropriately applied within a single sentence because of the simultaneous appearance of relations and so forth through the distinction between the primary and the metaphorical, due to the connection of difference and non-difference. He resolves this [objection] with the words: "precisely by virtue of the reality of the manifestation. This is not merely a metaphor; rather, it is a metaphor only in relation to the state of *māyā*.
As it is said:
"Because it is presided over by the Blessed One, the Blessed One alone is everything.
Therefore, in this case, there is no difference whatsoever between the manifestation and that which is manifested. Thus he says:

"Because it has that nature. Thus, even in the case of the level of *māyā*, the term has been explained as a *karmadhāraya* compound without abandoning the level of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Now, by resorting to the *bahuvrīhi* alternative:
(page 37)
He explains by relying on the very term *māyāpada*, using the words "or rather" (*athavā*).

The phrase "of these" (*amīṣām*) refers to [the categories] beginning with relation (*sambandha*). The word "that too" (*so'pi*) refers to the functional utility (*upayoga*). The phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) means: for the very reason that there is a functional utility regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through the very arguments established by us; it is for this cause—thus [he speaks] in a non-co-referential construction (*vaiyadhikaraṇyena*).

The two words "tasmin" and "pañcamyau" should be joined; otherwise, the two uses of the particle *eva* would be entirely inconsistent. "These" refers to relation (*sambandha*) and the rest. He explains this very point with the verse beginning "saṃvṛti," and so forth. By what statement are these [relations] said to be distinct from both sensory and mental error? He says: "And thus... (*tathā ca*). For if...

If the distinction of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*) were intended to consist merely in its being of the nature of an error, then it would not be logical to designate it separately from the mental error denoted by the word "delusion" (*bhrānti*), nor from the sensory error characterized by ophthalmia (*taimira*). Such a designation [of conventional reality] as distinct from error must arise from some specific perspective regarding the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
The phrase "by a mere trace of distinction" (*viśeṣaleśataḥ*) refers to the explanation of the ancient authorities (*prāmāṇika*) for the purpose of refutation;

[the author] introduces it with the words "that, however" (*tat punaḥ*). By this, the distinction from his own explanation is indicated. He does not tolerate this, saying "in this way indeed" (*evaṃ khalu*).
The word *khalu* indicates derision. By this, he says the following: [it arises] from another error (*bhrāntyantarāt*).
Not even a trace of a distinction is found here in this explanation by which it would deserve to be mentioned separately.

[Objection: But how can the visible object be covered by silver, which is a conceptual construction (*vikalpita*)? [Response: Then how could it be covered by a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth as well? [Objection: If you say it is because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) through the support of the visible object, then it is the same in both cases.
He determines this [error] as being "in the location of the mother-of-pearl. Now, one might object:

concealment (*avacchādana*) is not merely the occupation of that location; rather, it is a state of constant pervasion even when a sublation (*bādhaka*) occurs, such that the object distinct from that [concealer] is never perceived in its own form. Such is the nature of concealment.

The gift is perceived as a mere generality (*sāmānya*) and so forth, which are subject to conceptual construction (*vikalpanīya*), and not as silver and so forth; for this reason, error is mentioned separately [from the object]. Having restated this with the words "Now, moreover" (*athāpi*) and so forth, he refutes it with the words "This very [point]" (*tad etat*). In this context, the cause is the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*), like a cataract (*timira*).

Just as [cognition] ceases with respect to the eyes and eyebrows, or with respect to silver due to distance, dissimilarity, and lack of focused attention, one should not think that there is thereby some specific distinction regarding its status as an error;
for it is not by another [means].
(Page 38)
It has been stated that "there is no erroneous conventional usage here. The word "even" (*api*) is to be construed with "in the case of subverting cognition" (*bādhajñāne*).

The pronoun "of that" (*tasya*) refers to the subverting cognition. By the word "for" (*hi*), which indicates its causal nature, this meaning is expressed: because activity does not occur toward things such as a double moon when their falsity is known.

Furthermore, for one who has not acted upon it, there can be no deception consisting of fraud, precisely because of that non-engagement; nevertheless, since it does not grasp an object in its true form, it is logical according to your own view that the cognition of two moons is indeed an error. As for that which...
Regarding the statement "And if the determination were an error" (1.3.5),

it was said there that the magician's perception of unreal objects is not designated as an error when it is known precisely as being unreal; therefore, that [objection] was intended with reference to the views of others.
There is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. "Because of remaining in that state" means because it is indistinguishable from other errors.

"Otherwise" means if there were distinction, since [error] would then consist merely of delusion. "Therefore" means for that reason. Now, one might object: conventional cognition is an obscuration only if it is not itself produced by another cognition.

If it is argued that even though the superimposition is the same—since whatever has been seen at any time is superimposed as a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth—the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) is mentioned separately for this specific reason; [the author] refutes this with "nor even... If it is claimed that the very perception of the moon's duality is the issue, then [we reply that] even a single thing, which is common to multiple perceivers...

The rule is the same, namely that [the object] is simply perceived as such. Thus, having established that there is no further distinction regarding its being an error (*bhrāntitva*), he states with the words "having superimposed" (*samāropya*) and so forth that even the status of being a particular type of error is not accepted by the author himself, as he indicates it by means of a copulative compound (*dvandva*). This refers to the case where they occupy the same locus simultaneously.

It is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). And that [coexistence] occurs only between two things of identical nature. Furthermore, a universal (*sāmānya*), while subsisting by encompassing all its particulars, embraces the intended particular even though it possesses other particulars; thus, it causes that particular to receive a distinct verbal designation that it had not previously obtained.

"Directly" means by way of worldly convention (*lokapratīti*) that is clear. For it is precisely with words such as *dānta* (tamed) and *balīvarda* (bull) that both the noble and the worldly refer to bulls; however, with the word *go* (cow), they refer only to female cows—such is the conventional understanding.
Indeed, when it is said, "This city is rich in cattle" (*gomat*), what is intended is simply the abundance of curds and milk.

(Page 39) It appears. Regarding "the state of being conventional" (*sāṃvṛtatva*), even one who is unwilling must necessarily accept that this alone is the definition of the conventional; for that definition, together with the term denoting the definiendum (*lakṣyapada*), [is thus established].

He explains this with the words "that which is thus" (*tathā*) and so forth. With the intention that, regarding this definition, if the impossibility [of the object] is set aside by means of both its manifestation and its utility, then victory belongs to us; whereas if the utility is refuted by way of its impossibility, then victory belongs to the opponent.

He first states the dependence on another with the words "nanu" (surely). Since the collection of categories, such as relation and so forth, shares the same status as the well-established whole (*avayavin*), this investigation is undertaken by taking that very whole as the established premise. The phrase "in that very way" means by way of a single, gross form.
And for that very reason, the reason [given] in the passage beginning with "of the gross" (*sthūlasya*) is that it is not so. Now, one might object: "Atoms are many;

how could they perform a single, determinate causal function (*arthakriyā*)? It is said in reply: "Just as distinct [factors] such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, being restricted, produce a single cognition, so too do atoms. [This refers to] individual instances (*vyakti*).
And thus, although distinct, they produce a cognition of a single form by means of the aforementioned principle.

Furthermore, it is precisely these distinct moments that result in the single fruit of the preparation of rice and are designated as "cooking. Anticipating the objection—"Why should this very rule apply everywhere?"—he states the reason with the words "For not... (na hi).
It would indeed be logical that the sense organs and so forth, being perceived and determined as distinct entities,
should produce a single cognition— the notion of a sprout— just as seeds, soil, water,
and sunlight do; however, in this case, it is a single thing that appears and is determined which performs its own specific function.

How could there be the postulation of something else? For even in the case of blue, which is both manifested and determined as performing a causal function, it would not be possible to postulate without basis that yellow performs that same causal function.
Anticipating the objection that "in this case, since there is an impossibility [of the manifestation], another thing must be postulated," he refutes that very point.

"And this very [appearance]..."—the opponent says "but not," meaning that here there is no appearance at all. He provides the reasoning for this with the words "for the appearance as gross... It is logical [to say this] because extension is indeed spatial differentiation, and that depends upon a difference in essential nature; thus, it is entirely contracted both in terms of form and in terms of time.

That which is devoid of the superimposition of contradictory properties is the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) and the ultimate moment (*kṣaṇa*). [Objection: But surely grossness (*sthūlatā*) does indeed appear. [Response: True; however, that [grossness] is merely a continuous multitude of—

The nature of [the cognition] is necessarily concomitant with the appearance of atoms, just as the appearance of two things is necessarily concomitant with the appearance of a jar and a cloth. [Objection: But if the gross object is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then what of it? [Reply: He says, "And it is non-conceptual. He refutes this with the word "that": the unreality [of the object] is based on its being a conceptual construct.

By perceiving that which is incompatible with the pervader of that [conceptualization]—namely, non-conceptuality—one must forcibly effect the negation of unreality, which is pervaded by being conceptualizable;
thus, there would follow the absurd consequence that the double moon, the yellow conch, and so forth are real. Furthermore, non-conceptuality... [is not...]

He shows that [this condition] pervades validity by saying "inference" (*anumāna*). This might be the case: some conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is rooted in a real entity (*vastu*), while some are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*). In the first case, where it is rooted in a real entity, the initial perception shines forth as being precisely non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*); validity resides there solely because it is rooted in that [real entity]. But in the second case...

There would be a total lack of validity, and the conceptualization of the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth would have its root in ignorance (*avidyā*). Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "And if... (*yadica*). [He asks: "From that"—if the latent impression of experience (*anubhava-vāsanā*) is what gives rise to those conceptual constructions, then what would be the cause for postulating the latent impression of ignorance? And therefore...

The word "api" (even/also) is indeed not to be taken [in its literal sense]. This very point is established by the words "ataśca" (and therefore). For if experience were abandoned, then the blue aspect being experienced, as well as the manifestation residing therein—which is the very nature of experience—[would be lost].

In a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is fixed solely upon a single object of conceptualization consisting of a gross self distinct from what is being experienced, [the experience] would be entirely lost. He says "But that" (*tattu*) to show that even when the latent impression of experience (*anubhavavāsanā*) is present, there remains room for the latent impression of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*). He clarifies this non-pursuit (*ananusaraṇa*):

Regarding the phrase "for experience": it expresses the understanding that many atoms, endowed with contradictory properties and possessing distinctions such as spatial direction, exist in the form of jars and so forth as gross particular natures (*svalakṣaṇa*);
for grossness consists of multiple properties, whereas atomhood consists of a single property.

For the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādī*), it is that experience in which [the object] appears; likewise, it is that experience in which there appears a gross, specific-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) form such as a jar— which is distinct from other jars in terms of place and time and is endowed with contradictory properties— but which is not a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*).

"But that which is the opposite of this is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)," he says, "namely, the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpābhāsa*). "Unity" means not many; "universality" (*anugatatva*) means not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). [Objection: But if this is so, conceptual construction would always be—

Anticipating the objection—"If it also subsists upon the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of knowledge, and therefore that [impression] is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), how can there be validity for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of inference?"—he provides the rebuttal with the words "merely" (*kevalam*).

Regarding the phrase "even though not grasping that": although it does not grasp the actual object (*vastu*), it [functions] toward that which does not perform that [object's] causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

That which consists of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), namely the turning away (*vyāvartana*) or removal (*apohana*) from an empty object—a negation by nature that is distinct from the affirmation of the form of consciousness—that very thing is the supreme duty for one [who performs it]; the state of being such is "that-ness" (*tadbhāva*). By that reason, whatever object is determined through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), from that...

The fitness of the reason regarding an external object belongs to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). [The text] says "he brings that very [fitness] about even with respect to the external," because when that conceptual construction exists—"therein" refers to inference (*anumāna*) and to the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) which occurs immediately after perception;
"elsewhere" refers to independent conceptual construction (*svatantra-vikalpa*); "for its sake" refers to conceptual construction. "For its sake" means...

Regarding that object which has produced a conceptual construction (vikalpa) handed down through tradition: [an objection is raised]—"But surely the object of conceptualization is unreal, and what is unreal has no utility anywhere. Having anticipated this, he says "that" (*tat*), meaning the cognition of that which has been made the object of conceptualization; for what, then, is the definition of the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*)?
Because it is universal and eternal, it does not cease; however, hair, silver, and the like do not manifest as universal or eternal,
and therefore the conventional dualistic pair is merely a specific kind of error,
since the term "error" applies [only] to hair, silver, and so forth due to their lack of consistency.

"But because it is well-known" is obtained precisely from your own counter-argument. Now, as for what we said—that the definition is useful in some cases—why is that being abandoned? He says: "Even its utility... [is not established].
"Otherwise" means by way of multiplicity (*anekatayā*) and by way of being unattached (*araktatayā*). "And that too" refers to the lamp. "Of that" refers to...
Of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). "In that way" means by way of a false form. "Desired" refers to the manifestation of objects and so forth.
When cataracts, ignorance (*avidyā*), and the like—which are unavoidable—have not been removed, that which appears "in that way" is manifold (*vicitra*).

False perception (*mithyādarśana*) is merely the means for attaining that [object], whether it be a lamp or an aggregate of atoms; from that alone arises causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and not from a non-entity through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For nothing at all appears within conceptual construction; there is only mere conceit (*abhimāna*) therein, but no appearance of anything whatsoever.

In this context, regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), that which is the appropriate response has already been stated; or rather, it refers back to the meaning of the subsequent sentence as "that whose elaboration (*prapañca*) has for the most part been stated. Alternatively, since the prima facie argument is of such a nature, there is nothing further to be said here concerning experience (*anubhava*).

Regarding that which was stated somehow as "non-following" (*ananusaraṇa*), [the author], intending to refute it, first states "even in conceptual construction" (*vikalpe 'pi*) concerning the following of experience (*anubhavānusaraṇa*). But how is there non-following? First of all, is it because of a difference in properties (*dharmabheda*) within that very [object] appearing [in the conceptual construction]?

Or [it is distinct] because it delineates another object that is different from the object not grasped by experience. He says "clearly" to show that there is no difference [between them] due to a difference in properties (*dharma*). "Investigated" refers to the specific characteristic of the manifestation of the object. (1.8.2)

In this very inquiry, it will be examined [in the verse] "by virtue of being distant or near" (2.3.10). He refutes the second position as well with the words beginning "the universal," for that which indeed...

That which has been experienced appears as such in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Indeed, in the conceptual construction "this is a jar," it is only the perceived nature that appears—nothing more than the red object with a broad base and belly. Even in the case of "the cow is pure," it is only the form possessing a dewlap and so forth that is seen; there is nothing additional to what is perceived that could be denoted by the word "whole" (*avayavin*).

Or rather, it is the worldly [object] denoted by a general term that appears. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that whatever is seen appearing is itself the universal, because of identity with it or because of inherence in it, since [the cognition] proceeds in the form of that [universal];
or else, from the perspective of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because there is no desire to introduce any other appearance that would qualify it?"
That which is perceived, such as blue and so forth, is itself the universal (*sāmānya*). By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), actions, wholes (*avayavin*), and the like are meant.
If that is the case, since it is an external object of such a nature, why is it not apprehended even by non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perception?
[It is because] it arises through the power of a proximate object.

(Page 43) For that is proclaimed. And therefore, as for what was stated— namely, "not [of] relation, part, action, universal, and so forth"— which was intended to support one's own proposed theory, it is merely a fallacious conceptual construction (*vikalpābhāsa*), because it follows upon a sense of oneness.

If it were argued that [the universal] manifests through the suffix *tva* and so forth, rather than as a manifestation of experience (*anubhavābhāsa*), then that very point would be abandoned by you yourself;

for if it is accepted as having an external form in its nature as a universal, it follows as a logical consequence that this [universal] must be graspable by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*). For this very reason, [there can be no connection] of the universal—which is of a conceptualized nature—with an external object.

In the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*), he stated that the nature of the object is non-different from cognition because it is not separate from it; in the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), it is not other than cognition because it is a non-entity. Now, one might object:
"A real entity such as a blue jar is not touched by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); therefore, how could it possess a form such as 'samāna' (common) and so forth?"

Even for non-conceptual [cognition], it would follow that its object is universals and the like; however, in reality, it touches only upon what is not the [actual] object, because activity and attainment proceed from conceptualization—which is characterized by superimposition based merely on conceit regarding a real entity. It is precisely for this reason that its validity in certain cases was established in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

With the passage beginning "only that which has been made the object of experience," he refutes that [position] with the words "and even determination (*adhyavasāya*). In the case of a verb with two objects, such as *āropayati* ("he superimposes") or *nayati* ("he leads"), the primary object is the external one, which stands in the place of the goat; the secondary object, however, is the non-external.

That which possesses a possible difference of locus (saṃbhāvyavyadhikaraṇatāka) stands in the place of the village. "He enters into" (abhiniviśate) means "he conceives" (abhimanyate). And this is merely a variety of verbal expression, not a difference in meaning. Furthermore, it is not logical that that which is non-conscious in nature (asaṃvidrūpa) should be the activity (vyāpāra) of that which is conscious in nature (saṃvidrūpa); for what indeed is called "activity"?

The very nature of that [self] is said to be delimited by its fruit. For this very reason, the claim that "the property of self-conceit (*abhimāna*) is like consciousness, pleasure, and so forth" is also incorrect; for, just like pleasure and the rest, it would entail the undesirable consequence of being incapable of acting upon the object. Now, it might be argued that there is no distinction between the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpya*).

It is said that pride (*abhimāna*) is indeed *kāśa*; regarding this, he says "yadi hi" (if indeed). The locative and nominative cases in the phrase "avabhāsamāna eva" (while appearing) are used through *śleṣa* (punning juxtaposition) to characterize the manifestation of both the object of superimposition (*āropya*) and the locus of superimposition (*āropasthāna*). The word "prāk" (previously) [is used].
Regarding the statement "(page 44) *bhrāntitve cāvasāyasya*...
and so forth, that which was expressed there by the word "abhimāna" (*seti*) refers to [the thought] of a fool: "I am a scholar."

Just as there is the application of a word, so too would there be [the application] in the conceptual construction (vikalpa) "this is a jar. Concluding this point, he refutes what was stated in the prima facie position—that utility belongs not to that which is perceived through conceptual construction, but only to atoms—by stating "And thus," etc., asserting the opposite of that view. For indeed...
No causal efficiency whatsoever occurs for that which does not manifest. And manifestation does not occur for that which is not reflected upon (*avimṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, no one has ever had a reflection (*vimarśa*) upon atoms during the cognition of a jar or the like, even in a dream or in a mental construction (*saṅkalpa*).
According to this principle—that when division leads to an infinite regress of smaller and smaller parts, there can be no abiding in anything more minute—[atoms cannot be the ultimate reality].

Even while it exists, this [cognition] is never directed toward the jar; rather, when there is the conceptualization of its destruction, it has as its object another thing that is spatially remote and separated. Nor is it logical that the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of one thing should be determined by the conceptual determination of another, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). All of this is stated on the back of the commentary (*vṛtti*).

He joins [the argument] by stating "it is joined and stated. Thus, this formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the cognitions of substance and so forth do not have unreal objects, because their objects possess a form that performs uncontradicted purposeful action (*abādhitārthakriyākārin*).
This is the perception of this reason (*hetu*), which is pervaded by having real objects—a state that is the opposite of having unreal objects.

Atoms are never at any time the performers of purposeful action (arthakriyā) regarding objects such as jars, because they have never been so determined. In the conventional usage "this is the purposeful action of this [thing]," the cause is such a determination; and its opposite is non-determination. Thus it is said.
This is because of the perception of what is incompatible with the cause;
by this, the establishment of the reason is uncontradicted.
Otherwise, the reason—that atoms possess causal efficiency—would be unestablished. 1.
Now, one might object: even so, the reason is not established because the qualification "uncontradicted" is impossible;

for by you who assert that substances and other categories possess a nature that is both one and many, you yourself have stated the contradiction—namely, that whatever is one is also many—and how could that be? Thus is the objection.
In that regard, one internal reality is to be rejected— that very [reality] which is perceivable by the senses.
Having attained multiplicity through place, time, and inherent nature, it becomes manifold.

In that regard, once the reality of action and so forth has been established, the unity and multiplicity attributed to action and so forth—though these have been treated as subordinate qualities (*guṇīkṛta*) in their respective contexts—are here to be demonstrated as the primary objects of knowledge (*pradhāna-prameya*). Having reflected upon this, the determination is made: between those two, unity alone is thus...

It is established that plurality is thus [unreal]; for when the ultimate reality of entities such as blue and so forth is the internal essence characterized solely by pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), there is no conceptual construction whatsoever therein, because even unity is absent due to its being a mass of non-duality. As for that which is internal, distinct from other appearances—
The internal [reality] is unmixed; it is a single principle that is internal and cognizable solely by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

That is one. Yet, while still not abandoning its oneness, having attained the state of being cognizable by the external senses, it attains multiplicity through distinctions of space and so forth—such as "here" and "there," "now" and "then," or "emaciated" and "non-emaciated."

Nor is there any contradiction, because perception remains unimpaired; for, just as in the case of causality and non-causality, it is easy to state that the distinction between objects exists merely as a matter of conventional usage (*vyavahāramātra*) while being ultimately real (*paramārtha*). Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between unity and multiplicity, as in the case of the action "Caitra moves," and likewise in the case of a relation.
The meaning of the sūtra is that [the reality] should be stated as being "either within or at the beginning. Reality is internally undivided by virtue of being pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*).

However, for the subject under the influence of *māyā*, the object is—due to the manifestation of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the external organs (*bāhyakaraṇa*)—externally divided; thus, in effect, it is both one and many. The reason for its multiplicity is "externally" (*bahiḥ*).
This constitutes the connection with the preceding narrative (*itivṛttasaṃgati*). "Thus being" (*evaṃ sati*) refers to the action and so forth being present, as well as the reality inherent therein;

this is a general statement. "In this way" (*evam*) is as stated by the first quarter of the verse, while "subsequently" (*parataḥ*) is as stated by the remaining three quarters. First, there is non-differentiation due to the absence of mental construction (*kalanā*).
He explains this with the words beginning "of all," and so forth. If the words *yat* and *tat* are used, then the construction is as follows:

that very internality is precisely this appearance of unity. However, if the reading includes the words *yadā* and *tadā*, it is clear [that they function as temporal correlatives]. The word "infinite" (*anantāni*) refers to [the appearances of] a single jar and so forth.
The meaning is: by means of making manifest on the wall of any one [of these] appearances. Taste (*rasa*) consists of the six kinds, beginning with sweet;
it is infinite through its internal subdivisions. Potency (*vīrya*)... [page 46]

The touch of heat and so forth, as well as specific potencies (*prabhāva-viśeṣa*), arise from the connection with the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*). However, that transformation of taste (*rasāntara*) such as sweetness and so on, produced by the connection with the internal fire, is *vipāka*. The other qualities (*guṇa*) are heaviness, unctuousness, and so forth. (2)
Now, as for what was said—that one thing may be both one and many due to a difference in objects—who is to grasp that?

First, through visual perception, Caitra appears as indeed divided by the difference of location; it has been said that this [perception] lacks the capacity to mix these distinct appearances because it is non-conceptual (*avicāraka*), whereas conceptualization (*vikalpa*)— [...is capable of such mixing... (Note: The provided fragment ends here).

But the mental [consciousness] does not touch the object at all. Regarding this, it is said in the Sūtra: "Having that [object] as its twofold objective support, the mind, acting as a subsequent determiner, performs the conceptualizations of action and so forth, consisting of the activity of the subject. (3)

In this context, although in a state free of conceptual construction (avikalpa), there may be the appearance of mere existence or mere jar— such as "it exists" or "it is a jar"— and during the perception of the expanded [universe], there may even be said to be the appearance of universals (sāmānya) and so forth for the yogin,
as well as the appearance of action and the appearance of time; nevertheless, at that time, those universals and so forth [are not truly external].
One does not regain one's own life. For instance:

the quality of being disoriented by conciliation (*sāman*), the intensification of distinctions between relatives, the apprehension of the identity of a continuous series of momentary differences, the aggregation of parts, and the relationship between the delimited and the delimiting—[these are the factors involved].

The appearance of existence (*bhāvāvabhāsa*) is the life-force of appearances such as universals, relations, actions, substances, and directions; and that [life-force] is clearly manifested in conceptualization (*vikalpana*). Conceptualization, moreover, occurs at the occasion of mental after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), wherein the illusory knower (*māyā-pramātṛ*) becomes manifest. Therefore, the mind is the agent of after-cognition.

While performing the subsequent reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) following the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), one produces conceptual cognitions (*vikalpajñāna*) whose objects are the connection with action and so forth; these are performed by emphasizing the activity of the independent subject (*svatantrapramātṛ*). As it was stated before, that which is characterized as both one and many—this duality...

Those [cognitions] which have such an objective support (ālambana) are characterized by that very conceptualizing intellect (vikalpadhī); thus, there is a contact with two forms—namely, the single and the multiple—but conceptualization does not touch the actual reality (vastu). Indeed, this is the operation of the knower (pramātṛ), and the knower, even during conceptualization, consists of self-reflexive awareness (svasaṃvedana) within the prior experience.
It does not abandon its prior nature; however, when its illusory character becomes manifest, there is indeed a mental after-cognition (*anu-vyavasāya*) of it.
(Page 47)

This is the occasion. Furthermore, the connection with ritual action and so forth pertains only to that [empirical level] and not to the state of Śiva, nor even to the plane of Sadāśiva and the rest; and during the time of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpaka*), there is the aggregate of forms such as Śiva and Sadāśiva—this is the purport of the Sūtra. He introduces this with the words "externally" (*bāhya*) and so forth, leading toward unification.

[This is explained] up to the end [of the verse] with the word *vantaḥ*. He explains that on such a level, rather, duality dissolves and thus there is no occasion for the state of being a subject (*pramātṛtā*); and he describes the departure from that state by means of the two subsequent verses.
Within each respective subject (*nijanije pramātari*), that internal organ characterized as the mind (*manas*) which is proximate—

Because it performs the function of common cognition, those [cognitions] are engaged in that very operation of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) which is their means of accomplishment. "Worldly course" (*lokayātrā*) refers to worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*), in which it is considered that only the connection with action and so forth is densely required. Why, then, is this burden placed upon the mind?

If [this is] so, he says: "Even though" (*yadyapi*) it is not to that extent in pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, for that very reason, there is no full purity here; thus this state is indeed unfit for worldly transaction (*avyavahārayogyā*), like the state of ash or the *sūtaka* [impurity] during the act of eating. "By means of the divisions of parts" (*aṃśabhedaiḥ*).

For it will be stated [later]: "Cognition has as its object that which is denoted by a single term" (2.3.2). He explains the word *anu* as "subsequently. The connection is: "the mind itself performs the conceptual constructions (*parikalpanāḥ*). The phrase ending with "instrument" (*karaṇam*) is a qualifying attribute of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
However, the two words ending in the suffix *śatṛ* (present participles) contain within them the sense of causality regarding the act of conceptualization (*kalpanā*).

Fearing that it might be suspected that the mind (*manas*) situated between the two [the object and the subject] was what was described as "active" (*vṛtta*), he shows by means of the passage beginning with "externally" (*bahiḥ*) and ending with "of that" (*tasya*) that it refers to the grasped and the grasper. [He further explains] the relationship of distinction (*bheda*) and connection (*saṃbandha*) with the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
For those for whom [the notions of] external and internal cannot be expressed when they rest upon their exclusion (*vyatireka*), [the word] "of him" refers to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).

He states the reason for this with the words "of the cognizer. That very thing which the cognizer determines as the object of conceptualization—whether external or internal—by means of various combinations, is what is being described.
"Action in general," and so forth. "He engages in worldly discourse" (*vyavaharati*) means he performs a mental application (*vṛtti-yojanā*), as indicated by the phrase "being mental," and so on.

"The cause" (*hetuḥ*) is the remainder of the three sentences. Now, who else indeed is called the "knower" (*pramātā*), whose activity consists of conceptual constructions such as action and the like?

(Page 48) Having stated this, and having raised the objection that the internal reality (*antastattva*) is merely a continuum of consciousness consisting of experience and conceptualization, he says: "For it is the subject alone... [referring to] the true subject (*satyapramātṛ*).
The meaning is that [the Lord] is indeed in the form of Maheśvara. The word "previously" (*prāk*) refers to the section beginning with [Sūtra 1.3.7]:

"If [it is argued that the Self is not the agent] because [the mind] has not been made internal... up to the end. Regarding the phrase "born of latent impressions" (*saṃskārajā*), for latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is indeed...

It has been stated that [the result] culminates in the unity of the subject (*pramātṛ*). Therefore, one should understand that it is not the case here as the Buddhists believe—that [knowledge] is produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experience.
The intended meaning of the passage beginning with "and in the eyes, etc. and ending with "because of its being established" has thus been explained.

At the very commencement of the commentary on the Sūtra, [the author] indicates everything beginning with the "connection" (*sambandha*) by means of the term "general" (*sāmānya*). The phrase "even though they are of a general nature" means that they are for the most part indistinct.
The expression "they are called general" does not mean that they are conventionally designated as "general. Herein lies the reason:

In order to provide space for what is about to be said, beginning with the words "of those" (*teṣām*), and to reveal its general nature, he says [the passage] ending with "that which follows the particulars" (*viśiṣṭānāmanugāmi*).
Now, at this point, one might ask: what should that single appearance be called? It cannot, for now, be called a "universal" (*sāmānya*).
You yourself have stated this: "And the world does not engage in practical activity (*vyavahāra*) with an object as something devoid of distinction. It is true that the world does not so engage;

however, the reason for its lack of engagement is that the world seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and a mere appearance (*ābhāsamātra*) is not capable of performing such action. This is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "tadarthakriyā" and so forth.

And the particle *ca* indicates a doubt; it was stated that [the state] is rare with the intention that it might even belong to those who are mostly practitioners (*yogin*). It does not mean that non-existence alone is what is desired, as in the expression "he puts on an existing garment.
Now, when one wonders whether something exists in the house or not, even by the mere appearance of existence—

The purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), characterized by the avoidance of heartbreak, is indeed performed. And this will be explained in the same way in the passage beginning with *tathaiva sadghaṭa* (2.3.5).
So how can it be said that purposeful action occurs only when there is a mixture with another appearance?

To this, he provides the answer beginning with the word "deśa" (place). Here, at present, that which is merely being cognized as existing (*sannitīyatā*) has become the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the appearance of existence; thus, by means of appearances such as form, blue, and so forth, [it appears] externally—

What function do colors serve in the state of *svalakṣaṇatā* (particularity), since they are not its determinants? Even when there is a confluence of thousands of appearances, the state of *svālakṣaṇya* (specific individuality) does not persist without the appearances of space and time—
as in the case of "a blue cloth, spread out, made of cotton, soft, thin," and so forth, where [the specific individuality] culminates in the universal.

Because there is a manifestation of the very nature of form (*rūpatā*). However, the convergence of the appearances of space and time—as in "this is that"—sets aside its universal nature (*sāmānyarūpatā*). Therefore, that [convergence] itself is internal when it results in specific individuality (*svālakṣaṇya*). He demonstrates this very point with the words "of those two alone," namely, of space and time.

Space manifests the variety of priority and posteriority characterized by distance and proximity through its nature as being prior, posterior, and so forth; time, however, manifests [the variety] characterized by newness, antiquity, and so forth.
But if all manifestations (ābhāsas) are equally combined with one another, what is the rule here [that determines their specific manifestation]?

The ever-shining [consciousness], conjoined with those two manifestations (*ābhāsa*), is called the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārī*); however, it is never the case that the manifestation of space or the manifestation of time is mixed with another manifestation. To this, it is said: "It is always indeed... That which, indeed—
It is logical that the very same entity, which is indicated as primary and has entered the path of distinct conceptualization,

is the principal substance (*dravya*) that performs purposeful action (*arthakriyākārī*). As for space and time, if they are likewise [considered primary], then that which is the entire nature of form (*rūpa*), dependent on something else— defined as "that by which one is directed" (*diśyate 'nena*) and "that by which one is calculated" (*kalyate 'nena*)— is precisely that [substance].

"Separated" means that, insofar as they consist of independent appearances, their status as specific particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) occurs precisely through their interpenetration with other appearances of space and time; this alone is the position that unfolds. If it is asked what those two do when they have become subordinate, he says:
Regarding the term "pervasive and eternal": it refers to that which desires to expand its manifestation through form and action, yet simultaneously undergoes contraction;

and once contracted, it serves the limited subject whose nature is contracted. Thus, what is called "fusion" (*melana*) is precisely the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Now, as for the unfolding of that eternal manifestation—

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is that constant manifestation which, having attained the state of being a differentiator, exists through identity with the body of the differentiated; it is logical that it should bear the condition of the differentiated. Furthermore, differentiation consists in the nature of a contracted particular characteristic; therefore, it is also logical that it should contract by means of that [differentiation].
The universal would be destroyed; and how then can it be said that the universal has a nature that is eternal and all-pervading? This [is the point].
(Page 50)

He maintains that [the qualifier] functions as a qualifier because the qualificand-portion is indeed the primary element, and it is logical that the assistance provided by a qualifier applies precisely there; it does not apply to the subordinate qualifier-portion. Therefore, just as in the case of "The cloth is blue and soft," the quality of softness (*mārdava*) is a qualifier with respect to the quality of blueness, which is itself a qualifier.

It is ineffective; likewise, when the group of manifestations constitutes the universal nature as its qualifier, the qualification by space and time does not effect any contraction [of that nature]. "Therein" means in the state of being a qualifier.
"Of that" refers to the universal. To the question, "What follows from this?", he says: "And that... [referring to] what was stated previously, and therefore...

The meaning is "because of the reason. They are "made manifest" because they appear as a single, unified state (*ekalolībhāva*). As for manifestation, its primary life-force is what is called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness); when that [awareness] assumes the specific form of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and designates [objects], it shows that "the state of being that" is the true nature (*tattva*), by saying "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*)...

This conceptualization of the meaning of a sentence also has only a universal as its object, because it is impossible for it to accept the specific reality of place and time— such that whenever there is the appearance of a jar situated before one, thinking "this is a jar here now," it arises in this manner [only through a general form]. For this very reason, he says:

It may be so. For in that case, because of the assistance provided by other means of valid cognition—such as the perception of the speaker and the listener present at that time—the comprehension of the intended specific detail from that sentence might well be possible;
however, the conceptual construction of the sentence-meaning is incapable of grasping its specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) with necessity. Precisely for this reason...

In such passages as "They lead forward the water with the *camasa*," "He sprinkles the rice," and "He draws the *ṣoḍaśin* cup," even the present tense (*laṭ*) is not capable of conveying a specific appearance of the present; thus,
the meaning understood from the word, in the absence of assistance such as a pointing finger, [does not establish] the location...

It is perceived precisely as unconditioned by time; thus, this matter is established without effort. This will be explained further in the section on the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). By this much, it is shown that the very operation of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) revives the reality of universals, actions, and so forth. He concludes that what was introduced has now been explained, stating: "And thus..."

Thus [it is said]. "In this" means in that [object] where the nature of both the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) is fit for reflection. "Not then" means at the time of mental determination (*mānasāvasāya*). The word break (*cheda*) occurs right after "the universal" (*sāmānyam*). The reason for this is [stated on page 51]:

"Place and so forth" (deśādi) and so on; "the relation also [is] then" (sambandho 'pi tadā) and "the action also [is] then" (kriyāpi tadā)—this is the connection. Another text provides the reason (*hetu*). It has been stated that "the mind is reflective" (*mano 'nuvyavasāyi*) and "these are conceptual constructions" (*kalpanāḥ*). "Conceptual constructions take [them] as their objective support. (2.2.5) || 3 ||

Thus, by this much, it has been established that the so-called conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisattva*) of universals (*sāmānya*) and the like— which manifest in the conceptualizing consciousness within the conventional realm— is indeed a specific kind of existence,
and not a state of unreality like that of a double moon or similar illusions. In this regard, the sequence of the introduction is as follows:

All this— whether it be relation, generality, or the like— is the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which is characterized by the self-referential awareness of absolute freedom (*svātantryāmarśana*). Even therein, the very nature of relation, defined as the state of being both manifold and one, is the ultimate reality everywhere.

In that case, however, when there is a connection with another uncommon form, there is a different name. Regarding the relation which is of a unitary nature among a multitude of individual instances, there is the capacity for the designation "cows" (gāvaḥ); therein, the expression of a universal becomes unified and moves by virtue of its substratum within the flow of multiple moments.

Thus, by the force of such designations, there is the linguistic usage of "action"; when there is unity among threads, there is the linguistic usage of the "cloth" as a substance; and when there is unity among states such as childhood and so forth, there is the linguistic usage of the "substratum of the states.
The same applies elsewhere. However, in the absence of the knot-like binding of other designations, it is devoid of distinctions.

It is indeed the discourse on relation; for whatever appears as something in excess of the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha), all that is precisely relation. From that alone is established every object, consisting of the relation whose nature is both difference and non-difference.

"Worldly conduct... (Śloka 1). Thus it was stated in the *Sambandhasiddhi* that even by those who maintain the theory of distinct universals (*bhinnasāmānyavādin*), the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) is supported by the principle that "the relation [itself] is a relation," or by means of a relation.

Because [the object] is accepted as being favored [by consciousness]. And this relation consists of both unity and multiplicity, by virtue of the power of action whose nature is the sovereignty of the subject. Therefore, relation itself is the root for establishing the oneness of the subject.
(page 52) "Because of the statement: 'There must be vigilance regarding the relationship' (Vi.bhai.
106), the Sūtra is intended to investigate that very [relationship]."

Entities, which are established in their own selves and possess a distinct appearance, become the locus of the cognition of relation when they are joined with a unity consisting of mutual interpenetration within a single cognizer. (4)

Since the king and the man appear as external entities due to their state of isolation (*viviktatva*), when they reach completion within their own self (*svātman*), they attain unity within a single subject (*pramātṛ*) while remaining exactly as they were. And this is not merely a unity, for if their essential nature (*svarūpa*) were to dissolve, a relationship would be impossible; rather, it is a unity of mutual forms—

The characteristic of continuity (*anvaya*) consists of a swing-like mechanism (*dolāyantra*) of two poles—difference and non-difference—which sink and emerge simultaneously through their mutual cohesion. Furthermore, this does not exist merely with the subject (*pramātṛ*), but rather mutually, as in "the king's servant" or "the servant of him [the king]. Only upon entering into that state of being is there contact with consciousness (*saṃvit*).
These [two] are accepted as being merely instrumental, like fire in the fusion of gold and mercury, without destroying their own essential natures.
When those two entities are joined by such a unity, they become the locus—the objective domain—of the cognition of relation, such as "the king's man. In all cases, [this relation] resides in both.
