Although the relationship is indeed as described by the aforementioned method, nevertheless, the plural number is used in the sūtra to express the infinity of the individual instances of that relationship. Now, one might object: in the non-māyic state, non-duality is the single essence, whereas in the māyic state, duality is the single essence; yet the relationship has both duality and non-duality as its very life.

Anticipating the question of what state they might occupy, [the author] shows by means of the passage beginning with "agent and object" and ending with "intellect" that they exist precisely in the state of *māyā*, which includes within itself the state of purity (*śuddhadaśā*). At the occasion of the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), when the subject of *māyā* has emerged, worldly transactions (*lokavyavahāra*) take place.

They function [only] then, and not previously; for at that time, the transmigrating subject (*saṃsārī pramātā*) is unmanifest. Now, even then, the entire external organ (*bāhyendriya-karaṇa*)—just as an axe, despite its contact with the object to be cut, does not [necessarily] come into contact with the person who wields it—does not [automatically] come into contact with the subject or the object of cognition (*prameya*).

He restates and then refutes the objection: "If it is indeed abandoned [in one respect], then there is certainly difference with respect to the external and non-difference with respect to the internal; why, then, is worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which consists of a relationship characterized by both difference and non-difference, said to be unmanifest?"
"Of that same extent" means this: for it has already been established that even for the bound soul (*paśu*), there exists the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara;
and in that state, there is repose solely in non-duality (*abheda*) because the aspect of duality is concealed. Now, [one might object] regarding the subject (*pramātṛ*) of Māyā...

If manifestation is indeed nothing but a single essence (*ekarasa*), then once again, how can there be worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) consisting of both difference and non-difference? He resolves this as well with the word "primary" (*mukhya*). For the state of being composed of light (*prakāśamayatva*) never wavers from the reality; yet at that time, the light itself participates in the appearance of the contraction of the body and so forth.

"Even while not deviating from its own essential nature, the establishment of the non-inert subject must belong to it through that very self; how then could there be any constraint by means of the vital breath? (Śloka 21).
Therefore, even though duality persists within the realm of Māyā, non-duality does not waver due to the majesty of Light.

"Each one" means that this activity of the subject of māyā is indeed singular, by which those two entities—consisting of a relationship—are both created and manifested, and are also reflected upon. "Distinct" means different from the previous state of non-relationship; for this very reason, it is conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Because it is manifested by an activity belonging to the subject (*pramātṛ*) and because it is unique insofar as it is accessible to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),

there is no fault in the fact that the state of relation occurs through the diversity of relations of an entity according to the difference between subjects. For, in some cases, indeed, in the aspect of manifestation (*ābhāsa*):

It has been stated many times that the Supreme Lord sometimes unites the subjects [with objects] and at other times separates them. Now, if the very definition of a relation consists in being composed of both difference and non-difference,
then from what cause does the diversity of the related entities arise through the predominance or subordination [of one over the other], and from what cause [does this diversity arise]?

With the words "And that," he dispels the doubt that there might be a variety of relations through distinctions such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the collection of distinctions enumerated in the *Daṇḍaka* list;
for it has indeed been stated that the conjunction of appearances occurs precisely through their single flavor (*ekarasa*). [Objection: But surely, in the mental...

In order to dispel the doubt that "if conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is not external, its external form cannot possibly manifest," he reminds us of his own system with the words "even by the mind. The phrase "for this very reason" means that because it was stated [previously] that [the Lord] exists both externally and internally, for that reason this [conclusion] stands firm. Thus, the contradiction has been resolved.
He clarifies exactly what was stated [on page 54] with the words "by way of being external and internal.
Now, one might object: "In this way, while the contradiction has indeed been avoided by means of different objects—since that which is external is distinct—"

Regarding the phrase "internally differentiated": by this much alone, it is not established that "this is the form of one [single entity]," because there is a distinction between the two appearances based on their being external and internal. He resolves this as well with the words: "precisely by the power of reflective awareness" (vimarśabalāt). || 4 ||

Now, although [the appearances] consist of both unity and diversity due to the favor of their mutual relationship, he begins to describe another distinction, just as there is a distinct difference among the appearances of genus and so forth.

Conceptual constructions take as their objective support both the apparent unity of universals and substances even when they appear externally, as well as the difference between individuals and parts. (5)

Those conceptual constructions and discriminative cognitions which grasp and reflect upon universals— which are appearances that are [ultimately] non-existent in the ultimate sense— do not merely apprehend unity internally and diversity externally; rather, they also [apprehend] the persistence of a single universal (gotva) even with respect to external objects.

The purpose of employing a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is that it takes as its basis, reveals, and reflects the individual differences residing in the entities— which necessarily involve the apprehension of the individuals that serve as the substrata for the application of the plural number—
precisely through an outward orientation, as in the expression "these cows," despite the underlying non-difference.

For difference is perceived as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), while [the object] is perceived as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) by virtue of being colored [by it]. Thus, even externally, the conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) that manifest as substances take as their objective support both unity and the difference of parts— as in the case of "a jar" (*ghaṭa*), which appears as a single entity without gaps and as something extended.

The meaning of the *sūtra* is as follows: since there is a cognition of multiple parts, and because its essence consists of appearances (*ābhāsa*), there is no contradiction whatsoever—even when there is a distinction such as red and non-red—just as in the case of the perception of a variegated [color]. He introduces this with the word "connection" (*saṃbandha*). Now, one might object: "Granted that other appearances may not manifest in visual perception..."
But how do the appearances of space and time depart here [in this state] "now"? He says "thus" (*ittham*), meaning "when" (*yadā*);

that is, when there is manifestation in a general sense, without the determination of space and time—such as for a bound soul (*paśu*) at occasions such as the first awakening immediately following deep sleep, a swoon, or intoxication—at that time.
It is the manifestation of the mere object. For, having established the distinction of its own nature (*svarūpa*), no other distinction appears therein;
and the own nature is nothing but manifestation alone.
(Page 55)

"That" refers to the visual appearance of the measure of a cow; if the reading is "in the visual" (*cākṣuṣe*), it should be understood as "in common usage. The nominative reading, however, is clear. "That" refers to that which was stated as the definition of generality—the state of being similar among things. "Even then" means not in the appearance of a single [particular].
Nor does it mean that there is no appearance of multiplicity; rather, he considers that this "is accomplished" even according to the Kaṇāda school.
And thus, the reason is "inseparable" (*ayuta*) and so forth. For it is said by that venerable one:
"By which [power], the Self appears as if it were the very Self of another Self" (Vākyapadīya 3.3.9).

Thus. For this very reason, it was stated: "Such a nature of being both one and many does not appear in visual perception"—the meaning is that this follows from that detailed argument. It may be so; indeed, it is rendered probable by reasoning (*yukti*), because visual perception manifests a proximate object, and because universals (*sāmānya*), wholes (*avayavin*), and so forth, are common to all [perceptions].
Because that which is manifest by its very nature remains present even then; as the sage Kaṇavrata said:
"Universals are perceptible by the eye due to their inherence in corporeal substances" (VS 4.1.11).
[The phrase] "due to non-manifestation" refers primarily to the characteristic of form (*rūpa*) consisting of differentiation (*bheda*).
The meaning is "because of the cessation of cognition. Regarding the example "Caitra":

although even a jar or the like is indeed accepted as a whole (*avayavin*), as he will state later in the passage beginning with "from one sesame seed [to] another," nevertheless, there is no way for the reflective awareness of oneness—such as "I am this much, I go, or I stay"—[to apply to them].

This was stated in this manner to demonstrate that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the living body. For it might be possible to conceive that a jar, although being of the nature of a composite whole—like a house, a chariot, a village, or an army—could nevertheless perform a single purposeful action (ekārthakriyākārī). As for the states of childhood and so forth: [this is] not the case here.

What is intended here is the contemplation of the identity of the states, for that [identity] is not the cause of the cognition of a whole; rather, the purport lies in this much: "I am now so much [greater], and this [object] is today so much different from its former form, being entirely without connection."

Therefore, it has been stated that "the one is permeated by differentiated forms of the whole"; thus, the beauty of the form of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is such that its manifestation occurs within the conceptualizing intellect (*kalpanābuddhi*).
(Page 56)

It has been stated [previously]. Now, however, by examining the very nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*), he shows that it is likewise appropriate, adopting an alternative position with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*).
And the subject is one conditioned by *māyā*. Furthermore, all appearances of genus (*jāti*) and so forth depend upon the relation [of the subject] as their primary focus.
By means of the conjunction "and," he shows the third mode—that even by way of the pervader, it is precisely thus that the pervaded is logical—through the phrase "of the relations and so forth.

The phrase "also because of its connection with that" is used because they share a single flavor (*ekarasa*) as part of the same continuous section (*ekapraghaṭṭaka*). It is just like the case of the relation itself.

In this case, it is appropriate that [the object] is the domain of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, since the relation is pervasive (*vyāpaka*), it should also be understood that the very same nature follows for the pervaded (*vyāpya*). Now, one might object: "In that case, when using the singular number, only a single universal (*sāmānya*) is apprehended, and not the distinction of specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, [the application of the term] would not occur there."

The cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) takes the form "the state of being similar among equals. To this, it is replied: even in that case, since there is no contact with the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), what is the connection between [the word] "bring" and so forth? [Objection: But surely many particulars do not manifest to the cognizer or the speaker here; [rather,] these are cows...

Because, as in such cases, plurality is not perceived; this is what he means by saying "even though. Here the resolution is "nevertheless. By the words "even a shadow," it is meant that only the universal in its purity [is present]. What, then, flashes forth? He says: "of these"—that is, one particular individual among the individuals of the cow-class which resides in the heart.
Whether it be dark, with lowered horns, raised, or otherwise different,

in whatever way that very same [form] vibrates here, it does not appear to the user or another as "that very same thing vibrating," by virtue of such a restrictive rule; rather, it appears through the perspective of taking that [vibration] as primary, in the sense of "it is like that" or "it is also that."

If it is argued that "it is precisely that [universal] which is of the nature of non-existence," then by this form, that object appears as indeed indeterminate; and because of this indeterminacy, although it is distinct from particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it nevertheless accepts those particular characteristics as non-different from itself. He states another argument for its indeterminacy with the words "and therefore" (*ataśca*). If...
This word *nāmapada* is unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*), or it is [the word] *tama*; alternatively, the reading is *ekatama*.
Now, the suffix *ḍatamaj* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 5.3.94: *ekācca prācām*.
(Page 57)

Then, by virtue of its inclusion in the list beginning with *itará*, the substitution of *aḍḍ* occurs, resulting in *ekatamadam*. Here, both the "speaker" (*prayoktṛ*) and the "comprehender" (*pratipattṛ*) are intended. The state of being a performer of what is understood resides in the speaker;
the state of being a communicator of what is understood resides in the comprehender; and the state of being a bringer of what is understood [resides in the one who fetches]. This is what is meant:
When the speaker employs a word while having the cow with a black shadow present before him in his mind, the listener likewise takes as the primary object the cow with a white shadow;
yet, if the speaker brings even a tawny-colored cow, both of them will surely consider themselves successful. Therefore, if...

There would be no lack of restriction; how, then, could it be established in this way? And because there is no lack of restriction, the comprehension of all particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is accomplished without effort. "Where" refers to the appearance of a chariot.
"Immediately thereafter" refers to the logical principle of the relationship between a king and his servant, and so forth. "By means of conjunction" (*saṃyogena*).

The meaning is: by means of two conjunctions, or by means of many conjunctions, appearing as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). "An effect-substance" (*kāryadravya*) refers to that whose unity is not merely internal, but has a second [unity] which is external. He clarifies this very point with the words "of which. This is its distinction—
"But [the word] 'nyam' indicates [connection] in the case of a chariot and so forth; for it says, 'in chariots and the like. Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) also [is internal].
For such is the perception there: 'Ah, this is well-knit, this is well-joined, this is well-fitted—wood, metal, clay, and so on—with the hide,' but not [this perception] regarding a jar."
"The appearance [is such that] these potsherds appear as if joined together. [Objection:
But surely, even in the manifestation of a jar, Caitra, or the like, it is only the potsherds, hands, and so forth that appear;
and this [appearance] manifests as an extension (*vaitatya*) which performs the function of grasping objects divided by different spatial directions. To this, he replies:
"Caitra," and so forth. We do not deny the manifestation of the parts;

rather, we say that the manifestation of the whole—which is a single, compact, and seamless unity—occurs precisely by way of implying the manifestation of its parts. [Objection: But those very parts...

Having raised the objection that [the atoms] might appear as a unity—like a chariot and so forth—due to the distinction of their limiting conditions (*upādhi*) in performing a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākaraṇa*), [the author] shows that a single appearance (*ekapratibhāsa*) here cannot be denied by stating "And if... and "absolutely...". By this [phrase], [he indicates] that they are of a similar kind to what is observed.

There too, he eliminates the possibility of the statement "it is an appearance of identity" by saying "only a single part. For a Southerner does not remember only the neck of a camel; "that" refers to that single part.

"Pratheta" means "in perception. Regarding "pratyuta": that manifestation of extension (*vaitatya*) which has been made the reason by the opponent for the claim that "only the parts are manifested here," by that very [reason], the manifestation of the whole (*avayavin*) is also implied; for that which appears as extended appears as a unity. However, this is where [the case] involves many [parts].
The perception of extension in jars is merely an error, since it is through the imposition of unity that extension appears therein.

Thus, this is a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*). The phrase "even in the externalist doctrine" means "in the pure Vaiśeṣika system," let alone in our own system. Upon hearing the word "externalist doctrine" here—
By the passage beginning with "atha" and ending with "syāt," [the opponent] is suspected of being a *pūrvapakṣin* (an objector) while asserting his own position.

By the passage beginning with "asambhavam," the response is given: "And there is no limit to the conclusion. Furthermore, the phrase "tadāpi vā" refers to the expression "atyantādṛṣṭapūrvam" (never before seen).
The resolution: A camel, which is essentially a collection of atoms, may indeed produce pleasure characterized by wonder for a Southerner, or pain characterized by fear for a child;
it is solely through the power of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of such causal efficacy that its "oneness" is merely conditional.

He concludes his own position with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*). Now, one might object: "The density and grossness that appear do not exist in atoms at all; from where, then, could they appear? To this he replies: "of the many" (*anekasya*). For when five fingers are perceived simultaneously—

It appears as a gross form distinct from the appearance of a single [atom], or rather, there is no appearance of the intervening space because it does not exist; or else, even if it were present—as in the case of white and other colors within a blue form—it is not perceived by that sense organ, just like taste and so forth. This is precisely because the intervening space does not appear.
The appearance "this is a single solid mass" is like the appearance "the forest is a single solid mass" from a distance;
such is the appearance when multiple [objects] are perceived simultaneously and their intervening spaces are not perceived.
It is established by virtue of appropriateness that [the object] is gross and a single solid mass, but not otherwise.
Therefore, when there is an appearance, this property appears as belonging either to the external [object] or to the appearance itself.
In the doctrine of the cognition of forms (*sākārasaṃvedanavāda*), this property belongs to that which is characterized by the form of cognition, not to the external object;

therefore, it is not correct to say that "this appearance is the manifestation of a whole" (*avayavin*). Thus, the means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa*) that has been presented by the opponent for the sake of establishing the whole is [invalidated].
This [objection] is refuted by the sūtra: "There would be no perception of anything at all, because the whole (avayavin) is not established" (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.34).
Furthermore, it is refuted by the sūtra:
"And because holding and pulling are possible" (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.35).

Thus, he refutes the inference that was stated by demonstrating that its reason (*hetu*) is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*), beginning with the words "an accumulation of atoms" (*paramāṇusañcaya*). [He says] "due to the diversity of intrinsic natures" (*svabhāvavaicitryāt*): because those atoms which constitute jars and other such things arise through the power of their own causes, being invariably concomitant with their respective existence.
And those who are the enjoyers of jars and other such things—their karmas constitute the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) therein.

The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). This [explanation] is also intended by the proponent of the whole (*avayavin*) to preserve the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) of conjunctions, [referring to] the possible arising of wind-conjunctions and so forth.

The cause for the non-arising of the action that initiates the parts is necessarily present. Having thus refuted the proving evidence (*prasādhaka-pramāṇa*), he demonstrates the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) regarding the whole (*avayavin*) with the words "one," and so forth. This is a subverting argument based on its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). It is also [a subversion] by way of the properties of supporting, qualities, prior commencement, and so on.

He says of that: "the dyad and so forth. Likewise, when the colors residing in the threads and the color residing in the cloth are perceived by another, they would further produce an excess of weight due to their possession of color; thus, from the weighing of each respective part, there would be an increasingly greater weight in the cloth on the scale.
"Namanaṃ bhavet" (there would be bowing). Here, the refutation of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated.
In that regard, first of all, he renders all of this untenable in brief with the passage beginning with "syāt" and ending with "arthāḥ".
"Eṣa doṣaḥ" (this fault) consists in the absence of proof and the presence of sublation (*bādhaka*). Now, this very [point]...
He clarifies this with the words "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*), meaning: while this summary remains established;
and regarding what was stated by the opponent—that it is merely an aggregate (*samūha*) of atoms that appears in this way—concerning that appearance of the aggregate:

(60) That which is well-known as the appearance of division— namely, that which is called "conjunction" arising from the non-perception of the interval— is pervasive because it emerges from a single essence through differentiation, being produced solely by its concomitants such as pervasiveness.

He demonstrates this with the word "aggregate" (*rāśi*). He connects its non-perception to the present context with the passage beginning, "This appearance as Caitra," and so forth. Now, if there is only one [entity], how then was it stated that "the whole (*avayavin*) has a nature that is both one and many"? To this he says: "Furthermore, because no division is perceived," and so on.

To this, the reply is "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). That is to say: because the manifestation of Caitra—which takes the form of the manifestation of extension (*vaitatya*)—transcends that manifestation of multiplicity which belongs to the hands and other limbs as distinct entities; therefore, there is both unity and multiplicity. For this very reason, it has been said:

Extension appearing as such shines forth only when there is an underlying reality of unity, as in the cognition, "This one cloth is extended. In cases such as "the forest is extensive," however, this appearance arises from the very unity residing in the spherical earth which serves as the substratum. He clarifies this very point with the words, "For in the case of Caitra... and so on.

"Of that very [whole]" means belonging to the whole (*avayavin*). It is precisely because they appear as pervading a single whole that those [parts] appear as parts; otherwise, being entirely independent like a multitude of iron balls, for what could they appear as parts? He summarizes this with the words "for this very reason."

By the words "divided" and so forth, [it is shown that] it is internal and not external. Thus, having purified perception itself as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the whole (*avayavin*), he refutes the sublation pertaining to its own nature without placing any reliance on inference; this is why he says "for this very reason. Likewise, it is not red.

Or rather, it is not at all [composed of] red; rather, the color of that whole (*avayavin*) is variegated (*citra*) itself. Furthermore, [the author] will refute [the opponent's view] by stating that "it is equal," meaning that objects such as pots and cloths—existing like those in a dream, an illusion, or a mental construction—arise entirely without regard for the sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). This will be explained under the section on "without material cause" (*nirupādāna*).

Nor can one describe the creation of entities as being based merely upon the assumption of one's own desire; for, by the power of necessity (*niyati*), even though they appear in such a sequence, let gravity—which causes the falling of the composite whole—be eternally present in the atoms themselves, but let it not be produced in the composite whole. Or rather, even if gravity exists [in the whole],...

Thus, it is not produced in such a way that it would cause an excess of falling; for the intrinsic natures of phenomena are diverse. Salt situated in a solid state [becomes fluid] when joined with water.
(Page 61)

It causes a specific bending of the scale, yet it does not cause that very same [scale] to bend quickly even when present, because of the perception of an excellence in taste. Furthermore, even a thousand flies or a swarm of bees do not cause the scale to bend further when in a vessel filled with honey. For this very reason...

Since there are multiple components, there is plurality here. The meaning is that what was introduced as "having a single or multiple substrata" has already been determined in this sūtra. "Expounded" means in the commentary (vṛtti). || 5 ||
In this aphorism, both difference and non-difference are examined even within the relationship between action and its factors;
and as a consequence thereof, the nature of space and so forth, the scope of the investigation into action, and the coordination of the factors of action are addressed.
The cognition of direction and so forth has as its objective support the relation between the delimited and the delimiting.
In this context, the meaning of "object" (*viṣaya*) is the state of being a cause characterized by non-separability (*ananyatrabhāva*). This is also the case in the *Vṛtti* text.
"Factor" (*kāraka*) refers both to substance (*dravya*) and to power (*śakti*). Thus, the construction is as follows:
the integration (*samanvaya*) of substances which are the substrata of powers is the action that occupies the place of the glue (*jatū*) that binds them together.

Just as the relationship between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is caused by the act of knowing (*pramā*), and the act of knowing consists in its resting within the knower (*pramātṛ*), so too, that very convergence (*samanvaya*) is the movement toward non-difference within the agent, whose nature is consciousness, even though the causal factors (*kāraka*) are distinct. This applies likewise to [the factors] such as the wood and the cooking pot.

It should be stated regarding the agent (*paktṛ*). In this way, even the coordination of the powers of the factors of action (*kāraka-śakti*) culminates only in their resting within the agent, because they emerge through the medium of action and because action itself rests within the agent.
Thus, there is a distinction between action with respect to its own specific characteristic and with respect to the primary factors of action, and that which...

Non-difference [is established] through the resting in a single agent and through the unity of the fruit; that alone is the life-force of all relations. Even that cognition of space and time—such as "this is beyond that" or "this is below that"—is a reflection upon difference preceded by an internal differentiation, wherein the limit (*avadhi*) and the limited (*avadhimat*) exist as indeed distinct.
By uniting [the levels] through the culmination of the differentiation of the middle state, she is primarily characterized by the nature of relation (*sambandha*).
Furthermore, it is precisely that activity of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) belonging to consciousness which unfolds there;
thus, all this belongs to the Blessed One’s power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
(page 62) "Sphāra" means "the intended meaning"; this is the sense of the sūtra. [The rule] *grahaṇaka-sūtra* concerns the connection with action—(2|2|1).

And so forth. In this regard, demonstrating the difference and non-difference of action itself by way of the factors of action (*kāraka*), he first states its difference with the words "of the factors of action," and so on. And because action appears through the penetration of the coloring of those [factors], it possesses a nature of difference. Thus he says in the *Kārakavārtika*:

"The nature of *paci* (the verbal root) appears as divided due to the difference in its factors (*kāraka*), because of the cognition thereof"—this refers to the cognition of the action (*kriyā*). Now, he states that it is also non-different by means of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and [it is] 'pacati'";
with this "and," he conjoins non-difference together with difference. This is in reference to the term "pacati" there.

The cognition of action has a non-differentiated object; for that action—which consists of the independence of cooking—is made an object by that cognition through its being pervaded by that single agent. And the ultimate reality of that agent is his state of being a single essence. This is what is meant: [by means of] the wood...

The meaning conveyed by the sentence "Caitra cooks rice in a pot" is, in reality, that action (*kriyā*); for this very reason, the venerable [teacher] states that the verb (*ākhyāta-śabda*) is the sentence. And therein, there is that which resides in the fuel, such as burning; that which resides in the pot, such as heating; and that which resides in the rice, such as bursting open.
Even when there is a manifestation through differentiation— such as the reflective awareness "this is the form of the cooked"—
it ultimately results in non-difference alone, because it rests within the freedom of Caitra’s consciousness.
He concludes this object of knowledge with the words "even the cognition of action," meaning that it is not only the cognition of relation that is manifold.

The word "api" [in the phrase] "viṣayā api" [is used for emphasis]. Now, it might be objected: "But was this not already stated previously: 'And this sequential nature belongs to worldly action' (2.1.2)"? True; however, this is a different way of defining the distinction. Thus he says: "not only."

"And because of the identity of the agent"— this means not only because of the identity of the fruit. Having thus established that action is both single and manifold, he explains with full intent the meaning of the relevant portion of the *Vṛtti* text ending with the word "cognition" (*mati*), as well as the half-verse commented upon therein, by means of the words "therein" (*tatra*) in the *Vṛtti*.
And in the half-verse: "That cognition of being a factor (*kāraka*),
which occurs even with respect to distinct substantial factors (*kārakadravya*), though having a single object, is manifold..."

It has been stated here that "the intellect [is the agent] in the state of being an object. Since the cognition of the relation between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka*) and the cognition of the residual relation (*śeṣa-sambandha*) are equal in terms of having one or multiple objects, he states the distinction by saying "of the king," which means "of the cognition. Now, even in the case of a residual relation—

Anticipating the objection that action is preceded by its factors (kārakas), he says: "Or even here," meaning that these are not to be grasped as separate from it. This is because direction, space, and time, when reflected upon, take refuge in a single internal unity, according to the previously explained perception of relationship.

They are made objects of cognition. For they are established as prior and posterior in relation to a second correlate. He demonstrates this very point by means of an example with the words "this," "that," and so forth;
the apprehension of the middle, the distant, and the near occurs in this sequence. The same applies to time, and so on.

An illustration of time (*kāla*): the word "now" (*adhunā*) refers to a distinct point in time; "this" (*ayam*), however, refers to the present which shares a single nature with the action of remaining within an existing state;
and "that" (*saḥ*) refers to the past and the future. In both cases, the term "being examined" (*vimṛśyamānaḥ*) is a present participle derived from the root *mṛś* with the suffix *śānac*.

It is to be connected [to the previous context]. Thus, since space and time are investigated, these directions and so forth, being investigated in their entirety as having the nature of prior and posterior, are established;
consequently, they take as their basis an internal non-difference, even though their external objects are distinct—this is the logical connection. "Even though not explicitly stated" means...

In the Sūtra: [The author] raises the objection, "But if it is thus the case that the state of consisting of both difference and non-difference is the same everywhere, then what is the distinction between [the systems of] the Sāṅkhyas and others? To pacify this doubt, he states: "It is not the case that the manifestation of appearances everywhere reaches rest in the subject solely through a single flavor; rather, it is for the subject..."
He demonstrates this by saying "he enumerates," [meaning] with infinite variety through his own sovereignty.
When an object being enumerated is perceived as a number through mutual exclusion, it is not merely in the form of a negation like "blue" versus "non-blue," but rather—
It is by way of mutual dependence, and not by that alone as in the case of the cognition of reciprocal conjunction; rather, it is by way of their being mutually exclusive.
(Page 64)

This is what is meant: here, when it is necessary to quell the suspicion of another appearance regarding an appearing entity, then that entity, being delimited by the other appearance which is being excluded, is called "one. Precisely for that reason, even by means of the mere grammatical refinement of the singular number (*ekavacana*), [it is established as one].

When two things that can be accomplished by a single word are expressed together, a distinction is perceived—such as "Śiva alone is our refuge. Thus, by means of the exclusion of other objects, this specific object is established here as the task at hand; this is the number "two. It is for this very reason that it is said, "there are only two persons."

The application [of this principle] is as follows: for in that case, there is the realization that no other [entity] can gain entry. However, since two cakes have been mentioned, the non-entry of another is not at all a rejection of those two; for without them, another cannot be employed in that action. Thus the cognizer combines these appearances. In this way, three...

In such cases, up to the end of the highest number (*parārdha*), one should understand that its application through mutual delimitation (*parasparāvaccheda*) has many branches; and therein occurs a convergence of thousands of purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*), such as wonder, non-wonder, joy, and despondency. For this very reason, it is said to be "correct" (*samyak*).

If the description of an entity is intended to be primary, then there necessarily follows a delimitation of its own nature by means of another appearance, whether that appearance is dependent or independent [of it]. Therefore,
it is said:

"No entity existing as a sentient being is ever expressed without number. In that case, however, the appearance of number belonging to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) assumes a subordinate status (*upasarjana*). For this is the inherent nature of the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*): that [it qualifies] the meaning of the nominal stem.
There is a state of subordination. Consequently, through words such as "one" and so forth, the appearance of mutual exclusion is primarily apprehended.
And by that [apprehension], the very nature of the object consists of number and its various divisions. For it is said that number consists of the calculation of distinctions.
"Dimension also" refers to minute, large, short, and long;
that is, regarding the dimension well-known to the followers of Kaṇāda, it consists of short and long.
This much,
for now, shall be the measure of its length.

Thus, it possesses the defining characteristic of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And since a means of valid cognition is necessarily dependent upon another delimited object, that which is the appearance of equality [produced] by means of that which is well-known as a "hand" consisting of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), is not merely an external conjunction; that is what it is. For this very reason, he says:

Magnitude (*parimāṇa*) also, like intermediate dimension (*antaraikya*), is understood through the hand in relation to the cloth being measured; thus, the mention of the staff (*yaṣṭi*) is for the purpose of establishing the distinction between short and long. As for what is called "atomic" (*aṇu*) or "large" (*mahat*), therein—

If atomicity (*aṇutva*) were merely the state of being partless, then it would belong to qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth, which are themselves partless. Alternatively, if atomicity were the state of being a substance (*dravyatva*) that is partless, then it would also apply to space (*ākāśa*).
Therefore, [atomicity] is established by way of extreme subtlety, as distinguished from mustard seeds, granaries, small boxes, and chests.

That which is the very state of being most minimal, such that it is capable of being delimited on all sides, is precisely atomicity (*aṇutva*); anything other than that is magnitude (*mahattva*). This, then, is dimension (*parimāṇa*) in its entirety.

This is what is grasped by this [definition]. Thus he says: "A *prastha* or a *kuḍava*" refers not merely to conjunction, but to that measurement which consists in the appearance of equalization everywhere, achieved in dependence on the object to be measured—such as sesame seeds—and which is essentially like a wooden box or container.

That too occurs only within the state of internal unity. As for that which is defined as "measurement" (*unmāna*)—namely, measurement by height—that has been described by the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) as being merely heaviness (*gurutva*) which causes the action of falling; however, it is not so, because there is no conventional usage of the term "measurement" with respect to heaviness alone. Rather, it is that which is well-known [as measurement].

The Grammarians maintain that the weight of the *prativartaka* (the counterweight) and so forth, and the balancing thereof, is what constitutes *unmāna* (measurement by weight). Thus, the status of being a "measure" (*mānatā*) is common to all three [types of measurement]; the distinction lies in the fact that here it is a measure (*māna*) by virtue of its being preeminent (*prakṛṣṭa*), pervasive (*paritaḥ*), or vertical (*ūrdhvatayā*). And this very point...

He says it is appropriate that "a *māṣaka* is a *raktikā*. Measurement (*parimāṇa*) is characterized by the appearance of equalizing weight through a counterweight (*prativartaka*) in relation to the object to be measured, such as gold; thus, in worldly transactions like buying and selling, it functions as a factor of unity within the division [of the scale].

Since measurement is employed solely through the two types of excellence (*apakarṣa*), two examples for each have been written with this intention. Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) as well is preceded by the apprehension of difference; it is an appearance of difference that is internally suspected to be non-different in its midst.

That very [quality] is delimited by number, beginning with the singularity of separateness (*eka-pṛthaktva*) and ending with the highest number of separateness (*parārdha-pṛthaktva*). Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also the appearance of connection between two things whose nature was previously unconnected; likewise, disjunction (*vibhāga*) is preceded by the appearance of connection.

The appearance "it is not" (*na iti*), from which distinctness (*viviktatā*) shines forth, is itself explained by the explanation of space and time as "remoteness" (*paratva*) and "proximity" (*aparatva*). Whatever else is included here that appears in dependence upon another— such as mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*)— is likewise [to be understood].

The properties of the objects of dyadic relations (*dvandva*), as well as conjunction (*samuccaya*), the "et cetera" (*ādi*) construction, and the "remainder" (*avaśeṣa*) construction— all of these he demonstrates with the words beginning "the *dhava* tree," etc., to be merely an expansion of relation (*sambandha*). Furthermore, even that which begins with the specific types of option (*vikalpa*) and inclusion (*anvācaya*)— [is likewise such].

Even that which consists of the meaning of particles such as *ca* and so forth, and even that which is purely of the nature of concomitance (*samanvaya*)— namely, the creation of bound souls (*pāśava-sṛṣṭi*)— all of this, with the intention that it arises from the rule of commonality (*sādhāraṇībhāva*), was not counted by the followers of Kaṇāda as a separate category of reality (*padārtha*) such as mutual conjunction (*itaretara-yoga*).

The Teacher, however, considers that even though [the self] is as uncommon as pleasure and so forth, its inclusion in the enumeration is indeed appropriate; for this very reason, it has not been excluded from such enumerations by the Grammarians who maintain that *dharma* is a distinct category (*padārtha*). He demonstrates this with the passage beginning "What is the use of... and so on. It is "for this very reason" because...

The linguistic and practical transactions (*vyavahāra*) are based precisely on that appearance of non-difference even among things that are distinct; for this reason, "therein" (*tatra*), the *samavāya* (inherence) favored by the Kaṇāda school is accepted. For that [inherence], while existing among things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), renders them—though they are devoid of the capacity for separate existence—as manifold in form.

It causes [the objects] to have the nature of appearing as non-different. Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be a state of resting in non-difference in the case of a relation characterized by inherence (*samavāya*), but in the case of a relation between two separately established things, such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), that is not the case. To this, he replies: "The 'staff-bearer' (*daṇḍin*). For conjunction indeed [occurs] through the inherence of the staff and the person.
Existing through conjunction, it culminates by manifesting those two as non-different. Now, one might object:

"If this is exactly what is desired by the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas), then that alone is logical; what is the use of this partiality for another philosophical system? It is said in reply: "But for them... For substance and the other categories...

If categories are held to be distinct based on their appearance, then, because inherence is a single entity, there would be a confusion of all categories— characterized by substance— due to the relation of substance with its generic property of "substanceness" (dravyatva). This is the inherence [that causes such confusion].

(Page 67) Even the term "particular" (*viśeṣaka*) is a mere word. For instance, it might be merely an adventitious characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), like a crow on a house, or like the blueness of a lotus, or like the redness of a crystal. In the first case, nothing [is established].

The distinction of the qualified object arises from the distinction of its qualifiers. For a house, whether characterized by the three qualifiers—crow, sparrow, and hawk—either successively or simultaneously, remains that very same house. In the second case, even the relationship of qualifier and qualified exists through inherence (*samavāya*) alone, whether [the property] is of the nature of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) or of the nature of a quality (*dharma*).
In the case of "the manifested," there is likewise no difference [from the other two]. In the third [category], the visible portion is inherence (*samavāya*),

which, variegated by the coloring of all forms, would cause whatever it favors to appear as permeated by the variegation of universal identity (*sārvātmya-śavalatā*), even when the instances of inherence are distinct.
If [inherence] were to be admitted even in those cases, then inherence itself would be a universal (*sāmānya*), and there would be another inherence in that as well,

leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, if inherence were to manifest as non-different from entities whose distinctions are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then because it would be manifested as being constantly present, it could not be sublated.

Apart from this, what other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists by which the distinctions between substances, qualities, and so forth could be established? If it is argued that inference (*anumāna*) exists [as such a means], then that is not an inference at all, because it is sublated by uncontradicted perception (*abādhita-pratyakṣa*). Alternatively, if there is an appearance as non-distinct...

In that case, inherence (*samavāya*) would be the cause of error; and consequently, how could there be a necessary variety in cognition? As for the claim that things appear as if identical due to inherence, even there the meaning of "as if" must be either similarity (*sādṛśya*) or poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). And as for this similarity—

Whether it be imagined (*kalpita*) or unimagined (*akalpita*): in the case of imagination, its essence consists merely of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and this same rule applies to poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*); so enough with deliberating upon the object itself. As for the unimagined, with what could there be a commonality (*sādharmya*)? Between "jar-ness" and a jar? Between "jar-ness" and redness? Or between a jar and the act of lifting?

Because of the absence of commonality (*sādharmya*). Now, if it is argued that this inherence (*samavāya*) itself acts in such a way and is thus beyond questioning, then this indeterminable form of ignorance (*avidyā*), postulated by other scriptural traditions, would simply be designated by the term "inherence. Or, if [it is argued] that such a nature belongs to inherence itself...
If it is independence, then it must be the Supreme Lord himself, or his power, that is denoted by this name;
thus, our own philosophical system alone must be accepted as the refuge—enough with these intermediate arguments.
(page 68)
In short, this is what is stated by the phrase: "by means of the refutations consisting in the occurrence of contradictions such as difference and non-difference. (6)

In this context, the claim that "existence" (*sattva*) consists in a relation to existence is undermined by the fallacies of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and pointlessness (*vyarthatva*).
Furthermore, the definition as "causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*) is misplaced (*vyadhikaraṇa*); its capacity to perform such action is not eternal.

Nor is it tenable to argue that its nature is eternal by virtue of producing cognition, for [the object] is not present at the time its own cognition is produced, just as a seed is not present at the time the sprout is produced.

Since causality cannot be determined due to the absence of the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding what is intended [as a cause], the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is difficult to ascertain for both the real and the unreal. Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if one were to rely on another causal efficiency [to establish the first]. And if all of this were not manifest (*aprakāśe*), it would be equivalent to the horn of a hare; thus, manifestation—*prakāśa*.

Existence (*sattva*) is precisely that reflective awareness which has not yet been uprooted; and since that [awareness] remains free from any distress regarding relation and the like, even though this is established, if someone—due to a misconception—should say: "The world desires purposeful action (*arthakriyā*);
does such action exist for relation and the like? then for him...
The Sūtra consoles the heart: "In this very way, the accomplishment of the goal shall come to the mother who seeks purposeful action;
therefore, there is no such error regarding the object that possesses both difference and non-difference. (7)

If you accept this as true, then no purposeful activity whatsoever exists on the plane of worldly convention without a relationship consisting of both difference and non-difference. Even in cases where that [relationship] is not perceived, it necessarily remains manifesting within. For instance, when one seeks pleasure and so forth...

One might thus seek it if one knew it; and one would know it if it were indeed that very thing; yet even so, it would remain unattainable because of its [inherent] perfection. Therefore, this unavoidable conclusion follows: that there exists a state of both difference and non-difference between that which possesses such a nature and that which does not.

Regarding the phrase "in the form of a relation, generality, and so forth": if this [form] is unreal, what then is called real? Therefore, he who engages in the conventional usage of error here is himself the one who is truly deluded.
Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is that the permanence and utility established by the introductory sūtra are indeed logical.
He introduces this [point] with the words "of appearances alone," meaning that manifestation itself is existence.
"External organ" refers to the external sense faculty. And "that too" means: let one thing be desired [as such].
(Page 69)

He speaks by way of its being the form of that which is being remembered; however, it is connected with the phrase "but another thing. "Illusory" (māyīya) means that here, difference alone is the ultimate reality—this is the sense. "Or rather" (sa vā): in this interpretation, the performance of the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of an entity while accepting its nature as both one and many is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Thus has "utility" (upayoga) been described as being of such a nature, while "stability" (sthairya), however, is "corroboration" (saṃvāda). In the subsequent explanation, however, the distinction is that stability is the absence of sublation (bādhakābhāva), whereas utility is corroboration (saṃvāda). May there be auspiciousness! || 7 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, the Examination of Difference and Non-difference, in the *Kriyādhikāra* of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*, composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara, the venerable Ācārya Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the third reflection:
[The first state is] a single bliss, filled with the three powers, beginning from the form of the Absolute (anuttara).
I salute Śiva, whose mouth is nectar and who is the authoritative standard for this world.

In order to declare that "this is the manifestation of the power of action" (*kriyā-śakti-vijṛmbhā*), the nature of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth was established as a preliminary to the discussion of relation (*sambandha*); now, however, the very nature of relation itself is established in detail. In that regard, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), relation is indeed of two kinds.

The relationship between the known and the knower (jñāpya-jñāpaka-bhāva) resides in both the insentient and the sentient, while the relationship between cause and effect (kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva) resides only in the insentient. Of these, the former—consisting of the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge—is that upon which what has been stated and what is yet to be stated depends for its establishment; for the establishment of entities is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
This is well known. Therefore, for the purpose of supporting the subject matter already stated and yet to be stated,

and by way of establishing the nature of their relationship, another investigation is undertaken through seventeen aphorisms to define the conventional usage of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), which must necessarily be determined.
By such statements as "this is such-and-such," and so forth, the conventional usage of [terms like] "Īśa" and others is set in motion.
With these two verses ending thus, the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) are defined here;

thereafter, for the purpose of defining the reality of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the function of the means of knowledge operates with respect to each individual manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*), and not necessarily restricted solely to a single entity consisting of a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)— this is the intended meaning.

The establishment of appearances through the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is explained by ten [verses]; following that, the nature of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is treated in one [verse]; and the nature of the object of cognition (*prameya*), which is the very subject at hand, is shown to be consistent with the doctrine of the Lord (*īśvara*) in one [verse];

furthermore, the distinction between the means of knowledge, the object, and the result is only possible when the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) exists in the manner described above, and for that very reason, it does not [arise otherwise].

The meaning of this section is as follows: by means of these three [arguments], its status as an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is established such that it may serve as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) even regarding the Blessed Lord in a direct sense; for here, the proof is merely for the sake of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). However, the specific meaning of each sūtra will be examined individually. As it has been said:

In order to determine that cognitions such as those of action and so forth are not erroneous, the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is indeed well-established.
This is restated in two verses:

"That by virtue of which a thing is established as being 'thus' or 'of such a kind' is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and that [means] is itself a novel arising of its own manifestation. (1)

Thus, that cognition whose essence is internal reflective awareness is an uncontradicted valid knowledge regarding an object that is the referent of a single designation, [even though] it is undivided by space, time, and so forth. (2)
The entity (*vastu*)— whether external, such as blue and so forth, or internal, such as pleasure and so forth— is that by virtue of which,
through whose capacity, it remains fixed, not overstepping its distinct and determined boundary (*maryādā*),
both in terms of its own nature as "this," and in terms of its association with other qualifying attributes such as permanence and so forth as "of such a kind."

That it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is well-established in the world. However, as long as an investigator reflects upon what that [means of valid cognition] might be, the following consequence arises: here, an object does not establish itself by its own power alone; for if it did, there would be no such distinction as "blue appears to me" or "it appears to Caitra. Therefore, this [establishment] occurs through the power of something else.
It remains established [as such]. And if the other were insentient (*jaḍa*), that would be like a blind man showing the way to another blind man;

therefore, this other one must be of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*). Even if that [consciousness] were devoid of distinctions, how could it establish blue, yellow, and so forth in their distinct divisions? Therefore, it is colored by the blue and directed toward the blue.
The manifestation "blue-manifestation" is the establisher of the blue;
for there is no other establisher of its nature as a blue-manifestation. And if this manifestation were non-different from the blue, then why would it not also be the case for yellow and so forth?

Because there is no distinction in the identity with the reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) for everything, that manifestation (*ābhāsa*)— the light— is [identical to] the blue which is not separate from it. And thus, its separateness exists if,
even while non-separateness from the Great Light remains as the ultimate reality, separateness nevertheless appears.

And from this, the following arises: that very contraction of the Light (prakāśa) caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as emptiness is itself the manifestation of the subject, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, through the single power of emanation (sṛṣṭi-śakti).
As it has been said by the Siddhapādas:
"A single unified light arises, born from the means of knowledge, the object, and the knower" (p.
By this, [it is meant that] for one who possesses the contraction caused by limiting adjuncts such as the body, there exists an infinite internal awareness...
For as long as that manifestation— which, in an instant, has been as it were separated from the illusory subject (māyā-pramātṛ) and is oriented toward the external object of knowledge (prameya)—

persists, so long does it arise ever-newly in each moment with a different form, colored by the space and time inherent in the object of knowledge; yet it remains within that very one thing which is denoted by its own name.

Since that very manifestation— which appears as being related to the subject of Māyā, who pervades infinite time— in the form "this appearance of blue and so forth belongs to me," or "this appearance of yellow and so forth belongs to him," is itself the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because that manifestation possesses an operative function (*savyāpāra*) in the production of valid cognition (*pramā*). What indeed...

If it is asked, "What is valid cognition (*pramā*)?", he says: that very self of consciousness (*bodhātman*), which is the manifestation, is the "measure" (*miti*); this is the connection [with the statement] that it is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Nor are these terms synonyms, because it is a means of knowledge insofar as it has the nature of light (*prakāśa*) directed toward the external, whereas it is merely [the fruit] in its inward-turned nature as reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

The fruit [of cognition] belongs to that whose nature is sound (śabda), which has been contracted by the coloring of the object. For, just as heroism and victory—which reside in a single locus—are determined by the discerning person to be cause and effect, so too are the manifestation of blue and its reflective awareness (vimarśa). Precisely for this reason, it has been said:
"Because it is established by virtue of that [the agent]," as stated in Pāṇini-vārttika 3.3.18.

For the fruit of the instrument is indeed of the nature of an operation (*vyāpāra*), since it is the first thing to be accomplished. And this operation is not essentially different from the agent who is performing the action or the instrument which is being employed.

Thus, since it is properly joined [with the means], the non-difference of the instrument (*pramāṇa*) and the result (*phala*) is logically primary; however, let there be a distinction by way of the result—which is synonymous with the purpose (*prayojana*)—consisting of activity, attainment, and so forth. Therefore, reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is the result; by its power, cognition (*bodha*) is the instrument.

And reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) depends upon the word as its very life, [the word] which comes to rest in the manifestation of a universal form that is not embraced by specific manifestations of space and time. For even that which is "this"— being present and right before one— [is so only through such a word].

He states just this much: what need is there for more? Even in the case of [the cognition], "This Caitra stands here now"—as long as it remains within the range of words, this very same path applies. However, the state of being grounded in a particular [object] arises through the power of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇya*) of the object, which consists of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) residing in the speaker; thus, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) pertains only to the manifestation (*ābhāsa*).

The operation [of the means of knowledge] is as follows: even when there is an appearance of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the means of knowledge functions only within that which is pure, having the nature of an appearance of non-mixture. And that—

In the case of those [cognitions] that appear as mixed with the immediately preceding ones, they are not valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because they merely grasp what has already been grasped. Therefore, the reality of the class of appearances that partakes in the domain of a valid means of knowledge is indeed distinct. Furthermore, that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), even if it arises from the cognition of two moons, is capable of uprooting them in the end, and it is so even previously.
It has indeed been uprooted. For with an inward-turned body, it is that very same [consciousness], not another;
and here, one's own self-awareness alone is the witness, because at that very moment there is the realization: "This is not silver.
Even when showing a double moon to another for their amazement...

Being made an object of others' ridicule, contempt, pity, and so forth, one considers that very previous reflection on the double moon—though it was present at that time and brought about by the power of its manifestation—to have been utterly uprooted. Therefore, it is said: "That [is] within. In this way, he introduces the meaning of the aphorism.

Regarding the passage beginning with "now" (*idānīm*): for this very reason, because it was stated in the *Ādisiddhasūtra*, one must rely on what has been previously mentioned [even though it is] separated [in the text]. If that is so, then why was there no mention of it at the beginning? Why, instead, is it placed here? He replies: it is "incidental" (*ānuṣaṅgika*), consisting as it does of the context of the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

Those factors such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which arise from association (*anuṣaṅga*) and have as their purpose the association characterized by resting within the reality of a single cognizer (*ekapramātṛtattva*), are designated as "established from the beginning" (*ādisiddha*) in order that no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) or similar fallacy occurs; thus, they are not like [external] objects of cognition (*prameya*), and for that very reason, they are distinct [from them].

The meaning is that it is endowed with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Now, one might object: "Are not qualifiers such as permanence and so forth perceived by every direct perception? Let even a few be perceived; how then can it be said that 'it is also a qualifier'? To this he replies: "Permanence and so forth. Now, [one might ask] what is distinct from the qualifier...

Anticipating the question, "What else could its own nature (svarūpa) be?", he says: "by the mere thing-in-itself" (vastumātreṇa). For even by one who maintains the doctrine of absolute relation (saṃsargaikāntavādin), the nature of the substratum of attributes must indeed be admitted; it is precisely because that [nature] resides in a single locus that there is the cognition of its co-referentiality with a thousand attributes—such as, "This jar is red."

“The great golden heart. Now, one might ask: is not non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāditva*) the very definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and has that been abandoned here? It has not been abandoned; rather, he shows that it is [retained] because it pertains to the worldly (*laukika*) by using the word “object” (*vastu*).
Object... (page 74)

For by the phrase "it is established," that very point has been stated. The use of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the commentary is intended to manifest its dependence upon the subject (*pramātṛ-adhīna*).

He clarifies this dependence upon the subject with the words "for when awareness arises" (*vimarśodaye hi*); the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇij-artha*) is "it is made to be reflected upon" (*vimṛśyate*).

It has been shown that even the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the phrase "it remains established" (*vyavatiṣṭhate*) is subordinate to the primary meaning of the verbal root; thus, the "establishment" (*vyavasthāna*) mentioned in the Sūtra is also followed [in this sense]. The phrase "of this very [consciousness]" means of that which has been brought to the state of being an object (*prameyatā*) by the power of Māyā. The phrase "due to causing agitation" refers to the adoption of an outward-directed orientation.
Because even when introversion manifests, it remains unperceived;

and in this context, the manifestation, while arising as a related entity, shines forth in this manner through its own self-luminosity. Now, one might object: "Is this not contradicted by the fact that self-awareness [is denied]? Why so?

It might be suspected [that this is not so]; therefore he says, "the double moon, etc. He establishes that even in a mistaken cognition, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is non-mistaken in all cases. Regarding the phrase "for here": although a cognition is produced through the cooperation of the eye, light, and awareness with respect to an external object, its nature as awareness arises solely from awareness itself.

Regarding the claim that "the form of the object [arises] from the sense-faculty": consequently, just as a defect produced by the potter's cognition might corrupt only the configuration of the jar but not even its clay-portion,
so too [an error] would only cause the objective portion— the object which colors the eye— to be mistaken, but not the cognitive portion.

The syntactical connection of the sentence is as follows: visual [cognition] is erroneous with respect to the external [object], whereas self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is always non-erroneous. The intervening passage, however, is for the purpose of establishing its error with respect to the external. Since the eye is impaired, therefore, with respect to the external...

Whence [can it be said] that it is erroneous? For the assumption of the form of the object arises from the object itself, not from the sense organ. He says: "And not... Indeed, valid cognition (*pramā*) becomes such by being conjoined with the coloring (*uparāga*) of the object. And the object—whether it is in contact with the sense organ or fallen within the range of the sense-organ's activity—would act in that way only when there is a modification (*vikāra*) of the sense organ.

The error is not sensory. But surely, in cases such as seeing a mirage while walking, there is no modification of the sense organ, and yet the sensory nature of this error is accepted. Who says that there is no modification of the sense organ here? He shows this by stating "merely that much," meaning it is indeed a modification of the sense organ.
It is solely the cause of sensory delusion.
For if it occurred while the sense organ was unimpaired, how could it be a sensory delusion? He explains this very point:

Regarding the phrase "by means of ships and so forth": through rapid spinning, travel by ship, disturbances of the bodily humors (*vāta*), and the like, the sense organ itself is rendered incapable and mounted upon the form of whirling; thus, in those cases, the modification belongs to the eye alone.
Now, self-awareness here is not independent as it is for the Buddhists, but rather [it is] the Great Awakening—

[The cognition] is attached to the limited subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*) at its furthest limit. Consequently, the state of being pure consciousness would be established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), but not the state of perceiving two moons—which is what is seen [in error]; nor, in the present case, would there be the form "blue appears.
He refutes this with the words beginning "unerring" (*avyabhicarita*), [stating that the object] is absolutely non-different [from consciousness].
Even for one who has not yet attained the stage of differentiation (*pṛthaktā-bhūmi*) but dwells in the state of Sadāśiva,
that specific manifestation such as a double moon or a blue object, its corresponding mode of being—
which is the nature of consciousness, the state of being manifest— and which is invariably concomitant with it, non-erroneous, and imperishable; [that is what is meant].

"Of which"—that is, "of that which is thus. This is what is meant: that which is considered distinct, such as blue, a double moon, and so forth, must necessarily be suspected [as being other than consciousness]. However, that which appears within cognition like a reflection in a mirror is established by the very establishment of cognition itself; therefore, in this case, regarding the form of the appearances of the double moon, blue, and so on—

Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is indeed non-erroneous. Having established the example "like the appearance of two moons," he states another example by way of conjunction, saying "just as" (*yathā ca*):
just as at the time of a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) in which blue appears, it is understood through self-awareness alone in a universal manner; [so too is the case here].

The construction of the sentence is as follows: even that which was under discussion—the fact that "it appears to me in this way"—is understood precisely through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). In this regard, he shows that the self-awareness stated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this object must necessarily be accepted even by the proponent of cognition with forms (*sākāravādī*), by using the words "for this very reason."

Just as it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone—and not from any other means of valid cognition—that [objects] are the forms of consciousness, that they belong to consciousness, and that they are objects by virtue of being invariably established as the objective case (*karman*) of consciousness; so too [is this established]. Nevertheless...

As for what was stated— that [the object] is indeed established by virtue of being related— by the establishment of that, another object of knowledge under discussion is also established; thus, by this very passage, the status of an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by the context) is also [demonstrated].
(Page 76) He demonstrates this: "For this very reason" means that because [blue and so forth] are established as being related to consciousness,
the object of inquiry under discussion— that blue and so forth have consciousness alone as their ultimate reality— is likewise established.

Because a relationship has its very life rooted in non-difference, it culminates in identity (*tādātmya*). For when one says, "That form which consists of blue manifests," this is subsumed within manifestation through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And that manifestation, being related to consciousness, possesses identity with consciousness.
It has been understood. What else remains that could be the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of blue apart from cognition?

[Objection: But if this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) appearing as blue is established through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), why is it not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding external blue? To this he says: "And because... The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a doubt. Regarding the internal...

In conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is only this much: "Blue appears to me," but not in the sense of having an outward-turned form. Here, however, there exists an appearance within consciousness itself in the form "this is blue";
for precisely because it appears thus to me, it is "this blue. And therefore, by means of the perception of the external senses—

That which is cognized as "this has been apprehended" is called external, such as blue and so forth; however, that which is cognized through the self-awareness of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-svasaṃvedana*) is not called external. Thus, having explained the manifestation of itself (*svabhāsa*) in this way, [the author] does not see anything to be excluded in the phrase "arising anew" (*abhinavodaya*).

To remove this delusion, he says: "And that [consciousness] again and again. This means that, due to the distinction of time, there is no manifestation whatsoever that is not always new; rather, the sense is that within that [manifestation], the states of being other than or non-other than the object of cognition arise through the power of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), and these [states] belong to the object of cognition as well by virtue of that same power.

The phrase "the non-difference of reality" means that it resides in manifestation alone; by these words of the commentary (*vṛtti*), he states that non-difference has been expressed by those who maintain that there exists nothing else whatsoever—neither something established, nor something rooted, nor anything real—that stands apart from manifestation.
Having thus explained the commentary on the aphorism concerning the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he now explains the aphorism concerning the fruit (*phala*).
And thus: "here" refers to the sentence of the *vṛtti*. "Even here" implies that it is not only the case previously; this is established by the sense.
In the Buddhist view, since there is a difference in time between the perception (*darśana*) and the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), how could there be identity?
Thus, there is no non-difference between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*). [This objection applies] even in your own system, just as it does in their view.
He raises the doubt, "How is this so?
with the passage beginning "The eye, etc. and ending with "even though," and he provides the answer here with the passage beginning "nevertheless."

Even from the Buddhist perspective, since conceptual constructions indeed appear as direct perception (*pratyakṣāyante*), there is a conventional usage that treats perception and determination as one. Having thus established this with reference to the viewpoint of others, he now establishes it with reference to the viewpoint of his own established doctrine, beginning with "Alternatively (*athavā*)," in this very same [work] where [reality] is undifferentiated.
In the form whose nature is light and reflective awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*), it is indeed said:

"At the moment of direct realization... (1.5.19). He establishes that very point with the words "For it is one alone," because in a single cognition, by virtue of its being pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

To that extent, the state of Īśvara—which consists of the nature of the ultimate subject, is colored by the reflection of the object of knowledge, and is of the nature of consciousness—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This will be explained in the section on Revelation (*āgama*). Now, one might ask: "The state of Śiva is the stage of the subject (*pramātṛ*); the state of Īśvara is the stage of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); but what is the stage of the result (*phala*)? He replies:

And that very [result] is "this" — it is self-evident (*svasaṃvedya*). The flash of subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) through the accomplishment of an activity, which consists of a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) accompanied by that activity, is the essence of the *vidyā-tattva*.

Whether this reflective awareness pertains to the mere nature of an object, to a qualifier, or to both, that alone is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); [it is the cessation of] transmigratory existence—

However, on the level of the manifest world (*bhūmi*), all this is "stained" because it is touched by *māyā*; such is the underlying intention (*āśaya*). Now, one might object: since the commentary began with the words "by means of the qualifiers of the reality," there ought to have been another commentary stating "this" or "eternal"; so what is the intention behind the masculine designation "he" (*ayam*)? To this, he says: "This," he says.

"Only an appearance" (*ābhāsa eva*). The meaning is that in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the very same appearance which was stated to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is here designated with respect to its immediate proximity; this indicates the actual non-difference between the means of valid cognition and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*) under discussion. But if this is so...

How can it be said that cognition consists of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? For it is logical that first there is the knower, then the instrument (*karaṇa*) operated by him, and finally the object of that [instrument], the knowable (*prameya*). He says "when" (*sati*) to show that this is not so. But if this is the case, how does this worldly convention proceed—first...?
"Regarding the passage beginning with 'the knower' (*pramātā*) and so forth, it is said: 'But at other times' (*anyadā tu*). This has been explained by us [as follows]:
'All this is touched by *māyā*' (p. 78)."
Having thus analyzed that very [point], he explains the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with "having a single designation" (*ekābhidhāna*) as follows:

"And of the conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*).
