Conventional means that which arises from, has as its purpose, or exists within worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which itself consists of coming together (*saṃbhūya*), concealing (*saṃvṛttya*), and contraction (*saṃkocena*). Of such a cognizer (*pramātṛ*); "previously" (*prāk*).

In the section beginning with "tadatatpratibhābhājā" (1.6.3), [it is said]: "That which is common through verbal expression—that very object which is the referent of verbal expression—is its 'tadbhāva' (the state of being that); by means of that [state]. And it is common through verbal expression because of its [inseparable] connection with verbal expression."

That which manifests is, in other words, permeated by verbal expression (*abhilāpa*). Although the fact that [the object] is common to verbal expression is the reason for its having a single universal as its object, nevertheless, with the intention of merely providing a prior explanation, these two are stated together, just as in the case of the word.

It has been stated that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) [are the grounds for inference]. By this much, the function (*vṛtti*)—namely, that which follows a specific deliberation (*vimarśaviśeṣa*) such that "whatever is a single word, that alone is its denotable object"—has been explained. For this very reason, because the cognitive operation of the knower (*pramātṛvyāpāra*) pertains to a single universal (*sāmānya*), and each universal is indeed singular.

"Because it is a real entity (*vastu*), because it is determined by the cognizer, and because it is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-yoga*)"—thus says someone that "the synthesis of the different and the non-different" is the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Real entity" (*vastu*) refers to the primary substance (*dravya*). The term "exists" (*bhavati*) is a designation made in terms of persistence (*sthiti*) with respect to the entity to be predicated; the same applies hereafter.
[The question is: "In dependence upon a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), why does that very [substance] possess the status of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)? It is said: "Because it is within that" (*tadantar*).

By those very [parts] which are engaged in making it variegated, or by those whose purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is to be accomplished through the shape of a broad base and belly, the purposeful activity is carried out. And although each of them has its own various [qualities], it is not the case that they do not [possess them].

It is desired precisely because of the distinct intention [behind it]; nevertheless, that which is to be performed by means of a variegated cloth (*citrapaṭa*) in the form of a covering—consisting of its warp and woof—it is into that very [act] that the sense of beauty, pride, and so forth enter as that which imparts variety. For a woman united with her lover in private does not don a variegated cloth.
With the intention that the king might bestow splendor upon the assembly hall, or even place a golden pitcher studded with jewels upon his own head,
(page 79).

He says "mostly" because of this very reason—that it is not desired as something separate. Here, however, [the word] "this" denotes a substance (*dravya*) which is the primary referent of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*). As was stated previously, it becomes some kind of entity.
Thus,
the self, the entity, and the intrinsic nature are the body;
and so it is said "furthermore" at the beginning.
Likewise, in the passage "sadghaṭadravya...
(2.3.5), by the words "of conceptualization alone," he confirms that [conceptualization] follows precisely the distinctions of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
By the phrase "at times," he means that even among those things present before one, only a single one is sought; however, by that much alone—[the object is not thereby established].

The meaning is that there is an absence of so many [individuals]. The word "in every respect" (*sarvathā*) refers to whether the deliberation (*vimarśa*) pertains to a single universal or to its collection;

however, he states by means of the term "transactional usage" (*vyavahāra*) that this [deliberation] is not to be abandoned within the sphere of *māyā*. "For this very reason" (*ata eva*) means: because it brings about purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Thus [it is established].
Now, one might object: "Let there be both the capacity to bring about purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and sublation (*bādhyatva*); what is the contradiction?

Anticipating this doubt, he demonstrates the contradiction with the words "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*). That which performs purposeful action is external and common [to all]; this is not the case here—such is the nature of sublation. And the opposite of this is...

There is a logical contradiction in [the claim that] that which has been apprehended by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, that which leads to the attainment of an object capable of causal efficiency—is sublated. Now, one might ask: what does the sublater do to that which possesses the nature of being capable of causal efficiency? It is said in reply:
two examples were given to distinguish between sensory and mental errors. [The sublater] does not obstruct it.

Or rather, [it is removed] either instantly upon arising, or by uprooting it from within. He clarifies the meaning of the word "eva" (only/indeed) himself by means of the phrase "by causing the breaking of continuity," for uprooting generally refers to the cessation of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);

however, he uses the word "nanu" and so forth to clarify that, in the case of a sublater (*bādhaka*), there is actually a contradiction regarding its very arising. This is why he says "ata eva" (for this very reason).
Since a perfected manifestation remains perfected even by hundreds of sublaters or hundreds of curses, for that reason, non-sublation constitutes validity,
while sublatability constitutes invalidity.

(Page 80) By this, the contradiction between [the nature of] invalidation (*bādha*) and being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is resolved. He shows that this is necessarily required in the realm of *māyā* with the words "for a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇaṃ hi*), meaning that cognition itself is the means of valid cognition. It is useful—

"It is employed as a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatayopayujyate*). Thus, the purpose has been shown by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the words "for such a purpose," and by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "ascertained by that. Therefore, since those who fear non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) seek a means of valid cognition, a means of valid cognition is precisely that which is concordant (*saṃvādaka*). Now, what [is this]?

"Let it be so by virtue of mere conformity and mere incitement to action"—no, he says: "Even [in the case of] one who acts," because of the word "even" (*api*), this refers to even an ignorant person or one who possesses contrary knowledge, due to the gradation of their desire for an object. For even a fool proceeds to act upon learning that food contains poison; otherwise, [he would not act] even when a visible transgression is present.
"How could one who is certain that [an act] is harmful proceed to such things as stealing the property of others?

Thus, having established the validity [of cognition] within this sphere of illusion (*māyāpada*) just as in the externalist view (*bāhyadarśana*), the Vijñānavādin refutes it by entering into the very heart of the Siddhāntin's own position, saying "If that is so... and so forth.

The meaning is: "By what means must this be accepted by you? up until the end [of the passage]. Alternatively, the proponent (siddhāntin) reflects upon his own system with this text in order to resolve the suspected contradiction between earlier and later statements; or else, the disciple reflects upon it.

"Speaking thus": the meaning is that it might be possible to conceive that "it is determined"—that is, even by its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamarthatā*), it is precisely its luminosity that is determined. "Of the power of necessity" (*niyatiśakteḥ*) is in the ablative case;
the connection with the preceding [phrase] is that it is "capable of causal efficiency" by virtue of that [power] acting as the cause. For it has been said:
In the *Cinmayatvasūtra*, it is said:
"Even causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) exists in the case of externality; it [varies] according to the difference in diverse appearances" (1.8.6), and this will be explained further.
"Even causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not innate to objects...
(2.3.12). "It occurs" (*bhavati*) refers to what is being considered possible. "And thus" (*tathā ca*) means "this being the case.
From the mere perception of hair and so forth, no distinction can be determined, from the words "this" (*ayam*) up to the end of the passage.

Even that which was stated—that the form of the particular (*viśeṣa*) may indeed extend this far—is refuted by the fact that [the cognition] occurs even at the moment of the knowledge of causal efficiency (*arthakriyājñāna*). Regarding the phrase "in the manifestation of this": [it refers to] the appearance of hair and so forth.

In the appearance of activity, there is the attracting of people and so forth by a beautiful woman; for even from a counterfeit coin, the acquisition of value occurs. By the force of circumstances, this happens even in the case of that which causes misfortune—meaning, even for that which is not intended to be a producer of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). "Even from that" means even from such purposeful action as pleasure and so forth, it is not [necessarily] a real object.

It is determined that "this alone is thus capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā), but this other is not so. Nor is it proper to say that reality consists in performing the purposeful action as determined by the cognizer, because we observe that what is intended by the cognizer is frequently found to be otherwise. For he himself...

A particular form may sometimes result in a hundred blades of grass, and sometimes in fifty; thus, there is great lack of restriction. For this very reason, just as its capacity for causal efficiency is restricted, so too is its being produced by that specific cause. To explain:

Among fires produced from fire-drills, iron, machines, cow-dung, wood, or stones, which one should we designate as "fire"? Therefore, it is incorrect to say that being produced from those [specific causes] is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the appearance of an entity (*bhāvābhāsa*),
for the appearance of an entity is not seen to possess at once all the range of exclusions (*vyāvṛttivarga*) that might be observed in such a case.

It must always be so, because otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence that even the appearances of "that place" and "that time" would persist as something other than what they are; for even though such persistence is illogical, it would result [if the identity were not maintained]. Now, to whatever extent the collection of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) or the aggregate of universals (*sāmānya-samūha*) necessarily pervades that body of the entity, to that extent it belongs to it.

Regarding the body (*vapuḥ*), we do not know its exact extent even in that case. Furthermore, through the examination of cognition, it is established that a thing does not abandon its appearing form to assume another form. Therefore, how could even a hair that is admitted to be unreal not be real when it appears as a hair?

Having thus established the impossibility of ascertaining a form capable of causal efficiency, he establishes its futility with the words "at a later time. For since activity proceeds precisely from that whose validity has not yet been ascertained, even when causal efficiency is subsequently obtained, [the cognition] remains a means of valid knowledge.
The examination [of the means of knowledge] is not useful for determining validity therein;
thus, "a means of knowledge is purposeful because its activity is effective"—this view of Vātsyāyana is also indeed untenable. Having thus subverted perception, [he proceeds].
Inference also acts in that same way; for if the validity of perception were not ascertained, then [the inference] would be... [pakṣadharm-]

The essential nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*), which primarily consists in its presence in the subject (*pakṣa*), its existence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), must be ascertained at its very root through perception itself; yet even that [ascertainment] is not established, because that whose true nature has not been grasped by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot function as a logical mark.
Therefore, inference—which is defined as "the vision of an object through a logical mark"—is also of no consequence whatsoever. Thus, it is not [the case that inference is a means of knowledge].

There is a certain systematic establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the fruitlessness that was asserted by accepting the impossibility of ascertaining validity, he first refutes it with the intention that such impossibility has been undermined by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) himself, who demonstrated his own acceptance [of the possibility].

By the words beginning with "here" (*iha*), validity (*prāmāṇya*) must be ascertained for the sake of discerning [the true from the false]. And that [ascertainment] is certainly necessary regarding what is to be avoided through effort and what is to be acquired through effort. Thus he says: "sometimes.
[The phrase] "even without" refers to one returning to his own home from the village [and finding] that it has not been burnt, nor plundered, nor...

Then, how could one determine that "wealth, sons, and wife have been carried off by someone"? And likewise, the meaning is: "from that cause," namely, from such repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). He states that this is logical with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*), [meaning] "but in another configuration" (*sanniveśāntare tu*), that is, when there is a distant location, defective sense organs, dim light, and so forth.

The connection is as follows: "objects" means that the very nature of the cognition whose object is the thing becomes thus. "By that" refers to the correspondence. He shows its nature with the words "that which," meaning it is simply what is well-known in the world, and not something unprecedented or defined by his own technical terminology that is produced by the cognizer alone. [This pertains to] the cognizer.

He demonstrates that which was stated regarding independence with the words "infallible [knowledge] of another object," and so forth. "It is established" means that the established doctrine is that knowledge [occurs] regarding an imperceptible object. This is what is meant: perception [arises] from the power of the object itself; inference, from the power of another object; and scripture—

The distinction is that [the cognition occurs] through the capacity of the cognizer, as well as through the capacity of other cognizers, whether they be expanded or unexpanded. Regarding the phrase "even for animals": for they, upon seeing a raised staff, infer the impending blow, receive instruction, and respect the conventions established within their own species.

By means of the example that "even when practiced repeatedly, there must be the preservation of attentiveness during instruction" (p. 83), he connects [the point] with the words beginning with "repeatedly. Thus, the means for its acquisition is taught.

The Connection. Anticipating the objection raised in the verse by the opponent, the Lokāyata, [the author] asks: "Why should this delusion, born of inattention regarding the subject of authority (*prāmāṇya*), be removed through effort? He replies with the words "And in the unseen" (*adṛṣṭe ca*). First, even regarding what is seen, a person who acts according to authority...

One who has engaged [in action] fears mockery because of its fruitlessness; however, when it is not seen, there is a great transgression consisting of the experience of suffering in hell, and there is an infinite bliss characterized by heaven and liberation, which must necessarily be the object of avoidance or attainment according to its progressive gradations.

For discerning people, "harm" should be understood as pertaining to the perceptible realm. For instance, it is evident to a person of discrimination that one who, having mistaken a non-venomous snake for a garland, takes hold of it, is joined with death and the subsequent fall into hell; thus, inference should also be applied in that regard.

"In such a vast wilderness, how could there be the production of a garland woven with variegated flowers? Thus, since perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) have only observed objects as their domain, there exists [the need for] scripture (*āgama*) to support the search for that which is superior and to be sought— such as truth (*satya*) and so forth— which, like a painting (*citra*), falls within the domain of what has been observed.

By demonstrating "capacity" (*sāmarthya*), it is stated that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are dependent upon mutual assistance. For instance, even an object perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) must indeed depend upon the established consensus (*prasiddhi*) characterized by scripture (*āgama*), when it is being applied by the learned toward purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*). This is that [consensus].

The milk of a cow is wholesome and pure, whereas the milk of this she-ass is a source of destruction for fire and is impure; it will be stated that activity proceeds from precisely such a collection of means of valid cognition.
"But that [perception], beginning with space and so forth... (2.3.9).
And that [perception] consists of self-awareness, wherein appearances are joined and disjoined by an inward-turned, autonomous reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
The doctrine of the absolute freedom (svātantrya) of the Supreme Lord, whose nature is grace, alone is logical—this too will be established further on;

let it suffice for now. Furthermore, regarding that which was stated as necessarily to be followed, we have already explained this in the very first sentence, while the author of the Vivṛti [explains it as follows]:

Having previously explained [this], he now recites [the verse] beginning with "well-known" (prasiddhaḥ) in order to provide a concise exposition (page 84). "Established" (pratīti) means firmness through conventional usage; it is the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) that consists of the nature of the word.

Since the internal nature of the conscious self (*citsvabhāva*) is its innermost form, which is as vital as life itself even for perception and other means of knowledge, whatever is deliberated by it becomes exactly so; there is no dispute about this, just as when one says, "I am Garuḍa himself; I sport with serpents and turn their poison into nectar. And so they have said:
"For as one meditates upon oneself here, so indeed does one become";
and, "As one knows oneself, so do the gods know him."

And thus: that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is primarily called "scripture" (*āgama*); however, by way of metaphorical usage based on its utility, the collection of words (*śabdarāśi*) which produces it is also so called. Its authority (*prāmāṇya*) pertains to objects that are beyond direct perception; for when an object is already cognized through direct perception, the result [of scripture] is of no consequence, just as smoke is [redundant] with respect to fire. And so forth.

It is merely not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). For this [scripture], among the various means of valid cognition—whether as that which is to be negated, or through another utility, or by defining distinctions of place, time, creation, and so forth—assumes the status of a means of valid cognition;
indeed, it attains the character of direct perception (*pratyakṣatām*), like collyrium and other such things. Thus he explains the phrase "wherever" and "when."

"Of whatever object" (*yathā yasyārthasya*)—by this, the following objection is answered: as some have said, "Who is this [author]? [The answer is: "By the elders. Likewise, regarding the question "Whose is which scripture?": for scriptures indeed contain mutually contradictory teachings; yet it is not logical that what is a scripture for one person should be a non-scripture for another.
"Because valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is impartial. For instance, what kind of impartiality belongs to valid cognition?
Indeed, sir, how could perception and inference be impartial toward Caitra when they manifest blue, fire, and so forth to Maitra, yet [are not so] toward Caitra?
Or, if that authoritative instruction (*siddhādeśa*) which was obtained— namely, "you will obtain a treasure"—

is indeed an *āgama* for Maitra; or if, in the case of such [cognitions], perception and inference also sometimes occur for Maitra, and thus there is no partiality [toward one source over another], then that lack of distinction applies equally to *āgama* as well.
For indeed, even for the followers of the Buddha, the Cārvākas, and others,
there must necessarily be an established conviction in some trustworthy person’s word. To illustrate this, [consider] a firm...
The scripture is the verbal testimony that conveys the meaning in its entirety;

in this regard, just as light, the sense organs, and so forth, though they serve as instruments for the cognition of two moons— which is not a valid means of knowledge— are themselves not valid means of knowledge, yet it does not follow from this that they are incorrect.
A certain partiality of perception would result; likewise, in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such Vedic injunctions,

even that which is not a valid means of knowledge— functioning as a semblance of scripture consisting of weak reflection— would find application among a twice-born person possessed of faith and reverence, even though he is otherwise ineligible, such as a Śūdra.
When employed as a verbal expression in the form of a valid scripture characterized by firm discernment,
it attains the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is not subject to being described as partiality or the like; for every scripture,
having taken into account specific qualifications, locations, times, conditions, auxiliary factors, and so forth, [establishes] injunctions and prohibitions.

It consists of the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the letters beginning with *ka* and *dha*. Consequently, a certain person is created by the Lord through the union with his own self, reflecting upon a specific awareness appropriate for a particular deity, a Siddha, or another such being;
while another reflects upon a different awareness. Thus it is said: "of the empty creature."

This is incorrect. It has been shown by the Śruti itself that firm and well-established conviction (*dṛḍhanirūḍhi*) alone is the primary characteristic of those qualified for each respective path, in such passages as: "He who knows this thus," and "The knower should sacrifice.
And for that very purpose it was said: "This person consists of faith" (*śraddhāmaya*), and so forth. This will be explained further ahead.

"It will become clear" means that he explains [the passage] beginning with "it is logical," etc., by [the phrase] "and of that," which refers to the firm establishment of cognition. "Nyāya" means inference (*anumāna*). For indeed, regarding the existence of God, there exists an inference arising from signs such as the nature of being an artifact (*sanniveśa*) and the nature of being an effect (*kārya*); however, [this does not apply] to the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth.
Regarding the question of "how much" (iyattā), there is no means of inference; thus, scripture alone is the refuge in that matter.

Having thus explained both [aspects] as they are established in the treatises, he explains the case where [the measure] is not fixed by worldly convention with the words "even in the world. As for the phrase "in Kashmir," it refers to the intellect [of those] in regions such as Madhyadeśa and Pūrvadeśa.
The excellent [cognizers] mostly perform the duties of household life;

however, when relying on scripture, inference (*anumiti*) is that reasoning which has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through the scripture, and its "conformity" (*anugama*)—that is, its corroboration—is primary.

Thus, once the ascertainment of the object is effected by that very [inference], the reasoning possesses the character of apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*). Now, one might object:

Anticipating the objection as to why there is no error, he says "because": for first of all, by means of direct perception— namely, that produced by the sense organs, self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and that born from the practice of yoga— one [perceives] blue, pleasure, Brahman, and so forth...

The meaning of *kādira* manifests directly. Since there is no doubt in that regard, it is not appropriate to say that it "is joined" (*yujyate*). For where there is indirectness (*parokṣatva*), and precisely because of that, there is the state of being a locus for doubt, there the certainty regarding the object—that is, the objective status of the thing—is designated as "being joined. This is indeed the case with a mountain.

When another person has seen [something] and asks, "Is there fire here?", and one replies, "There is fire here," and is asked again, "How so?", and says, "Because of smoke"—the first person says, "It is logical. This means that the reason (*hetu*) is not something yet to be established.
And thus the venerable one said:
"The word *yukti* is cited in the Bhāṣya as meaning 'the application of well-known logical principles' (*prasiddhanyāyakaraṇa*).
Therefore, that collection of factors (*sāmagrī*) by which an object is established is called *yukti*, and it is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*). As for what has been stated by some..."

"The intellect perceives those entities..."—this is reasoning (*yukti*). "This is indeed reasoning," "this is the non-dullness of wisdom," and "this is the equipment for inference"—thus the nature of reasoning has been stated; this will be examined later in the *Yoginirmāṇatāsūtra* regarding the connection (*pratibandha*).
In that regard: [the opponent objects], "If reasoning (*yukti*) is indeed inference (*anumāna*), then how can this [reasoning] be secondary? He replies:

"And that" refers to inference. "Effect and so forth" means the effect, which consists of two forms—effect and essential nature—or else it is of five forms, as stated in the definition of the inferential mark (*laiṅgika*): "the effect, the cause, the conjoined, the inherent, and the contradictory."

The mark (*liṅga*) is that which consists of the state of being an effect and so forth— such as "this is its effect," "this is its nature," "this is its cause," "this is its conjunct," "this is its inherent," or "this is its contradictory"— which, though difficult to perceive, cannot be determined with certainty. Such is the mark.

Furthermore, as for what was stated beginning with "well-discriminated" (*suvivecitam*), that is simply impossible to carry out, like the destruction of a disease that is to be accomplished by wearing the crest-jewel of Śeṣa. Having thus stated that even though [the cause] exists, its status as an effect and so forth— which is restricted to a specific object— is undeterminable, he shows that even that does not exist, saying "the yogin."
Nor can it be determined whether this is something created by a yogin or something else that is mundane; as stated previously.
"Even causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), if [the object] were external, would be distinct... (1.8.6).
Here [it may be objected]: "But surely, just as the whiteness, rising nature, and so forth of smoke are its forms, so too is its being born from fire (*agnijatva*);
that which is not born from fire is not smoke at all. If it were [not born from fire], then in this case too, its very nature would be non-origination from fire."

Fearing that [the relation] might not belong to fire—thinking that it might fall [on something else]—he says: "And the causal relation is non-intrinsic. For if there were some such thing as fire or smoke, then the necessity between them characterized by priority and posteriority would be their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); however, those two do not exist [as independent entities].
Apart from being a manifestation of consciousness, it is consciousness itself that manifests in such a way—

as in the case of dreams, mental constructs, yogic emanations, and so forth. However, when the necessity of immediate succession is made to appear through the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) solely by virtue of the expansion of consciousness, there arises the worldly convention of "waking."

And there is the ascertainment of causality. In that regard, from what does this ascertainment arise—that smoke must necessarily exist immediately after fire? For a single observation at a particular time is not pervasive across all instances, and even with repeated observation, there is no certainty. Furthermore, regarding repeated observation, it occurs within the context of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Since the presence of one's own self has been introduced [as the basis for perception], it might even be the case that smoke does not exist when there is no observer presiding over this specific portion of space within me; if such a certainty were reached by relying on the perceptions of others, then scripture would have been accepted as the authority.
Now, what is the nature of smoke in this case? He says: it is the "single reflective awareness" (*ekapratyavamarśa*).
For the very appearance of smoke as smoke, having attained firmness through reflective awareness, is its true nature;
it is not its being posterior to fire, nor is it its being preceded by the movement of the throat and eyes [in the act of perceiving]. If that were so, what would be the nature of fire as well?

If form (*rūpa*) were internal to the fuel and so forth, and if it were preceded by smoke and so forth, then by this sequence there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). Likewise, even in the case of the movement of the throat and eyes,
there would be mutual dependence with respect to smoke, and a lack of finality (*aviśrānti*) with respect to its own effects.

Smoke would never be seen; consequently, everyone would become blind and deaf due to the non-perception of the true nature of entities. Furthermore, as many exclusions (vyāvṛttis) as are observed at one time need not necessarily exist at all times.

Because it would follow that [the object] is not connected with other places and times, it would result in being nothing but a single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the nature of an entity (*bhāva*) defined as the conjunction of a few exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) would be merely a conventional designation (*paribhāṣita*), for [it lacks] the few...

If it is argued that while the limit (*avadhi*) is visible, the act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) itself is the cause for determining that limit, then this results in exactly what we have already stated: that smoke is "the smoke to be reflected upon," but not "this is the effect" or "this is the cause. For [the notions] "in this place," "at this time," and "visible as this" do not, in the same way, constitute a portion of the positive entity (*bhāvāṃśa*).

This is already established because it is a different kind of manifestation (*ābhāsa*); likewise, even the manifestation of cause and effect may indeed bring about the emergence of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) simply through the intermingling of different manifestations of permanence,
yet that manifestation of smoke does not [cease to exist] merely because something is not its cause or not its effect.
The appearance of smoke. Here he provides an example with the words "as follows" (*yathā*). For the common understanding of the world is this:

"Oh, how great is the power of the jewel, the mantra, and so forth, that even this fire, though complete in its parts, does not burn! In this way, he shows that just as there is no necessity regarding the effect of an entity, so too there is none regarding its cause; thus he says, "and the lotus-root" (*śālūkaṃ ca*).

Thus [is explained] the *utpalakanda*. Furthermore, because the conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*) of it as a *śālūka* does not cease, it must belong to that same genus. How so? According to the principle that "a difference in effect arises from a difference in cause," the *kanda* produced from a seed and the *kanda* produced from a *kanda*—namely, the birth of a plantain tree—are two distinct *kandas* that emerge separately due to the intervention [of the intervening cause].
Then even the two plantain trees arising from those two bulbs would have to be distinct, and from that distinction,

there would also be a distinction among the plantain fruits and so forth. Consequently, as for what is said— that an immediate cause leads to the inference of its effect, such that things of similar form are similar— [that would be undermined].

In the case of two plantain trees growing from a bulb, there is an emergence from a bulb; however, where there is a direct difference in cause, there is also a difference in form, as in those very same two cases—one growing from a seed and one growing from a bulb. Thus, that [objection] would be refuted by the first distinction of causes, since in every effect there is a direct difference in cause.
Because they are equal. Just as a fool living in the Maru desert, restricting cow-dung alone to be the cause of fire, might likewise postulate that for smoke as well;
for if fire were not made of cow-dung, this [smoke] would also be [non-existent], but it does exist, therefore fire must also be something other than cow-dung.

It is thus: in this case, only the fuel itself must be conceived as the cause; what difference is there [between that] and the mere thing in general immediately following smoke? Well then, let it be so for those two types of plantain trees as well.
This is a distinction. He restates even this for the sake of refutation with the words "let that be so.
By saying "even having accepted what we have established," he shows that there is no attainment of the result; this is indicated by the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
The word "this" (*asau*) refers to the distinction. For instance, is this speech an expression of the desire to speak arising from passion, or...

Regarding the phrase "out of compassion": just as even when a cause exists, the distinction between causes makes the distinction between effects difficult to discern, so it is in all cases here; because there is no means for thorough investigation, this instruction is impossible to carry out, [the implication being] "if that excellence could indeed be known by you yourselves."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is the cause in all cases; and if, within that totality, a diverse set of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) brings about a difference in the effect, then those fires produced from blowing, from the force of wind, and from friction are entirely distinct. Therefore, why should smoke now be considered the effect of [only] one [of these]? It is not so.

We know this; therefore, inference is difficult to establish. For the touch of a fisherman brings about sin because it is a touch involving sin; this is either an inference from cause to effect or an inference from capacity. In that case, due to the possibility of an obstructing factor or the manifestation of destiny, it might not even be a cause of sin.

In that regard, disregarding inference (*anumāna*), it is indeed the scripture (*āgama*)—in the form of clear and well-established tradition—that becomes a factor for the avoidance of contact. He says "that" (*tat*).
[The phrase] "only for those possessed of higher discernment" (*prasaṃkhyānavatām eva*) refers to those who are attentive, discriminative, and fearful of mockery. For such is the nature of scripture.
This is the body of the transmission through sound. As the Lord Ananta said:
"For the sake of transmitting one's own realization to another, it is taught by means of sound.
In this context, one's own realization is [attained] through direct perception in the form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and sound is [perceived] by the sense organ of hearing.

If there were weakness regarding the validity of perception on the grounds that "it is an object of cognition by means of a perceiver," then one might fear that the same would apply to scripture as well; [the author] dispels this doubt with the words "and perception.
Here, "perception" is the agent qualified by the preceding term, while "general [nature]" (*sāmānyam*) is the object being established.

An example here is as follows: "Precisely from perception" (*pratyakṣād eva*). For by means of perception, the appearance of the house is indeed determined as being the object of the desire to reach it. Now, regarding such a determination...
(page 90)

"How can doubt, which is contrary to that [certainty], be said to arise even from doubt? To this he replies with the word "kevalam" (only/merely): the meaning is that it is merely a semblance of doubt when it is regarded as invalid in another context. As for the example "guḍa" (molasses):
the conventional usage of the term *guḍa* does not apply to anything merely sweet, merely hard, or merely red.

Because that [nature] is absent in honey, a clod of earth, and lacquer, the conventional usage of terms such as "form" (*rūpa*) applies only when they are combined. "From that very [source]" means from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It does not exist [otherwise], for it is established directly by that manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) which is confirmed by uncontradicted reflective awareness (*abādhitavimarśa*). That...

Otherwise, how could it be so? Would it not then be that there is either "it might be silver" or "it is not," rather than "this is indeed silver"? For once silver has been determined by a perception that grasps the very essence of silver all at once, how could there be a distinction between doubt, certainty, and error? It is precisely because [the cognition] consists of certainty itself...

Indeed, it ought to be endowed with a single flavor (ekarasa). This is true; however, doubt and error regarding the aspect of the appearance of silver arise through the power of that appearance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) which is preceded by the intermingling of another appearance of space and time. Thus, the threefold nature [of the cognition] is not untenable.

Regarding this, he says: "And everywhere," and "as before. As was previously stated in the section beginning with "(1.8.3) ...in the case of pleasure and so forth, as well as in the causes of pleasure and so forth," there is an investigation into the intermingling of other appearances, such as being graspable or external.

The same should be followed here as well. Alternatively, what was previously stated in this very commentary—namely, that "immediately thereafter, it is solely due to the distinction of place and time"—is extended by the phrase "as before. Now, it has been said that the emergence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) occurs at least with respect to the universal alone; that...

What is the point of this [objection] beginning with "Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as qualified by place and so forth"? He replies: "And when [the object] is ascertained. Although through perception validity is attained only with respect to a single universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, nevertheless, validity remains entirely unimpaired regarding the aspect that appears as a mixture; thus, the universal—

It is established that [the universal] pertains to all places and times, whereas the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not; this distinction regarding the establishment [of the universal] is made even though it extends to all places and times. "In the same way" means as qualified by place and so forth.
The word "again" (*punar*) refers to two distinct statements. The terms "object" (*viṣaya*) and "in the universal, etc. (*sāmānyādau*) are used in a non-co-referential sense (*vaiyadhikaraṇyena*).
That which was stated up to the end—"by the combination of multiple universals, [the object] is established from that very [combination]"—is precisely this.

In common practice (*vyavahāra*), one relies upon it as a reason (*hetu*) for establishing the essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), [expressed as] "for this very reason. Here, "herein" refers to the state of being a *śiṃśipā* tree; "of that" refers to the state of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*). And "that which" is this very state of being a *śiṃśipā* which, by the power of necessity (*niyati*), includes the state of being a tree even throughout the three times (*traikālya*); this is that.
The connection with that alone is the state of being drawn forth by the mere nature of a *śiṃśipā* tree; as it has been said:
"The reason, which possesses a nature that follows from the existence of that alone, resides in itself.
This may indeed be possible, since these two appearances are distinct. Is this not so?
Having abandoned the state of being a tree, how could a *śiṃśapā* be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?
To this, he says "ahead" (*agre*) in the *Yoginirmāṇatāsūtra*. "In that way" (*tathā*) means, as in direct perception and scripture.
But what harm is done to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvyavahāra*) by its application according to logic (*nyāya*)? Precisely for that reason—

Since it is rooted in the well-known tradition of the Supreme Lord, that uncontradicted consensus which exists even among other specific places, times, and persons, and which follows the very nature of necessity (*niyati*), only those inferences based upon it—
such as the inferences regarding instruments and agents— possess indisputable validity.
But not [the case] of those [notions] such as "being one of two" (sadvitīyānyataratva) that have arisen from one's own conceptual construction (*svayaṃkalpa*). Rather,

it is by the force of the habitual cultivation of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) from birth, or reaching back to thousands of millions of prior births, or by depending upon the matured intuition (*pratibhā*) of others.

Alternatively, when the maturation of intuition (*pratibhā*) occurs through the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the function of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in ascertaining the reality of all things is unimpeded. Thus he says: "from practice" (*abhyāsāt*). And for this very reason: since it happens thus precisely from practice, therefore that which was stated—[the passage beginning with] *paś-*... [is established].

The objection, "What is the use of correspondence? is thereby refuted, because its utility lies in the aspect of repeated practice; this is the intended meaning. "Then" means at the time of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). From this, the establishment of the reality arises; that direct realization occurs at its own proper time.

(Page 92) That which is the certainty that "this is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is, at that time, the certainty of the establishment of that object. "Otherwise" means in the absence of the certainty regarding the nature of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) due to a lack of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). For instance, in that case, there would be no further corroboration (*saṃvāda*).

...they look toward. Furthermore, "correspondence" (*saṃvāda*) means this: the attainment of that [object], such as its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) or its concomitance with its effects; this is the connection. All of this, although accepted in the establishment of external objects, is in no way tenable in that [Yogācāra] view, because of the [lack of] mental impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) and so forth.

Because that [consciousness] is the essence, and because its identity with the subject is logically established— this has indeed been demonstrated in the introductory sections beginning with "The Seer is self-luminous" (1.3.2). However, with the intention that this is logically consistent within our own philosophical system, it is here once again set forth in detail.

That which is to be contemplated has been shown; however, the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) must be introduced there because it is the essence of the Great Manifestation (*mahābhāsa*). This much is sufficient. And thus, the meaning of "by this" is "by this manner of cause," referring to the object of knowledge (*prameya*) that has been stated. The word "so far" (*tāvat*) is understood as referring to the domain of perception within conventional discourse (*saṃvyavahāra*).

"What indeed?"— this refers to perception (*pratyakṣa*), which consists in the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the manifestation of blue and so forth that has entered into a contracted light in the form of a single cognizer;
[it is contrasted with] the uncontracted light, which is devoid of the determination (*pariccheda*) consisting of universally non-disputed reflective awareness.
The meaning is that scripture (*āgama*) is powerful because its essential nature consists in the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the manifestation of the reality of the state of rest.
He analyzes this scripture, characterized by uncontradicted renown, with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*).
For when the meaning of the Vedas, Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, and so forth, is being reflected upon...
Established through mutual practice, it is expressed by this very [word], produced by this very [word],
and having proceeded from that very time onwards, it does not admit of limitation; thus,
the Supreme Lord Himself is the self of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), whose nature is uninterrupted light.

In this regard, there is indeed beginninglessness. For the well-known performance [of rituals] by Kaṭha and others, by Bhārgava, Mataṅga, and others, and by Nārada and the rest, is established as beginningless, since it is expressed through words composed of sentences arranged in both concise and expanded forms. And this [expression] is not something to be accomplished through effort.
He shows that she possesses the nature of the Supreme Goddess by saying, "all indeed. That [knowledge] has been established;
therein, knowledge is self-evident. (1.1.5) (p.
In such passages as these,
it will be demonstrated that "in this way" or "thus" refers to the appearances of jars, cloths, and so forth,
in places such as [Tantrāloka 2.4.21]. If all activity— whether mental or verbal— [is of this nature]...
[Objection: If it belongs to the Supreme Lord, then how can that activity—even in the case of a kingdom of the mind and so forth—be non-concordant?

[The author] replies: "But of that... This refers to the primordial activity of sovereignty belonging to her, which is characterized by being either existent or non-existent through its extension toward external objects.

Although a distinct individual difference (*prātisvika-viśeṣa*)—a divergence in form arising from the operations of the speech and mind of bound beings (*pāśava*)—is possible, it is difficult to perceive; thus, the worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) is justified. Furthermore, in the case of such engagement, even contradiction (*visaṃvāda*) is justified when there occurs the state of being the operation of the speech and mind of bound beings. In that regard:

Furthermore, because its nature is distinct from form due to the presence or absence of external objects reaching their limit, it is difficult to perceive; and thus, even when there is a discrepancy in activity, this should be applied as the reason, namely, "by the will of the Supreme Lord. The phrase "even while being obstructed" (nirudhyamānāpi) means "even though it is intended to be obstructed."

"Immovable" means that even when being moved by the desire for cessation, they remain unshakable. "The notion of appearance" means that this very scripture called the cultivation of sound (*śabdabhāvanā*) has the characteristic of appearing; that is to say, it is the tradition itself.
"Cultivated" means...
"Whether there is poison or no poison, there is indeed poison; O fool!"—

with such specific instructions, whose inner organ (antahkarana)— composed of the three functions of volition (saṅkalpa), self-identification (abhimāna), and determination (niścaya)— is interwoven and pervaded by words in the form of sounds, even the mantras [are thus affected].
The nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is characterized by a single, eternally established form belonging to the Supreme Lord whose essence is pure consciousness,
pervades the reflective awareness of whichever subject it may be; for that very subject,
its state of being of such a nature follows necessarily.

"Thus, [the mantras], bestowing such distinguished fruits, cause [the consciousness] to shine forth; for that very reason it is said: 'Together with the mind of the worshipper' (Svacchandatantra-kārikā 27).
Now, one might ask: how can that which is the specific form of verbalization consisting of the conceit (*abhimāna*) of the limited subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*) [be so]?
Anticipating the objection that the speech of the Supreme Lord is [omnipresent], it is replied that the nature of the Supreme Lord is indeed unobstructed everywhere;
however, solely by His will, its emergence and submergence occur within various particular portions.
Thus he shows [this] with the words "for the transmigrating soul" (*saṃsāriṇo hi*). "At that time" means at the time when the state of being the Supreme Lord is set aside;
because of its lack of autonomy, like a clod of earth and so forth. "The state of being a subject" (*pramātṛtā*) refers to what is called the subjectivity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest.

It is merely designated as "supreme," meaning it is not ultimately real. From that [union] comes the yoga of supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya*), which consists of the manifestation and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of everything without exception. This is what is meant: just as the Supreme Lord is the self-nature of the manifestation of the universe, so too is He the self-nature of the reflective awareness of the universe. In that regard—

Just as there is manifestation (*prakāśa*) of the external, the state of being an object (*grāhyatva*), purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and the class of its auxiliary factors, so too is there reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Therefore, by the will of the Lord alone, whatever is unified within the aspect of reflective awareness cannot be abandoned even if one desires to abandon it; for that very reason.
"One who is a portion of Rudra and a devotee of Rudra...

and so forth; by such passages, the predominance of the aspect of disposition (*bhāvāṃśaka*) is demonstrated in the Āgamas. "That" refers to such a cognition—that is to say, that which determines the actual state of an object to be cognized as being exactly so, resulting in omniscience.

But surely, if that which is established by the will of the Lord alone as a verbal designation is itself its scripture (āgama), then what excellence can there be for those who claim to be authoritative? Ah! Who are these wretched "authoritative" ones? It is the Lord alone who thus appears, reflects, and causes [others] to reflect. But surely...

Thus, let one remain silent; what is the use of composing treatises, listening to instructions, or practicing them? True, one remains [in silence] if the Supreme Lord himself were to abide in that manner; for even the carrying of a vessel of nectar [would then be unnecessary].
It is simply the will of the Lord. And so, the *Śivadṛṣṭi* states:
"He alone, in his capacity as the author of the scriptures... (3.75), and so forth.

"...as long as one is intent upon its performance. Thus it is said. Having thus examined the mental activity (*mānasī vṛtti*), he now examines that which consists of speech (*vāṅmayī*), [saying] "speech also" (*vāk api*).

And so it is: since [speech], having become firmly rooted (*prarūḍhā*), is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), therefore, among those belonging to other schools (*parayūthya*), there is no further rooting [of doubt].

That which is rendered non-investigative by the sublation of its ontological characteristic is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at all. Is it not the case that it is not a *pramāṇa* because of its conventional currency (*nirūḍhatvāt*), rather than because it is established by a *pramāṇa*?
(Page)
He says "not so," [adding] "but the portion consisting of reasoning. First of all, the principle does not hold everywhere;

even where it does hold, it is weak there too because, according to the previously mentioned perspective, that which takes the form of an effect and so forth is difficult to know. Though strong in its own domain, it is weak when viewed through another principle raised by a different proponent.

Thus it is. Nevertheless, even now, as long as saṃsāra continues, no finality whatsoever is found for the systems of reasoning that are being raised by the six categories of agents and their thousands of subdivisions. As it has been said:
"Even an object inferred with great effort... (Vākyapadīya 1.34);
thus, everyone understands all objects suitable for their results through scripture (*āgama*).

And it can be stated everywhere in the scripture that this is the opposite [of what you claim]: "Thus it is said in the *Vākyapadīya* (1.142): 'The [property] belonging to another' refers to succession and simultaneity as the pervaders of the capacity to produce effects in succession. Regarding this, is it said with reference to a real entity (*vastu*), or is it merely possible? It cannot be both, for two contradictory things cannot coexist.

Since it is impossible for one thing that ought to be a pervader to be so for another, how could there be pervasion in this manner? Furthermore, there can be neither successive nor simultaneous action, and since such [action] is in fact inconceivable, the second category does not exist at all from its perspective; thus, the determination of what is of that nature and what is not—
Since there is no certainty regarding the non-existence of a third category through [the arguments of] exclusion and inclusion, there is likewise no destruction of any other possible state.

Probability, however, is merely a conceptual construction; the relationship of pervader and pervaded, even when triggered by such probability, does not enter into the reality of things. Thus, even that which is momentary does not act sequentially.

Because it does not possess the property of non-conformity [to change], it cannot produce an effect simultaneously through a single form, since a distinction between those forms would be impossible; nor can it produce them through multiple forms, since simultaneity would be impossible. If it were to act in such a way due to the convergence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), then that [convergence] itself would be the pervasive factor, and not the sequential or simultaneous [nature of the entity]—and so forth.

The logic propounded by the Naiyāyikas becomes weak; this is merely the speech of a Piśāca, for the objection raised by another can be easily refuted. Thus, reasoning (*tarka*) is entirely unstable, for it was created by the Supreme Lord in that very manner. Therefore, in this world, through the process of increasing power (*śakti*), [it functions].
By means of drawing forth the power of internal, contracted reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
and thus being employed as that which is conducive to both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), it is created by the Supreme Lord as *tarka* (logical reasoning).

Saṃsāra is indeed something other, like the world of poetry; for these worlds are truly manifold. Even though reasoning (*tarka*) is not firmly established, there is no refutation whatsoever of our philosophical system (*darśana*).
For in the doctrine that objects are mere appearances (*ābhāsa*), this restriction of appearance is governed by the will of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). That [will]...

And by producing appearances through manifold variety, and by making subjects diverse through the manifold ways of joining them with or separating them from those appearances, [consciousness] remains beyond questioning; this much alone constitutes the established principle. Therefore, it is only when it has not yet reached its depths that reasoning appears to be effective. But in this case—

Let it be whether he is a fool who, out of pride in his own intellect, sees [his own view] as established— like a child mimicking an adult and imagining himself to be at the North Pole at the center of the entire earth— or whether he is a mere mockery; in any case, this does not hold for inference.
One must take refuge in scripture alone; moreover, it is that very scripture which has taken firm root in one's heart.

But surely, what is the case for one in whom nothing at all has taken root? Surely, what is the case for one who has no eyes? If you say, "In that case, there would be an absence of the relinquishing of what should be abandoned and the adoption of what should be adopted," [we reply] that this is the same here as well.
It is simply the absence of the attainment of enjoyment and liberation—which are to be accomplished through specific scriptures—and the lack of avoidance of falling into hell and so forth.
As the leader of the Mīmāṃsakas, Bhaṭṭanāyaka, said:
"The gods declare that great sins exist only by virtue of their command."
Salutations to that purifying Hara, who is independent and self-willed.

Thus, here the application of injunction and restatement must be explained in three ways. Scripture is an authority by virtue of its established tradition (*nirūḍhatayā*). He says this with the words "But what is well-known" (*prasiddhaṃ tu*); in this sequence—namely, "whatever," "when," "as," and "wherein"—the validity of all scriptures is established. For even the scripture of the Mlecchas and others is authoritative to that extent.
Even though you exist, your mere semblance of passion is subject to withering through association with the ignoble; likewise,
regarding those very things prescribed by the Vedas,
such as "one should sacrifice a large goat or a large bull"—
From among such duties to be performed, by the force of his will, even in the case of the sprinkling of a great bull— an act that is utterly contradictory [to his status]—
(page 97).
Among those who have lived for a long time and are mostly sages, such an understanding arises: "This is appropriate today," and thus it is not performed today;

however, they do not think, "We were formerly doers of what was inappropriate. But where, through the integration of other scriptures, the cognizer first develops the conviction, "I was previously a doer of what was inappropriate," [then the situation is different].

In that regard, it is not merely a matter of scriptural authority (*āgamatva*). Even there, O Blessed One, when such a cognition arises through the necessity of destiny (*niyati*) within the Supreme Lord’s own scripture (*pārameśvarāgama*), the conventional treatment as "dissolution" (*vilaya*) results in infinite transgression (*pratyavāya*); whereas, when such [cognition] arises elsewhere, the conventional treatment as "grace" (*anugraha*) results in infinite [merit] based on confidence in the Supreme Lord’s scripture.

This is because of the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Furthermore, even in that regard, the avoidance of the transgression incurred by abandoning those [lower] scriptures has been established by the Supreme Lord Himself through initiations such as the removal of sectarian marks (*liṅgoddhāra*); it has not been shown in that way for Vaiṣṇavas and others who lack faith in the Śaiva scriptures and so forth.

The scriptures follow the reality of things (*vastutattva*), whereas human intellects, possessed of partiality aroused by their own [preconceptions], bring about elevation or depreciation by their own power and are subject to potential sublation; enough of this excessive talk. But if it were not so:
If the speech of the Supreme Lord is indeed of unknown authorship, then the authority of the Siddhānta scriptures and so forth would be established [by this very fact],
since they proceed from the supreme cause, Śiva, who is peaceful and whose form is invisible.
This scripture, which has emerged in the form of sound, is extremely difficult to obtain.
Just as a great thunderclap arises from the formless sky,
so too does the scripture known as "Sound" arise from the tranquil [Reality] consisting of pure consciousness.

In this sequence, because [the Supreme Lord] is beginningless and His nature is light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there is no emergence of time within Him; however, because they were composed by Buddha and others, the Buddhist scriptures and so forth could not have originated from Him. Regarding this, the resolution is as follows: "Buddha" [is used here]. For there is no fixed individual named Buddha; rather, it is [the state of] meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—

The firm contemplation of momentariness and so forth is attained through strength; its teacher who instructs in the cultivation of momentariness and so forth is a former Buddha, and his too was another—thus, because the speakers are indefinite in this sequence, in reality, it consists solely of the contemplation of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara). In this way, the cultivation of the twenty-four principles (tattvas)—

Kapila should be considered liberated (*vīta*); for this very reason, all the scriptures (*āgamas*) are indeed beginningless. And thus, even in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*), there are accounts of his life.
It is indeed heard that the Buddhists abide in the principle of the intellect (buddhi-tattva), while the Pāñcarātrikas abide in the unmanifest (avyakta).
Thus it is said.
Whatever verbal composition exists in the world— whether Buddhist, Ārhata, Vedic, Vaimala,
Pāñcarātra, Lākula, or Sāṃkhya— [is all derived from that source].
"One should cause him to grasp that; there is no doubt"—
thus,
for those proponents who speak in this manner, there are three hundred [verses].
"And sixty-three [thousand] more—" (Sva. 10.680).
Thus, this knowledge of the Puruṣa was [taught] to the great-souled Kapila.
Thus it was spoken by me.

And so forth. Therefore, the word of the Sugata (Buddha) in that context is like a direct statement from his own throat, but its authority does not derive from being composed by him. For if its authorship by him were established apart from common renown (*prasiddhi*), what proof would there be for it? Thus, renown alone is the sole authority. Furthermore, by the power of the Supreme Lord’s will, even the Sugata, Kapila, and others [attain their status] in accordance with that renown.

Having entered [the path], they have been made objects of favor; [this is for the purpose] of favoring them and others as well. "World-renowned" (*lokaprasiddhi*) means that whoever is a practitioner in a particular transaction is the "world" (*loka*) in that regard. "In the region" (*deśe*) means in the locus of those respective transactions. He confirms this with the word "at will" (*kāmam*). Even if, by some certainty based on scripture (*āgama*), [it were otherwise]...
Even such conduct and activity as is contrary to the customs of other worlds, which they have fashioned for themselves—that too many undertake with one voice and accept it;
the meaning is that no doubt arises in them regarding that. For in that case...

The meaning is that speech is the cause of such contradictory worldly transactions. [An objection is raised: "If the word of the Supreme Lord is authoritative, then how is it that the Veda [is so]? He replies: "For it is the command of the Lord," meaning that it is entirely unimpeded on all sides.

From the attainment of the fruit until its accomplishment, it remains active; from the lack of discipline until the heart is moved to tears, it persists in the form of deliberation. This is the command.
"We bow to you, who are beyond the *śukra*—the essence—of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* Vedas;
whose command, consisting of the Vedas, is indeed profound and beautiful. (Sta.
Ci. 69). Regarding the word "whose" (*yasya*), it refers first to the threefold speech, which is the *śukra*—the essence or potency—of the *Ṛg* and the other Vedas.
The triad consisting of the powers of will, knowledge, and action has been explained. Beyond that is the abode of bliss, whose nature is the supreme power (*paraśakti*).
Beyond that is the abode of repose in the supreme power, which is the form in which all powers are established. That we praise. Oh!
Manifesting the excellence of its profundity and beauty,
and declaring that it contains within it a thousandfold meanings concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*), the elements (*adhibhūta*), the deities (*adhidaiva*), and so forth,
he states that the Vedic scripture is not in contradiction with any other tradition. As it has been said:
"For he consists of all-knowledge.

Thus, "both" refers to that which is established and that which is unestablished. The connection is as follows: it is possible that a contradictory well-known fact (*prasiddhi*) would extend to the definition of validity (*prāmāṇya*). And so it is.

"The twice-born must not drink liquor from the time of their initiation (śukra) onwards"—such [teachings] are heard; thus, that too is indeed a well-known tradition (prasiddhi). And that tradition is beginningless, for all traditions have existed since time immemorial. Among them, however, some emerge at certain times, while others submerge.
He clarifies the process of emergence and submergence by means of an illustration with the words "and so" (*tathā ca*).

Even though the syllables of the name "the object of metaphorical designation" (*tadupacāravastu*) are brought within the range of the ear and the mind, they are nevertheless applied to the written script because of their firm establishment through long-term familiarity with linguistic usage practiced over many lifetimes. By the Supreme [Lord]...

By virtue of following the command of the Lord, and likewise through the concordance with reality as it is followed by the venerable Sarvavīra, Bhargaśikhā, and others, they are designated by means of firm reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
And the reality of this firm reflective awareness consists in its being of the nature of nourishment, affliction, and so forth toward those [entities].
Either by means of the application of phonemes and letters endowed with excellent primary colors and secondary refinements,
or by means of the application of nourishing and scorching— such as the sprinkling of milk and the heating with *khadira* charcoal.
Or, by means of the application of lines metaphorically designated as the phonemes expressing ritual injunctions such as those for nourishing (*āpyāyana*) and so forth; or,
when [the phonemes] have been nourished or, alternatively, heated,
they take on the form of phonemes contemplated as being identical with the letters of that script.

This person (puruṣa), whose nature is light attained through non-differentiation from reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa), becomes either nourished or distressed. In that regard, by the will of the Lord (īśvara), that entity is created as a reflection within the Light, consisting of the manifestation of specific forms and so forth; likewise, it consists of the [manifestation of] specific forms...

Since [words] consist of specific reflections (*vimarśa*) variegated by passion (*rāga*), how could words of this kind fail to touch upon their actual objects? To confirm this very point, he states another illustration: "And in the case of a name and a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)," etc. In the deliberation regarding the afflictions caused by the six lunar mansions and so forth, even more than one's birth-mansion (*janmanakṣatra*), the primary name—

In the *Svarodaya*, the asterism (*nakṣatra*) that arrives through the gateway of the letters in the wheels (*cakra*) such as *avaka* and *haḍā* is primarily reckoned; and that has been observed to be extremely consistent. Thus, according to the direction of the scriptures, having demonstrated that the word possesses the nature of its meaning by virtue of its efficacy in producing results, [the author proceeds].

He has also stated "so it is" by way of worldly convention (*lokapratibhā*). Although the will of the animal—which is like that of a parent—is active therein, nevertheless, it is the will of the Lord alone that unfolds as the primary factor here, according to the actual intended meaning. The definition of scripture (*āgama*), made clear by these examples, applies everywhere.

"He transfers [the notion] thus" means in this manner. "Here" refers to in worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*). "By him" refers to by the Lord (*īśvara*). "Otherwise" means without that superimposition (*adhyāsa*). And this [is illustrated by] the determination "this is a jar. (1.5.20)

This has been analyzed in the Sūtra. "Formally composed" (*nibaddha*) refers to those [works] with specific arrangements of sentences; however, "informal" (*anibaddha*) refers to those where such [arrangement] does not exist. "The great person" (*mahājana*) should be understood as that group which has attained renown regarding a particular duty—for instance, the Vedic scholar (*cchāndasa*) in the performance of Vedic rites, and the Vaiṣṇava in the performance of Vaiṣṇava rites.
[The devotees] are known as Bhāgavatas. As Varāhamihira has said: "The Bhāgavatas belong to Viṣṇu; those of Maghā to Savitṛ; the twice-born smeared with ashes to Śambhu;
then the Brahmins who know the Mātṛmaṇḍala to the Mothers; and then [the devotees] to Brahmā."

The Śākyas [should perform the rite] for the benefit of sentient beings; likewise, the naked ones for the Arhats; and by whichever deity one is worshipped according to one's own rule, by them the ritual for that deity should be performed.
(Page 101) Thus it is said.

For those [individuals], through the experience of realizing identity with various specific reflective awarenesses (*vimarśa*), are capable of effortlessly manifesting the respective fruits. Furthermore, a certain scripture [speaks] of the characteristic of non-differentiation from the state of the Great Lord (*maheśatva*).

Becoming one whose fruit is supreme nirvāṇa, by accepting infinite manifestations—just as a jar that accepts a collection of common [reflections] appears with those reflections—he remains capable of both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) as taught in the lower scriptures;
however, the lower [teaching] is not capable of bestowing the higher fruit. Therefore...
It is said:
those established in the meanings of the scriptures of the Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Buddhists,
and Ārhats possess progressively greater capacities, while each preceding one is sublated by the following.

Therefore, while remaining established in the Śaiva Āgama, one who desires to favor others should learn the doctrines of the various Āgamas from those who are experts in the Vaiṣṇava and other traditions.
However, for one who has been consecrated by the Vaiṣṇava initiation and other rites,
there is never eligibility for the Śaiva Āgama without that [Śaiva] initiation once again.

Thus: by that, [it means] by the discourse in the form of what is well-known (*prasiddhi*). By "by that," [it means] by the cognizer (*pratipattr*). Therein, [it means] in that place. At that time, [it means] at that moment. By the particle *eva* (only), he says that even if there is contradiction with other treatises or worldly custom, one should not entertain doubt;
thus he says "in the case of disagreement" (*vigāne*), which refers to the arising of a conflicting deliberation. "Even though unrecorded" (*anibaddhāpi*)...

[The practice] exists merely as a remnant of the performance by the great multitude. Now, one might object: "In a matter beyond perception, there ought to be a final attainment of the fruit through established tradition; however, how can it be determined from any source of valid knowledge that this [tradition] does not touch upon the actual reality? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "free from doubt. For instance:

The nature of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*), which consists in having branches and so forth, is ascertained by a single instance of direct perception that, occurring in the interim, does not encounter any subverting evidence; this ascertainment holds throughout the three times and the three worlds. Thus, because of its establishment beyond doubt, the status of being an external object extends even to names, constellations, and the like.

And in cases such as poison, spirits, or planetary influences, the determination of validity occurs through perception alone. Now, one might ask: "How can it be said that no sublation will arise in the interim? To this, he replies: "It is precisely regarding the unseen object.
[Thus,] liberation comes from initiation.
(102) "There is no liberation equal to initiation"—
from such scriptural authority (*āgama*), there is no possibility of sublation (*bādhaka*) once [the realization] is firmly established; however, in the interim, when a sublation has arisen...

Due to its dissolution, it lacks authority precisely for that reason; "for this very reason" means because scripture (*āgama*) consists of nothing other than what is well-known (*prasiddhi*), for that cause. Thus he says:
"But others, not knowing this, having heard it from others, worship [it]."
Even they, being devoted to sacred learning, surely transcend death.
"Thus:
'This is merit'—[and so forth]. This statement by the Sage [Vyāsa] was cited by Bhartṛhari (*Vākyapadīya* 1.40) to establish the authority of the *āgama*."

Since it was presented for recitation (*ḍhyāya*), it has been written here by way of that [reciter]. Likewise, he shows that the composition of specific sentences is called "treatise" (*śāstra*) here precisely for the sake of strengthening the context, by means of the word "nanu.
Thus, it is threefold: as intuition (*pratibhā*), and as consisting of both the established and the unestablished.
Having shown the first [type of] renown, he now shows another form of it as well with the words "another also.

Among these three types of renown, one need not seek a basis in another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, in the case of the word of a reliable person (*āptavāda*), that must indeed be sought. Reliability (*āpti*) is the thorough comprehension of the object to be spoken; and from that...
One who possesses the realization of the subject matter to be expressed is an *āpta* (a reliable authority). For this very reason,
even if it occurs in the form of worldly speech or the form of scriptural discourse, and even though it depends upon a specific form and an author, it remains indeed subject to doubt.
Because doubt is absent when that which serves as its fundamental basis—the means of valid cognition—is present. Thus he says, "and [he is] authoritative" (*āptaśca*).
The term "free from doubt" (*nirvicikitsā*) is a qualifier of "cognition" (*pratīti*) when taken separately, or of "practice" (*anuṣṭhāna*) when taken as a whole.
By the phrase "by that also," it is meant "by what is agreed upon by the authoritative. "It certainly exists" refers to experience, meaning it is not the case that it does not exist.

He states its non-deniability: that person who is to be instructed, whose knowledge derived from a trustworthy person (āpta) has arisen as being rooted in another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), does not suspect it, nor does he conceive of it as being of the nature of doubt, error, or ignorance; him—the person to be instructed—he [the teacher] [instructs] in that manner.

No one is capable of turning back, by any means whatsoever, that person who has attained the realization of the reality taught in the words of trustworthy beings (*āpta*)— realization which culminates in the performance [of the teaching] through further instruction— since he is the one to be instructed.

In that regard, concerning knowledge connected with a reliable person (*āpta*), one stands by resorting to the category of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). When it is said by a reliable person, "This was known by me directly," the person being instructed conceives [the knowledge] thus: "I myself have perceived this directly. And even a child does not [doubt] what has been directly perceived, even by means of hundreds of arguments.
It is capable of being turned back. As others have said:

"The nature of reality, which is free from affliction and is the true object, cannot be subverted by erroneous cognitions, even if there is effort [to do so], because the intellect has a partiality for that [true nature]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.223)

Thus, it has been explained that because the inclination of the intellect (*buddhi*) is so firmly established as to be incapable of being uprooted by doubt, this very state is the pervasive basis for validity (*prāmāṇya*). Therefore, wherever this [inclination] exists, there validity itself exists; hence, cognitions such as those concerning the connection with action and so forth are true.

Prior [to that] (2|2|1): It is the very nature of tradition (*āgama*) that it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it consists of uncontradicted reflection. If it is asked, "How is its reliability (*āptatva*) ascertained?", he says: "By specific activities. For even in that case, why is the easy discernment of the effect not accepted? "At every step" refers to the authoritative statement of the scripture.
For instance, the status of being an authoritative person (*āptatā*) is well-established in the grammars of Pāṇini, Vararuci, and others, but not in those of Akṣapāda and the like.

By the term "the word of an authoritative person" (*puruṣāptavāda*), the inclusion of the "word of an authoritative person in the world" (*lokāptavāda*) is intended. Thus it is said: "the word of an authoritative person belonging to a [specific] school (*caraṇāptavāda*). And this "word of an authoritative person" [encompasses] the previously mentioned divisions of scripture (*āgama*) as appropriate.

He favors [beings] by means of exposition and other such methods. For that very reason, all scripture (*āgama*) has been subsumed under the term "instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśa*) by the venerable Patañjali and others. Having stated the essential nature of scripture, it was demonstrated that both perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture are more powerful than inference (*anumāna*).
