He concludes with "tadevam" (thus, in this way) in order to corroborate that very point. "Sarvameva" (all indeed) [is used] because the validity of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) does not fail even in the case of error. "In the manner described" means by means of practice (*abhyāsa*) and so forth.
"Ārṣam" (the state of a seer) refers to that which consists of worldly renown arising from the constant presence of the Veda and other scriptures in the form of intuitive flash (*pratibhā*).
That which has been set forth by the Sage—who is accepted as a correct seer and an authoritative person—is indeed a sublater of inference;
for [it is] perception and scripture that [sublate it].
(page 104)

That which is to be manifested and that which is to be reflected upon are, respectively, devoid of dependence on anything else through the medium of manifestation and reflection. For in perception, reflection occurs by way of manifestation, whereas in other cases the reverse is true. But in inference, however—

In the case of an object of inference (*anumeya*), there is no connection with manifestation and reflective awareness (*prakāśa-vimarśa*) that does not depend upon the manifestation and reflection of another entity that is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*). Because it thus depends [on something else], this cognition (*pramiti*) is remote from the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Furthermore, it has been stated that even in that case, the knowledge of such invariable concomitance is difficult to obtain. Nor should it be argued regarding the scripture (*āgama*):
Since the investigation of meaning is preceded by the investigation of the word, there too [in the case of meaning] there would be dependence and so forth;
for there is no investigation of meaning other than the investigation of the word, because the word consists of the investigation of both itself and others.

This jar—[as demonstrated] in [the passage] "ghaṭo'yam" (1.5.20)—is established. Now, an objection: since not everyone accepts the authority of scripture (*āgama*), how can you assert its independence (*anapekṣatva*) when it has fallen into a state of dispute? [We reply: It is indeed accepted...
He says, "It is known through common usage (*prasiddhi*). [Objection: But surely the meaning of words such as *chāga* (goat) will be understood through a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*);

what is the use of common usage here? To this he replies, "By its four-footedness. That too is included within the defining characteristic. [Objection: If it is argued that it will be understood from usage in the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth—
In that regard as well, he says "even previously" (*purāpi ca*) to show that the status of relying upon what is well-known (*prasiddhi-śaraṇatva*) is not contradicted. And thus he says:

"in whatever matters [are known] in the world. "Even previously" means even in the very first sūtra. An authoritative person (*āpta*) is not only one whose objects are perceived or inferred; he is also one who relies upon other authorities—thus he says "instruction" (*upadeśa*).

Thus [it is said]. For in the scriptures (āgamas), the teachers are indeed recited as authoritative (āpta) in this very way. Now, regarding those who themselves do not know the meaning of the scripture, yet understand its meaning through traditional succession—does their authority in that matter exist or not? To this he says: "Even in the case of the succession of instruction."

Even without the comprehension of scriptural texts, if there were only a tradition of oral instruction, it would follow that the scripture of a reliable person (*āptāgama*) itself would be [the basis] therein; thus, its status as a reliable scripture and its established nature would result, by virtue of being both intermediate and fundamental through the quality of reliability (*āptatā*).
Because they possess the nature of being established as the beginningless tradition of the Supreme Lord,
such gurus also become instructors for others; for this very reason, it is so stated in all the scriptures of the Āgamas.
"It is recited as knowledge passed from mouth to mouth, having come from ear to ear," and so forth.
In the reading "from the recitation of all the scriptural texts" (*samastāgamagranthapāṭhāt*), others read *nañ* (the negative particle) and explain [it as follows]:

And as for the objection regarding the "wound": it is not the case that some read the entire corpus of scriptural texts (*āgama*), but rather they proceed through the instruction of the guru-paramparā alone;
or alternatively, even if some do read them, they do not read them all, and yet they too are gurus; or else, the introduction [to the objection] is as follows:

There is a certain form of scripture that benefits only oneself, which pertains to the triad beginning with the *samayin*; in that case, there is merely the oral tradition of instruction (*upadeśapāramparya*). However, that which benefits both oneself and others exists when one possesses the status of a Guru; it arises precisely from the recitation of the entire scriptural text for the sake of understanding its meaning, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, the status of being an authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) does not apply there, nor does established consensus (*prasiddhi*) culminate therein. For this very reason, it is stated in various scriptures:
"One should again appoint as a Guru one who is proficient in the *Catuṣpāt-saṃhitā*."
Thus,
even if he is devoid of all [external] characteristics, a guru who possesses knowledge is desired.
Thus.

"And because it has been declared that a guru who possesses well-practiced knowledge is the giver of liberation. Thus, this was previously explained with the intention of referring to the status of a "guru" in the sense of being one who is proficient in a single portion of the worldly conventions well-known to the people; however, [the other type] is that which pertains to the entirety [of the teachings] as stated in the scriptures, arrived at through the sequence of the ritual procedure (*prakriyā*).
"By way of emphasizing the importance [of the teacher]"—this has been explained by our teachers in both ways:

that the authoritative person (āpta) is situated in the middle, and that renown is rooted in him; thus, he is primary, because in all the scriptures of the tradition (āgama), the teachers are recited [at the beginning].
Thus has this been handed down through successive tradition.
(Page 106)
"I too previously obtained this from Aghora...
and so forth. Regarding the authority that has been stated, he analyzes whether that [authority] is eternal or otherwise:
"And that" refers to what was stated as being authoritative.

And regarding the passage "only [that which is] distinct from the object of cognition... (1.5.21), this was stated previously: "Just as in the case of perception," the aspect of appearance (*ābhāsāṃśa*) is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśāṃśa*) is the fruit (*phala*). Now, one might object: let this be so in the case of inference, which consists of cognition; but what of it?
Since scripture (*āgama*) consists of the form of sound, it is insentient (*jaḍa*); how then can this established order [of authority] apply to it?
Anticipating this doubt, he demonstrates that even in our system, scripture is not insentient, by saying "even scripture.
Now, let this be so regarding what is bound and unbound within the form of common consensus; but what of authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*)?

How could that cognition consisting of words, which is connected to a reliable person (*āpta*), be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for another in the form of a direct experience? For [the cognition] that arises in the cognizer by way of the words uttered by him rests solely within that cognizer and is distinct from the reliable person.

How could there be a relationship with a trustworthy person (*āpta*)? He shows that there is no fault in either case by saying, "even of the trustworthy person. The particle *ca* indicates the previously mentioned doubt, and the phrase "let there be the status of subordinate and principal" has been stated.
"For this very reason" means: because at that time there would be the consequence of their non-distinction; for, in the case of the speaker...

This sequential sound has its root in a cognition whose essence is non-sequential reflective awareness; thus, when it is transmitted [to another], it culminates in cognition because it is non-different from that [original awareness]. The term "utility" (*upayoga*) implies "as scripture" (*āgamatvena*). For if it were merely accessible to auditory perception, it would be like color and other such objects.

It is merely the object, not the form of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, [one might object]: "The signifier (*vācaka*) is the *āgama* (scriptural tradition), and that first resides in the speaker and then in the listener; how, then, can there be identity (*tādātmya*) between two things existing at different times? He says "the state of being the subject" (*pramātṛtā*) to show this is not so. The status of being a signifier exists on the plane of internal self-awareness (*antaḥsaṃvedana*), and that [plane]...

It is untouched by time; however, due to the metaphorical application [of properties] such as the body, there is the conventional usage of temporal distinctions—thus, everything is faultless. By this much, it has been established that that which is the eternal nature of consciousness in the Lord is not an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for within the Lord, there is no object of knowledge (*prameya*) ending with the principle of *vidyā*.
Because it rests solely in the form "I am," there is no separate manifestation whatsoever,
even for the omniscient when touched by time.

Due to the contraction of that subjectivity, even knowledge which extends to all objects of cognition is indeed touched by time; it is only when there is an intensification of the eternally active present state that their knowledge is conventionally expressed as "they know everything. || 2 ||

But has it not been stated that "cognition has as its object a single denotation" (2.3.2)? If, in that case, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is so [the object], then there would be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for every appearance.

How could this be logical? For when there is a mixing of appearances, the sūtra is differentiated according to preference, according to need, and according to proficiency, in order to pacify the doubt that [the object] is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Even the appearance [of an object] is a single entity when established through synthesis.

Although, at first glance, it is well known to the world through habit and lack of discrimination that "the jar" refers to a single object, nevertheless, this [object] does not fail to admit of being analyzed into distinct parts through discrimination (*viveka*). And this discrimination is threefold: by way of independence, according to purpose, and by relying on prior established knowledge.

[Objection: "If that is so, how can there be unity of the object? [The author] replies: Reflection (*vimarśa*), which constitutes the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for appearances manifesting as distinct, sometimes rests upon each individual appearance where the linguistic usage of a universal (*sāmānya*) occurs; at other times, it does so by way of the distinction between the subordinate and the principal (*guṇapradhānatayā*).
In this context, that which is called "synthesis" (*anusandhāna*) is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consisting of the mixing [of cognitions] such as "this is thus. Therein,

even when a single object consisting of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been established by the final [cognition], the appearances [arise] without transgressing either a preference or autonomy, or the desire for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), or the conventional usage of elders.

"They are divided" is the meaning of the Sūtra. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), even though the verb is used in the singular, it is not incorrect; for [the author] is stating that unity is indeed appropriate there. Therefore, one should consider the fact that it was not discussed in the introduction (*avatāraṇikā*) as the reason for the restriction to a single [interpretation]. Hereafter...
Thus,
regarding the phrase "of the lights of separate lamps" (2.3.7),
since it will be stated in this manner, how then can that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) be a configuration?

It is an object of mere cognition; and how could it consist merely of the nature of being made of clay? For one manifestation cannot be of the same nature as another manifestation that is apprehended by a different manifestation—even in the case of a jar.
The objection that is raised— that there would be the undesirable consequence of identity with the cloth— is not valid; the reason for this is stated as "because it is prior."

In this section beginning with *tātkālikākṣa* (1.8.1), the variety of appearances has been established as the Lord’s sovereignty (*svātantrya*) in joining and separating them. By which— by which power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-sāmarthya*), that very [consciousness] is thus...

That which exists as "earth" and so forth is that which is designated merely by its configuration (*sanniveśa*), without regard for its being made of clay, silver, or other such qualities. What is it like? It is said: it is a single form qualified by other appearances—such as "made of clay," "red," or "elevated"—and because it is the very nature of the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), it is purely a configuration.

Even when there is an appearance distinct from the appearance of the universal (sāmānya), that which arises is non-different from the form of color (*rūpa*), which was previously apprehended as the mere configuration (*saṃniveśamātra*) of the universal. The same applies to "being made of clay" (*mṛṇmayatā*).
He extends this [principle] to other cases with the word "thus" (*evam*), referring to "largeness" (*mahattva*) and so forth. That which is each one, unmixed, and manifold—
The universal (*sāmānya*) is manifold; those reflective cognitions (*parāmarśa*) which are determined as having that [universal] as their object,
when they subsequently operate upon a single particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), [perceive] that universal-nature even though it has become a particular,
by means of what was previously apprehended at the time of the conventional usage of the cognition of the universal.

They bring about unity through a generality (*sāmānya*) that is distinct, unmixed, numerous, and has as its object the apprehension of that [thing] alone; and this very process is the "attainment of unity" (*ekatvāpādana*). By this much, the commentary on the portion of the sūtra beginning with "in one" (*ekasmin*) and ending with "in the object" (*vastuni*) has been explained.

He explains the commentary on the remainder of the sūtra with the word "punar" (again). By the word "hi," he states that this meaning serves as the reason for the function of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vyāpāra*) which consists in the re-manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*) of the object within the scope of the preceding sūtra. He shows that one's own will (*svecchā*) is operative either in the external organs (*bahiṣkaraṇa*) or in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

"Part by part" (*bhāgaśaḥ*) and "effort" (*prayatna*) [are the two factors]. "Now" (*atha*) means "if" (*yadiva*), that is to say. Even regarding the configuration (*sanniveśa*), he shows another variety arising from one's own will: "in a painting" (*citre*). Whether it be the variety consisting of a broad base and so forth, or merely the state of being a configuration, that generality (*sāmānya*) appears. Here he states an illustration.
For instance: the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is like a wall, and the division of universals (*sāmānyavibhāga*) is like the division of lines;
thus it occurs even in a single thing according to one's preference.

When the meaning of "distinct appearance" has been clarified by the analogy of lines in a mural painting, [the author] analyzes the phrase "according to the object" (*yathārthatvam*) with the words "as mere formlessness" (*arūpamātratayā*), which means "without regard for the division of its parts. He explains the phrase "according to proficiency" (*yathāvyutpatti*) with the words "without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇaiva*). This too—

This [particular] also possesses branches and so forth as its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); for that very reason, there arises the cognition: "These objects possess branches and so forth. Even in that case, through proficiency in the linguistic usage of elders, there occurs a manifestation of distinctions—such as "This is a *dhava* tree," "This is a *khadira* tree," and "This is a *kadara* tree"—for the sake of clear identification.
Interest, purposefulness, and proficiency have been demonstrated through various examples; yet even with respect to a single particular (svalakṣaṇa), such as a jar, all three can indeed be applied.
Just as appearances are differentiated by being long, round, upright, human, smoke, sandalwood, and so forth, even though they do not differ in terms of space and time.
In the same way, the various appearances such as the pot, the substance, the gold, and the brilliance—which produce distinct effects—are the referents of words. (5)

The purport of these two sūtras is as follows: by means of a well-known distinction—pertaining to both the insentient and the sentient, arising from [the subject's] inclination (ruci), and consisting in the manifestation of a universal (sāmānya) as described in the first verse—he clarifies, in the subsequent verse, an unknown distinction of manifestations residing in the jar. Thus, the commentator explains the pair.

Explaining that the two [previous] examples have different objects, he explains one example that is non-insentient (ajaḍa-rūpa). For indeed, when one’s eyes are fixed precisely on the upper parts of a jar, it appears as long. Thus he says: "in another part," which refers to that which belongs to the other parts.

The "place" (*deśa*) refers to those very [objects], or it is the place by excluding them; therein lies the application of the eye and the mind. The term *tryaśra* is a *dvigu* compound ending in a suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*). The phrase "according to one's preference" (*yathāruci*) is an illustration of what was stated in the preceding sūtra (the example concerning the teeth has been made); [it refers to] long and round.

Thus much [has been said]. He provides an example according to the intended meaning (*yathārthitva*) with the word *ūrdhvapuruṣa* (upright person), whereas for the case of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the example is *dhūmacāndanatā* (the state of being smoke-white). And since no other illustration was shown there regarding the derivative sense (*vṛtti*), he says "in the case of derivation" (*vyutpattau*). Not only is there an example here, [but...]
The word "also" (*api*) indicates that even in the case of an illustration (*udāharaṇa*), another well-known example has been stated. Now,
[on page 110]:

Perceptual knowledge is being investigated here; raising the doubt as to whether that is possible in the case of an illustration, he shows by means of the words of Bhartṛhari that it is indeed possible:
"That which cannot be described to others arises only from practice."
"In [the case of] jewels, silver, and so forth... (*Vākyapadīya* 1.35).

By this, [the author], demonstrating that [the knowledge of these objects] does not derive from the word of a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) nor from inference (*ānumānikatva*), has stated that it is perceptual through practice (*ābhyāsika-pratyakṣatva*). Consequently, it is clearly shown that this [knowledge] arises from proficiency (*vyutpatti*). And here, "iti" [indicates the end of the citation].
In all three examples as well, the reason for the claim that "it is not a different particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)" is the phrase beginning with "place" (*deśa*).

He explains [the phrase] "does not touch" by saying "here. The state of being a single particular characteristic refers to the stage of reflecting upon the pair, such as "long" and "round. "Possessing smoke" (*sadhūmatva*) is the universal (*jāti*).

"Sandalwood-ness" is the universal (jāti); "oneness" is the state of being a single particular (ekasvalakṣaṇatā). Having thus explained the illustrative verse, he explains the corresponding statement with the word "evam" (thus).
He establishes its status as the subject of the illustration with the phrase "anupalakṣya," meaning it is impossible to perceive [the universal therein].

Therefore, in that particular where there is a distinction among unestablished appearances (*ābhāsa*), the possibility of a distinction in manifestation—that is, a distinction in luminosity (*prakāśana*)—regarding the various properties (*dharma*) which are themselves distinctions of appearance, should be followed according to the analogy. How so? He says: "the desire to speak" (*avadhitsādi*).

The meaning is: "by relying on the threefold distinction of inclination (ruci) and so forth. Thus, in this context, the pot itself is stated as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) by way of its well-known distinctions, such as the appearance of height and length;

however, the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) is by way of its less well-known distinctions, such as existence (*sattva*) and potness (*ghaṭatva*). Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that here..."
The distinctness of the manifestation [is such that] the word "existent" (*san*) is simply something else; this [the opponent] does not tolerate, saying "no.
For in that case, there would be a mere synonymy, as in "existent jar" (*san ghaṭaḥ*), and it is not thus—this is the intention. [Objection:
But surely, since the manifestation "existent" also rests upon the jar...
A manifestation such as a cloth or a cart implies another manifestation, and therefore it is distinct from the manifestation of a jar;
however, he refutes the notion that there is some other thing called a "manifestation of existence" by saying "nor even...
This is precisely what you yourself have accepted. He says "for when... because this [distinction] is logical according to our view.
At the point of formal admission (*abhyupagama*) [on page 111], the phrase "among them" refers to the pot and so forth, out of the midst of those appearances such as cloth and the like.
The manifestation of some particular, indeterminate, existent object is possible within this cognition,

because the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) intended to be established here pertains to the real particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), and not to a cloth or a jar. For example, it is like a dispute between two parties over a wager concerning whether or not there is [something] in this house.

By the statement "something exists, something exists," he shows that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is possible here; thus, "existence" (*sattā*) refers to the appearance of "being" (*sat*), which— whether as a particular delimited by space and so forth,
or as a universal characterized by the absence of such delimitation— is mutually distinct from one another and distinct from anything else.

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "it exists because of the appearance as cloth," and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "But 'existent' is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) residing within another appearance; how can that be called causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? For causal efficiency is an effect, not an essential nature (*svabhāva*. To this, he replies with the words beginning "reflective awareness," and so on.
The mental steadfastness (*dhṛti*) that serves as the cause for avoiding the breaking of the heart is also a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

The suspicion of redundancy regarding the constant appearance (*sadābhāsa*) is countered by the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*) in the commentary; for when a single word is employed, its nature as both a universal and a particular is understood.

But surely, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), regarding the appearances such as "pot" and "gold" that are to be discussed, the exclusion of other-natures (*anyātmatā-parihāra*) will be stated: namely, that the appearance of "pot" which exists in a pot does not exist in cloth and so forth, and the appearance of "gold" which exists in gold does not exist in earthenware and so forth; in the same way, the appearance of existence (*sattābhāsa*) is also [to be understood].

Why was it so stated? To this it is replied: "Because it is excluded [from the category of external objects]. For the manifestation as "existent" (sat) is indeed distinct from the manifestations of jars and the like; it is merely that which is subsequently determined by the mind. (2.2.3)
According to the principle thus stated, this [pure object] is manifested by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and not by the external organs; therefore, it cannot be attained in its pure state.
Consequently, the refutation of those other non-existent manifestations of objects—which are distinct from the real—is not mentioned in the commentary (*vṛtti*).

That which appears as "existent" does not exist in absences that are distinct from jars and so forth; this is what is meant by "not stated" in the commentary (*vṛtti*). "That" refers to the state of having cloth and so forth as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*), as stated in the commentary.
"The general term" refers to what occurs in the commentary. "Therein" means among the modifications of clay.
"By means of inclusion and exclusion" (ūhāpohābhyām) means by means of the cognitions of concomitance and non-concomitance; for it is not the case that whatever is [the object of] concomitance—

"That which is to be grasped by [valid] cognition is precisely the object of the awareness of exclusion"—thus, the connection is that since a distinction between manifestations (*ābhāsa*) must necessarily exist here, there is the establishment of difference. By the phrase "of one's own self," he asserts the non-deniability [of this] as established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). In this way, due to the distinction between manifestations...

Having explained the phrase "producing distinct objects," he explains the term "of the resonance" (*dhvani*) with the words "likewise by means of sounds. To provide even a slight explanation of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) from the sūtra, he analyzes the commentary beginning with "Caitra" and so forth, using the passage starting with "state" (*avasthā*) and so on. This is done because [the object] possesses the singular nature of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

He demonstrates that the word "Caitra" functions by way of a universal form (*sāmānyarūpatva*), even for one who is agreed upon [as such], with the verse beginning "svalakṣaṇaikā... and so forth. [The opponent might argue: "Recognition will occur merely through the fact of being a single continuum;
there is no need for a universal here, as the Buddhist (*saugata*) maintains. He refutes this:

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means if one does not accept its nature as a universal (*sāmānya-rūpatā*). "By the unseen" (*adṛṣṭena*) means where there is an uninterrupted continuity of the cognition of successive similar arisings; that is to say, [it refers to the case] up until that point. Now, if in this way a universal nature enters into everything, when would there ever be a pure particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)?

He dispels the doubt that "it exists" with the words beginning "because of being a universal," and so forth. "Because of non-manifestation" means that while this [universal] has arisen, it is indistinct; however, when it has not yet arisen, for the subject of Māyā, this entire state of "I am all this"—the level of Śrī Sadāśiva—is the nature of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Precisely for that reason...
He says, "simultaneous with this," by which he indicates the non-application of inference due to the non-application of the [necessary] convention (*samaya*).

"At another time" means when there is an absence of predominance of states. "Like a whole whose parts are extended" means that the whole (*avayavin*) appears as extended in space, whereas the substratum of the states (*avasthātṛ*), on the other hand, [is not so], because of the distinction between the states.
When there is the intention to express a continuity and unity— such as "Oh, how indeed this long-lived one has perceived the reality of worldly transactions"—
then a single [entity] extended over time should be made to appear, just like the appearance of a whole (avayavin). For instance,
just as a solid mass manifests many parts such as the head and hands in a single moment, so too [does the person appear].
Likewise, the cognition of a whole that apprehends form either accepts from birth onwards the appearance of its own infinite states.

The cognition of the substratum (*avasthātṛ-buddhi*) grasps a single, solid form. Now, just as when an object extended over time is perceived through its distinct individualities at each successive state, a single unifying continuity—a universal form following after the individual states—is conceptually constructed; so too [is it] in the case of what is extended in space.

He dispels the misconception—namely, "Why then could that [cognition] not be postulated even at a single moment?"—with the word "nanu" (surely). For in that case, the cognition of Caitra does not arise for each individual part independently of the synthesis of the parts;

this is because there is no such perception as "the head alone is Caitra. However, in the case of one who possesses any one of the states beginning with childhood, [the cognition arises] regarding the possessor of those states...

Even in the absence of synthesis, the cognition of Caitra arises; however, when the cognition of the head occurs, it necessarily brings about the synthesis of other limbs such as the hand. Therefore, even with respect to the head, such a cognition of Caitra occurs—it is not that it does not occur at all—and thus the term "primary" (mukhya) is employed. That very point—

Causal efficiency does not belong to a single manifestation alone; rather, because it is invariably accompanied by the search for another manifestation—just as when one seeks fire, one simultaneously seeks a vessel for it—one searches for that which is indeterminate precisely through those manifestations, reflections, and causal efficiencies. Thus, the manifestation itself is the reality.

Based on the intention of what is more well-known, what is well-known, and what is not well-known, even a single object is divided into various forms in the Sūtra, such as "long," "round," "smoke," and "an existing jar. || 5 ||
[Objection: But in this way, a single object consisting of [attributes] such as "pot-ness" and "redness" would not be a real entity (*vastu*).
[Reply: To this, he says by means of the Sūtra:
"Furthermore, due to the difference in appearances, there is restricted causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for entities."
Because they appear as having a common substratum, they are non-different.

When manifestations are mixed, a certain manifestation is primary; it is the common substratum for the others. The relation they have with that [primary manifestation] is *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical coreferentiality). The appearance characterized by that [relation], which conforms to its own nature, is here [expressed as] "this" (*eṣa*) and "now" (*idānīm*).

Sustained by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the sentence-meaning "the jar exists," those [entities] which, due to that cause, become non-different and attain the state of a single particular (*ekasvalakṣaṇa*), yet do not abandon their own individual differences, possess another kind of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) consisting of a collective form; however, when there is a difference in the reflective awareness of appearances (*ābhāsa-vimarśa-bheda*), there is yet another, determined [causal efficiency].

(114) It has the nature of being exclusively one by one. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates a specific distinction. And because it does not abandon its particularity (*bhedāparityāga*), even though it is a unique characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*), that which consists of the mere form of appearance is precisely what is colored by a common individual (*samānavyakti*).

The meaning of the aphorism is this: in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no universal; however, when there is a reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) solely of the appearance of a pure jar, it possesses the nature of a universal by virtue of its mere capacity (*yogyatāmātreṇa*). In the commentary on the phrase "the unity of the manifold," the form of relation was recalled. [Objection: But how can that which performs manifold causal functions (*arthakriyā*) be one?
He says: "By means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For even when one makes [something] one, it is not by the mere act of making it so that one's parents are pleased;

rather, it must be accepted as being [so] by means of valid cognition. And that [valid cognition] consists of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of appearances, and it does not uproot that reflective awareness—this he states by employing the term "force" (*bala*). He explains the intended meaning of the commentary (*vṛtti*).

Regarding the phrase "pratyābhāsam" (for each manifestation): here, "atra" (here) refers to the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with "in one [manifestation]" (*ekasmin*). Now, if things manifest in that way, from where does their state of being internally latent (*antarlīnatva*) arise? He dispels this delusion by stating:
"because the reality of things consists of manifestation itself" (*prathātmaikatvācca vastutattvasya*). Now, if those very causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*) [belong] to those manifestations...

If they are distinct, then let them remain so; why is this unity superimposed upon them in vain? He says it is "in vain" by the phrase "the manifestation as one. This will be explained in the *Pṛthagdīpa-sūtra* (2.3.7).

Furthermore, from that [text], unity is established through both appearance (*ābhāsana*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), as well as through the performance of a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*).

The word *api* implies: "What fault could there be if even their state of being an agent (*yākāritva*), cherished by another, were to place itself in their hand? The term *niruktaḥ* is explained by splitting it as *nir-bhajya*. By the word *punaḥ*, a distinction that is essentially non-dual (*abheda-ātmā*) is illuminated;
specifically, the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) exists simultaneously through both multiplicity and unity, and not otherwise.
The word *punaḥ* here denotes repetition, as in expressions such as *punar bhuṅkte* ("he eats again"). Thus he says, "but not...

Having raised the objection, "How can there be the conventional usage of a 'locus' (*adhikaraṇa*) when there is only the appearance of separateness? he replies, "And the locus... "Being so" (*tathātva*) means inherence (*samavāya*). This is what is intended by the phrase beginning with "this is what is meant," and so forth.

Regarding the term *samānādhikaraṇa*: although the specific verbal usage— that "having a common substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇatva*) is "co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)— is not intended here, nevertheless, in reality, there is indeed a difference in meaning between the words *nīla* (blue) and *utpala* (lotus), whereas for Caitra and Maitra there is co-referentiality.

(Page 115) Because there is an absolute difference between the two cognitions [of] "the same substratum" (*samānam adhikaraṇam*) and so forth. Now, one might object: "This co-referentiality and the like is produced by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); it is not a real entity (*vastu*), and that [reality] has nothing to do with it. To this he says: "The cognition... (*buddhi*).

Although inherence (*samavāya*) and the like are indeed the nature of relation, and relation itself is the unification of the manifold into one, nevertheless, inherence is a distinct category (*pṛthak-padārtha*).
Likewise, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth are either an unseen form (*adṛṣṭa-rūpa*) or a separate entity.

For those whose view is that the nature of *dharma* is indeed distinct [from the substance], with that intention it was stated separately that the connection possesses the quality of favoring all; yet, even so, the unity of the manifold is real. For instance, after describing the nature of inherence (*samavāya*), His Honor declared:

"The tradition from the predecessors states: 'He favors that power called inherence (samavāya), which manifests both difference and non-difference; this is what is meant by 'relation'. (Vākyapadīya 3.11)

"She is the power even of powers; she is the quality even of qualities" (Vākyapadīya 3.5), and so forth. "For this purpose" means that [the term] denotes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and not merely appearance (*ābhāsa*).
The connection is: "considering unity to be contradictory. The reason for such a misconception is as follows:

The incapacity to provide support. The suffix *śatṛ* is used for the present participle. Just as one rolling down a mountain, while clutching at kusha and kāśa grass, falls along with it and that [grass] does not provide even the slightest protection for him; likewise, the recourse to logic (*nyāya*), even when being employed, does not [protect].

It serves to nourish the subject at hand; thus it is said: "Their grasping at *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses [is futile], for their nature as a distinct category of entity from *samavāya* and the like, as well as their inherent capacity for function, is like the purity of the waters of the Gaṅgā," and so forth. For in this position:

"Those two entities and that which is other than them"—thus the thorn of this objection is truly impossible to extract; however, in this philosophical system there is no contradiction whatsoever, as he demonstrates with the word "intellect" (*buddhi*). Being manifested by the intellect is the defining characteristic of existence. In that regard also, the object—
If existence (*sattva*) is characterized by its capacity for causal efficiency (*kriyākaraṇa*), then "the reality of the thing" (*vastusattva*) is merely an additional name for it.
This much must be distinguished: namely, that which constitutes the multiplicity of what is essentially one.
(Page 116)
"Would that object be real or not? To this also it is said: "In this way, between the real and the unreal," and so forth.

He demonstrates the impossibility of its appearing [as such] with the words "for if it were a being" (*bhāve hi*); for it is "transformed" (*rupyate*) on all sides (*samantāt*), and thus that which is transformed in every respect cannot in any way be said not to have been transformed. This is what is meant by "the manifestation of a single [form]" (*ekaprathā*).
The meaning is that it is called "first" because of its oneness. || 6 ||

Now, is it not the case that there is no single causal efficiency here for the sake of which a single particular (svalakṣaṇa) is accepted? Indeed, let it be granted that there are many causal efficiencies from many appearances;
on the contrary, distinct appearances intermingle.

When this is said, the cause of the restriction must be stated; therefore, the Sūtra is provided to convince one who asks how it is that the appearances of water and fire, or the appearances of jars, cloths, and so forth, do not become intermingled.
Just as the lights of separate lamps [merging] in the ocean, or the currents [of rivers],
have non-contradictory appearances and yet perform a single function, so too is the cognition of unity.

Individual lamp-flames, being extremely subtle, do not provide the capacity for vision when separate; however, when they coalesce within a single dwelling, they do so. In that case, there are no causal functions (*arthakriyā*) which existed previously even when they were separate. This is like the streams fallen into the ocean.
Let those things be called "wondrously impetuous undertakings" because they are produced by a mass of exceedingly numerous waves;
what collection of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is there in this? Similarly, [the expressions] "a golden pot," "red," or "large"—therefore, it is fit for the ritual bathing of the Śiva-liṅga.

Since it performs only a single purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) consisting of intense pleasure, how could that which performs it be a single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)? For it has been stated that the reality of an object for worldly people consists in its capacity to perform a purposeful action.
As for what was said regarding the "cause of restriction" and so forth, it is replied: for those very [things]...
Their compatibility consists precisely in their being mixed together, not in the case of the appearance of form, the appearance of wind, and so forth;

moreover, even their opposition exists solely by virtue of the power of *niyati* (destiny). That which is a single object belonging to separate lamp-lights—namely, that which consists of their convergence within a house, or in a vast receptacle such as the ocean—[is the result of this power].
Just as there is a single object related to streams, which consists of the form of a large aggregate of water; by means of that single [object], an effect is produced.
(page 117)

"The cognition of unity" (*aikyadhīḥ*) refers to the cognition of oneness (*aikyabuddhiḥ*) and the single reflective awareness (*ekavimarśaḥ*) characterized by it, as well as the single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*); likewise, the cognition of unity—whose nature has been explained—is to be produced through the merging of those appearances, such as "jar," "red," and "elevated," which are mutually non-contradictory, into a single essence consisting of their own specific character (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus [it is said].

This is the meaning of the Sūtra: "ekadhā" (in one way). The form "aikadhyam" is derived from "ekasya bhāvaḥ" (the state of being one), and thus its ending in the vowel "a" is justified; however, others remember that according to the rule "anudarśanam amuñcantāt svārthe," the suffix *dhyamuñ* is applied even after a word ending in *dhyam*. The connection is that by means of this explanation found in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the following is stated. What is that?

He says, "In the Sūtra," and so forth. Now, one might ask: "Should there be three *ca*s in the commentary, or only one? To this he replies: "By the *ca*. This means that by a single, indivisible *ca*, the action beginning with "is gathered" (*samuccitā*) is drawn in;
however, the remaining intention is that by the second [the particle], there is a gathering of substances (*dravya-samuccaya*). Precisely because it is contained therein...

Thus, even that which has entered into thought may become a real entity (*vastu*), and here "entity" means a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). Now, one might object: "The state of being a qualifier is observed [in cases] such as 'blue' and 'yellow,' just as you have a blue cloth, while yellow is most pleasing; therefore, let that too be fastened by you. To this, someone says in reply: "Only blue."

"‘It is drunk by me’—this supports [the distinction between] quality (guṇa) and possessor of quality (guṇin), and so forth. It is called a ‘quality’ (guṇa) because it is multiplied—that is, superimposed—upon something through a common property such as loveliness; that upon which it is superimposed is the ‘possessor of quality. Therefore, it is stated that such grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is metaphorical (aupacārika)."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), he provides an example for the metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) such as "the prohibited [food] and so forth," or "it is yellow, it is blue," or "it is not," using the phrase beginning with "lion" and so on. Now, one might object:
even in the absence of a single, variegated, or wondrous causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the cognition of a "beverage" (*pānaka*) is observed.
"No," he says, [referring to] "the unlearned. He explains the commentary (*vṛtti*) with the words "appearances such as whiteness" and so forth.

Having explained the commentary by dividing the sentence in accordance with the first established usage, he now explains it as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) by relying on the logic of the treatise (*śāstra-nyāya*), beginning with "atha. No.

He considers that the compound *abrāhmaṇaḥ* is not a negative (*nañ*) compound because the sentence has the same meaning as the term *vṛtti* (conduct/lifestyle), and because negative compounds are non-eternal (*anitya*). Furthermore, the learned (*śiṣṭa*) employ it in this very way;
for instance, the sage Akṣapāda [states]: [text follows].
(Page 118) "Among these, delusion is the most evil, because for one who is not deluded, the others do not arise" (4.1.6), so he said.
For this is the meaning here: "because for one who is not deluded, the others do not arise. Although [the causes] are manifold—

Although the yoga of manifestation has been taught, there is still no fullness regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, the word "also" (*api*) applies to that as well. And for that reason, the second "also" indicates that other things—namely, those whose form consists of the manifestation of space and time—must also be joined therein. Without such joining, however, there is no fullness; but when they are joined, there is fullness even if other things are not joined. *Sva-* [refers to] self...

Regarding the characteristic [of the universal], he says: "Precisely because of the difference in place and time. Now, someone might argue: "Let that which appears as a single entity in the manner described above be an illusion; rather, it is the appearances of the universal alone that are real entities. He refutes this with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*); here, the particle *ca* indicates an objection. "In that way" (*tathā*) means by that aforementioned method.
Likewise, the status of being the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntikatā*) by means of whiteness is indicated by the word "likewise" (*tathā*).

The connection is: "there exists some such specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyāviśeṣa*). And thus, "from that" means from the possibility of a specific causal efficiency. "At another time" means...

Because it is impossible to apprehend two contradictory things simultaneously as being of equal status with respect to a single object; nevertheless, the meaning is that there is no apprehension here as being of equal status, but rather by way of the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*). "Or otherwise" means that it is not perceived here through such properties as being a collection or a non-collection.

The point is that we have no insistence on providing an internal justification. "Otherwise" means that if even then such an appearance did not occur, then that light which does not tolerate any difference from that much reflection would not exist.
Here is the illustration: "just as," [for example], many things that are not being experienced...

If a particular flavor appears as only pungent or only sweet to a cognizer due to the predominance of one or another humor such as bile (pitta), that cognizer has not truly apprehended the taste of the beverage. Now, if even in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) both the one and the many appear, then...

He cuts through the doubt— namely, "How was it stated [in the verse] that 'these [cognitions] have those two as their objects, being subsequent mental determinations'?"— with the word *kevalam* ("only").
For by whichever cognizer pepper, molasses, and so forth have never been tasted, there is only the *pānaka* (the mixed drink).

"It is tasted"; its distinct flavor, though appearing directly to perception (*pratyakṣāvabhāsa*), cannot be brought into the sphere of conceptual linguistic usage (*vikalpena vyavahāryatām*). However, for another [object], it can be so brought; therefore, it is said:

Because they depend upon prior mental impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), difference and non-difference are made manifest through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). It is not merely the capacity for reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that constitutes the nature of Light; rather, it is precisely this [capacity] that is the cause for the possibility of manifold appearances, as well as for the distinctness found between cause and effect.

He shows that "even existence" means even the relationship of cause and effect. "Of another" refers to [factors] such as clay, a staff, and so forth. But surely, let there be only a multiplicity of appearances due to the difference in reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the difference in effects, and the difference in causes; from where does the unity of appearance come? He replies:

"And [it is] a single manifestation" (*ekābhāsaśca*): the word "and" (*ca*) implies that this [single manifestation] also occurs upon the basis of their multiple manifestations. He states "a single manifestation" not only by the force of the reflective awareness of experience (*anubhavavimarśabalāt*), but also by the force of the effect (*kāryabalāt*), saying "difference in purposeful action" (*arthakriyābheda*). "Of them" (*teṣām*) refers to those who possess discernment (*vivekinām*). "Then" (*tadā*) means when the denial of the single manifestation is true, there is purposeful action. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: ...Indeed... [the rest of the passage follows].

By the principle of "the alleviation of fever and so forth," even from many [substances], there may be a single [result]. To this he says, "No," with the words "and not" (*na ca*). But how can the alleviation of fever and so forth belong to the *pañcamūla* (five roots) and other such groups? It is said: "by another substance. For in that case, whatever part of the humors (*doṣa*) is pacified by whichever [substance] through its own specific taste, potency, and so forth—[that is what is meant].
The established principle is that the very nature of a substance is augmented through contact with another substance, while its capacity to aggravate other humors is preserved. || 7 ||

[Objection: But surely, through contact with other substances such as molasses, a different taste will arise in long pepper and the like, just as a different color arises in a betel leaf due to the addition of lime, white chalk, and catechu. [Response: He shows that this is not the same in the present case with the words "or, upon its manifestation. And there exists for a skilled physician such a [remedy].
The sense is that thorough knowledge by way of distinction is produced by [the addition of] pepper and so forth, because of the cognition "this has been prepared with pepper.
Furthermore, the cause—though it exists as a well-known appearance of a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*)—has not been shown here.
Now, one might object: "But there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the case of pepper and so forth, as there is in the case of the appearance of whiteness and the like."
This is because these [qualities] are established as having the nature of distinct ultimate composite substances;
however, this is not the case regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
(Page 120)

This is the illustration. Where, then, does it apply? He says: "In the case of the logical possibility of becoming one. Now, it may be argued that the establishment of a reality does not occur through an illustration alone. To this it is replied: because there is a means of proof (*sādhana*) for the appearance as distinct and manifold, as well as for the appearance as one when there is a state of intermingling.

There exists a characteristic consisting in the appearance of the distinction and non-distinction between the causes and effects of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); for that reason, and not by means of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). If one asks, "What then is the use of an illustrative example? he says: "Of the *marica* [pepper] and so forth," and so on.
This refers to those things whose nature consists of a substance possessing multiple, distinct qualities such as form, touch, taste, and so forth.

"Separately" means that when there is a mutual intermingling (*vyāmiśratā*)— that is, an entry— of distinct substances such as black pepper and the like into other substances such as molasses and curd, each occupying its own distinct location, and likewise among things of different classes possessing dissimilar qualities, a manifestation of unity (*aikyāvabhāsa*) is indeed perceived and encountered.
And this is not by mere chance (*kākatālīya*), but rather repeatedly. Thus, when such [identity] is perceived within empirical usage,

since existence (*sattva*) and the other categories have never been experienced as having an independent nature apart from that empirical usage, what room is there for disagreement regarding the appearance of their identity?— this is the opponent’s view.

This example—"nanu" (surely)—is given to refute the impossibility [of the coexistence of contradictory qualities], even though the cause exists. He establishes this very point with "na hi" (for not). For in the case of black pepper, jaggery, and curd, there is no manifestation (*prakhyā*) nor designation (*upākhyā*) on the basis of a beverage, such that jaggery itself is the curd, or black pepper itself is the jaggery, by way of a relationship between attribute and substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*).

Anticipating the objection that— just as the qualities of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Vitastā, and so forth exist in the ocean, and as the quality of redness exists in a substance such as a jar, and as properties belonging to consciousness (caitanya) exist within the category of "dharma" in the case of Caitra who has been apprehended— the relation of property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is indeed real, [the author] introduces the aphorism.
In that regard, with respect to fire and so forth which are indistinct [in their nature], the fact that they possess the character of being cause and effect,
or of being hot, or of being the referent of this or that word, is understood from a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Regarding the word "ekaika" (each one), the particle "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "even though," indicating that the object is being questioned.

Even though the validity of perception has been accepted even with respect to a mere semblance of perception (*pratyābhāsa*), nevertheless, when a mere appearance of fire is grasped by perception without distinction, the appearance of being an effect of fuel [is not established], as is the case with smoke as a cause.
The group of manifestations such as "the appearance of that" which depends on other entities, and the manifestation of heat which is independent—
this much is the uncreated [nature] existing in all places and times by the power of necessity (*niyati*).

That which has been made [is as follows]: the appearance of being denotable by this or that specific word—the nature (ātman) or intrinsic character (svabhāva) of each object—which is restricted to certain places and times, depends upon the manifestation of convention (saṅketa), and is produced by necessity; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), its connection with the upward direction and its distinction from taste and smell are also included.

Regarding the phrase "opposition to water": that Self is established as being perceived through direct perception from a single [source], namely, from one who looks upon the face of Niyati (the principle of necessity). This is the meaning of the aphorism, briefly explained by the words beginning with "all" (*sarva*).
By the word "all," the totality of space and time as regulated by the appropriate constraints of *niyati* is expressed. In the aphorism—

The second and third quarters are entirely compound words; for in the *Vṛtti*, the compound itself has been made explicit. "There is a pause at the end of the even quarter" — this is the convention in poetry (*kāvyam*), not in the technical treatise (*śāstram*).

The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used here to demonstrate the distinction between dependence, independence, authorship, and so forth. Now, it may be argued that in practical discourse, the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not perceived with respect to every individual appearance (*pratyābhāsa*), because [appearances] such as space and time are ultimately present everywhere.
Repeating the objection that [the definition] lacks deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he refutes it with the words "although for the most part" (*prācuryeṇa yadyapi*).
[An objection: But for what purpose does one seek to know the nature of the thing through another method? He says: "that" (*tat*).
That inquiry regarding each appearance (*pratyābhāsa*) would be useful precisely for that practical transaction (*vyavahāra*).

For the sake of accomplishing the specific portion of each respective effect, the gathering of the specific portion of each respective cause is possible only when the distinction [between them] has been practiced through the processes of inclusion (*ūha*) and exclusion (*apoha*), and not otherwise. "Sometimes" means at the occasion of inquiry (*jijñāsā*). Why, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), are only the appearances of space and time mentioned as things to be abandoned?

Anticipating this objection, he says "place" (*deśa*). For it is these two alone that establish the distinction of the form—that is, of the object being formed—and its non-extension to other places and other times;
for in their absence, even though the mixing with other appearances might bestow a specific character, it would not [be established].
It challenges the specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*). It demonstrates this with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*).

The sense is that [the cognition] does not deviate even from the infinite appearances of existence, substantiality, animateness, cowness, and so forth—such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) and the rest.
Therefore, by means of these two relative factors, namely having a large scope and having a small scope, [the distinction is established].
The nature of being both universal and particular is indeterminate, whereas specific individuality (*svālakṣaṇya*) is determinate. Thus,
one should understand the exclusion of specific individuality from space and time, as well as its absence in other appearances.

Having demonstrated this, he shows the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of that [consciousness] with those two [space and time], and their absence in its absence, by means of the passage beginning with "the appearance of space and time. He explains this very point with the word "space" (*deśa*). By the word "that" (*tat*), he refers to the abandonment of space and time.
And in order to establish that even to this extent, necessity (*niyati*) alone is the vitalizing principle, he recalls what was stated previously, beginning with "space."

Regarding the phrase "even the difference of time" and so forth, the intended meaning here is as follows: when considering for whom this renunciation mentioned here applies—namely, for space and time—it should be understood as referring to those two which have become one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), consisting of the manifestation of form and the manifestation of activity. For that [renunciation] is necessarily concomitant with the very nature of duality. Therefore, always—

Even a manifestation (*bhāsa*) is nothing other than a particular form of the body (*mūrti*), arising from what is not a non-manifestation. However, in that case—such as when there is the manifestation "this is a jar"—there is a commingling with another manifestation of a body; thus, it possesses the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*).
Furthermore, this relationship of universal and particular exists everywhere in relation to the Light (*prakāśa*). But where [the manifestation] resides at the ultimate limit...

In the absence of the manifestation of form and action, the impossibility of commingling with anything else constitutes its very particularity (*viśeṣa*). This is what he expresses by saying, "and the existence and non-existence of manifestations. For those [particulars], the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—the essential nature—is distinguished from other manifestations, such as the manifestation of heat and so forth.

Since those appearances of form and so forth are created as being exactly as they appear, there would be no abandonment of the space and time that have become their very nature; however, connection with a separate space and time must be abandoned.
Even that [separate space and time] can be abandoned in its specific form, but not in its general form. For this is not the case.
The appearance of luminous form is not qualified by any particular place or time;

with this intention, it was stated in the commentary that even when there is a connection with commonality of place and time, the universal nature of that appearance of form and so forth is not lost. This is intended to demonstrate that very point.
Now, one might ask: why should the appearance of commonality regarding place and so forth not be abandoned? To this he says: "Because [it is] its own nature.

Since it is implied by the manifestation of the difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), that very thing is what has been described. He demonstrates this implication with the words "for not," etc. The phrase "having the form of real entities" means those which perform distinct causal functions (*arthakriyā*).
The earth and so forth, as well as the rising of the sun and so forth, indeed possess the nature of space and time. Regarding this, [the author] says on page 123:
"Even though... [The term] *upacaryeta* means it would be designated (*vyavahriyeta*), or rather, by way of secondary usage (*gauṇavṛttyā*).
The meaning is "it should be said. "Precisely by the manifestation of difference" means "by that which culminates in the difference of essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*).
He demonstrates that manifestation of difference with the words "and by the distinct," where "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also" (*api*).
He concludes this with "therefore" (*tat*), meaning "for that reason. [This refers to] the manifestation of one's own self characterized by form and so forth.

In the absence of a connection with a specific place or time, there would be no distinction; therefore, that manifestation of generality must necessarily occur either in some particular place and time, or everywhere. However, a connection with something distinct—such as a staff with a person—comes about by differentiating the very nature [of the person], and thus it appears in such a way. This is what is meant:
Space and time are indeed the contraction of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Even therein, due to further internal contractions, there is a state of generality (*sāmānyatā*);

however, as long as it cannot tolerate another internal contraction—that is, another difference in form—it is merely a particular (*viśeṣa*) and not a universal. But that which can tolerate the inclusion of differences in form...

Great generality (*mahāsāmānya*) is existence (*sattā*). He clarifies this with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). A location (*deśa*), even while connecting [objects] despite differences such as distance, is beneficial only by imparting clarity;
thus, its being remembered has not been illustrated here, unlike [the case of] days and so forth. Time (*kāla*), however, existing in three ways...

The present self is [perceived] with clarity, whereas the other [past self] is helpful by virtue of its lack of clarity; thus he says, "Alternatively" (*athavā*). That for which a specific action appears accompanied by that which is being remembered—and for this very reason, by its non-manifest appearance—is the "past" (*bhūta*). The word "previously" (*prāk*) refers to a consideration of time. And here:

Even that which is being imagined, though it is characterized by what is being remembered, is included by the word "ca" (and); or rather, because the manifestation of a future object cannot be established with certainty due to its abundance [of uncertainty], it has not been shown. Now, is it not the case that even the movement of the sun and so forth, just as in the present...?

There is a destination; how is that? He shows it to be "in one's very self" (*svātmany eva*). Although there is a temporal distinction [of the sun and so forth] due to the variety of bodily states and the coming and going of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), nevertheless, in the end, having abandoned even the vital breaths and so forth, [one remains] in the intellect (*buddhi*) which consists of the mind (*citta*).
When [the mind] comes to rest through the conceit of being a knower or as an object of knowledge,
then there is the suppression of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the state of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impression of restraint (*nirodha*). (Yoga Sūtra)
According to the principle stated in the *Yogasūtra* (3.12), "Thus,
the subsided and the arisen are identical in their nature," it is indeed possible for there to be both manifest and unmanifest forms. Now, one might object:

In what form does the activity of the mind possess clarity or lack of clarity? The mind is of the nature of determination (*vyavasāya*), and determination is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); and that [awareness] is the very self of light (*prakāśa*), while light is not limited by space or time. To this, it is replied: "It is precisely the manifestation of the object."

For it is precisely because of its contraction through the coloring (uparāga) by objects that the mind (citta) is so called; otherwise, it would be consciousness (cit) itself, and not something called "mind" at all. Furthermore, the object—whether in the form of an object of knowledge (vedya), or in the form of an object of meditation (dhyeya), and so forth—is either the very nature of the mind persisting after its dissolution, or [the external object]; thus, its connection with clarity or lack of clarity as that [object's] self-nature is logical.
Thus, it has been established that although appearances such as form (rūpa) possess a connection with general space and time, they lack a connection with their specific [particular] qualities;
therefore, they consist only of a general form, and the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) pertains precisely to that.
Now, one might object: what about cases where there is the nature of a single individual, such as "Caitra" or "Maitra"? In those cases...

By stating "in a single composite whole" (*ekāvayavin*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates a forgetfulness regarding the objection: "Upon what is the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based when there is no universal (*sāmānya*)? For it has been established that in that case, the single universal is the nature of the persisting entity (*avasthātṛ*).

Having established the nature of each individual generality, he applies the meaning of the present sūtra to that context with the words "and when it is thus. Those natures, which are like the foundation wall, consist of the diversity of the substrata (*dharmin*). Now, as for the visual means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends form—

How then does that very same [perception] grasp heat? For heat is tactile (*spārśana*), not visual (*cākṣuṣa*). To this he replies: "And the oneness... We have not said that by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which the luminous form is grasped, by that very same [means] heat is [grasped]; rather, it is stated thus: by whichever...
By the very first cognition that has arisen,
heat and so forth— which possess the nature of a specific luminous configuration— are apprehended as being non-deviant;
by that same [cognition], [the existence] of a specific luminous form and configuration throughout the three worlds and the three times [is established].
Since the non-deviation of heat from fire is thus ascertained, there is no utility for another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in that regard.
Likewise, a specific instance of heat is also [ascertained] by whatever means of knowledge through its non-deviation from that very form.

It was first ascertained, and by that very [means] it was established in that same way as being universal. But what would that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be which is thus consecrated for the sake of ascertaining non-deviation? This will be explained shortly. "In this" refers to the commentary (*vṛtti*). Now, let it be so in the case of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); however—
But regarding the connection with cause and effect and so forth, which depends upon something else, how [could it exist], and how could it not exist? To this he says:

"Because of being an effect," and so on. First of all, it is impossible to say that "it has not been made an object by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)," because that would entail the denial of what is perceived; and if it has been made an object, then that [connection] is indeed its very nature.
Even though [the cognition] is dependent on others once it has arisen, it is nonetheless employed in linguistic usage.
Indicating the logical justification for this very point, he says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), implying that this same principle applies even to the denotation of those various words,
provided that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which has functioned once is [accepted as] determining the existence [of an object] in a universal manner.

If it were to become dull, then how could one who has grasped the convention "this is fire" in the kitchen apply the usage "this fire is burning" in a cremation ground? And where [the convention applies] even to that which is conventional, what indeed [could be said] regarding that which is non-artificial, such as its being an effect or a cause?

The phrase "for this very reason" was explained in the middle [of the commentary] as meaning that one cannot say [the world] is "unfitting"; however, it was not stated that [the world] is of a single flavor, nor that it is denotable by the word "fire," and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "etc.
(*ādi*), both from the *Vṛtti* and from the word "etc. in the *Ṭīkā*, there is the inclusion of such qualities as being the "companion of the wind" (*pavanasakhatva*).

By the word "svabhāva" [used] in the commentary (*vṛtti*). Now he elaborates upon that which was stated: "What would that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be? In this regard, he first presents the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "And here... The particle *ca* serves to aggregate the objects of cognition (*prameya*). In this aphorism (*sūtra*), whatever other relevant matter of this kind is to be stated, this [is it].

The connection with the phrase "how is it to be established? is through a very long [intervening] distance. If one asks, "What is the difficulty in establishing this?", he says: "From one"—meaning another object whose existence is doubtful, such as a treasure buried within the ground—and so forth. "Mutually" refers to that which...

"It is existent; it is hot. Having thus established the incapacity of each individual [element] to grasp the mutual nature of the others, he establishes the same for the aggregate as well with the words "even by many," through the very perception of that which stands upon the peak.

(House, shop, chariot, elephant, etc.)—Now, one might object: "Will not the synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanājñāna*), which is conceptual in nature and arises immediately after the collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), establish the mutual identity [of these objects]? He says: "No."

Regarding the term "synthesis" (*saṃkalanā*): the response is that this will be like the synthesis of a staff and a person; however, [the opponent] refutes this with the objection: "That which is established by what is itself unestablished is not established. Thus, he distinguishes [the two cases]: "staff" is [cognized] by means of appearance (*avabhāsa*), while "appearance" is [cognized] by means of appearance. But surely...

That consciousness which possesses manifold appearances would become a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only if it were performing a synthesis of its objects. It has been stated in this regard that the synthesis of elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth does not occur within a single visual perception.

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, he states another defect with the words "otherwise. If a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to exist only by depending upon the nature of its respective object, then the means of valid cognition that perceives the sky would be valid regarding the sky only in dependence upon the double moon.

The statement "there is no double moon" would itself be invalid; or, if it were valid with respect to the sky, then since the sky is a distinct entity or consists of light and so forth, that [statement] would also be valid with respect to the double moon by virtue of depending upon it. Now, if this [cognition] regarding the double moon is separate—

If it is argued that its function is the object of a separate cognition, then even regarding the objects of knowledge (prameyas) which are the truths, its validity would be entirely independent, not mutually dependent. Now, let there be singularity;
however, each [truth] is said to be of the nature of a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), and that—

It is merely a state of properties that must be conceptualized through various exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*); by that very [conceptualization], the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire—consisting of its form, configuration, and upward movement—is grasped.
Even in your own view, a single specific characteristic consists of a synthesis of multiple universals (*sāmānya*).

By the power of grasping the unique particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each single [object], even the mutual dependence of those many [objects] would indeed be established. He refutes this with the words "even though there is the appearance of many," the connection being that the validity [of cognition] belongs only to the knowledge that reflects [the object]. Here he states the reason according to the Buddhist view:
Even though momentariness and so forth appear, let there be no validity for perception if [the object] remains undetermined;
for if validity were granted even to one who does not reflect upon it, then [validity would also follow] regarding momentariness.
Or, if it were apprehended as being excluded [from the subject], then perception would indeed be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); however, this is not accepted by the opponent.

[The opponent objects: "But if validity belongs only to that which is subsequently reflected upon (*parāmṛśat*), what is the point of all this? [The author] replies: "And of the subsequent reflections... and so forth.

According to the principle stated in the *Pādukā-vārttika* (1.51): "As many as there are superimpositions of objects, so many indeed are the certainties regarding their negation," the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that functions through the distinction of each individual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In each individual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which is of a universal form, it causes [the cognition] to terminate precisely in that which exists separately. Now, by that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the appearances of universals in the form of all those exclusions rest upon a single particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The non-difference of the manifestations has been grasped. True, it has been grasped; however, even though it has been grasped, it is proper that validity be considered as something distinct. The reason for this disregard is that this manifestation, being of the nature of apprehension, is rendered useful only through the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Validity is attained through its capacity to initiate [cognition] and so forth. He concludes the discussion on the object of cognition (*prameya*) with the words "tataśca" (and therefore), which means that validity arises from distinct and separate exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). Regarding one's own object, the state of being a qualifier and a qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva*) consists merely in a single exclusion: that which is luminous is hot; that which is...
It would be impossible to know that "that which belongs to the class of smoke is an effect of fire. Consequently,
the aforementioned activity— both that indicated by this sūtra and that which will be shown by the subsequent sūtra—
would not occur, since no specific object could ever be established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for one who lacks a desire for that specific object.

Because it has not been demonstrated. [Objection: But was it not stated that activity proceeds from the force of desire? [Reply: True; however, even when there is desire, it occurs only when there is doubt regarding the object and so forth, since in some cases there is an absence of activity initiated by desire.
Moreover, because one has never at any time seen anything specific [as being the case], it is precisely the doubt regarding the object and so forth [that motivates action].

If a discerning person (*prekṣaka*) were not to act at all because [he thought] "this would not come to pass," then his status as a discerning person would consist precisely in his non-activity at that time. Thus it is said: "the discerning person. Furthermore, the world of fools acts according to the varying degrees of their desire, but the authoritative person (*prāmāṇika*) does not; yet even he is seen acting when [the opportunity] arises.

Its occurrence would not happen at all according to the stated sequence; this too he states with the words "the discerning," and so forth. "Of those" refers to the followers of Saugata, Kaṇāda, and others. "Inevitable" means that there is no way to avoid this in any respect.
For instance, as for what they say— that fire, by abandoning its status as the cause of smoke, and smoke,
by abandoning its status as the effect of fire, would become causeless; and that by abandoning heat and so forth,
it would indeed be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)— that [objection] is addressed together with the appearance of causality and the like which has already been established.

It is said that [the object] such as the appearance of smoke exists through identity with [the cognition]; however, that very [identity] is not established when the means of knowledge appear as distinct. For it has been shown that the extent of the grasper is determined by the power of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and thus [the object] is indeed distinct from that reflective awareness.
