If it is argued that there is a single objective essence consisting of as many exclusions (vyāvṛtti) as there are reflective cognitions (parāmarśa) whose objects are grasped by a single act of apprehension— then this very point is difficult to know: how much is grasped by a single act of apprehension, and how many such reflective cognitions there are?
It is even more difficult to know that these [cognitions] are preceded by the grasping of this [object], for it has been stated:
"Perception is indeed self-luminous... (1.3.2).
Therefore, by what third means could this be known?

"Subsequent ascertainment (adhyavasāya) consists of reflective awareness (parāmarśa) immediately following perception. Indeed, by virtue of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), both cognitions may know themselves, but they are not capable of knowing anything further. Therefore, this statement is also incorrect: "That which exists where there is no fire is not smoke at all."

It might be so. For that [entity] has a nature immediately following fire; if it were otherwise, it would not exist as such even once. If this were established even once, its permanence for all time would be understood—like a knot tied around one's neck—and no medicine could then be applied or extracted.

This collection of faults arises from that very [source]; for even a thousand such verbal arguments— such as [the claim] that "the state of possessing smoke" and so forth [proves] "the state of possessing fire" and so forth, because it has that alone as its cause, that alone as its nature, that alone as its objective, that alone as its concomitant, and that alone as its defining characteristic— are likewise [invalid].
When the planet [Jupiter] has waxed strong, the clamor of the Vairāṭas is as powerful as it may be, yet it is ineffective;
therefore, our very vision—herein, the splendor of Arjuna acquired through the grace of the Lord—is that which must be sought as a refuge.
Thus he says: "But by us," meaning that it is appropriate and logical that there is no difference in their fundamental nature.
Such cognitions have been established as having an ultimate nature consisting of self-awareness alone; and this is not [achieved] by mere unity that is dry [i.e., devoid of such awareness].
(Page 129)

It carries through. Therefore, it is declared that "reflective awareness" (*pratyavamarśa*) must attain sovereignty in order to effect a fixed unification of appearances. "That" refers to consciousness (*saṃvit*). "Means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) refers to that which is characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Now, [one might ask]: by that consciousness which grasps unity...

If the specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*) is not grasped, then non-difference alone is made out to be the ultimate reality; thus, the theory that appearances (*ābhāsa*)—which are essentially universal in nature—are the ultimate reality falls apart. He shows that it does not fall apart by saying "and even unity," referring to the "other fire-word" as being like the denotative part (*vācyabhāga*).
The meaning is that even in the expressive aspect (*vācakabhāga*), the non-dual nature is primary precisely by virtue of its being a universal (*sāmānyarūpa*).

Furthermore, that consciousness has the universal as its very object, because it cognizes even unity through the form of a universal; such is the logical connection. And "in this very way" means by way of spatial location, insofar as it consists of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
The relation [is expressed] as "there is fire on the earth," "in the summer there is forest fire due to the time," or "the wind is its inflamer and opposed to water" due to another substance;
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it refers to the category of attributes such as the action of upward flaming and so forth.

The connection [is as follows]. And "it is exactly thus" has been established repeatedly. Now, what is the status of that which the Buddhists call the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic), which is said to be absolutely non-conforming? He says:
"But as for that... In that case, there is merely the conceit of absolute non-conformity due to the power of the illusionary capacity (*māyā-śakti*).
But the state of being accompanied [by the subject] alone is the ultimate reality. For instance, when this entity, whose nature is existence,

enters the path of illusory reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), then even the reflective awareness of the meaning of the sentence— "Now, this specific jar is being measured here by me, Caitra"— is of precisely that same kind.

It is fit for arising again and again; therefore, its nature as a universal alone is real. Even when the state of being "illusory" (māyīyatva) does not arise, that which is the pure "thisness" (idantā)—namely, "I am this"—which does not depend on linguistic convention, is precisely because of that [universal nature] devoid of specific characteristics such as persistence over time.

That [limited state] also dissolves into the undivided "I-ness" because the nature of Māyā is no longer manifested; so what occasion is there for this, and where could duality find any reality, except as a mere conceit produced by Māyā? For in every case...
(Page 130) By the principle stated in [Abhinavagupta’s] *Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa* (APV),

"All this whose nature rests precisely in subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) according to the rule ‘this’— of that reflective awareness which is [otherwise] fragmented... and so forth, the entire essential nature (*svarūpa*) comes to rest in subjectivity alone, and subjectivity...
[The state of being] undivided. This is what is stated by the passage beginning with "yat punaḥ" and ending with "upapāditāvibhedatvam.

This is an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) applied to a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Now, while it is true that the non-difference of the cognizer has been established, nevertheless, the cognition of the particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue rests upon the cognizer who is subject to *māyā*; and he—
He dispels the doubt— namely, "How can there be non-difference for that which is delimited by blue?"—

with the words "such an object. Even the subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) of the particular blue (*nīla-svalakṣaṇa*) consists in the reflective awareness of the aforementioned meaning of the sentence, and is thus common to all space and time.

"Even though it is of such a nature" means even though its essence is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). "Real" (*tāttvika*) means that the distinction [between objects] is produced merely by the conceit of *māyā*; in other words, its sole essence consists in the manifestation of the form of one's own perfect self. Thus he says:
"But as for the two portions, real and unreal, which are established in every individual entity:
that which is real therein is the universal (*jāti*); the unreal are the situated individuals (*vyakti*)" (Vākya-padīya 3.32).
He concludes this with the word "therefore" (*tena*), referring to how even the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been established with effort as previously explained.
He shows this by means of the term "universal" (sāmānya). "In this very [context]" means in the state of being a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇatā).

"From mere difference" means from the non-distinction from the state of being a particular characteristic. For it is well known that the quality of coloring [the cognition] as common is itself the definition. Thus, in his own system...

Having established that principle, the opponent might propose his own view as follows: "Granted, let there be no validity [of cognition] based on the exclusion of others through the force of conceptual determination; rather, let validity reside solely in the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, in its form as something luminous and upward-tending. What fault is there in this?"

He says, "This [is] in that very same [instance]. The word "that" (tad) refers to the reason consisting of that very admission: it is fitting that there be a distinction of objects such that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the aspect of momentariness, while there is a means of valid cognition regarding the aspect of stability; however, this is not the case when there is a single object. Thus it has been stated.
These are the supreme weapons for crushing all opposing doctrines, which bring about contradictory properties.
[Page 131] Now, let this system of distinguishing between valid and invalid means of cognition not even exist; for what indeed is the use of it?

By shifting to another argument: first, it is established that the subject under discussion is proven—namely, that fire has a single nature and is not established by means of valid cognition as having a nature consisting of exclusions (*vyāvṛttyātmā*). He shows that the subject itself is not established with the words "and by those," meaning by the Buddhists (*saugataiḥ*), through [the properties] such as luminosity, configuration, upward movement, and so forth, which are perceived by a single sense-faculty (*ekendriya-*)...

This is the sequence for an object of apprehension [perceived by a single sense]; however, when it is impossible for that which is apprehended by different senses to be grasped by a single cognition, how can there be an establishment of a single nature, such as "fire is luminous and hot"? And therefore, it is luminous.
If it is argued that because [the object] is not known as "that which dispels cold," even upon seeing something luminous, one who desires to dispel the cold would not approach it—

and thus there would be a lapse in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)— nevertheless, perception has no function in the cognition of the relationship consisting of the qualifier and the qualified, expressed as "if indeed... (yadi nāma).

Furthermore, since there is no arising of a single, compact (ekaghana) determination, what "compact" thing could possibly be grasped? This [objection] is essentially nonsensical. Here too, he shows contempt for that which consists of mental cognition (manovijñāna), i.e., that which is of the nature of conceptual construction (vikalpa). For that [mental cognition], even if it were to grasp many [objects] in a single moment, [is not truly compact].

This [non-conceptual cognition] might take as its object a general form consisting merely of the exclusion of things such as color-form, which is indeterminate; however, it is not capable of performing a mutual conjunction that has never been performed before by non-conceptual [cognition]. For in this regard—that is, with respect to an object accepted as a unity—there could not be such a mode of apprehension.

The connection is that such is the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of consciousness. The locative case [in "rūpe"] is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). Here, he raises the objection of the opponent's view with the word "atha": "as the substratum of form" (*rūpāśraya*);
that is, in that which is the substratum, locus, or inherent substance (*samavāyidravya*) of form, or else, in form itself.

The common formulation is that "the proximity of form" (*rūpasannikarṣa*) consists in the substrate (*āśraya*) being extremely near. For this very reason, he will conclude: "But it is not [a matter of] occupying the same location, nor is it [simply] proximity or non-proximity," because when there is contact with the hand, both the perception of touch and the perception of form are apprehended in that very same place. And this...

That third consciousness is established as ultimate in the view of the Siddhānta; however, [the opponent] objects, challenging the supreme [view], by means of the word "nanu" (surely), suggesting that this is not logically tenable. The phrase "atrāpi" (even here) means: even though this reality of things remains as it is, how can this be so for you? For indeed, the hand...

(Page 132) That which is conceptually constructed there as being essentially form and touch— namely, the internal touch of the hand, which, due to its purity, is capable of grasping the touch of an object and is thus designated as a sense faculty— is [the eye].

It is first logical that it occurs without interruption. With this intention, having formulated two alternatives, he establishes the final alternative: for the sense organ is indeed the tactile contact itself; its status as an object of inference, however, arises because it [contact] exists in a restricted location with a restricted form, such as hardness, softness, cold, and so forth.

Although it has been stated that "this must be understood," he shows that it must be investigated as far as possible by saying, "In that case, if... He rejects this position precisely on the grounds of its impossibility by asking, "By what?
For it is by an organ grasping both color and touch that the proximity between color and touch is perceived, and yet—

That cognition exists. [Objection: But surely one perceives touch only after perceiving form, or vice versa; or else there is a simultaneous perception of both by a single intellect. Or rather, in the case of vision, there is a simultaneous perception of both form and touch.
[Response: Let it be so for now; however, he shows that what is under discussion is not thereby established, with the words "merely" (*kevalam*).
From a fixed temporal sequence, the relation of cause and effect would be established; from simultaneity, the state of having a single effect would be established.

However, there is no such rule that cause and effect—or things that share a single effect—must necessarily occupy the same location or be in close proximity, as is the case with *dharma*, *adharma*, and so forth.

Furthermore, because ashes, smoke, and so forth— indeed, the entire universe consisting of preceding, succeeding, and simultaneous moments, or even that which takes the form of a common causal complex— are perceived as being in close proximity;
and this very fact is established only within our own philosophical system.

By the phrase "if indeed" (*yadi nāma*), he indicates with the intended meaning of the previously stated reasoning—that "this is merely a concession"—that [the following] is not based on direct perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). Now, as for the touch of the hand, that is not the sense organ which perceives touch; rather, [it is the tactile faculty].
"Based on that consciousness, the eye and so forth are translucent matter" (Abhidharmakośa 1.9).

According to this Abhidharma principle, the matter of the hand is what perceives touch, and matter is apprehended through visual perception by both the hand and fire. This is due to the contact with the matter of fire.
And it is closely associated with the form of the hand that has been grasped, by means of that very form which possesses the designation of the tactile faculty (*sparśanendriya*).

As for the claim that "the touch of the fire is perceived," this too he refutes by stating that it is imperceptible (*parokṣa*). For that which has been made an organ—the form of the hand—is not [itself] perceived; therefore, its proximity to the form of the fire is difficult to know, and must either be accepted as a premise or supplied as an ellipsis.

For the form of the hand is apprehended by visual cognition, and the form of fire as well as the touch of fire are apprehended by another cognition produced from the very nature of the hand, which is consecrated as the tactile sense-organ; thus, no single cognition that grasps two [objects] has been established. This is likewise the case for color and touch.
Having established that nothing is capable of perceiving either proximity or co-location,

you— displaying the confidence of one who has won the argument— show that it is equally difficult to establish that the hand's contiguity is the same as the contact with fire; thus, your statement "by the very contiguity of the hand" is a mere verbal assertion.

He shows that this is logical with the words "athāpi" (even so). The meaning is that even by one who accepts a logical position while abandoning what is faulty, [the following] remains difficult to establish. By the word "anena" (by this), he indicates the instrumentality of the sense organ. And by the words "naca" (nor), he [denies] that color is the instrument for touch.

He states the abandonment of the position that [the self] is dependent [on the senses]. By "by that," he means by the touch of the hand, taking it as the locus of the sense-faculties. "Another touch" refers to the touch of fire. Indeed, "not so," because its internality consists in its existing as non-different from the Self; thus, if the Self is not known, how [can there be such internality]?
It would be known. And the word "tataḥ" (thence) means "even from that. This is the meaning:
it is utterly extraordinary [and contrary to common experience] to claim that a sense organ, which is perceptible, illuminates both itself and others;
even more so than that, it would follow—given what has been accepted—that the touch of fire is continuous with the touch of the hand, which is not the case.
"Continuously in the form of the hand. Now, this is stated by relying merely on worldly convention.

"Of one" means that the color is proximate to the touch of the hand; for fire as well, it is likewise because it belongs to that same class. Furthermore, "of one" refers to that which is proximate to the touch associated with the hand.

The form of the hand; for even this touch, being related to fire, belongs to the same class as touch. And from that, this [cognition] arises; thus he says "by which," meaning by such an establishment. Here, he cuts the very root with the words "even there. "Of those two cognitions" refers to the cognitions of the form and the touch related to the hand.

For, according to the opponent's view, [these] would be restricted solely to their own selves; thus, in the case of the specific characteristic of color and the specific characteristic of touch, it would be impossible to determine their contiguity through spatial succession or internal sequence.
Having thus established this, he says "yathā ca" (and just as) to show that even through the sequence of time, such determination is impossible.

In the sequence of time, the state of being the object of cognitions by different senses need not be relied upon. "Tathaiva" (in the same way) means by virtue of abiding in its own fixed nature. "Ekatra" (in one place) refers to those two whose sequence is being investigated.

How could two [things] appear in a single cognition? The point is that even in that case, whether one says "it is a conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) or "it is real" (*vāstava*), [the problem remains].
Anticipating the objection that "let there simply be a sequence as the appearance within a single conceptual construction," he says: "Not so" (*na hi*).
Thus, having incidentally refuted the opponent's view regarding the sequence of time in the interim, [he proceeds].

He examines the very subject at hand, namely spatial sequence, by means of the example "Devadatta. For if someone were to say that the perception of the distinct individual forms of two entities is itself the apprehension of their difference in space, time, and so forth, then this [argument] refutes that misconception by demonstrating that it is not so; for in reality, there is no such continuity. That very [point]...

Thus, is there a sense of "secondness" due to the doubt that "this is the one who has returned, or perhaps it is that very same one previously seen, and not another"? No, there can be no such certainty; for when the specific location is not apprehended along with the expectation [of identity], it is only appropriate to perceive the jar itself. As for the notion "it is the second," this refers to the perception of a second object.
That [cognition] of the constellation does not depend upon that cognition for the perception of another constellation;
for it has been stated that the validity of even a single cognition is established separately with respect to its own respective object.
By this, it is shown that even if simultaneous apprehension were admitted, this point cannot be established in any way according to the opponent's own view.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the cognition of the continuous proximity of two stars is erroneous, because the stars are separated by an extreme distance? To this, he replies: "The connection is that even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of 'contiguity' is intended [as real]. The phrase 'always indeed' applies even to cases such as daydreaming (*manorājya*). And therefore..."
The intention is that this would be a theory of appearing objects (*ābhāsavastuvāda*). He concludes this with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
"Established" (*vyavasthitam*) means that, according to the actual state of things, it exists even as a sequence of space and time. Thus, in the investigation of sequence...
By that principle which was stated in [the verse] "The sequence depends on differentiation" (2.1.4), [it is characterized] by those two: the appearance and the non-existence [of the object].
That which is to be proven would not be established according to the opponent's view, because those two [the existence and non-existence of the jar] remain undetermined.

By the word "hi" (for), he states that for this reason—namely, because those two are undetermined—it would certainly not be established for the opponent. Therefore, by the word "tasmāt" (therefore), he refers to that very state characterized by the absence of the manifestation of the jar as it was previously perceived.

The two qualifiers—"immediately preceding" and "prior"—are employed by relying on the worldly perspective and the perspective of those who maintain the reality of external objects (*padārthavādin*). For in the system of Kaṇāda, priority and posteriority are effects produced by conjunction with spatial direction (*dik-saṃyoga*). Furthermore, it should be understood in the same way regarding pastness (*bhūtatā*) and prior-ness (*pūrvatā*).
In such cases, "sequence" (krama) means priority and posteriority; "interruption" (vyavadhāna) means being separated by an interval; and from the word "etc.
(ādi), one understands distance and so forth. All of this—regarding these objects such as jars and the like—exists independently of the body of the cognizer and other such factors.

It has been stated that the mutual appearance and non-appearance of things occurs in relation to one another, having been brought forth by the power of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the independent light (*prakāśa*) of the single subject (*pramātṛ*). As for "priority and posteriority, etc.," this means: "this is before," "this is after," "this is to the right," and so on.

"From the north this," and so forth. By the word "also" (*api*), he permits that [the spatial order] is also produced by the existence and non-existence of mutual appearances, because there is even the conventional usage: "To the south of the jar is the cloth. Having thus established that the sequence of space depends upon the reality of a single cognizer (*pramātṛ*), the sequence of time is now likewise established. Time...
By the words "and so forth," the meaning is that "in this way" refers to the very same manner as in the case of location, because it depends upon the existence or non-existence of the manifestation.
Having thus examined independent substances, he now examines that same sequence with respect to those whose nature is attributes, in the phrase "and of color, taste, and so forth."
The first category includes dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*), inherence in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyitva*), non-contradictoriness (*avirodhitva*), and so forth.

Having thus investigated those residing in the insentient (*jaḍagatatvena*), he now investigates those residing in the sentient (*cetanagatam*) with the words "of cognitions as well" (*jñānānām api*).
It should be understood that the sequence of color, taste, and so forth is to be established by the cognizers themselves, and these too are to be investigated.
He demonstrates this. And therefore, although it was established in the preceding section—
namely, in the context of [the verse] "evamanyonyabhinnānām" (1.3.6)— nevertheless, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) situated within a single continuous passage [is now being discussed].

He reminds us here that [this is said] "at some time" in the case of the position that accepts the simultaneous existence of cognitions. Regarding the phrase "of that," it means that non-existence cannot be known by itself as being non-existent.
(Page 136)

The connection is with what precedes. "That" means from that knowledge of taste (*rasajñāna*). "Always" means even when the existence of the knowledge of taste is admitted. By saying "always," it is determined that even when the knowledge of taste exists, there is no separate knowledge of taste; thus its non-existence is established. "That" refers to that which belongs to the knowledge of taste itself.

It is an absence by its very nature; therefore, that [absence] itself is the cause for the determination of absence and the establishment of non-existence, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [non-existence]. And it has been stated that this [absence], being of the nature of blue, does not manifest. Here, the author addresses an objection from another with "Now" (*atha*). "Of that" refers to the cognition of taste. He refutes this with "That" (*tat*).
Therefore, if the capacity of the cognition of form (*rūpa-jñāna*) is of such a nature— as you have stated—

that it determines the absence of the cognition of taste (*rasa-jñāna*), then the previously mentioned refutation remains entirely unrefuted. The connection is that [the cognition] does not exist in that location (*pradeśa*).

For an entity always abides solely in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Now, one might object: "Just as spatial location (*pradeśajñāna*) becomes conjoined with and mixed with a jar, so too will it be here. He refutes this by saying, "It is not so here. The reason for this is "because it is self-luminous" (*svaprakāśasya*). This [reason] would apply there...

The intention is that the certainty regarding the absence of the cognition of taste would be possible only if there were no mixing [of the objects]. He concludes this with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Now, by which sense organ might one mix color and taste, or how could one bring about their simultaneous perception? He replies: "By way of a channel" (*praṇālikayā*); it is not the case that his entire range of activity is dependent upon the sense organs.

Because that [perception] is accomplished by the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) alone; however, when assuming the state of a subject under *māyā*, *niyati* (the principle of necessity), unfolding before him, first displays the employment of the senses as instruments (*karaṇa*). But thereafter...

He establishes entities through that which is called conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), which consists of the expansion of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) that animates sensory cognition; this takes the form of the activity of the subject (*pramātṛ-vyāpāra*).

He says this very thing with the words "for he" (*sa hi*): [he] is the one subject (*ekaḥ pramātā*). "In himself" (*ātmani*) means in his own essential nature (*svarūpe*). "As if distinct" (*vyatirikta iva*)...

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: why would one not establish the simultaneity of those two—which are of the nature of *dharma* and are denoted by the word "knowledge"—just as one does for color and taste;
and conversely, why would one not establish their non-simultaneity? Regarding this non-simultaneity:

"The reason is 'because it appears otherwise'. Now, one might object: "In another philosophical system, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) itself will bring about this [appearance], and its contact with entities such as color and taste is not difficult to establish."
For conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are indeed [of the nature of] experience. To the objection that this very point undermines the subject at hand, he says:

"the experience of form itself," with reference to the time of the self and the time of the experience. Thus, one would determine it as being simultaneous with that experience. But [what of] conceptual constructions in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)?

[Objection: There is some dependence on prior experience; how then can it be said that "they have no life of their own"? [Response: To this he says: "In the aspect of self-awareness (*svasaṃvid-aṃśe*). In the state of being awareness itself (*saṃvedana-rūpatāyām*), time—which is a property of the object of knowledge (*vedya-dharma*)—does not manifest. Even if it were to manifest, it would be as ineffective for [the perception of] color and taste as it is for [the perception of] sound.

To this he says: "And because of the absence of extroversion. If it is argued that self-awareness itself will perform the function of the conceptualization of the awareness of form, taste, and conceptualization, he replies:
even by way of the sequence of self-awareness, it is not logical for it to establish the distinctions of time—such as simultaneous or non-simultaneous—and so forth.

For even in that case of imagined self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), there is no single distinct experience having both form and taste as its object, because those two are cognized by different sense faculties. But surely, that very conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) appears as an experience. True; this applies where it possesses the nature of a conceptual construction.

Regarding the portions of form and taste that are distinct from the nature consisting of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), [the cognition] is directed toward their experience; however, for the sake of that very experience, the restriction of the subject matter [of the present discussion] would be obstructed. This is what he says with the words "But where...
By this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no connection with the perception of time for these two, form and taste. For that [perception of time]...

It exists through mutual dependence; yet that [dependence] does not exist, because those two appear to that conceptual construction precisely as they are unjoined. "Just as by one's own experience" is an example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Just as those two would be perceived by their respective experiences as being indeed unjoined, so too it is by that which follows them.

They appear by the power of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), and not otherwise. The connection is: "it would attain [the object], but not [otherwise]. Now, one might object: "By whichever other conceptualization that conceptualization is itself conceptualized, it will be treated in this way; those two, form and taste, which were previously conceptualized, [will then be] simultaneous. To this he says: "No."

Regarding "of conceptual construction" (*vikalpasya*): that which has color and taste as its object is sensory (*aindriyika*), following precisely the primary experience (*maulānubhava*); that too is another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Now, by this [statement], is it not the case that conceptual construction...?

It is conceptualized, not experienced; why, then, does one follow that [conceptualization]? To this he says "and not" (*na ca*): a conceptualization does not conceptualize the activity of conceptualizing itself, for conceptualization is not self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And this has been stated:
"For its own nature is incapable of being conventionally designated... (*Pāṇini-vārttika* 3.2.49).
By saying this, the opponent has admitted that the activity of conceptual construction (*vikalpavyāpāra*) is a secondary aspect (*paramāṃśa*),

and thus the experience which is its very foundation must necessarily be relied upon. Consequently, how could that which does not exist there— like [a mark] on the forehead, or like [the result of] a thousand efforts at threatening— exist even through a thousand conceptual constructions?

Regarding this, he says: when there is a final resting point— meaning a culmination— in that very state of occurrence or event (vṛtti/vṛttānta) of an object such as form which is manifested by direct experience, [an object] characterized by being devoid of any temporal distinction based on mutual dependence,
then even amidst hundreds of successions of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), [the object remains as it is].

"Nor is there," he says, reminding us again and again that once [the object] has arisen, there is no operation of manifesting the object that is distinct from the experience itself, and yet experience does not act in such a manner. But surely, even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that falls on your side—[that is, one that takes you as its object]—how could it act in this way? True, it would act so. For in our view, this [conceptual construction]...
He has indeed attained a state that is his very life-breath:
that the members of his retinue possess virtue, fortitude, intellect, and prowess through their acquaintance with the Lord Abhinavabhāratī, and never manifest their own individual impulses.
Behold these moments: those that took refuge in the night and attained a state of wretchedness through darkness, yet having entered the day, what do they become?

Thus [it is said]. He says "but it might be" (*syāt punar*). The word "also" (*api*) indicates that the partiality toward your own position regarding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has just now been refuted. "This" refers to the conceptual construction. By the phrase "without division of time," space (*deśa*) is also implied here. Although [the object] is not touched by space and time in its own nature...

Having descended to the level of the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*), while manifesting time and space within his own self, he simultaneously manifests the spatiality and temporality of an object along with that [time and space], thereby manifesting that object together with other objects. Thus it is said.
Nothing is problematic here. [The text] establishes that there is an appearance of time with the words "for instance," whereas there is a difference of location.

"Even the difference in location" (*deśabheda*)—this is because the unity of a single substance (*ekadravyātmatā*) has been established as the reality of the cognition of substance. The word "also" (*api*) indicates the *sannikarṣa* (contact) accepted by the Buddhists; it is stated with the phrase "but he who... (*yaḥ punar*) in order to refute what is criticized in the perspective of others and to establish it within one's own perspective. For *sannikarṣa* indeed...

"Continuity" (*nairantarya*) means the absence of an interval (*antarābhāva*). And the perception of that [continuity] occurs in this way: if that intervening space, which acts as a separator, were to reach the conditions for apprehension (*upalambhalakṣaṇaprāptatva*), but that is not the case; such is the intended meaning. Now, if there is no spatial sequence between two houses experienced separately in this manner...
If it is being perceived, then why do those two appear as devoid of sequence? This is indeed true;
for whatever sequence appears there with respect to spatial order, that belongs to time, not to space.
He shows this by saying "separately. But if they are experienced separately, how can there even be a temporal sequence?

Is it not true that even for that [simultaneous manifestation], its very life consists in mutual dependence? If so, what temporal sequence could there be in simultaneous experience? How, then, is this to be explained? He shows it thus:
"In conceptualization"—that which appears simultaneously at the time of conceptualization does not do so as a single essence, but rather with distinct clarity.

And another [reason] is due to their non-manifestation; because of the very power of experiencing those two separately, when they exist in such a state, it is only a temporal sequence (*kālakrama*) that appears despite the difference in manifestation, not a spatial sequence (*deśakrama*).
However, in the case of Kashmir, Kanyakubja, and so forth, since there is no simultaneous experience, a spatial sequence is inferred, but not—

It is perceptible. By this, that which was stated—"in the case of two jars placed without an interval"—is also shown to have its ultimate reality demonstrated. For in that case, when there is a temporal sequence dependent on the act of experience, the subsequent conceptual construction (vikalpa) depends upon the experience in that manner, relative to the state previously determined.

It makes the sequence of spatial location inferable if that previous jar has been removed; otherwise, the sequence of these two locations is conceptualized as being directly perceived through the force of a subsequent simultaneous experience. Now, as for what was said regarding "the two stars," he says in response:

Regarding the phrase "and of two constellations," this refers to two objects in the form of constellations that are either considered distant according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), or are accepted as such through scripture and other means; when these two appear together in a single expansion,
the proximity or contiguity that manifests is exactly so— that is, it is of the nature of truth itself.
For if there were an interval that had attained the conditions for perception, it would be perceived; but it is not so.
The interval is indeed non-existent, though it may be conceptually imagined like a *piśāca* or similar entity; this "possessing an interval" is not the cause for conventional usage.
For this very reason, it is stated even in the *Āgama*:
"Today there is a conjunction of these two, being situated in the same lunar mansion (*ekarkṣagatatvam*)."

And so forth. Having thus established his own system, and considering that this [system] is a source of intense delusion for the ignorant, he— desiring to convince others who, despite the great difference existing between his own system and those of others, remain undecided— resorted to repeated weighings on a scale.

Not wishing to establish any distinction between those two, he again demonstrates the impossibility of perceiving another [object] by means of the words "from experience" (*anubhavāt*) and so forth. If, at most,
those two such entities are indeed perceived as being near, distant, or existing in the present time;

It is thought that [the cognition] is established by the subsequent [cognition] alone; however, the intention is that even here, mutual dependence cannot be sustained. This should be understood as referring to the specific time of mere presentness, and not to that which is cognizable by a wise person, even if it is immediate.

The connection is as follows: the manifestation of distinctions of place and time occurs when there is a distinction of place, a distinction of time, or a distinction of sense organs. Now, one might object that a distinction of sense organs alone must necessarily suffice. To this he replies, "No," stating "by means of a single sense organ. The reason for this is given by the words "within range" (*arvāk*), and so forth. But [one might ask]: [The text continues: ...Now, [one might ask]: [Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly after "nanu". The translation reflects the available portion.]

"Even while conceptualizing one object, one sees another before oneself" (Pāṇini-vārttika 3.2.107)—according to this principle, one might experience a jar and simultaneously conceptualize a cloth indistinctly; this alone would be the difference in time between the two. Anticipating the objection that "this is not so," he says: "even though" (*yadyapi ca*) and "by which" (*yena*).

Independently. His own time is the presentness of conceptualization due to its clarity; however, in his own philosophical system (*svadarśana*), this fault does not exist because it is accepted as such, and thus he connects [the argument] with the words "all," and so forth.
When there is an interval between all experiential cognitions...
The single nature of consciousness, by virtue of its sovereignty, reflects upon that extroversion consisting of experience; because of the unification of its own nature and the experience,
it considers itself as both self-made and experience-made— thus, this is indeed a real entity.

Not otherwise. This very point is established by the phrase "for he" (sahi), which refers to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). "Otherwise" means independently of the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*). For the yogi is not...

[Objection: But how could that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is intended to be distinct from previous cognitions because its apprehension depends upon other prior experiences, be oriented toward an object and be a knower of that object? Such a thing has been stated [previously] and will be stated [further].
And for this very reason, there is a distinction between this [our] view and that accepted by others, because of its being the cause;
it demonstrates that very object belonging to the internal cognizer, whose characteristic is self-awareness (*saṃvedana*), and which is manifold.

"Thus" refers to the grasping of the stage of direct experience (*anubhavabhūmikā*). "That very [consciousness]" refers to the immersion in the stage of conceptualization (*vikalpabhūmikā*). "But not" implies that it is not like the view of the Sautrāntikas and others; for even within the systems of Kaṇāda, this [position] is difficult to establish, since when there is an absence of a single form among cognitions, there can be no connection based merely on their being grounded in a single consciousness (*saṃvid*).

"It is of no avail," as was already stated previously. "He himself fulfills his own doctrine in due order"—that is to say, "in such a manner. "Consisting of many natures" means composed of form, touch, and so forth.
He clarifies the meaning of the Sūtra, which is tossed by the waves of manifold objects of knowledge, by stabilizing it.

"Thus" means "not otherwise. "The nature of the object" means having the form of each individual appearance. Regarding the phrase "this much," he says "even that which... in order to state that another object of cognition (prameya) indicated by this [statement] is now established. "The thing" refers to a single entity whose essence consists of multiple appearances.

"Up to the point where... refers to the cognition of a single fire, such as that which burns, and so forth. "In both cases" means in the case of the various manifestations (*ābhāsa*) and in the case of their single manifestation. "From that" refers to the subject (*pramātṛ*). "Therefore" means that since, in reality, the subject alone is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), from this [fact] the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) arises; such is the meaning.
The connection is as follows: through contraction, that subject attains the nature of the visual means of knowledge (*cākṣuṣapramāṇa*).
"In relation to its own self" means in relation to the unity of the manifestation that exists in identity with the light of the subject. "In this very way" [is said].
And its name, when being given, is appropriately "yukti" (reasoning/conjunction),
because it consists of the joining of various appearances apprehended by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the art of perfumery (*gandhayukti*). For this very reason,
to the extent that the joining of various appearances residing in multiple subjects becomes clearer, so too [does the object].
Likewise,
wisdom is brought to excellence in one way, and in another way it is brought to deficiency. And this also—
Since this is merely the manifestation of the Lord’s own independent power of will (*icchā-śakti*), that alone is the refuge everywhere. Thus it has been said:
"Intellect, knowledge, freedom from delusion... (BhG 10.4).
And so forth. Here too, "iti" refers to the appearance of the blending of the various forms, tastes, and so on.

"This" refers to perception (*pratyakṣa*), which consists in the direct realization of a single [entity] that is manifold in nature. Reasoning (*yukti*) does not consist solely of the application of direct experience; it also occurs by way of memory.
By demonstrating that this [cognition] consists in the unification of experience,

it is shown through the passage beginning with "autumn" (*śarat*) that the establishment of objects across extended time is possible in the same way as the establishment of objects across extended space. At that very time, by the cognizer alone...

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having established that it has the nature of a single direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such an extended form (*vitatākārā*) sequence is thus cognized. But this is not possible for the opponent; thus he says, "For not... (*na hi*). "That" (*tat*) refers to the reality whose essence consists in the appearance of a continuous sequence. Now, one might object: "If this has been accepted by the opponent..."

What, then, is the partiality for one's own position? He says: "And this very thing"—namely, that which has been accepted by the opponent—is capable of being established through the reasoning and terminology of our own school as being a single, unitary consciousness distinct from successive experiences, their conceptualizations, and the memory thereof; it is not [otherwise].

"Otherwise" means as follows: that which is the very essence of the flower within the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) appearing as a unity—that is the nature of the flower consisting of the recollection of the flower.
Thus, by establishing the arrangement of objects across expanded time, [the text refers to] everything from a moment (*muhūrta*) up to the end of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*).

Having established the reality of the manifestation, he establishes the truth of that manifestation— which is non-dual in nature— even as it extends across all distances such as a *krośa* or a *yojana*, and encompasses the entire range of worlds from the fire at the end of time and the primordial world up to the realm of Sadāśiva, by means of establishing the reality of objects occupying extensive space.

By the words "proximity" (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth: that in which two objects— regarded as proximate or remote— are manifested, and in which the smallness and largeness of other objects appear as they are being manifested, those two [objects] appear therein.
In that case, proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and its opposite can be established in relation to cognition according to their respective order.
As for one who thinks that those two are merely objects, whether they be proximity or something else— his [position is as follows]:

Even if other intervening objects were not perceived, those two [distances] would still be capable of being established as residing solely within the two perceived objects; however, this is not the case.
Thus he says: "But not in the interval. And in every perception of distance and so forth, there is a perception of the interval.

He establishes that it must be considered the motivating cause (*prayojaka*) with the words "as for what... (*yattu*). By the phrase "at the time of midnight" (*niśīthasamaye*), the intention is that at such a time, the perception of intervening objects such as rivers and mountains is impossible.
From the mention of "proximity" (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth, one should understand "distance" (*viprakarṣa*); and even there, there is a gradation (*tāratamya*).

For the cognizer who establishes [the object], there is a variety in his activity here, such as "one must go quickly" or "one must not go"; in that case, it is not that the intermediate space is not perceived, but rather it is indeed perceived. He shows this with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). "The pair" (*dvayam*) means that which has arisen from two directions. "Of that" (*tasya*)...

Of the two streams of sound. Now, it may be objected that the stream is not perceived as existing in two locations; rather, it is perceived only in the portion of space delimited by the ear-cavity, as the followers of Kaṇāda maintain, or it is perceived at the very location of its production, as the followers of Kapila maintain, [the latter] holding that there is a movement of the auditory organ (*śrotravṛtti*).

"The very place where the sound originates transforms into the nature of the direct perception of the sound; however, there is no apprehension at both places, nor is there apprehension of the intervening space. He refutes this by employing experience as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the passage beginning with "and in the location of the ear itself," etc. "At that very time" means at the time of its origination. And thus, due to the difference in time...

[Otherwise] there would be no perception [of the sound], yet such perception does exist; thus he says, "And not so. When the place of origin is distant, perception is observed after the time of production has passed by a long interval; when it is extremely distant, it occurs after an even longer interval.
Therefore, this sound is understood to have the nature of a continuous stream (pravāha) existing between both locations.

This must be accepted. Furthermore, even for one who says that the sound is not perceived by the auditory organ at the location of its production, but rather through inference based on the mark (liṅga) of the final particularity of the sound, relying upon the space of the auditory ether—by him too, the perception of the intervening space is indeed admitted as being inferential. Therefore...
It is difficult to ascertain whether a sound has come from one specific direction or from two directions. For while the particular qualities of a sound—
such as its distance and so forth— may indeed be known, its directional qualifiers and the like cannot.
Because that [causal relation] is not cognized at the very time the relation is grasped— even when the causes, such as the conjunction of the drum and the stick, are observed by the eye,
it is not necessarily the case that the causes [are thereby known].
Thus, according to this logic, since doubt persists when the possibility of another cause is entertained,

the final sound produced by a sound originating from a specific direction must possess a distinction— just as there is a distinction for persons situated in the south, north, east, or west who perceive momentary objects.

"Of those falling before the eyes"—enough with this digression. In any case, sound is perceived even at its place of origin, and not only at the very end as something extremely faint. And for this very reason, when one hears a song from a great distance, one perceives it thus: "He is singing very loudly. Therefore, there too, there is another [quality], namely intensity (*tīvratā*).

It is perceived. Just as an object being perceived from a distance is cognized as indistinct due to the obstruction of intervening entities such as particles of dust that fall between, so too is that [sound] initiated with a sharp sound;
and although it is sharp, it is accompanied by an aerial element that stands in the place of the intermediate particles of dust.
Due to the influence of the obscuration caused by other sounds, [the word] is perceived indistinctly; however, it is only at the end that it is perceived clearly.
And this is witnessed by experience: that very sound which is heard from a distance on a noiseless night appears with distinct phonemes.

"In the presence of the sun, where the movement of people is active, [the word] is indeed indistinct in its phonemes, existing merely as sound. He concludes this with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). "Is seen" (*dṛśyate*) means it is observed as being established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, for what purpose?

If it is maintained that another sound is produced, and if it is further argued that this occurs in another location such that there is a "dual stream" [of sounds], then let that very same sound persist for that duration of time;
or, if it does produce [another sound], let it do so in that very same place; or, if it is indeed produced elsewhere, what [cause] is there for this?

There is the occasion for [the following] objection: "If [the sense organ were all-pervasive], there would be the consequence of hearing sound from all directions simultaneously. He dispels these doubts with the words, "And it is situated right in front.
Therefore, there is no hearing from all four directions. It is "unobstructed" because it is not impeded by air and other such elements.

It ceases, so to speak. By means of this—namely, by the production of another sound—remote perceivers hear the sound for exactly as long a duration [as it takes for that other sound to reach them]. (Page 145)

Even if cognizers situated in the place of origin were to hear it at that time, provided that the sound remains stable, it would either remain right there or produce another sound. For in either case, being situated there, it does not transcend the state of being perceivable by the ears of the cognizers located there. And this is not so.

For indeed, due to the conjunction of the wood and the axe, that sound is heard by those situated right there at that very moment, whereas by those situated at a distance, it is heard only at the time the axe is raised. Therefore,
the perception of the sound's distance and so forth is necessarily preceded by the perception of the intervening sounds.

It remains as stated. As for what was said regarding sound, touch, and so forth, it should be understood that therein it was asserted that no sound is perceived apart from that continuous flow. || 8 ||

In this way, the determination of the intrinsic nature of entities is effected by a means of valid cognition that rests upon each individual manifestation; so too is the mutual restriction of the natures of these manifestations.

Then, by means of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which possesses both an inward and outward orientation— thereby sustaining distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) determined by those respective appearances— and which, although grasping what has already been grasped in each individual appearance,
functions as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the aspect of their synthesis, [the object] is thus cognized within the mental sphere.

The utility of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated in relation to [theoretical] engagement (*pravṛtti*); however, to demonstrate how the operation of the means of valid cognition is useful in relation to physical engagement (*kāyapravṛtti*), another aphorism is cited:
"In a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinct from other perceptions such as those of place and so forth..."
Even for one who seeks a goal, activity would be merely momentary, even if based on inference.

The particle *tu* indicates a distinction from what precedes. Although the specific forms (*viśeṣa*) of things that perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) indeed dissolve their particularity by resting within the nature of consciousness—which consists of light and reflective awareness—nevertheless, they appear as if solidified by the power of *māyā*; thus, [this occurs] through that which is to be accomplished by specific forms.

For one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), that activity of speech, mind, and body which is useful for that particular unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) at that very moment— but not, like the establishment of the nature of an entity, useful at another time— is [the means of cognition] with respect to place, time, and essential nature.

Furthermore, regarding the investigation of another intrinsic nature and so forth, those many other perceptions—those various direct cognitions—are possible only when there is a distinction [between them]; not otherwise.
That is to say, it arises from a collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not from each individual means of valid cognition. Or else:

Since the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are differentiated by those other appearances— such as place and so forth— which have become objects of other direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*), [the cognition] has them as its cause.

"Engagement" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the connection (*saṅgati*). Here too, by way of the multiplicity of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), it is precisely the collection of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is stated to be the cause; or else, the construction is made with reference solely to the ultimate form (*pāramārthika-rūpa*).
Even when there is a state of particularity through the conjunction of appearances, provided that the perceptible [objects] such as space and so forth are present.
When these very perceptions of the supervisor exist,

there is an activity directed toward that specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is non-different from them on the plane of the subject. This sequence applies not only to activity produced by perception, but also to that immediate activity which arises from inference.
It arises precisely from a collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For example: perception apprehending the mountain; inference apprehending fire;

inference based on what was inferred (*anumitānumāna*) apprehending the removal of cold; and authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*) apprehending the absence of harm from thieves and the like. Therefore:

The meaning of the sūtra is that activity culminates in self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) which is entirely inward-turned, arising from a collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He introduces this with the words "wherein" (*yatra*). The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is explained by the terms *mātra* and *api*. In no way is there an establishment of the intrinsic nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*).

He says it is prohibited: "If there were an activity directed toward the relation itself, then since that [relation] would be grasped by a single causal means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the activity [of inference] would necessarily be abandoned as proceeding from a collection of means of knowledge;
however, the activity does not proceed toward the relation. The reason for this is given as "internally" (*antar*); [the cognition] proceeds externally.

And connection (*saṃbandha*) is identity through internal unity (*antaraikya*). As it has been said: "Entities [reside] in a single cognizer, joined by an identity consisting of mutual interpenetration" (2.2.4).

Thus [it is asked]: why does the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone perform such diverse purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*)? He replies: "Because of the universal" (*sāmānyasya*). For by its luminosity (*bhāsvaratā*), it would manifest as something else, but it could not burn or cook.
However, when that luminosity merges with the manifestation of heat (*auṣṇya*), then burning, cooking, and so forth occur. Thus he says:
Furthermore, when there is a unity of those very natures whose essence is manifestation,

that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends their conjunction takes as its object those other manifestations which, although coexistent and sharing a single nature with it, are by no means entirely devoid of difference.
Moreover, they bring about activity like particles of gold that give rise to various arrangements joined upon the surface of a bracelet; this is even by means of inference— this is the point.
In order to explain the process of inference, he first states it briefly: "And inference...

It has been stated more than once that the state of being denotable by words pertains to each individual manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*). Now, as for what was said here—namely, "also in this case"—in order to exclude the non-connection with [other] locations, if that is not demonstrated;

What is the fault of inference? None at all; however, he demonstrates with the passage beginning "smoke" (*dhūma*) and so forth that it would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), providing two examples of the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*). The phrase "nor even" (*nāpi*) implies "by means of perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*). "In a restricted place" (*niyate*) means in a location suitable for action based on that very [perception]. "By the force of that" (*tadbalāt*)...

"By the power of smoke that is non-deviant with respect to fire located in that place. The meaning is: "That" refers to the cognition which is of such a nature; that is inference. He clarifies this very point with the words "for not," [referring to] those cognitions belonging to all possible perceptible things.
Since the object [of the fire] is not within the scope of the activity [of perception], it can be reached and known only through inference.
[Objection: But in that case, perception has no role here at all. [Reply:
Not so; he says "perception" because here there is the perception that apprehends the smoke.

The appearance of fire is projected by virtue of the generality of the perception that grasps the pervasion (vyāpti); thus, those two [the perception and the memory] also possess an operation. Even though they exist, if that appearance of fire were to manifest by its own power through its innate nature, then inference would not have been proclaimed as a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). But it is not so; therefore—

Inference is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Objection: In that case, then, there is no purpose for the collection [of the three marks]. [Reply: How is it that there is no purpose? He says: "And not... By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the logical mark (*liṅga*), and so forth are included. Regarding the phrase "wherein," it refers to where inference itself is proclaimed as being of the nature of a certainty that is independent of anything else.

And regarding this, if someone were to attempt to argue: "Surely, other means of valid cognition such as perception, which apprehend the locus (*dharmin*) and so forth, constitute the very equipment (*parikara*) for inference itself";
even there, since activity proceeds from the entire collection of means of valid cognition, how much more so in the case of perception?

For in this case, inference is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to the relation itself, namely that "there is fire. Yet, activity does not occur toward that [relation], but rather toward the related object; and even there, it is restricted by specific locations and so forth.
Thus, perceptions rest upon other appearances (*ābhāsa*).

How could they not become factors of its manifestation? Furthermore, that very [consciousness] cannot itself be of the nature of an accessory (*parikara*), because it is illogical for something to be its own accessory. If it were distinct [from consciousness], would it be insentient (*jaḍa*) or sentient (*ajaḍa*)?
If it were insentient (*jaḍa*), it would necessarily require another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend it, since it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Even if it were non-insentient, if it were unrestricted (*asaṃkucita*), its having a fixed set of adjuncts (*parikara*) would not be logical. If it were restricted (*saṃkucita*), then by the very rule that it takes the form of another means of knowledge, this discourse on ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) cannot be refuted even by positive injunction.
Therefore, it is established that in all cases, reasoning consisting of a collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the motivator for activity.
With the words "not one" and so forth, he reiterates for those of dull intellect the very same logic already stated regarding perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The phrase "in mere oneness" refers to the internal, connected form. Now, [one might object]:
Thus, because they function as a single operation, there is only one such means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). To this he says, "No;

for these... By implying a difference in time through a difference in object, a difference in essential nature (svarūpa) must necessarily be admitted. For perception, which grasps a property (dharma), [does not grasp another].
Since inference consists merely in the knowledge of fire produced from a logical mark (liṅga), it is logical that activity proceeds from the [cognitive] aggregate alone. || 9 ||

In this way, the determination of difference and non-difference arises solely from the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). For that very freedom (*svātantrya*) is the sovereignty of the Lord whose nature is consciousness. Furthermore, the non-difference of objects at various distances and so forth, which is asserted by others, is established only through the power of reflective awareness, and not merely through the power of appearance (*ābhāsa*).
He says by means of two verses:
"By way of the remoteness or proximity of objects, by their being imperceptible or perceptible, by being external or internal, by defects, or otherwise through the manifestor. (10)
Even for those things that appear with distinct shadows, their unity is not precluded by virtue of a primary manifestation known as a single reflective awareness. (11)

Establishing a determination based on mere appearance alone, how could one maintain the unity of things that are reached through distinct appearances— such as those that are distant or near, whole or partial, covered or uncovered, clear or unclear, red or black, facing toward oneself or turned away? But surely, even reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)...

Each individual manifestation is indeed distinct, as if possessing its own life; this is true. However, there is another factor therein, which is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that "this very [object] has been [perceived] by me.

That very [object] which was seen incompletely from a distance is seen completely when near; thus, by that means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is a complete manifestation (*ākhyāna*) or expansion (*prathana*) on all sides of that primary appearance— which, in relation to the previous appearance, exists as an identity with a single reflective awareness (*ekavimarśa*).

Relying upon that [consciousness], there is the unimpeded unity even of entities whose shadows appear as distinct; this is "conjunction" (*saṅgati*). They are distinct in their manifestation—that is, in their appearance—but not in their essential ultimate nature, which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśamaya*).
"Of those who are divided" means of those for whom there is division. "Always" means even at the occasion of [its] being real.
"That very same" refers to the form of the initial manifestation (*ādyābhāsa*). "And of that" refers to the fruit whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
"For this very reason" means because the distinction between reality and unreality is not established by the non-sublation of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but rather...

"Only by the non-sublation of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); for that reason. "They" refers to the Buddhists. "Suchness" (*tathātva*)—and not the non-apprehension of it—is indeed their refuge of oaths, not something arrived at through the operation of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor is this [definition] over-extensive, as he says: "In the case of mother-of-pearl," because there the reflective awareness is indeed uprooted.

Up to this point, "uprooting" (*unmūlana*) is understood as a conjunction brought about by the power of the identity of the subject (*pramātṛaikya*), whether through its own manifestation or through that of another, because the manifestation of negation (*neti-ābhāsa*) consists in the uprooting of whatever else might be conjoined. And this uprooting occurs precisely in the state of commonality; for that very reason...
It has been stated more than once that there is no lack of awareness regarding internal states such as pleasure and so forth. Furthermore,

that which was previously observed as being mixed with the appearance of being made of clay— due to an appearance of a different nature— is likewise perceived when mixed with the manifestation of silver-ness.

The causal efficiency (arthakriyā) consists in sustaining a mass of water that pervades a spatial region of the sky; "of that" refers to the manifestation of the universal (sāmānyābhāsa). Having explained [the phrase] "by means of distance and proximity," the phrase "or otherwise" is now explained by the words beginning with "in this way" (*evam*), following from that context. Now begins the section starting with "imperceptible" (*parokṣa*).

He explains [the phrase] "even from smoke" as follows: "by other perceivers" means by forest-dwellers, by omniscient ones such as the Mantreśvaras and others, and by yogis whose perception of the imperceptible has arisen through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). He concludes this with the word "therefore" (*tat*), meaning "for that reason. The phrase "as external and internal" refers to the distinction between the two.
(150) He explains it as "thus" (*tathā*). According to the principle stated previously, this [nature] exists as something innate (*naisargika*). (1.6.10)
Regarding this, he explains the phrase "by the defects of the manifestor" (*doṣair vyañjakasya*) with the verse beginning "the sun," and so forth.

That very red lotus which was seen as blue by means of a lamp appears as red when viewed in the light of the sun. "In the same way" (*yathā*) refers to by which method or principle; "so" (*tathā*) refers to by that [same method].

In accordance with the manner of the *vṛtti* on the authoritative texts, he now connects the commentary (*vṛtti*) with the sūtra by means of the passage beginning with "of the imperceptible" (*parokṣasya*) and ending with "otherwise the meaning of the word" (*anyathāśabdārtha*).
[The phrase] "it has not been explained" refers to the *vṛtti*. And this is not merely a summary; rather, it is also a demonstration of mastery (*prauḍhi*).
He demonstrates that [the text] explains the logic by means of the passage beginning with "mere appearance" (*avabhāsamātra*). The phrase "stated additionally" refers to the Sūtra.

By this, the suspicion of redundancy between the expressions "by way of distance and proximity" (*dūrāntikatayā*) and "by way of externality and internality" (*bāhyāntaratayā*) is dispelled. "For this very reason" (*ata eva*) means because of [the distinction between] externality and internality.

And that state of being manifest or unmanifest has been explained in the *Vṛtti*, for which reason all phenomena (*dharma*) are subsumed; therefore, it was not further elaborated upon by the author of the *Vṛtti*. Furthermore, even though there is a difference or non-difference in the manifestors (*vyañjaka*), there is unity because of the identity of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Thus, this is the true meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) here.
The neuter gender [of the word *anyathā*] is used because it refers back [to the preceding term]. Nor has the meaning of the word *anyathā* from the Sūtra been explained otherwise.

Therefore, the connection is with the words "for this very reason. By the passage beginning with "that which is primary," he explains the commentary (*vṛtti*) while reiterating the matter previously stated with the words "cognition" (*mitiḥ*), etc., [referring to] "of the appearance" (*ābhāsasya*).

Regarding light: that which is the nature of the crystal within consciousness is its purity; therefore, blue and so forth are said to be a "reflection" (*chāyā*) therein. In the same way, the nature of light within the self-awareness of consciousness is not sublated by that [object]; thus the construction is: "not sublated by the nature of consciousness" (*saṃvidrūpānupahata*).

Regarding the reading *āvaham*: if the reading is *āvaham*, the meaning is as follows—just as the reflection of blue or other colors does not bring about the nature of consciousness in the crystal by itself, so it is with the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) of light; rather, it is *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) alone that brings this [consciousness] about for it, and thus that alone is primary. || 10, 11 ||

(151) Now, one might object: let it be that in cases such as "distant" and "near," that very same object exists because its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is identical; however, since this is not the case regarding "external" and "internal," how can there be identity? To this, the author provides the answer by means of a *sūtra*.
Even the causal efficiency of objects is innate and not determined by the will of a Lord;
for that [efficiency] is fixed by Him, and thus its non-activity cannot be anything other than [the absence of] activity.

Regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as well: it has already been stated that it is not the [entity's] own nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, being non-natural, it is not independent, because it depends upon the will of God (*īśvara*) and necessity (*niyati*).

Therefore, since it does not produce [the effect] by itself, it is neither distinct [from the entity] nor is it a separate reality; rather, it is either a non-entity (*avastu*) or a different entity (*vastvantara*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is that [the object] ought to exist. The meaning of the Vṛtti is that although these very mental images (ullekha), such as a jar and so forth, are devoid of the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) belonging to an external particular (svalakṣaṇa), [they nonetheless appear]. "Otherwise" means that the nature [of the jar] would be non-existent; for if it were being differentiated [as absent], it would effect the state of non-existence of the jar in that location.

The connection is as follows: its own nature (*svabhāva*) would constitute a distinct entity (*vastvantaratā*) in relation to that very thing, depending on whether it is a jar or a cloth. Regarding the phrase "previously" (*purastāt*):
that which is non-existent is... [2.4.3]

Thus, in this context: "in the difference of manifestation" means in a particular manifestation, whether it be of the nature of a universal or of a particular; "another manifestation" refers to the universal form. || 12 ||

Having raised the objection that the unity of objects which was stated on the basis of the unity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because it would destroy the account of error, the Sūtra states: "Even when there is a reflective awareness of the identity with silver, there is no status as silver in the mother-of-pearl."
Because there is no contradiction with the location of the substrate, the sky remains otherwise even in the case of the double moon.
Although the identity of the shell-silver with silver is contemplated, nevertheless,

that which appears as "silver" in the mental consciousness within the shell has no established existence through identity with real silver; its externality, reality, and suitability for common transactions such as sale do not exist.

That doubt is uprooted because, in this location which serves as the substrate, there is a lack of correspondence— due to its being uprooted— with the nature of the superimposing factor, namely the mother-of-pearl, which appears in the form of "this is silver" in that location.
(152) Due to the stability of doubt that has become its counter-thesis, [one thinks] "this form is not silver.
Correct speech is a cognition whose nature consists in the reflective awareness of manifestation.

Its opposite is non-correspondence (*asaṃvāda*). Just as in a mental error, so too in an error recognized as sensory—such as [the illusion of] two moons—there is no stability; for in that region of the sky occupied by the second moon which was perceived, another subverting reflection arises that is contrary to reality.

The meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) is: "In this region of space, there is no second moon. The commentary (*vṛtti*) connects the words as follows: "In silver" means in real silver; "and in mother-of-pearl" means in that which is determined (*adhyavasita*) as being silver; and "the cognition is false even in the case of the double moon. He introduces the meaning of the aphorism with the word "likewise" (*tathā*), which [refers to] that which is distinct.

The appearance [is such] through disregard for that [distinction]; the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*). "That" (*tat*) refers to the unity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). "What is this?

means that it does not effect a division between the domains of the real and the unreal. By this method, the aphorism (*sūtra*), although it constitutes the remainder of the immediately preceding subject matter, [is explained].

It has been joined [to the discussion] as being supplementary to the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), which is useful for establishing the relationship between the primary subject matter of the treatise and its objects of cognition (*prameya*). "In order to establish" means to settle the states of reality and unreality by way of a distinction between objects. "The generality of silver" (*rajata-sāmānya*) refers to [silver] apart from its specific place, time, and so forth.

It is merely an appearance as silver. Now, if it were created by the *kṣetrajña*, then since it would have the form of an appearance of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), how could we say [it is an error]? He says: "And not... It will be elaborated that the very designation of it as being created by the *kṣetrajña* is itself the delusion.
The point that "it is merely instability," and so forth, has already been determined in its true nature.
Now, raising the objection, "But how can there be error in the absence of corroboration? he says: "For [it is] a means of valid cognition...
Indeed, that which is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) arises through the reversal of the characteristics of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is the true nature of error.
In order to investigate [the matter], he establishes the foundation for the objection with the words "nanu ca" (but surely). Then,

by means of the passage beginning with "athāpi" and ending with "astyevam," he sequentially concludes his analysis of the theories of non-existent manifestation (*asatkhyāti*), unstable manifestation (*asthirakhyāti*), uncommon manifestation (*asādhāraṇakhyāti*), manifestation of that which does not perform a purposeful action (*anarthakriyākārikhyāti*), and erroneous manifestation (*viparītakhyāti*).

By the words "But that [error] alone," etc., he will first cause even that [theory] to rest upon the theory of non-apprehension (*asatkhyāti*), and then proceed to establish the ultimate reality of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*)— this much [is intended].
(Page 153)
By such statements as these, it is stated that "contradictory" means that being manifest is itself existence, as in the case of a flame and so forth.

Regarding this, whatever remains to be said—namely, that a flame and the like are indeed of such a nature—that has not been stated separately because it is identical in principle to what will be said later concerning objects such as pleasure and the like. That too...
