Since such a fixed form has been shown by you, how [could it exist], and in what manner, given the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that serves as the cause for such a restriction? He states that very point with the words "by which" (*yehi*). In that context—that is, when things are situated thus—"thus" (*evam*) means having a unique, uncommon nature; "that" (*tat*) refers to...
Silver and so forth; from the seed-tuber and from the tuber-tuber, the plantain is of one and the same species, as it is used for its tactile quality and falls away like a myrobalan fruit;

and the blue lotus tuber, whether born from a tuber or born from cow dung, is likewise of one and the same species. By this [it is meant that] the unity of reflective awareness alone shines forth everywhere—this is the sense.

"It is indeed otherwise" means that it is devoid of the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and is not common to other cognizers. By the words "distinct," and so forth, he clarifies exactly what was employed [in the previous statement] to demonstrate its nature as a misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*).

He provides the illustration itself with the words "taddhi" (for that), meaning "causality and so forth. Here, even while providing the illustration, he states a *vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta* (an illustration by contrast) with the word "yathā" (just as). The word "punaḥ" (again) means "furthermore," in the sense of being more than what has been previously mentioned. The phrase "by purity" (*śuddhatvena*) means by way of genus (*jāti*) and so forth. [An objection: But if causality and so forth do not...
Anticipating the objection that [the blue and so forth] would then be mere synonyms for something additional, he says "only" (*kevalam*).

Let it be said "just this": a relative designation does not alter the actual existence of a thing, just as we do not say, "This gold of ours is existent. "This" (*etat*) refers to that which is manifesting.

Since the fact that [an object] is the domain of another subject does not manifest as its opposite, this error is indeed a form of "non-apprehension" (*akhyāti*), consisting in an incomplete manifestation due to the absence of full manifestation.
Although every occurrence within the narrative of transmigratory existence is an error, nevertheless, it is like a dream within a dream, or a boil upon a boil.

According to the principle of *sphoṭa*, even within the realm of *māyā*, this empirical usage of delusion occurs because, even at that level, there is an absence of the full manifestation of the appropriate and functional [reality]. One might ask: "Does this [full manifestation] ever appear, which would contradict the former state? He says: "True."

"In one's own self" refers to those by whom an impairment characterized as cataract—a visual defect—is determined. "This is not [the case]" refers to hair-locks and the like. "But here," however, refers to the state of being an error. Or, "in such a case" refers to what is relative.

It consists of a specific form of dharma. Having thus examined the absence of difference (*vyatirekābhāva*), he now examines the absence of identity (*tadātmyābhāva*) as well, [expressing it as] "the jar is not the cloth.
Now, why is the *kṣetrajña* (individual soul), whose sovereignty has not been contemplated, the creator here? Is it not rather the Lord (*īśvara*) himself?
Anticipating the objection that "this knower of the field (kṣetrajña) might also have his freedom cultivated through the contemplation of reflective awareness and recognition," he says:
"because [it] is not common to other subjects," and "from another."

Immediately after the usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it appears as "not" (*na*). For this very reason—meaning, because first there is a superimposition (*samāropa*) consisting of coreferentiality, and subsequently there is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) consisting of exclusion (*vyāvartana*) whose nature is emptiness—it is said "of that very [thing]"; that is, of that which is identity (*aikya*).

Thus, by the force of the reflective awareness that "this very jar has the property called emptiness upon the cloth," [the two are linked]. For this very reason, proponents of positive entities (padārthavādins) consider mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) to be a qualifier of a positive entity. Such is the nature of error as non-apprehension (akhyāti).

Even the application of the names "apprehension of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*) and "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*) occurs by the force of the reflection and subsequent conceptualization; thus, he says "tadevam" and so forth, because such [names] cannot be tolerated by the proponents of ultimate reality (*paramārthavastuvāda*). However, it is precisely non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) that constitutes error.

He shows that this is a case of erroneous conventional usage by stating "in reality, however. He shows that the nature of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*) does not serve as the foundational basis here by stating "self-apprehension is not [the cause]," meaning that nothing more than this is required;
for in cases such as the cognition of two moons, it is simply that the non-apprehension of memory is not manifest.

The meaning is that the pervasive [cause] must be stated as being of the nature of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) alone, wherein even the non-apprehension of memory would be included. Even in this great delusion characterized by transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), it proclaims that non-apprehension alone is the reality, [saying] "by the power of *māyā*. The "cognition of difference" here is of a positive form. In this regard—
The cause of differentiation is [the fact] that what is manifest has as its ultimate reality a manifestation without beginning or end; as stated in the *Nareśvaraviveka* (p.
"Even here in the cognition 'this is blue,' name and form consist of manifestation;
they are not to be abandoned, for that which is to be abandoned is precisely the non-manifestation of the sense of 'I'.
Thus, it is not only in this [cognition] common to all subjects within transmigratory existence...

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the non-manifestation within the great delusion; even though this great delusion—which consists of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the cognizer—is restricted to each individual cognizer, he shows that it alone is the truth by using the term "māyā.
The activity of the *māyā*-cognizer is the conceptual construction: "this is mine."

The phrase beginning with "the means of happiness" refers to that delusion which is identified as saṃsāra and of which [the former] is the form; the connection with what precedes is that all such delusion, existing individually and distinctively within every cognizer, consists of the non-manifestation (akhyāti) of non-duality. It is not, however—

Error is the non-manifestation of that form which consists in the manifestation of an unprecedented object—that is, a manifestation in various forms. Now, with what is there the non-manifestation of the non-dual? He says: "without appearance," meaning devoid of the appearance of anything unprecedented.

The ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātā*) is of the nature of eternal light, the ultimate limit for the emergence of specific manifestations such as jars and the like, pure, devoid of the contraction caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body, and consisting of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).
That which is non-different from him is the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātā*); it is precisely the state of being the form of his activity.

The nature (*prakṛti*) of that delusion (*bhrānti*), which consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is such that for the transmigrating subject, the non-dual reality does not manifest when compared with the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*). Therefore, the activity of conceptual construction is called "delusion" because its nature is the creation of bound beings (*pāśava-sṛṣṭi*); otherwise, however—
The intended meaning is that this is indeed the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the direct path for entering into sovereignty;
it is from my very self that there issues forth a mass of submarine fire, dense with flickering flames, from the waters.

How wondrous is this marvel: that from the breaking of the thunderbolt-like teeth of the serpent Pūrṇādi—who is like a pillar of nectar—there arises, through the power of conceptualization, a path for the expansion of sovereignty that tears asunder the cycle of worldly existence;
yet how even more wondrous is it that this proceeds from the destruction of the obstacles posed by fate!

Thus it will be stated in the section on scripture (*āgamādhikāra*) and in the summary (*saṃgraha*). Having thus elaborated upon the account of the great delusion as a digression, he now examines the very subject at hand— the error regarding silver and so forth— under the heading "non-existence" (*abhāva*), because non-existence is not common to other subjects of cognition (*pramātṛ*).

(Page 156) By demonstrating that the designations of non-existence and its opposite are appropriate for the narrative solely by virtue of its greatness through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the author] states "by which otherwise" (*yena anyathā*) as the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

To support what has been stated, he shows an illustration containing the underlying reason with the words "of hair, etc. For one who considers himself afflicted by ophthalmia (*taimirika*), there is no designation of hair and so forth as being non-existent, nor as being erroneous. For, from his perspective, this is not [treated] as an object for another cognizer.
It is certain. That [refers to] hair and so forth. For (hi) because it is thus, therefore the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is logical.

Regarding the example as well, he states the illustration: "as toward a magician" (aindrajālikam)—that is, toward one who moves about by means of an illusionary adjunct such as a mantra, sleight of hand, or the Śambara art. Just as [in that case]...
For false things such as gems and the like— which possess an appearance that is their ultimate reality— there is neither non-existence nor any kind of error; therefore,
since non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) alone pervades the conventional usage of "non-existence" and "error," in the absence of that pervader [the latter two cannot occur].

The determination is that there is an absence of that [silver]. For this very reason— the sense being that since non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) alone is the cause of error because it lacks the status of being an object for another cognizer, therefore the apprehension (*khyāti*) belongs to one whose error has ceased—
[the term] "mere" refers to the mother-of-pearl as qualified by that property of silver called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).

This very manifestation is precisely the prior manifestation of this form [of the object] as "this is not the domain of other subjects. And in the case of the double moon, the connection is that there is the manifestation of its lack of being an object.
The phrase "it has been said" refers to the recurrence of the previously explained sentence from the *Vṛtti*.

The condition of reality (*bhūtapratyaya*) is established; and because it follows from that context, the statement in the commentary (*vṛtti*) regarding "the region of space" (*nabhodeśa*) is also said to have been stated precisely for this reason. Now, one might ask:

what is the purpose here in manifesting the fact that the shell, the region of space, and so forth, are indistinguishable from being devoid of that [silver], rather than manifesting the silver itself?

To dispel the doubt as to why the manifestation of non-existence (*abhāvaprathā*) is not mentioned, he states the reason: "because of its emptiness" (*tacchūnyatvāt*). This means that the shell and so forth manifest precisely as empty of that [silver], and not because silver manifests in the form of non-existence. For that alone is logically consistent with absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).

Because it is impossible for the mere appearance of silver—which is apprehended as identical with the mere appearance of silver qualified by another place and so forth—to be non-existent; he demonstrates this very point with the words: "But of the silver, etc. (13).

(Page 157) By demonstrating to this extent that only appearances possess the nature of reality (*vastutva*), it has been shown that the principles established by scripture (*āgama*) are indeed real entities (*vastu*).
For instance, the appearance of solidity is earth, and the appearance of redness is...

Form (*rūpa*) is the manifestation of an entity as a fixed form and its configuration (*sanniveśa*); "here" is the appearance of space, "now" is the appearance of time, the quality of passion (*rajo-guṇa*) is the appearance of conjunction, and up to the nature of Śiva is the appearance of luminosity— just as there is a perception of both difference and non-difference in a jar, so it is here.

Even this conventional usage of the term "light" (*prakāśa*) in the *Pārameśvara* [Tantra] is, on the contrary, a means for those graced by the Lord to enter into ultimate reality, rather than being contradictory to it. Thus, the establishment of all objects of knowledge, which consist of both difference and non-difference, depends solely upon the Supreme Lord; so it is stated in the Sūtra.
It is said: through qualities such as sound and so forth there is distinction, while through genus and so forth there is non-distinction;
in this way, the cultivation [of these] is established within a single cognizer.
Since entities manifest with both a recurring and an exclusive nature,

and since it is impossible for anything that causes their re-emergence or cessation— and which would contradict ultimate reality— to exist in any part of them, both recurrence and exclusion arise from the sovereignty of consciousness itself.

They do not deserve censure while they are manifesting. Furthermore, just as non-difference, ultimate reality, action, relation, and so forth are appropriate only when there exists a cognizer who synthesizes [the experiences], so too is difference appropriate only when the Blessed One exists—who is capable of synthesizing that very difference; it is for this reason alone.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that the inclusion of the term "self" (*sva*) in the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) indicates the primacy of the knower (*pramātṛ*); thus, this is the extent of the method of investigation for the definition of the means of valid cognition itself. By the words "not merely," etc., this much has already been established; what more is there to say here? Yet, this [which follows] is truly marvelous.

He explains the second quarter of the verse as an illustration for one who asserts that [the subject] must be accepted, because this point is well known. The word "ca" (and) indicates a reason: not only does the state of having a single or multiple objects imply the identity of the cognizer, but this also applies to the case where there is a single nature despite the presence of differentiation.

If the explanation were explicit, one would have to connect [the statement] that the qualities (*guṇa*) also have both single and multiple objects; however, that is not appropriate. For in that case, they would not possess their nature as differentiators (*bhedaka*). Therefore, the previous method of interpretation is the correct one here. [Objection: But what about the universal (*jāti*)?
Anticipating the objection that [the word] would be a differentiator, [the author says] "nevertheless": "The body of 'cowness' is 'cow, cow'";
thus, it is produced solely by its own qualities—namely, whatever inherent property belongs to cowness and horseness.

Because it brings about the manifestation of the wealth and perfection of purity (*pavitratā*), and so forth, [the quality] resides in [the substratum]. It is either the existence (*astitva*), the knowability (*meyatva*), and so on, which is the *brahmacārī* (the celibate student), or its occurrence (*tadvṛtti*) as that which inheres in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*). By this, a distinction is made.
And thus, in the state of being differentiated (*bhidyamānatāyām*). Now, the white quality (*śuklaguṇa*) persists in swans, snow, nectar, and so forth.

He says "not so" [in the phrase] "and also by way of whiteness. "The same" means that for qualities such as color and for categories such as genus, there is a fixed capacity to differentiate and a fixed capacity not to differentiate, respectively.
And it is precisely by means of words and so forth, existing as qualifiers, that [the objects of knowledge of] yogins, omniscient beings, and others [are distinguished].
Since the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛttapratyaya*) is established in relation to atoms and so forth, what is the use of other "ultimate particulars" (*antyaviśeṣas*)?

Having refuted the objection that [the term "particular"] might denote a genus (*jāti*) by virtue of being expressible by a word denoting a form (*ākṛti*), it is now established that configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is indeed a quality (*guṇa*). He shows that this is also accepted by others with the words "paramāṇu," etc.

For they designate the dimension of the atom as *pārimāṇḍalya* (sphericality), and that is simply a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) consisting of roundness. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the dimension of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is understood to be long in form. As for the dimensions of the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and those beyond, however—

It is perfectly clear that the state of being triangular, quadrangular, and so forth belongs to those things accompanied by conjunctions with specific spatial parts; thus, this is indeed the quality of configuration (*saṃsthāna*). Now, it was stated that an object within the range of the eyes and other senses is a quality, and that it possesses a nature that is exclusively differentiating.

This was demonstrated at that time: how could the spatial arrangement of directions such as "below" and "above," the composite whole (avayavin) such as "this is one jar," the universal (jāti) such as "jar, jar," the state (avasthātā) such as "Caitra, Caitra," and so forth—which are all perceptible by the eye and yet consist essentially of non-difference—be possible? To this, he says: "only this much."

The group of six beginning with form (*rūpa*). By way of that [group], however, it is precisely form and the others which, existing as subtle, agitated, solitary, and mixed, constitute the essence of the principles (*tattva*) consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*mahābhūta*). Of those very [principles]...
This [notion] of "direction" and so forth, produced by the intermingling of other appearances, exists on the plane of *māyā* as a form characterized by duality;

it is grasped primarily through the object-aspect by means of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*)— which is appropriate for *māyā*-validity and consists of conceptualization (*vikalpa*)— and not as the unfolding of a non-dual form.

(Page 159) But surely, what is the status of this ground which is of a non-conceptual nature? He says: "The first. "Not that," because that state of Śrī Sadāśiva is not an object of conventional discourse. "Beyond that," etc.

After the manifestation of the "this-ness" (*idantā*)— which is appropriate for becoming dissolved within the "I-ness" (*ahantā*)— the subject of Māyā becomes manifest. Now, if by the word "white," which reaches as far as the universal (*jāti*), difference itself is directly implied, then [the same would apply] to "cowness" (*gotva*) as well.

"Let it be stated thus. [The opponent] says, "It is not possible to speak of that in such a way," for its very nature consists in following along with the individual life. [Objection: But is it not the case that the form of "cowness" (*gotva*) is the specific arrangement of parts such as the dewlap? [Reply: If that were so, then it would not be a universal (*sāmānya*), but rather—

It is indeed a quality (*guṇa*), and that [quality] is precisely what differentiates; as for the statement that "non-differentiation, however, extends up to the universal (*jāti*)," that remains non-differentiated. Thus he says: "even though it remains. But surely only an implication (*ākṣepa*) is experienced, not those two—differentiation and non-differentiation—and by the weak [evidence], the unity of the cognizer [is established].

This must be postulated. For instance, the single subject, by virtue of resting within himself, manifests that which is delimited by difference as being capable of non-difference. To this, he replies: "Difference and non-difference also.
It is not only the object consisting of the difference that serves as the limit and the non-difference that the subject projects.

He shows that the cognizer himself is employed therein even while establishing their very own nature, by saying "the cognizer himself. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that differentiation, namely *svālakṣaṇya* (particularity), arises precisely from the difference in space and time?
In that case, what is to be done by the cognizer? To this it is replied: "It is the difference in manifestation (*avabhāsabheda*). For without that [difference in manifestation],...

Whence indeed could there be a distinction of space and time? Furthermore, that the distinction of manifestation depends upon the subject (*pramātṛ*) has already been discussed at length in the investigation of succession (*krama*). From this, it follows that what was stated—that the subject alone even constructs the distinction of space and time—is established. Now, [one might object]: "In that case, the distinction of manifestation itself is the differentiator."

It is contradicted [to say] that sound and the other [objects] are the differentiators. He says "no," for that [difference], namely the difference in manifestation, manifests only in the objects of knowledge—sound and so forth—which possess the nature of being both manifesting and manifested. For this very reason, the scripture states that the five categories of reality alone are the objects of knowledge. But if this is so...
If sound and the rest are qualities by virtue of being differentiators, what else could "universal" (*jāti*) be?
There is nothing else; rather, those very appearances of sound and so forth, whose natures are not embraced by the appearances of space and time, [constitute it].
Regarding the universal (*jāti*): since its essence consists in manifestation, even in the theory that it is omnipresent in every individual (*vyakti*),
there is no room for objections such as "it does not come [into being] there" or "it was not there before," because in reality, nothing at all exists in those locations.

Even in the doctrine of the omnipresence of all things, although the manifestation of universal selfhood is admitted across the stages of the negation and superimposition of the delusion regarding the Omniscient One, it is not [the case that] everything [is perceived as such], because the power of necessity (niyati-śakti) acts as a regulator through its propriety in determining the diversity of subjects, places, times, and conditions.

This is stated to address the suspicion of such defects as "it would perform all actions for all selves," and so forth; thus he says, "And of that very [object]," etc. Now, one might object: "In that case, let that from which there is exclusion and that in which there is inclusion also be manifested by the sense organ; what is the use of the identity of the subject (pramātṛ) in that regard? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"But the meaning of 'implication' (ākṣepārtha) is as follows": for it is not the case that the entire multitude of individuals appears there [in the cognition], since that which is excluded from it and that which is continuous with it [would otherwise appear]. Indeed, if it were to appear in such a way, what would be the purpose of implication? And he shows that this [purpose] exists here by the word "clearly" (sphuṭa). "Precisely for this reason" means because there is a clear manifestation.
There is no absence of characteristics, yet there is manifestation; such is the meaning. The word "api" (also/even) is used in the commentary (*vṛtti*).

The intention is that the phrase "the shadow of contradiction" (*virodhacchāyām*) serves to indicate autonomy (*svātantrya*); the word "shadow" (*chāyā*) is used because, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no actual contradiction. And [it refers to] hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
The point that the subject (*pramātā*) is established through the sequence beginning with [Pāṇini 2.2.1] *kriyāsambandha*... and so forth, is not something to be proven;

rather, it is already established. What need is there for that here? This is a hyperbolic statement (*atiśayokti*) even regarding a matter where there is no possibility of delusion on the part of people.
He states that [the subject matter] is a source of confusion: "This matter is difficult to accomplish;

therefore, how can it be endured? This is the fruit of the hyperbole (atiśayokti), intended to reassure the disciples who might lose heart by entertaining such thoughts. He expresses this as "the necessity of its being undertaken."

With this very intention, the establishment of the distinction between the *vṛtti* and the *vivṛti* has been concluded; and in the *vivṛti*, the introduction was made precisely by making that [distinction] the primary focus. || 14 ||
(Page 161) Now,

if it is the case that the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is the locus of rest where all objects of knowledge (*prameya*), consisting of both difference and non-difference, find their unhesitating repose, then the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) should be presented with respect to that [cognizer] alone, not with respect to the object of knowledge. As it has been said regarding the primary [subject]:

For effort is fruitful [only when the goal is already attained]. Anticipating this objection, that very state of being established from the beginning—which was mentioned at the outset of the treatise—is now clearly evident once the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been understood.
For such is the nature of the means of knowledge; how, then, could it apply to the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*)?
He demonstrates this with two verses:

"In the Lord, who is ultimately real, who is untouched by contradictory states, and who is comparable to the even surface of a wall upon which the variegated painting of the universe's diversity is depicted. (15)
But regarding the primordial knower, whose form is ever-shining and who partakes in all cognitions, what new manifestation could serve as a means of knowledge? (16)

It has been stated that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the ever-new manifestation directed toward the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which is attached to the contracted subject (*pramātṛ*). How can that be so in relation to that which is already established as having the nature of pure luminosity?
For instance, when that [pure luminosity] exists, its form—which appears as the contraction of the body and so forth—is attached to it.

While the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishes the object of knowledge (*prameya*), on what basis is the establishment of the knower (*pramātṛ*) itself? For the manifold variety that constitutes the universe shines forth as resting within that knower— like a painting upon a plain wall— without which wall-like light it could not manifest.
Because the appearance of variegated colors such as vermilion, yellow orpiment, and so forth is impossible [in a single locus], for instance,
on a single wall surface devoid of actual depressions and elevations, yet possessing divisions of depression and elevation produced by lines,
there arises the visual appearance of a painting: "This woman has a depressed waist, broad hips, and elevated jar-like breasts."

Thus, on the very wall of light, while there is a state of perpetual luminosity, there arises the manifestation of the manifold variety of the universe, consisting of both difference and non-difference, as being attached to that [light].
Since that [light] is by nature eternally self-luminous and indestructible, what need is there for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding it?

[The Self exists] by way of having a nature that is ever-new manifestation. Nor should it be said that its manifestation did not previously exist, but comes into being when a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is present; for in that case, it would follow that the [Self] itself does not exist. For manifestation alone is its very form. And it is not logical to say that "it itself does not exist," because of its ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*) and its sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
For it is that very [reality] which exists in truth, and not anything else; however, something else may arise as its form of sovereignty.
Therefore, how can there be contact between this [subject], whose nature is being, and non-being, given their contradiction?
It might be argued: "His sovereignty, though unmanifest, is manifested by a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). But that too is not so.
For if this cognizer (*pramātā*) does not appear, who would exert such an effort? And if he does appear, he appears as the cognizer.

In that case, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is precisely this: His form (*vigraha*) is always manifest, and His unique nature consists of various modes of perception. Furthermore, since the conventional usage of time is pervaded by its entry into non-existence, and because no pervader is perceived in that which is untouched by non-existence, [time] does not exist.

This [world] is ancient. In such a case, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and for what purpose is there a means of valid cognition? The meaning is that this is entirely useless. Nor should it be argued that there will be some [means of cognition] distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest; for every means of valid cognition is nothing but a new manifestation.
Form (*rūpa*) exists by virtue of its capacity for valid cognition (*pramitikāritva*). Furthermore, all acts of valid cognition find their rest (*viśrāmyanti*) in that cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
Therefore, when that [cognizer] is the object of desire to know (*pramitsita*), where else could the valid cognition of it find its rest—whether in the insentient (*jaḍa*) or the sentient (*ajaḍa*)?
This should be understood exactly as stated in the *Ādisiddha-sūtra*. As I have said myself:
Since everyone feels ashamed within themselves at the thought, "I have been made an object of cognition," how could that Great Lord endure being made an object of cognition?

Thus, in brief, is the meaning of the Sūtra. Now, one might object: "Without first specifying the particular means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one ought to state what that means of valid cognition is; why then are they not defined in the Sūtra? Anticipating this doubt, he introduces the Sūtra with the words "In this way," and so forth. Likewise:

Thus, regarding "as a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatayā*): here, *iti* refers to number. "A specific cognizer" (*pramātṛviśeṣam*) refers to the cognizer who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). [This occurs] by means of an object that possesses both difference and non-difference. (2.2.7)
Thus,
according to one's preference— (2.3.3)—
thus.

The meaning is that [the author] has established the subject who perceives through *māyā* by means of the passage beginning with: "The activity of one who seeks an object would be merely momentary" (2.3.9, p. 163).

It has been established by the passage beginning with "ekābhidhānaviṣaye" (2.3.2) and the subsequent remainder that the reality is that an object consists solely of manifestations whose nature is universal form;
furthermore, it possesses the character of being both differentiated and non-differentiated. Now, [one might object]:

"Free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), free from appearance (*nirābhāsa*)... (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 2.42). This is the scriptural authority (*āgama*). How then do you say in your commentary, "of that which is eternally manifest"? To this he replies: "It is mere luminosity (*prakāśamātra*). However, in the scripture, the prefix *ā-* has the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*).

The meaning is that the property of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*) is expressed by the word "appearance" (*ābhāsa*). As for the word "the rest" (*śeṣa*), otherwise, due to the rule [of case endings], the instrumental case would be required. For it is the appearance of the object (*arthāvabhāsa*) that is spoken of as a property (*dharma*), and not the appearance of the essential nature (*svarūpāvabhāsa*); this is the intended sense. He demonstrates this with the words: "of that which shines eternally by its own light."

Thus [it is said]. "Immediately after" refers to the sūtra *apravartita* (2.3.17). "Previously" refers to the sūtra *ādisiddha*. "Previously" refers to the occasion of refuting the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding external objects and so forth. Here, in the context of the diversity [of manifestation], the logical ground or cause is stated in the commentary by the words "from His will" (*tadicchātaḥ*). Now, one might object:

Regarding the phrase "by the power of *māyā*," how is it explained in the immediately following text? It says: "A particular *icchā* (will). Even though a single, uniform form is logically untenable, that *icchā*—the power of *māyā* which brings about the most difficult-to-accomplish [task]—is what makes differentiation possible;
thus, that *icchā* is said to be created by the power of *māyā*. For example, it is like a wall appearing as a circle.

The so-called breast appears as such due to the influence of bodily contours; likewise, the jar is nothing but light manifesting itself through its broad base and other features. Although that [manifestation] is not additional to the light, it appears as if additional due to the power of *māyā*. Thus he explains that it exists in the ultimate sense.
Now, [the author] says "prathaikavapuṣaḥ" and so forth. The phrase "yeṣāṃ tu" refers to those things such as blue and so on, which are considered insentient (*jaḍa*).
As it has been stated:
"In this way, they are like non-existent things in relation to the Self... (*Aparokṣānubhūtiprakaraṇa-siddhi* 13).
And so forth. With the words "or in the Kālottara," he corroborates his own position using the terminology of the scriptures (*āgama*).
The diversity of forms is animated by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and that [diversity] gives rise to directions and locations.
(Page 164)

He demonstrates by means of the passage beginning with "merely the first [cognition]," etc., that it has already been stated in the section beginning with "aham-pratyavamarśa... (1.6.1) that mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) in the form of exclusion (*apoha*) is not possible for the Blessed One.
The diversity of forms, animated by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), brings about spatial distinction.

That which exists here in this treatise as being implied in the passage beginning with "by mere primacy" (*prathāmātreṇa*) serves as the basis for the refutation of the views of others; therefore, [it follows that] cognitions [are established].

They are of the singular nature of self-luminosity, and for them, being cognizable by another cognition is contradictory. Furthermore, those who maintain that these [cognitions] are manifold— who assert external objects as well as both wholes and atoms—
hold that cognitions are themselves of the form of blue and so forth.

Because they exist simultaneously within the continuums of oneself and others, and because they exclude one another's essential natures (*svarūpa*), they are distinct in terms of their spatial location according to the definition of their own nature; and for that reason, they possess corporeality (*mūrtimat*). If it is asked, "What follows from this?", he says: "Thus... Therefore, due to the reason of possessing corporeality, just as in the case of external atoms...

From the conjunction of the six [senses], non-existence alone results, and the same applies to those [objects] as well. For if the object is extended and not one, how could the cognition of it be one? This is because the perception of its various spatial divisions remains as it is. Therefore, the cognition of an extended object is merely an accumulation of multiple cognitions, and that [accumulation] is manifold.

If it is argued that many cognitions each rest in their own self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), and thus, due to the impossibility of expanded appearances, there is no spatial distinction whatsoever that could bring about contradiction,
then what other temporal distinction could there be that would entail contradiction? [Therefore,] how could there be any externality to cognition?

"And not," because of the non-existence of external objects. Now, let it be granted that this [object] is external; in that case, by virtue of being an interposer, it must necessarily fall within the space between the two things to be separated, and thus it would come into contact with that which is to be separated by it. Consequently, due to that contact, [the object] would possess parts. Alternatively:

By the passage beginning with "of the cognitions" and ending with "precisely the consequence," the multiplicity of cognitions having been refuted, the unity of the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) follows as a matter of course; in that regard,
the previously mentioned [arguments concerning] posteriority in terms of time, space, and direction are adduced as the reason.
(Page 165) It has been explained.

"For this very reason" means that, due to the absence of any difference in essence, location, or time, the single *cittattva* (consciousness-principle) alone remains; such is the sense. He concludes the subject under discussion with the words "tadevam" (thus, therefore).

The term *pratipadyate* is used in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*). The word *tam* refers to the knower of truth (*satyapramātāram*). The phrase *pramātaiva* means that he remains precisely the agent (*anujjhitakartṛbhāva*) himself; otherwise, he would neither have attained realization nor been made to realize it. Thus it has been said:

"You are the knower, you are the agent, and you are eternally perfected; even action appears only through the state of being a true agent. If it is asked, "In that case, how is there the state of being an object? [the author] recalls what was stated previously with the words beginning with "pūrva" (previously), etc. "By means of the instruments of knowledge, etc. refers to the relationship between teacher and disciple, and so forth. "Because it is said to be real," as has been stated.
"Even though the stability of objects... (*Āgamaprāmāṇya* 20), and so forth.

With the words "And therefore," he concludes this state of being the recipient of all valid cognitions: in the Blessed Maheśvara, who is the true subject and whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), as well as in that which is insentient in nature, such as blue and the void (*śūnya*).
When the manifold objects of knowledge—both insentient and sentient—are being cognized, having been rendered non-inert through the act of subjectification, there is a cognition;
by virtue of its role as the foundational support for that cognition, the primary subject, whose nature is consciousness, remains non-deviant because it is manifest in every way. || 16 ||

If neither the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor the application of reasoning (*upapatti*) apply to the Blessed One in every respect, then what is the purpose of the scripture? To dispel such a doubt, the Sūtra states:
"This [teaching] has never before been set in motion here, except solely through the power of delusion."
Through the manifestation of power (śakti), the conventional usage of [the categories] beginning with Īśa is set in motion. || 17 ||
Here, the meaning of the commentary (*vṛtti*) has been clarified;

however, due to delusion—[as in the case of] *ityatra* (in this regard)—only a mere coordination (*yojanā*) is being made. [The phrase] "one becomes accomplished" (*kṛtī bhavati*) does not mean that, having attained what is to be accomplished by the pot, [one remains there].

"Is afflicted" means [he suffers]. "In the self of all people" means in one and the same [self]; this is the sense. "In such a way" means by whatever method of proof. "He" refers to the self of transmigrating beings. "In that manner" means manifesting in the form of the Lord (Īśvara).

(Page 166) From that delusion which takes the form "this conventional usage of 'cow' based on the possession of a dewlap and so forth is concomitant with shortness," he states the point of application (*dārṣṭāntika*) as being on exactly the same footing elsewhere:

The word "or" (*vā*) indicates that although [the Lord] was known as the basis for knowledge and so forth, one did not proceed [to worship Him] due to delusion (*moha*). For instance, he says this later by means of the terms "presiding over the universe" (*viśvādhiṣṭhātṛ*) and "eightfold form" (*aṣṭamūrti*).
Even by the proponents of dualism (*bhedavādin*), the universe has been accepted as the body of that Blessed One; therein—

The insentient is not separate from consciousness, nor is consciousness separate from another consciousness; thus, the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other scriptures are established solely on the basis of the ultimate truth of non-duality (*abheda*).
Consequently, since the Lord is proven by those authorities, the non-difference of the Self is also established through the non-difference of the universe.

The essence of this differentiation is indeed delusion (*moha*). He provides a description of this delusion, which is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), by way of its form: "another" [person], because of existing in a different world far away and being invisible to people such as ourselves, and so forth—[an entity] unprecedented for us.

This linguistic usage of "sovereignty" (aiśvarya), which by its very nature cannot coexist with an object that is not manifesting, is contradictory when applied to one's own self—which lacks such a previously non-existent form. How could one whose heart is permeated by the delusion [that it exists] engage in such usage? Thus it is said: "He is impelled by the world."

And since we, while teaching, cause the world to proceed by means of performing what is conducive to that [purpose], the two actions (*kārita*) should also be explained in the Sūtra through the shadow of a pun (*śleṣacchāyayā*). Even when the object is known and even when the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) has been attained, the accomplishment of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-sādhana*) is indeed useful for it.
Regarding how that distinguished effect is to be accomplished, he says "that which" (yat tat). That effect,

which is known as being preceded by the state of being within the scope of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) to be conveyed by the word "distinguished," proceeds from that [cause] as the engagement in verbal usage characterized by such a designation.

Because it is conceivable that [the object] is not attained without the mantra, for this reason [it is used]. Now, whether expressed by a word or unexpressed, the meaning is indeed just that much. Indeed, even when cognized through valid means of knowledge (*pramita*), the meaning is just that much. What follows from that? What follows from that here as well? If you ask, "What is the purpose of the application of the word?"— [The answer is: It serves to indicate the specific manner of the action. For example, in the case of the injunction "One should sacrifice with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the word "curd" does not denote anything other than the substance curd; however, it indicates that the act of offering is to be performed in the manner of using curd as the instrument. Similarly, in the case of the injunction "One should sacrifice with the *mantra* 'agnaye tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi'," the *mantra* does not denote anything other than the *mantra* itself; however, it indicates that the act of offering is to be performed in the manner of employing that *mantra*. Therefore, since there is no contradiction, it is established that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of indicating the manner of the action. Furthermore, because the *mantra* is recited at the time of the action, it is understood that it indicates the manner of the action. Thus, it is concluded that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of indicating the manner of the action. This is the view of Bhaṭṭa. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of reminding (*smaraṇārtham*). That is to say, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of reminding one of the action to be performed. For example, in the case of the injunction "One should sacrifice with the *mantra* 'agnaye tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi'," the *mantra* reminds one of the act of offering to Agni. Therefore, it is established that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of reminding. This is the view of Prabhākara. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of praise (*stutyartham*). That is to say, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of praising the deity. For example, in the case of the *mantra* "O Agni, come hither with the gods," the *mantra* praises Agni by stating his qualities. Therefore, it is established that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of praise. This is the view of the followers of the *Bhāṣya*. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of recitation (*pāṭhārtham*). That is to say, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of mere recitation. For example, in the case of the *mantra* "O Brahman, protect the sacrifice," the *mantra* is merely recited. Therefore, it is established that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of recitation. This is the view of some. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). That is to say, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of restricting the order of the ritual acts. For example, in the case of the *mantra* "I cut off the head of the enemy who hates us and whom we hate," the *mantra* restricts the order of the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Therefore, it is established that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of restriction. This is the view of others. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of both reminding and praising. That is to say, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of both reminding one of the action to be performed and praising the deity. For example, in the case of the *mantra* "O Agni, come hither with the gods," the *mantra* reminds one of the act of offering to Agni and also praises Agni by stating his qualities. Therefore, it is established that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of both reminding and praising. This is the view of the *Mīmāṃsā-nyāya-prakāśa*. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of both reminding and restriction. That is to say, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of both reminding one of the action to be performed and restricting the order of the ritual acts. For example, in the case of the *mantra* "I cut off the head of the enemy who hates us and whom we hate," the *mantra* reminds one of the act of cutting the sacrificial grass and also restricts the order of the cutting. Therefore, it is established that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of both reminding and restriction. This is the view of some. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of all three: reminding, praising, and restriction. That is to say, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of all three: reminding one of the action to be performed, praising the deity, and restricting the order of the ritual acts. For example, in the case of the *mantra* "O Agni, come hither with the gods," the *mantra* reminds one of the act of offering to Agni, praises Agni by stating his qualities, and also restricts the order of the offering. Therefore, it is established that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of all three: reminding, praising, and restriction. This is the view of the *Tantravārttika*. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of recitation, reminding, praising, and restriction. That is to say, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of all four: mere recitation, reminding one of the action to be performed, praising the deity, and restricting the order of the ritual acts. For example, in the case of the *mantra* "O Brahman, protect the sacrifice," the *mantra* is merely recited, reminds one of the protection of the sacrifice, praises the Brahman priest, and also restricts the order of the ritual acts. Therefore, it is established that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of all four: recitation, reminding, praising, and restriction. This is the view of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-bhāṣya-vivaraṇa*. Thus, it is concluded that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of indicating the manner of the action, or for the purpose of reminding, or for the purpose of praise, or for the purpose of recitation, or for the purpose of restriction, or for the purpose of both reminding and praising, or for the purpose of both reminding and restriction, or for the purpose of all three: reminding, praising, and restriction, or for the purpose of all four: recitation, reminding, praising, and restriction. This is the final conclusion. This is the view of the *Mīmāṃsā-nyāya-prakāśa*. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of indicating the manner of the action, or for the purpose of reminding, or for the purpose of praise, or for the purpose of recitation, or for the purpose of restriction, or for the purpose of both reminding and praising, or for the purpose of both reminding and restriction, or for the purpose of all three: reminding, praising, and restriction, or for the purpose of all four: recitation, reminding, praising, and restriction. This is the view of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-bhāṣya-vivaraṇa*. Thus, it is concluded that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of indicating the manner of the action, or for the purpose of reminding, or for the purpose of praise, or for the purpose of recitation, or for the purpose of restriction, or for the purpose of both reminding and praising, or for the purpose of both reminding and restriction, or for the purpose of all three: reminding, praising, and restriction, or for the purpose of all four: recitation, reminding, praising, and restriction. This is the final conclusion. This is the view of the *Mīmāṃsā-nyāya-prakāśa*. Alternatively, the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of indicating the manner of the action, or for the purpose of reminding, or for the purpose of praise, or for the purpose of recitation, or for the purpose of restriction, or for the purpose of both reminding and praising, or for the purpose of both reminding and restriction, or for the purpose of all three: reminding, praising, and restriction, or for the purpose of all four: recitation, reminding, praising, and restriction. This is the view of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-bhāṣya-vivaraṇa*. Thus, it is concluded that the *mantra* is employed for the purpose of indicating the manner of the action, or for the purpose of reminding, or for the purpose of praise, or for the

Nevertheless, what is the purpose of the functioning of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If it is argued that it is useful for the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), the solution is the same. This is shown by [the statement]: "For the cognizer...

Thus, the meaning is that the very life and fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is its reflective discernment (*vimarśa*), and it is precisely this that is nourished through verbal usage (*śabdavyavahāra*). Just as the appearance of the specific quality of being a *śāvaleyā* (the brindled cow) is additional to the appearance of "cowness," so too, even when verbal usage has been set in motion, there is no [such addition] for that external object which has fallen under the category of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

Its own nature appears as another manifestation through differentiation; for it has been stated that in the portion consisting of the manifestation of the word, there is no entry into "this-ness" (*idantā*), such as in the determination "this is a jar. (1.5.20)

Regarding this point: [the opponent objects], "But even if a word is applied in this way, if there is no addition to its form which performs the causal function (*arthakriyā*), then what is the point of its application? It is said: "Only" (*kevalam*).
Having stated this in the example, he applies it to the subject at hand with the word "thus" (*evam*). "This one" (*asau*)...
The cognizer is intent on accomplishing worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*). "Established" means resting in the sense of "I.

"He undertakes" means that even though there exists the conceit of "I-ness" regarding the body and so forth—which arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of *māyā*—he firmly identifies his own self with that very [subject] which is the agent of that undertaking; this is the meaning.
"But surely, living beings are constantly observed who lack conviction in the supreme lordship of the Self, even through hundreds of means for worldly practice.
He replies, "True," with the words beginning "kadācit" (sometimes), and so forth. "Saḥ" (that) refers to the delusion in the form of a cow; by this [statement], he further [explains] the Supreme.

Thinking that some task of the Supreme Lord must be accomplished, even that which is impossible becomes possible; for "effort" exists because it is the vitalizing force of the fourfold task. "Only through His grace" means wherever the Self of the Supreme Lord is pleased.

By abandoning the impurity of identification with the body and so forth, he alone is capable of crossing over the great ocean of delusion. "That" refers to the scripture spoken by the Supreme Lord; therein, that which has been established through "bhāva"—namely, the purification (*saṃskāra*), the ritual acts such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), the yoga of meditation and so forth, the yoga, and the knowledge—belongs to that [scripture].

By virtue of its omnipresence, it [perceives] "this and that"— namely, the ground (*bhūmi*) consisting of the various forms to be abandoned, composed of the body, vital breath, the city-of-eight (*puryaṣṭaka*), the voids, and other subjects; characterized by the locus of enjoyment and the objects of enjoyment, and consisting of the worlds (*bhuvana*) and objective entities (*bhāva*).
Abandoning [worldly life] by himself, through the grace of the Supreme Lord and the Guru in matters such as meditation, yoga, knowledge, and initiation, he— being favored by the Supreme Lord—
brings sovereignty into his own self; thus it is connected with what preceded.

(168) The Connection: It has been stated that the efficacy of all [practices], beginning with initiation (*dīkṣā*), lies in this very fact— that the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratva*) is attained in this very birth— even though yoga and knowledge (*jñāna*) hold primary importance.
Because it must be preceded by the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*). As the scripture states:
"There is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śiva without initiation;
and that [initiation] is said to be twofold, according to the distinction between action (*kriyā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.6)

Thus [it is said]. When, however, one does not practice the yoga of meditation but is instead fully confident through the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*), then what happens to him? To this he says: "Meditative cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). "Some" refers to the yogis. "A portion of the sovereign powers" (*vibhūtibhāga*) means a part of omniscience and omnipotence—the capacity for the instruments of superior knowledge, such as *aṇimā* (the power of atomization).

The eightfold characteristics of divine prosperity pertain to specific particular worlds. Having thus demonstrated by direct perception that there is no loss of the subject at hand even when something superior exists, he says "for not" (*na hi*) to show that this very point is established by reasoning as well. The terms "in its own nature" (*ātmabhāve*) and "of the Supreme Self" (*paramātmanaḥ*) [are used].

It has been stated that there is no contradiction between the two types of proximity, namely, mutual proximity and proximity to the Supreme Self. Now, one might object: "Granted that there is no contradiction in the proximity of the Supreme Self to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth due to their proximity to the nature of the Self;
however, there would still be a contradiction regarding its self-luminosity consisting of self-awareness. This is not so.
If the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is present, then it is of the sole nature of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*). Thus he says, "And not...
Now, if the Supreme Self is self-luminous, then how can there be the state of being the Self for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth? [The answer is:
"That manifestation" (*tatprathā*) refers to that manifestation of the Supreme Self through its own sovereignty.

It is solely by virtue of its power that there is the manifestation of that—of the vital breath and so forth—in such a manner, namely as the Self. He confirms this very point with the words "of others also," meaning that even for the vital breath and so forth, there exists a contact with the state of being the knower even while they are objects of knowledge; hence the use of the singular term. "Of entities" means of things. This is it.
He clarifies this by showing that "it is thus even for non-entities," meaning "even for non-existence. [An objection:

"Granted that in the case of the principle of consciousness (*saṃvit-tattva*), there may be no need to establish a new state of lordship (*īśvaratva*); however, in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, let the negation of their being the Self (*ātmatā*) be established as something entirely new. To this he replies: "That too is not new."
"Of the vital breaths and so forth," etc. (p. 169).
"In that manner" means by way of being an object of cognition (*prameyatayā*). For an object of cognition is remembered through the power of the interruption of direct experience.
However, as for that which is the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*), whose essence is uninterrupted luminosity, in that case recollection is not possible. For this very reason it has been said:
"But that reality does not attain the state of being recollected" (Svacchandakalpa 13).
"Thus. "By virtue of which" means by the power of establishing the conventional usage of negation. "Priorly" refers to [the discussion of] mutual...
[etc.]—this has been demonstrated in the *Ṭīkā* on [verse] 1.3.6. As for the phrase "of that which is of the nature of consciousness," it was indeed stated by you yourself.

This has been established in detail in the passage: "For there would indeed be an appearance of two distinct [entities]" (1.6.2). Here, *param* refers to the state of being *idam* (this-ness). *Upajātāḥ* means that they have reached a state of firm establishment (*nirūḍhim gatā*).
"Previously," [it was said] that "liberation arises immediately upon the mere stiffening of the eyes" (Vi.bhai.
113). With the words "from another," he recalls the instruction regarding the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

"In the manifestation of the subject of illusion" (māyāpramātṛ); "having saṃsāra as its fruit" means that it brings about the process of saṃsāra, which consists of the continuous cycle of taking up and casting off birth, lifespan, and experience, all of which are bound by merit and demerit. "Wherein"—from this, what was stated is indeed appropriate, and that...

The underlying intention is that [the error] is removed precisely by the manifestation of the contradictory nature [of the object]. "For this very reason" means: because objects are indeed composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), therefore. "In this context" means: in our own philosophical system. "But not" connects with "is primary. However, for the Sāṃkhyas, this very [error] is accepted as the primary delusion (*moha*).
Now, one might object: "If objects consist solely of consciousness (*saṃvinmaya*), then the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth would be the Self itself, not the non-Self (*anātman*);
so how can it be said that [the notion of 'I'] occurs with respect to the non-Self such as the vital breath? To dispel this doubt, he says:
"But that... [The notion of the Self arises with respect to the non-Self] when, from objects such as jars which are appropriate for the sense of "I," [the mind withdraws].
Having turned away [from the Self], one comes to identify with the vital breath, the body, and so forth—which are like jars and other objects—as the locus of "this-ness" (*idantā*).
At that time, when the vital breath and the rest are fixed as the very nature of the Self, the entire essence of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) resides in them alone.
(Page 170)

"Arising from superimposition (samāropaṇa)": this means "in relation to that," i.e., in relation even to that which has attained the fortune of subjectivity through being thoroughly embraced by the attachment of "I-ness," yet still possesses the stain of "this-ness" and the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth, which have not been abandoned. He says the same thing: "That too..."

"Thus" and "indeed": by whatever mode all objects belong to the locus of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) for the Lord, they arise as if they were something slight; at that time, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth do not belong to the locus of "I-ness"—this is the construction.
He establishes this very point with the word "since" (*yataḥ*). "This" refers to the vital breath and so forth. "I-ness" refers to...

In the state of the Lord (īśvaradaśā). Having thus, by way of digression, described the nature of the subject of Māyā (māyā-pramātṛ), he now connects that very object of knowledge which was introduced—the conventional usage of negation regarding that [nature]—with the phrase "tatra ca" (and there), meaning in the body, vital breath, and so forth. "Gradually" means through the practice of contemplative cultivation (bhāvanā). For previously... [the text continues].

In the absence of the process of cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*), the reason for non-cessation is that [the mind] acts as a grasper with respect to jars and other such objects. For in both cases—both in cessation and in activity—the cause exists;
therein, it is bound by the thread of firm latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are the cause of activity, and it is also present.
Even though it exists as a cause for cessation, it remains indifferent;

it will bear fruit once the present state has vanished and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been exhausted. Thus he says "merely" (*kevalam*), meaning [after] the fall of the body, which is denoted by the term "departure" (*prayāṇa*). "Afterwards" (*ūrdhvam*) means at the end of that departure, as previously defined.

"To that extent" means: for one whose sense of "I-ness" regarding the body has dissolved, there is an absence of the commencement of another body bound by merit and demerit brought about through connection with the body;
thus, when the body has vanished, he remains in a state where expansion, dissolution, and so forth no longer exist, having thereby transcended the path ending with the intellect (*buddhi*).
As it has been stated:

"And from karma, for the embodied one," and so forth. Likewise, the crossing over of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the rest will also be explained in the section on scripture (*āgama*). [The phrase] "this very day" refers to this.

"Even while the body has not fallen": by the word "even" (api), he explains that because a small portion remains, there is still the persistence of the ego-inclination (*ahaṃkāra-abhiniveśa*) toward the vital breath, the body, and so forth;
for if there were a total cessation [of such inclination], the expression "now" would be inappropriate, as it would necessarily entail the falling away of the body. But then, at that time—
Wherein does this yogin possess the firmness of egoity (*ahaṃtādārḍhya*)? He says: "Then indeed" (p.
[This occurs] when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth have been made into objects of knowledge (*vedyīkṛta*); or even in the case of jars and other such things.

The meaning is that when the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is firm, even though one has emerged from it, one does not—due to the firmness of that impression—identify with the body and so forth as the subject (*grāhaka*). "In that same way" means by means of a limited state arising from the power of differentiation (*pṛthagbhāva*). He equates this with the well-known body and so forth by saying "just as. But [an objection may be raised]: nanu...

Even at the time when the body and so forth function as perceivers, they are clearly objects of perception (*grāhya*) in relation to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other such factors; so how can it be said that they possess "capacity" (*yogyatva*)? He refutes this with the words "but not" (*na tu*). The phrase "it will be explained" refers to the section on scripture (*āgama*). By this much, the following has been stated:

As long as the succession of distinctions between the grasped and the grasper has not ceased, this infinite regress is an ornament within the realm of *māyā*; however, since the state of being a subject (*pramātṛtā*) does not entail the state of being an object (*prameyatā*), there is no fault of the non-establishment of the object. But if another void were [to exist] within the void...

If it is held that there is a grasper even in that [emptiness], then there too there must be another emptiness; let there be an infinite regress (anavasthā) if you wish. But if the true nature of consciousness (cittattva) is held to be the grasper within emptiness, and from that [nature] comes manifestation, then what is the infinite regress?
Anticipating this objection, he says "and not" (na ca). The reason for its impossibility is "because of the absence of its being a grasper."
In that case as well, the preceding is the cause; in that case too, the preceding [is the cause]—thus it should be understood. And "of that" refers to the reality of consciousness (*cittattva*).
"Without appearance" (*nirābhāsa*) means in the state of pure Śiva-nature. "Appearance of the universe" (*viśvābhāsa*) means up to the level of Īśvara.
By using the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the word "Śiva-nature" (*śivatva*), the author here indicates that this is a state of being, referring to the Perfect One (*paripūrṇa*).
He states that the subject (*dharmī*), which is the substratum, is inexpressible in its fullness, as was previously stated:

"But in the Full [Reality], everything exists," and so forth. Now, one might ask: is this practice of negating the sense of "I" (*ahaṃtā*) with respect to the body and other such things of any use here at all? If one says "yes," then it must certainly be mentioned in the aphorism as well.

To this he replies: "And that" means that having recognized their own nature as Śiva-hood and Īśvara-hood, they attain perfection and become of the very form of Śiva. The essential nature of this recognition itself has been stated:
for one possessed of devotion, it is a state of self-identification that is so firmly grasped by force that it cannot be removed; such is the meaning.

In that regard, the reason has been stated by the words "it has been said," and so forth; therein too, [the reason] has been stated by the words "the tradition," and so forth. For a body devoid of pleasure and the like, consciousness does not exist as the subject (*pramātṛ*), because [the body] is insentient (*gauḥ*).
(Page 172)
For the cognition of the subject is indeed "I am happy"; therefore, it was not said [to occur] "in the state of the body.

This is what is meant: some, by ascending the stages in succession through the process of practice, having clearly made even the Void—which had been rendered as the subject—subordinate to their experience as an object of knowledge, [attain this state].
The path has been cleared so that they might grasp the conceit (*abhimāna*) in the ultimate subject (*paramārthapramātṛ*).

However, those who are bound by attachment to the body, the vital breaths, and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), even while practicing the abandonment of those [lower levels], do not disregard the sequence of transcendence; rather, remaining unimpeded in their identification with those [levels], they [focus] upon the body.

Moreover, for those who have established their footing on the Wheel-support (cakrādhāra) and so forth, as well as on the stages of bliss such as Mahāvideha and so forth, they instead become the Self of the universe through the further nourishment of identification with other objects of knowledge; thus, for them,
there is no purpose whatsoever in the practice of negating the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) regarding the body and so forth.

It is precisely for those who lack the qualification for such a tradition that [the practice] is useful, for the purpose of abandoning the habitual identification with the body and so forth as the self; yet in the end, even they must take recourse in this very [tradition] out of fear of infinite regress. Now, [regarding] this...
He concludes the discussion on the contradiction between "this-ness" (*idantā*) and "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) with the words "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*). Now, one might object:

just as the worldly usage of a cow characterized by movement was previously established for one who was ignorant [of its true nature] without effort, so too, when there is the usage of the Self (*ātman*), where is the usage of God (*īśvara*) established? If, however, even in that case...

If it is unestablished, then there is an infinite regress. He avoids this by means of an example; thus, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates a distinction from the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). For here, the conventional usage that "the Self is the Lord" has not been previously established. He expresses this very point with the restrictive particle *eva*: for the Self alone is distinguished.
"Lord" (Īśvara) is how those who maintain that doctrine describe Him. This is stated in the passage beginning with "the city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), and so forth.

Because [the Lord] is not distinct from—that is, inseparable from—the light [of consciousness], even though He is devoid of the nature of that which belongs to Māyā, such as the body consisting of the "city of eight" and the rest, and because He is endowed with the powers of knowledge and the other [faculties].

The conventional usage of "selfhood" and "lordship" is unestablished; rather, it is established by those very two grounds within one's own self, which is differentiated as Caitra, Maitra, and so forth. It is not, however, a state of non-separation or non-distinction from the Light (prakāśa), and that [Light] is what is to be conventionally designated as "I"; whereas the notion "this is the Self" is [designated] by this [differentiated self].

It is treated as if distinct from light. Furthermore, the possession of powers such as knowledge and so forth is the basis for the very usage of "I" in the form of "I know" and "I act," but not for the usage of "the Lord.
Having raised this doubt himself:

He refutes [the objection] with the words "Even though... and so forth, while reminding us of what was previously stated with the words "Nevertheless... and so forth. The word "here" (*iha*) implies that this is not merely the case previously. Now, one might ask: is it not the case that linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is being set in motion by this sūtra?

By this statement, it is declared that the means of accomplishing worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and through that instrument, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of this treatise consists of action (*kriyā*). However, previously, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) was demonstrated. (1.1.3)
Having raised the doubt as to how this recognition (pratyabhijñāna) is to be reconciled,
he establishes that the reality of things consists in a single consciousness by means of the passage beginning with "recognition" (pratyabhijñā). Furthermore,
since the instrument is employed for the sake of the action, it is the action itself that constitutes the subject matter of the treatise.

It has been defined. And since action (*kriyā*) is to be expressed by means of the discernment of the nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*), recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this treatise;

its subject matter (*abhidheya*) is that which is to be characterized, and its purpose (*prayojana*) is the exposition thereof, namely, the realization of the nature of the means of valid cognition, the fruit of which is [liberation].
Its operation is that [process], and its fruit is the arising of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

Beyond that, the ultimate fruit—which cannot be further questioned—is the manifestation of the nature of the Supreme Lord, who consists of infinite power and perfect bliss; this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object:

Anticipating the objection that, according to the maxim "the scripture is purposeful regarding what has not yet been attained," there is no need for the operation of scripture with respect to the Self which is already established, he says: "For [regarding] scriptures... in the world..."—meaning either in relation to the means of valid cognition concerning worldly ends such as wealth and pleasure, or in relation to the objects of human pursuit. This is as was stated previously.

"The treatise is for the removal of delusion. Thus [it is said]. "As if unestablished" (*asiddha*) means that one does not become fit for conventional usage (*vyavahārya*); this is to be connected with what precedes.

"Again" (*punaḥ*) means by way of another commentary (*vṛttyantara*). Now, [one might object]: purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) results from the object of cognition (*prameya*), and from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)...
Since the establishment of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) depends upon both the object itself and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

let an investigation be undertaken into the means of valid cognition that establish the logical reasons for dispelling the erroneous delusions regarding those objects; but where, then, is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*)?

That by which the removal of delusion regarding that [object] is effected is what is employed; and because it is not employed, the notion of its existence is cast far away. Therefore, this too should not be asserted: "It will have the fruit of non-return, even in the absence of having worldly transaction as its fruit."
(Page 174) [The objection is raised:

"By the method of such statements as 'the Self is to be known; he does not return again,' [it is implied that liberation occurs] through the removal of delusion regarding the cognizer. To this, [the author replies] by returning to the meaning of the *Ādisiddha* sūtra: [The answer follows: ...by way of returning to the meaning of the *Ādisiddha* sūtra.

"Even though it pacifies," and so forth. Indeed, in every respect, that very Blessed One is both employed and manifested. This is logically consistent provided that he is not objectified; on the contrary, this entire category of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) does not exist anywhere, nor does it manifest anywhere.

The intended meaning is that [consciousness] is employed in some instances as something independent. For instance, he will demonstrate that the entire range of subjects and objects existing within the world is essentially like one who is asleep, with the underlying intention that they are grounded solely in one's own Self. Indeed, in this context, there are three states of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The prior limit (*prākkoṭi*), the state of being present (*vartamānatā*), and the culmination in the fruit (*phalaparyantatā*). Among these, he demonstrates that at the prior limit it is the subject alone who unfolds, by saying "in the desire to know the object of knowledge" (*prameyajijñāsāyām*); for in every case, this subject is present.
"Averse to the contact with suffering and devoted to the savoring of the taste of pleasure"—
by this principle, one is entirely pervaded by the desire to know the objects of cognition (*prameya*). Even when traveling on a path or similar occasions,
even for one who possesses such a desire to know, doubt arises in the interim solely through the power of non-discrimination (*aviveka*).
It is for the sake of such determination that one who acts with circumspection exerts himself.

For even while looking at his own body, this seeker desiring to know the truth raises a doubt through the power of discrimination: "Is this very body of mine, which is the locus of the 'I'-notion," and so forth.

It might be so, or it might be otherwise. Therefore, desiring to employ a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in order to dispel that doubt, one recalls [the relevant knowledge]. Even in cases where doubt arises from the very nature of things themselves—such as when a post or a person is seen from a distance due to their height—the same process applies.

This is the course [of the process]. Thus, this specific form of conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), which consists of the desire to engage the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), unifies the subjects, their two properties, the determination that restricts those properties, and the means of valid cognition that serves as its cause; it is called "investigation" (*vicāra*) because it proceeds by operating in various ways.

The "shifting" (*saṃcāraṇa*) of the object of cognition consists in the arousal of inquiry through the application of discrimination; and the "moving toward the particular" (*viśeṣe cāraṇa*) is characterized by the search for the means of valid cognition that serves as the basis for the specific comprehension of that object of cognition.

The deliberation consists in performing that which is capable of accomplishing what is to be done; it is a comprehensive examination and a thorough discernment from all sides, involving the exclusion of other [alternatives].
(Page 175)

"Ālocana" is the presentation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); "paryālocana" is the thorough consideration of a possible object as something that is plausible because it is capable of occurring.
That very [consideration] is called "upapādana," which is the performance of what is possible and established through reasoning. Thus, preceded by desire—
The operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), consisting of conceptualization and effort, is called "investigation" (*vicāra*). As for the one who says:
