"Having reflected on whether that which is thus is indeed so or not so, its establishment as 'it is exactly so' by the rejection of what is undesired is investigation"—this is the five-limbed investigation (*pañcapada-vicāra*).

He should be asked: what is intended by "investigation" (vicāra)—is it a sentence, or the meaning of a sentence? And as for the meaning of a sentence, is it considered insentient or of the nature of cognition? Furthermore, is cognition a single unit or a series of cognitions? And as for words, are they those ending in nominal or verbal suffixes, or are they of the nature of their respective meanings?

These too are to be distinguished according to the division of knowledge (*jñāna*) and non-knowledge (*ajñāna*). It is first conceivable that by the word "pada" (word/foot) one means either the constituent parts (*bhāga*), or the objects (*viṣaya*), or perhaps knowledge itself, or a series of cognitions (*jñānamālā*), or even deliberation (*vicāra*). And in that regard, there is occasion for [the discussion of] nouns and verbs (*suptiṅanta*); this remains true even on the occasion of other discourses (*saṃjalpa*).

In a single cognition—whether of the nature of doubt or of certainty—that is accepted as being deliberative (vicāra), what room is there for many words? But in the case of conceptual construction (kalpanā), what restriction is there on its extent? By this same reasoning, the rejection of a fixed number of words is established even in the case of a series of cognitions. Now, regarding a single [cognition]...

The five components of knowledge are of the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). In that case, let it be granted that the two components—"the mountain" and "possessing smoke"—are indeed objects of knowledge; however, what follows thereafter—the cognition consisting of the doubt as to whether this [mountain] possesses fire or does not possess fire—is not itself an objective form.
This consists of two words. If it is argued that the presence and absence of fire are the objects [of cognition], let it be so; but what is the connection?

If the five—the mountain, smoke, the presence of fire, the absence of fire, and the rule regarding fire—were to become objects within a single cognition, just as jars, cloths, and so forth are objects in the cognition of one standing on a peak, then...

How could there be a mutual dependence for the establishment [of the inference] that "the mountain possesses fire," given that the restriction to fire is based on the presence and absence of fire? Since this very presence of fire is what is being established, this would not constitute a fifth category; for it would be a single cognition occurring at one and the same time regarding both the presence and the absence of fire in one and the same place.

It must be stated: how could it be made an object? Now, if it is argued that the cognition which synthesizes the five objects—each of which has been made an object by separate cognitions—is called "reflection on the five words" (*pañcapada-vicāra*), [we reply:]...

In that regard, let there be two objects for the two cognitions— namely, the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) and the cognition of smoke (*dhūmajñāna*). However, as for the subsequent cognition of doubt known as "deliberation" (*vimarśa*), its [object]—

A single object, when conceived as having a dual nature— as in the case of "Is it a post?"— is introduced into the oscillation between alternative positions through the entry of the sentence itself; otherwise, if there were two objects, whether the cognition be one or many, what would be the purpose of doubt in either case?

Therefore, since this doubt (*saṃśaya*) has a single nature despite such differences in words as "what is this? and so forth, how can it consist of two words? Furthermore, the establishment [of a point] as being "exactly thus" is called ascertainment (*nirṇaya*). How then could its constituent words be such as "the cognition of the property-bearer and the property" (*dharmidharmasaṃvedana*) and so on?
[The opponent argues: "They may be of the nature of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Since they serve as its [the cognition's] functional applications (*upayoga*), they are its 'terms' (*pada*).
[The author replies: If that were so, why would even the exclusion of the undesired (*aniṣṭaparākaraṇa*) not be counted as another term?
In that case, how could there be a state of having five terms (*pañcapadatva*)? And what is this conceit here—that it has five terms?
No one has realized this "investigation" (vicāra); we alone have dispelled the blinding darkness for the world.
For even children, having first studied the aphorisms of grammar, study the aphorisms of logic (nyāya), wherein it is said:
"Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the determination of the object through the examination of the thesis and the counter-thesis" (NS 1.1.40).

For "examination" (*vimarśa*) is indeed doubt (*saṃśaya*). And that [doubt] occurs when there is the perception of a substratum (*dharmī*), as well as the refutation of the counter-position and the removal of what is undesirable; so what is this pretension of demonstrating something unprecedented?

Even such a manifestation of conceit is, in fact, the very sovereignty of the Blessed One; therefore, he is most worthy of our veneration. Furthermore, the establishment [of the system] is what is meant by "investigation" (vicāra), according to the thesis [stated] at the occasion of defining the characteristics, words, and purposes: that if one were not to state "this is thus," [the investigation would not occur].
Since there is no wall [to obstruct it] and because reflection (*vimarśa*) is not a constituent part [of the inquiry], the investigation would be without support; let that be so.

As for the objection raised—that if the two words "what" (*kim*) and "thus" (*evam*) were not expressed, the investigation would be formless—that speaks of an excessive devotion of the heart to its own [logical] consistency. For by this statement, reflection...
Thus, the definition of inquiry (*vicāra*) would have been stated as being characterized by doubt, rather than its establishment.
Furthermore, it was stated that if the word "just so" (*evam eva*) were not present, inquiry would be fruitless and without limit; therefore, by this [word] as well—
(Page 177) [If it were] "establishment" (*sthāpana*) and "investigation" (*vicāra*), the previously introduced grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be contradicted.
For that very same thing cannot be both the fruit and the limit (*avadhi*) within itself. Therefore, by this investigation...

While investigating, one has not investigated the preceding and the succeeding; nor is it the case that investigative skill or the status of being an examiner is renowned in the world solely through the application of inferential determination—according to the principle that "it is in the final consciousness"—since even the investigation into the true nature of a gem is possible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, inferential investigation...

If it is said that the self consists of a garland of cognitions, then it must be called "the sixteen-fold," since [the self] arises by means of that many [cognitions]. Furthermore, "ascertainment" (nirṇaya) is well known as "investigation" (vicāra), for this has been investigated by the learned; yet, because of the common usage [of the term], it is not ascertained even today. For instance, the author of the Mahābhāṣya [states]:
In this *Sandhyakṣaravārttika*,
the following is deliberated:
when a doubt arises as expressed in [Pāṇini 2.3.4], the very search for authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) is established as the means for entering into discernment (*viveka*).
He has treated it as being of the nature of *vicāra* (investigation). Even in the scripture (*āgama*), it is said:
"The yogin should investigate until he perceives the reality (*tattva*).
Thus, the state prior to the definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) characterized by the vision of reality is precisely what constitutes the state of being an investigator.
It has been explained [by Patañjali]: "Even for one who possesses a great guru, immediately after the meditative attainment with deliberation (*savicāra-samāpatti*),
there is internal clarity (*adhyātma-prasāda*) in the state of fearlessness regarding the absence of deliberation (*nirvicāra-vaiśāradya*)" (Yoga Sūtra 1.47),
having thus stated.
"Then, wisdom is that which bears truth" (Yoga Sūtra 1.48).

By thus stating the essential nature of wisdom—which consists of ascertainment—subsequent to [the stages of] discernment, it is implied that the very desire for ascertainment (*nirṇinīṣā*) constitutes the state of inquiry (*vicāra*). Furthermore, it is *vitarka* itself, when directed toward a subtle object, that becomes [the stage of] *vicāra*.
Thus, *vicāra* (investigation) has been shown. Nor is it correct to say that *vitarka* (initial inquiry) is a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*).
Investigation is simply the desire to reach a definitive conclusion, taking the form of presenting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Enough with this digression.
Having thus explained the utility of the means of valid cognition—or rather, of the knower alone—at the prior stage, [he now speaks] regarding the subsequent stage as well.

He shows that [the proof] exists even beyond [that point]. The ablative case in "pravṛtteḥ" is used in the sense of direction (*digyoga*) and as a causal reason (*hetu*), due to its connection with what precedes and follows. However, in the middle position, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), though it is being observed, shines forth.

(Page 178) It shows that [the light] actually illuminates the cognizer alone. "With respect to him" means with respect to the cognizer. Thus, let the means of knowledge shine forth in the middle position; however, as for that—
It becomes one that has accomplished its purpose; thus it is determined that it merely pursues the prior and posterior limits (*pūrvāparakoṭi*).

Nevertheless, the prior limit and the posterior limit are exactly the same. This was already shown previously by the statement beginning with "it arises precisely through the savoring of the object," and so forth. [Regarding] the foundation...
The connection is that the object causes the form of firm determination to be taken up by the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).

He clarifies what was stated as "in the agent of worldly transaction" (*vyavahartṛ*) with the words beginning "the dewlap, etc. Furthermore, inference is that which is employed in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) due to its universal applicability.

He takes refuge [in this]. And that has, in every case, as its sole fruit the cessation of mere delusion (*moha*). "Reflecting" means desiring to employ the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He concludes here that the primary status of the knower (*pramātṛ*) consists precisely in these two alternatives, while the intermediate alternative lacks primacy because of the other alternative.

Because it lacks the capacity for conventional transaction (*vyavahāryatva*) at its conclusion, he examines it within the systems of the Sugatas and others by means of the word "thence" (*tataḥ*). Although the prior limit characterized by investigation exists, it is not clearly perceived everywhere;
therefore, it is mentioned later. It is as if one were asleep amidst the entire range of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) existing within the world.
By these and other such statements, the middle alternative is indicated. Even though the mere result is the removal of delusion,
in a case where the state of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*)— as perceived by the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa)— is not put forward as the reason,
but rather the state of being a *śiṃśapā* (*śiṃśapātva*) alone is, there that state of being a tree is intended to be unestablished (*apramita*).

In that context, the inference based on the essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) establishes what has not been previously established. Even there, it is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) alone who is instrumental, employing perception universally; thus he says, "Whichever... [yā yā...]. Now, if that operation belongs to the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can it be [effected] by the cognizer?

It is employed as something universal. Now, if it were not so, then that [activity] would not belong to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather only to the knower (*pramātṛ*). He says, "The activity also," acknowledging that this is indeed true.
"Of the cause" refers to [the activity] such as raising and lowering, like that of an axe. "Here" refers to our own philosophical system.

Where a new manifestation (*navābhāsa*) is centered upon the subject (*pramātṛ*), that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And by this very text, even within the dimension of presentness, the means of knowledge relies solely upon the primacy of the subject.

As has been shown—thus, in all three states of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is the cognizer alone who unfolds; therefore, the exertion to explain the means of establishing that [cognizer] for the sake of the deluded is appropriate. For he alone...

The cognizer employs the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) both for the establishment of the real object (*vastu-sādhana*) and for the accomplishment of practical activity (*vyavahāra-sādhana*). Therefore, he shows that the functioning of the means of knowledge is entirely dependent upon that [cognizer] by the word "tena" (by that), which means "tasmāt" (therefore). It is in grammatical apposition with the cognizer (*pramātṛ-samānādhikaraṇa*).

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— characterized by perception, inference, and the instruction of authoritative persons— is not operative for people like us regarding such things as heaven, nor regarding the fixed enumeration of principles, such as "there are thirty-six principles," nor, by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), regarding the power of mantras, spiritual influence, initiation, and the like.

"By way of the scripture" means that it extends its own self-reflection, in the form of the Vedas, Śaivism, and so forth, until it reaches common consensus. "Is made" is to be connected with "by that very subject (pramātṛ) in the form of the author of the scripture. For as many scriptures of self-knowledge as there are—

Those [scriptures] which take the form of the secret tantras of the ultimate conclusions of the Vedas do not at all produce a novel kind of realization within the Self; therefore, the sense is that they have as their fruit only the accomplishment of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). For this very reason, it is said: "that which [belongs] to him alone in all three categories."

The state of being the burner has been explained; therefore, because of that very reason—the primacy of the cognizer—this also is established which was stated previously: "In the case of fire and so forth, which are indistinguishable [to different subjects], the relation of cause and effect [is determined] by means of a single valid cognition alone" (2.3.8). For when the cognizer is the primary factor in a single instance...

The determination of difference and non-difference regarding the primary [subject] arises from the power of reflecting upon its activity. And since this reflection is one and the same throughout all time, it constitutes a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, in our own system, [the distinction between cognitions] would arise from the coloring by different objects of perception, whereas in the view of others, it would arise from the force of the contraction of one's own nature.

Since cognitions possess temporal distinctions and are therefore distinct, and even their corresponding determinations (*adhyavasāya*) are likewise distinct and momentary by nature, how can there be a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that culminates in the illumination of an object at a specific time, following along with its own [momentary] nature?

Producing a conceptual determination (*vikalpādhyavasāya*) which is the cause for the practical application of truth (*satyavyavahāra*), it would be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in its universal scope; however, since every [cognition] among distinct cognitions consists solely of the apprehension of what was not previously known, what "apprehension of the already-apprehended" (*gṛhītagrāhitā*) could there be, as in the case of what has been apprehended by another cognizer?
And therefore, how can it be proclaimed that in a stream of consciousness (*dhārāvāhivijñānamālā*), only the very first cognition is [valid]? (Page 180)

"Valid cognition," and so forth. Now, if it is argued that validity has already been attained by this means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which grasps the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities such as fire at the very moment of their birth, then subsequent cognitions would necessarily be invalid. For [subsequent cognitions] would be nothing more than mere appearances (*ābhāsa*).
In this very way, let the venerable one proceed;
yet their lack of measure is not absolute, whether in the case of other appearances previously ungrasped,
or in the case of the appearance of a synthesis (*yojanā*) where the characteristic of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) has not previously arisen.

Because of the manifestation of the activity of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Now, one might object: "The activity of the cognizer is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and since that too has the nature of cognition, it is momentary; how, then, is it appropriate for there to be any unity whatsoever in the activity of the cognizer? He dispels this doubt with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

As long as this [subject], existing primarily through inwardness, is not severed from his autonomy by the cognizer, he remains one and the same. Now, one might object: "Is it not accepted that his very nature is inward-turned?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that... [referring to the subject] due to the latent impressions of the duality belonging to Māyā.

This very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), though pure, is proclaimed to be conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Now, one might object: the fruitfulness of the means of knowledge does not arise from a reflective awareness that is inward-turned and consists merely of the form "I"—which, being conceptual by nature—but rather from an outward-turned awareness such as "this is a jar. And yet, it is not by that [outward-turned awareness] alone...

"How is it said that the external object is touched [by cognition], given that the determination of the object occurs primarily through reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)? To this, the answer is: "And even that which... [and so on]. "From the operation of the sense organs" means from the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) arising therefrom. That too is not without an object; rather, in its universal nature...

[It] has a universal as its object; otherwise, however, [it] has the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object. This was stated [in the passage beginning] "And because the determination is erroneous" (1.3.5), etc. Now, is that which appears before one a universal or a particular?

Since there is both clear manifestation and unclear manifestation within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), how can it be said that [the object] has that [consciousness] alone as its domain? To this, he replies: "Nor even...
because even for those things which have distinct shadows of appearance, they exist primarily as appearances.
"It is stated [in the verse]: 'Oneness is unimpeded due to what is called a single reflective awareness' (2.3.11).
By the use of the word *tāvat* ('at least' or 'for now'), it is shown that, according to our own system (*svamata*), this is not difficult to establish."
He says "even the other" (*yo 'pi*) because even the Buddhist (*bauddhaḥ*) does not dare to speak of a distinction here.

He demonstrates the very lack of determination with the word "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpam*), which is the subject term (*kartṛpada*). "Its own" (*sva*) means having a form other than its own manifestation. "From that" (*tataḥ*) refers to the reason why this is so, even according to the opponent's view.

By this [argument], the difference between appearances cannot be determined. Furthermore, he shows that by establishing identity through the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), one does not gain a firm grasp even regarding the object of knowledge at hand;
thus, in the case of the conceptual construction of words, the Lord—the all-powerful Self—is the cognizer.

At the occasion of instruction, although [the Self] is brought to the state of being an object of knowledge by words—having been established through the force of worldly transaction—it finds its rest in the "I-self" (ahantātman) upon the ultimate reflection of the supreme reality. This is the intended meaning here:
this alone is the sovereignty of the Lord, which is exceedingly difficult for the world of bound souls (paśuloka) to achieve.
Even in accomplishing that, there is no obstruction; what else could be more difficult than this:
that while the light itself is shining, there is the denial of its luminosity, which is nothing but the conceit of non-luminosity? Such is that which...
Sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is precisely that which causes the manifestation of the subject (*grāhaka*), and through that, the manifestation of the object (*grāhya*) as well.

This very power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) is called "the deluder. It is by means of this [power] that, although one's own self is independent, eternal, pervasive, and manifest—due to its connection with memory and so forth, and its lack of connection with time and space—[it appears otherwise].

When there exists a dense misconception of non-manifestation—defined by synonyms such as "delusion" (*moha*), "impurity" (*mala*), and so forth—a particular kind of appearance (*ābhāsa-viśeṣa*) arises; due to its influence, the deluded person does not engage in the full-fledged worldly activity of the Lord (*īśvara*) within his own self. This [text] is intended to proclaim the power of the energies of will (*icchā*) and the rest.

It is made known by means of the treatise called *Pratyabhijñā* (Recognition), which establishes conventional practice in the form of a complete inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). For instance, just as a certain fool, thinking he has been robbed due to delusion, is thus instructed: "Who indeed are you, whose face is such and whose garment is such? if [he asks], [the answer is given].

Behold this within yourself—thus saying again and again, nothing new has been produced for him; rather, the world of bound souls (*paśu*), while their own self is appearing exactly as it is, is awakened from the delusion of thinking "I am not the Lord" and so forth. Indeed, in that [state] where...
The powers such as knowledge and so forth are designated as "Īśvara" (the Lord), because that designation is based solely on those [powers], just as it is well-known in the Purāṇas and other texts.

"And those [qualities] exist in you as well. Alternatively, wherever something is dependent, that [support] is the sovereign there, like a king in his own kingdom; and so it is with you, for the universe [depends on you]. Whatever is attached to something and whatever shines forth, that is filled by it, like a treasure-pot with jewels; and the universe is attached to you and shines forth—this is how it is for whomsoever.
That which shines as internal must pervade its extent, just as the nature of a gem pervades gems,
or as "treeness" pervades *śiṃśapā* trees and the like. And within you, whose nature is consciousness,
the entire universe— from the earth up to Sadāśiva— as understood through the systematic procedures (*prakriyā*) of the scriptures, shines as internal.

Whatever arises and dissolves when something else exists must pervade its prior and posterior parts, just as a sprout pervades the ground; and so it is with the universe within You, whose nature is light.
In this way, the attributes of lordship, omnipresence, and eternity are to be understood, as are others as well.
The properties denoted by the term "power" (*śakti*), as taught in the scriptures, are thousands in number. To reveal them, this work— which consists of a complete inference for the sake of others—
is composed correctly by means of a treatise on the sixteen categories, beginning with the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and ending with the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

A treatise (*śāstra*) is that which is capable of effecting the thorough understanding of others. For it is in this way that another is correctly instructed regarding the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful;
and thus, by such statements, the sixteen categories beginning with perception (*pratyakṣa*) are established as having the purpose of instructing others.

If [the validity of inference] were established otherwise than by its nature as an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), then even opponents— possessing unwholesome faults acquired through their hatred for the sage who knows the reality of logic (*nyāyatattva*)— would have demonstrated that it is indeed false within their own treatises. This should be understood in detail from my very *Kathāmukhatilaka*.

Thus, by means of establishing conventional usage, that misconception which holds that what is manifesting does not manifest—denoted by the term "saṃsāra"—is removed. The removal of that very misconception is liberation. For bondage and liberation have as their ultimate reality nothing more than the appearance of such misconceptions.

This is merely the manifestation of the Blessed One’s will for one who is deluded even regarding the factor of the logical reason (*hetu*). In that case as well, it is simply the removal of delusion that must be accomplished; thus, nothing unprecedented or unestablished is being proven.
However, for one whose heart is consoled by the power of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), [the goal is attained].

When the Supreme Lord, through a portion of the impurity of delusion (*mohasaṅkara*), maintains for a certain period the identification with the body and so forth— which is sustained by effort— for the sake of accomplishing his tasks such as the desire to manifest the other world (*parojjihīrṣā*).
(Page 183)

He is called "awakened" because, like one who has understood the true nature of a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), he perceives it without error even while seeing it; for it is said that his [realization] is distinguished by the stages of hearing, reflection, and meditation reaching their full intensity.
However, through the firmness of the practice of meditation by means of the methods taught in the teachings of Śiva, preceded by the prescribed rules—

In that very context, it is stated in the scripture that a yogi who has infused the continuous stream of the supreme Lord’s attributes into the vital breath and so forth within the body, or even into objects such as a jar, becomes a vessel for supernatural powers (siddhi).

The distinction between the accomplished (siddha) and the most accomplished (siddhatama), whose nature is consistent with their respective meanings, has been described as occurring upon the attainment of the state of *ghaṭamāna*. However, even at this stage, there remains a complete residue of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of delusion. Upon the destruction of these, however, because the restrictive sense of "I-ness" regarding the body and so forth dissolves, there is nothing other than the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratā*).

However, by the power of the Lord's will alone, recognition does not arise for some even through hundreds of efforts. Even for such a person, merely upon its reaching the path of the ears, the attainment of one's true nature necessarily occurs through the gradual ripening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). As it has been said in the Āgama:
One who is unwavering in self-awareness is called liberated while living;
however, one who still harbors conceptual constructions regarding reality shall go to Śiva upon the falling of the body.
Thus it has been explained by me as well:
that because of the internal nature of volition— which is like a cluster of roots for the withered tree of saṃsāra— it is [the fuel] for the fire of ultimate reality.
Even if there were but a tiny spark,
the mass of the fire of pure awakening would blaze forth within it.

Thus, by this [argument], nothing new is established regarding the self itself. Therefore, that which was stated at the beginning of the treatise—"In the agent, the knower, the self, which is established from the very beginning"—has now been fully demonstrated in its ultimate sense. (1.1.2)
"Thus, and so forth"—may there be auspiciousness.

Thus ends the third chapter, the investigation into the ultimate reality of the means of knowledge, their results, and the objects of knowledge, within the *Kriyādhikāra* of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*, composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara, the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth reflection:

Through the digit of the supreme reality of oneness, I remember Hara— the Great Cause whose form is the manifestation of universal diversity composed of the three powers, whose body is nectar, and who is the expansion of bodiless consciousness.

It has been stated that the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) itself is the relationship; and that [relationship] was determined to consist in the nature of the signified and the signifier (*jñāpyajñāpakabhāva*). Now, however, its form as cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*) is examined in twenty-one verses.
And because he possesses infinite power, [he is the cause];
by such [statements],
his causality, agency, and action [are established].

Thus, with this [final] verse: having introduced the view of our own school—that in that context, the very nature of cause and effect consists precisely in the relationship between agent and object—[the author] refutes the causality of the insentient (*jaḍa*) by means of three verses, and establishes by means of six verses that causality belongs only to the sentient (*cetana*), whose essence is agency (*kartṛtātman*). This is done as an incidental discussion following the investigation into causes.

By three [verses], it is shown that in inference, the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) must necessarily be relied upon; by another three, it is shown that even the notions of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*) asserted by the Śākyas take refuge in our very system, for otherwise they would be entirely devoid of reality; and by yet another three, it is shown that the same applies to those asserted by the followers of Kapila. By this much, [the nature] of the conscious principle (*cetana*)...

The summary is as follows: having established [the Lord's] agency, it is shown that even that [agency] would not be tenable if He were non-supreme (anīśvara); this is demonstrated by two [sūtras]. However, an effort will be made with respect to each sūtra. Thus, the status of being a knower (*pramātṛtā*) in the Supreme Lord has been established through the medium of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), while His nature as an agent (*kartṛ-rūpa*) follows from that very same [power].
He shows by means of the aphorism that [the world] is fashioned without effort:
"And he, because of his infinite power, causes these entities to appear in this way; by the force of his will, this is his activity, which is his state of being the creator. (1)
This very primordial subject causes these entities to appear without interruption.
How? By the power of that will which has been described as non-conceptual and non-sequential, being inseparable from the Lord. Where do these entities of his reside?
If this is argued, he says: "Because of having infinite power. For it has been stated that all infinite entities are indeed His powers.
In the passage beginning with "svāmina...

(1.5.10), the meaning of the aphorism is as follows: that which is such an appearance, animated by the Will—that alone is called the Lord's instrument, His state of being the fashioner, and His state of being the creator. He now introduces this [aphorism].

By such statements as these, [the author] intends to refute [the opponent's view] through the series of arguments beginning with "But for the insentient, that... (2.4.2). The sense is that this [view] is accepted by the other [party], namely the eternalist.

He states his own view with the words "nor indeed" (*nāpi*). By the phrase "but of that" (*tasya tu*), he shatters the opponent's delusion that sequence and simultaneity alone exist. And by this much, that which they say is refuted: "If the will were eternal at the beginning of creation, then creation and dissolution would occur simultaneously; but if it is occasional (*kādācitkatva*), however..."

"Or another reason must be stated," and so forth. With the intention of showing the distinction in the coloring (*uparāga*) of what is to be sought, the reading of the plural "desires" (*icchāḥ*) is indeed not faulty. By the phrase "the manifestation of succession" and so on, he reminds us of what was previously stated: that there is no connection with time in the Blessed One, who is free from appearances and beyond succession.
The word "also" (*api*) implies that even the potter and others are like this; as will be stated later:

"Even for the transmigrating subject, it is desire alone," and so forth. "Because" means that the connection with time (*kālayoga*) would occur in the state of conceptualization (*vikalparūpatā*) through contact with the quality of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*), which arises from the coloring by the aspect of "this-ness" (*idantā*); however, it does not [occur] in that [state of pure consciousness].
The creator is of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because effects such as the movement toward a location arise even in its absence—
as in the case of running swiftly— and because it would follow that one person would be enveloped by it while a second person would not,
since the accomplishment of gestures such as the circular motion of the chest (*ura-maṇḍala*) and so forth is not achieved [without it]. For in that regard:
The existence of the cognizer’s self-awareness is characterized by a specific intensity, consisting of unimpeded effort— the unwavering intuition that "this has already been accomplished by me"—
and not [the state] of that which is yet to be done.

He who is accomplished in the swift recitation and so forth is indeed "accomplished" (*saṃpanna*); by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), he alone is the form of emanation (*nirmāṇarūpa*) of the universe. This very point is stated with the words beginning "in the recitation" (*vācana*).
(Page 186)

But surely, even conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), when associated with such a manifestation, is seen to function toward emanation in certain cases, such as in slow walking or reading; so how can it be said to be non-sequential? To this it is replied: "Even that which... and so forth.

It was stated in [the verse] "This is a jar" (*ghaṭo'yam*) and so forth (1.5.20). Furthermore, he says "and of the Lord" (*īśvarasya ca*) to indicate that the power of construction belongs to conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) at the level of *māyā*, but not to the creation of the Lord (*īśvara*) under discussion here. "That very same... (*saiva*).

It consists of mere will. It has been established that the consciousness of the potter is indeed the Lord; however, by the power of His decree, the appearance of the potter's causal agency—consisting of the collection of the wheel, the staff, and so forth—is like that in dreams or mental constructs, as has been stated more than once.
Thus it was reported. || 1 ||

"But surely, if the sprout arises from the seed, there is no entry of consciousness at all; therefore, it is the nature of consciousness alone that illuminates the universe—what does this mean? To this, the answer is given by the aphorism: "But the insentient lacks that power, [namely] the existence [of bringing forth] that which was non-existent into existence."
Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect consists precisely in the reality of the agent and the object.

Whether the sprout exists or does not exist, that existence which is perceived therein belongs neither to the seed nor to the sprout. For if it is said that "the sprout is born," this is merely the occurrence of the sprout; how then can there be a power belonging to another, namely the seed, when at that time the sprout is nothing at all? Therefore, [it is] by way of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
The action being manifested is itself the effect, and the manifester is itself the cause;

this means that [the cause] is either of the nature of the non-existent or of the existent. However, the previous explanation included the sense of the word "or" (vā), namely: "of the non-existent sprout or of the existent seed," or alternatively:
The subsequent mention of what has been enumerated applies to each individual category; thus, the application should be made according to what is possible. || 1 ||
That which is non-existent is not joined with existence; for that which is non-existent cannot possess the nature of existence.
Nor, again, is there any purpose served for that which already exists by obtaining existence once more. (3)
In the world, the relationship of cause and effect belongs to that which exists internally within [the object];
its being perceivable by both types of sense-faculties occurs through the power of some particular [cause]. (Verse 4)
Whether real or unreal, an effect is conceived as having a dual nature;

however, to claim it is "of neither form" and "inexpressible" contradicts one's own words. In that case, if non-existence were the nature of the jar, then [it would possess] existence, which is contrary to its own nature.

In what manner could one accept [the existence of a universal] even through prostrations at the feet or even by royal pressure, any more than one could accept that the color blue has become yellow? Furthermore, if its nature consists of existence (*sattā*), then why should it beg from punishments and the like? Even properties such as being the object of a particular manifestation or clarity are to be questioned in terms of their existence or non-existence.

Nor is it fitting for one who accepts valid authority (*prāmāṇika*) to remain silent on this account alone; for in the world, unimpeded practical activity (*vyavahāra*) prevails, and that is established as follows:
even though [the pot] has attained the status of being an object within the mental range of the potter’s heart...

In the primordial state, within one’s own internal consciousness, the universe— which consists of both difference and non-difference— manifests in its manifold variety through identity. It is then projected such that pleasure and the like are perceived solely by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), while objects such as a jar are perceived by both the internal and external organs.

This very thing is the relationship of cause and effect in the world. "Of someone" means of one whose power is inconceivable to people such as ourselves. For instance, just as in the case of reflections in a mirror, dreams, or mental constructs—even when there is the appearance, "This is a jar being fashioned by a potter"—in reality...

This is merely the power (*mahimā*) of the mirror and such; likewise, it is the power of consciousness alone that manifests as the appearance of a jar, even in the arousal of the appearance of the conceit that it is being fashioned by a potter. Thus, by the power of consciousness, while the jar, the staff, the wheel, the potter’s body, and so forth exist and appear, by this—

This appears as a "created" [manifestation]. And since an insentient object such as a staff is not a locus for such a conceit, agency is established as residing in the nature of consciousness (*cit*).
It is characterized by being clearly perceived through both types of sense organs and by appearing in the form of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: "Non-existent" (*asat*) means that the sprout is non-existent; by this, no specific nature (*svarūpa*) of the sprout is stated that would be contradicted by its existence. Furthermore, the so-called "existence" of a non-existent thing is its state of being an effect (*kāryatva*); by this, [the sūtra does not negate] any property of the sprout.
It was stated that for one who has previously accepted [a position], there is the admission of a property contrary to it. Now, if both of these [cases] are...
(page 188)
If it is optional, then what is the reality? He says: "But in reality... "Of otherness" means of non-existence.
[Objection: But that is insubstantial; therefore, he is all the more to be questioned. To this he says:
"Because of its remaining in that state," since the insubstantial cannot subvert the form of the non-insubstantial. [Objection: But when the seed exists...
By stating "the sprout exists," the nature of the sprout has been expressed; therefore, by setting aside those two words, how can there be a challenge?

This [statement] dispels the delusion of the opponent. The connection with the word *iti* extends up to the end [of the sentence], namely *na ca*. That which is the position of the opponent—what is that position of the opponent? He says: "In the seed," and so forth.

[The phrase] "up to the point of the consequence" (*prasaṅgapadāntam*). By the word "previously," the subsequent state (*parāvasthā*) is also indicated, because by the statement "only when the seed exists is there a sprout," it is stated that [the sprout] has an essential nature (*svabhāva*) of existence for only a single moment immediately following the seed.
Now, why is this view of the opponent not accepted? He says: "Because... (*yataḥ*). Even though... (*yadyapi ca*)... [he continues].

"In the opinion of others" (*paramate*) refers to the view of the opponent; "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) refers to our own view (*asmanmate*). He explains the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with the words "established" (*siddhā*).

In the commentary, the novelty of the nature of existence—namely, that which was previously unobtained by the non-existent—is presented; through its proximity to this, the contradiction with the established existence (*sattā*) is explained.
But surely, in that case, one should state that there is a contradiction even with the Sūtra, rather than its pointlessness.

True; however, [the opponent] speaks by way of a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*), thinking: "Let there be no contradiction with the Sūtra, yet there remains its lack of purpose. For this very reason, he provides an alternative interpretation of the function (*vṛtti*) in accordance with the Sūtra.
The phrase "or rather" (*yadvā*) means that one should not connect the word "contradictory" (*viruddhāḥ*) here with what precedes it.

Furthermore, the phrase "even so" (*tathāpi ca*) means even when there is an inappropriate doubling [of existence]. Now, if that second existence is not distinct from the prior existence, then how can there be the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryatā*)? In that case, what is the use of that other [existence]?

He says this [in the words] "But of the prior existence... and "At a distance... For the doctrine that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryavāda*) can indeed be introduced within one's own system. Precisely for this reason [he says] "And this...
And this [is] the external adjunct (*upādhi*) of appearances as existence and non-existence.
This has already been shown in the aforementioned enumerations; however, by relying on the necessity of a single fixed form, the contradiction has been established.
(Page 189)
"Being cognizable by two sense-faculties" means, in other words, that it appears as an object capable of performing a clearly manifest and complete purposeful action. (3–4)
He shows that by this investigation, the subject at hand is also established:

"In this way, this very single action, which possesses both internal and external sequential states, has been demonstrated to belong to one and the same [agent] who is capable of assuming both forms. (5)

"This very one"—she who has long been perceived by others both in her essential nature (*svarūpa*) and in her locus (*āśraya*)—now triumphs through sovereign empire. For it is thus: in the state that begins from the internal form of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*) and extends to its attainment of the status of being an object for the external senses;
Succession is appropriate because of its identity with a single substratum, and its unity [is established] by this very fact.

This single substratum is the Lord, whose nature is consciousness; through His absolute freedom (*svacchandatva*) and transparency (*svacchatva*), He indeed accommodates both the internal and external forms. The term "of the one" refers to both the agent and the object.

For action is well known to reside either in the agent or in the object; moreover, the object possesses both internal and external aspects due to the non-difference of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). That [action] has another as its agent has already been explained by us previously, and therefore it is not written again here.
"Of the cognition of an object" means [of that which] has the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*). "But in self-awareness," however, refers to [awareness] in the form of the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Now, one might object: "In the production of pleasure and so forth, there is only an internal state, not an external state;
so how can there be succession for this [self-awareness]? To this we reply: even in that case, there is indeed an internal-external nature, though it is inverted.

He explains "supreme" with the words "of pleasure and so forth. By the word "and so forth," this same rule applies to conceptual objects such as jars and the like. Regarding the word "previously": this was stated earlier while establishing that pleasure and so forth belong only to sound and the other [objects], even in the case of the *pañcabrahmannyāsa*.
In this context, he establishes that even when there is no dependence on words and the like, there is still a sequential order, by saying "or pleasure, etc.

Right here, he provides an example established in his own system, saying "just as," which will be explained at the beginning of the section on scripture (*āgama*). For indeed, in the case of pleasure being desired, whatever...

"Appearance" (ābhāsa) means that [the action] itself would result in the non-utilization of the gain upon its acquisition; "due to its differentiation" (tadbhedāt) means due to the differentiation of appearances within a single action; "manifold" (aneka) means even when there is a conjunction of differentiated appearances.

(Page 190) All action indeed resides in the agent, though some also resides in the object; due to the excellence of the perception of its specific qualities, it is said to reside in the object. Designations occur by way of common usage, as for example, "cooking" (*pāka*).

And thus, due to the difference in the object (*karman*), its difference will be explained; however, this does not apply to the act of going (*gamana*), because it is located in the agent (*kartṛstha*) and does not impart any specific quality to the object. But the act of creation (*nirmāṇakriyā*), even while imparting a specific quality to the object, [is distinct] from the object itself as it appears.

Because they have as their essence the subject whose nature is consciousness (*saṃvid-ātman*), the action residing in the agent and the action residing in the object are said to be of equal status. Regarding the phrase "of the act of cooking," this refers to [cooking] taking place in the kitchen of a single king. Now, one might object: "If the actions are distinct, how can they be denoted by a single word? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Only... (*kevalam*).

Thus it is said. For this very reason, it has been stated that "verbal suffixes (tiṅanta) do not necessitate a *ekaśeṣa* [retention of one of several identical forms]. Now, one might ask: why must its unity be established solely through the identity of its substratum (*āśraya*), rather than allowing it to be one by its own nature? To this he replies: "For [in the case] of action... One might object: if action is one because of the identity of its substratum as characterized by the object (*karman*), then...

"Why is the unity of the agent (*kartṛaikya*) alone consecrated with the burden of the effect, such that it belongs to some [single] agent?"—it was in this context of defining the nature of the agent that it was stated, "the action is one or many. To this, it is replied:
by the force of the reference in the words "for even of the action" (*karmaṇo 'pi hi*), it is indeed the unity of the action itself that has been stated.

Even for that which appears as divided through the connection with the prior and posterior parts of an action, the reflective awareness belongs only to the agent; and since this awareness consists in the synthesis of diverse appearances through the process of subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), it is the Lord, the Agent alone, who is said to be the primary reality. || 5 ||
Now, one might object: "In the case of an insentient seed, since it is devoid of activity, its causality is properly understood as being merely latent.
To this he replies: "That which exists within is the effect of that very [cause] which is external, in relation to which [the internal exists]."
And with respect to the subject, the twofold state of being external or internal has been described.

Manifestation as externality is itself the creation (*nirmāṇa*). Furthermore, whatever object is said to be externalized in relation to something else, that object is the effect of that very [subject]; and since the state of being internal or external is relative to the subject (*pramātṛ*), insentient things such as seeds do not possess causality at all. To illustrate this: [the text continues with] *vaśanam*.
The capacity to empower, sovereign power (*prabhāva*), strength (*bala*), and independence (*svātantrya*)— all these, being of the nature of will,
belong solely to consciousness. However, when preceded by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), they appear as if belonging to the form of consciousness within its own body-like [manifestation].

In the case of insentient things such as seeds and the like, that [agency] is used figuratively; by virtue of them—that is, through their capacity—such conventional expressions are employed, but there is nothing whatsoever that depends on the will of the insentient. Furthermore, the connection is that even if it were postulated, it could not be one [single cause];
rather, it would necessarily take the form of being produced in various specific places and so forth. This is the meaning.

He demonstrates the form of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) by means of the words "the seed," and so forth. He sets forth the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to explain the restrictive particle (*evakāra*) found in the Sūtra with the words "even so. Here, the response is as follows:
the term "restriction" (*niyamagrahaṇa*) is used because even in the case of externality, internality remains unbroken. And not...

With the intention that internality may be conceived in relation to the seed (*bīja*), he says, "in relation to the form of consciousness" (*cidrūpam apekṣya*). The underlying meaning is that even the entry [of the seed] into the interior of the seed is acceptable here precisely because it has been transferred into non-difference from the form of consciousness. The phrase "only of the potter and so forth" refers to that which has been multiplied over a long time.
It is appropriate to stop at this point, having turned [the opponent] away from the doctrine of an insentient cause, so that he may understand the ultimate [truth].
However, the reality is that even for the potter, his rest lies only in the consciousness of the Supreme Lord. 6.

If the effect does not belong to the insentient, then the cause does not reside in the insentient; thus, it is established that causality belongs to consciousness alone, and that [causality] consists precisely of action.
Therefore, the aphorism states: "The knower alone is the cause, and he [abides] in the state of the two-fold manifestation."
While the effect remains as one alone, the activity of that single entity is said to have arisen.

The two appearances are distinguished as external and internal. "As an object" means by way of the unification of the reflection upon the previously experienced external form; thus, in this case, the previous experience itself is merely the first stage of cognitive engagement (*ābhoga*). As was stated previously regarding pleasure and the other [feelings].

"External appearance preceded by a prior and subsequent appearance. Alternatively, "as an object" means as a distinct entity from the portion of the subject (*pramātṛ*) by way of a manifest form. As it has been said: "In conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), this which is the mental representation... (1.8.8).
And so forth. At that time, the first manifestation is merely the desire to act externally.
This should also be applied to pleasure and the like. || 7 ||
(Page 192) This very point is further strengthened by the following:
"For this very reason, even in the case of a sprout, the Supreme Lord is accepted as the efficient cause."
For that reason, it is also not tenable for other things, such as seeds and the like, to possess the status of being a cause. || 8 ||

Even though God exists as the cause, that causality which they accept for something else— namely, for the insentient (jaḍa) distinct from God— is not possible, because [the insentient] does not act with foresight.
For what is called "structure" (sanniveśa) is that which brings about the distinction between the homogeneous and the heterogeneous.

In the case of jars, bowls, basins, and the like, which are produced from the material cause of clay, their form consists of being assembled and situated together; thus, they are effects whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Once this has been observed even a single time, it follows by necessity that everything must exist in that very same way through its configuration. As for what is said:

The claim that there is a cognition of something being produced by [an agent] even when that agent is not perceived, and so forth, is merely an utterance distorted by the delusion of partiality toward one's own views, for this same [fallacy] applies equally to smoke as well;
enough with this digression. Indeed, this has already been elaborated by the author himself in the *Īśvarasiddhi*, whereas here it is...

The ultimate truth is this: the Lord himself, conforming to his own power of necessity (niyati-śakti), manifests himself as a sprout by means of the preceding appearances of seed, earth, and water, within that which is pure and self-luminous. || 8 ||

Since an insentient entity cannot function as a cause anywhere without consciousness, and since the conscious agent must ultimately be none other than God, the Sūtra states: "For instance, this potter [acts] only through the arrangement of God’s sovereignty."
One should produce a jar through the sequential process of refining that particular clay and other materials.

The pot serves as an illustration for establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*). If the causal relationship between insentient things were merely a sequence of prior and subsequent forms, independent of a conscious agent, then what would be the need for a potter in the case of a palanquin or a stack of bricks? Consequently, even the cognition of movement toward an object [would be inexplicable].

A conscious agent would not be required anywhere; for even that [conscious agent] is occupied with the regulation of one place to another, and that very [regulation] is called "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*). Therefore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
whatever is non-conscious yet performs an effect depends upon a conscious agent, like clay and other materials; and seeds and the like are likewise [non-conscious].
This is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For the capacity of an insentient thing to produce an effect is occasional; it is neither causeless nor does it have any other cause.
(Page 193)
The pervasion is established. Consequently, the potter alone is the Lord in that case, because by performing the various refinements of the clay,
staff, wheel, and so forth— such as kneading, preparing, and turning— he produces the jar through that sequence, starting from the lump of clay and ending with the finished vessel.
This is the *niyoga* (the divine ordinance). And it is the Lord alone who, having assumed such a form through the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), appears as such;

whether as a potter or a weaver, He alone is the agent in every case. Otherwise, how could clay, the staff, and other tools follow the will of the potter, or even how could threads proceed toward the making of a cloth?
Why would they not conform? As for the potter’s fixed sense of agency and the persistence of his merit, demerit, and so forth, even that exists solely through the arrangement of the Lord,
who clearly arouses the sense of ego— just as the status of a debtor exists for a guarantor— in every case.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that the Blessed One alone is the agent. If God is accepted as the agent on the grounds that an effect does not arise in the absence of a conscious being— this being the case for seeds and the like, and since for jars and the like there is indeed the presence of a conscious being such as a potter— then how can God be the agent in all cases?
He introduces the Sūtra with the words "buddhimat" (to the intelligent one) with the intent of removing that delusion.

The phrase "udāhṛtām" (stated) means "spoken by way of introducing an illustration," as indicated by the words "tathā hi" (for instance). It should be understood that he "explains" [the meaning] by means of the entire sentence of the commentary, which is indicated by a single part [of it]. [This occurs] when the intelligent person is present.

With the intention that "the specific distinction must be stated," he explains the intended meaning regarding a portion of the sentence by means of this single part, namely the term "potter" (*anena hi*), which denotes the form of the potter. [Objection:
But if this is so, what other specific distinction, distinct from the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*), is required for the intelligent agent?

"Even the wise man destroys delusion. Regarding "refinement" (*saṃskāra*), that potter is employed for [clay] such as that from Mount Mandara. [Objection: But surely a jar is produced from clay and so forth once they have been refined;
what is the use of a specific quality of God (*īśvaratā*)? To this he says here: "And refinement also... [meaning] "even when [the material] has been refined."

Even if clay and other materials are intended to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the potter, despite being present, is not capable of bestowing upon the clay and so forth the quality of consciousness— the property of being a conscious agent (*anusandhātṛtva*). Nor [is this possible] for that which is insentient.

The state of being the cause, whose essence consists in the supreme agency of the ultimate reflective awareness of the sequence of internal and external manifestations, is thus appropriately established.
(Page 194)

The word "again" (*punarapi*) is used even though it has already been stated that [the object] is accumulated; the meaning is that it is produced by the agent of action (*kartṛ*). Regarding its lack of utility, he provides the previously mentioned object of knowledge (*prameya*) as the reason through a concise statement: "even in the case of a mental impression" (*saṃskāre'pi*), where the particle *api* implies that even such a thing is not possible. And thus, "if" (*yadi*) [the effect arises] merely by the vibration of the mind (*cetaḥ-parisphuraṇa-mātreṇa*).

The meaning is that he should perform [it]. Even the refinement (*saṃskāra*) has been accepted by way of a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*), yet even that is not tenable; thus he says "nor" (*na ca*). If the refinement were due to his will alone, then he could, by his own will, refine space itself and thereby bring forth the imagined universe.

Now, let it be granted that this is a criticism directed against the proponent of the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*); however, in the view of the proponent of the existent effect (*satkāryavāda*), only a specific thing serves as the cause for a specific effect, and not everything arises from everything. Consequently, depending upon consciousness, only a particular [effect] will arise from a particular [cause], with consciousness serving merely as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*); what is the use of postulating the nature of a Lord (*īśvara*)?

Here is the point to be established: that [the seed] does not tolerate even that [state], nor does it [attain it]. For the nature of consciousness never belongs to the seed, such that the sprout could exist within it. This will be explained in this very investigation (*vimarśa*).
Having refuted the opposing position as faulty, he concludes his own position with the word "therefore" (*tat*): therefore, of both...
Furthermore, whatever utilization there is of that which is both conscious and unconscious, that is by the will of the Lord; such is the connection. || 9 ||
The independence of the conscious agent (cetanasya) in the process of cause and effect is indeed observed; thus, he speaks by means of a well-known example:
"Even for yogins, that [effect] occurs through the power of their will alone, even without clay or seeds."
A jar or other such objects arise, each performing its own stable purposeful activity.

The connection is "even without clay and seed"; since the causality here is based on the primacy of the individual (vyakti), it is appropriate that the reference be to the genus (jāti), and not to a singular collective form. Both [clay and seed] are mentioned to illustrate that there are two kinds of effects: those well-known in the world as having a single insentient cause, and those dependent upon a sentient agent. Now, one might object:
In that regard, there is merely a similarity of words concerning things such as jars and sprouts; however, in reality, they are entirely different.
Therefore, he provides the qualification "that which is stable in each respective case" and so forth, as the means for dispelling the supreme delusion.
The term "each respective" (*tattat*) refers to their diverse forms. And "stable" (*sthira*) means that which performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
And this is the construction made by the author of the commentary: [the cognition] apprehends each respective stable object-character possessing various forms,
which is connected with subsequent causal efficiency, through its own causal efficiency by way of being a cause, having that as its nature, or being in conformity with it.

There is no fault even in the compound *karoti* ("he does"). He first restates the opponent's view—that even the will of a yogi could not produce an effect without a material cause (*upādāna*)—in order to refute it, saying "and this is not so. Then, introducing the reason for that refutation with the word "because" (*yataḥ*), he presents what is to be said, which is useful for enlivening that [point].
The author restates the opponent’s position as it truly is with the words "because," meaning from the nature of its own material cause (*upādāna*).
"Of the same class" means that cognition [arises] from cognition. "That which conceals" refers to the seed [concealing] the sprout.
And this, according to the circumstances—either collectively or individually—is the definition of the material cause (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*) held by the opponents.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is a collection of the distinctions stated by others, such as "the object," "the cause," and "the dominant condition. As they say:
"For those other than the existent, the cause is the causal factor (hetu)..."

And so forth. Having restated the opponent’s position along with its underlying principle, he demonstrates the reason for the negation—which was introduced by the word "since" (*yataḥ*)—with the passage beginning "of the sprout," and so on. [He asks: "If there were even a slight transgression of the well-established worldly order, which is pervaded by specificities such as place, time, form, and auxiliary conditions..."

Is it endured? Then what is the point of the yogin’s wretchedness regarding the grasping of the substratum (*upādāna*)? Or, if it is not endured, then the yogin would become nothing more than a broken potter—this is the intended meaning. "Of them" refers to the yogins.
And this [distinction] is to be applied to both the preceding and the following [verses]. As for the word "subtle" (*sūkṣma*), here it is merely an admission of that [state]; for at that time—
The view that atoms, the primal matter (pradhāna), and so forth [are the causes] is entirely useless. Furthermore, even that [view] is established only by means of well-known causes;
for while the primal matter is by nature imperceptible, atoms and the like are already well-established as being beyond the range of the eyes and other senses.

"The cause for direct realization exists as established in the world"—this is the point. Now, one might object: "Let 'yogic-ness' be simply the capacity for subtle vision; nothing more than that is required. To this, he replies: "All indeed," meaning [all] up to the point of being an agent of desired results.
The term "of the perfected ones" (*siddhānām*) is an epithet for yogis, referring to those who have attained stages such as *ghaṭamāna* (striving) and so forth.

For the sake of exclusion: for yogins here on earth, whose excellence of power unfolds in successive stages, possess unimpeded power in accomplishing their desired ends precisely by transcending all worldly necessity (*niyati*).
Because:

"From some cause of causes," meaning even from one that is remote. "Then" means at that stage; the sense is that at that time it is that very [proximate] cause which is the cause, and not that remote cause.

"From the non-existent" means from emptiness itself, or from a non-existent effect. For how could there be a rule of occasional occurrence for that which is causeless and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? "Concomitant causes" refers to space, time, ether, and so forth.
Now, if it is argued that a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not observed therein—on the grounds of the principle that what is eternal lacks negative concomitance—then:

Let the will of the yogi alone be the material cause; furthermore, even the creation of a yogi—like the work of a weaver—is in reality nothing more than the essence of the conceit produced by *māyā*, since it is ultimately the creation of the Lord (*īśvara*) itself.
He applies this object of knowledge to the present context as an illustrative example with the words "just as that very [thing]."

He states that even a world-renowned example, such as "hair and so forth," [serves as an illustration] because there is no fixed rule regarding its material cause (*upādāna*); furthermore, it is not a separate entity because it lacks connection with that [notion of] "that-ness" (*tat-parāmarśa*). Moreover, even by an opponent, in certain places—such as in the sections on "determination" (*viniścaya*) where it says "in some regions, certain substances... and so on—[this is accepted].

The intention is as follows: although a multitude of entities belonging to a single genus—such as the *āmalaka* fruit—does not transcend its generic nature due to differences in field, time, processing (*saṃskāra*), and so forth, it nevertheless possesses a manifold variety of qualities such as taste and potency that is fully admitted.
Thus, in some way, it indeed performs purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) by producing pleasure, pain, or other effects.
"Even from that"—that is, from the aforementioned example; for in that case, the Lord's status as creator is established precisely by disregarding his own well-known material causes. || 10 ||
Is it not the case that the stability of inference has now been shaken?

For, in the restriction of one thing—whether imagined or unimagined—to another, the cause characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*) is observed to remain intact; for there is no such thing as a thing devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Nor is it of a different nature in its various aspects (*paryāyaśaḥ*), for if each one were abandoned, there would be a total absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). The same should be said regarding the case of being causeless or having different causes.
Both of these [cases] are [resolved] precisely because of the restriction of causes; for the *śiṃśapā* possesses the nature of a tree [only] due to such causal necessity.

For this reason, [the fire] arises from its cause and possesses the specific nature of being a consumer of fuel that produces smoke. However, according to the path of reasoning already explained, there would be a total collapse of all logic; for by the mere will of a yogin, even a *śiṃśapā* tree could possess the nature of being a non-tree.

(Page 197) It might be so; however, in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), this [uncertainty] would be twofold: smoke could be produced even without fire, and a specific kind of fire could fail to produce smoke. Thus, how could there be a reliable inference? This is true; however, in this way:
This [logical reason] is applicable when the absence of a yogic creation has been ascertained by another means of valid cognition;
for only then does the effect-reason or the essential-nature-reason arise from its origin in production. (11)

Regarding what was stated— that the yogi’s will is unimpeded— it is for this very reason that the qualification "in the absence of the yogi’s emanation" (*yoginirmāṇatābhāve*) must be ascertained by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Only then do the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*) become valid reasons when the cause or the essential nature is to be inferred, and not otherwise.

Now, one might object: "What is this weakness regarding the essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*)? For in that case, it matters nothing whether there is a restriction or lack of restriction on causality. How can it be that it matters nothing?
Since even an essential nature is restricted by another essential nature; in that which has arisen, its very production consists in the relation of cause and effect.
Root text: For instance,

according to the principle that "that which depends on the same causal complex [as another thing arises from that very cause]," since the *śiṃśapā* tree was produced from its own [cause], from that very [cause]...
"This universal has arisen as excluded from non-treeness. But what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there that apprehends the qualifier?
It has already been stated by others:
it is either rational perception (*yauktika-pratyakṣa*), mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), worldly consensus, or scripture (*āgama*).

Whether this distinction of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) is rooted in the practice of infinite lifetimes, produced at that very moment, or is a matter of presumptive necessity (*arthāpatti*), what does it matter to us? For, since it is useful for our conventional discourse and does not obstruct the subject at hand, we need not concern ourselves with it.
Indeed, what is the nature of this object of knowledge (*prameya*)—the Lord, who is self-luminous and the soul of the universe?
"The opportunity for refutation exists when inference is weak"—this is the introduction to the meaning of the sūtra.
"It has been established," and so forth, is the explanation of that portion of the sūtra beginning with "for this very reason.
"This is not the subject matter under discussion for us"—this is the phrase indicating the context of the incidental argument (*prasaṅga*). By the words "he cognizes," and so forth...

The distinction between inference for oneself and inference for others has been shown. Here, the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is of two kinds: that which clearly implies a relationship of cause and effect, or its opposite. Of these, he provides an example of the first (page 198):

"Fire-possessing" (*agnimān*): for fire-possessingness would indeed be the very nature (*svabhāva*) of that which possesses smoke, provided that smoke were established as belonging to fire alone. He gives a second example: "being a *śiṃśapā* tree," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of the Buddhists": the followers of Kaṇāda and others, however, do not say this, as they maintain that these two universals (*sāmānya*) are distinct.
They accept [this] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatā*). Regarding the term "of the probandum" (*sādhyasya*): that which is the probandum is "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*);

its concomitance with the mere *śiṃśapā*—namely, the fact that it exists only when that [the *śiṃśapā*] exists—is established precisely by way of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Why is this so?
If this is asked, he says: "No. For a cause is necessarily connected to its effect;

it is logical that its presence must be necessarily concomitant with the presence of the effect. Now, just as fire is the cause of smoke in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), is [the universal] likewise the cause of being a *śiṃśapā*?

Tree-ness is the cause. For *śiṃśapā*-ness is indeed of the very nature of tree-ness; therefore, since there is no difference at all in the case of a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*), how can it be said that "it is something else here"? To this, he replies:
"In the case of non-difference. If that [tree-ness] is of the very nature of that [śiṃśapā-ness], then necessarily, upon the establishment of *śiṃśapā*-ness...

That too would necessarily be established. For if that which is not established when something else is established were identical in essence with it, then the entire universe would likewise be identical with the universe. Therefore, if it is not established, it must necessarily be other than it. And it is not logical for one thing to be invariably concomitant with another, except in the case of identity.

Thus it is established that [the relation] is by way of cause and effect. Now, one thing is not said to be connected to another through its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) if the relation of cause and effect were to be applied; rather, it is through the medium of cognition (*pratīti*).
For when the state of being a *śiṃśapā* is cognized, the state of being a tree is cognized; therefore—
"That which is invariably concomitant with the mere state of being a *śiṃśapā* is so described. He refutes this with the words "And not...

For when the state of being a *śiṃśapā* has been apprehended, one who desires to apprehend the state of being a tree may be questioned as follows: "Why, when one thing has been apprehended, have you begun to apprehend another? If he should say: "But surely..."

Since the cognition of "treeness" necessarily occurs in one who cognizes that [tree], this very question would have been answered by itself. If, however, the reality of the answer is that this is simply the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*) and thus not subject to questioning, then one should be questioned in this way: "But how could even a resident of the Coconut Island [cognize it]?"
Thus one should not perceive it;
for the intrinsic nature of a thing does not arise through partiality. But surely by that—
The fact that this [cognition] is necessarily concomitant with those [objects] is not known. But why is it not known?

For that [concomitance] is mediated by cognition, and it has been stated that cognition arises from the very nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*). And how could the nature of one thing be the cause for the cognition of another, in the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*)?
If [the object] is already present, what is the use of inference? This is stated up to the words "because of its fruitlessness" (*vaiphalyāt*). Now, one might object:

when this person perceives a tall *śiṃśapā* tree—possessing branches and so forth—as being of the nature of a tree, then at that time, the fact that "treeness" is perceived as necessarily following from that [specific instance] would mean that [the universal] is short-lived (*vāmanāṃ*) over time.

Seeing a *śiṃśapā* tree but not seeing its height, one might— due to delusion— not perceive "treeness" here; yet, whether by oneself or through the assistance of another, once awakened, one follows after "treeness" as something whose cognition is invariably concomitant with that [the *śiṃśapā*] alone, and by following after that...

The cognition of "treeness" (vṛkṣatva) when [the tree] is obstructed is called inference. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the word "atha": even when a *śiṃśapā* tree is present before one's eyes, how could this person perceive its "treeness"?

If it is argued that it is because the latter is of the same nature (*svabhāva*) as the former, then [we reply]: since it is of that very same nature, it should be perceived in the subject (*pakṣa*) as well.

Inference would be contradicted; for inference is not possible with respect to a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) as a corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is what he says: "Just as in the case of the similar instance," and so forth;
thus, because it is a cognition invariably concomitant with that alone, one thing [is established] elsewhere as being invariably concomitant with that alone.

Having accepted the refutation that "it exists," he states another objection regarding its necessary connection through cognition alone: "Even as for the necessary connection through cognition. For a necessary connection through cognition is said to mean that one thing invariably produces the cognition of another; in that case, how can this necessity exist?
"Without a necessary connection. [Objection: But surely, only when a necessary connection exists will there be a concomitance with cognition;

what is the fault? [The author] replies: "And merely being inferable. What is the meaning of "concomitant with that alone by way of cognition"? It means that it is to be inferred by means of a logical reason (*hetu*). And this is its characteristic form.
