"Even for that which is to be inferred from an effect-reason, there exists a nature that is concomitant with the mere presence of that [effect]; thus, the reason is [established] by its own nature."

And the statement, "The reason [is] either an essential nature (*svabhāva*) or a presence that is invariably concomitant with mere existence," which describes a distinction of the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) by way of its object, would not be possible.
Therefore, because the appearance is distinct and likewise real as an entity, the state of being a tree and the state of being a *śiṃśapā* are indeed different in the ultimate sense; however,
by means of the cause consisting of the power of the Supreme Lord’s necessity (*niyati-śakti*), there is the appearance of a *śiṃśapā*.
Regarding what was previously stated in the verse beginning with *pṛthagdīpa* (2.3.7)— namely, that [the tree] is "created" as being conjoined with the appearance of treeness—
let this much of the text be used to designate it as a "reason based on essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*).

[The author] states his intention: Now, it has been said that this entire conventional practice of inference and the object of inference proceeds according to the principle of the property (*dharma*) and the locus of the property (*dharmin*) as they are mounted upon the intellect; therefore, even though the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is partless, nevertheless...
According to the principle stated in [Pāṇini-vārttika 1.51], "As many as are the superimpositions of objects...

and so forth, identity is asserted because the exclusion from non-śiṃśapā-hood and the exclusion from non-tree-hood both have exclusion as their basis, and because that which is excluded [from these] is one.

But what is the fault in [saying] that the distinction is conceptual? This [objection] is not tenable, for even that which is conceptual [cannot be so]. Here, if the two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are real entities or if they are non-entities, how could there be identity (*tādātmya*) between them, or with that [thing] from which they are mutually excluded, as in the case of a jar and a cloth?
And it would be like the horn of a rabbit, the horn of a donkey, or a cart. Furthermore, how could there be a distinction characterized by plurality between two non-entities?

If two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) possess the relationship of signifier and signified, one must assert their identity (*tādātmya*), just as in the case of causal production (*tadutpatti*), and not [identity] with some other entity. For indeed—

Since the relationship of cause and effect exists between a jar and a cloth along with another entity, the relationship of the signifier and the signified (gamyagamakabhāva) is logical. Therefore, regarding that single object which is established through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), there can be no status as signifier and signified due to the absence of differentiation. Now, if that conceptual construction does not apply to the actual entity...

When [an object] is determined through the power of ascertainment (*vyavasāya*), then there is the establishment (*siddhi*) of the real entity (*vastu*); and since that which is not a real entity (*avastu*) is nothing at all, it would be said that there is neither any establishment of a real entity nor any non-establishment. By this very statement, one informs the opponent regarding "the real entity. This much, however, concerns the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

He demonstrates that what has been stated by us as the object of cognition (*prameya*) has indeed been accepted by others, even if not expressed in words, with the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), meaning from the aforementioned object of cognition. For this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) for the opponents.

It is agreed. In that case, it is logical that "cowness" (*gotva*) alone is the probandum (*sādhya*), and not the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), because the latter is not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) since it is something distinct from it. If it is argued that being the object of conventional usage is indeed its intrinsic nature, this is a conceptual construction and is not tenable. Therefore, [the probandum is] the conventional usage.

For those who say "it is established," the fact that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is already established implies that, on the basis of that very nature, what is to be established is merely another entity, and not the nature itself—this is clearly manifest in their hearts.

Now, one might object: even in the case of the reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*), in all instances, the relationship of the signifier and the signified exists only between two specific exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).

Just as in the case of smoke, fire, and so forth, why this frantic effort to find fault with the essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*)? To this, he replies: "Exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*). By way of the exclusion of non-fire, it is determined that the external fire itself is established. As he said:

"Validity has a real entity as its object"—thus [it is said]. But in the case of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), we do not understand what is established by inference. It cannot be the real entity, because that is already determined precisely by the determination [of the reason] through the means of proof; nor can it be the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), because that is not a real entity.
Having thus refuted the opposing view, he establishes his own position with the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way).

Even that which is an object of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—meaning that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) must not be held to be without an object. Consequently, the two appearances are conceptually constructed, and they are indeed distinct; however, they have attained the status of a single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
According to the method already explained, and therein [in that system], since the very root is the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) which depends upon necessity (*niyati*),

the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) has been established by his own doctrine through the theory of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) consisting of a mass of appearances. Now, even within the theory of the partless particular (*niraṃśasvalakṣaṇa*), [he establishes it] by way of a provisional admission (*abhyupagamavāda*).
Others say that when the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is accepted as the logical reason (*hetu*), one must necessarily rely upon the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*);

thus, they describe this object of cognition (*prameya*) as being extremely firm by saying "because it has such an essential nature. Furthermore, some divide even what is a single entity into distinct parts, and they analyze that very same thing.
For the natures of conceptual constructions indeed unify [their objects] through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of what has been differentiated;
therefore, by the power of such a determination of conceptual construction, there will exist both the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) and identity (*tādātmya*).
Because all conventional transactions depend upon the face of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
To this it is replied: "even so" (*tathāpi*). The phrase "as if distinct" means that [the object] can be differentiated by the power of conceptual determination.

Up to this point, the relationship between the signifier and the signified has been explained. By the phrase "only partless," the nature of the reason as a *svabhāvahetu* (essential identity) has been stated. Having thus restated the opponent's position, [the author] applies his own intended view—rooted in the principle of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*)—to the object of cognition (*prameya*) following this, using the words "and so it is" (*tathā ca*). He reiterates his own statement: [The text continues: "Just as... and so forth. This indicates that the relationship between the signifier and the signified is established through the causal relation of origination. Thus, the logical reason is not merely a matter of essential identity, but is grounded in the fact that the effect arises from its specific cause. Therefore, on the basis of the object of cognition, he demonstrates how the conclusion follows from the premise by means of the principle of causal origination. This confirms his own position.

He clarifies this with the words "the reason," and so forth. With the intention that in a *svabhāva-hetu* (essential-reason) characterized by symmetrical pervasion (*samavyāptika*), there is no variety in the concomitance of that [reason] alone, whereas in one characterized by asymmetrical pervasion (*viṣamavyāptika*) there is, he says "but not.
"Of the reason" means the causality of the producing reason toward the produced [effect], such as being produced (*kṛtaka*). That very [causality]...

It establishes momentariness therein. That which is the seed-nature of a specific *śiṃśapā* seed—that is, its being the cause of a *śiṃśapā*—is itself what establishes treeness therein; thus, with respect to the probans (*svabhāva*), the probandum is necessarily concomitant with that alone.

It is established that [the reason] does not exist in that which is to be inferred by means of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). For it is not the case that the cause of smoke itself establishes the fire as the probandum (*sādhya*). Indeed, the causality of smoke belongs to fire alone;
and it is solely by the power of the cause characterized as fire that the mountain possesses smoke, but not from that [smoke] itself.

The state of possessing fire; for that [possession of fire] occurs through the power of other causes such as fuel and the like, and thus there is no necessary concomitance (*tanmātrānubandha*) with it here. Indeed, the kind of necessary concomitance intended by the Teacher is one where "whenever this exists, that necessarily exists," and not "when this exists, that may also exist"—how then could this apply to the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*)?

"It would have to be rooted in identity (*tādātmya*). By this, it has been shown that what the Bhaṭṭa [Kumārila] maintained—that among the types of necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) is primary—does not follow the logic of reason (*nyāya*). And therefore, regarding one who speaks in accordance with that [position] alone:

The claim that "the state of possessing fire in that which possesses smoke" is the definition of the essence (*svabhāva*) as an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) nature is to be understood as refuted; for this [definition] relies on the determination of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) manifested through the force of formal application (*prayoga*), in order to justify the definition of a reason (*hetu*) according to the system (*tāntrika*).
This is merely a conceit of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatva*), for there is no actual intrinsic nature here. To explain:

when smoke is perceived in reality, fire is cognized; yet fire is not the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of smoke. If it is argued that being produced by fire is its characteristic, let it be so for the moment; however, as for fire—

To this extent, what constitutes the nature of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatā*)? It is not the state of being produced by fire that is to be inferred; rather, for those who seek the removal of cold, cooking, and so forth, it is fire itself that is ultimately to be inferred.

For the fulfillment of that [desire] does not arise from the nature of smoke as being produced by fire, but rather from fire itself; nor is it logical to say that "possessing fire" is the definition of "possessing smoke. For what is meant by "possessing smoke"?
According to the Buddhist (Saugata) view, it is "smoke and the mountain," whereas in the system of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣika),...
Conjunction, inherence, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth would have to be added. Likewise, one should consider the state of "possessing fire.
In that case, how could the nature of these two positions—whether considered part by part, in pairs, in threes, or as a whole—be consistent with one thing [serving] as the nature of another?

Because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If, due to the ultimate unity of inherence (*samavāya*), there were such a conceit [of identity], then nothing would have an intrinsic nature for anyone. Furthermore, it is precisely intrinsic nature that is called a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), because it makes known its exclusion from heterogeneous things, being defined as that by which something is characterized; but it is not...

The conventional usage of a "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) is useful for the purpose of production; or, if that were the case, the characteristic would be nothing other than the cause itself. Having thus refuted the opponent's position that it is merely a cause, what more has been achieved by accepting that it is merely a characteristic? It is merely a synonym.

Because there is no distinction in the object to be denoted; furthermore, it is not mere intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that constitutes a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), but rather that which makes [the nature] known (*jñāpaka*). And it is logical that the maker known is that which is situated within the totality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-sāmagrī*), not the object of cognition (*prameya*). Therefore:
And as for the definition of that which is to be made known—
whatever is stated in accordance with the difficult-to-comprehend doctrine of Dharmottara is indeed incorrect. For instance,
[the claim] that there is [a distinction] of perception, which is a specific type of cognition, from other cognitions such as inference...
A definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which makes known a distinct form; it is non-conceptual and free from error.
In this regard, it is stated that a definition is formulated in order to dispel misconceptions, such that the definition is prescribed while the definiendum is restated.
Whatever such a definition of this [reality] is well-known in the world, that indeed does not exist for the deluded.
That which is known as a point of dispute is called "to be enjoined" because it is being elucidated by means of a treatise;
as was stated previously:
"The means of valid cognition are well-known."
Thus [ends the section on] the treatise that removes delusion. (Page 204)

And so it is said. Furthermore, at the time of inference, it is not the case that the presence of fire is already established merely by observing the presence of smoke, such that even here the definition would have as its sole fruit the removal of delusion and thus the pervaded (vyāpya) would be [the object of] the definition.
And what is the harm in using the word "nimitta" (cause/occasion) instead of the word "tanmātra" (only that)?

Furthermore, we do not understand how it is that [the object] is "characterized" by the word *lakṣaṇa*, for the objection and its refutation are symmetrical. To explain: from what [source] is it known that this alone is its cause? Since this alone is its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), if someone were to ask, "From what is it known that this alone is its characteristic? then he—

If it is argued that the second category— which is distinct from the collection of things accepted as possessing this definition— is not its definition because it would involve the fallacies of impossibility, under-extension, or over-extension; then,
this alone must be its cause, since no other cause for it exists.
If it is said that [the definition] is due to its connection with impossibility and so forth, why would the face be distorted by such crookedness?

If you argue that these faults are well-known in the refutation of [its being] a definition, are they not likewise well-known in the refutation of [its being] a cause among the faults of impossibility and so forth?

Because the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) is untenable, as it is well-established in the world. Whatever is indeed censured, that is done by way of attributing a fault; and these faults, such as impossibility and so forth, are present everywhere—so what is new in this? For instance, the earth is not inherent (*samavāyinī*) in sound, nor does it [inhere] in it.

Because [the probandum] is impossible even when [the reason] exists, and possible even when it does not exist, "belonging to that" (tasya) is raised as a fault by way of a *prasaṅga* proof, due to such defects as non-existence and lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Furthermore, the definition of an entity (*bhāva*) is not merely a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because [properties] such as being an effect, a cause, or a concomitant are non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) characteristics;
if it is argued that the very nature of being its cause and so forth is the characteristic, we say no, because that [nature] is itself what is to be characterized.
Furthermore, the state of not possessing fire is not a characteristic of the state of possessing smoke.

Because of the consequence of [logical] impossibility and so forth, the absence of being a definition or the linguistic usage thereof is what is to be proven (*sādhya*). In that regard, in some cases, that very [absence] is the probandum, as in the case of other types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
In this context, perceptuality (*pratyakṣatva*) is not, for its part, the absence of being a definition.

Because, such being the case, it would be impossible to set forth [objections] regarding its non-existence; therefore, this certainty concerning existence must be declared as inferential (*ānumānika*). Thus, once again, that very point which the ancients maintain has returned: [the certainty of existence is inferential].

"The removal of the mass of undesirable [consequences] by means of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*). Now, is there not an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in inference? Indeed, do defects of the object, such as impossibility (*asaṃbhava*), cease merely because the name has been changed? For even when "reasoning" (*yukti*) is mentioned, would there not likewise be an infinite regress? To explain:

The impossibility of smoke in the absence of fire is the non-existence of its occurrence; and "occurrence" (saṃbhava) is said to be smoke itself—namely, the existence of smoke as its own cause, or its inherence (samavāya). And if the non-existence of that [inherence] is internal, having the nature of cognition and consisting in non-apprehension, then...

This [self-awareness] is self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*); however, that which is external is of the nature of another entity and must be apprehended by another means of valid cognition, such as perception itself. And regarding that [external object], whatever objection is raised concerning its being a universal cause, its omnipresence, and so forth, that same objection can be raised here as well, even if there were no fire in the wall.

The occurrence of smoke has never been observed in the absence of fire; however, as for the claim that its occurrence cannot possibly exist in the case of something like a *piśāca*, from where does this certainty come? Indeed, if there were an impossibility of [smoke] even in that case, then in the absence of that very thing here, smoke would not occur. To this, the following is said:

It might be argued: "There is no such invisible entity here, comparable to a *piśāca*, who could be the producer of smoke; how then can there be such a cognition? To this it is replied: If smoke were to arise from such a source anywhere, fire would not be required for it, and thus it would exist even in the absence of fire; but this is not the case.
Well then, this means of valid cognition characterized by non-apprehension, which grasps exclusion (*vyatireka*),

arises from the very fivefold direct perception and non-apprehension; thus, the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*)— which is independent and characterized by inward-turned self-awareness— is established in accordance with our own philosophical system.
The establishment of the relationship between cause and effect occurs precisely through rest; and even therein, the certainty of its universal applicability is determined—

whether through worldly convention, through linguistic training, through scripture, or through one’s own intuition arising from practice in previous lives— solely by the power of the Lord’s destiny (*niyati*).

That which is capable [of proving a point] must be examined, and not impossibilities and the like. Even those [impossibilities], when brought forward in the form of *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum), do not transcend the nature of inference (*anumāna*), as they establish the intended conclusion through their own mode of operation. For [inference] consists of proof and refutation.

Sometimes, by means of an instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), one correctly understands both correctness and faultiness through proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*); and indeed, the very capacity to cause such understanding constitutes the nature of being a *pramāṇa*.
(Page 206)

And as for what is said— that from the mere observation of two individual instances, the operation of the causal factors upon the effects is determined, since even thousands of fires produced from straw are but a single individuality— it can also be argued in that regard that [individuals] produced from straw, wood, cow-dung, and so forth...

Even when thousands of fires have been seen, that very same fire-individuality (vahnivyakti) produced from fuel is not seen as such, because individuals arising from Indra’s head or from sun-crystals are not observed; and therefore, how can fuel even be considered the cause of fire?

If one were to accept that those [other things] also possess causality, then even the non-perception of other things that lack fuel would be possible; thus, the claim that "Śakra’s head does not have the nature of fire" is merely the result of a lack of understanding. Likewise, because [the absence of] impossibility and so forth is not universal, [it cannot serve as a valid reason].

There is a means for certain determination. Now, if it is argued that only one who is proficient through universal worldly consensus is an authoritative person entitled to engage in inference, then that is simply the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*). Furthermore, the state of being "uncharacterized" by impossibility and so forth is pervaded in this way only if [the definition] were possible.

The nature of being a definition is pervaded by both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and non-over-pervasion (*anativyāpti*). This being the case, since the definition is ascertained precisely through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), it does not escape the domain of inference (*anumāna*). Now, [one might object]:
"Inference is that which establishes a state; therefore, what [is the point] regarding impossibility (*asambhava*) and so forth?"

Those things which have been excluded from being denotable by inference or verbal testimony, even if they serve as a means for comprehension, are certainly not valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); and what objective reality can be established from that which is not a valid means of knowledge?
Or, what among them could possibly be a valid means of knowledge? Now, you yourself must explain how this [reality] is established.
If he is unable to say this, then the very impossibilities and other points we have stated become established.
Thus, by these words, it is the first disciples who are truly convinced, not those of long standing.
For instance, if a man on the street were to say, "I am the legitimate son of Brahmā," [the first disciples would be startled, whereas the long-standing ones would remain unmoved].
Someone asks: "What is the proof for this? He replies:
"Indeed, I have already arisen, and I am not without a cause. If you can point out another father for me, then I shall accept him; if not, then let my own statement stand as 'Om'."

And "worthy of worship" and "to be received with respect like the nectar of immortality"—this is the speech of one who shares the same religious life (*sabrahmacārin*). Furthermore, a contradiction must be understood to exist between these [qualities] and the definition of impossibility (*asambhava*) and so forth. And that [contradiction] occurs as follows—if:

Non-existence (*asaṃbhava*) and the others are pervaders (*vyāpaka*) of the state of being a definition (*lakṣaṇatva*), and their status as pervaders must be apprehended by means of further instances of non-existence and so forth; thus, there is that very same infinite regress (*anavasthā*). [This involves] infinite regress and mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Furthermore, those defects such as circularity (*kāryaprabhṛti*) which are mentioned depend upon the nature of entities (*bhāvasvabhāva*) as observed by valid cognition— being mutually dependent, established, and non-confused; yet even though they exist as forms of absolute non-existence, when delineated by the intellect, they [function as] the unreal [characterizing] the real, or the unreal [characterizing] the unreal.

According to the principle that "only what is real can be the signifier of what is real, or what is real can be the signifier of what is unreal," how could those things proceeding as causes for the sake of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) ever be released from the shadow of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception?
For instance, the Blessed Lord Anantanātha [said]:
And mutually dependent [arguments] are not tenable;
having stated this, he spoke the following example to demonstrate dependence upon the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa):
"For a boat tied to another boat [does not cross over]."
Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: how can we place our trust in perception to establish its universal validity? Alas!
To lack confidence in perception and instead rely merely on a conjecture is a great mark of integrity. For these [opponents] are driven by mere imagination characterized as a mere possibility.

The impossibilities and so forth have been stated by you; furthermore, poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And every conceptual construction depends, at its root, upon perception alone. For since conceptual constructions arise from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of experience, it is perception itself that shines forth even there, and nothing else. Precisely for that reason—
"The first Sage [Gautama] was the creator of the system of logic (*tarkatantra*), and inference is threefold, preceded by that [perception]" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.5).
Thus, he declared that inference is indeed preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa*). Now, how is perception...?
It functions toward universality. Now, how does even probability function?
For it is not the case that [the object] is not seen, nor is there a subsequent [perception], even when it has been directly perceived, as in the case of [the suspicion] "it was eaten by dogs.
Indeed, some say that such is logical perception (*yauktika-pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, probability...

If such [cognition] is indeed free from deviation, then it must be admitted that mental perception itself is capable of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*). On the other hand, if one maintains its impossibility and so forth,
that [position] becomes inconsistent.

(Page 208) Regarding "presumption" (*saṃbhāvanā*): in that case, this would simply be presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). For instance, smoke has indeed been observed in fire through direct perceptions and non-perceptions; and since it cannot exist otherwise—that is, if it were possible for it to exist in what is not fire—[it follows that there is fire].
"It arises" means that its non-existence in the absence of fire is postulated; this is quite clear.

Furthermore, in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*), so the same infinite regress (*anavasthā*) follows. To resolve that, perception itself must be accepted as the foundation. Nevertheless, by the Sāṃkhyas, through the employment of the *āvīta* form of logical reason—

When the refutation of the opposing view has been established, direct perception alone is ultimately resorted to as the refuge. For a non-existent thing is never seen to be a cause; nor is it observed that everything arises from everything;
nor is it seen that what is incapable of acting can produce what is impossible to produce—thus, when impossibility and other such arguments are examined, [perception remains the final authority].

They must be brought to rest in perception alone. Furthermore, as for the claim that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), what purpose is served by stating something so entirely contrary to all established doctrines?
For it is well known in the *Ṣaṭtarka* that logical reasons (*hetu*) which subsist in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) are indeed capable of producing knowledge.

What is established by this [definition] being thus inverted? If it is argued that "in this way, the nature of a definition becomes faultless," we say no, because it has been refuted. For fire is not the definition of smoke, such that the possession of smoke would have the possession of fire as its definition. It is not as, for example:
The very nature of consciousness, which is devoid of the form of delusive conceptualization, is itself the nature of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*);

apart from that, no other body of it appears, nor is it pointed out. Likewise, the state of possessing fire [is known] through the state of possessing smoke; for indeed, by means of smoke that has already established its own presence, [fire is known] as something distinct.

Even by one who has not touched upon the news of the day, it is said that "the mountain is smoky"; for otherwise, if the nature of fire were accepted, and by that fire its own cause were accepted, then the entire universe would be accepted here.
If that much did not appear, nothing at all would manifest, and there would be nothing but blindness.

As for the objection raised by others— that the definition [of a logical reason] is accepted by us as applying to all forms of inference, whereas it was accepted by them only as the object of purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) inference—
that too is false; for the definition of the reason was indeed accepted by the ancients, but by you, on the other hand—

There is a great difference [between this] and [the case of] that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). Therefore, it is by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone that proof and refutation must be carried out; and from that, the determination of the reality (*vastu-nirṇaya*) follows. As the Sage said (p. 209):
"Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the determination of a matter through the examination of the proponent's position (*pakṣa*) and the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*).
(Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.41). By the word "position," the proof residing therein is meant; and by the word "counter-position," that which is directed against it [is meant].

In that regard, what other logical justification (*yukti*) could there be for [calling it] a "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*)? By the expression "it is the equipment (*parikara*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," the purpose of the word is merely to attract [the listener], not because one is fond of the actual reality. For "equipment" (*parikara*) is either a cause, an effect, an auxiliary factor (*sahakārin*), or an auxiliary object (*sahakārya*), but nothing else.

It is a certain "accessory" (*parikara*). Therefore, the Sāṃkhyas and others maintain that *yukti* is indeed nothing but inference (*anumāna*), for they desire the exclusion of the counter-example (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*) through *āvīta* reasons. However, the venerable Bhartṛhari and others hold that it is intuition (*pratibhā*) consisting of the purity of mental composure (*samādhānanairmalyātmikā*). And it is precisely in accordance with that [view]...
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that this is an *arthāpatti* (presumption) regarding the non-dullness of wisdom;

for they hold that inference, which consists of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), culminates in perception and conceptualization according to the principle of "the experience of a single apprehension" (*ekopalambhānubhava*).

The Buddhists maintain that [reality] is established within one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*). The Knower of the Reality of Pratyabhijñā holds that the very sovereignty of the subject (*pramātṛ-svātantrya*), which consists in the application of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yojanā*), is what constitutes reasoning (*yukti*). Furthermore, for anyone who would accept even the slightest thing as real, it must necessarily be the sovereignty of the subject alone in the final analysis.

It has been stated more than once that one must accept [the reality] as consisting of the union of the powers of knowledge and action. Even in the world, it is well known that "reasoning" (*yukti*) is precisely the application of means brought forth by autonomy—as in the expressions, "Act with reason," or "I have emerged from this difficulty through reasoning. Therefore, the wise should pay close attention to this very point here.

Enough; we have composed this treatise, and it is not out of mere self-aggrandizement. Thus, having established that even for that which is the very life of the subject matter of the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)—namely, its being invariably concomitant with that [the probandum]—the root is indeed the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), this alone is the [intention] of the Master.
He establishes that this is "agreed upon" by the words "for this very reason, by them. [An objection: But what is gained by saying this?

Does it mean that what you yourself intend has been stated? He says: "it does," by means of the passage cited and indicated by the word "iti"—namely, that which was said by them even regarding an impartite entity (*niraṃśa-vastu*).
The phrase beginning with "of the indicator" (*gamakasya*) and so forth is what is referred to by the word "iti. Now, one might ask: what is established by this much? He replies:
"And thus," (*evaṃ ca*).
(Page 210)

"Of this too" means: even of that [inference] in which the state of containing a cause and effect does not appear at first glance to those of dull intellect—not only of such [inferences] as "possessing fire because of possessing smoke," and so forth. "From that too" refers to the fact that this preceding passage was employed for the purpose of qualifying the *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).
It has been explained that [the term] "only some" refers to this.

However, the distinction in the explanation is that the qualifier is employed now to inform others that every such essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) must be understood as being of this nature. And thus, the purpose of this designation is out of compassion.

The instruction is that the supreme state is to be ascended from this path by means of a ladder-like sequence, so that one may find rest from the great dark well of delusion (*moha*). He establishes this very position of his own through the passage beginning with "for the nature" (*svabhāvo hi*), and so forth. The term "primary" (*mukhya*) means that which distinguishes [it] from everything else, and it is also that which makes [the meaning] known.

"Another," however, is that which distinguishes [an object] from something else, and it is the object to be understood (*gamya*). It is "established" (*siddha*) because it is accepted as being distinguished from everything else by that very [distinguishing mark]. "The other" refers to the nature (*svabhāva*) which is the object to be understood through a probans (*gamaka*) such as "having an origin" (*utpattimattva*), namely, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) or impermanence (*anityatva*).

In another view, [the properties] such as being dependent (*āśritatva*) and so forth— that very nature— is not established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the indicator (*gamaka*); for when a momentary entity (*bhāvakṣaṇa*) is observed— whether it is arising, being produced, generated by effort, or manifested by a lamp and the like— the doubt arises whether this will exist in the subsequent moment or not, and so forth.

No consideration was made at all; rather, by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends *śiṃśapā*-ness as having the specific form of possessing branches and so forth, only the mere possession of branches and so forth is accepted. Therefore, there is no establishment of a real entity (*vastu*) therein. Consequently, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), which was not [established] by that means of valid cognition apprehending the indicator (*gamaka*),...

This has been accepted; it can be inferred in this way from the "possibility of origination" (*utpattimattva*) and so forth as a means of proof (*gamaka*), provided that the very cause which is the inherent reason (*nija-kāraṇa*) for that "possibility of origination" and so forth is the same cause by which it was made both "possessing origination" and "momentary. [Objection: But in that case, would it not be a mere "invariable concomitance with that alone" (*tanmātrānubandhitva*)?

Fearing that it might be argued that what is to be proven (sādhya) refers only to a momentary entity and not to "treeness" (vṛkṣatva), he explains that this is the case here as well by stating "in the case of *śiṃśapā*-ness.
"Because of its being thus" means because of [its being] treeness (*vṛkṣatva*). "Residing in the *śiṃśapā*" means being swallowed up by the form of the *śiṃśapā*.
"If at most" means that this is a means for establishing conventional usage through synonyms (*paryāya*),
but it is not a means for establishing the conventional usage of the actual entity (*vastu*). "Another exclusion" refers to the cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*).

It has direct perception as its fruit; for one does not determine, upon seeing a pure *śiṃśapā*, that "this is equal to a *dhava* tree," but rather [that it is] accompanied by a *dhava*. Thus, here, because the determination (*adhyavasāya*) is different, there is a dependence on another exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), namely, "it is not a non-*śiṃśapā*"; for by this much alone, it is not a tree.

For in this way, the *dhava* tree would not be a tree, since it is not a *śiṃśapā*; therefore, depending upon that appearance of its own nature— namely, "it is not a non-tree" as the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) other than the exclusion [of being a *śiṃśapā*]— that "treeness" appears in each respective manifestation.

Alternatively, because the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) rest upon each individual determination (adhyavasāya), that which was not accepted by a preceding pramāṇa must be accepted by a subsequent perception itself, up to the point of such a determination;
furthermore, even if something has been accepted, if it is not ascertained due to delusion, then—

Inference is the means for establishing the conventional usage regarding real entities (*vastu*). Even in that case, it is the power of the cause alone that must be inferred. However, inference such as that of momentariness and so forth establishes the real entity itself; thus, the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is explained in three ways. The word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) in the phrase "the cause of being produced" (*kṛtakatvakāraṇa*) refers to the agent (*kartṛ*).

The word "śiṃśapātva" (the state of being a *śiṃśapā*) is the object (*karman*), and "the cause of *śiṃśapātva*" is likewise [the object]; thus, by implication, the agent (*kartṛ*) is obtained. The word "tat" (that) is drawn from the preceding context and should be understood as referring to this very point. "Nyāya" refers to the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He demonstrates this with the words "for not... (*na hi*). If, by that reason, the eternal were produced...

Because its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not abandoned, it cannot have a connection with another place, time, or entity. [Objection: But even if it is indestructible, once produced, will it not depend upon that which is contradictory to it when there is destruction caused by place and so forth? [The author] refutes this by stating "of place and so forth," because [place and so forth] would entail the acquisition of a different intrinsic nature.

The meaning is "of those things that are agreed upon. [This is] by way of its having the nature of blue; and thus, since it does not produce an entity, its status as a producer (*karaṇatva*) would be refuted, but its status as a producer of destruction would not have been stated.
This was said regarding the state of being a counter-example (*vyatireka-pakṣa*); however, regarding the other position, he says: "perishable. But surely—

"Let the causes of its destruction at another time impart to the entity its perishable nature. He says "perishable"; "of them" refers to those intended as the causes of destruction; this genitive case is used in the sense of the agent with a residual meaning (*śeṣavivakṣā*). "By the aforementioned reasoning" refers to the [reasoning] regarding non-existence (*abhāva*).
By means of the characterization consisting in the expression of the exclusion of both substantiality and non-substantiality.
And thus, "tathāca" means "given that it is imperishable. And this is indeed observed; for it is indeed imperishable.

It must necessarily be admitted that it persists for a period of time, and that very persistence is itself perishability, because it consists in the relinquishing of its prior nature. He refutes this [objection] with the word "tat" (that):
what was to be said has already been stated; or else, "tat" serves as a reminder by drawing the heart toward the commencement of the subsequent argument.

It illuminates this: that the very fact of being acquired through just means cannot be maintained without relying on destiny. For it is heard thus regarding the village of the deaf: once, when the king was sleeping late at night in a certain region, the sounding of the drum was not performed with such effort out of fear of waking him.

Then, even by deaf people gathering together, a legal principle is established; yet, even when it is being applied there hundreds of times, we have never seen the sleep of anyone interrupted. So what else could it be? It is simply that the inherent nature of things has changed. Therefore, what is called "legal principle" (nyāya) is merely [the nature] of things.
The means of valid cognition is said to be that which establishes [an object]. If these [cognitions] have manifestation as their essence, why should they not tolerate [the presence of] form?

Even blue would tolerate yellowness, as in the case of a variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*). As it has been said regarding variegated cognition consisting of blue and so forth, where it is impossible to perceive it as having distinct parts: "In the case of variegated cognition such as blue, it is impossible to perceive it as having separate portions."

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, in the case of mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*), dreams, and so forth, thousands of varieties of conjunctions and disjunctions of appearances (*avabhāsa*) are observed. In that regard, who could determine which appearance is what, or which one is restricted to a single appearance?
He clarifies this intention with the words beginning "the essence is appearance" (*avabhāsasāra*). [Objection: But let it be that...

In the absence of the *dhava* and other [specific trees], there is the appearance of "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) which is common to them; but by what could that which is unique [to each] be prevented? To this he says: "in the presence of the *dhava* and others. For that which is unique is indeed the state of being a *śiṃśapā* (*śiṃśapātva*) itself, and nothing else is understood through it. But surely—
The creation of an appearance of a *śiṃśapā* tree devoid of the nature of being a tree after the creation of a *dhava* tree and so forth is conceivable;
but how could there be the creation of a produced thing (*kṛtaka*) devoid of impermanence? To the question "How indeed? he says:
"Because of its being produced," and so forth—[meaning] that this garment has fortunately arisen from the operation of its causes.

The appearance [of clothing and so forth] produces delight; that very appearance will not perish—hence it is called "appearance"—but rather, it is something else entirely, like the breaking of the heart.
(Page 213)
Bestowing [the fruit] upon those who have shared their merit: for that class of subjects whose sole essence is the first manifestation, a second manifestation has not been created at all.

For them, it is as if a form were invisible to the blind; for the Lord has not created it for them by way of unifying them with another class of subjects. Furthermore, the followers of Kapila hold that the effect is pre-existent.

By declaring that a produced thing possesses non-decay across its prior and subsequent states, they indeed declare its very permanence. Now, one might object: even for that person to whom this entity appears as "produced," it does not appear as "impermanent"; how then, upon seeing that same entity in another location, could he perceive it through a difference in intrinsic nature?

One should understand it thus; he says "this very thing" (*tad etat*). For at that time, by virtue of being in a different location, impermanence is known through this [reason] by means of the abandonment of its previous nature, and not through the fact of being produced (*kṛtakatā*).
But surely, then, that so-called "abandonment of nature" is easily established as a reason dependent upon a restricted capacity?
Anticipating the objection that there is an absence of any possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he says: "Even though there is a difference of location...

This is not a proof for the actual entity (*vastu*), nor even for the practical usage of the entity, but rather for verbal usage (*śabda-vyavahāra*); the word "only" (*mātra*) is used for that purpose, and such is verbal usage.
What is surprising about this dependence on necessity (*niyati*), given that it is well-known to be merely conventional?

He concludes this with the words "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*). If the two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) intended as the signified and the signifier are merely synonymous, then the object of proof is mere conventional usage; however, if...

The intended meaning is that the objection— namely, that because appearances are distinct, they cannot be synonymous, and therefore a single appearance must necessarily persist even while excluding other appearances through the power of the influence of masters of yoga and the like— must certainly be dispelled. He clarifies this by means of an illustration.
The word *sattvam* means "for it is so," because there exists such a clear demonstration;

therefore, the meaning is that this is logical. "For this very reason" refers to the appearance of succession and simultaneity. At that time, that very momentariness—characterized by the abandonment of its own nature—is indeed the performance [of an action] without having performed [it] sequentially.
But simultaneity is established by means of non-production; at that time, the linguistic usage of "sound" itself is what is to be proven.

"Otherwise" means: if it were not stated that the appearance of causal efficiency consists precisely in the ultimate reality of the appearances of succession and simultaneity, then [the object] would not be [established] by those two.
(Page 214) From what [source] is it established that [the object] is pervaded? Now, if impermanence is established from that very [reason], then what is the point regarding the subject at hand?

He replies with the words "successive" (*kramika*), etc. Furthermore, he states that even by another mode [of reasoning], there is an entry into the object to be known (*gamya*) within the means of knowledge (*gamaka*).

By the words "succession" (*krama*) and so forth: the intended meaning is that when the principle of exclusion (*vyatireka*) is being investigated, the inclusion of the semblance of the probandum (*sādhyābhāsa*)—which emerges as the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—makes manifest the semblance of the prover (*gamakābhāsa*).
"In the counter-example" (*vipakṣe*) means in the eternal (*nitye*). "That nature" (*tatsvabhāva*) means the nature of the semblances of succession and simultaneity (*kramayaugapadyābhāsa*).

"In our own position" means "it is impermanent. "That" means "therefore. Now, if causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) consists precisely in that which has the nature of appearing as successive or simultaneous—that is, that which is momentary—and if that alone is existence (*sattva*), then there is no need at all for establishing the conventional usage of reality and momentariness.
The power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) is required. This might be so if that [power] were the very essence (*sattva*) of things; however, it is not so.
Demonstrating this, [the author states]:
"Even the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not innate to objects" (2.3.12).

With the words "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*) and so forth, he recalls what was stated previously. "That too" refers to the capacity for purposeful action. Regarding that which God does, what is the restriction—that He does only such-and-such a thing? To this he says: "because of acting without restriction. "In relation to the eternal" means at the time of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
[Objection: "In that case, regarding conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), is momentariness itself the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)? [Reply: No;
he says, "But perishability..."—no entity possesses any intrinsic form (*vapuḥ*) of its own, whether eternal or non-eternal.
However, the Lord (*īśvara*), manifesting the universe within the mirror of his own consciousness, [reveals] even momentariness.
"It would cause [it] to appear"—this is our position. || 11 ||
Now, in the doctrine that things are mere appearances (*ābhāsa-vastu-vāda*), the relation of cause and effect exists only between two appearances;

therefore, fire that has not appeared is of no form whatsoever. How, then, can it be said that the appearance of smoke is produced by it? [If one asks: "From the appearance of a jar comes the appearance of smoke, and from the appearance of smoke..."

Immediately following [the appearance of smoke], there is the appearance of fire; since the sequence of appearances is fixed, he dispels the doubt—namely, "How can one infer fire from smoke even when relying on such necessity?"—by stating:
"Furthermore, it arises from the single appearance of fire belonging to that respective subject."
Even from a remote sovereign, there arises something new, such as the appearance of smoke and so forth.
The effect is the non-deviating mark (*liṅga*) of this [perceiver] with respect to another perceiver;
however, the appearance thereof [is known] from the appearance thereof itself, while the supreme [perceiver], the sovereign, [is known] from that very [appearance]. (13)
The Vijñānavādin, asserting that appearances differ within each individual continuum, perceives a causal relationship only between the appearances of smoke and fire belonging to his own [continuum],
because he does not perceive the mere occurrence of appearances belonging to another continuum. This is now [the case].

For him, there is only the appearance of smoke; how, then, could there be an inference of the appearance of fire from that? In our system, however, within such an appearance, there is a creation by the Blessed One through the unity of the subjects (*pramātṛ*); thus, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), just as in the external school (*bāhyadarśana*), the appearance of smoke residing in the various subjects is indeed one and the same.

And there is the appearance of fire. Consequently, by abandoning the distinction between subjects [of cognition] and through the force of perception and non-perception, the appearance of smoke arises from the appearance of fire;
thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) can be grasped even once. Furthermore, it may be grasped repeatedly or by means of many [instances].

By way of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), for all those subjects—from worms up to the omniscient—who are not restricted [to a single continuum], there is only one appearance of fire, and it is not differentiated by a difference in mental streams (*santāna*); by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), this refers to the appearance of seeds and so forth; for that very reason.

The appearance of smoke, the appearance of a sprout, and so forth, are capable of arising [from their respective causes], and not from anything else. And since that appearance of fire and so forth is imperceptible (*parokṣa*) to the inferrer, it is therefore called the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Moreover, that [fire] is something new; it is not like the smoke produced by smoke. And that [fire] belongs to him...
The sign (*liṅga*) in the form of an effect, which is non-deviant with respect to the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) regarding the appearance of fire and so forth,

indeed operates toward its inference. Insofar as it is one with those subjects (*pramātṛ*) regarding the general aspect of the appearance of fire, that inferer is said by the Blessed One to have been created by Him.

This is the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). However, that which is "other" (*para*)—namely, something distinct from the new [perception], such as the appearance of smoke—is produced from the very appearance of smoke and so forth, which exists in another cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and serves as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) from the perspective of the inferrer; therefore, it is for the sake of inferring that very cause of its own.

The effect would be the logical mark (*liṅga*), but not that which consists of the cause, such as a mere semblance of fire; thus, everything is in its proper place—this is the meaning of the aphorism. A semblance of smoke, being produced from a semblance of fire itself, is the indicator of that very [fire]; however, once it has attained full development, it arises from a semblance of smoke alone.

The commentary connects [the phrase] "being born, it is the indicator of that very [object]" with the preceding [sentence]; this is the construction of the *vṛtti*. Thus says the author of the *vivṛti* (p.
Having raised an objection, he briefly restates the meaning of the Sūtra with the words "tad etad evam" and so forth,

up until the end of the passage ending with "sā ca āśaṅkā na syāt. And this objection is raised by the Vijñānavādin, who maintains that for each individual stream of consciousness (pramātṛ-santāna), there exists a distinct object in the form of a manifestation.
The intention here is that this [argument] is difficult to establish; "even from another" means from the appearance of a jar or the like.

Or, "of the contrary" means that even for one who has ascended a mountain, the appearance of fire is indeed seen immediately after the appearance of smoke. This is shown by the passage beginning with "even one situated on the back of a mountain."

Intending to explain the meaning of the word *bhūyaḥ* (again/furthermore), [the author] first sets forth the circumstances at the time of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "in that which exists in a proximate place," and so forth. The word *tadā* (then) means "from that aforementioned reason consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The word *tāvat* refers to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) devoid of that [reason].

This means that it is certainly not the cause. By the phrase "established by scripture" (āgamasiddha), he states that one must be a person who relies on valid cognition (pramāṇika) by employing reasoning (yukti) consisting of the application of a collection of means of valid cognition.
For the rule regarding the nature of cause and effect and so forth is indeed scriptural (āgamika).

"By the power of necessity" (*niyatervaśāt*). He explains the word "only" (*mātra*) with the words "elsewhere," and so forth. He establishes the persistence of the power of *māyā* with the word "that" (*tam*). He clarifies the meaning of the word "only" (*mātra*) in the phrase "just that much" (*tāvanmātram*). The phrase "the manifestation of objects" (*viṣayāvabhāsastu*), however, refers to its general form.

Only manifestations (*ābhāsas*) are denoted by the word "reality" (*tattva*); and it has been stated more than once that these were indeed created prior to the [current] creation. He explains the word "that" (*tat*) from the Sūtra as follows: "even worms, insects, and so forth.
The distinction between these two [types of beings] based on subtlety and non-subtlety is found in the *Āgamas*. Furthermore, even a manifestation can be imperceptible (*parokṣa*).
By the words "it happens" (*bhavati*) and so forth, he shows that the matter just mentioned is not contrary to the Sūtra by saying "and this.
By the word "more numerous" (*bahutara*), he demonstrates another interpretation of the word "furthermore" (*bhūyas*), [stating] "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
This is in case, as in the Vijñānavāda school, there were only two appearances fixed for each individual cognizer.

If the causal relationship is accepted, then one might say "there is fire on the mountain"; however, for that reason, fire is not inferred there [in that specific instance]. For the manifestation of smoke residing in the cognizer located on the mountain is one thing, which was cognized by that cognizer as the effect of the manifestation of fire, while the other is [the present manifestation].
It resides in the subject who is considered the inferrer (*anumātṛ*).
And one might suspect that it arises from the appearance of the body and so forth; here, "here" means on the mountain. And therefore—

The intention is that, in commonality, there is only a single appearance of smoke (*dhūmābhāsa*). By stating "established by scripture" (*āgamasiddha*), he recalls [this] as being dependent upon the application of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And it has been stated that undisputed renown (*prasiddhi*) is indeed scripture. Consequently, there is the mastery of all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*); this is precisely what constitutes the knowledge of the reality of scripture.

The fruit of the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). For indeed, the supreme state of being cultivated consists precisely in the knowledge of texts such as the Vedas, Āyurveda, Daṇḍanīti, Kāmasūtra, and the *Prayogamālā*.
Thus, when the theory of uncommon fallacies has been refuted, the opponent—
Desiring to revive [the argument], he raises a doubt with the word "atha" (now/if). He refutes this by means of an equalization with the word "tarhi" (then).

The reason for this is given by the word "antara" (internal/within). Again, he anticipates the opponent's objection with "atha," noting that it is observed as such only in the kitchen; for one does not perceive an appearance of smoke emerging from a mere semblance of a body.

One perceives [the fire], but only from the appearance of fire itself; furthermore, since the appearance of smoke elsewhere belongs to that same class, it is logical that it must have that [fire] as its cause, and thus its emergence does not proceed from the appearance of a wall. Therefore, the appearance of fire is not an errant cause with respect to the appearance of smoke.
This is the remainder of the intention. Thus, when smoke has arisen and one has entered the kitchen,
at the moment the gaze is employed as it moves from above downward, then from the appearance of smoke itself—
conjoined with the appearance of activity characterized by upward movement— the appearance of fire arises.

The relationship of cause and effect could also exist in the reverse order. But surely, even then, the cognition of other subjects is that the appearance of smoke arises precisely from the appearance of fire. What follows from this?
It follows that the appearance of fire alone possesses causality; and for that reason, this [conclusion] holds even when [the fire] is imperceptible.
"Fire-like appearance is the cause of smoke"—this might indeed be so for those who maintain a single appearance common to all cognizers, but not for the Buddhists;
this he shows by saying "for each cognizer. Therefore, because [the cause] is remote, it is invisible even though it is a cause.
"Because it is perceived by another single cognizer; for this reason, the connection is that it is indeed previously arisen.
By the phrase "in this very [place]," he shows that even the appearance of the kitchen is useful as something common. Although not explicitly explained...

Thus [it is said] by the Buddhists and others. "Of something" means of an effect. "Of that" means of the effect. If it is asked, "From what does this definition of a sovereign arise? he says, "And thus," meaning that the definition is postulated from the object to be defined (*lakṣya*).

"...up to 'and [its] effort' (samīhāṃ ca), which refers to the object of activity and so forth. Regarding the phrase 'in another continuum' (santānāntara), it means in another cognizer. As for the inclusion of the word 'when' (yadā) in the Sūtra, it was omitted in the Vṛtti; therefore, he says [this] in response to one who might be deluded by that: 'In the Vṛtti,' that which was included in the Sūtra has not been excluded from the Vṛtti."
This has been explained with the intention of indicating [the nature of the relationship], but not with the intention of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

He concludes the meaning of the Sūtra— from the mention of smoke and fire up to "because this mark is thus non-deviant"— with the words "this being so," and so forth, including the passage beginning with "from the perspective of another cognizer."

He explains this with the words beginning with "gopāla" (the cowherd). By the term "line" (*lekhā*), he indicates the direction of the distinction between the smoke of fire and other things. "Thence" means from the appearance of fire. "Of Devadatta" means of one who has entered the state of an inferer. || 12-13 ||

If it is argued that "the appearance of smoke follows from the appearance of fire" is accepted, then by that same logic, it would be equally appropriate to say "the appearance of a sprout follows from the appearance of a seed," and so forth; why then was it said [in the previous verse] that it is not at all logical for anything other than that—such as a seed—to be the cause? (2.4.8)

If it is argued that "the conscious being alone is the agent," this is refuted by the Sūtra: "When this exists, that comes to be"; for even that relationship of cause and effect is not possible for insentient things that lack mutual dependence. (14)

Because of insentience (*jaḍatva*), there is no dependence; because of the absence of that [dependence], there is no restriction (*niyama*); and because of the absence of that [restriction], there is no sequence characterized by restriction—that is, no causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

These are the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*) and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). As for that which belongs to one [thing] being [found] in another...

The rule [of causality] is not inherent in the nature [of things], because all entities are established in themselves (*svaniṣṭha*). Therefore, dependence, which consists of a mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*), pervades that [rule]. And since that [dependence] does not exist in insentient things—this is the meaning of the aphorism. Furthermore, in this very aphorism, it is stated that "the existence of the subsequent [effect] is due to the capacity of the preceding [cause]."
The two positions—that prior capacity constitutes the existence of the subsequent, and that existence itself [constitutes it]—have indeed been indicated;
for there is a restricted existence of both the jar and the cloth within mere existence.
(Page 219)

Furthermore, there is no relation of cause and effect between two co-existent things that depend upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*). Therefore, by the passage beginning with "of the two," he demonstrates through a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) that the opponent accepts as the nature of causality a state of existence characterized by a necessary sequence where one follows the other, which ultimately amounts to the relationship of the prompted and the prompter (*prayojyaprayojakatā*).

By this much of the text. "And of the location" (*pradeśasya ca*): here, "location" (*pradeśa*) refers to the ground at the same time [as the action]. "By the word 'becomes'" (*bhavatiśabdena*): by way of explaining "exists" (*asti*), as found in the commentary (*vṛtti*). "Even so" (*evam api*): for in that case, there is the manifestation (*prādurbhāva*) of what has come into being (*bhūta*). "Even then" (*tadā api*).

The meaning is that there can be inference even of that which is qualified by a future time. By "simultaneity" (sahabhāvena), it is meant that the continua of fire and smoke proceed as a continuous stream;
therein, regarding those two moments of smoke and fire which exist at the same time, there is [inference] by virtue of their co-existence.

The relation is qualified by necessity (*avaśyambhāva*), but it does not exist when the sprout has already arisen; for since the relation itself is absent, of what could there be a restriction (*niyama*) characterized by necessity? From the context, the word "not having occurred before" (*abhūtapūrva*) conveys existence (*sattā*). In this sūtra, [the locative case] is used in the sense of the seventh case (*saptamī*).

If one asks how this was accepted, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). Regarding the rule "and that which [indicates] a state by means of another state" (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*, Pāṇini 2.3.37), he shows together with it that the locative case prescribed by this sūtra expresses this very qualifier.

Thus [it is said]. "In the beginning" means that since, even when fire is present, there is no indication of that smoke by means of a particular location, for that reason [the inference does not occur]; such is the meaning. Having refuted coexistence (*sahabhāva*), he refutes its occurrence at a later time as well with the words "later," etc. "Of that" refers to the fire. Now, [one might object]: "Even at a later time..."

Anticipating the objection, "What is not established for you by fire?", he says: "At its own time. He demonstrates the pervasiveness of this form [of fire] by means of the term "by the seed" (*bījena*). Alternatively, previously it was explained that fire is the cause of smoke characterized as a *sahakārin* (auxiliary), whereas by this [present statement], the distinction is that it is characterized as the *upādāna* (material cause).
He concludes this by way of its essential meaning with the words "by that" (*tena*). The word "of those two" (*tayoḥ*) is in the ablative case used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
The connection is that this restriction is thereby established. Furthermore, the phrase "even that" refers to non-existence (*abhāva*).
Even at the outset, in order to demonstrate the predominance of the sentence-meaning— which consists of a relative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)— as being of a non-existent nature,
that which is suspected when there is an absence of fire, namely, "smoke does not arise from anything other than fire (i.e., from non-fire)," is [addressed].
"No"—this is the meaning of the sentence. [Objection: But how can the locative case imply a restriction?

[Reply: He says, "In another," and so forth. For even when a cloth exists despite the absence of a jar, that cloth, though observed in the proximity of a jar, is not designated as "it exists when the jar exists. Precisely for this reason...
The meaning is that since the locative sense of "yataḥ" (from which) rests [there], the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also understood from it.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, because the commentary consists in explaining the aphorism (*sūtra*), the negative concomitance is shown within it by the phrase "for the commentary is... [and so on]. Now, as for the qualification "the sequence is fixed": and this sequence...

There are two types of existence (*bhāva*). When that [existence] has been defined as qualified by a restriction, how can its negative counterpart (*vyatireka*) be shown? For that [negative counterpart], being of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), is said to be expressed through a qualification of existence (*bhāva*); what does this mean? He refutes this with the words "restricted" (*niyata*) and so forth. For here, what is called "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*) is the companion of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

The nature of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) has been introduced. Since the causal relationship exists only between two real entities (*vastu*), its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), like its positive concomitance (*anvaya*), is ultimately nothing other than two restricted, real entities. Now, if that is so, how does this [relationship] differ from non-duality (*advaya*), and how can it be [established] through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)?

It would have to be understood through a specific kind of non-existence; yet it is proclaimed that positive concomitance (anvaya) is established by perception, and negative concomitance (vyatireka) is established by non-perception. Thus, the causal relation—which consists of positive and negative concomitance and is grounded in existence—is established by means of both perception and non-perception, or by those [two] respectively.

Thus, he dispels these two objections with the words "by non-apprehension" (*anupalambhena*). For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity is determined in this way only if it is treated through affirmation and negation.
In this manner, its own form would be treated as excluded from others; therefore—
In the phrase "its own nature" (*svarūpam*), the positive form of connection and its being established by direct perception are stated.
In the phrase "restricted and excluded" (*niyataṃ vyāvṛttam*), he first demonstrates the restriction of the cause: "the causal complex of fire and so forth is restricted to smoke."

Thus [it is said on page 221]. By the mention of the "totality of conditions" (*sāmagrī*), he indicates the causality of fire by virtue of its having reached its final stage. Here, he states that non-perception is the means of proof at the time when smoke is intended to be pervaded.

In that moment, there is no jar or the like consisting of the negation of smoke; for even if a jar or the like exists, it is necessarily accompanied by smoke. Furthermore, the jar or the like does not exist only in the moment immediately following fire, because it exists at other times as well.
Having thus demonstrated the necessity of the cause with respect to the effect, [the author now demonstrates] the necessity of the effect with respect to the cause.
He shows that smoke also [is absent] by the words "smoke too. To prove this, he demonstrates non-perception with the word "fire":

for smoke does not arise from a location or from earth and so forth that is animated by the absence of fire, but rather only from that which possesses existing fire; moreover, smoke does not arise from a location, earth, and so forth, even when those are present [without fire].

Because [the effect] is absent when fire is absent. Thus, by demonstrating that the rule applies to both, it is shown that the pervasion is symmetrical between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*); this demonstrates that the Buddhist alone accepts that there is a rule for the signifier even with respect to the signified. As the *Vārttika* states:
"For fire has the nature of having smoke as its cause and possesses a specific capacity for it.

Thus, as for the conceit that "this [logical relation] is our own invention" and that the object of inference is devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*), let it suffice to say that such a conceit is merely conceit. Now, what is the use of this necessity of the object of inference?

As has been stated: even if that [non-existence] exists in reality, it is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of inference. For inference proceeds by the power of a reason (*hetu*), and since the reason is the cause, it must be said that the nature of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) belongs to that [cause] alone—namely, that "it does not exist when there is no fire. Having taken this into account, he says: "And of the effect alone," and so forth. Here too...
He shows that the previously mentioned fault is indeed refuted in this alternative by stating, "But [it is] mere negation.
For this very reason—namely, because it was stated that linguistic usage regarding a real entity occurs precisely through the form of affirmation and negation—for that cause.
Now, one might object: the causal relation is not merely two entities, but rather...

That [object] is qualified by a restriction (niyama), and that restriction also brings about a dependence upon another. It is said: "the restriction also. Regarding "a specific restriction": that is the object which is conventionally designated as "restricted" (niyata). Then, what indeed is this so-called "restriction"? He says: "in such a way," meaning by its own respective [nature].
By way of their own form. How so? It is because this alone is the nature of the restriction:
that entities, being of the nature of existence, do not exist in any form other than how they are mutually perceived. Not otherwise.
He clarifies the manner in which there is no [independent] existence with the words "for this... The phrase "of these two" refers to fire and smoke.
The question "what is it? means that, apart from the two entities, no further dependence whatsoever manifests here;
thus, having elaborated upon and restated the Buddhist position that "when the prior exists, the subsequent comes to be," [the author proceeds].
He refutes this with the words "It might be so" (*syādetat*), which implies an admission. However, he adds that while this may be true, it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Alternatively, the phrase "this might be so" could be understood through the skill of elegant expression (*vācoyukti-vaidagdhyena*) as meaning: "What you have said may indeed be sustained by such cleverness. He then demonstrates how this leads to an over-extension and other logical faults.
"Even so" means as follows: "the state of being thus" refers to the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

By means of what is understood through previous observation—namely, from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) and other sources—it is known that "the Rohiṇīs do not arise from the Kṛttikās. Therefore, there is the state of having been previously observed.

The meaning is that it is understood from these [words] that they do not arise from the *kṛttikās*. "The rising of Rohiṇī" means the observation of Rohiṇī at a specific location; he clarifies this very point with the passage beginning "And the rising...
and ending with "...is indeed born. In this very context, he provides an illustration with the words "Just as a cowherd... and so forth.
"Insofar as that [rohiṇī] is indeed the cause of the specific smoke-characterized [effect], [it is not a cause]. Now, one might object: "Let it be so;
with respect to moments, let there be the state of being an effect of the kṛttikās for the rohiṇīs. To this he says, "No," with the words "And not...
"In this way" means by the logic of smoke. "Even though they have become such" means even though they have arisen in a specific form.

[The word] *api* [is used here]. It is not the common understanding of the world that the Rohiṇīs—being effects arising from the Kṛttikās which serve as their causes—are "beings" (*bhūtāḥ*) in the sense of being endowed with manifestation (*prādurbhāva-yoginī*). And this refers to what was stated regarding the fact that [the notion of] priority and posteriority leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Since that [causal relationship] is possible if it is characterized by the nature of cause and effect, one might accept it; however, he says "again" (*punaḥ*) to indicate that such a [relationship] does not exist at all. Even if, by chance, a person were to see a cloth immediately after a jar on two or three occasions—does this much suffice to establish a causal relation between the two entities?
Some relationship of kinship (*jñāteya*) might arise as a regulator for two things that are mutually independent.
He demonstrates this very independence with the words "for not" (*na hi*). [The word] "ahead" (*agre*) refers to that [point], for there...

The capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the former is its own nature (*svabhāva*); it will be explained that this is not the case for the latter, whose nature consists in existence (*sattā*). Just as capacity is a nature, so too is intrinsic form (*svarūpa*); therefore, it is likewise logical that even that does not belong to the former, but rather to the latter. [Objection: Let there be dependence (*apekṣā*) between two positive entities (*bhāva*) alone. [Response: In that case, then—
It brings about a state of mutual intrinsic nature (*parasparasvabhāvatā*). Thus he says, "Or, in that case" (*tathātve vā*);

this means that when dependence (*sāpekṣatva*) is asserted as the denotation, that very dependence would result in—or entail—the identity of mutual intrinsic nature (*anyonyasvabhāvatādātmya*). Now, [an objection]:

What is the use of accepting identity (*tādātmya*) here? Let it be that what is called "dependence" is simply a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) that rests solely within the respective essential natures of cause and effect. He refutes this with the words "And not... (*na ca*). [The opponent asks: "But let it be accepted in this way; what is the fault? He says "For in this way... (*evaṃ hi*), meaning: for that which belongs to another...

That particularity exists even when that particularity is abandoned, just as a tree exists apart from its specific nature as a *śiṃśapā* tree; and thus, smoke and fire would exist even while being devoid of such a particularity consisting of mutual dependence, [which leads to the conclusion] "it would be smoke alone"—this is the connection. By the word "alone" (*eva*), the essential nature [is excluded].

He states the possibility of it being otherwise. By the inclusion of the word "or" (vā), he means this: although the causal complex of fire and so forth, having reached its final stage, is accepted as being capable of producing smoke—because, due to the non-discrimination of moments, it cannot be obstructed, and that which is incapable of acting cannot be an obstructor—[it may nonetheless fail to produce it].
