Even so, by the force of worldly reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), one views even an infinite collection of causes such as fire and so forth as being that very same [collection];

thus, there might indeed be room for the statement that "causes do not necessarily possess their effects. However, the fact that smoke is not produced from non-fire is not tolerated even in a dream. Thus he says:

And so it is said: "Thus. He demonstrates that very point with the words "in the object" (*arthe*). Regarding the mere essential nature (*svarūpamātra*) of the object, it is precisely therein that they have accepted the determination: "this is the cause alone," and "this is the effect alone. Now, one might object: "Is everything not already established by that very determination? Furthermore, regarding the position of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there was the doubt expressed concerning the abandonment of that [determination]."

She also suspects the intention of the opponent— that [the definition] has been refuted— starting with "Now" (*atha*) and ending with "and the usage of all established conventions" (*sarvasiddhivyavahāraśca*). The suspicion regarding the abandonment of the qualifier is addressed starting with "But surely" (*nanu*).

(Page 224) It has been refuted. By the words "in what is not fire" (*anagnau*) and so forth, he shows the nature of that dependence which is being negated by means of the locative case. However, in the phrase "but in mere conventional usage" (*vyavahāramātre tu*), the locative case is used [to indicate the locus of the convention].

The designation characterized by the relation of cause and effect and so forth is conventional (*sāṅketika*). In this very context, he explains three examples regarding direction, number, and spatial arrangement with the words "just as" (*yathā*) and so on.
That specific form of an entity which is distinguished from others—that alone [is the basis] for the conventional...

The word, while being denoted, gives rise to a conceptual determination based on relative expectation, even in the absence of a specific quality consisting of the number five. "Things alone" refers either to those in the form of atoms or those in the form of jars and so forth. He applies this to the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*).

In the same way, because there is no other related entity existing as a separate thing, the causal relationship—though characterized by the conceptual construction of conventions such as the locative case—is nevertheless distinguished [from them]. It arises from that very nature of the two entities which constitutes its root; for if it were rootless, [it would not exist].

For he demonstrates that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not necessarily arise in such a manner by means of the word "not" (*na*), because it has not been brought into its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
He refutes this position of the opponent—which begins with the critique of the illustrative example—by the word "this" (*etat*);
for [in the case of] jars, cloths, and so forth, which exist in an indefinite state, there is no fixed sequence of priority and posteriority.

It may be supposed that even for those [entities], their sequence—whether produced by space or time—is baseless and merely projected by conceptual construction; however, even that is not tenable, as was previously demonstrated regarding the connection with action. (2.2.1)

In this context, "the state of cause and effect" means a sequence consisting of priority and posteriority among entities that abide in a fixed order. He clarifies this very necessity with the words "as long as," meaning that whose nature is precisely that fixed mutual non-separation.
The nature of that dependence is the essence of its own body, belonging to that relation of cause and effect.
Even if there were a fixed priority and posteriority, it would not be possible in the absence of the existence of space and so forth;
for space and the rest are animated by relations, and a relation culminates in identity—thus, dependence as well [is grounded in them].

The underlying intention is that the relationship between smoke and fire consists precisely in identity (*tādātmya*). He clarifies this very point with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). And "in that very way" (*tathaiva ca*) means that [the self] is established by perception itself as residing solely in the self, unmixed with anything else. "In this manner" (*evam*) refers to what is about to be stated.
By way of this manner: "these two" refers to fire and smoke; "thus" means having the nature of that which is to be adopted and that which indicates it;
"even in the absence of dependence" means even when such [dependence] is impossible in the case of something distinct.

The meaning is "in dependence. He states that even by the opponent this is almost admitted, saying "And thus," which means that the cause, having reached its final state, is indeed of the nature of the drawn-in effect, and the effect is also indeed of the nature of the drawn-in cause; however, it is impossible for those of limited vision to perceive that form.
The word "as if" (*iva*) is employed with the sense of providing a justification. For this very reason,

in passages such as "Therefore, because its effect is not distinct from the nature of the cause due to the non-deviation of the causal pervasion, its non-perception is stated to be simply the non-perception of its own nature," a figurative usage (*upacāra*) has been resorted to.

In reality, however, its nature is precisely that [of being a reason]. It is for this very purpose that the Noble One (Dignāga) employed the term "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) in such passages as "when there is a necessary connection through essential nature" (*svabhāvapratibandhe sati*). Bhaṭṭa also maintained that the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established only through an essential nature. The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the form of the reason (*hetu*).
He will demonstrate that this cannot be further contested by the words beginning with "tena" (by that).

He summarizes this with the word "sarvathā" (in every way): although there is no external unity for that other object which is characterized by the distinction between appearance (*ābhāsa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there exists within it a unity characterized by internal synthesis.

Thus, otherwise there would be no sense of dependence at all; the meaning is that "it comes into being" does not possess the nature of something to be depended upon. This should be applied to the three statements beginning with "prior" and so forth, as well as to "that which is to be depended upon.
Furthermore, in the external view, there is differentiation outside [the self], whereas in the subject...
He explains that this consequence arises because the nature of such an entity as "oneness" is not admitted;

thus he says, "by that," "the two would be," and "but it is not seen thus externally"—this is the intended meaning. "As a jar" means they are mutually undetermined. "Even more so" refers to the case where there is perception accompanied by a rule (niyama).

The meaning is that they are essentially nothing more than each other. He repeats what was stated previously—that "the nature of fire alone is the cause of smoke," and so forth—in order to refute it with the words "therefore. What else [could there be]?
Since it possesses no form beyond that of fire and so forth, it would be nothing at all; this would be a mere matter of words.

And regarding the phrase "the cause of smoke"— and so forth— the term "mutually" implies, according to the logic of "the man with the staff" (*daṇḍin*) and "the one with the horns" (*viṣāṇin*), that they must necessarily be of a nature that is mutually conjoined. Yet even that is not tenable.

He declares that "not so" because all objects are established in their own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*). Likewise, there is no non-conceptual experience (*nirvikalpaka-anubhava*) of fire and smoke as being mutually connected;
therefore, he states—by virtue of the underlying intention—that this consequence follows when all other alternatives have been exhausted.

Thus: for one who is thirsty is not perceived due to being attached to water, and he is dependent upon the water; for that [thirst] has returned toward its manifestation within his consciousness. In the same way, smoke [is dependent] upon fire, and there would also be a dependence of that [fire] upon smoke. This "dependence" is one produced by intention (*abhiprāya*). Thus, whatever...

This was previously introduced and stated as an admission; thus, that has been resolved. Now, one might ask: what is the use of this admission? Why was the refutation found in the Sūtra not presented directly in the Vṛtti?
It has indeed been presented; however, this [admission] is stated as an additional refutation, intended to demonstrate an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

"He demonstrates," and so forth. This matter will be explained in detail in the commentary (*vṛtti*). How is it that the capacity of the former is the existence of the latter? Because there will be the position of capacity;
by reason of its being conjoined with that [capacity], its being of one kind, and its sharing the same security and vulnerability (*yogakṣema*), this is what has been stated.

That which the Sūtra refers to as "bhāva" when stating "it exists in this"— namely, both the state (*bhāva*) and the capacity (*sāmarthya*)— is precisely what is demonstrated here in the Vṛtti; however, the position of capacity (*sāmarthyapakṣa*) has been introduced merely by pointing out that the former interpretation leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Regarding the phrase "to refute": by means of the great sentence beginning with "Thus" (*evam*) and ending with "he says this" (*etad āha*), [the author] introduces the subsequent position while concluding the preceding one.
Having established that this relationship of cause and effect is beset by two faults, he states this matter as follows.

What is that? This causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇatā*) is also not tenable for the reason already stated; yet it is not outside the Sūtra, but rather is indicated by the Sūtra itself—and for this reason, it is adopted as something to be maintained in the commentary (*vṛtti*). And for this reason, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in this position.
He states "Kṛttikā" and so forth together with the word *hi* (for/indeed) to indicate that this position might be suspected [of being untenable]:
"This wheel of constellations, fixed to the pole star situated at the navel,
though remaining simultaneously in place, is thus constantly in motion."

(Page 227) It is seen merely revolving in succession like a water-wheel, but it does not arise in succession. What has happened to the intrinsic nature of an entity just because there is a fixed priority and posteriority in its perception?

He shows this with the words "nanu" and so forth. With the intention that this position also leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since capacity (*sāmarthya*) is equally conceptualized as being cognizable through perception and non-perception, he says: "Even though... Although the causal capacity of the *kṛttikās* might be suspected [to belong] to the *rohiṇīs*, [it is not].

If it is argued that, unlike smoke, the sprout does not possess the nature of being an effect characterized by rising upward from its source, and thus [the objection] is to be doubted; to that also it is replied: "The nature of being an effect [remains]. For a sprout, unlike smoke, does not have the nature of spreading outwards, and yet it is said to emerge gradually from the seed. Likewise...

The sense is that this applies to Rohiṇī as well. Regarding the phrase "by another means of valid cognition," since the ascertainment of its continuity has already been produced by perception, the specific point stated—that the mere observation [of the moon] devoid of rising from Kṛttikā is itself sequential—is incorrect; this is what he expresses by saying "not mere observation."

But surely Rohiṇī was seen on previous days as well. Now, why was smoke not seen on those previous days? If you say it was seen, but only another fire [was present], then Rohiṇī was also seen, yet there was no such capacity; since that capacity exists in the case of fire and so forth, this distinction is groundless.

How could this be believed? To that he says, "In suchness," and so forth. [An objection: But if they are equal in this way, what is the distinction of this [position] from the previous one? [The author replies: "Nevertheless," he says;
for in this position, the mere acceptance of the authority of the *jyotiḥśāstra* (astronomy/astronomy) is the seed of its acceptance.

The intention [of the author] is as follows: the phrase "having a cause and so forth" includes, by the word "and so forth," the state of being an effect; likewise, it also includes the necessity of priority and posteriority, and so on. Now, one might ask: when it should have been said "that" (*saḥ*) in the commentary, why is there the designation "it" (*tat*)? He replies with the words "of the other," and so forth. Here, the relationship of cause and effect is not what is being referred to.
Rather, the intended meaning is that the sentence-meaning is a specific entity, characterized as such and existing as a real being (*sattvabhūta*).
"That too" refers to both [the preceding and following], which are appropriately situated everywhere without distinction.
"From mere restriction" means from the form of the sequence consisting of mere existence. It pervades their own nature.

(Page 228) Thus it is universal. For instance, how could dependence—which is characterized by being grounded in another—pervade that which is defined by being grounded in itself, such as heat, since being grounded in another is its opposite? This is one [point].
"Expectation is not tenable for that long, and it is even less so for a second [object]," he says with the words "intention" (*abhiprāya*) and so forth.

The phrase "being connected to another" (*anyānuṣaṅgitā*)—whether in the form of being established in another or in the form of a mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*)—is raised by the locative case. The phrase "merely a cognition" (*pratītimātra*) refers to either "the *dhava* and the *khadira*" or simply "the *dhava*."

For in cases such as "khadira or [something else]," what manifests is the state of mutual dependence or being conceptually constructed (*vikalpyamānatva*) as established by the conceit (*abhimāna*) of the cognizer regarding cutting and so forth;
it is not some objective form of the thing itself. Precisely for that reason, because it is a property of internal cognition, the meaning of the particle *vā* [is understood].

Since it is not logical for this [entity] to possess properties such as augmentation or the property of number—just like the external meaning of a nominal stem—it is devoid of gender and number. Thus, on the view that [the suffix] has semantic force (*sāmarthya*), the sense of the locative case is undermined; therefore, since there is no other alternative, that which is appropriate for the opponent to accept here is as follows: *atha*...

With the words beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "iti," he raises an objection. Regarding the word "tasya," it refers to the preceding [cause]. Now, one might object: "The existence of the subsequent [effect] consists in its being an effect; how then can this capacity of the preceding [cause], which is distinct from that [existence], be manifested?
To this he replies with "ittham" and "tasya": when, first of all, the subsequent [effect] does not exist, it is precisely then that it is called an "effect"; and at that time—
It follows that causal efficiency (*sāmarthya*) belongs only to that which exists previously, and this alone constitutes the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
For how could there be an excellence (*atiśaya*) characterized as being an effect in something non-existent, which lacks any essential nature (*niḥsvarūpa*)? [The opponent says:
"Then it will belong to that which has been produced. [The author replies: "Produced" means, in other words, "existent."

Indeed, it is the very arising [of an effect] that falls into the sphere of dispute; for it is improper that something non-existent should possess the status of being an effect—this is the sense of the word "api" (even/also).
Even for that which exists, no excellence characterized as "effectness," exceeding its own nature, can be obtained through the capacity of the cause; likewise, this smoke is the effect of fire.
The same applies here as well. This is the meaning: the capacity of fire is that by which this smoke comes to be.
In that context, "it comes to be" refers both to the nature of the smoke and to the capacity of its cause, the fire;
that alone constitutes the complete relationship of cause and effect. [Objection: But surely, [this capacity] resides solely in the smoke.
The claim that "being an effect of fire" is logical—namely, that which is merely smoke—is not tenable; for that [smoke] alone cannot logically be the sole effect of fire.
(Page 229)
For that [inference] is indeed grounded in fire; therefore, once smoke has been apprehended, the fact of its being grounded in fire would also be apprehended.

Consequently, there would be a recourse to another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the removal of delusion, just as there is in the case of momentariness. If this is argued, it follows that what is unestablished is being proven by means of what is unestablished.
For it is not logical that when the nature of an entity is apprehended, that which is non-different from it remains unapprehended;
if it were apprehended, how could there be any delusion? How, then, could there be delusion even regarding the nature of smoke?
[Objection: But surely the nature of smoke is its being an effect of fire; therefore, as long as it does not abandon that [nature]...

"How can this [inference] be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)? Do not say so. For it was precisely this—that "it is its own essential nature"—that was undertaken to be analyzed, yet it does not hold up. Thus he says: "Therefore" (*tataḥ*). But if both [the production and the presence] are the capacity of fire alone, then how does smoke enter into the cognition here? Ka...

Thus he says, "it enters. For, by means of mere conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) in the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), a relation characterized by dependence, or the nature of another characterized by being established in another, is determined.
He says this with the words "mere conventional usage. This too is refuted by the words "this also. [The opponent claims: "The prior existence..."

If the [causal capacity] of smoke were unreal, then that very efficacy belonging even to fire which constitutes its being the cause of that [smoke] would likewise be unreal; thus, there would be no such things as cause and effect at all. On the other hand, if it is real, then that prior existence of smoke—
The statement "by the power of fire" would be equivalent to saying "this jar is red" or "this cloth is white. To this, he says: "of another" (anyasya). || 14 ||

In the preceding sūtra, a mere proposition was stated regarding the subject of the reason—that [entities] are devoid of mutual dependence. Now, the reason for proving that is set forth by means of another sūtra:
"For [those things] which are restricted solely to their own selves and are devoid of synthesis..."
This same meaning of the locative case is also postulated for the terms "existence" (sat) and "non-existence" (asat). || 15 ||

In the *Vṛtti* and *Vivṛti*, however, this point is taken up in the preceding sūtra in order to demonstrate that they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). Therein, by the first quarter-verse (*pāda*), dependence characterized by mutual contact is excluded; by the second, that which is based on intention (*abhiprāya*) is excluded.
Since all four positions— namely, that both cause and effect exist, that neither exists, or that either one of them exists or does not exist— are conceivable, there can be no mutual dependence.
The phrase "the previous reason is not tenable" concludes the intermediate argument;

the meaning is that this is a restatement because the reason has already been stated for the previous proposition (*pratijñā*). The inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) is in view of what follows. The term "in existence" (*sattāyām*) refers to the external form, and not to the second [moment].
Or rather, it is optional (*vaikalpika*) depending on [context]. And in both cases of dependence, optionality is the lifeblood [of the distinction].

For the optional distinction between fire and heat is merely conceptualized as a differentiation. If "fire" refers to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of luminous form, then its particular characteristic of touch—

Even if it were to have a common cause, how could it possess its own nature? For this very reason, with the intention that this dependence is in reality of a single kind and has its life in synthesis (*anusandhāna*), it was stated in the previous aphorism simply as "of insentient things" (*jaḍānām*).
With this same intention, we have [stated] in the *Sūtravimarśinī* precisely by way of being of one flavor (*ekarasa*).

This sūtra has been explained; however, here, in order to investigate the extent of the [possible] destinies (*gati*), dependence (*apekṣā*) has been explained through this kind of analysis. Having asserted that neither [of the two] exists, he first establishes the impossibility of the former with the passage beginning with "if" and ending with "does not exist."

It has already been stated that the seed itself is not the sprout; thus, there is no such appearance as "an entity characterized by a diverse sequence. Just as in a variegated painting, where there is a spatial sequence, the conceptualization of causality part by part is merely a conceptual construction, so too would it be in the case of a temporal sequence.

If there is no effect whatsoever, how can the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkārya*) be established? For instance, that which is a single [reality] variegated by the succession of space and time would itself be the universe. By saying "let it be," the sense is expressed that even though it exists, it is the effect because its time for manifestation has arrived; thus it is said "in this way."

The meaning is: "precisely because of the difference in time. Otherwise—that is, if the nature of the cause were established solely in the effect, and the nature of the effect were established solely in the cause, such that both possessed this very mode of being—then fire would be perceived by its form as it is when not yet joined with smoke.
"Even smoke [is perceived] as not conjoined with fire"—this very thing would not possess a fixed form;
for it has no pure form of its own devoid of heat, just as fire has none devoid of heat.
And that which was considered possible—the arising through mutual forms—is indeed of two kinds. If [both are the case], then...

(Page 231) Anticipating the objection that "there is no [logical] dependence [on the locative], so why should the meaning of the seventh case not be assumed here?", he says: "And thus," [meaning] why would the seventh case be purposeless? Therefore, it is meaningful precisely by expressing the mere sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Is it by means of an optional meaning that exceeds the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), or rather by means of a real entity (*vastubhūta*) that exceeds the meaning of the nominal stem? Among those three positions, the first three are in fact equivalent to what has not been stated. He states the fourth position with the words "or else" (*utasvit*) and "some real thing" (*kiñcidbhūtam*).
"Real" means "unconstructed. In that regard, he refutes the charge of meaninglessness with the words "In that case.
By using the term "at least," he indicates that the reason here—the contradiction with universal consensus—is already established.
Then, having raised the fourth alternative with the word "Now," he refutes it with the passage beginning "This very [point]," and so forth.
He specifies that qualified form with the words ending in "vidyamānam.

In the reading where there is "ādīti" following the nominative case, the word "ādi" (and so forth) is for the purpose of including the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). "Tad etat" refers to that which is qualified by the aforementioned attributes. "Tāvat" means whatever [is required].

First, that which consists of the relationship between the potencies of the factors of action (kārakas) such as karma, and their distinctions—all of that has been refuted by the arguments stated above. Now, why has everything been refuted? He says:
[The self] does not desire or pursue another object regarded as primary within its own nature.

This very form of mutual orientation comes to rest; for indeed, the second and subsequent case-endings (*vibhakti*) are called "qualifiers" (*guṇa*). Therefore, by means of them, the state of being a qualifier must be imparted to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), and it is not mutual orientation that is expressed—rather, that very [state] is what is called being a qualifier. Thus he says: "attained."

That [word] by which the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) has been brought to such a state—characterized as having the nature of resting within its own self—is that which possesses the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*). The root *ās-* (in *āsādita*) has the sense of "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*) and takes two objects (*dvikarmaka*). By this, the commentary’s statements "it is the primary [object]" (*pradhāna*) and "the case-ending is for the subordinate" (*guṇavibhakti*) are explained. As in: "When there is a seed, there is a sprout"; "The sprout from the seed"; "By means of the seed."
He concludes with the words beginning "the seventh case," etc., that such a relationship of cause and effect—as in "the sprout [arises] from the seed as its cause"—is simply not tenable. || 15 ||
Having thus demonstrated that the relationship between cause and effect is not tenable according to the views of the Saugatas and others, he establishes it within his own system.
(Page 232)

Therefore, the meaning of the case-ending, which consists of the relation between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva), is properly understood as a connection of entities that rests solely upon the knowing subject. (16)
Since insentient things possess no dependence [upon anything else], for this very reason, the connection expressed by the case-endings—

such as the seventh (locative) and fifth (ablative)— which pertains to entities, exists only as a relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-bhāva*), established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of resting within the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).

Such is the meaning of the Sūtra. Intending to explain the Sūtra phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) by introducing it through a summary, [the author] relies upon everything previously stated as the underlying cause with the words "and since" (*yataśca*).
Regarding the "actual state of things," it has been stated that one seeking smoke takes up fire, for it is from smoke that fire is cognized.

He explains the state of consisting of both difference and non-difference by means of two reasons: "mutually" and "the single unifier. "Of others" refers to those things that are not of the nature of cause and effect, such as the master and his property and so forth.
"Designatable" means worthy of designation. "The farmer" refers to the one whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).
In [the case of] Śṛṅgāditya and others, the Lord is of the nature of consciousness; furthermore, the qualification "Lord" applies even to the farmer. || 16 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that there is no need for dependence when seeds, sprouts, and so forth are each established solely within their own selves; however, what fault is there in the Sāṅkhya view where they are mutually identical in nature? Anticipating this, [the author states:
"Even in the case of cause and effect, if they were of a mutually identical nature..."
For if there were indeed oneness despite difference, there would be no mutual distinctness of essential natures.

"This [position] is first of all contradicted by direct perception through scripture (*sūtra*), and it also contradicts the doctrine under discussion, namely the theory of effects such as *kārya* and so forth," he says. The rest is clear. || 17 ||

There is only one reality whose nature is manifold through its successive manifestations. Within that category of natures, the preceding nature is the cause and the subsequent is the effect; thus, according to the Sāṅkhya view, the relationship of cause and effect is indeed dry. But even there, it is not dry.
He states in the aphorism that it is precisely because the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva) is manifested:
"The differentiation of the single self is action, which follows the sequence of time;
likewise, agency arises in this way through such a process of transformation. (18)

Therefore, these [entities] such as pleasure and so forth, which partake in various forms of inequality, are that very seed which, through its own specific excellence (*ātma-atiśaya*), has reached the state of the sprout and so on. (Page 233)
By the power of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) based on any one of the means of valid cognition— perception, inference, or scripture—

that which is the single essence, whether it be the seed (*bīja*) for those of contracted vision or *pradhāna* for those of expanded vision, [belongs] to that which has a single substratum (*ekāśraya*). Its...

The distinction of intrinsic nature, supported by the divisions of time consisting of a sequence produced by manifestation and non-manifestation, is this very action characterized by transformation; it occurs through the relinquishing of the prior intrinsic nature, by the avoidance and removal of that which was intended to be manifested, [and] in relation to the subsequent [nature].
Bending toward another nature is humility (*prahvatā*) and eagerness (*autsukya*). Consequently,

even for that primary cause (*pradhāna*), seed, and so forth— which are considered to have a dry (inert) form— there would indeed be agency (*kartṛtva*) due to their possession of independence in the activity of transformation characterized by following [the object] in processes such as abandoning and taking up.

This is the meaning of the sutra. He introduces it with the words "of that which consists of the three guṇas," because [the world] is recognized as existing through the power of its pervasive connection (*samanvaya*) with the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion; thus it is established as eternal, remaining in its own undivided state.
Or, it refers to that which serves as the material cause for the entirety of the subsequent ten stages. "Great" (*mahat*) is the cognition [of the intellect].
"Up to the earth" means up to the limit of the entire subtle array of manifestations;
this is according to the worldly perspective. "Up to the sprout" refers to the seed.

The intention is that [the transformation] is preceded by an excellence consisting of the modification of its own kind (*sajātīya-pariṇāma*) and so forth. He applies what was stated previously regarding the characteristic of action (*kriyā-lakṣaṇa*) in the context of modification, namely the passages beginning with "for action" (*kriyā hi*) and "due to the inherent nature of the *guṇas*" (*guṇa-svābhāvyāt*). The phrase "the functioning of the *guṇas*" (*guṇa-vṛtta*) is used because it alone is capable of assuming the form of the universe, which consists of various diversities; it is not [merely] the *guṇas* themselves.

It becomes variegated as if blue; however, when *sattva* and *tamas* are mutually distinct, they are led by the restless and diverse *rajas* into thousands of transformations through their variegated nature, such as mutual overcoming and so forth. Therefore, a manifold variety (*vaiśvarūpya*) is appropriate. Thus it is said: "The unmingled does not transform."

By way of distinction: "as the goal of the Puruṣa" means as that which has the nature of being an object of experience (*bhogya*). The *pradhāna* is the "object of vision" (*dṛśya*) through non-discrimination; and through discrimination, vision is designated as liberation for the Puruṣa because it is the cause of isolation (*kaivalya*), being synonymous with the state of being an object of experience.

It is said that [the unmanifest] effects the purpose of the Puruṣa by making the power of the seer fulfilled; thus far is the restatement of the opponent's view. The remainder is to be understood as its refutation within one's own system. "Of this manifest" refers to the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth. || 18 ||
(Page 234) One might object: "By what has been stated thus far, the agency of *pradhāna* would be established, not that of the conscious principle (*cidrūpa*);
and that is not undesirable for the opponent. Anticipating this objection, the Sūtra [states]:
And this is not possible for that which is insentient, because of the contradiction between difference and non-difference;
however, it is logical in the case of the single conscious self due to the diversity of its manifestations.

Thus, that agency of the act of transformation— which was described as consisting in the independence [of the subject] in the integration of the various evolving attributes within a substrate (dharmin) whose form is undivided— is not tenable for the Pradhāna or other such [causes].

Because it is insentient (*jaḍatvāt*). For that which is insentient has its own nature definitively established; because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatvāt*), it is established as if distinct from the perspective of "that is this," just as blue is [distinguished] in relation to non-blue. However, in relation to itself, it is indeed non-distinct.
It is not the case that the very same nature is both distinct and non-distinct, because that would be a contradiction.
If there were a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could there be oneness?

For according to the principle: "In this way, the very distinction between difference and non-difference would be destroyed. Therefore, an insentient entity cannot possess multiple forms, because it is an object of cognition (*prameya*), just like blue and other such objects.

Unity is opposed to multiplicity; knowability is pervaded by that [multiplicity], for knowability consists in being established as having a definitively determined form. This is the perception of the pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
However, as for the conscious self (*cidātman*), when it has not yet entered the state of being an object of knowledge, it is like a mirror—pure and translucent.

The meaning of the sūtra is that a group of appearances, which are like reflections, can logically belong even to a single independent manifold consciousness, just as in the case of a variegated perception. He introduces this [sūtra] by concluding the preceding [section] with the words "Thus," etc. [The term] *śuṣkaḥ* [means] dry.

[The state of being] devoid of that essence which consists of the union of both [aspects], characterized by agency and the autonomy of the Self—this, first of all, arises as the cause; however, the word "api" (even/also) implies that this [cause] is not tenable within the perspective of the Supreme (paradṛśi). Therefore, because insentience is untenable as a cause, its opposite, non-insentience, is the cause for its tenability.
It is established without effort. Now, one might ask: why do elephants, mountains, and so forth not contradict unity there?
They would contradict it if they existed as something with their own independent nature; but this is not the case. For those [images] are nothing but the mirror itself.
Thus he says: "For not... Even when devoid of autonomy, this belongs to mere transparency.

The word "also" (*api*) [in the phrase] "even greatness" (*mahimāpi*) implies this: even if this were the case, it would not contradict our position; furthermore, from the very root, this is simply untenable.

Regarding the statement "in both ways, that which was undertaken, and not even in the case of difference," he analyzes it sequentially with the passages beginning with "even through delusion" (*bhrāntyāpi*) and "nor is there delusion" (*na ca bhrāntiḥ*). "Just that much" (*tāvanmātram*) refers to appearing in such a manner. He clarifies this very point with the passage beginning with "one" (*ekam*). Now, [an objection is raised]: "Is it not as in a mirror?"

"Let even the lump of clay appear as manifold. To this, he says: "And not... For in that which is not transparent, the multiplicity of reflections—consisting in the capacity to bear various reflections—is lost; it is not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And the lump of clay is not transparent when compared with a jar, a bowl, and so forth; thus, it is one.

That [consciousness], being existent, does not become manifold. Now, if it were said that some purely transparent object, such as a jar, is joined with multiple reflections, then this would not be the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), because in the theory of transformation the various transformations are admitted to have a reality distinct [from the original substance]. Nor, moreover, is it...

However, if the reading is *svacchaṃ* (clear), the meaning is as follows: even a clear object, having abandoned the multiplicity of reflections, cannot logically be many while remaining one in any other way; for in the present case, the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) is not abandoned because there is no subverting evidence, and this is confirmed by universal consensus.

This means "because of the failure to uproot [the object] through critical inquiry. Now, one might raise the objection: "Even though there is consensus from all experience regarding universals (*sāmānya*), wholes (*avayavin*), and so forth, they are nonetheless sublated by reasoning; could the same not apply to the present case as well? He dispels this doubt with the words beginning "of the one" (*ekasya*). For even in the case of universals and the like—

It has already been examined that the uprooting of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose object is the manifestation common to all is nothing at all; this is because it occurs through experience itself—meaning, universally and eternally. Now, [one might ask]: "In this way, how can there be the manifestation of the Pradhāna, which consists of a multitude of extremely subtle qualities and is translucent?"

Even for that which is insentient, such as a mirror, there will not be a form consisting of a reflection, as in the case of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest. True; however, with the intention of showing that this results in a flaw in the Sāṅkhya view, he states their position: "But for the insentient," etc. [The phrase] "the existence of real entities" is used, and not because the Pradhāna alone is the ultimate reality.

They are mutually devoid of any real nature. This very point is stated by the words "but not. In the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), existence produced by ignorance is not accepted as it is in the vision of Brahman. [An objection: But ignorance is of the nature of the insubstantial (*tuccha*); how could it produce existence? [The author] says:

That existence is of the nature of a delusion and is, therefore, empty; or rather, those for whom even that existence produced by ignorance possesses a form that is essentially a delusion and empty are not such [as they appear].
The compound *iṣyante sāṅkhyaiḥ* is to be connected with the preceding [term]. Therefore, as for what is said:
"The supreme state of the guṇas does not come within the range of vision."
But that which has come within the range of vision is utterly void, like an illusion.

Thus, this should be understood as referring to the doctrine of Brahman as the primary cause (*pradhāna-brahma-vāda*), and not to the doctrine of the transformation of the primary cause (*pradhāna-pariṇāma-vāda*). He confirms this very point with the words "this indeed. For since it is so, therefore our distinction is justified. And this is not merely a fabrication of our own intellect, because:

In the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) as its attributes (*dharma*), and the nature of the attributes as the substratum, is indeed accepted. Thus, by way of being both attribute and substratum; having thus demonstrated the process of transformation, he states the process of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) as it is accepted by others.

Regarding the phrase "of Brahman": the expression "of the one" implies by its very oneness that [Brahman] is not fallen from reality (*tattva*); thus, it was not written separately. Furthermore, the phrase "by following after differentiation" is accepted precisely through the designation of unreal distinctness. [This refers to] the apprehension of the differentiated form of the one.
By means of assuming forms such as a bowl from a mound of clay, there is a deviation from the reality of the mound's nature;

thus, through the assumption of unreal forms, a distinction is stated from the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*). If it were said that "the form is unreal and undivided," one might suspect that it is merely an undivided form, like the appearance of a garland or a snake in a rope.

This is another point. Now, if those forms are unreal, how can they be other than Brahman? What kind of distinction could there be? Or, if they are not other than Brahman, then indeed there is a state of non-distinction, but from where does their unreality arise? To this, he replies with the qualification: "from the reality of Brahman, which is the nature of consciousness."
He demonstrates the non-negatability of this light—that is, of Brahman—by the word "asya" (of this).

In all philosophical systems (*pravāda*), the very essence of ignorance (*avidyā*) is its lack of beauty when subjected to inquiry; for inquiry, which is of the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*), is like light, whereas the true nature of ignorance is like darkness.
Because there is no room for [the object] to be examined [as such]. By this much, it has been demonstrated that, at least in the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), there is no reality.
(Page 237)

"Surely, let this [Pradhāna doctrine] not be; however, there will be the doctrine of Brahman as the Primal Cause (pradhāna-brahma-vāda), as it is stated in the Upaniṣads. This is not tolerated, for it has been explained at length that in those [Upaniṣadic passages], the identity of the insentient—which is of the nature of an object of cognition—with [Brahman] is untenable due to its association with contradictory attributes.
"Thus, the very distinction between difference and non-difference is destroyed...

Therefore, the doctrine of an insentient Brahman is not tenable; rather, the doctrine of consciousness as Brahman is established in its own system, as it concludes with the words "in the conscious Self."
The very nature of consciousness (*citi*) is the sovereignty of undifferentiated luminosity; this refers to these "entities" (*bhāvānām*).

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the state of being ignorance (*avidyārūpatva*)—just as in the case of the conscious Brahman (*cidbrahman*)—will also serve as the Brahmā-missile for shattering the entire array of objections against the inert Brahman (*jaḍabrahman*)? Not so.

For that very power of consciousness—which, by virtue of its sovereignty, consists in the capacity to accomplish the most difficult feats—is that which brings forth *akhyāti* (non-apprehension), whose ultimate nature is incomplete manifestation;
it does so by manifesting within the light of consciousness a nature characterized by the awareness of the negation (*nañ-artha*) in the form of fragmentation. It is this very [power]...

Let it be called *māyā* because it gives rise to ignorance (*avidyā*), and thus it is termed *avidyā*; however, this [ignorance] does not belong to the insentient (*jaḍa*). For if that [insentient] were to exist, what indeed would constitute its insentience? Indeed, this [Brahman] is entirely non-insentient. "In this" means in the non-dual Brahman. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [it refers to] the Blessed Lord.
Demonstrating that it is impossible to calculate the accumulation of such capacities, he says this:

if our view is not accepted, the theory of Brahman’s transformation (*brahmavivartavāda*) becomes nothing other than a theory of the transformation of the insentient (*jaḍavivartavāda*). And in that case, even ignorance (*avidyā*) cannot be established as that which accounts for the reality of the transformation; this has already been elaborated upon.
In the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*, this has been stated by the passage beginning with "yadi" and ending with "syāt.

That true nature of consciousness— which consists of the forms of Paramaśiva and so forth, extending from the supreme (parā) through the intermediate (madhyama) to the ultimate (para)— is not perceived by the proponents of Vedānta on a clear path.
The intention is that [the reflection] would indeed occur in the union with the non-dual Supreme Lord.

Now, regarding what was stated—that it occurs "by the principle of reflection" because the conscious self is absolutely pure—the author dispels an objection from others with the words "And not... The grammatical connection is: "And this cannot be said."

He states the reason: "Insofar as it exists... (page 238). For it has been explained that even when a clear object displays a form distinct from itself, the nature of that which is clear remains unconditioned (*anupādhika*).

This is said to be the power of transparency (*svacchatva*), and not of reflectivity (*pratibimbatā*), because that which consists of reflections and the like is itself insubstantial; and since what is insubstantial cannot be discussed in terms of "power," this must be described as the power of transparent essence alone. That, however, is a form distinct from itself.

Whatever else there is, that should be understood as being in relation to its similarity [to the original]; in that case, there is the conventional usage of "reflection" (*pratibimba*), but in the absence of another object that serves as the source, there is the conventional usage of "creation" (*nirmeya*). For this very reason, it was not said "by way of being a reflection," but rather "by way of the principle of reflection. Thus he says: "In that case, however... with reference to the mirror.

And even though the genitive case (*saptamy-arthopakrame*) is employed [in the compound], the use of the genitive in *cittattvasya* (of the consciousness-principle) serves to establish its connection with the power of sovereignty (*aiśvarya-śakti*), which constitutes the nature of the subject matter under discussion. Now, one might object:
in this way, even *pradhāna* (primordial matter), being like a mirror, would be variegated by the reflections of *mahat* and the other evolutes.
"It will not be so," he says, [referring to] "of one" (*ekasya*), which means of that whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has not been abandoned. It must be accepted as such;

otherwise, it would not be the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*). For in that case, it would be merely an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), and even that is untenable because, in the absence of another supporting medium, it could not be a reflection, and because of its insentience (*jāḍya*).

Because it would be impossible for something to be created by the power of creation [if it were not already present]. Now, does a clear mirror actually become the form of a mountain and so forth, or does it merely appear as such? He says, "But of that which is clear," [implying] that there is no fault in either case.
But how is it logical for [the reflection] to reside within itself?

Because the consequence of the imposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) cannot be avoided. He says, "Precisely because it is observed to be so," meaning that there is no contradiction at all. Now, one might ask: for what purpose were the words "due to the difference in appearances" (*ābhāsabhedāt*) and "in the conscious self" (*cidātmani*) stated in the Sūtra? For even in the case of something transparent, whether it be insentient or otherwise, [the distinction] would be established as residing in itself (*svaniṣṭha*).

Anticipating the objection that "difference indeed exists," he says, "And that [difference] is as follows": in whatever manner— that is, by way of being perceived as such— that difference is rendered non-contradictory, in that same manner it ultimately comes to rest in its manifestation (*ābhāsa*), since perception is the activity of the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Because it rests upon appearances.

For even though a mirror reflects a multitude of images such as cities and mountains that have not been grasped [as external objects], its true essence is in reality nothing but appearance; for a mirror is so called because "appearance (ābhāsa) is seen here."

Now, one might object: since it is contradictory for an insentient entity to grasp a reflection, it is logical that only the single conscious self exists in a state of apparent division; however, this is not tenable for the insentient, as it is non-different [from the self].

Since the persistence of difference is contradictory [to the nature of consciousness], why is the maintenance of a reflection (*pratibimba*) shown in the commentary? Furthermore, the state of being an object of measurement (*nirmeyatā*) for entities exists in relation to consciousness, not as a reflection. To this, he says "reflection" (*pratibimba*).
This is stated with the intention of providing an illustration; or rather, that without which [something else] cannot exist.

Even that which is formless and non-different appears as if it were different; that is the reflection there. Thus, with respect to consciousness, this is the general definition of a reflection for all entities. Furthermore, even the mirror is not some independent, insentient thing; for it too—

The intention here, to be described in the commentary (*ṭīkā*), is that because the ultimate reality consists solely in appearing as such, the insentient (*jaḍa*) is simply impossible as a reflection. Now, anticipating [an objection], he refutes the view of the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) with the words beginning "And not... and ending with the word "iti."

What has been stated by Ācārya Dharmottara and others is not worthy of being spoken, because of the connection with the passage beginning with "since it is thus" (*yata evam*). What have they stated? He says: from "even though" (*yadyapi*) up to "of the object" (*arthasya*). By the section beginning with "even though" and ending with "because of the impossibility" (*anupapatteḥ*), that which is accepted by the proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātravādin*) [is addressed].

He restates that inference—namely, "that which manifests is non-different from manifestation"—in order to demonstrate the contradiction between the reason (*hetu*) and the similarity (*sāmya*) within this very syllogism; he does so with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), and so forth. For blue manifests, and its very blueness [is non-different] from the nature of consciousness characterized as "I-ness" (*ahantā*).

[If there were] difference from manifestation and the state of being self-luminous, then, because blue would not be non-different from the manifestation of "I," the blue would not exist as anything at all. [Objection: But this is indeed so, for consciousness alone is the ultimate reality of the blue. [The author] refutes this with the words beginning with "pure consciousness" (cinmātra). That which...
"That whose form does not shine forth is its ultimate reality"— this is a great illusion. Indeed,

to refute the opponent's view that just as the mirror is the actual form of the mountain, so too consciousness is the [actual] form of the blue object, he dispels that very example with the words beginning "the mirror," and so forth.

The elephant, while remaining in its own location, is transferred into the mirror merely by way of the configuration of its form; or rather, that elephant, though appearing as something else entirely from the elephant situated in its own location, exists only through the mere configuration of its form.
Since it is produced in this very way, its nature as a mirror is not its reality. [Objection:
But how could form—given that it possesses the property of resistance (*sapratigha*)—be mixed with [it]? To this, he says: "Not so. In that regard:

If "that perception" means non-obstructiveness (*niṣpratighatva*), then that exists even in the case of light-form, since thousands of jars and other objects are contained within it. However, the attainment of oneness (*ekatāpatti*) does not occur here between the form of the elephant and the form of the mirror, as it does between the two forms of the jars; thus, the situation is the same. Now, one might object: "But this mirror itself is of such a nature."

[This is] the practice. Here he says: "For it is indeed an error. "This" refers to the nature of the jar as being identical with the mirror, which is fashioned by erroneous cognition, and not the reality. Now, one might raise the objection: "In this case, how can there be the manifestation of the blue [object], since the property of manifestation belongs only to consciousness? To this [he replies]:

"And thus [it] removes [the objection] regarding knowledge. Indeed, it is not the case that blue is manifested; rather, knowledge itself, while manifesting by its own nature, manifests also by way of what is not itself.
Thus, it follows that what is necessarily to be accepted is this: the manifestation of the knowledge whose form is the manifestation of blue is itself the manifestation of blue. Why?
It has been stated:

because the manifestation of an object as an object cannot be denied, and because the nature of the object—which is characterized by cognition—is established as having such a nature from beginningless time.
But surely, since self and non-self are contradictory, how can the manifestation of both of them constitute a single form?
[Otherwise] it would follow that the object consists of both atoms and gross forms, and is thus corrupted by the defects of the sixfold conjunction, being both red and non-red, and so forth.

To this, he says: "Right here," meaning that in establishing the dual nature of consciousness, by means of the term "ascertainment" (*avasāya*), he states this: in reality, sublation (*bādha*) is already excluded here precisely because it is impossible for an actual entity (*vastu*).
Since there is no contradiction for a consciousness that is limited in space and time, atomic in form, and momentary— given that it is established as beginningless and is its very nature—
those who are merely unable to ascertain it as such are defeated by others through dry logic, harsh reasoning, and fallacious arguments.

Regarding the word "asya" (of this): if one were to transgress [the existence of] that which has the nature of cognition, that which appears, and that which is external and attested by uncontradicted experience, one would fall into the position of a mere arbitrary speaker; therefore, one who desires a comprehensive exposition should here recall the *Bāhyārthasiddhi* treatise. This is not so.

Regarding what was stated, he provides the reason with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). By this support of the example, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been stated through the capacity of a clear [surface] to manifest other distinct forms.
The phrase "in the same way" (*tathaiva*) refers to its remaining within the mirror.
The intention [of the author] is as follows: by saying "it is established by your own cognition and cannot be denied," he indicates that it is not to be rejected.
"From that" means because of such a statement. "Situated in another place" refers to that elephant which is accepted as real.
Thus, first of all, it does not appear as distinct from that [mirror] by way of spatial separation; for that very reason, it is not transferred therefrom.

Therefore, this [notion] is devoid of reality and is mere speech. Nor is it of the same nature as another elephant, because that would entail the consequence of lacking the necessary restriction of appearing as dependent upon the mirror. Thus he says:

"Because there is no manifestation in that manner. As for what was also said—that this [reflection] is something entirely different—that too he refutes with the words "within the mirror. To begin with, the elephant, whose essence is its form, is not independent, because it does not appear apart from the location of the mirror, just as [it does not appear] inside a house.

If it is argued that [the reflection] appears within the mirror, he says: "in the form of the mirror. For the form of the mirror is dense; how, then, could this [reflection] enter therein? Or, if there were spaces between its atoms, then only two arrangements—the mirror and the mountain—would appear.

Furthermore, objects such as jars are perceived precisely by the removal of the form of light, and not as the mere form of that location. This has indeed been investigated at length in the *Piśāca-ṭīkā* (1.7.11). And [the author] says "And that... to show that this consequence follows for one who maintains that perception cannot be denied.
"It is seen"—and yet, such is not the actual state of affairs. He points to that very fact as the reason by saying "that.
"Elsewhere" means in the middle of the mirror, on its back, in its rear portion, or in some other independent location.
Now, one might object: what is established by non-erroneous perception should not be denied; and this [perception] is indeed erroneous.

Having raised the doubt that "this is the perception of a mountain in a mirror," he first establishes its identity [with the object] in order to refute its erroneous nature, stating "it is indeed yellow. This is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa dṛṣṭāntaḥ*) with respect to non-obstruction, or else [it refers] to other perceivers.

Since even the yellow form manifests [as white], why should it not be of the nature of a mirror by virtue of that very similarity? With this in mind, however, the example of similarity is given as the primary one. For, just as the yellow form is accepted as having white as its ultimate reality, precisely through its white form;
Because it generates cognition in that very way, it is logical that the form of the mountain is the ultimate reality of the mirror-form,
whereas the yellow form is unreal.
(Page 242)

This is another matter. He says "no" because [the error occurs] in that very case, such as with a yellow conch and the like, but not in the case of a mirror, a mountain, and so forth, because the other form—namely, the white color which is ultimately real—is not manifested.
And it has already been established that the very non-manifestation (*akhyāti*), consisting of incomplete manifestation, is the essence of error.

In the present case, however, he shows that there is no such thing as non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) by stating "of both," namely, of the mirror and the mountain. By that very [means], namely by the manifestation of the two, the form of the mirror is thus established even without being pervaded by the form of the mountain, and likewise the form of the mountain.

Regarding the phrase "by not being overcome by the form of the mirror," he says "for it is not so" in the case of a yellow conch and the like. It cannot be established that the white [color] is pervaded by the yellow, and the yellow by the pervasion of the white form, because those with jaundice do not perceive the white, while others do.

Regarding the yellow [reflection]: But surely the mirror occupies a small space and has a small dimension, whereas the mountain is the opposite; thus, since there is a contradiction in terms of location and dimension, how can there be a contradiction characterized by mutual identity?
As it has been said:
In objects of contradictory dimensions, such as the surface of a diamond or a mirror,
there can be no occurrence of entities possessing the same form as mountains and the like.

Thus [it is said]. He refutes this by stating "even though it is extended," and so forth, asserting that there is no contradiction regarding spatial dimensions at all. This is because there is no spreading of that—namely, the mountain's location and the mountain's dimension—beyond the location and dimension of the mirror. Now, one might object:
If it is argued that there is no outward diffusion, then let there be delusion, just as in the case of yellow [perception] when white is not perceived due to the lack of diffusion.
To this it is replied: "And because of non-obscuration. For by the yellow, the white is indeed obscured, since it does not appear.
But is it not the case that saying "the mountain is of the same nature as a mirror" is extremely preposterous? No, there is nothing of the sort here.

He says "danturatā" (unevenness) and "of such a thing" (*tathābhūtasya*); that is, of an object whose location and dimension are not contradictory, which is non-erroneous, and whose establishment depends solely upon its non-perception. And he says "by way of possibility" (*saṃbhavitvena*)—the instrumental case here is used in the sense of "being in such a state"—to show that this [establishment] is not impossible. The reason for this is as follows:

"Because of such a capacity for illumination. He clarifies this very point with the words "contradictory": although a contradiction may appear to be conceived at first glance, nevertheless it is not [the case].
(Page 243)

"This is the contradiction. To this he says: "Being [existent] precisely because of such manifestation. Now, one might ask: "How can the contradiction being urged actually contradict [itself]? He explains this with the words beginning "In case of contradiction," and so forth. For this very point clearly extols and defines the mirror's nature of transparency.
The reality of existence (*bhāvatattva*). Now, one might object: "Is this not merely a delusion?
What is the point of such effort in establishing its substantiality? Anticipating this doubt, he says "nanu" (surely).
And here, in the manifestation that is full of both, and in the manifestation of such a nature as being transparent in form, there is no...
The sense is that there is no such thing as non-manifestation (*akhyāti*). Now, if there were no mutual contradiction, why could it not be that the reality of the mountain is the form of the mirror?

And from that, it would follow that the ultimate reality of blue and so forth is the nature of consciousness (*cittattva*), which would imply that blue and so forth possess ultimate reality. He refutes this with the words "the mountain and so forth."

Even in the absence of mountains and other objects, because the nature of consciousness exists through its pure transparency and performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in that very same way, this same rule must be followed for the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*).
Even if the capacity to contain the forms of boats and mirrors is established, how could there be the state of being of the same nature as the mirror?
The phrase "nor even" shatters the delusion that it might somehow be non-existent;

for it cannot be said that it is not of the nature of a mirror, nor can it be said that it is non-existent. The reason for this is the obstruction by the form of the mirror—that is, its support in ultimate reality.
"Even though it is appearing. Now, one might object: "In that case, let it be described as such [as appearing].
He replies: "Just like a mirror. He clarifies this very point with the words "of that," meaning of the form of the mountain. "From that," meaning from the mirror.
If, when examined through reasoning, even that which is manifesting does not [exist],...

If someone were to say, "Let that which arises [in this way] be its non-existence," one would inform him that it is also "purity" (*nairmalya*). For this very thing is purity: the manifestation of that which is not distinct from one's own self as if it were distinct. "By way of separation" means by way of the "this-ness" (*idantā*). And thus...
Even in the appearance of separation, we maintain that all this multitude of objects has manifestation as its sole essence. Nevertheless, due to the power of the energy of *māyā*,
we say that just as blue and other such things are indeed externalized, so too is the mountain in the mirror.
Even for the Vijñānavādins,
this [cognition] does not manifest through its own reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) aspect, but rather just like blue and other [objects].

By the aforementioned fact of its being mere consciousness (*vijñānamātratā*), there is no disruption whatsoever of our own original example. Now, having summarized the point already stated, he says "In this way" and so forth; however, the subject at hand is the distinction from error.

"It shows 'yellow'" means that independence (*svātantrya*) consists precisely in being independent of the appearance of a white conch; this is shown by the words "and not," where the connection is "it is not erroneous" [in the sense of] "the yellow conch. He applies this to the present context with the words "but not. For it appears as such from the mirror, but not like a white conch.
The emphasis lies on the word "shines" (*ābhāti*). Having thus established the analogy, he applies it to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "that" (*tat*);
that is, for this reason, this analogy has been fully constructed. With the word "thus" (*ittham*), he brings about the correspondence in the subject of the illustration. [Objection:
But [if it is argued] by way of non-difference from the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)...

Anticipating the objection that manifestation is unestablished because blue and other objects are perceived as excluded from the state of "I-ness," he says: "of the illusory subject" (*māyāpramātuḥ*). The genitive case here is used in relation to the verb "appears.
In that context, it should be understood that [the subject] is "from the nature of consciousness" (*citsvarūpāt*), meaning from the Supreme Lord.
Or, [the fifth case] may be used in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); in that case, the meaning is as follows:

even for that cognizer (*pramātṛ*) who undergoes contraction and [identifies] "I," it is precisely from that non-conscious aspect (*acid-aṃśa*) that blue and other objects appear as distinct, and not from the conscious aspect (*cid-aṃśa*).
This is what is meant by the emergence of one who is devoid of a body and so forth as a cognizer.
Because this is a delusion produced by the operation of the power of *māyā* from the very beginning, for this reason:
"this" (*etat*) refers to that manifestation of blue and so forth as distinct from that [consciousness];
and in relation to that, there is the state of being external to the "I-sense" (*ahambhāva*). Let that be so—it is not that this has not been admitted. And that...

He is the protagonist of saṃsāra— which is like a dance of delusion, which exists as non-ultimate reality, and which is brought within the range of perception by the light of the Supreme Lord who acts like a dancer by not relinquishing his own essential nature.

The Sūtradhāra is the primary agent who initiates the narrative, or the protagonist through whom the entire history of the universe shines forth; for this reason, he is the first. Now, one might ask: why is this very act of making the insentient [world] into a subject of cognition considered the first delusion?

For it is logical that the process of making manifest— that which consists of light— such as bodies, jars, and so forth, constitutes a primary delusion; [the author] says "not so" because it is the fundamental basis (page 245).

Thus [it is said]. For here, priority does not arise from the operation of time, because that very [time] is absent. As the *Nareśvaraviveka* states: "Therefore, the power called Māyā produces the pair simultaneously."
All objects of knowledge, both existent and non-existent, as well as certain objects of knowledge and their knowers.

Thus [it is said]. But then, how can there be even the state of being the root? For instance, the delusion characterized by the appearance of difference between the objects of perception and those perceptions, as well as between the perceptions and those objects—this is produced by the activity of *māyā*.
Having entered into the form of delusion, that very delusion becomes further filled with hundreds of branches of darkness; this is the meaning.
It is true that this is so, yet nevertheless all delusions fall back upon the nature of the Self, which is characterized as the grāhaka (the subject). But if this is so—
This would indeed be the case for the knower of truth (*satyapramātṛ*) alone, according to the principle:

"Even though the stability of the object [is established in this way]" (*Aparokṣānubhūti-prakaraṇa-siddhi* 20). He shows that the ultimate realization does not find its rest here [in the object] by means of the phrase "tattat" ("this and that").

The illusory nature of the subject, which serves as the substratum for each respective delusion—this is what is meant: when the illusory subject exists, other delusions arise appropriately in dependence upon it; thus, the manifestation of the illusory subject alone is the fundamental basis, since...

That alone is the root; however, the other—the sense of "I" even toward objects of knowledge—is the individual impurity (*āṇavamala*). Thus, it has been stated that with respect to the subject conditioned by *māyā*, non-duality is not in the least compromised; but with respect to the true nature of consciousness, he says "as for that which... to indicate that such [non-duality] does not exist. Now, [one might object]:

He addresses the objection that even in relation to pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), there exists a difference between blue and other objects, because the Mantra-Īśvaras and others possess the nature of pure consciousness, and because blue and other objects manifest through their differentiation—
this he refutes with the words "let it be an error. Even though they are devoid of bodies and the like, they do not have the nature of pure consciousness.

Moreover, they were created by the Lord as having a nature of consciousness in which the impurity of māyā— consisting of the contraction of the conceit of being separate from their own kind and from the object of knowledge— is predominant; as will be stated:
Even for those who possess the state of being an agent of cognitions, when the impurity of action (*kārmamala*) has been destroyed,
yet they still possess distinct objects of knowledge, they are the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s), characterized by the impurity of Māyā (*māyāmala*). (3.2.9)

Thus [it is said]. By the word "eva" (only/precisely) in the phrase "idantayaiva" (only as this-ness), the difference from the state of the subject Śrī Sadāśiva which was indicated is clarified by the words "nanu" (surely). For in the state of Sadāśiva, when there is the unfolding of "this-ness" (idantā), there is also a veiling of "I-ness" (ahantā); these [subjects] possess the conceit of difference even from those of their own kind.

The word "api" (also) indicates that [the Lord] manifests not only the class of objects to be known (*vedyavarga*), but also Himself within His own self; for even He, whose differentiation is impossible because His ultimate reality is solely Light, appears as if differentiated. To demonstrate that this supreme power of the Lord—the performance of the seemingly impossible—is designated in the scriptures as *mahāmāyā* and *vidyā*, [the author says]:
The second [verse] as well: "That which he will say:
'The cognition of difference itself regarding entities...
(3.1.6), etc. For this very reason—that is, because [the world arises] from the class of subjects (*pramātṛ*) and the class of objects (*prameya*).

[Their] nature is contracted consciousness; therefore, they are produced, for otherwise, if they were of the nature of pure consciousness, being eternal, their state of being produced would be impossible. Anticipating the objection, "In that case, since they are merely products of *māyā*, why are they said to exist above the *māyā-tattva*? he says: "And for that long... (*tāvacca*).

The meaning is that these are called "non-māyic" because of the absence of the full operation of *māyā*, which is characterized by the manifestation of the lack of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*), knowledge, and agency regarding the body and the objects of cognition; this is so even while that much of the operation of *māyā* still exists. If that is so, then [they are so called] by virtue of having transcended *māyā*.
As for what is called "consisting of pure knowledge" (*śuddhavidyāmayatva*), where does that apply? He says: "But of the Lord" (*īśvarasya tu*).
This means that the state of consisting of knowledge belongs precisely to that whose state of "this-ness" (*idantā*) has been concealed by "I-ness" (*ahantā*). As he will say:
"For those possessed of the state of 'this-ness'... (3.1.4).

And so forth. Now, there certainly exists this possibility: that the power of the Lord causes duality to appear even to the subject whose nature is consciousness and who is not limited by the body and so on.
Therefore, at present, all beings from Brahmā down to insects, while existing as subjects possessing bodies and so forth, [perceive] duality...

Regarding the statement "they grasp," he restates and refutes the doubt—"Why is this proclaimed? Let them too be of the nature of subjects consisting of pure consciousness"—by saying "it is not tenable," meaning:
it is not [tenable] for us [to accept that], because otherwise the conceit of duality would be inexplicable.
(Page 247) The status of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtā*) has been attributed to the body and so forth. For this status manifests through self-awareness itself,
as seen in the individual experience of such cognitions as "I am thin" or "I am happy."

Because it cannot be denied; he states that a logical justification (*upapatti*) for this point is also possible by saying "in the very self of consciousness" (*bodhātmanyeva*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin the reasons. For there is no cognition to be brought forth for the cognizer who consists of pure consciousness, wherein the employment of the collection of causes such as the sense organs would be required.

For its nature as the cognition of blue and so forth arises merely through the coloring of the object of knowledge; and since the object of knowledge is always present, omniscience alone is appropriate for it—
by what form indeed would the Supreme Lord not manifest?
And by this method, even omniscience must be made to appear as nothing more than that [consciousness]; the intention is that these subjects, such as the body and so forth, are merely that.
Thus, the subject matter at hand—the meaning of the Sūtra—is presented, having been interspersed with other points of doctrine that arose incidentally.
With the words "tat" and so forth, he connects [the preceding] with the conclusion, beginning with "abhāsabhedādekatra" (due to the difference in appearances, in one place, etc.). || 19 ||

Now, as for the delusion that thinks: "Is it not said that Brahman itself, in the form of consciousness, appears as the universe; what then is the need for [conceiving it] as the Lord (Īśvara)?"—this [delusion] is dispelled by the following:
Even though there is a single reality of consciousness, there would be no [identity] between two things that appear distinct due to their manifestations.
Action [does not occur] without the reflective awareness of oneness characterized by the desire to act. (20)

Even if it is accepted that the unity of consciousness (*citta*) is real while its differentiation is due to ignorance (*avidyā*), the relation between action and its instrument is not logically established; for unless there exists a single unifying awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) regarding the jar and the conscious subject— which appear as distinct through manifestation— there can be no action, or rather, action would be impossible.
The genitive case is used for the general relation; subsequently, however, that relation is to be divided into the states of objecthood (*karmatva*) and agenthood (*kartṛtva*) according to propriety.

Or rather, it means "without that single reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by resting in the supreme consciousness, which [unifies] the inert and the conscious—'this' and 'I'—which appear as distinct. By that [reflective awareness], one performs the action.
The genitive compound is formed by depending on either the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) or the reflection (*parāmarśa*), because it is inherently dependent.

What is meant is this: if the unity of consciousness is said to be real, established by its own nature—just as "pot-ness" is the nature of an insentient object like a pot—then duality is merely ignorance (*avidyā*).

(Page 248) Then it must be determined whose this [avidyā] is. For avidyā, which is of the nature of the absence of that [knowledge], cannot belong to Brahman, who is of a single uniform nature consisting solely of knowledge; nor can it belong to any others, such as individual souls (*jīva*) and so forth.

For they must indeed be raised up by ignorance alone. If you say that ignorance is "indescribable" (*anirvācya*), we do not know to whom it belongs. To say both "it appears" and "it is indescribable" is the language of a *yakṣa*. If you say it is not logically tenable, then what logic is there for transcending its appearance? In the non-conceptual state, pure Brahman alone shines forth.

If it is argued that "it" (the distinction) exists in conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), then it must be stated—as before—of what that [cognition] itself is. Furthermore, if it is claimed that conceptual cognition is unreal while non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpaka*) is real, then how can such a division be made when there is no difference in their being manifest? If you say it is due to sublation (*bādha*), then the sublation would be equally mutual in the case of their being contrary. As for the firm establishment of experience regarding their difference, it is just as [it appears].
If there were no difference [between them], then it would be logical that only difference possesses reality. Furthermore, sublation (*bādha*) is real precisely because it appears;
