likewise, difference is also real. Therefore, how could that [difference] be ignorance? Moreover, since sublation is itself a form of difference, it too would be ignorance.
This would be like saying that a rabbit’s horn is the cutter of a flower in the sky—an argument derived from scripture (*āgama*).
If it is argued that "everything" [is not so] because of its appearance, then even scripture is ignorance; thus, this entire web of arguments is a snare.
As he will state:
"Even Brahman is desired [to exist] along with ignorance," therefore this is not an absolute doctrine either.

This is the intended meaning of the Sūtra. Thus he says in the Vṛtti: "Suddenly" (*akasmāt*) means "due to the non-attainment of a cause"—this is the sense. By the words "the difference of appearance" (*ābhāsabheda*) and so forth, the form residing in the object of cognition (*vedya*) is stated.
Since that [form] is the object, the state called "action-ness" (*kriyātva*), which bestows agency (*kartṛtā*), is not possible.
Form is said to have reached the state of Brahman. "That" refers to the synthesis of the various appearances, which constitutes the nature of action.
Now, is the agency of an insentient object not observed?
In the northern direction, there is the sovereign of mountains named Himālaya, whose self is divine.

Thus [it was said]. He says "this is not so" with the words "of the insentient," which is to be connected with "the state of being a non-agent. "That" refers to the insentient; "he" refers to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). This is precisely what is intended by the author of the *Sārasvata*, who qualifies [the subject] as "the self of the deity.

He introduces the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) with the words "of the consciousness-principle" (*cittattvasya*), etc. By the word "not," that which resides in the object to be measured is [negated].
Nor indeed—
by stating that the form belongs to the creator (*nirmātṛ*)— is the Sūtra’s phrase "of the two distinct appearances" made clear. (Page 249)
Out of compassion, he briefly recalls what has been established with the words "Just as...

and so forth. The connection is as follows: without the power of sovereignty (*aiśvarya-śakti*), because there would be no cause, and due to the absence of a cause for the sequence, the sequence—which is occasional and diverse—could not exist.

For since its very nature is the radiance of all internal appearances, simultaneity alone is appropriate; thus he says, "always indeed. But the power of sovereignty is capable of resolving this objection; thus he says, "because of lordship. "That and that" means occurring in various sequences. It is precisely the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
The connection is that [the agent] is "properly characterized by action" (*kriyālakṣaṇa*). He demonstrates this characteristic with the words "even though successive" (*kramiko 'pi*) and so forth.

He refers, in sequence, to both the commentary passages—the reason for succession being "internally" (*antar*) and so forth, and the objection regarding the unity [of the agent] as "the agent's operation" (*kartṛvyāpāra*) and "that" (*tat*), along with the response—by reciting them.

If even an action (*kriyā*) were to be cognized, it would then be something to be produced (*nirmeya*), and within that [production] there would be another action, and within that yet another—lest anyone suspect such an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the author recalls the previously stated reality of reflective awareness (*parāmarśatattva*) with the words "And this... (*sā caiṣā*). As for other [actions]...
The sense is that while such a thought might occasionally arise regarding actions such as cooking, it certainly does not apply here. Now,

if reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is non-different from the knower’s nature of consciousness and does not descend into the realm of the object of cognition, then— given the absence of sequential form— how can it possess the nature of action (*kriyātva*)?

Regarding this, it is said: "But [it] appears through the non-difference from the subject. And this account of the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) occurs solely through the power of the Supreme Lord;
thus, even in that case, the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) has been stated. And this has been explained.

And the state of being sequential [is taught] in the passage: "And the worldly [activity] is sequential" (2.1.2). This refers to the state of being sequential. Now, one might object: since the Lord’s very act of intention (*parāmarśa*) is his creative activity (*kriyā*), how can it be said in the commentary that there is a triad, beginning with "by the desire to act" (*cikīrṣayā*)? To this, [the author replies]: this...

"He avoids [the objection] by means of a prior admission, and also through reflection. In the phrase "of that and that" (*tasya tasya*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). By the inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*), [on page 250...]
He states the non-emergence of action [from that state]. Why, then, would there be distance from that very [state]?
He explains this for the sake of the commentary in the passage beginning with "atra hi" in the *Vṛtti* text. Manifestation (*ābhāsanā*) is an activity;
its defining characteristic is the primary reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). That very [awareness] extends up to manifestation, which consists in externalization. Therefore—

This differentiation of forms is merely an act of reflective awareness performed with the intention of making a distinction within manifestation itself. Therefore, although these three appear at the outset as a duality, the intended meaning is that they are in fact one. This is so not only because of the coloring by that which is being reflected upon, but also...

The meaning is: "also because [the agent] consists of effort according to desire. He begins the commentary on the passage starting with "of the insentient" by means of an objection, [saying] "and thus," which means "if that were so. [He says] "of the great element," for this [activity] is appropriate only if it has the form of a deity; and he considers that a deity does not burn, because such is observed [in experience].

But surely, even in desire there is a lack of sentience (*acaityanya*). True; however, that [lack of sentience] belongs to the object of desire, not to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Thus he says, "name and form.
And this refers to the determination (*adhyavasāya*) such as "this is a jar" [1.5.20].

This has been stated here. It was established in this very sūtra that [the term] "immediately following" (*anantaram*) refers to the mere manifestation of word and meaning—consisting of the signifier and the signified—as objects of cognition. To this, he provides an answer by way of concession, beginning with the words "let it be," etc., regarding the arising of existence and so forth within itself.

Precisely because of its stability, there is no change of form; thus, where could there be a synthesis? However, in the case of vibration and the like—which are intransitive—there exists a single synthesis whose object is both the preceding and succeeding moments, since it consists of the nature of flowing.
But in the case of burning and the like—which are transitive—there is not only a synthesis whose object is the preceding and succeeding moments...

This consists precisely of ascending the stream of continuous connection (anusandhānadhārā), including even that characterized by the unification of distinct actions; he shows how this could not occur in the case of the insentient with the words "let it be for now. The word "this" (asau) refers to the activity (vyāpāra). The connection [of the sentence] is: "even when it is said [that the insentient acts], then also..."
The phrase "mere existence" (*sattāmātra*) means existence that is both stable and characterized by having come into being after not having existed previously.

Now, one might object: in reality, those [entities] certainly do exist as independent; so why was it stated in the *Vṛtti* that they lack independence? To this, [the author replies]: [The passage continues: ...here...
(Page 251) He says:

"Independence," and so forth. That "this appears to me, while that necessarily appears to him"—this alone is called the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*), and not anything else. And therefore, even the act of coming into being...

Since an entity that is attached to manifestation becomes such [only] through its own freedom (*svātantrya*), what would be gained by looking toward the face of manifestation? That very freedom which does not look to any other face in the act of manifesting is what is called "freedom"; and that does not exist for insentient things.

"The reasoning is indeed correct because of the absence of autonomy. And that which is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), whose essence is pure wonder, belonging to Light in its supreme state—that alone is autonomy, and not the form of will (*icchā*);
however, in the intermediate state (*parāpara*), it takes the form of will due to the emergence of the object of desire, and in the lower state (*apara*), it is that very same [will].
He shows that [the subject] is not incomplete with the passage beginning "prakāśo 'pi" and ending with "cikīrṣaiva.

For "camatkāra" (wonder) is indeed resting within one's own self, which is independent of anything else. Thus, "camattva" (the state of being wondrous) consists in the nature of the enjoyer; that very state acts with intensity (*saṃrambha*), but it does not reflect (*vimṛśati*).

It pursues [the object] elsewhere. *Camat* is an adverbial modifier; or rather, it is the word *akhaṇḍa* (indivisible) itself, whose function is the unimpeded savoring [of the aesthetic experience]. Or, *camat* is an onomatopoeic imitation of the indistinct sound consisting of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) arising from the vibration and oscillation of the internal resonance (*āntaraspanda*). This applies even in the context of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) of poetry and drama.

Elsewhere it has been stated that aesthetic savor (*āsvāda*), which consists of relish and wonder, is indeed free from obstacles whose nature is the emergence of other future mental fluctuations. However, regarding the creation of the universe,
starting from the worlds of Śrī Sadāśiva and the others, [this occurs] by way of being desired as both distinct and non-distinct.

Through the gradual unfolding of the process of contraction within the veiling of the sense of "I" (ahambhāva), [the Lord] demonstrates the nature of both the transcendent (parā) and the immanent (aparā) as it remains established in such a state— from Ananta down to the Vidyeśvaras— according to the gradations of the sense of "this-ness" (idambhāva); for when differentiation has not yet sprouted, there is an absence of the functioning of the instruments of action.

However, the notion that "it has been done" is firmly established only within the specific distinctions of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) for both [beings] beginning with Brahmā and those beginning with potters. Thus he says: "in the creation consisting of *māyā*," and likewise "even in the state of contracted form. This means that even though there is a distinction between Brahmā and others on one hand, and the weaver and others on the other, [the same principle applies].

He says "thus" because there is a distinction between that which is being desired and its measurelessness or measurability; for in the supreme state (*paradaśā*), which is devoid of measurement, there is no conventional usage of desire—
this is according to the intention of the doctrines of Śāntaśiva and others.

(Page 252) Having stated that Śiva is indeed permeated by the nature of the eternal power (*sadāśakti*), [the author] says "Or else" (*athavā*) by relying on the perspective of Śiva-dṛṣṭi, which takes its basis in such a vision. For in every case, wonder (*camatkāra*) itself is will (*icchā*).
And that [power] exists even on the level of the other; as it was said:
"That very desire is of such an extent" (1.3). For it is precisely this [desire]—namely, the state of being a consumer characterized by wonder—that is defined as resting within one's own self.

Desire (*icchā*) exists everywhere; however, in certain cases, it arises as a repose within one's own self with respect to another object whose specific qualities have not yet been grasped, and in that state it is called "attachment" (*rāga*). But when its specific qualities have been grasped, it is called "lust" (*kāma*). By the inclusion of the word "and so forth," the impurity of longing (*abhilāṣa-mala*) is indicated, wherein there is another state of being.
Or rather, even the universal form remains by virtue of a mere residual impression (*vāsanā*), as it has been said:
"Affections from other births remain established within one's being.
And longing is simply the desire permeated by the absence of fear due to the constant proximity of that [object].

In this way, other points are to be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "and its absence," the connection is that the absence of will (*icchābhāva*) has been stated as the cause for the absence of autonomy (*svātantryābhāva*). By this much, the state of being active (*vṛtti*) is shown to be twofold:
[first] that which is autonomy through its association with the desire to become (*bubhūṣā*); and [second], through its dissociation from that, that which is [the absence thereof].
"Consequently, there is an absence of autonomy. [Objection: But how can it be said that "the Himavat exists" in this way? [Response:

He says, "But there is a metaphorical attribution of agency (*kartṛtva-upacāra*). The meaning is that the ground for such a superimposition (*āropaṇa*) is its being situated in that [substratum], which consists in dependence upon it. In this case, there is a superimposition of autonomy, which is understood here.

With the words "the bank," etc., he provides an illustration of the superimposition of independence upon an object that is being denoted. Regarding the statement—"Or rather, [there is no such thing] because of the equality of causes; for desire is perceived through its resulting activity"—which was intended to refute the objection concerning insentient things, therein:

The intended meaning is that the reality to be understood is precisely the superimposition of the sovereignty of the subject (*pramātṛ-svātantrya*). For this very reason, considering the position that [the word] arises from desire (*icchā-sambhava*) to be weak, he stated another solution:
"or it is established through analogy" (*upamānād vā siddham*). However, that was not accepted by the third sage (Patañjali).
Regarding the statement that there is no comparison using a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*): let that matter rest for now. The phrase "all indeed" refers to their state of being in constant flux.
(Page 253)
This was stated with reference to the subject under the influence of *māyā* while [the Lord] is manifesting [the world];

however, he indicates his intention by saying "or rather," suggesting that from the perspective of the true subject (*satyapramātṛ*), this is indeed non-metaphorical (*anupacarita*). He further states that from the perspective of the subject under the influence of *māyā*, this is indeed non-metaphorical.

With the intention that even at the level of the illusory subject (māyīya-pramātṛtā), there is no contradiction with the true subject (satya-pramātṛ), the word "api" (even/also) indicates, by means of the term "sprout" (aṅkura), the manifestation of what was previously non-existent. This capacity [of the sprout] exists only with reference to the illusory subject as "my subject"; however, it does not exist in the ultimate subject (paramārtha-pramātṛ).
He says that something is to be undertaken here: || 20 ||
Thus, for Him who desires to abide in this manner as the world-soul appearing as jars, cloths, and so forth, His very will is the cause, His agency, and His action. (21)

The meaning is clear. Regarding what was stated—that this very [power] is the power of action (kriyā-śakti)—someone might ask: "In the scripture, there is a division of powers such that the power of will (icchā-śakti) resides in the Blessed Lord, the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) in Śrī Sadāśiva, and the power of action (kriyā-śakti) in Īśvara; how is this so? To that, he says:

The particle *ca* in the phrase "the illumination of all" (*viśvāvabhāsana*) indicates a doubt or a qualification. The particle *api* signifies that this [illumination] is not merely an action well-known in the world in the form of physical vibration, but is also of this nature. The two indeclinables *yadā* and *tadā* indicate the relationship between cause and effect; alternatively, they function with the meaning of "even though—nevertheless" (*yadyapi—tathāpi*).

Having thus explained that "power" (śakti) resides in action (kriyā), he also explains his own intended sense of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the words "or rather, in that [action] as well. Here, "power" is essentially the nature of action,
as it has been stated:

"The triad of extremely subtle powers exists in a state of aesthetic equilibrium" (Śivadṛṣṭi 1.4). "By means of that [agency]" means by means of the agency of the mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*). As for the phrase "as they say," it refers to the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).
And by those who speak thus, even when there is the disappearance of other factors of action (*kāraka*), the reality of action resides in the agent.
But when [the agent] is absent, there is non-perception even though the collection of other causal factors (*kāraka-sāmagrī*) is present;

thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that action (*kriyā*) rests solely upon the agent. Even in cases such as "it is cooked here" (*iha pacyate*), those things fit for the enjoyment of the cooking and so forth appear as being merely implied by the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Thus they are the agents; however, it is not the case that the penetration of activity into the object is possible, because of the absence of desire—this is what follows from above. And in the case of metaphorical usage...
The indicative mark (*nimitta*) is the observation of a specific quality that has been deposited or intended in the object by means of that [action] residing in the agent.

Regarding this, having raised the objection that "the sentence which was recited after saying 'iti' does not exist in such a way in the *vṛtti*, because the word *sambandhinī* is not read in the *vṛtti*," he says: "the remainder" (*śeṣa*).

The meaning is that there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). By the word "of the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ*), which is heard in the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is thus stated that this [sūtra] has been recited with an ellipsis supplied. And the connection is: "of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, there is the status of being a *kāraka*. Now, if one follows the etymological derivation of *kāraka* as "that which acts" (*karoti iti kārakam*), then it refers to the agent (*kartṛ*).

Metaphorical usage (upacāra) is inevitable; however, one might raise the objection: "In this view where the cause is synonymous with the effect, what is the need for metaphorical usage? He dispels this doubt with the words "and the state of being a cause.
For, in the investigation of the doctrines of the existence or non-existence of the effect (sadasatkāryavāda), the dry (abstract) relationship between cause and effect has already been refuted.

"Of these" refers to the instruments and so forth. "This" refers to their status as causal conditions (*nimittatva*). Consequently, even in a state such as "he cooks with wood," the status of being a *kāraka* arises solely through the entry of the sovereignty of the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattvasvātantrya*), and not otherwise. [Objection: But surely they possess sovereignty over the action of their own constituent parts?

Because one observes agency in the statement "the pieces of wood burn," when that [agency] is intended as being subsumed within the primary act of cooking (*pāk*), then what is there to undermine its status as a *kāraka* even while it functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*)? Why, then, bring in the nature of consciousness (*cittattva*) here? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The pieces of wood."
It is appropriate that the agency of igniting belongs only to that which desires to ignite; this and other points should be understood as previously stated.
May there be auspiciousness.
Thus [ends the section].

In the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the illustrious Great Māheśvara, this is the fourth chapter, the investigation of the relationship between cause and effect, within the section on Action (*kriyādhikāra*). || 4 ||
The *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*, composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the Great Mahāmaheśvara. The Section on Scripture (*Āgamādhikāra*).
Now begins the first reflection:
I bow to Him who, having pierced through everything woven like warp and woof, spontaneously makes all things consist of Śiva;
He who, arising within the unsurpassed abode, is Himself the sprinkling of nectar.
Thus, having extensively established knowledge and action through the two preceding sections, it is now said within the section on action regarding that which was stated [in verse 2.3.15]:
"of the variegated painting of the manifold universe..."

In such passages, the very nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is defined as being characterized by the stainless manifestation of all categories of objects (*padārtha*). In that regard, it must be stated: what is this collection of categories? In this matter, the perception (*pratyakṣa*) of people like us does not directly perceive everything; nor does inference (*anumāna*), for it likewise depends upon the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) of a logical mark (*liṅga*) for all things.

Because there is no possibility of attaining [knowledge] through other means, the sacred tradition (āgama)—which consists of the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the Supreme Lord whose nature is uncontracted luminosity—is capable of cognizing the universe; for that very reason, it is introduced in this commentary for the purpose of establishing the reality of categories. Thus, it is the sacred tradition of the Supreme Lord alone that establishes the truth.

It is capable of being demonstrated; however, logical reasoning serves only to reinforce that [demonstration]. Furthermore, the reduction of the entire universe to the status of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) is not useful for the present purpose, which is the recognition of the Lord (*īśvarapratyabhijñā*).
For in the process of making the universe an object of knowledge, [the subject] transcends the very state of being an object of knowledge.
To that extent, the state of being a true subject (*satya-pramātṛtā*), having attained fullness within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), becomes realized in the heart. As it has been said:
"When [the Self] abides pervading all objects as if out of a desire to see them..."
"Then what is the use of much speaking? One will understand for oneself. (Svacchanda Tantra 4.43, p. 256).
Thus, by the word *samastasampat* ("all-accomplishing"), when analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it serves as a qualification of *prajñā* (wisdom).

This has been made clear: for when the entire manifold of space, time, and mental activity—including form and action—manifests within consciousness, it is that very self-luminosity which shines forth, being all-powerful, eternal in nature, and its own essence unconditioned by those [manifestations]. Even so, due to the veil of *māyā*, it may otherwise appear.
If one fears [the consequences], even in that case, one must take refuge in the scripture of the Lord. As it has been said:
"His word alone is the single authority; that which is spoken by the Lord is true.
His utterance is not sublated by the gross means of knowledge belonging to humans."
Thus, with this intention, the section on scripture (*āgamādhikāra*) is stated. Therein, by means of eleven verses beginning with "In this way, internally and externally...
and so forth—

By the end of this [passage], beginning with "through the distinction of grossness and subtlety," he demonstrates the individual nature of each of the principles (tattvas) from Śiva down to the Earth, as established in the Pārameśvara Āgama and further supported by reasoning. Those very [principles]...

In other systems of philosophy, real entities— which consist of the appearance of each [particular] as the object of the operation of a means of valid cognition— are treated as universals. Yet, it is precisely through these [entities] that there arises an infinite manifestation of particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*), characterized by the diversity of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), which are grasped by the favoring of restricted capacities.

The purport of this section is that this entire creation— consisting of bodies, worlds, and so forth— is composed of the specific manifestation of the Great Array (*makavyūha*), woven like warp and woof. In this regard, by relying on the meaning already stated, [the author] establishes the connection with the subject matter (*adhikāra-saṅgati*),
concludes the refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa-nirākriyā*), and [affirms] the very principle of Śiva.

And all this indeed is the reality of all entities; thus, he first demonstrates its essential nature as consisting of manifestation and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) through the union of knowledge and action: "In this way, activity, which functions internally and externally, follows the succession of time."
In that case, knowledge and action are mutually inseparable from the Mother alone. || 1 ||
The relationship of cause and effect is not possible in that which is insentient (*jaḍa*); rather, it exists only in that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*),
whose ultimate reality is solely light and self-reflection (*prakāśavimarśa*), yet which, through its sovereignty, possesses both an internal and external aspect.
Shining forth and bringing about the sequence of time, being the substratum (*dharmī*) by virtue of having the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) as its body,

it assumes as its own attribute (*dharma*) that very power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which consists of internal and external aspects and manifests sequentially. Thus, because it has been stated "that," therefore...

The two powers of knowledge and action, whose nature is illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), are mutually inseparable from the Cause. This very [inseparability] is the ultimate body of all entities. Therefore, it is the sovereignty that unfolds the manifestation of the fivefold cosmic functions (*pañcakṛtya*), having assumed them all through the gateway of the power of action.
Even that which is manifested as a mere appearance through instruction for the sake of its utility in meditation and so forth is called the Śiva-tattva.
Thus it has been said in the *Śvātantryamukta*: (1.5.16) [The text continues: "That which is not liberated from autonomy... etc.
Thus, it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"How can the supreme reality of Śiva, who transcends Māyā, manifest within the mind?"
To this question,

it has been established that the downward pervasion belongs to Śiva alone, who is self-luminous. For self-luminosity is indeed autonomy, and downward pervasion is likewise nothing other than emanation itself.

This is the meaning of the aphorism. The commentator states that, regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) proposed in [Sūtra 1.1.4], "Knowledge and action belong to the elements," it must be explained that [the soul] possesses within itself the nature of a Lord (*īśvara*), which consists in self-cognition.

The entire subject matter has been stated; now, holding in mind the objection of others— namely, "Is there now some other object of cognition for the sake of which this new section is undertaken?"— he introduces the meaning of the treatise in brief with the words beginning with "Thus" and ending with "having shown," thereby establishing the connection to the present topic.

By the word "begins" (*upakramate*), even the seed of doubt has been addressed, and the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) has also been introduced. For the Śiva-principle is the body of all entities; and since the variegated manifestation of all phenomena occurs upon its surface, the very mention of that [Śiva-principle] constitutes the commencement of their exposition.

Furthermore, by the manner [of stating] that "the intended meaning of the entire scripture is precisely the Śiva-principle," the introduction of the sūtra has indeed already been accomplished; thus, the previous style has also been followed.
In the introduction: Now, it would be more appropriate to say "the action of the agent" rather than "the action of the knower.

To this, [the author] replies with the word "manifestation" (*avabhāsana*). Although the assumption of external existence is indeed nothing but manifestation, nevertheless, [it involves] hands, feet, and so forth, which produce forms common to all worldly knowers.

It is precisely that which culminates in the excellence of divine activity that is intended, as it is well-known among worldly people; and he indicates this very thing by means of a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*), with the intention that the supreme subject, whose characteristic is the *śiva*-tattva, cannot be defined because of its transcendence of the worldly. Even though...

The principle of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*) has been explained by way of the illusory subject (*māyīya-pramātṛ*); yet, although the collection of principles and worlds (*tattva-bhuvana-varga*) is not its creation, nevertheless, the principle of the illusory subject will ultimately be shown to reside within the Śiva-principle itself, because it is common to both modes [of manifestation] and because it is of one and the same nature as that.

The mention of "principles" (*tattva*) and so forth is intended with this in mind; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of objects such as jars and bodies, which are manifested by the subject under the influence of *māyā*. In the commentary, the phrase "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*) is used because principles, worlds, and other such entities are specified as being distinct from the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Therefore, the action— which takes as its support the very Self designated as the subject, both in the form of the object and the form of the agent—
being analyzed either as residing in the object or as residing in the agent,
exists as having a single locus and is in reality one alone; for the manifestation of a jar is [not distinct] from the manifestation of a cloth.

For indeed, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no difference between a jar and a cloth, because they are non-different insofar as their ultimate reality is solely consciousness (*bodha*). However, let it be granted that there is a difference among actions, as they appear colored by the distinctions created by *māyā*; this is the apprehension of the actual state of things. Now, as for that [consciousness] which has as its object the entities appearing [to it]...

Anticipating the objection that the "performance of what is capable" (samarthācaraṇa) belongs to the cognizer, and asking how it could be anything other than devoid of cognition, he says: "of the nature of consciousness" (bodhātman).

For the cognizer, whose sole form is consciousness, whatever additional element is of the nature of non-consciousness is relegated to the category of that which is to be manifested; such is his [position].

That which is one's own essential nature (*nijam śakti-rūpam*), designated as *dharma*, is appropriately of the very nature of consciousness (*bodha-rūpam*); such is the meaning. Furthermore, there is no qualification for ritual action (*karmani adhikāraḥ*) for the wise man, nor for one engaged in rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), worship (*samarcana*), and meditation (*dhyāna*).
Although this scripture has been explained in the sense that it is the "attainment of the knowledge of reality," nevertheless...
(page 259)
This very point is logical only when it is rooted in this specific purpose. Otherwise, if knowledge were to be useful for action, let that be so; but how could action increase knowledge?
For its accomplishment is seen even through mere contemplation (*bhāvanā*). However, when action is indeed supreme—

Furthermore, when reflective awareness (vimarśa), having become firm by extending itself to the very limits of the body, offers all this—such as flowers and ointments within the heart—to the Supreme Lord, reflecting that "I contemplate [them] as non-different from Him," that is worship (pūjana). In that case, it is rightly said: "Knowledge devoid of acts such as ritual worship does not [exist]."

"It becomes firm. And thus says the venerable *Sadāgama*: "Yoga is not one thing and action another; for that intellect which is ascended upon reality, when it pacifies the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of its own mind, is designated as 'action'."
Thus it is said. And this has been explained by me in the Vārtika:
"The latent impressions (vāsanās) in one's own mind are born from karma, impurity (mala), and māyā;
that cognition which is the innate nature of consciousness exists for the purpose of their pacification."
That very activity, which presides over the multitude of principles— both those that initiate the body and those situated externally—
is also yoga, because it effects the dissolution of the principles into consciousness.
Even in the world, that which is called the action of "going" is indeed nothing but an internal vibration;
it is this [vibration] that enters the body, the senses, and the location.
Therefore, even that which is known as action is in fact nothing but knowledge.
(Tantraloka 1.155).

This very point he demonstrates with the words "mutual non-separation," and so forth. "Otherwise" means that if they were not considered non-different from one another, then identity would be asserted between them, as in the case of "treeness" and "śiṃśapā-ness."

In order to demonstrate that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is indeed a distinction [between the two] due to the difference between appearance (*ābhāsa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), both the terms "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and "distinction" (*vyatireka*) have been employed. If it is thought that action belongs to the conscious subject alone, while in cases such as "the chariot runs," it is merely a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), then that very point is easily stated.
The intention [behind this] is as follows: surely the Supreme Lord possesses both knowledge and action, which are not mutually exclusive;
for his very nature is consciousness (*bodha*).
(Page 260)

For the Supreme Lord is by nature constantly manifesting the fivefold activity that is ever-new; however, for bound subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*), at the moment of perceiving blue and other objects existing within the universe as previously constructed, there is no such new manifestation. He resolves this [objection] with the words beginning "māyā," etc. Regarding the word "mukhena" (by way of): [The text continues: ...by way of [the door of] Māyā. Here, "mukha" means the door (*dvāra*). It is said that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. This is because the power of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Therefore, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*kāraṇa*). For example, in the phrase "he eats through the mouth" (*mukhena bhuṅkte*), the mouth is the cause of eating. Similarly, in the phrase "he sees through the eyes" (*cakṣurbhyām paśyati*), the eyes are the cause of seeing. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*nimitta*). For example, in the phrase "he drinks through the nose" (*nāsikayā pibati*), the nose is the cause of drinking. Similarly, in the phrase "he hears through the ears" (*karṇābhyām śṛṇoti*), the ears are the cause of hearing. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*hetu*). For example, in the phrase "he lives by means of water" (*udakena jīvati*), water is the cause of living. Similarly, in the phrase "he acts by means of the body" (*dehena ceṣṭate*), the body is the cause of acting. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*pratyaya*). For example, in the phrase "he understands through inference" (*anumānena budhyate*), inference is the cause of understanding. Similarly, in the phrase "he knows through verbal testimony" (*āgamena jānāti*), verbal testimony is the cause of knowing. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*upāya*). For example, in the phrase "he attains heaven by means of sacrifice" (*yajñena svargaṃ prāpnoti*), sacrifice is the cause of attaining heaven. Similarly, in the phrase "he attains liberation by means of knowledge" (*jñānena mokṣaṃ prāpnoti*), knowledge is the cause of attaining liberation. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*kāraka*). For example, in the phrase "he cuts with an axe" (*paraśunā chinatti*), the axe is the instrument of cutting. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*sādhana*). For example, in the phrase "he goes by means of a horse" (*aśvena gacchati*), the horse is the means of going. Similarly, in the phrase "he obtains wealth by means of trade" (*vāṇijyena dhanaṃ labhate*), trade is the means of obtaining wealth. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature.
