Similarly, in the phrase "he weeps because of sorrow" (*duḥkhena roditi*), sorrow is the cause of weeping. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). For example, in the phrase "he makes a cloth from threads" (*tantubhiḥ paṭaṃ karoti*), the threads are the inherent cause of the cloth. Similarly, in the phrase "he makes a pot from clay" (*mṛdā ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the clay is the inherent cause of the pot. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). For example, in the phrase "he produces sound by striking a drum" (*murajenāhanyamānena śabdaṃ janayati*), the drum being struck is the non-inherent cause of the sound. Similarly, in the phrase "he produces color by heating gold" (*suvarṇena tāpyamānena rūpaṃ janayati*), the gold being heated is the non-inherent cause of the color. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*pratyayakāraṇa*). For example, in the phrase "he perceives form by means of light" (*ālokena rūpaṃ pratyeti*), light is the causal condition for perceiving form. Similarly, in the phrase "he perceives taste by means of moisture" (*snehena rasaṃ pratyeti*), moisture is the causal condition for perceiving taste. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). For example, in the phrase "he builds a house with bricks" (*iṣṭakābhir gṛhaṃ karoti*), the bricks are the material cause of the house. Similarly, in the phrase "he fashions a statue from clay" (*mṛdā pratimāṃ karoti*), the clay is the material cause of the statue. Thus, the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Consequently, it is established that the door of Māyā is the cause of the concealment of one's own nature. Furthermore, the word "mukha" here signifies the cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). For example, in the phrase "he creates a jar by means of a potter's wheel" (*cakreṇa ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the potter's wheel is the instrumental cause of the jar. Similarly, in the phrase "he fashions a crown by means of a goldsmith's hammer" (*ghaṇṭayā mukuṭaṃ karoti*), the goldsmith's hammer is the instrumental cause of the crown. Thus, the door of Māyā is

The connection with the preceding [phrase] is: "the mutual non-separation is logical. Since sovereignty is the very nature of that consciousness (*cit*), and there is no consciousness whatsoever apart from sovereignty consisting of knowledge and action—it is through this means, by way of that [sovereignty], that it is logical even for bound souls (*paśu*).

There is a mutual inseparability of knowledge and action. As stated in the *Nareśvaraviveka*: "Individual souls (*aṇu*) consist of both consciousness and non-consciousness; because of their consciousness, they are one with Maheśvara. Therefore, how can some, due to their lack of consciousness, be grounds for objection?"

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might raise the doubt: "How is it that even for the Blessed One, constant manifestation does not fail to occur?"—this he dispels with the words beginning with "blue" (*nīla*). Alternatively, that sovereignty of the Lord which was previously established, by way of that very sovereignty, [he establishes] the creation of even the subjects of *māyā*.

It has been established that the text should be interpreted as having a single, uniform sense. In the *Vṛtti*, the genitive case in the phrase "the actions of the cognizer" (*pramātuḥ kriyāḥ*) denotes a relationship (*sambandha*), rather than the agent (*kartṛ*) in the sense of being excluded [from the action]. Even in that case, there is no absolute prohibition, because the rule "it is optional in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*) permits it, provided that it is not merely a suffix expressing the feminine gender.
The remainder [of the verse] is as follows: "Or independently" means without depending on the creation of Īśvara; the connection is that "the manifestation" is thus established. For it has been said:
"Because of the appearance of a form according to one's desire within the range of the intellect..."
Therefore, as it is said: "Just as desired... (1.6.11), and so forth. Now, one might ask: for what purpose is this investigation undertaken by beginning with the limited subject (*paśu*)?
To this, he replies: "Pure sovereignty" (*śuddhaiśvarya*). [One might further object: "But if, in the ultimate sense, these [limited subjects] do not differ [from the Lord], then..."

What is the use of investigating this "excessiveness"? By the word "merely" (*kevalam*), he shows that even this excessiveness, while appearing, is not absolutely impossible. Regarding the phrase "in the state of the creator" (*nirmātṛpade*):
it refers to that activity which previously [belonged] to those subject to *māyā*, from humans down to insects, at the time of performing their own respective functions.

It vibrates within the heart; although in that state of the vibration of duality within the heart there is a sequence— namely, that duality is preceded by non-duality— and although there is also an action brought about by that sequence, nevertheless, it does not amount to that alone.
The world, desiring commonality with other perceivers,

requires a sequence characterized by the transition from the nature of being cognizable by the external senses to the internal nature of the self; therefore, even action, which consists of the intended reflective awareness, is considered an incomplete sequence.

It is not appropriate to treat that which is incomplete as if it were a mere mental construction (tāmasa-kalpa) and then proceed with discourse based solely on that cognition. The word "ucyate" means "is so treated in discourse. Now, if the manifestation or creation of pleasure and the like, as well as of objects such as jars produced through volition, occurs only within the internal field of the intellect (*buddhi-bhūmi*), then how can there be action?
He says: "internally. Immediately after this, the word "api" (also) should be supplied. The particle "api" indicates that it is not only externally;
"ca" (and) serves to indicate the aforementioned doubt and so forth. The same applies elsewhere. In that case, with respect to what is there a sequence?
He says: "internally also. For, on the plane of the intellect...

And by the principle stated in [the aphorism] "svāminaśca... (1.5.10), there is an externalization of that which exists precisely within the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*). Now, one might ask: how can there be a temporal sequence in that pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)? He says, "pure consciousness," [implying] that this is indeed accepted as such.
"And the state of being sequential belongs to the worldly [power]," so it has been said. Now, one might ask: "How is such a sovereign (*prābhavī*) action not shown in the Sūtra and its Commentary?
Who says it is not shown? For as much as was said—namely, "the internal and external function"—just that much [is intended].
By the demonstration of its internal nature, its state of being the innermost of all is also necessarily implied.

The word "power" (*śakti*) is used to clarify the intention that, in this context, "action" is simply the capacity for sequential manifestation. The phrase "of this" means "of this very one whose nature is the fullness of consciousness. It is where the pure, divine creation (*aiśvara-śuddha-sarga*) is said to occur.
"Śiva is the agent on the impure path"—thus [it is said]; whereas that which is impure belongs to Māyā, concerning which it is stated:
"Ananta is declared to be the Lord in the dark [path]."
Thus, although in reality Śiva alone is the agent in all cases, the agency of another is spoken of due to the conceit produced by His will. As the Guru of Vidyā says (page 262):
Even for one who perceives the lower [truth] through successive graspings of the higher,
there remains the grasping of one's own conviction regarding the means of proof.
In this case, O Lord, the mirages are the cause.

Thus it is said. In that regard, within the creation of Īśvara, the existence of the internal-external relationship occurs in relation to the purely internal consciousness; however, in the creation of Māyā, this relationship has many branches in relation to the internal increase of the Lord and so forth. Both of these creations belong to the Blessed One, Paramaśiva.

The unfolding of power (*śaktivijṛmbhā*). Therefore, that power, by virtue of its nature manifesting internally, is called the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*); however, when characterized by the firmness of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) intensified by the gradual expansion of externalized forms, it is designated as the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). As the scripture says:
"It must be known that this is so, and not otherwise"—
this firm conviction which makes it known here in the world is called the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Furthermore, when [one intends] "let this object be thus," [that is the power of action].
At that very moment, that which brings about such-and-such [results] is here called "action" (kriyā).
(Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.8).

Thus, although the Blessed One, Paramaśiva, is indeed beyond succession (*akrama*), his union with the powers of knowledge and action is logical. Now, one might object: "In the creation pertaining to Māyā, let it be so because of the manifestation of the category of Time (*kālatattva*)."

As for the sequence: at the end of the *vidyā*-tattva, since there is no emergence of *māyā* and thus an absence of connection with time, how can this sequential yoga (*kramayoga*) be said to exist? To this, he says: "And here... In this context, the subjects belonging to *māyā* who possess duality are those to be instructed, and they are subject to the succession of time.

Even in the state of Sadāśiva, those who posit the possibility of the emergence of "this-ness" (idantā), which is to be concealed by "I-ness" (ahantā), must necessarily admit this [concealment]. For immersion into another state arises precisely from that. Therefore, with respect to them, a sequence certainly exists; however, since it is not fully developed, what is the use of further elaboration?

By this [it is meant]: "possessing duality" (*dvaitavat*) is [formed] with the suffix *matup* as appropriate in the case of the "plenitude" (*bhūman*) and so forth. Since this is so, therefore that which is stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* (p.
But when, through the unfolding of the joy of the manifestation of his own conscious nature, he proceeds to create various effects through manifold and diverse arrangements;
"The state of being oriented toward [the object] is the mind's first *tuṭi* of will" (2.8).

Thus, even in the Lord Paramaśiva, the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), which consists of orientation (*aunmukhya*), possesses primacy— that is, the quality of occurring prior to— the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).

The term *tuṭi* is appropriately understood as having the nature of a temporal fraction (*kālāṃśa*); otherwise, in the absence of succession, how could there be the conventional usage of "prior" and "subsequent"? However, this [usage] is justified in relation to the person being instructed and in relation to the subject who is still within the sphere of *māyā*. But [one might ask]: in this aphorism...
Successive illusory subjects have been created, but not the Śiva-principle.
He says, "because of the commonality of the subject. For even there, the existence of succession has been demonstrated.
Therefore it was said, "Thus, in this way. Or else, he states the truly real position with the words, "or rather, they are none at all. || 1 ||

Now, if the Śiva-tattva is indeed of such a nature, then what other distinct principle (tattvāntara) could there be beyond it? Specifically, how could Sadāśiva and Īśvara be separate principles? As the scripture says:
"Because it demonstrates the teaching on the three principles (*tattva*)—laya, adhikāra, and bhoga—the category named *pati* is proclaimed as the first. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.1.14).
By this, the sovereignty of the *pati* alone is stated; and for those who rest in the single principle of consciousness...

Since the principles (tattvas) are devoid of spatial and temporal sequence, what order could there be? Anticipating this very objection, he establishes [the order] by means of the aphorism: "However, due to the predominance of the intermediate state, the principle called Sādākhya comes first."
But when it has as its ultimate object external existence, then the Pārameśvara [scripture] is extrinsic (parataḥ).

Truth is indeed the single reality that is Śiva-tattva; yet there exists another distinction. This is stated as follows: for that [reality], by means of its own power, manifesting variety within itself like a reflection, must necessarily manifest the sequence of time and space, because variety consists of the differentiation of action and form. Therefore...
In the manifestation of the intensification of the internal state whose nature is knowledge (jñānarūpā),
that which pertains to *sadākhya*— arising within *sadākhya*— is primary in the instruction on the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) and so forth. (Page 264)

From the moment that reality, which is worthy of being seen, is manifested as "it exists, it exists," it is then designated by the term *Sadāśiva*. Even when there is the emergence of the "this-ness" (*idantā*), it is called *Śivatā* by means of the word *Sat*.
This occurs when the external object, which consists of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), is perceived in its supreme state through its overflowing manifestation.

Because it is appropriate to fully nourish the Blessed One’s performance of what is extremely difficult to accomplish, the principle of Īśvara, denoted by the word *Parameśvara*, is fit to be described after *Sādākhya*. This is what is meant: here, "principle" (*tattva*) refers to the state of being that [which is denoted].
A universal (sāmānya) is said to be the cause for the unification of specific forms within their respective classes,
such as earth for clay, stone, wood, bone, flesh, and so forth, or water for rivers, wells, lakes, oceans, and so forth. This has been stated in the venerable Mataṅga-āgama:
That which is the nature of reality (tattva) is the form of the object, whose essence is the manifestation of its own attributes;
in the vision of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), that reality is clearly and distinctly the state of the object.

"That which has not fallen from its own state, which is pervasive, and has come under its own control, is not pervaded by another; therefore, that is the *tattva* within the continuum of *tattvas*" (1.5.4).
In this regard, [it refers to] that which belongs to the class of pure consciousness called the Mantramaheśvaras.

In the first creation, the wheel of existence (*bhāvacakra*)—which resembles the mass of objects perceivable by the internal organs of beings such as ourselves—is manifested as something predominantly dark, like a painting just begun; and at the time of reabsorption, it appears as a reflection, as if on the verge of dissolution. Within that wheel of existence, of that [Self]...

The manifestation of the group of conscious subjects as such, which is the generality of specific consciousness, is the *sadāśiva-tattva*; however, the state of persistence in a complete and variegated reflection that resembles the objects of the external senses for those in the form of the Mantreśvaras and others is the *īśvara-tattva*. As the scripture says:
"Established in that very reality of Īśvara, all the Supreme Lords (Parameśvaras),
authorized by the will of Śiva, are the sovereigns of the universe" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.5.5),
and so forth. Sadāśiva and the Lord Īśvara, however, are the presiding deities over such a reality.
Where [the object of worship] is like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth, this [objection] has no scope:
namely, why are Brahmā and the others not included among the categories of reality (*tattva*)? This is the meaning of the sūtra.
The commentary (*vṛtti*) and the sub-commentary (*vivṛti*) are clear. By means of the two words "internal" (*āntara*) and "state" (*daśā*),...
(Page 265) That the Śiva-tattva is implied [in the term "Lord"] is shown in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the words "of the Lord" (*īśituḥ*). || 2 ||
These two very principles have been stated under different names; one should not be confused as to what they might be here. He says this in a half-verse:
"Īśvara is the outward expansion (unmeṣa); Sadāśiva is the inward contraction (nimeṣa)."

In the passage, "From whose unfolding (unmeṣa) the world arises," the term *unmeṣa* refers to that power of consciousness which constitutes the principle of Īśvara, bestowing externality and clarity upon the universe. This is what is indicated here.
In the passage beginning "By whose blink [occurs] dissolution," the word *nimeṣa* (blink) refers here to the *sadāśiva-tattva*, which brings forth the internal form in an indistinct manner.

Both of these [the *sadāśiva-tattva* and the *māyā-tattva*] function by causing the appearance of movement within the *cittattva* (the principle of consciousness), even though that *cittattva* is itself immovable.

That which is characterized by slight movement is called this "pure vibration" (śuddhaspanda). For all principles (tattvas) are indeed the power-forms (śaktirūpa) of the Lord and are nothing but vibration. As it has been said:
"The outpourings (niḥṣyanda) of the qualities and so forth arise from their dependence upon the universal vibration."
"Having attained their own self-nature... (Sp. Kārikā 19).

Thus, one particular power, existing by drawing forth infinite powers toward itself, is most proximate to the Blessed Lord; others, however, are more distant, very distant, or most distant. Therefore, worship is manifold.
They have been shown in the Āgamas.

Thus, by means of this half-verse, it is stated that the Śiva-tattva— consisting of all the principles (tattvas) assumed as the two forms characterized by Īśvara and Sadāśiva, which are of the nature of opening and closing— is that which was previously mentioned in the preceding sūtra; however,
its function belongs to that very same [Śiva] when he possesses full sovereignty.

That which is characterized by reflective awareness (vimarśa) through the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the notions of "I" and "this"— that is the state of coreferentiality between the consciousness of Being (sadvidyā) and the cognition of "I" and "this. (3)
*Satī* is pure *vidyā*; *aśuddhavidyā* is something other than that—this is the intermediate meaning.
The intended sense (*tātparya*) is this: "I" is the light and its self-reflexive awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*) which is not directed toward anything else.
(Page 266)
"This" refers to one who is oriented toward another. One [aspect] resides in the venerable Lord Śiva, while the second resides in the group of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
And in the subject constituted by Māyā, those two—characterized as the grasper and the grasped—are established as having separate substrates.
However, when they rest in the middle position like a balanced scale, then it is "I am this."

Precisely for this reason, the superimposition of the object (*grāhya*) upon the subject (*grāhaka*) constitutes the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the Lord Sadāśiva, wherein the objective aspect remains somewhat obscured. In the venerable Lord Īśvara, when the object has become manifest as "this," reflective awareness consists in the superimposition of "I" upon it, resulting in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This [awareness]...

He introduces the meaning of the Sūtra with the words "unmeṣa" (the unfolding), etc. "Of the authors of the Śāstras" refers to the composers of the *Spanda* and other treatises. And "of that" [refers to] that by which the sovereignty of Śiva, beginning from the *Sadāśiva-tattva*, is fulfilled; therefore, this activity belongs to both.

It is called "knowledge" (vidyā). Both of these consist of its activity and constitute the single, compact sovereignty of the Lord Paramaśiva. Now, if the universe is withdrawn [into Him], then "I-ness" (ahantā) alone is appropriate, and since that is Śiva-hood, how can the withdrawal (nimeṣa) be the nature of Sadāśiva? And if so, how...

The teachers [have spoken of] the opening (*unmeṣa*); how then can even the closing (*nimeṣa*) of the Lord be designated as distinct from that, such that by means of His opening and closing—[as in *Spandakārikā* 1]?
Here, he dispels this doubt with the words "but not" (*na tu*). For [the statement] "the universe is closed" refers to the universe...
This very state of non-contact with "this-ness" (*idantā*) must be described as having some form; yet in the state of Śiva, the universe is nothing at all.
For it will be stated [later]: "In every way, however, it is dissolved within" (4.1.14). Indeed, in the Āgama:
"For this very reason, saṃsāra—which is by its very nature peaceful in essence—is indeed terrible;
therefore, it is not desired by the Lord, whose heart is non-terrible" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.4.14).
Thus it is recited. And consequently, that which is "within" the universe—that which revolves within the *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness)—[is the Supreme].

Obscurity (*dhyāmalatā*) is that very state of *nimeṣa* (the closing of the eyes). For this very reason, at that time, that universe is said to be "dissolved" because it lacks the capacity for empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*). This is what is meant by the phrase "the state of Sadāśiva," which refers to the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) of all persons who are subjects under the influence of *māyā*.

(Page 267) Indeed, [these objects] do not manifest externally; for this very reason, they are to be known individually by their own respective consciousnesses due to their uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatā*), and consequently, because they lack commonality (*sādhāraṇya*), they are inexpressible (*avyavahāryatā*).

The state of Sadāśiva is the manifestation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those objects denoted by the word "dissolved" (*pralīna*) due to their being absorbed into the state of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Although this has been demonstrated equally as "I am this" in the Vivṛti, nevertheless, regarding this "this-ness" (*etattā*)...

Because of the description of non-manifestation (*asphuṭatva*), there is an emphasis on "I" (*aham*) in the prior state; however, because of the mention of manifestation (*sphuṭatva*) in the state of Īśvara, there is an emphasis on "this" (*etat*). Now, one might raise this doubt: since sovereignty is complete here, it is called "Īśvara-hood," but why is the conventional usage of "Śiva" characterized by [the presence of] Īśvara applied to the former state? It is always so.

Recalling that this is not distinct from the state of Īśvara, he explains the station of Sadāśiva with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*). First, the station of Īśvara was described as *idantā* (the state of "this-ness") due to its clarity, and for that very reason, it is intensely radiant. However, when that same state is characterized by tranquility, it is indistinct due to its lack of luminosity.

When that occurs, even while in conjunction with the object of knowledge (*vedya*), because Śiva-nature emerges, it is called Sadāśivatā— the state of Śiva— by virtue of every mode of differentiation. And that is the complete dissolution of those beings established in the realm of Māyā,
who consist of the forms of both subject and object.

Because of the dissolution of the form consisting of *māyā*. At that time, the elements (*bhūtāni*) are deposited within the *māyā-tattva*, and that [tattva], being of the nature of the power of the Supreme Lord, comes to rest in the state of Sadāśiva through contact with the aspect of "this-ness" (*idamaṃśa*);
thus, the closing of the eyes (*nimeṣaḥ*) is the state of Sadāśiva. In this way, this passage is to be understood, and not the previous one. Now, [an objection]: "But..."
With the intention that the meaning of the passage beginning with these words should be recalled here, *paramaśivatā* (the state of Supreme Śiva) is to be explained;
for otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the statement that "dissolution occurs in a mere moment" and that "this is the activity of Sadāśiva.
Now, one might object: let it be so when there is the great dissolution of all subjects and objects; but what about when...
When *māyā* has not dissolved, there occurs the dissolution of the entire range of objects of knowledge— such as those composed of earth or primordial matter (*prākṛta*)—

while the *puruṣa*-principles remain as the subjects. At that time, the universe exists within the internal organs of the *puruṣa*-principles themselves in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), like one in deep sleep.

[If it were] dissolution (*pralaya*), and not the entry into the interior of the "I-sense" (*ahantā*), then how can it be said that "the closing of the eyes (*nimeṣa*) occurs within"? To this, he says: "The grasper," and so forth. "Within" means within the principles of the Person (*puṃstattva*); "closing of the eyes" means the state of having only residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
[Objection: But even so, [this would apply to] Sadāśiva...
(Page 268) This portion of the sūtra has not been treated as an explicit statement, yet it has been treated as such; thus he says,
"And at that time," referring to that state which exists even during the stage of having experience (*savedyāvasthā*).
The "twinkling" (*nimeṣa*) consists of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is of the nature of the illusory subject;
even that, in reality, belongs to this [consciousness] characterized by the fragmented reflective awareness of "this-ness. (Aparokṣānubhūtiprakaraṇa 15)

By this logic, resting in the word "I" (aham), one touches the very state of Sadāśiva, which is "I-this" (ahamidam). However, when its essence consists of residual impression (*saṃskāra*), then its true nature is simply "I-ness" (*ahantā*); at that point, the state of Sadāśiva is primary, while the state of Māyā—whether as "this-ness" (*idantā*) or as the "I-ness" of Māyā—is merely a residual impression. For this is what he will state later.

He states that both explanations are also logical with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). Since dissolution (*pralaya*) is twofold—either as the state where the principle of the Person (*puruṣatattva*) remains, in which case objects of knowledge (*vedya*), possessing the nature of their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), exist in a state of being perceivable; or [the other], where even the principles of the Persons...

Because, through dissolution into the power of *māyā*, one enters the state of Sadāśiva; since there is no longer a separate subject-hood (*pramātṛtva*) with respect to that [state], objects of knowledge (*vedya*) do not exist as such, being devoid of objectivity (*apavedyatā*). And therefore, even for one who is in such a state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*),...
The state of possessing both forms will be explained [later];
meanwhile, it has been stated in the verse, "That which remains as mere [consciousness] is called the state of deep sleep, comparable to cosmic dissolution" (3.2.15).
Having thus explained that "from whose closing of the eyes comes dissolution," [it follows that] "from whose opening [of the eyes] comes emergence."

While explaining [this], he states the distinction between the state of Īśvara and the state of Sadāśiva with the words "the state of Īśvara. Here, the word *daśā* has the meaning of the word *avasthā* (state). Objects characterized by a clearly manifest sense of "this-ness" (*idantā*) arise within the state of Īśvara; it is precisely there that they exist in the ultimate sense.
Because this would result in the state [of the object] becoming manifest. Now, in the passage beginning with "By whose opening and closing...
(*Spanda-kārikā* 1), why is only the category of the knowable (*vedya*) included by the mention of the "world" (*jagat*), when—
Even up to Sadāśiva, dissolution and creation are heard of in the Āgama:

"O lady of good vows, everything from the earthly element up to Sadāśiva is to be known as *prākṛta* (of the nature of primordial matter), being subject to destruction and origination" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1264).
Thus [it is said on page 269].

Consequently, even for those two, a designation must be made based on their arising and dissolution, which are themselves comprised of opening and closing. Furthermore, just as the operations of Śiva’s opening and closing—

Sadāśiva and Īśvara have been declared to be distinct principles (*tattvāntara*); likewise, why have their functions of expansion (*unmeṣa*) and contraction (*nimeṣa*) not also been declared as distinct principles? He dispels these two doubts with a single sentence beginning with "Sadāśiva," etc. [He states that] it is precisely the aspect of "thisness" (*idantā*), which is the other form...
In that scripture, the dissolution and emergence should be understood as being spoken of from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). And with that very intention, it is stated there:
"Having multiplied the duration of Māyā by a hundred parārdhas..."
He rules over day and night in this manner—
In this sequence, even up to the end of the Śakti-tattva, according to the *Śrī Svacchanda* and other texts,
having multiplied the time of Īśvara by one hundred *parārdhas*,
a day and night of Sadāśiva is established; [the end of] that is the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

By such statements, the connection with time has been designated. Now, one might object: "The dissolution and emergence of those two, which consist of the power of the Lord (īśvara-śakti), are logical;

likewise, that which constitutes their state of possessing the activity of dissolution and emergence belongs in ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ) to Śiva alone. Therefore, no separate further activity has been stated for those two. To this extent [is the objection].

Because it has the nature of the perfect Śiva. He says this very thing with the words "for it is one alone. "In which" means among those objects; "and at that time" means at the moment of manifestation. The word "api" implies not only the objects of perception (*grāhya*). "Of the nature of emptiness" means in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) during dissolution, when there is nothing to be known.

For those whose form is the *puryaṣṭaka*, the state of being known consists solely in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*); and since objects of cognition (*grāhya*) depend upon the subject (*grāhaka*) when there is something to be known, this [state of being known] also occurs during dissolution (*pralaya*). Therefore, it is not mentioned as distinct [from Śiva].
And thus, Sadāśiva and Īśvara do not differ from the Śiva-tattva. Consequently, how could there be [a distinction] between those two?

In order to carry forward the present topic—that creation and dissolution are designated as distinct functions—it is not something that can be accomplished through mere effort; with this intention, he defines another object of knowledge (prameya) with the passage beginning "tadetādṛśa" and ending with "pratyupasthāpayanti. [The number] is thirty.

The twentyfold group consisting of the gross elements, the subtle elements, the organs of cognition, and the organs of action; as well as the mind, ego, intellect, primordial nature, the individual soul, attachment, necessity, knowledge, limited agency, and time.

"Enter" refers to the hundreds [of powers]. "Will" (*icchā*) is the compendium of the *śakti-tattva*; by the suffix *-maya*, it indicates that each subsequent principle is vitalized by its respective preceding one. Knowledge and action (*jñāna* and *kriyā*) are Sadāśiva and Īśvara; their activity, which is the *vidyā-tattva*, is likewise included within that very same [category].

The *māyātattva* is not accepted as a separate entity in the body merely by virtue of being its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), but rather as the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord. For instance, an object such as clay is itself nothing other than the power of the Supreme Lord, yet by the force of His will, it also serves as the cause for a jar.

Manifesting within the causal determination (*niyatī*), it is called the distinct cause. For this very reason, according to the intention expressed in the *Spandaśāstra*, Śiva is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all things; for without Him, everything would be devoid of essence.

"It is said [in the *Svacchandatantra*] that 'one's own nature by way of being the presiding subject' (*svabhāvam adhiṣṭhātṛbhāvena*, Sva. Kā. 11); and in the commentary (*vṛtti*) as well, it is stated that it is precisely one's own nature, which consists of Śiva" (*svasvabhāvasyaiva śivātmakasya*, Sva. Kā. Vṛ. 1).

And so forth. For in the *Śrītriśiromata*, it is stated that "the totality of the principles (tattvas), their collective nature, and Śiva [himself]—all this consists of the essence of Śiva’s power. In the same way, Māyā is also [included]. These five are the principles (tattvas).

"Even from those" means even from those principles (*tattva*) which serve as causes. The connection is that there is "no division" of the thirty-sixth principle, Śiva-tattva. Regarding the phrase "due to non-differentiation": the intention is that while in a reflection a division appears even though it is non-existent, in the Power (*śakti*), even that [appearance of division] does not exist. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*),...
[Niyati and Rāga] belong to them—that is, to the powers of time and so forth. "In the state of Śiva-hood" means as follows:
just as the capacity to fetch water, which does not appear as separate from the jar, appears as if it were separate in relation to the mirror, yet that [capacity] does not belong to the mirror.

The appearance as "power" (śakti) is, in ultimate reality, indeed called a reflection; this should be understood to apply to the present case as well. And this is what is meant: time and the other factors are employed in the capacity of the subject (grāhaka).
For [one thinks], "Now I am doing nothing," or "I am attached, even though I know."

The individual soul (*aṇu*), permeated by time, portions of time, ignorance, and passion, and animated by necessity (*niyati*), is called the "grasper" (*grāhaka*)— so say others, namely the commentators on the Śaiva tradition.
For thus it has been explained by the venerable Guru in the *Śivabrahmatanugrantha*:
"This group of thirty-five principles is said to be the power (*śakti*) of Lord Śiva alone;
therein, four are supreme (*parā*), while the final twenty-five are indeed gross (*sthūlā*)."
"The intermediate ones, however, are subtle forms of power (*śakti*), but here they are indeed accompanied by *añjana* (impurity)," and so forth.

Although the powers of time (*kāla*) and the rest also touch upon the object of cognition (*grāhya*), since the state of being a subject (*grāhakatā*) is dependent upon the object, they do so only in a general sense and not in a specific one.

The powers of the cognitive and active organs, however, touch the object of perception specifically as both the knowable and the effect; this is the intended meaning of the term "beginning with sound" (*śabdādi*). These too are twofold, being both gross and subtle. Even for the subject under the influence of *māyā*, from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), there is only consciousness (*cit*).
"Reality" (*tattva*) refers precisely to these powers of Śiva. For it is according to the principle stated in the *Svacchandatantra* (6.1): "Since this entire group of instruments...
and so forth; in reality, he alone knows and acts as everything. This is what [the author] says:

"Even the subjects" means [they exist] in the state of being without appearance (*nirābhāsa*), that is, in the singular form of the knower. "Having the nature of exertion" means that the essence of the powers of hearing and speech consists in [the notions]:

"I know the sound" and "I produce it. For this very reason, he says "of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)," because these [powers] are specific forms of the reflective awareness "I," and reflective awareness is...
"It is said that power belongs to the Blessed One alone: 'The reflective awareness (vimarśa) itself is the Lord's [power]'—thus it has been stated.
This is what was said.
The outflows of the vibration of the qualities and so forth obtain their own self-nature by depending upon the universal vibration.

(Spanda Kārikā 19) Thus, having established that even for those subjects whose form is a reflection, their conscious portion (*cidbhāga*) is indeed Śiva, it is further shown that their unconscious portion (*acidbhāga*), consisting of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), is likewise his very power (*tacchakti*) in the form of Sadāśiva.
He establishes that "the apprehenders, too," and this has already been examined by us previously.

The connection is as follows: "The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), though assuming all forms, does not touch excess. Consciousness manifests its wondrous nature through its capacity to accomplish the most difficult tasks and so forth. He summarizes this by connecting it with the words "yo hi" (for he) and "idantābhāk" (possessing the character of 'this-ness'). The connection is: "the manifestation of an object possessing established 'this-ness'."

He applies this object of knowledge to the present context with the word "thus" (*evam*). The connection is as follows: "Īśvara and so forth are designated as distinct from Śiva. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), Sadāśiva and the others are included. Now, one might object: "We have not heard that all these principles are dissolved into Śiva. To show that this will indeed be heard, he says:

Regarding the phrase "to be described": the intention is that in the plane of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇabhūmi*), there is stability precisely in the state of Sadāśiva, whereas in the plane of reality (*vastubhūmi*), there is dissolution; thus, both "emanation and stability" (*sargasthitī*) and "emanation and dissolution" (*sargapralayau*) have been shown.

Now, one might object: "The state of Sadāśiva exists even in the preceding peak (*pūrvakūṭa*); how then can this [state] be characterized solely by dissolution? To this, [the author replies]: "In this regard..."

He says: "It is called *prapañca* (the manifold). For it is precisely the state of being unmanifest that is expressed by the pure term *pralaya* (dissolution). He states the reason for this designation with the words "of dissolution" (*pralayasya*).
The word *pralaya*, being devoid of the manifestation of distinctness, clarity, and the like, [denotes that state].

In common worldly usage, it is established that the perception of a previous state as clearly manifest—which occurs without [the object] becoming unmanifest—is designated by the word "destruction" (*vināśa*). Having thus explained the half-verse, he clarifies the intermediate point with the words "And of that" (*tasya ca*): [it refers to] that which belongs to the dual form of both Sadāśiva and Īśvara.

The reality called *tattva* is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of non-difference from one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). With the intention of defining the meaning of the word "Being" (*sat*) precisely in this context, he states the reason with the words beginning "the radiance of one's own self" (*svātmollāsa*). The word "of that" (*tasya*) refers to the group [of letters]. Now, one might object: is there not only difference as it is perceived?

Anticipating the objection that [the world] might have its birth dependent on a succession of its own causes, he recalls what was stated previously as the reason for this, with the words "from manifestation" (*prakāśāt*). The word "here" (*atra*) refers to the *vṛtti*. By this, he states that the nature of jars and other objects—which consists in their being rooted within the ground of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is not such here [in the case of the world]. Now, one might object:
In the state of the Lord (Īśvara), that very subject is the knower of the void, the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), and so forth;

therein, the state of being an object of knowledge is of a single essence. Consequently, what other knower could there be there, for whom it would not be appropriate to find rest within the same substratum—the self consisting of pure consciousness—along with that which is the object of knowledge?
Anticipating an objection, he says: "And the knower" (*vedakaś ca*). It will be stated [later]:
"But those objects have distinct appearances" (4.1.8).

In these and other such enumerations: [the opponent] objects, "Just as the blue quality and the lotus species find their rest in a third locus, namely the substance itself, so too must the rest of 'I-ness' (ahantā) and 'this-ness' (idantā) be stated; for a third [category] does not exist, since it has been established with effort in the introduction that there is only the duality of consciousness and the unconscious. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that..."

Thus: "The knower" means that very nature of consciousness which, by completely casting off contraction, is as if transferred to another locus; this is what is meant by the third substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). According to the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says "by the word *mati*. By this, *mati* is the operation of the mind (*manas*); that [is what is meant].

It cuts through the doubt as to how there could be cognition independent of the collection of sense-faculties in the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign (Īśvara), by the words "tataḥ" and "ī": from that Īśvara, whose nature is consciousness (*citsvarūpa*). The phrase "just as" (*yathaiva*) means by way of a distinction brought about through conceptual construction for the sake of instruction, meditative cultivation, and so forth.

[Objection: In that case, since *vidyā* would then be included within the *śakti-tattva* itself, how can it be a separate *tattva*? To this, he says: "by which indeed... [as stated] in the commentary (*vṛtti*) with the word "pure" (*śuddha*). And this [power], following the question of the sage Mataṅga, is that which, by the Lord who is the object of knowledge (*prameśvara*), effects the total appropriation of "this-ness" (*idam*) within consciousness as "I-am-ness" (*aham*).
Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) has been defined. For it is said therein in the text of the inquiry: "The bound souls (paśus) residing within Māyā have been described as being subject to bonds;
Pure Knowledge, which transcends Māyā, is that which reveals the path of purification."
How is that [multiplicity] logically consistent? Cut through the darkness born of doubt regarding the atoms! (1.10.22) As for the subsequent text:
this path, which extends from Śiva down to the earth, is exceedingly vast.
"He should be known as the totality within consciousness; because he is not Śiva, he is not liberated. (1.10.23).
Here, "this" refers to the state of "this-ness" (idantā), while "within consciousness" refers to the state of "I-ness" (ahantā). || 3 ||

In response to the doubt as to how this vidyā is pure, the Sūtra states: "Because the essence of all entities—which have attained the state of being and have entered the sphere of the knowable—is consciousness, [this vidyā is pure] due to its perception of things as they truly are. (4)

Avalokana is knowledge (*vidyā*). And because it follows after the object, it is pure (*śuddhā*). For even for those who have accepted the state of being the object of cognition (*vedya*), it is for this very reason [pure] by virtue of its suitability.

The very essence of the objects of cognition, which are perceived through the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*), is consciousness itself, whose nature is light (*prakāśa*); and this light consists of the self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is not directed toward anything other than itself. It is precisely within that [light] that "this-ness," having attained full development, becomes "I am this," such that there arises the pure cognition: "This is I."
This is the meaning of the sūtra. He introduces this with the words "impure," and so forth.

Having in mind that the essential nature of both pure and impure vidyās becomes characterized through the examination of another cloth by way of their mutual distinction, he first [discusses] impure vidyā.

This is shown by the passage beginning with "māyā" and ending with "vakṣyate. In order to demonstrate the utility of impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*), he describes the nature of the bound soul (*paśu*) with the word "prathita"; the meaning is that for this [soul], only his own self appears as supreme, and nothing else. Of those belonging to *māyā*...

This refers to the connection with a difference in time, but not to Māyā, which is of the nature of the power of the Supreme Lord. Therefore, although the impurity (mala) has Māyā as its root, it is indeed beginningless; thus, the bound soul (paśu) is eternal. As stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*: "The bound soul is indeed eternal, formless, ignorant, inactive, devoid of qualities, and powerless."

Thus, because of that very contraction from all sides, [the self] is atomic (*aṇu*). The connection is as follows: that which is atomic, by virtue of which the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*) become distinct, belongs to *māyā* (*māyīya*). "I shall explain its state of belonging to *māyā*"—by this, the distinction from Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is shown. Now, with the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely), [the author explains] "by non-difference from that," meaning by non-difference from Knowledge (*vidyā*). "The supreme" (*param*).
That which is other than that is non-illusory. || 4 ||
In order to demonstrate by way of a specific formulation that these two principles (tattva) are indeed distinct from the presiding deities and bear those very names, the aphorism states:
"In this context, the 'inferiority' of entities arises because they appear as non-self."
Indeed, that state of "other" and "self" arises from the concealment of otherness by means of the ego-sense.

Otherness (*aparatva*) is incompleteness, characterized by the desire for another and the sense of "this"; supremacy (*paratva*) is fullness, characterized by "I. For this very reason, both of these aspects exist within each of the two principles (*tattva*). Thus, the state established in the objective being (*vedyabhāva*) is the nature of the principle itself, which serves as the means for the pure subject who illumines it and for the object to be known.

However, the state of consciousness established upon that which is to be known is Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), which consists in its presiding over the class of [deities] such as the Mantra-Maheśvaras, who are the nature of that subject.
The intended meaning of the aphorism is that [the Self] has the form of the venerable Lord Sadāśiveśvara Bhaṭṭāraka.

He states this concisely with the words "In the Āgamas," and so forth. By the term "pertaining to the principles" (*tattvagata*), a distinction from the form of the deity is indicated. Because [this state] is made manifest in the state of Īśvara, it is characterized by the sense of "this-ness."

With the intention that both "remoteness" (*paratva*) and "proximity" (*aparatva*) are maintained, he says "the state of Īśvara. The underlying meaning is that by means of this [state], even the stage of Sadāśiva would not be accepted as distinct. He shows that here, unlike in the Sāṃkhya system, there is no designation of stages according to a sequence of transformation (*pariṇāma*).

Regarding the phrase "independence belonging to oneself": in response to the inquiry as to what kind of pure higher and lower states there might be, he says "therein" (*tatra*) in order to first define the state of being higher (*paratva*).
With the words "the opposite of that" (*tadviparītam*), and so forth, he describes the pure state of being lower (*aparatva*). The word "first" (*tāvat*) [indicates the sequence].

The intention is this: even when the second type of error (*viparyāsa*) has not arisen, the state of being "other" (*aparatva*) is manifested to this same extent, as is the case with the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*); however, upon the arising of that [second error], that very state will become fully manifest for all beings from Brahmā down to the smallest insect.
In that context, the phrase "there too" refers to the manifestation of the second [error]. The word "situated" (*sthita*) means that it is superior to that.

Regarding the phrase "of one who is fit for fullness": indeed, by being an object of reference as "this," fullness is rendered without scope—just as in the case of a king who, due to misfortune, has fallen into the state of a servant.
Since he must possess the state of being referred to as "I," fullness ought to exist; yet, because that [fullness] does not exist [in him], it is obstructed.
The state of being most pitiable belongs to him alone, even when he has attained the status of a master, just as in the case of the non-assignment of the three powers [to the soul].

This is indicated by the commentary (*vṛtti*) from the words "by this" up to "the state of otherness. Although Brahmā and others are included by the inclusion of the *puruṣa*-principle, [they remain pitiable] because of the predominance of the portion of power belonging to *māyā*.

The separate mention [of the third state] is because one should not imagine its equality with other worldly beings of limited intellect; this is indicated by the phrase "by this" up to "the state of transcendence" in the commentary (*vṛtti*). Having defined the two pure states, he describes the third through their combination in the commentary, and therefore—

This state, called "the condition of the higher and lower," arises due to the influence of both aspects of the cause; this is according to the proponent of totality (*sākalyavādin*), and not according to one who has arrived at the [view] called "denoting a genus" (*jātyākhyā*), but rather one who expresses a plurality of individuals.
The connection is that "fullness is fulfilled. One might then ask: what, then, would be the state of the Vidyeśvaras?

(Page 276) In order to demonstrate the consequence of [the state's] distinctness (*vyatireka*), he touches upon another state once more with the words "the meaning of the second," and so forth. The word "absolutely" (*atyantam*) implies that there is a state of otherness, but not one equal to that of transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*).

Having thus determined that they are indeed equal to transmigrating beings with respect to the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*), he demonstrates their superiority by way of the subjective aspect (*vedakāṃśa*) through another perspective: "or because of the immobility of the nature of consciousness" (verse 5).

Thus, it has been established that in the cognition "I am this," when the aspect of the form "I" acts as the concealer, the operation characterized by its predominance is called *śuddhavidyā*; however, to show another view, [it is said] that when the aspect of "this"— the portion to be concealed here— acts with predominance, [that is the case].

Others maintain that even for the conscious agent, the cognition of difference regarding existing things is *vidyā*, just as it is for the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), being like the power of *māyā*. (6)

Even when there is no manifestation of the subject (pramātṛ) consisting of Māyā— such as that which perceives emptiness and so forth— it is within pure consciousness alone, acting as both the cognizer and the agent, that there exists a sovereignty characterized by the manifestation of difference among entities that are essentially identical to it;
this sovereignty, though appearing as if it were the power of Māyā, is not subject to subversion within the aspect of the subject.
Śuddhavidyā is that state by which the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta-bhaṭṭāraka, exist.

For they, whose sense of "I" (ahambhāva) is bound solely to pure consciousness, perceive the manifold category of objects as if through a dualistic vision, like Īśvara. Thus, it subsists upon the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord.

The purport of the sūtra is that the power of the Vidyeśvaras is Śuddhavidyā. This he states with the words "of the Vidyeśvaras," and so forth. Furthermore, the term "athaca" (and yet) implies inferiority; this inferiority arises because the sense of "this-ness" (idambhāva) has become firmly rooted. He explains that very [power] as "Vidyā. The connection is with the word "śabdena" (by the word). Therefore...

"Thus" (*eva*) means because of the non-manifestation of the clearly evident state of being a bound soul (*paśubhāva*). "Of actions" (*karmaṇām*) refers to those belonging to the worldly and Vedic domains. However, the attainment of that [state] occurs only through initiation (*dīkṣā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*arcana*), and so forth, performed under its influence; and one who has not performed atonement (*akṛtaprāyaścitta*), even if he has received the authority (*adhikāra*), remains as one who has not truly acquired the authority.
Even upon obtaining the rite of qualification, one attains that state; as the scripture says:
"If he does not exercise authority, he shall become a Vidyeśa at the dissolution of the body.
Thus, the scripture must also necessarily be accepted; so he says, beginning with "Īśvara," etc.

(Page 277) One should understand that "possessing meaning" refers to the Lords (*īśvara*) who abide in the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*); they are omniscient and all-doers, and thus they are the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*). Now, even so, why is it that they do not constitute a separate ontological principle (*tattvāntara*)?
Anticipating the objection that this implies attachment (*saṅga*), he says: "And of the principles (*tattvānām*)," and "in *māyā*.

Brahmā resides in the earthly [principle], Viṣṇu in the primordial material (*prākṛta*), and Rudra in the state of *māyā*; and since this is an expansion of the power of *māyā*, it is stated generally as "in *māyā*. He explains the function (*vṛtti*) [of the mantra] as "the knowledge of the mantra (*mantra-vidyā*)."
Regarding the word "iti": unity [is established] by virtue of having as its essence the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) whose core is the pure, beginningless reflective awareness;

whereas the internal distinction [between them] arises from the respective predominance of liberation and accomplishment, of consciousness and the denotable, and of the possessor of power and power itself, in that order. Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other scriptures.
The Vidyārājñīs, beginning with Ambikā, are described as being entirely distinct from the Vidyeśvaras. || 6 ||

The power (*śakti*) of the Lord is indeed will (*icchā*), whose essence is autonomy (*svātantrya*). That [will], however, is metaphorically designated in many ways according to the distinction of its functions. In that regard, when there is the manifestation of the sense of "this-ness" (*idantā*)—whether it has fully emerged, is clear, or is indistinct—the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara consist of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), even though they grasp only pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

When the sense of "this-ness" (idantā) has not yet fully emerged, Mahāmāyā is the power of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa), consisting essentially of the residual form of the power of action (kriyāśakti). When there is the inversion of the grasped and the grasper among the bound subjects (paśupramātṛ), it is the power of Māyā. Likewise, even when there remains only the latent impression (saṃskāra) of the inversion of both the grasper and the grasped, that which is the object of the knowledge of yogis and the wise— [The text continues: ...is the power of Śuddhavidyā, which consists of the residual form of the power of cognition (jñānaśakti). Thus, the powers of Māyā, Vidyeśvara, and Śuddhavidyā are established as the three powers of action, will, and cognition respectively. Therefore, the Lord is indeed the possessor of all powers. The manifestation of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) consists in that sovereignty of the Blessed One which is the reverse of the power of *māyā*; this must necessarily be a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*). That which will be explained as having a separate purpose is precisely the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*). By means of the aphorism, he demonstrates its nature as being distinct from *māyā*.
The power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) manifests that nature of sovereignty within the state of bondage (paśu-bhāva), while the power called illusion (māyā) again effects its concealment.

Even while the state of being a limited subject (*paśubhāva*)— which consists of the duality of the grasper and the grasped, is characterized by bondage, and remains present— is established, that power of the Lord which illuminates the essential nature of that [subject], which is in reality the supreme subject and characterized by sovereignty, resides within those subjects who are free from parts (*niṣkalapramātṛ*).
The present science; that which will be stated [on page 278]:
"His sovereignty is made manifest by knowledge" (3.2.2).
Thus, the operation of the power of *māyā* does not apply here; for she effects concealment, which is the nature of obscuration,
by means of causality, habitual tendency, and so forth, such that this subject will become blinded by *māyā*, a transmigrating being— (3.2.2).

Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is that this [power] is indeed distinct from the power of manifesting one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). He introduces this with the words "māyā," etc. The word "tathā" means "by way of sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*). In order to explain the distinction from *māyā*, he explains the sūtra’s statement beginning with "that which causes concealment" (*tirodhānakarī*), etc., by means of [the discussion of] the nature of sovereignty.

By the words "bhāva" and so forth: concealment (*tirodhāna*), which is obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), the non-manifestation of one's own nature, and impurity (*mala*)—that is, ignorance (*ajñāna*) consisting of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)—is one [aspect]. Immediately following that, however, there is a second [aspect], which consists of a contrary mode of operation by way of relative negation (*paryudāsa*) supported by that [first aspect]. He says this with the word "anyat" (the other).
Thus, it is "well-known" merely by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*); however, everything is likewise produced by the power of *māyā*. It is for this very purpose that [the text says]:
"Now, [the impurities] called *ātma-mala* and *māyā*..."

Thus ends the section on the mention of names in the Śrī Raurava Sūtra. It has been stated that "creation" and "maintenance" are the opposites of dissolution (*pralaya*), and "waking" and "dreaming" are the opposites of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). One should understand that the distinction between dissolution and deep sleep lies in their being common to all or not, and in qualities such as being other than [the waking state], rapid, or long-lasting. Thus...

Having explained the three activities beginning with creation (*sṛṣṭi*), which are of the nature of concealment (*tirodhāna*), he now describes the fourth activity, called dissolution (*vilaya*), which is also well-known by the term "concealment" and is an effect of *māyā*, using the words "in hell," and so forth. Now, [one might ask]: from acts such as the killing of a Brahmin...

"Going to hell" refers precisely to these three [stages] beginning with emission (sṛṣṭi). To this he says, "beyond the fruit of karma. For indeed, even for one who has accepted the supreme Lord's convention (samaya), if there is internal impurity consisting of hatred toward that [convention], that occurs independently of karma, by means of purity alone.

It occurs solely through the will of the Supreme Lord, which is synonymous with His wrath; therefore, those pleasures and pains that arise by the force of good and evil as perceived by the mouth of Niyati have dharma and adharma as their cause,
whereas those that occur even without following good and evil arise from the will of the Supreme Lord.
Thus [it is said] regarding that which is solitary alone. In that regard, the attainment of suffering caused by it is called dissolution (*vilaya*) and concealment (*tirodhāna*). And that—
Whether it be merely momentary or persisting over a period of time— the former [referring] to Kāma, Andhaka, Tripura, Rāvaṇa, and others,
while the latter consists of the fall into hell for those who hate Śiva, their Guru, the scriptures, and the *samaya*— it is "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), because of that.

Another ritual act has been mentioned; what then is that fifth one? He says: "And grace. That too is gradual, consisting of the granting of boons as in the case of Nandīśvara and others; however, the non-gradual [grace] bestows liberation instantaneously through the attainment of initiation and so forth. When "everything" is said, grace is also included.
It has been stated that [the deity] is the effect of *māyā*; therefore, one might raise the doubt: "What is the need for another operation here?

To dispel this, he says: "even the granting of boons (*varadāna*) and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he refers to that which is performed through the desire for supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the longing for wealth and the like, or the wish to alleviate suffering, as well as the exposition of the conventions (*samaya*) of the Supreme Lord.

He states that even that [act of] giving is indeed of the nature of grace (*anugraha*). By using the word "unmeṣa" (opening/expansion), he indicates the intensity of the *vidyā* therein; thus, one who is possessed by the power of Rudra through the force of the grace produced by intense *vidyā*, and who desires liberation alone, proceeds with such acts as approaching a teacher (*gurūpasadana*).
He demonstrates that initiation, knowledge, yoga, conduct, and so forth, yield the fruit of liberation (*apavarga*) precisely upon the fall of this body;

this is indicated by the word "it may be" (*syāt*). Although there is no cessation of *māyā* at the time of the granting of boons and the like, and everything was said with that intention, nevertheless—

In this case, a slight possession (*āveśa*) produced by the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) is indeed possible, which, upon its full ripening, results in liberation. For this very reason, it is sung:
"They worship Me in four ways... (7.16).
Having said this,
"all these [beings] are indeed noble," thus [it is stated].
In this way, the grace of the intense power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) has been demonstrated.

"But the man of knowledge is the Self itself" (7.18). This has been elaborated upon right from the beginning; likewise, it has been thoroughly analyzed in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* and other works that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is primarily ninefold. (7)
(Page 280) In order to clarify the true nature of *vidyā*, that which must be stated is its distinction from *māyā*;
it is with this intention that the nature of *māyā* was described as "that which causes concealment. That very [nature]...
This is clarified by another scriptural passage:
"When difference appears as having a single flavor, when the non-self is perceived through the sense of 'I', and when the intellect or the body is seen as empty, the power of Māyā unfolds. (8)

Therefore, in the *Avatāraṇī*, it says "the cause of the two-fold error" (*viparyayadvayahetu*); the meaning is that this is by way of its being clearly manifest as the cause thereof. [The phrase] "in deep sleep or in dissolution" refers to the state of non-existence (*abhāvasamādhi*), wherein that which appears like space, as if it were the form of the non-self, is [perceived] through the process of recollection.

The object of knowledge (*vedya*) is clung to as the self through the sense of "I am," by way of its own autonomy. In the notions "I breathe in" and "I breathe out," it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is like wind; in the cognition "I hunger" and "I thirst," as well as in the kindling of anger and so forth, that same [breath] is augmented by fire (*tejas*). Internally, I know: "I am."

In states such as "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded," the intellect (*buddhi*) is like a reservoir of clear water; whereas in instances such as "I am thin," "I am fat," or "I am fair," it is the body itself, consisting primarily of earth, [that is so perceived].
And herein, even though the ultimate reality is pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*), that which appears as an object of cognition (*vedyatābhāsana*) is this primordial [condition].

The illusory nature is perversion; however, that which, though insentient, appears as "I" through the state of selfhood while its status as an object of cognition remains entirely unobscured—that is the second [form].
This [power] consists in the non-obstruction of the accomplishment of such an extremely difficult operation of delusion.
The phrase "it expands to speak" (kathayituṁ vijṛmbhate) indicates that by the inclusion of the word "speech" (vāk), even though [the state] is understood through discernment (viveka),

there is no distinction in the fact that the status of being a subject consisting of intellect, vital breath, and the void is to be abandoned; thus, it suggests a profound sense of non-egoity (amahantā) even toward one's wife, children, wealth, house, and so forth.
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows:
[the Sūtra] "And there is grammatical coreferentiality" (3.1.3) restates that knowledge which was previously shown, in order to distinguish it from the power of Māyā.
By the words "of the Lord," etc., [the author] indicates the perishability of the body; by the words "old age," etc., he shows its state of decay.
"The form of fire" means that which is invariably concomitant with it.
(Page 281)

Up to this point, they maintain that the state of being the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) arises from the entry of the five groups and the triad into the very vital breath (*prāṇa*). [This is incorrect] because it is something being remembered;
for how can that which is of the nature of consciousness—whose essential character is uninterrupted luminosity—be remembered? As it has been said:
Beginning with "Not non-existence" (*nābhāvaḥ*) [from *Sparśakārikā* 12],
and so forth, it concludes:
"Because of contact with application (*abhiyoga*), there is the certainty that 'it was'."
Having said this, [it continues]:
"In this way, that reality (tattva) does not become something that is merely recollected" (Svacchanda Tantra 13).
Thus, when it is so, then the non-self alone is apprehended as the "I" (ahantā).

This connects with the great statement: "All this is the second type of misconception. The phrase "in that very way" means by way of being the Self (*ātmatayā*). Furthermore, it is precisely this second misconception—known as the cultivation of the notion of Self in what is not-Self—that is established everywhere in the Sāṃkhya and other scriptures as something to be abandoned, and not the former one. And for that very reason...
This second misconception is indeed already subsumed within the first;

as he will conclude, "this is just one," and not by treating these two misconceptions as equals, he establishes its nature as a defilement (*mala*) with the words beginning "and non-perception" (*adarśanaṃ ca*).

[Objection: "Surely, even though the *puryaṣṭaka* and so forth are not perceptible [by external senses], they may be postulated as being manifest, just like a jar or similar objects. But what is the need for the additional factor of the 'I-cognition' (*ahaṃpratīti*) in its case, such that it was said [in the verse], 'in cognition' (*pratītau*)? [Reply: He says, "of that very [I-consciousness]" (*tasyaiva*). The word "merely" (*kevalam*) implies that this much more must necessarily be accepted.

This is the point to be established: for if the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) were absent, that very collection of entities such as blue and so forth—which is not perceived as having the nature of the Self because it is accompanied by pure objectivity (*śuddhājñatva*)—would not manifest at all; yet it does manifest. For this [state] where one thinks "this is blue" is certainly not the condition of a swoon or dense darkness. Therefore, there must necessarily be the sense of "I."
There must be something additional here by which, having accomplished the state of isolation (*kaivalya*), ignorance does not remain there.

To the objection—"Is it not the case that the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) belonging to the Lord is already the concealer; so what is the use of another distinct [entity]?"—he provides the following rebuttal:
(282) "The city-of-eight (*puryaṣṭaka*) and so forth as well. By that sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*), ignorance is entirely concealed;
thus, [the thought] "this is blue" would not sprout again. Therefore, another such sense of "I" exists here.

The remaining intention is that he who is to be distinguished therein cannot be set aside by the purity of knowledge; "the first" means the initial one and the primary one. As stated in the *Nareśvaraviveka*:
The impurity called *māyā* is said to be that which causes objects to become objects of cognition.
The impurity—

Thus, it is with reference to its nature as a *mala* (impurity) that the Lord has established its designation as *māyīya* (the impurity called Māyā) in the Āgamas, based on its underlying cause (*nidāna*); however, for the second *mala*, the designation *āṇava* is used based on its object and purpose. Regarding this first [impurity], he states its pure object: "Wherein the *āṇava* does not exist."

This is shown by the passage beginning with "tat yathā" and so forth. Precisely because of omniscience, there is an absence of the *āṇava* [impurity]. The term "designator" (*vācaka*) has as its essence reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and is not merely a specific word-form that is an object of hearing alone, nor is it *amāyīya* (non-māyic) in the sense of animating the *māyīya* phonemes. As it has been said:

"Being embraced by them... (*Mālinīvijayottara-tantra* 3.28), and so forth. That Self is the locus of the sense of "I" for those [beings]; because they consist of the body of sound (*śabda-śarīra*), they are contracted both from the class of objects of knowledge (*vedya-varga*) and from one another, and because sound is entirely [dependent upon] light (*prakāśa*).

There is no loss of omniscience because there is an absence of the nature of a dense obscuration; and this has been indicated by the inclusion of the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) and by the employment of qualifiers such as "the knower" (*pramātṛ*). The subsequent text is intended to support this very point. And here:

The subject matter of this commentary on the aphorism, "This is a jar" (1.5.20), must be accepted. First, one should consider the group of mantras, which are mutually distinct, as having a common nature through a universal form.

Following along as the very form of the portions of the root-mantra within the faces of the limbs of Brahmā, they appear differentiated according to the logic of the universal and the particular—such as "cowness" and "horseness"—yet they themselves consist solely of the body of expressive sound. Thus it is said: "And both..."

Thus are the mantras and the lords of mantras (*mantreśas*). The lords of mantras (*mantreśvaras*) are also those who preside over specific mantras whose nature consists of the lords of mantras— the body of expressive sound.
In this context, the very nature of the Mantreśvaras is subsumed; as he will state, beginning with: "Even for those who possess agency through their cognitions...
(3.2.9), and so forth.
"And they are the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras).
With reference to that,
[the text speaks of] the connection with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of a body whose nature is a specific expressive word.

The meaning is: "by virtue of having attained contraction. With the intention that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) possesses the nature of a specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) through mutual exclusion, he distinguishes the subjects of *māyā* and the subjects of *vidyā* by means of an investigation into their internal differentiation, starting with the words "the subjects of *māyā*" and so forth, for [the sake of] the mantras.

And so on. Indeed, it is "this-ness" (*idantā*) alone that constitutes the primary element within the body, intellect, vital breath, and so forth. For these [factors] do not enter into consciousness in the same way as sound or form; rather, by constricting consciousness, they obscure it most densely. Thus, the mantra-nature has sound as its body.

Revolving within the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) in the form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it is for this very reason the mantra that is eternally arisen and designated by the term "unstruck sound" (*anāhata-śabda*). He demonstrates its identity [with all things] by the words "of touch, etc. This has been stated briefly; however, the inclusion of the word "speech" (*vāk*) indicates that this is the appropriate description. For this very reason:

Furthermore, regarding the initial phrase: "of that which exists within another entity" means of that which has the nature of a single object of cognition (*meyai-karūpa*), such as the sounds *khaṭakhaṭa* or *chalacchala*. In that case as well, when there is an imitation of a word consisting of a specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) that constitutes an unmanifest object of cognition (*avyakta-prameya-bhūta*), that which refers to it—

It is not sung by the grammarians; rather, that which belongs to space (*ākāśīya*) is indeed the signifier (*vācaka*), whose true essence is its repose within the subject (*pramātṛ*). By this, the exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) of the term "belonging to space" is shown. "Even Śiva-hood" refers to the state of the subject when the manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā*) has not yet emerged. "Even Īśvara-hood" refers to... [the same].

In this opening [of the eyes] onto the plane of valid cognition (*pramāṇabhūmi*), that which is designated as "that"— the agency of the Blessed One whose nature is the freedom of "I"— is metaphorically applied or superimposed upon touch and the other [objects]. Since that object consists solely of the nature of the knowable (*vedya*), therefore both Śiva-hood and Īśvara-hood also proceed toward non-differentiation from identity with it.

The contraction of space and time appears as if it were inherent solely in the touch, sound, form, taste, smell, and so forth, residing within that body and its extensions. [This occurs] through the aspect of luminosity, termed "intellect" (*buddhi*), and as "visionary speech" (*paśyantī*).
By means of the reflective portion (*vimarśāṃśa*). For that very reason, being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) and being denotable (*vācyatā*) were previously mentioned separately.

By the word "of those two" (*tayośca*), which expresses selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), it is shown that this is a clarification of the very same preceding point. "From that" (*tataḥ*) means from the [distinction between] the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
It possesses the limitations of space and time; therefore, the consciousness of the object, being dependent upon those two, appears in that very same way.

It is "primary" because it resides in the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as the instrument (*karaṇa*), and not because the state of being an object (*karman*) or the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) is established therein. At that time, it is primary and complete.

The state of being a subject characterized by the relation of the known and the knower does not exist [in its true sense] for the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*), yet due to the contraction caused by the imposition of the limiting adjuncts of the objects of knowledge (*vedya-upādhi*), it certainly exists there as incomplete. "By way of the Mantra-self" means by way of the nature of pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). "This" refers to that contraction. And "that" refers to the letter *ka* and so forth.

It consists of differentiation. The phrase "resembling a reflection" implies that everything appears precisely by virtue of resembling a reflection. In this context, even things such as the body or a jar are, in reality, essentially like reflections; for in them, the state of being an object of cognition does not appear as something clearly distinct.

But the distinction between the letter *ka* and so forth is not established in this way as being based on a reflective awareness of the denotator (*vācaka*). This is what he means by saying "but not of a different class" (*na tu vijātīyam*), which amounts to saying it is not to be experienced as an object of separate reflective awareness. In that [sentence], "that" (*tat*)—referring to the form of the distinction between phonemes—is the agent; "ignorance" (*ajñatvam*) is the object; and the example is one of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).
Having stated the reason "because it appears as if it were a reflection," he states another reason as well:
"and because of the absence of its own primacy. For all [beings], the primary locus of attachment for the subjects of māyā appears within the body and so forth as the very place of bondage.

This is because their very nature is fearful of its own dissolution. However, the collection of phonemes beginning with *ka* appears to the subjects of limited knowledge (*vidyā-pramātṛs*) as an external adjunct, like the blue and other objects of difference residing in the subject of illusion (*māyā-pramātṛ*), serving as instruments for their own specific functions. For their sense of selfhood is rooted solely in consciousness itself.
He demonstrates that very state of being an adjunct (*upādhānatā*) with the word "merely" (*kevalam*). But [it may be objected]: "Are not bodies produced from karma? (p.
Thus much has been said. But what is the cause for the manifestation of those [powers] consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*)?
