He says: "The will of the Supreme Lord. And that will is said to be independent of karma and other such factors. Thus, by way of its objects, the impure nature of the impurity called *māyā* has been described; now [the author] concludes:

"Rati" means "that very thing. "Param" means "only. He clarifies this very point with the word "nanu. "Agre" refers to the passage [3.2.9]: "even for cognitions that possess agency... In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the singular ending is used in relation to the phrase "the body and so forth," by means of the particle "ca" (and).

This was stated with the intention that a distinction between sentences (*vākya-bheda*) has been introduced here by way of explicitness. Regarding the phrase "therein," it refers to the fact that the *kalana* (differentiation) of the *kalā* named *vimohinī-māyā* is established;
for such is the statement from the *Śrīrudrayāmalasāra*. The phrase "by its power alone" refers to [the power of] *vivarta* and *pariṇāma*.
Since the theories of causality have indeed been refuted at length, it is the Power (śakti) of the Lord alone that constitutes Māyā;

through the sequence of the previously mentioned misconceptions which project further distortions, she brings about the appearance of objective entities within her own self. Thus ends the eighth [verse].

Now, one might raise this objection: "As long as that which is non-self, such as the void (*śūnya*) and so forth, is adhered to as being the self, for that long one remains adhered to [only] as having the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). And since that [consciousness-nature] is unobscured, it is again only the possession of pure sovereignty (*viśuddhaiśvarya-yoga*) that is appropriate for him. To address this doubt:

And that cognizer, whether the void or another, who excludes [the object] by demonstrating the principle of the individual soul (puruṣa-tattva) as conjoined with the five principles, being himself an object of cognition,
is enveloped by the pentad beginning with time. (9)
This fault would indeed arise if, in the state of being the subject (*pramātṛtā*), the void and so forth were to abandon their status as objects (*meyatā*);

but this is not the case. For if that were so, how could there be a subject when the object is distinct? Indeed, in this context, limitation (*pārimitya*) is the life-force (*prāṇa*) in the state of being an object and in the separation from the subject. And that very [limitation]...

The meaning of the aphorism is that [the Self] is enveloped by the fivefold sheath beginning with Time. He introduces this in brief with the words "now" (*idānīm*). It may be so (*syāt*)—[as stated on page 286].

"However, by the principle that 'through the touch of one's own power' (Spanda Kārikā 8), 'that' refers to the sovereign consciousness as 'I am this'; 'here' refers to the body; and it will be stated [later]: 'And this is intensified by *kalā*... (3.2.11)."

In this sūtra, [the phrase] "having that nature" (*tadrūpatā*) means that even while existing within the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), the nature of the Self (*ātmarūpatā*) indeed ceases to manifest, just as [one's true nature is obscured] by the body, house, clothing, and so forth. By the word "other" (*anya*), he expresses a limited degree of authoritative validity (*prāmāṇikatva*). With the intention of avoiding the suspected fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), he qualifies [the term] with "ever-arisen" (*nityodita*) and so on.
"Not so," [it is argued], because it is dependent on that very [body], the ignorant one is a non-agent; thus, the definition of the *aṇu* (the individual soul) has been refuted here.
But surely, for women, children, and others, the *puryaṣṭaka* and so forth would not exist, since it is said that "the self is the body alone.
Consequently, they would be devoid of a future world (*aparaloka*). To this, he says: "Even for those who identify the body as the self. And this...

This has indeed been explained previously in this context: "For this is precisely the sequence for entering into the misconception of a self in what is not-self. When, through the power of practice, one abandons even the specific mental reflection on the negative particle (*nañ*) upon the removal of the eighteen kinds of objects to be negated;

"Abandon that by which you abandon"—when this is said, even the distinction of "no" (negation) sets, and thus the very nature of the mind shines forth in its purity; yet, due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that [distinction], differentiation persists here, and thus the possibility of emergence (*vyutthāna*) and so forth arises. It is contracted.

The phrase ending with "ityantaṃ" (up to this point) is the subject (*kartṛpada*). The phrase beginning with "anubhūtaḥ" (experienced) and so forth is the object (*karmapada*). The word "sā" refers to the nature of the Self (*ātmarūpatā*).

Although the pronoun "yat" refers back to the action (*kriyā*), since the action has its very body dependent upon its factors (*kāraka*), it is entirely appropriate for it to refer back to the instrument (*karaṇa*) which is the topic at hand; this gender [of the pronoun] is not dependent on the latent impression (*vāsanā*).

Furthermore, because it would follow that there would be another masculine designation in view of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Alternatively, the meaning is that [the self] is not to be known as "this" (*idantayā*), but rather it is logical that it is precisely that "I-ness" (*ahantā*) which, for the time being, possesses a form grasped through illusion (*māyīya*).
For it has been explained that the self indeed possesses latent impressions.
Thinking thus, he endeavors to explain [the passage], but he does not perceive those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) as distinct entities, as in the case of "the comparison of Rudra and so forth" (p.

And because of the reflective awareness of "I am that very one," he is indeed full of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); thus, the arising of pride, anger, and so forth is logical. Consciousness (*cit*), which possesses the latent impressions of the contraction it has itself produced, becomes identical with that [state] and is thus a single entity in which the specific forms of sound and other objects have dissolved and been removed.

It is distinct from the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka) and its internal states. He concludes the nature of the second misconception—which is invariably concomitant with the first misconception—by way of its objects, stating:
"Thus, this is so. By the word "ignorant" (ajña), he indicates that this is a different form [of the self] upon the foundation of the first misconception.

He speaks with an uncompounded word (*asamastapada*). Having thus explained up to the point "the mother is the object of measurement" (*meyah*), he begins to explain the passage beginning with "time and so forth" (*kālādika*) by saying "also another thing" (*anyad api*). This doubt as well has been resolved by this very [statement], namely, that the effects such as the reckoning (*kalana*) and the regulation (*niyamana*) are entirely objects of measurement (*prameya*).

Since that which is most inferior is observed, why are these factors such as time (*kāla*) and the rest described solely as attributes of the subject (*pramātṛdharma*)? Dependence (*pāratantrya*) consists in having capacity only when there is a connection with another principle (*tattvāntara*), whereas self-insufficiency is a lack of sovereignty; it is by this manner of analysis that their differentiation is established.

In that regard, time and the other categories have no intrinsic nature apart from their status as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). And a qualifier exists only as it has ascended into cognition. In this context, even qualifiers such as a staff do not exist by dividing the act of manifestation; rather, they exist only as the person and so forth [to whom they belong].

The qualificand [is perceived] by means of conjunction and so forth. Therefore, since these [factors] serve to delimit the object, their prior delimitation of the subject-aspect is required—as in "this one is a man with a staff"—for by this much alone the purpose is fulfilled. Time, moreover, [performs] the very act of manifestation in both its manifest and unmanifest forms.
It was created by the Supreme Lord, who manifests existence and non-existence;

and by the very act of manifestation, because it has fallen into the objective portion characterized by "this-ness" (idantā) while simultaneously being absorbed in the manifestation as "I," it first flashes forth within the subject alone. Through that medium, however—

Regarding the pot and other objects: "I, who am now clearly manifest, having been emaciated, shall become more robust through the use of aśvagandhā-ghṛta; and these co-existent pots and other things are currently clearly manifest."

Thus, by encompassing the limit of constant time whose nature consists in this very process, there is a resting in the object of knowledge (*prameya*) of the past and future which exist solely within the subject (*pramātṛ*).
(Page 288)

The two-fold time of the flowing breath is taught in the scriptures as being joined with the very person as his "mantle" (kañcuka). This same principle applies to Necessity (niyati) and the others. Indeed, the reflective awarenesses—such as "alas, alas," "something," "yesterday," and "it was"—consisting of Necessity, Attachment, Limited Agency, Time, and Ignorance, reside in consciousness alone, not in the object of knowledge.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that this category is neither independent nor is it a property of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) in a general sense. As it is said in the *Śrīkālapādā*:
"For as long as consciousness has arisen, it must become perfectly clear."
Is that present moment, or the eon, or something else, defined by its two limits?
Thus [it is said]. He clarifies this with the words "and likewise" (*tathā ca*) and so forth. The general rule here is that everything is of the nature of a manifestation (*ābhāsa*).

Anticipating the question—"In that case, what is the purpose of the word 'manifestation' (*ābhāsa-pada*) in the verse?"—he says: "For everything... The term "external object" (*bahir-vastu*) refers to externality precisely by virtue of being common to all; and that [externality] does not exist in the state of being a qualifier.
Because "blue" is the qualificand with respect to something else, and "lotus" is the qualifier;
for the Middle Sage [Nāgārjuna] stated that both the qualifier and the qualificand can function as qualifiers.

And so forth. The phrase "with respect to Devadatta" is to be applied to both cases: [the cognition] being unperceived and its connection with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Now, one might object: "Even if that [cognition] is unperceived, it will nonetheless perform another causal function"—to this he says:
"And not... For blue produces pleasure, pain, and so forth as something entirely distinct; it does not [produce them] by itself.

The qualification is stated. He clarifies this by means of an illustration with the words "for it is not," etc.; the meaning is that [the cognition] serves to delimit the intended person from among those suitable for the cognition of "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*). The phrase "tathā hi" means "this being so. The repetition "pramātṛbhūmau pramātṛbhūmau" is an *vīpsā* (iterative emphasis).

By means of the *avyayībhāva* compound, the absence of external nature in the form of commonality is expressed. "Consisting of oneness" (*ekatāmaya*) refers to its nature as a relationship. "It expands" (*prathate*) means that it is indeed a reality, being incapable of being denied. "Occasional" (*tātkālika*) means it is created in that very manner at that time; for at other times, this [reality] appears otherwise to that same cognizer.
It indeed throbs. Thus he applies the account of the qualification to the subject at hand with the words "and therefore" (tataśca).
For this reason—that such is the account of even a mere qualification—therefore, [the same applies] to time and so forth.

The meaning is: how could it be suspected that those [powers] which function through the medium of the act of manifestation exist outside of the cognizer's perception? By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the powers of] *niyati* and so forth are included. For this very reason, it is said in the *Āgamas*:
"O Dear One, his self is colored by *rāga* (attachment) and is fashioned by *kāla* (time)."
Restrained by necessity (niyati) and further augmented by the state of being a person (puṃbhāva).

It has been stated: "Consciousness is intensified by *kalā*, and its objects are revealed by *vidyā*. The categories such as *niyati* (restriction) are to be reflected upon through grammatical particles (*nipāta*), while *rāga* (attachment) and the rest, being reflected upon in such expressions as "he was born," exist within consciousness and thereby touch the objects of cognition.

"Of those that are non-separately established" means of those whose nature is the power of the cognizer (*pramātṛśakti*). Regarding the cognition of that qualifying activity—which consists of delimitation (*avaccheda*)—of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the establishment of those things which are useless for it and external to it is simply not possible. [This applies to] external qualifiers such as a staff (*daṇḍa*), etc.

The sense is that, in reality, it is appropriate for these [attributes] to belong exclusively to the subject (*pramātṛ*). By the phrase "of time," it is meant that even that which is universal to all [objects] is thereby qualified. By the word "only" (*mātra*), the commonality with all subjects is excluded. For this very reason, he says: "even the manifestation."
The act of delimitation is already far removed, and other causal efficiency is even further away.
Even manifestation, like a staff, does not exist externally as something separate from time that is common to all.
For one might perceive a succession of jasmine, mango, mallikā, kuṭaja, lotus, and mālatī flowers, but not—

Time, which is sequential in nature, is external to that cognition, like a staff [held by it]. This very point has been demonstrated in the *Śrīpūrvāgama* through the distinction between the primary definition of essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) and the subsequent mention of distinctions relative to the subject (*pramātṛ*).

"The earth-principle [is established] through the differentiation between the possessor of power and the power itself, together with its own essential nature" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.2), and so forth.
Now, let it be that time is thus attached to the subject (*pramātṛ*); but what of the Supreme Lord?
Anticipating the question, "How is there a connection with that power? he says, "variegated" (*vicitra*).
For [the mirror] possesses variegated appearances—appearances augmented by both non-appearances and appearances—consisting of jasmine flowers and so forth.
(Page 290)

The Supreme Lord acts; from that, the power of the Supreme Lord brings forth time as an attribute of the subject; thus, time becomes an attribute of the subject. For it is said that the subject, being himself limited (kalita), is the limiter (kalayitṛ) when limited by time. However, for the Supreme Lord, there is the power of time.
"Having the form of being animated by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Regarding the word "previously," this refers to the section [beginning with] *kramaḥ bhedāśrayaḥ* (2.1.4).
To show that this very same account applies elsewhere to the group of coverings (*kañcuka*), [the author says:]...

The activity of one who explains destiny (*niyati*) is as follows; he elucidates it with the words "and the relation of cause and effect. By the term "characteristic of the effect" (*kāryalakṣaṇa*), that state is expressed. And since that [state] culminates in agency (*kartṛtva*), there is a restriction of that agency—which is bestowed by the power of time (*kāla-śakti*) as will be described—by virtue of which...

From the attribute characterized by being a controller preceded by the state of being controlled, that *niyati* (necessity) is an attribute of the subject (*pramātṛ*). Its power, however, which is of the nature of a residual form of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), belongs to the Lord alone and is appropriate to consciousness (*cit*). Agency (*kartṛtā*) is the agency of consciousness. "Therein" means within the sphere of *niyati*. By the term "cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇa*), [the following is meant].

It is an appearance thereof. Consequently, the meaning is as follows: since it is established that, in reality, the Lord alone manifests in such a way, the seed does not possess the status of a material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the sprout, nor does the clay [possess it] with respect to the jar;
thus, both are equally incapable. Nevertheless, this is so by virtue of being common to all subjects (*pramātṛ*).

Thus, the seed is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the sprout, not the jar; yet the jar [is the cause] of that [sprout], not the seed. Such a property, characterized by being subject to restriction within the sphere of manifestation, exists in reality only in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), not in the object of cognition (*prameya*). However, in that regard—

"By means of the manifestation of the measures (mātrā)..."—thus has *niyati* (the principle of necessity) been declared by the Omniscient One as a property of the subject (*pramātṛ*). As it has been said:
"Furthermore, [the object] is constrained by *niyati*..."

Thus [it is said]. He demonstrates their commonality with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). Since the determination of action and its fruit is already established by this very [explanation], the separate mention of it is because of its predominance within the account of the process of saṃsāra. He states this with the words "And he who... If, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "action" (*karman*) refers to...
(Action: in that case, the result is the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by it which resides in the self;
or, if "action" refers to the act itself, then the result is heaven and so forth. In both ways, the application [of the term] has been explained. [Regarding] passion...)

He explains [the word] "of the agent" (*kartuḥ*). The group of mental fluctuations such as envy (*matsara*) and so forth, which is shown in the Abhidharma and in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, has its root solely in passion (*rāga*). For this very reason, [it is said]:
"In one who is free from passion... (*Nyāyasūtra* 3.1.25).

Thus, the disappearance of hatred, arrogance, envy, and so forth is indeed perceived in this [state]. Now, one might object: "In the Śaiva system, non-detachment (*avairāgya*) will also be stated as a property of the intellect (*buddhi*); so what is the need for a separate passion (*rāga*)? For the followers of Kaṇāda, however, there is no other [entity] than that; therefore, it is logical that desire and hatred are qualities of the self (*ātman*). Thus [it is argued].
And it dispels doubt, as well as being a quality of the intellect. "As a distinct category" means:

by this term "passion" (rāga), what is meant is its state as a sheath (kañcuka). For instance, hunger, thirst, and that exaltation characterized by the desire for sexual union with women—this is non-detachment (avairāgya). And therein it exists.

Attachment arises toward the elderly, the sick, and so forth, through the realization that "this shall be mine"; therefore, the principle of *rāga* (attachment) is predominant. Its outward expansion to its furthest limits is that for whose fulfillment [the following occurs].
Medicine will be for the elderly, the sick, and others; that is non-detachment (*avairāgya*).

Even dharma and the rest are merely sprouts of the latent impression of attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga-vāsanā*); thus, this entire category is one of passion (*rāga*). These, however, are enumerated as qualities of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*) because they consist of specific manifestations. Therefore, this [is so].

Everything indeed exists solely rooted in *māyā*. Accordingly, it is established in the *Śrī-svacchanda* and other scriptures that at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), everything contained within that [realm] is to be purified, because there is no further sprouting for that which has been burnt at its root. This applies to *rāga*, *niyati*, and the rest as well.
It is mostly in a state of budding and sprouting, yet in the intellect (*buddhi*), it is fully blossomed and even bears fruit.

All of this is stated by the passage beginning with "the quality of the intellect" (*buddhiguṇa*) and ending with "the specific object" (*viṣayaviśeṣa*). Having explained passion (*rāga*), [the text now addresses] consciousness (*caitanya*) which has blossomed in the form of agency and subjectivity.

The operation of the two [Kalā and Vidya] is for the purpose of manifesting that which has as its object the knowable (jñeya) whose effects are differentiated; thus, he defines Kalā and Vidya as being equal by the words "and from Śūnya," etc. The word "and" (ca) conjoins another attribute to the subject. Consciousness (caitanya) is unobstructed.

(Page 292) Anticipating the objection that since [consciousness] is eternally unobstructed, what need is there for manifestation, [the author replies]: "This is true indeed regarding ultimate consciousness (*paramārthacaitanya*); however, this discussion concerning consciousness as conceived in relation to distinct objects continues," with this intention.

And he says, "and consciousness. Here, "here" refers to the principle of the Person (puṃstattva). He states the reason for not intending that [consciousness] there with the words "because it consists of consciousness," and so forth. "The state of being an object" means being manifested through dependence on another. "Consciousness," and so forth, means that it is distinct from the subject; that is to say, it is distinct from any other entity.

It is distinct from other objects of cognition (*grāhya*); for that very reason, although it is undivided, it is brought into a state of division from the subject and the object. Even while existing in such a way, it does not abandon its own nature as pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) by virtue of being manifest as "itself"—that is, in its own form—even as blue and so forth.

It is called "insentient" (jaḍa). Why? Because it lacks the capacity for that variety of cognition which arises from the distinctness and differentiation of other objects. And the reason for this has been stated by the words "this-ness" (idantā) and so forth.
However, the manifestation of non-difference (abheda-prakāśana) is indeed never extinguished, even in the case of a corpse, a body, a jar, and so on.

Thus, this worldly distinction between the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*) is not produced by that [relation]; this is the sense. He says "but not" (*na tu*). Now, for this reason—that is, because of this manner—the relation is called insentient: because it does not perform that perception of another who is distinct, which must be performed in order to initiate worldly activity. It is not [sentient].

He states that this applies not only to emptiness (*śūnya*) and so forth, but likewise to jars (*ghaṭa*) and the like, with the words beginning "for this very reason" and ending with "by virtue of dependence on another. He then connects the subject at hand for which all this has been deliberated, namely, "by means of *vidyā* and *kalā*. The word "all" (*sarva*) [refers to] suitability (*yogyatā*).

He speaks by means of the diversity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); the word "object" (*artha*) indicates differentiation. Now, if those two—the powers of knowledge and agency—are manifested, let them be manifested in their real form as non-different in nature. To this he replies: "because they belong to *māyā*. Now, might they not exist with differentiation regarding all objects? It is said: "by *niyati* (the principle of necessity)."
For these sheaths (*kañcukas*) function through a process of union characterized by mutual assistance, like the filling of a sweetmeat with syrup;

for this very reason, it is stated in the *Āgamas* that [the soul] is "enveloped" (*veṣṭita*). Consequently, there is no contradiction in describing them according to various sequences of priority and posteriority. Thus, it is said in the *Mālinīsāra*:
Having begun with the statement: "The knot which resides in the heart is the regulator of that which is below and above," it is said:
Like the fibers within the core of a plantain tree, like the juices of sweetmeats and the like,
or like the whorls of a Kadamba flower, the production of the sheaths occurs from the variegated [consciousness] in a gradual sequence.

Thus [it is said]. With this very intention, he says: "And not here... This much indeed is both manifest and supported by scripture. Now, regarding the group of principles (*tattva*) consisting primarily of "I am he who knows this, acts, is impassioned, and possesses discipline"—the wise, for the sake of following after direct experience (*saṃvedana*), do not apply their attention [to it as an object].
He holds this in the highest regard. If there were indeed respect for this matter, he would have extended it further. What is that? He says:

"This very sequence, or otherwise," because the manifestation (*ullāsa*) possesses a variegated sequence. [The phrase] "of other principles" implies that no additional ones are included, or that they serve no purpose. This is the reason for his lack of emphasis.

"Because it is purposeless. To the question, "Where, then, is there any regard? he says, "But this much... He states the reason for the necessity of regard with the words, "And this much... He demonstrates the lack of purpose for those situated in the middle with the words, "But other... The connection is remote, as [the phrase] "is useless" relates [to that]. How is it useless?
He says, beginning with "now" (*idānīm*) and ending with "thus" (*evam*). By the term "cognized" (*saṃvidita*), its actual existence (*sadbhāva*) is indicated.

Consequently, this is the meaning: "at present this much exists, but at other times there may be more. For this very reason, he states another alternative view with the words "due to the absence of attention" (*avadhānābhāvāt*), etc. Now...
It might be suspected that even though the sixth object and so forth are present, they would be unperceived;
yet, upon perceiving that [sixth], there occurs the cessation of the possibility of a seventh object and so on. Thus he says, "inconceivable," and so forth.
By this, the enumeration of the middle objects of knowledge is established through the divisions of six, sixteen, and so on.
He shows that [the number of such things] is like the counting of grains of sand— impossible and useless—

because even substances such as mercury (pārata) exist which possess forms distinct from those of earth and other elements. He corroborates this very point with the words "it has been said," meaning that our subject matter under discussion appears as follows:
It arises and it is employed; yet, in the absence of the perception of the middle object of cognition, its [existence] as abiding in the highest state—

He says "there is no such refutation for us," and so on with "but this [is as follows]," etc. "Having that nature" means that one's own self is the knower, the agent, and the independent one. With the intention that "without this, nothing at all shines forth—let alone anything else being postulated," he says "nor is this [the case]," and so on, where...
This is useful; in that regard, all of this has been thoroughly established in the ritual procedures for initiation and so forth. || 9 ||

It was stated [in verse 3.1.8]: "When the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is that which possesses exclusion (*vyatirekin*). He states that object of knowledge by means of a pair of verses: "The object of knowledge is twenty-three-fold, consisting of effects and instruments."
Its undivided form is the one Pradhāna, the fundamental cause. || 10 ||
In this context, there is a series of thirteen external and internal instruments, and a group of ten effects, distinguished by their gross and subtle natures. (11)

This has been clearly stated in brief; however, as for the detailed elaboration, it exists only within the commentary (*vivṛti*), and thus has not been examined separately here. He begins with the objection starting from "nanu" and ending with "bhavet" in order to purify both the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and the statement. For this very reason, [it is said] "ata eva," meaning "because."

It is appropriate that they be subsumed under the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); this is the meaning of "from that. He states this very point by way of contrast with the words "and in the case of the unreal" (*avāstave ca*). "But that" (*tattu*) refers to the fact that these [objects] are not objects of cognition. This [point] should also be applied to the domain of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). Furthermore, it is inappropriate for these [organs of action] to possess the status of being instruments (*karaṇatva*).

He shows this with the words "in the same way. For time, its divisions (*kalā*), and so forth, while fulfilling the state of the subject (*pramātṛtā*), possess distinct natures for each individual subject; however, in certain instances—such as when watching a performance by actors or wrestlers—they may, through the will of the Lord (*īśvara*), become unified to that extent, or else they remain fixed on different objects due to being attached to one thing while [another] is elsewhere.

By means of the passage beginning with "that which is produced," [the author] raises an objection regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*), suggesting that since [the power] resides within the instrument (*karaṇa*) itself, what need is there for another instrument? He then states the objection concerning the verbal expression with the words "In that way" (*tathā*) and so forth. Here, it is appropriate to understand the reference as being to the *pradhāna* (the primary cause) alone; the sense is that it has not yet arisen, because it is impossible for it to be free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇa*).
The intention is that what was stated [previously] is likewise merely a verbal objection (*vacanacodya*). The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the objection. Furthermore... [iti].

This refers to the distinction between differentiation and non-differentiation. By the phrase "the worlds and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes various types of bodies and the like. "By being such" means by being an instrument;
that is, by being knowable through the application of instrumentality. "The transformation of the intellect and so forth" [is the meaning].

The sense organs (*buddhīndriyāṇi*) are those employed for the transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) into the forms of smell and so forth; however, the action organs (*karmendriyāṇi*) are for the transformation of external objects, such as a lump of clay, into jars and the like. This is what is expressed by the word "also" (*api*). [The author] says "for not... and so on. This has been merely recalled, as it was already stated in the *Ādisiddha-sūtra*: "In this world, the causes..."

Since the causality of seeds and the like toward sprouts and so forth is indeed inferred even when they are unperceived, the meaning is that there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) based on their actual preeminence, even though that [preeminence] is not touched upon by words. By "to that extent," it is meant that the actual state is not contradicted by the function of verbal expression. And this—
This was stated by way of bold assertion (*prauḍhavāditva*). However, the Sūtra can indeed be interpreted in this manner:

that all things consisting of the twenty-three categories of effects and instruments, as well as their fundamental cause, are objects of valid cognition (*prameya*); thus, this is what is excluded by the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*).
By demonstrating that the object of cognition (*prameyatā*) resides in the cognizer, he refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "for in conceptual cognition," and so forth.

Now, one might argue: "In this very way, let even *pradhāna* (primordial matter) lack direct perceptibility, since it is cognizable solely through conceptualization; and for this reason, the following [objection] was raised by the followers of Kapila:"
To one who might think that [the object] is reckoned precisely because it is beyond perception (*asaṃvedya*), he says "the Pradhāna.
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) illuminates the distinction of this subject (*pramātṛ*) and clarifies its direct perceptibility;
furthermore, it indicates that even in relation to those such as ourselves, there is the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*), as established by inference.

By these and other such statements, the following is meant: the self, appearing as "this" within conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), comes to rest within the primary reflective awareness (*mūlaparāmarśa*) of the "I," which is the ultimate reality of the single subject (*pramātṛ*).
And this has been stated:

In the passage [beginning with] "not due to a difference in the reflective awareness of 'I' and so forth" (1.5.17), although the *pradhāna* appears within the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is in fact of a single nature consisting solely of the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*). Because it shines as having a single flavor through the "this-ness" (*idantā*), it is that very same thing due to the unity of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). This too...
It has been stated [in verse 2.3.10] that [the distinction between near and far] is due to distance and proximity.
In this regard: [the opponent asks], "But why has its status as an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) not been stated by his own throat [i.e., directly]?
To this he replies with the word "merely" (*kevalam*). Now, he dispenses with everything in a single stroke with the words "and all of this.
The meaning of "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) is: because the utility for worldly life (*lokayātrā*) alone is the primary concern; otherwise, indeed...

The intention is that the section on the instruments (*karaṇavarga*) should be presented first in accordance with the Sūtra. By using the plural number (*bahuvacanena*), he shows that the very objection raised by the opponent—namely, that the members of the group (*vargin*) should be primary—is in fact the solution itself; for there is no group distinct from its members.

"Someone" means anyone whatsoever. Alternatively, by the plural number, the entire collection of entities well-known in the world is grasped; this is what is meant by the word "group" (*varga*) in the Sūtra. With the intention that the realization of the subtle occurs through the gross, whereas their origination is the reverse, the sequence in the Sūtra and its commentary is inverted.

The exposition: By the method of expression "the Great Principle" (*mahattattva*), from *prakṛti* comes the Great One (*mahat*); from that, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); from that which is devoid of existence (*niḥsattā*) comes existence (*sattā*); from that which is neither existent nor non-existent (*niḥsadasataḥ*) emerges pure existence (*sattāmātra*), whereby the Great One is manifested; from that, the Great Self (*mahātman*) [arises]—is consciousness (*saṃvit*) white?

By reminding us of such statements from the followers of Kapila, he establishes that the intellect (*buddhi*) is not merely a category of instruments (*karaṇaskandha*), like the mind, the eye, or speech, but rather possesses the status of a causal category (*kāraṇaskandha*) as well;
for the scope of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) extends even to things such as sound and ether, where "being a cause" (*kāraṇatva*) does not exist.

"Of them" means of those who possess the state of being composed of the eleven [senses], that is to say, of those devoid of the nature of gross elements such as space which have undergone transformation (*pariṇata*). "In that way" means by way of being an effect (*kāryatayā*).
Furthermore, by another manner of expression, that very statement of the Sāṅkhya is supported: "and [their] being an effect..."

For one who has come to rest from the activity of enjoyment performs an inquiry into the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and their instrument; thus, by way of being an effect (*kāryatvena*), he establishes the sequence pertaining to the functional states (*vṛtti*) through the determination of its origination, stating "and the effect" (*kāryaṃ ca*). By saying "manifesting" (*āvirbhavat*), he asserts the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) in the sense of being made manifest. [He says] "subtle" (*sūkṣma*); it is not...

It is the form of the atom; however, being devoid of further division and consisting of an extremely subtle essence, it is a pervasive form in relation to the category of effects. Coarseness, moreover, should be understood as the opposite of this.
(page 297)

He explains the word *mātra* [in the compound *tanmātra*] as "devoid of particularity" (*viśeṣarahitā*). This is the supreme universal (*paraṃ sāmānyam*) in the form of a cause, just as the nature of clay is to a jar and so forth;
whereas the subordinate universal (*aparaṃ sāmānyam*), characterized by similarity, is like "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) among jars. [The phrase] "further on" refers to what follows.

In the *Yoginirmāṇatā* and other sūtras (2.4.11), "and that" refers to the sequence. He demonstrates the power of necessity (*niyatiśakti*) through valid means of knowledge, stating "also from scripture," thereby implying that inference is weak in this matter. [The opponent asks: "But not repeatedly"? [The author replies: Indeed, there is no other scripture here that establishes a different sequence.

Whence comes this certainty? In that regard, it is indeed difficult to comprehend that this very sequence is the rule of necessity (*niyati*). Let it be so; however, in the present context, there is no lack of clarity whatsoever, as he says: "And even if [the object] is unestablished... This refers to that which is the nature of being an object of cognition belonging to consciousness—which is itself undeniable—and that which is the manifestation of that cognized object.
Lordship consists in the sovereignty of performing actions such as joining and separating, or bringing about external and internal states;

all of that is self-luminous. However, for the sake of instruction to the ignorant, this is here treated as an object of knowledge (*prameya*), yet there is no loss [to its nature] even if it remains unestablished [for them], because of the necessity of the order and enumeration of existing things.

This is the connection [of the words]. This is what is meant: one who has accomplished his purpose perceives only the omnipotence of consciousness; for a supreme yogin, what use is there in counting the grains of sand on the banks of the Gaṅgā—how much could there be of that which exists merely in the interval? As it has been said:

"Indeed, the knowledge of the number of insects is not useful for him," and so forth. By the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way) and so on, [the author], while summarizing the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), outlines the great elements (*mahābhūta*). The term "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*) is used for the purpose of including the underlying intention (*āśaya*). And [the phrase] "mutual contact" (*anyonyasamparka*)...
It has as its object another primary element (*bhūtāntara*). Or rather, it is the determination of two alternatives:

for when one perceives a gross primary element possessing a single quality, the perception of other qualities occurs due to contact with another primary element; thus, by way of its configuration, its nature as a primary element is gross.

In the view that each element possesses an increasing number of qualities, there is mutual contact among the subtle elements (*tanmātras*); however, in the case of space (*ākāśa*), the attainment of grossness consists merely in its arrangement, since it lacks contact. As for air (*vāyu*), its functions are motion and expansion. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the functions of fire, water, and earth—namely digestion, cohesion, and support—are also included.
[They] have been grasped.
(Page 298) Or rather, the phrase "yadvā" introduces an alternative position for the purpose of including space (*ākāśa*). He clarifies this very point through [the term] *sanniveśa*—

The word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "there is no mutual contact here" indicates a distinction. It is possible that the transformation of sound (*śabda-pariṇāma*) provides scope in two ways: first, for the denotative word (*vācaka-śabda*) which consists of resonance (*nāda*); and second, for that which is the seed of the multitude of phonemes (*varṇa-grāma*), which is the root of the various functions of speech and is capable of sustaining diverse linguistic conventions (*samaya*).
Since that which possesses the superimposition of multiple denotations is capable of providing space for all [other sounds],

this is one mode; or rather, whether it be a denoter or a non-denoter, even a sound such as *khaṭakhaṭa* is capable of accommodating all [other sounds], because, being devoid of association with tangibility due to the absence of corporeality, it is non-obstructive.
"Since" (*yataḥ*) indicates another method [of explanation]. He defines that with the words "consisting of sound" (*nādātmā*) and so forth, as well as "or else" (*yadvā*) and so forth.
The word "even" (*api*) implies that, for the time being, the capacity of earth and the other elements to provide space is not possible in any way whatsoever;
even though it is observed, it is not their inherent nature (*svabhāva*), but rather something concomitant with them.

The meaning is "of space alone. Regarding the phrase "having another reality as its essence": sound is that which does not have touch as its concomitant; whereas earth and other elements possess the quality of touch, which accompanies it and acts as an obstruction, [sound] enters into that space. Thus, it is of space alone that there is the quality of providing room (avakāśadātṛtā).
The commentary [states]: the intended meaning is that this applies to the qualities of sound alone, and not to the other elements as well.

That which constitutes the "gross portion"—characterized by its structural arrangement and having the nature of cavities—is space itself; it is not the subtle element (*tanmātra*), which is devoid of structural arrangement and consists of agitation.

The meaning is that sound is a quality of form (*rūpa*). For this very reason—because the nature of being a configuration of sound is invariably present therein—for that reason, space alone is the single locus of air, because it is invariably its own essential nature. This is precisely what is well-known in the world.

He provides proof by saying, "And so they have said": for everyone, both worldly and non-worldly, desires the non-deviation [of sound] from space and air; with this intention, it is stated that there is always an inseparability between wind and space, as in Bhagavad Gītā 9.6.
Thus,
as the wind is eternally situated in space— (page 299)
And such [passages] as these have not been read here because they are already established. He states another alternative with the words "or else" (*athavā*).

"For this very reason" (*ata eva*) means because the portion consisting of sound falls within the category of space (*ākāśa*). He corroborates this even according to another school of thought with the words "and likewise" (*tathā ca*). For if space itself, due to an excess of the quality of touch, is [called] air—this is the view.
If it were not so, then wind would arise from sound and touch, or from touch alone;

and likewise for the subsequent elements. Thus, the intention [of the objection] is: how could a preceding great element (*mahābhūta*) serve as the cause for a subsequent one? Now, for what purpose [were systems] such as Śaivism and Sāṅkhya established?
Thus they say: it is said that when this sequence has been mastered, once the earth-dhāraṇā is conquered, the yogi,
contemplating even the earth as dissolved in water, perceives only water and attains its perfections,
until [all elements] are dissolved into space alone and partake of the state of unity with the Void.

Meditating upon the primary elements (mahābhūtas) in their prior order, one attains the powers of space (ākāśasiddhi). Furthermore, it has been established in the *Yojanā* that at the time of initiation, the previously purified principle (tattva), namely Earth, is to be joined with Water in the subsequent stage.
For those who possess the resolve but lack the capacity for the [higher] knowledge,
this method of the Guru, which is an easy means, has been proclaimed.

Thus, in the scripture, the application of initiation (*dīkṣā-yojana*) is rightly established as that which bestows grace upon all; therein, "application" (*yojana*) consists in the dissolution of the effect into its cause. By the word "rightly" (*yuktaḥ*), it is meant that this very position is supported by the majority of scriptures. He demonstrates this same two-fold method regarding other elements as well.

"Even so," he says. This confirms that the elements possess only one quality each; for this very reason, the author of the Sūtra-bhāṣya states: "The activity directed toward objects has arisen as the cause of stability. Thus, [he explains] the perception of each single quality, such as odor, within the fields of earth and the other elements.
He explained this very point as follows: even in the venerable *Matanga-shastra*,

by means of the passage beginning with "From the agitated subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), wind arises as a twofold manifestation (*vyūha*)," he shows that while each [element] possesses its own single quality by nature, there occurs the manifestation (*vyūhana*) of the preceding elements.
The fact that they are double that size and so forth has already been established. He explains the commentary [on the verse] with the words "And those very same...
300) up to "...but not a different entity," by means of the phrase "because they are not perceived."

Because of their subtlety, they are perceived only through the medium of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*); otherwise, the actual state of reality is that there is only the single principle of *māyā* and the single principle of *śiva*. Now, one might object: "In that case, even jars and other such objects should be counted as being of the nature of *tattvas*. He says "no," for [the definition of a *tattva*] is based on transcendence (*paratva*), which is the subject at hand. This is indicated by the word "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*).

Among these, subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*) culminates at the level of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); extension (*vyūhatā*) culminates at the level of *dhāraṇā*, because the increase of qualities through the successive accumulation of each preceding stage has just been described. Beyond that is "pervasiveness" (*vibhava*), such as [the capacity to occupy] the body, a jar, and so forth. There is nothing further here than this extension (*vyūhana*). The word "of them" (*teṣām*) is used for the purpose of specification (*nirdhāraṇe*). Now, regarding these...
Regarding the objection that, according to [the verse] "of the five [faculties] with respect to form and so forth" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 28),

it is appropriate for these to be organs of perception (*ālocanendriya*) rather than organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), he refutes this by clarifying precisely this point— that they serve the function of cognition— by means of the fact that the sense organs possess the nature of determinative apprehension (*adhyavasāyātmatā*).

Because the cognition of objects is produced from them, they possess the nature of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*). But [it may be objected]: since these are entirely beyond perception—both in their specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*), in their commonality as being derived from *ahaṃkāra*, and in their form as powers of the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—how can they have the nature of determination (*adhyavasāya*)? True.
It is exactly so by these means; however, having transformed into the forms of their respective objects and entered into the intellect (*buddhi*), they impart those forms to the intellect.
Thus, through that transformation into the form of the object, they consist of determination (*adhyavasāya*), and not otherwise.
By means of the three forms, beginning with its own specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*). And that alone is what is useful for the worldly course of these [beings], not that [mere sensing].
But surely, since mere sensing (*ālocana*) is the root to this extent, why is there no designation by that? To this he says:
"by mere sensing"—that is, by that which reaches as far as the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore...
"This object is mine" is not the resting place of the cognizer; rather, that [resting] occurs when that [determination] exists.

He states "for determination... and "also elsewhere... because this is agreed upon even in the case of the perception of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, by saying that this is also accepted as logical by others, he [establishes] his own system.
He states its firmness through universal consensus by means of the passage beginning with "indriyavṛtteḥ" (page 301),
[explaining that] in the very state of *māyā*, perception (*ālocana*) is the door, while the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are the gatekeepers, and so forth.

He shows that this is a matter of *prakriyā* (methodological procedure) and not of the level of *vidyā* (spiritual realization) by the words "yataśca" ("and because"). The phrase "is followed" (*anugamyate*) means that it is certainly not denied even by us. Regarding the "sequence of subtlety and so forth": the sense of smell is gross, while the sense of hearing is the most subtle; thus, [the sequence] from the most subtle...

The organ of speech. Regarding the objects—sound and the rest—they describe their respective natures at the time of producing [objects] such as a jar. There is the pair of abandonment and grasping: externally, this pertains to the anus, the hands, and the feet; internally, to the organ of speech; and the repose of the agitation of those [functions] pertains to the generative organ.

Thus, the organs of action have uncommon functions, pervade the entire body, and possess distinct activities within fixed locations. By this, it is established that even one whose hand is paralyzed can still grasp with both arms, and so forth. The word "of these" (*eṣām*) is used for the purpose of specification (*nirdhāraṇe*). "Some" (*kecit*) say as follows.
But others, however, hold this view; such is the connection [of the text].

Therefore, as it is said: "The instrument is threefold: the doorkeeper and the doors are the remaining ones" (*Sāṅkhyakārikā* 35), that [statement] is indeed of a single essence. However, regarding the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is a mutual relationship of being doors—

In the state of being a gateway, the sequence is fixed, just as in the case of the divisions of time (*kāla-kalā*) and so forth. This is because, when [the subject] attains the state of the perceiver (*pramātṛ-bhāva*), first there is attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*), from that, sensation (*vedana*), and from that, the instrument (*karaṇa*);
or else, from sensation and the instrument, there is passion (*rāga*) and so forth—this being the sequence of the distinctions of the perceiver, space, time, and so on.

Because of their diversity. Now, one might raise this objection: "Is it not logical that all the instruments (karaṇas) exist externally, following the distinctions created by Māyā? Or, because they are employed by the subject of Māyā, should they not be considered internal as being 'within'? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] proceeds to establish the division between the internal and external instruments.

Although the essential nature of the cognitive and active organs has already been stated, he returns to it with the words "and among these," meaning "among those well-known to all. The compound term begins with "in another subject" (*pramātrantare*).

The phrase beginning with "the grasper in the mind" (*manasi grāhaka*) refers to the *ahaṅkāra*; that beginning with "residing in that" (*tanniṣṭha*) refers to the *buddhi*; and that beginning with "all" (*sarva*) refers to... [the *prakṛti*].

In all three cases as well, this should be applied as the reason for their being internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇatā*). "Others" refers to Vindhyavāsī and his followers; for they [hold that] between the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and the intellect (*buddhi*)...
(page 302)

They speak only of it as the aggregate of instruments (*kāraṇaskandha*), not as the aggregate of organs (*karaṇaskandha*). He states the logical consistency of his own view: here, however, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is spoken of as being twofold due to the power of its distinct functions;
for the application [of these functions] is threefold. Otherwise, indeed, it would have been stated that there is only one single reality. For this very reason, it is said in the *Āgama*:
"Mind, ego, and intellect—this is the gateway of the eternal Self; for the sake of prosperity, the Lord of Beings fashioned this instrument in three ways. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 18.83).
Thus, regarding "knowledge and action": it is the power of knowledge itself [that resides] in the subject conditioned by Māyā.
Existence (*sattva*) consists in having distinct objects of cognition as its domain; likewise, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is *rajas* because it has distinct effects as its domain;

and *māyā* itself, consisting of delusion regarding distinct entities, is said to be *tamas*. Thus, the knowledge of the Lord (*pati*) regarding the categories that constitute His own limbs will be described [in the following verse]. (3.2.3)

Thus, in the Sūtra: "Therefore, that manifestation of differentiation among them—which has as its object the expansion of various objects of knowledge and effects—is the Supreme Nature (parā prakṛti), the root cause. It is called 'Pradhāna' because the universe is first deposited within it during creation, and it is dissolved therein during dissolution. [The author asks: "But how [is this established]? and so forth, [referring to] the state of being characterized by division.
He explains: "That which is the primordial state of all principles (tattvas), and for that very reason the supreme primordial nature (parā-prakṛti);
its connection is that it is the principle of Pradhāna. He clarifies the nature of non-differentiation by stating:
"The non-manifestation of all distinctions is the state of non-differentiation. However, it is not a mere nothingness (tuccha).

He says that it is merely a non-affirming negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) regarding the reality that is the fundamental cause; by this, he explains that oneness is the state of being indivisible, which constitutes the very nature of that reality.
And its oneness exists everywhere. For this very reason, she is the non-differentiation of all distinctions.

And therefore, how could this [consciousness] possess various distinct forms, since it alone swallows up all distinctions? Now, one might object: "The primary cause (pradhāna), consisting of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, is of an undivided nature; furthermore, you will not tolerate that the principles (*tattvas*) and so forth are merely powers (*śakti*)."

In the determination of the meaning of the sūtra, "The possessor of power [is distinct] from the state of differentiation" (4.1.5), an objection is raised: "Why is there such a difference of opinion, since Patañjali and others designate this as 'power' (*śakti*)? To this, he provides the following reply:

(page 303) "Even though [the Self] consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*": we have denied its state of being a power (*śaktitā*) with the intention of maintaining the distinction [between the Self and the powers], but not according to its actual mode of existence. As will be stated:

"The Lord’s knowledge and action, with Māyā as the third... (4.1.4), and so forth; thus, having taken these principles into account, the designation of the power of Māyā is indeed appropriate in the Pātañjala [Yoga-bhāṣya] and other texts.
"The identity of the powers of seeing and the seer" (Yoga Sūtra 2.6);
for this sūtra [states that] the power of the primary nature (pradhāna) is [the object] of the person (puruṣa).

And such is the commentary. Regarding the state of unity, he states another perspective in the passage beginning with "the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*). Thus, the doctrine of an original plurality (*mūlapṛthaktvavāda*) is certainly not accepted here. For in this system, the Śaivas have pointed out that the *māyā*-principle is the material cause (*upādānakaraṇa*), and that very same principle is described as being in the form of the supreme primordial nature (*paraprakṛti*); whereas *māyā*— [The text continues: ...is [described as]... [Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly.]

The power of the Supreme Lord has been described. For this very reason, it is stated that just as there are countless earthly eggs (*pārthivāṇḍa*), so too there are countless primordial eggs (*prākṛtāṇḍa*):
"Two distinct [types of] eggs are said to be innumerable" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.50).

Thus, in that context, the differentiation of the manifold variety of the *guṇa-tattva* constitutes its life-force (*jīvita*), whereas the *māyā-tattva* and *śakti* are each one only; therefore, no division of cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa-vibhāga*) is shown for them in the scriptures. As it has been said:
"Two separate [categories] are innumerable; each one is a single [entity], and two are separate. (Mālinīvijaya Tantra 2.50)

Thus [it is said]. And here, by stating that "there is no difference with respect to each individual soul" (*pratipuṃstattvaṃ na bhedaḥ*), it is indicated that such a difference does exist for the principles (*tattva*) situated below that [level]. Now, what is the proof for this? He says: "And this...

This sequence of principles is established not only through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but also through inference (*anumāna*)—specifically, that which is preceded by perception and is characterized by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*).
It can be established. Now, it was argued that the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is difficult to ascertain by means of inference.
True; however, this very ascertainment is achieved by relying upon the power of the Supreme Lord’s destiny (*niyati*).
But then, how is that [power] known? It is said: through the authority of the scriptures of the Supreme Lord.

(Page 304) That sequence of reality (*tattvakrama*) is "thus" in the sense that the state of being an object with respect to the operation of the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) has been brought about and accomplished for it. This is what is meant: [it pertains] to the Supreme Lord.

Thus far, the unimpeachable authority of scripture has been established; and that scripture demonstrates a fixed order of things as follows: namely, that the gross is necessarily preceded by the subtle, action is preceded by the instrument, and division is preceded by the indivisible.

In that regard, is it not invalidated by the established [opposing] obstacle? Even through the gateway of the Supreme Lord’s scripture (*pārameśvarāgama*), because that which is manifested is maintained as a reality exactly as it appears, the fruits of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth are established precisely through their manifestation.
Anticipating the objection, "Well then, let the detailed account stated in the Supreme Lord’s scripture be explained," [the author says:]

He says: "Here. However, we have already demonstrated this in detail in our extensive works—such as the *Vārttika*, the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and the *Śrī Tantrāloka*—which are based upon the scriptures (*āgama*). This much, however, is the essential point here:
it is the manifestations (*ābhāsa*) of earth and the other elements that, having become intermingled, constitute the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of objects such as a jar.
Produced and approached by the organs of action, perceived by the organs of cognition, brought to the state of conceptualization, self-conceit, and determination by the internal organ,
and differentiated by impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā) along with the [tattvas] beginning with *kalā*.

Though they are non-different [from the Absolute], being colored by those who posit a limited cognizer, the state of objects nevertheless exists through the gateway of resting within the Māyic cognizer. (Āgamaprāmāṇya 20)

By this principle, when the true subject is present, things—having their own internal divisions dissolved according to the degrees of that dissolution—rest solely in the ultimate reality of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); thus all is auspicious (*śivam*).

Thus ends the first reflection on the principles (*tattva-vimarśa*) in the *Āgamādhikāra* (Section on Scripture) of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*, composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara, the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 1.

Now begins the second reflection: I salute the one whose form is nectar, who holds the trident that severs the three bonds, and who is the ultimate reality of the fullness of the three powers— the medicine for mental anguish and physical disease.

Thus, once the mass of reality has been determined by way of its objectivity (*prameyatā*), the principle of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*)— though already determined [in the previous section]— is here worthy of being determined in detail as the primary focus, since this scripture, whose essential subject matter is the recognition of one's own nature as Godhood (*īśvaratā-pratyabhijñāpana*), requires such an exposition. For that purpose, there follows another investigation.
In this regard, by the passage beginning with "this very state of being the Mother...
and so forth,
[it is shown that] Vyāna is the supreme, whose nature is the universe.

With these twenty verses, the exposition begins. Therein, one verse [describes] the essential nature of the triad beginning with Brahmā; then, by two verses, the distinction between the types of subjects (pramātṛ) as those to be abandoned and those to be accepted;
thereafter, for their utility, the nature of impurity (mala) and the diversity of subjects produced by it.

By seven [verses], the nature of the knower as that which is to be abandoned has been stated; by two [verses], the nature of "absorption" (samāveśa) is described in order to express his nature as that which is to be accepted; thereafter, by five [verses], the nature of the states of the knower—such as deep sleep and so forth—is explained as a related digression; and [finally] the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted among those very states [is established].
"By three"—this is the purport of the section. Now, the meaning of each sūtra is examined:
therein, when there is the state of mere motherhood, Rudra is the presiding deity;
when there is the expansion of distinct objects of knowledge, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are established. (1)

In this context— that is, while this group of principles (*tattvavarga*), established by scripture, reinforced by reasoning and perception, and consisting of the subject and object, is being determined and introduced— it is that very [group] which, enveloped by the sheaths (*kañcuka*) such as time and so forth,
becomes pure in that state where the status of being an object of cognition has been withdrawn. Thus, [it is pure] because it is no longer an object of cognition...
It becomes oriented toward that during the state [of manifestation]; in that state,

the Lord acts as its presiding authority by means of bringing that state into being, by bestowing that state upon His circle of devotees, and by bringing about His own orientation toward them for one who has entered meditative absorption in that state.
Paramaśiva himself, assuming the state of Īśvara, is the presiding deity in the form of Rudra; for that very reason, he [presides] even in the realm of Māyā as the nature of prāṇa and apāna.
(page 306)

Having opened his third eye through contact with his own essential nature— which exceeds the portion of the subject consisting of the middle light (madhyamajyotis) that serves as the basis for the distinction between dharma and adharma, sun and moon, day and night, the state of impurity (sūtaka) and purity (amṛta), and so forth, yet is itself devoid of such distinctions— he [remains] while the expansion of the differentiated object of knowledge proceeds.
Brahmā is the presiding deity over its accomplishment (*saṃpādana*), whereas Viṣṇu is the presiding deity over its expansion (*prasara*)— that is, the continuous flow of its manifestation. Therefore,

these two primarily emphasize this very object of knowledge (*prameya*) as being of the nature of "this" (*idam*) through the light of manifestation, while [the third deity emphasizes it] as "I" (*aham*).

The meaning of the aphorism is as follows: those who do not disparage the essential nature of the subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) are not "possessors of the third eye" [ordinary yogins], but rather the Deity itself;
for the Deity is the presiding deity (*adhidevatam*), being the form of the presider (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). He introduces this [aphorism] with the words "of Viśveśvara," and so forth. Of Viśveśvara...
How do those [powers] manifest in an impure form through the forms of Brahmā and others? He says:

by way of being qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*), and not as the nature of pure consciousness alone. Therefore, that sovereignty which exists as the substratum, characterized as agency, is autonomy (*svātantrya*).

Knowledge extends as far as the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); that is their form. If one asks, "In that case, from where does duality arise?", he says: "Sattva. That very quality (*guṇa*) which has become the principal member (*aṅgin*), its sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) has that [sattva] as its object; thus, insofar as it is of the nature of knowledge, there is a distinction. In the void (*śūnya*), there is the state of being the *puryaṣṭaka*, the extremely subtle body.
Explaining the commentary on the word *eva*, he analyzes the term *mātra* from the sūtra with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth.

[The Lord] is devoid of that limitation which, like a corporeal being, is restricted by a specific form (*mūrti*)—that is, by a particular configuration—and by a specific time, such that it possesses finitude (*pārimitya*); however, even for Him, there is a connection with universal time.

Whether it be time itself or the determined time mediated through form, the fact that the *puryaṣṭaka* possesses corporeality due to its association with the gross elements (*mahābhūta*) is indeed established; yet, even that need not be stated here.
The mention of "the body" (*deha*) is intended to dispel delusion by raising a doubt.

In order to designate its fitness for grasping (*upādāna*), he uses the term "extremely subtle" (*atyantasūkṣma*) rather than "gross body" (*sthūladeha*); furthermore, he states that even the metaphorical masculinity (*puṃstva*) exists [in it]. Now, one might object: "Since it is empty and consists of the quality of darkness (*tamas*), that is simply the principle of primordial matter (*pradhānatattva*); so what is the point of this different terminology? To this, he replies: "consisting of *sattva* and so forth."

It is included within the primary [principle], but it is not that very thing itself; such is the meaning. "Because it is perceived as such" means through the superimposition of the state of being a subject (*pramātṛ*) in the form of "I. He elaborates on this very point (page 307):
He dispels this doubt with the words "even now" (*adyāpi ca*) and so forth. The word "thus" (*evam*) means that what has been stated is logical:

although there is equality between the subtle and gross bodies for that reason, nevertheless, [the body] does not belong to the primary *puruṣa-tattva* of the parents; such is the connection. Regarding their non-difference—

"Not at all" means by way of non-difference from the *puryaṣṭaka*. For it has been stated that the subsequent state arises as such through the penetration (*āveśa*) of each preceding form. Now, one might object: "But the nature of consisting of form and so forth exists in the *puryaṣṭaka* as well.

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And because of the non-manifestation of objects of cognition (*prameya*). For the form and so forth belonging to that [subtle body] do not [function as external objects].

It appears. For it is consciousness itself, conditioned by that contraction, which shines forth as the subject (*pramātṛ*), and not the form and so forth that constitute the objects (*prameya*) contained therein; however, in the case of the body, that very [consciousness] is made into the subject, as seen in the cognition "I am fair. But surely—

One might object: "Since even the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body) and the void (*śūnya*) appear to the omniscient [Lord], they too possess the status of being objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*). Therefore, how can it be said that these two are merely the subject (*pramātṛmātra*)? Anticipating this doubt, he begins with another position: "Or rather... Let it be granted that those two are objects of knowledge; however, by means of them...

Anything else, such as a jar and so forth, is not cognized by means of the external body, because without contact [with that body], it would be impossible for it to produce experience. "For this very reason" means: since nothing other than those two is cognized, therefore [it is so].
"Of the Supreme Lord" means: for He alone, through His absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), manifests Himself in that manner.

This has been stated more than once: that they are of two kinds—namely, "with experience" (*savedya*) and the other. That which is designated as *āṇava* is a specific impurity (*mala*) consisting of ignorance, produced by *māyā* alone, as will be stated:
"By the power of *māyā* itself, that triad [is produced]. (3.2.5)

Thus; making that [object] extremely manifest within the aspect of cognition, the Lord Rudra suppresses the *tamas* quality in the intellect, withdraws its connection with differentiated appearances, and clarifies his very nature as the presiding subject by means of the words "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth. And here, "in this" (*atra*) refers to the pure subject alone, whose essence consists in the withdrawal of all things.

"He himself" refers to the Blessed Lord Rudra. Now, one might object: "If the destruction of all that is to be known has occurred, then that itself is the supreme state; what other 'fourth state' (turya) could there be, distinct from deep sleep? To this he says:
"And therein," even when [the objects] have perished.

(Page 308) Even now, the reality of the knower— which is the locus of attributes such as being transcendent to all, consisting of all, and being the Lord of all— remains within the realm of the knowable, such as the void (*śūnya*), due to its association with the contraction of consciousness (*saṃvit-saṅkoca*).

It is indeed appropriate that there is a distinction from the fourth state (*turyadaśā*), which has the manifestation of that [reality] as its essence, on the grounds that "the manifestation of the ultimate reality does not exist. Now, one might object: let the various mental constructs (*bhāvanā*) exist when the void is the contemplator and the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*) is present;
but when the void itself is the reality, who is this [agent] characterized primarily by the mental construction of duality?

The one who brings [the object] into being would be another; yet, from the perspective of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), there is no difference in that which is to be brought into being.

To this it is replied: "And in the void" (*śūnye ca*). When, at the very same time, by way of the consciousness situated on the peak, one brings both into being—whether as the grasping of speech or as something distinct such as the body, a jar, and so forth—then...
In relation to another void that is to be meditated upon as having entered into the midst of that [first void], it is said to be "another void";

that very [void] attains the state of the subject (*pramātṛtā*). Nor is there an infinite regress, for even if the stability of objects occurs through the penetration into the reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*)—(Aparapramāṇasiddhi 20).
Thus,

by the principle stated in [Svacchandatantra-kalpa] 8, "Moreover, through the touch of one's own power," because of the emergence of the subject (*pramātṛ*), he says "it is established. In this way, the half-verse of the *sūtra* [is explained].

Having explained the remainder, he explains the half-verse beginning with "jāgara" (waking) and so forth. The connection is as follows: that very meaning which the word *prasara* (expansion) has in the Sūtra is elucidated in the Vṛtti by the word *ābhāsa* (manifestation).
Having explained the two deities in their totality, he clarifies them through their individual division, starting with "jāgaraṃ ca" (and waking).
By such statements as these, he explains that [the Lord] is called "seated upon a lotus" (kamalāsana) precisely because He resides within the lotus of the heart;
for it is not merely that this manifestation of existence exists there at the very first moment,
but rather that He also attains the state of memory and even the state of dream— such is the continuous [description].

The Lord Viṣṇu, performing that expansion (*tana*), is called the Protector (*pālaka*). He resides in the region of the throat within the assembly of subjects, beginning from the Supreme Lord down to the limited subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*), in the state of the unfolding manifestation (*ullāsa*) that follows the nature of the Intermediate Vaikharī speech. For it is in the heart...
The primordial creation consists in the nature of *pratibhā* within the expansion of the first *paśyantī*, which is the state of the initial stage.

In accordance with the principle stated [in the *Svacchandatantra*]: "The Creator, when requested according to one's desire, [bestows] objects upon the waking state" (3.33), the state of Rudra— characterized by deep sleep (*suṣupta*) consisting of the withdrawal of everything— is located in the palate, which is the ground for the commencement of entering the reality of the unstruck supreme speech (*anāhata-paravāk*), the form in which all doctrines are withdrawn.

Since it is understood from the very fact that [the breath] moves to the position above that even when the throat region is examined, the palate is not mentioned by the author of the Vivṛti. Precisely for that reason, [it is said]: "Brahmā is the heart, Viṣṇu the throat, Rudra the palate, Īśvara the space between the eyebrows."
The Supreme Lord— whose cranial aperture (brahmarandhra) is Sadāśiva, who stands upon the steps of the power (śakti) consisting of Anāśrita,
and whose body is the six causal deities— is indicated by this scriptural meaning through the description of the essential nature of the Heart and the other centers.
Having divided himself by himself and created various kinds of entities,
the Lord of All, who consists of all things, proceeds as the enjoyer within a dream.

With this intention, he raises the doubt with the words "although" (*yadyapi*). "When" (*yadā*) means "because," and "then" (*tadā*) means "therefore"; or else, when there is a dream for one possessing latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), then there is the state of stability; but by virtue of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), that very [state] takes the form of waking even in a dream.

According to the principle stated in the *Svacchandakalpa* (3.34), "Likewise, even in a dream, desired objects do not transcend [the power of] affection," whenever that [principle] is mentioned by those two [authors], the novel manifestation of objects—
such as houses and jars manifested by architects, potters, and others— is indeed clearly evident.

Because of that commonality, there is again the perception of that very same thing; thus, the state of being a creation—which does not depend on such particularities—is what constitutes wakefulness. Now, one might object: "But surely this is also the case in dream"; to this, he provides a rebuttal by means of an alternative position with the words "or rather" (*yadivā*), [referring to] the cognition of non-difference expressed as "we all know [this] as one."

Or rather, it was previously manifested through its identity with other subjects as the locus for the cognition of difference—that is, the perception of its distinctness from previous creations. The phrase "having such a nature" (tathārūpatā) refers to its being of the nature of a creation, which connects back to the waking state. By the word "only" (eva) in the expression "only a quality of the intellect" (buddhiguṇa eva), [the author emphasizes this].
Even the touch of pure sovereignty does not belong to those two; however, for the venerable Lord Rudra, there is both pure sovereignty and knowledge.
(page 310)
He demonstrates that yoga is indeed the contact with the two qualities of the intellect, namely sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
He shows this very point through a clear scriptural sign (*abhijñāna*), saying "for this very reason":
when there is sovereignty, which is the power of ruling over the dissolution of the manifold world (*prapañca*), then indeed [there is] the quality of the intellect.
"The disappearance of sovereignty is the suppression of that which exists, not its absolute non-existence" (Spanda-kārikā 15).
Thus [it is said].
"Then, in that great void...

(Spandakārikā 25). Thus, even though there is no attainment of absolute oneness (*ekaghanatā*) within the great void that lies between these [states], there is nonetheless a mere entry; this occurs through the third eye by means of the awakening of the great splendor of *udāna*.
Yoga consists in the nature of burning away differentiation. || 1 ||

Explaining the differentiation of this very state of mere subjectivity (*mātṛtāmātra*), he establishes through a sūtra that its necessary connection with other principles, such as Time (*kāla*) and so forth, must be acknowledged:
"This cognizer (*pramātā*), blinded by *māyā*, is a transmigrating being bound by karma."
One whose sovereignty is made manifest through knowledge and higher powers is called a liberated being, a mass of consciousness. || 2 ||

Deluded by *māyā*, and for that very reason regarding actions as being binding, "this one"— enveloped by the divisions of time (*kālakalā*) and so forth, whose nature is consciousness contracted within the "empty city" (*puryaṣṭaka*),
