and whose character is to wander through transmigratory existence— is [liberated] by *vidyā*, which is the power of manifesting one's own true nature.

He whose sovereignty—pure autonomy—is attained through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and therefore whose consciousness (*cit*) is dense and compact, being free from any suspicion of the intrusion of insentient matter (*acid-rūpa*);
he is liberated even while in the body due to the absence of the bond of rebirth, and when this body has fallen, he is Śiva himself. Who [else could be so]?

The meaning of the aphorism is that although he was previously liberated by way of his prior state, he is designated as "Muktaśiva" (the Liberated Śiva) in the scriptures. He states this briefly with the words "now" (*idānīm*). With the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*), [he means]: otherwise, if his nature were pure consciousness, then Māyā would instead be subordinate to him; he would not be dependent upon it, such that she [Māyā] would [be his power].
The sense is that he should be called "he" (*saḥ*). It will be stated [later]:
"And for the gods and so forth... (3.2.10).
(Page 311)

Having begun thus, [it continues] in the sūtra: "There too, only the *kārmika* [bondage]" (3.2.10). And by the phrase "that very same," the meaning is that for whom there is bondage, for that very same person liberation is appropriate.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [the text refers to] gnosis, conduct, devotion, and so forth. As it is said in the venerable *Sarvavīramata*:
"At times, He favors those in the cycle of existence through the yoga of devotion, or by means of ritual action, or even by initiation."
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrīmataṅga*:
"Or rather, liberation [arises] from the fourfold [set].
Now, one might object: "But surely, in the Āgamas, the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*) is stated to be something to be abandoned."
But those who worship the Self do not go to the supreme state in Śivaism.
Having raised the objection that [the state] consisting of Śakti and Śiva has been described as something to be adopted—as stated in [Netratantra 8.4], he says: "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*);
the meaning is that this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*). The word "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*) is from the sūtra. Now, [one might ask]: "But..."

Anticipating the question, "How is the state of being a mass of consciousness (ciddhanatva) revealed by this? he says, "In pure consciousness," and so forth. The underlying intention is that "always" refers to liberation in relation to bondage. || 2 ||
He defines the various designations of this very cognizer according to their etymological derivation:
"The cognizer is called the *pati* (Lord) with respect to entities that are his own limbs;
through *māyā*, he is the *paśu* (bound soul), defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth, with respect to differentiated [entities]. (3)
He who is called "liberated" perceives all entities as his own limbs; thus, he is their master and, by bestowing the form of ultimate reality, their protector.
Therefore, being permeated by the nature of the Lord, he is described in the scripture as a "Lord" (pati), just like the Supreme Lord.
But when he perceives those [souls] as differentiated by the power of *māyā*, then— precisely because of that—

they become associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*), with auspicious and inauspicious actions (*karma*), and, by the force of the word "etcetera," with latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the enjoyments (*bhoga*) consisting of the maturation of karma, all of which are elaborated through the aforementioned manifold coverings (*kañcuka*).

Turbid, with its singular sovereignty of aesthetic flavor cast aside; then, because it is bound by those very fetters, it is called a *paśu* (bound soul). "Then" means in the state of *śivatā*, wherein that which is to be protected (*pālya*) must be awaited.

The meaning is that, in its state as the *pati* (Lord), there is no [state] distinct from that. Now, one might object: "In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the sūtra phrase 'among those differentiated from Māyā' was not touched upon; rather, something else was said, namely, 'in the state of being a person (*puṃstva-avasthāyām*)'. He shows that the sūtra itself was stated in this manner with the passage beginning with 'And then' and ending with 'precisely by the state of being a person'.

Now, if it is asked, "What is the purpose of this variety of expression? he replies: "The primary one" (*prādhānika*) [is understood] by the very state of masculinity (*puṃstvāvasthayā*), like the eye of a crow (which moves between two sockets). By that very statement, another thing to be accepted is implied: that which has come from the *Pradhāna* and exists therein—the universe (*viśva*). Thus, first of all, in the Pārameśvara system, in the supreme...

This has been accepted because it is admitted that the power of the Lord (*īśvaraśakti*) itself exists in such a manner. Furthermore, even those other philosophical systems, such as the Kāpila and Vaiṣṇava, must necessarily accept what we have stated, even if it is not explicitly recorded in their own texts.

There is a predominance of *rāga*, *kalā*, *avidyā*, *niyati*, *kāla*, and so forth. That which was stated as "the Lord (Īśvara) [is] the Lord" is clarified by the passage beginning with "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Now, one might object: "Let the non-Lord be the opposite of the Lord; but why should the individual soul (*puruṣa*) be so? To this he says: "And that very [non-Lord] is the individual soul. But then [one may ask]: "Indeed..."
Let the person be endowed with afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and the latencies of fruition (*vipākāśaya*); therein, among the afflictions, ignorance (*avidyā*)—
acting as delusion— is *māyā*, which, by obstructing right perception, fails to see the Self as the universe and, through egoism (*asmitā*), sees the non-self as the Self, [giving rise to] desire.

[It is] accepted; however, while passion (*rāga*) is included within the triad beginning with passion, how are necessity (*niyati*) and the others subsumed? He says: "By necessity," because necessity is the fundamental ground of action (*karman*). For the relationship of cause and effect arises from that, and the triad of the maturation of the latent impressions of action (*karmavāsanā-vipāka*) has that as its root; therefore, [the soul] is also joined with that [necessity].

And when *vidyā* and *kalā* are characterized by *rāga* (attachment), that which is the locus of attachment is precisely the object of *kalā* and *vidyā*, or its opposite; therefore, [the soul] is conjoined with those two. Furthermore, *karman* is of the nature of action (*kriyā*), and action is animated by time, which is characterized by succession; thus, [the soul is conjoined] by means of *karman*.

"Since time is also accepted by that which has been accepted, it is likewise joined with that"—this thought, though not yet ascended to their tongues, exists in their hearts. He demonstrates this with the words "silence"; however, for us, who have been graced by the vision of the Supreme Lord...

Everything has been clearly explained. Indeed, the pure and impure nature of the knower (*pramātṛ*) must be expounded in detail within the spiritual sciences (*adhyātmavidyā*), for this very subject constitutes their primary purpose.
Because it is worthy of being spread abroad. || 3 ||

The commentator himself establishes the connection [between the topics] by stating "of the bound soul" (*paśoḥ*), in order to elaborate upon and define the true nature of the bound soul through another aphorism. Regarding the term "supreme lordly" (*pārameśvara*), others—being ignorant of this true nature—are not properly liberated; having thus instructed them, [the author proceeds].
In our own system, when it comes to superimposition, this alone is the cause of liberation from the perspective of ultimate reality;
and this is accepted by the wise—this is the intended meaning. For that very reason, the scripture states:
"But those who worship the Self do not go to the supreme state in the Śaiva [tradition]" (Netratantra 8.4).

Thus, [the nature of] the three impurities (*mala*) has been explained by means of the seventh and third case endings. By this method, the three impurities will be made manifest according to their characteristics and their objects. Among these, he first states the *āṇava* [impurity] by means of a sūtra.
The loss of freedom of consciousness and the lack of awareness within freedom itself—
this is the twofold atomic impurity (āṇavamala), resulting from the deprivation of one's own true nature.

"Independent consciousness"—this is the reality (*tattva*). In that regard, by the loss of another portion, there is a removal of its own nature; thus, *mala* (impurity) bestows the state of being an individual soul (*aṇutā*), which is contraction. This [impurity] is of two kinds: the *āṇava* [mala] and so forth. Now, one might object: "Since *mala* is to be explained in this commentary, why is there this mention of a stainless nature? To this he says: "The pure... and so on.

Regarding the phrase "of the intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvasya*): for impurity (*mala*) is indeed a conjunction with something else of a different genus (*vijātīya*), like a particle of soot in its own substrate; and that particle [is also] of the soot. Therefore, that form which is of a single genus, compact, stainless, and pure, must first be stated. By the term "in general" (*sāmānyena*), it is meant that [it is] not yet manifest.

The meaning is that this applies even to the entire collection of attributes such as fullness (*pūrṇatva*) and sovereignty (*svātantryatva*). By the mention of the second [category], he states that *māyā*, *pradhāna*, and so forth, are indeed of the nature of its power (*tacchaktirūpatā*); thus he says "separately" (*pṛthak*). Those living beings who are *vijñānākalas* exist in the form of *mantreśvaras* according to their respective order; however, the *mantreśvaras* themselves—

They are indeed independent. The meaning is that this is known through perception, that is, through means of valid cognition such as scripture (*āgama*). Now, one might object: even for those such as the *vijñānākala*, who are devoid of the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) consisting of agency characterized by the wonder of the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*), [how can they be independent?]

(Page 314) First, regarding the definition of the bound soul (*paśu*), it was stated that its characteristic is ignorance: "The bound soul is eternal, formless, and ignorant; its nature is mere consciousness alone."
Thus, [if one objects that] that [limited agency] does not exist, and how can that which is conjoined with the impurity of *āṇava* be necessarily present?

Anticipating this doubt, he says "svātantrye" and so forth. For in that state, the nature of being a knower (*jñatva*) consisting of a separate perceiver has been negated; [only] by virtue of the grace of other principles in the form of *kalā* and *vidyā* does the *sakala* (the bound soul) [possess limited knowledge].

That which is called "the arisen" does not exist at all for the *vijñānākala*. Even within its own self, the state of being a knower (*vedakatva*) is not tenable as something separate; and even if it were non-separate, because the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of the wonder of "I" is obscured, it does not differ from what is non-existent. Thus he says regarding its own self:

Thus, the capacity to make something known (*bodhakatva*) is distinct [from its object], depending upon a separate thing to be known (*bodhya*); it does not exist within itself. Furthermore, a distinct thing to be known by it is neither logically established nor possible. Therefore, the conclusion is that there is only ignorance (*ajñatā*), and not knowledge (*jñatva*). That very point is stated as the cause for being atomic (*aṇutva*) in the Sūtra.
This has been accepted through the reasoning of the *Āṇavopāya*, and it is made explicit in the commentary by the word "only" (*mātra*). Now, one might object:
"Granted that the status of being a knower (*vedakatā*) is refuted by the word 'only' when the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is distinct; but when it is non-distinct, by what is that refuted?
It would be like [the case] of Īśvara. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "by the inclusion of the word 'only'."

The word "and" (ca) is to be understood here [as implying "only"]. For by the mention of "mere" (mātra), which likewise excludes the state of being the self of the universe as well as its manifestation, it is possible to exclude the state of having a distinct object and subject;
for that [state] is the aforementioned prior stage of non-conceptuality in which the divine nature exists.

Now, he explains the point that even autonomy (*svātantrya*) may be characterized by non-awareness, with the words "but for that which is excluded from awareness" (*bodhanirākṛtasya tu*). Regarding the phrase "it remains as such," if ignorance were not something to be remedied, then the definition of an atom would be clearly established. For the void (*śūnya*) and so forth manifest as objects of cognition due to their status as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); the same applies to the aspect of consciousness (*saṃvid-aṃśa*).
It is indeed permeated by the shadow of the object of knowledge (*vedya*). Regarding the "two-fold fruit":

it will be explained in due order that the fruits of this [impurity] are, respectively, the Vijñānākala and others, as well as the gods and others. [This concludes the section on] the root impurity (*mūlamalatā*).
Moreover, in the context of the command (*ājñapti*), the subject (*grāhaka*) is primary, and its state is dependent upon that [subject];

however, in the context of the yoga of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-yoga*), it is stated that what is called *māyā* is the root—thus there is no contradiction. Now, as for that which was said regarding the creation of mere consciousness (*bodha-mātra*) and mere sovereignty (*svātantrya-mātra*), by that—

One might think that by stating "impermanence has ensued," that which was declared as the preeminent permanence in the definition of the "bound soul" (paśu) would be abandoned. To show that this is not so, he says, beginning with "and mere consciousness" and ending with "this is indeed eternal.
"Of independent consciousness" means of that whose nature is consciousness in its aspect of sovereignty (*svātantrya*), and not...

Because, through the aspect of consciousness (*saṃvedanāṃśa*), the state of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) does not exclude the nature of "this-ness" (*idantātman*) due to its lack of the nature of self-awareness (*asaṃvidrūpatva*).

The phrase "nowhere" implies that even in objects such as a jar, where autonomy (*svātantrya*) is not superimposed, the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*) is present because their sole essence is manifestation (*prakāśa*); how then could that [consciousness] exist through a superimposed autonomy? Thus he says:

Regarding the term "viśeṣaṇa" (qualification): [the author asks] "But if someone were to perceive even a jar as having the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), would he not then indeed be non-deluded? He replies, "Yes, indeed," with the words "but of the insentient (*jaḍasya tu*). The phrase "it is indeed appropriate" (*yukta eva*) means that it is precisely fitting. For by means of *śakti*, which is of the nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), this [perception] is truly correct.

The meaning is that "penetration" (*āveśa*) refers to an entry into one's own essential nature from all sides (*ā-samantāt*), characterized by the predominance of the conscious nature (*cidrūpatā*) through the suppression of the state of insentience (*jaḍarūpatā*). As it has been said:
"From a blade of grass, from a leaf... [and so forth].
Thus [it is said]. For emergence is indeed a humiliation of the nature of the insentient (acid-rūpatā).

In the verse beginning "O you of eight forms, what [is this] in one...", that very [emergence] is the satisfaction. Now, [one might ask: is it not the conceit of selfhood (ātmatva-abhimanana) regarding that which is non-self and insentient?

"This ignorance consists in the non-apprehension of the [true] nature of the opposites"—this is the view of the Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and other schools, because they speak of the persistence of the impermanent, the impure, and suffering within the self, and so forth.
Anticipating the objection, "How then can it be said that this [ignorance] is indeed logical?", he says: "Precisely for this reason. Since it has been stated thus, therefore...

The meaning is that the Sāṅkhya position must be understood as simply untenable. For, in the state of non-discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, it is accepted that the conceit of being the *puruṣa* resides in *prakṛti* itself. [Objection: But surely, if one meditates on that [non-existence] even in the state of liberation, there would be the undesirable consequence of continued transmigratory existence, since it is merely a non-entity. This very point [is established] by logic...

(Page 316) "It does not connect," [it is said]. If the Self were not present in that which is non-self, then the identification with it would be a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*); but this is not the case in the house.

One who determines that the nearby space [is the self] becomes deluded. [The author] says "Now" (atha) to address the objection: "But this was not stated by the Sāṅkhyas. This refers to the manifestation of the object characterized as self and non-self;
and that has not been stated by them as being bondage, but rather that the non-self itself is [mistakenly] taken as the self.
"It appears"—this too he refutes with the words "What is this?

If it is the manifestation of light, then that object is exactly as it is; there is no other reality to it, so what delusion could there be? Alternatively, if delusion consists in a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) in that way even when there is no such manifestation, this too—

"It refutes by way of censure, but not [in the sense of] 'it is not'. "Attained" (*prāpta*) means "appropriate. "Related to the person" (*puruṣasambandhī*) means "appropriate as having the person as its object. He clarifies that concise statement with the passage beginning with "In the self" (*ātmani*) and ending with "is improper" (*ayuktaḥ*), taking it as a single syntactical unit without eliding the negative prefix *a-* (i.e., reading it as *na yuktaḥ*).
"This is not tenable. Here, the particle *tat* indicates the introduction of the point to be stated in this context.

In the Sāṅkhya view, the determination "I" is, on the contrary, appropriate only with respect to that which is non-self—the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) and ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)—but not with respect to the Self, whose essential nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Thus, however, it is as follows.

The sense is that what was taught by the Supreme Lord to the Sāṅkhyas was indeed incomplete, whereas this [teaching] is perfect knowledge. "One's own" (*svaka*) means uncreated; for that very reason, it is appropriate. "And that" refers to the form of the meaning of the sentence. "By them" refers to the Sāṅkhyas. That which, in connection with the object of knowledge (*prameya*), is this *āyā-*...

He concludes that very point with the summary: "But for us... Thus, the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*)—which has been established as the very nature of the Self in passages such as (1.6.1)—is precisely that.

The Lord's agency has been stated in such passages as "Agency belongs to the Lord precisely in His reflective awareness" (1.8.11); therefore, such agency is not possible with respect to an effect that is distinct [from Him].

Because the relationship between cause and effect has been refuted at length, the world, which is of the nature of an effect, consists of the Puruṣa alone. As the Śruti says: "The Puruṣa indeed is all this. Thus, the entire world is [the Puruṣa].

And by saying this, he demonstrates that even though one is indeed alone, such an identification with the body and so forth—due to their difference from objects like a jar—is nothing but a delusion (*viplava*). For it is precisely for this reason that it has been stated here and there: "This delusion is twofold."

Thus [it is said]. Therein, "thus" (*iti*) refers to the world. Furthermore, the collection of particles "pratyuta" indicates that the opponent's insistence here is improper because it is the reverse of the truth. Regarding "the binding of the root" (*mūlabandha*):

when that exists, from that very source—from a category (*varga*) that has not been made one's own—one [perceives] within a portion of the body and so forth, which are indeed non-self, that which is not yet discarded as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

Let there first be the conceit of self in the form of "I am," which is the subsequent bondage; it is with this intention that the power of Māyā is said to give rise to the emergence of the dual-fold corruption. || 4 ||
Now, with the words "here now" and so forth, he introduces the aphorism that defines the two impurities (*mala*):

"The manifestation of a distinct object of knowledge right here is that which is called *māyā*, bestowing birth and experience; while the *kārma* [impurity] resides in the agent's lack of awareness; thus, this triad arises through the power of *māyā* alone. (1.5)
With the words "this [is] the individual" (*etadāṇava*) and so forth, he explains [the phrase] "right here" (*atraiva*).
It will be stated that even for the Mantreśvaras there is the individual impurity (*āṇavaṃ malaṃ*), even though they possess [divine] consciousness. (3.2.9)

Thus, in the Sūtra and its commentary (Ṭīkā): "Therefore, when that very [āṇava-mala] exists, there is the conjunction with another impurity (mala). When the āṇava-mala exists in its twofold form—namely, in its state as 'vṛtti' (active) and as 'svarūpa-saṅkoca' (contraction of essential nature)—the manifestation of the divided [self] is that which is called 'māyā'; that whose designation is 'by means of māyā' is the impurity known as māyīya."

"By mere designation" (*saṃjñāmātreṇa*); however, that even the three impurities (*malatraya*) are created by illusion (*māyā*) is stated in the fourth quarter of this very verse. In that regard, when there is the manifestation of an object distinct from the body and so forth—which are the agent consisting of non-awareness—even with respect to inert actions that lack any [other] cause.

Error consists in the grasping of signs (*nimitta*). Furthermore, the karmic impurity (*kārma-mala*) is the cause of birth—which is projected with a fixed limit—and of experience, such as pleasure and pain. The power called *māyā* belongs to the Supreme Lord; it is that power which manifests the soul (*aṇu*) through the power of impure knowledge (*aśuddha-vidyā*).
(Page 318) Then, having presided over the internal and external senses, the individual soul (*aṇu*) perceives the differentiated object of knowledge.
At that time, this *aṇu* is said to be "defiled" by the impurity called *māyā*; for this reason as well—and not merely because of the former [impurity]—it is so designated.

The meaning is that this [error] which was described as consisting of the *āṇavamala* (the individual impurity) is also included. "Therein" means in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-āgama*). He asks, "How is it indicated? and replies, "Even the triad. Regarding "of this," he refers to the mention of the name. And he demonstrates that here, in particular, the designation by means of *māyā* is appropriate.

"Non-duality," and so forth. "Therein" means in that which is called Māyā. Precisely for that reason, by way of the sequence of emanation (*utpattikrama*), this [Māyā] is the root of roots, because the impurity of finitude (*āṇavamala*) depends upon the cognition whose nature is pure consciousness.
For this very reason, the making of objects into objects of knowledge is called the impurity known as Māyā.
The innate sense of "I-ness" (ahambhāva), however, which is rooted in the primordial matter (mūla-prakṛti) and persists even toward objects of knowledge, is the individual (āṇava) impurity.
In this regard, the teachers have explained that the word "root" (mūla) is to be understood [in both instances] like the eye of a crow (i.e., shared between the two).

He clarifies this very point with the words "and in the dualistic vision. The phrase "of the liberated souls" (muktāṇūnām) means of those such as the Mantramaheśvaras who have transcended the state of transmigratory existence. Thus, it would be possible.

Up to this point, that which is called *māyā* has been explained primarily; however, in the course of clarifying its nature, the other two impurities (*mala*) were also described. Now, he explains the *kārma* [impurity] as "subjection to karma. And that [subjection] is due to the state of being the impurity of karma.
Since its locus is characterized by a general state of inversion (*viparyāsa-sāmānya*), it lacks reality.
Why is it said that this is a general state of inversion? He replies: "Because of autonomy.
The very power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which is the nature of the subject’s autonomy, is itself the object; for it is precisely this [power] that renders the subject dependent upon another.

By the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), this [individual] becomes a partaker of diverse fruits even though he does not desire it; therefore, the meaning is that it arises from error (*viparyāsa*). "Previously" refers to the investigation into the relationship between cause and effect. "Will be stated" refers to the *Devādi-sūtra* (3.2.10). By means of consciousness (*vijñāna*), which consists of mere awareness, they are devoid of *kalās*.
The meaning is that they are devoid of enjoyment because of the absence of association with impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā), passion (rāga), and so forth, as characterized by the [previous] kalās.
He explains the fourth quarter with the compound beginning with "tad etat" and so on. || 5 ||
(319) Now, in order to clarify the nature of these impurities by demonstrating their distinct objects, [the author states]:
"The loss of the autonomy of consciousness... (3.2.4).
Thus he states the scope of this section:
"Even though they consist of pure consciousness, those who do not possess supreme agency have been created by the Lord as distinct from Himself due to the absence of that agency. (6)

Those who, although their ultimate reality is pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), are not supreme agents because they are joined with the concealment of the wonder of the bliss of supreme freedom— which is characterized by resting within one's own self as "I"—
are [treated] by the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, whose unimpeded and fully nourished freedom desires to manifest in that way.

By whom [they] have been fashioned as distinct from their own self, just like jars and other objects, such that they appear with the differentiation of the Mantramaheśvaras and others. The reason for their difference from the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is "due to the loss of agency"—
the underlying intention being that this is because the Supreme Lord consists of supreme sovereignty.

He explains with the words beginning "bodha" that purity here consists precisely in the removal of some portion of impurity, taking the form of the cessation of the density of impurity and the subsequent manifestation [of consciousness]. By the word "anena" (by this), he refers to the term "unaffected by objects of knowledge" (*vedyānuparakta*). "Kaivalyam" means the state of being absolute (*kevalatā*).
"The conjunction with the substratum" (*upādhyayoga*)—this very thing is the ultimate liberation (*paramārthāpavarga*) for the Sāṅkhyas and others;
this he indicates by the term "isolation" (*kaivalya*). He explains the fifth case-ending in the sense of cause (*hetu*) with the words "that which...
(*tad etat*), and so forth. Now, why is the creation of the Lord (*īśvara-nirmāṇa*) required there? He says:

Regarding the term *īśvaranirmiti*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which consists of sovereignty" (*svātantrya*), and so forth. For this very reason—namely, because even that which is difficult to accomplish (*durghaṭa*) gives rise to the appearance of being separated from its primary nature—it consists precisely of sovereignty; for there is not even the slightest lack of independence (*asvatantratā*) anywhere whatsoever.

[This concerns] the shadow of destruction and so forth. Now, if it is argued that the Lord shines even through His own self by means of His absolute freedom (*asvātantrya*), and if such is His supreme sovereignty, then how can it be said that they are distinct from the essential nature of the Lord? He resolves this with the words "by that very same [Lord]" (*tenaiva ca*) in the word "distinct" (*bhinna*).
[This occurs] in that which exists in a state of contraction. He clarifies this very point with the words "for not," etc.
For he appears as independent—according to this mode of expression, that independent form which exists when there is such an appearance is what has been accepted.

Thus, it follows that [the object] appears as dependent and indeed distinct from that [subject]. Now, one might object: "In this way, the Lord would surely abandon His sovereignty. To this he says: "And He too... [The objection continues: "There would indeed be a loss of sovereignty if another were to act upon Him in this manner; but such is not the case. Therefore he says: "Himself..."

Now, one might object: "In reality, these [entities] such as the *vijñānākala* and others are indeed non-different from the Supreme Lord; therefore, of whom can that sovereignty be said to belong? Is it of the Blessed One alone, or of them as well? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But the *sāṅkhya*-puruṣas and so forth... For he who desires to become thus and is not obstructed, he...

He is independent. And this [independence] belongs only to the Blessed One, because He alone is the Lord by virtue of His being complete in all respects—according to the principle stated in [Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā] 1.5.10, due to His union with the will characterized as the desire to exist (*bubhūṣā*). Thus, in this respect...

Those which exist, such as jars and the like; this is what he expresses by the words "the elements and so forth" (*bhūtādi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of worlds, principles (*tattva*), entities (*bhāva*), and so on is intended. The word "those" (*te*) refers to the Sāṅkhya *puruṣas* and others. Now, one might object:
these do not appear as distinct from the perspective of the Supreme Lord as the subject (*pramātṛ*) in the same way that jars and other objects do.
Anticipating the objection that these [entities] do not manifest to us, and asking in relation to what they might be differentiated, he says: "in relation to the Mantreśvaras and others.
For they perceive them as distinct from themselves, from one another, and from the class of subjects (*grāhakavarga*). Although...
Even for cognizers such as ourselves, those [objects] manifest with differentiation because the scriptures possess authority;

nevertheless, when rooted in direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), the manifestation of scripture is grounded in that which appears commonly to all externally. Otherwise, however, it would be merely an independent conceptual construction (*svatantra-vikalpa*).
The intention is that [these powers] possess only a non-commonality with respect to the perceivers (*bhāsava*), and not an external existence;
thus it was said "with reference to Mantreśvara and others. He states this very point: "established by their own scripture" (*tadāgamasiddha*).
This means that, such being the case, they are established by their own scripture and not otherwise. || 6 ||

Now, granted that there may be a distinction between the Vijñānākala beings and the Supreme Lord due to the reason already stated, how can there be a mutual distinction among them? For, since they consist of consciousness (*bodha*), there is no difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*); and as for a difference in space or time, [that too cannot exist].
And because they are non-different with respect to their nature as consciousness, how is it that they are designated by the plural "they" (*te*)? To resolve this objection, the Sūtra states:
Even though they are identical in their characteristics such as enlightenment, they are mutually distinct;
likewise, through the differentiation of the Lord's will, they are the Vijñānakevalas.

Although their characteristics—such as being of the nature of consciousness, eternality, and omnipresence—are not distinct, nevertheless, the will of the Lord causes them to appear as such through differentiation, [thinking]:
"I, who am indeed of the nature of eternal, all-pervading pure consciousness, manifest myself as differentiated"; therefore, for them...

It is indeed logical that there is a mutual distinction between them, as well as from the objects of perception and other subjects. And in the scripture, these are called *vijñānākala*s, described as having a nature that is pure consciousness (*vijñānamātra*), devoid of agency, and free from the appearance of illusory distinctions (*māyīyabhedāvabhāsa*). Nor should it be argued that if...

If the will of the Lord makes even mere cognitions differentiated, then let the subjecthood of cognition itself be established at all times within the diverse category of objects such as jars and the like; for what is the purpose of postulating other intervening subjects, from the void down to the body? This is because:

It has been stated more than once that what is manifest cannot be denied. And indeed, there manifests the state of being a subject (*pramātṛbhāva*) with respect to the body, vital breath, and so forth, in such forms as "I am thin," "I am hungry," "I am happy," and "I am transcendent of all.
He introduces the meaning of the aphorism with the words beginning "inconceivable" (*acintya*). If [it is argued] that there is duality...

"How can there be the nature of consciousness and so forth? And if that [nature] exists, how can there be difference?"—such an objection regarding both difference and the mutual identity of the characteristics of consciousness and so forth should not be raised at all. Explaining that the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the Sūtra includes such qualities as eternity and omnipresence, he now defines what is relevant to that point:
"Of those whose nature is awakening," and so forth. Now, one might ask: if [the world] is thus a manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), how could there be permanence and so on?

Manifestation is merely the appearance of mutual differentiation; it is not something additional beyond that, like another appearance such as blue, by which impermanence would occur as it does for blue and the like. This is the context.

"He employs it for the sake of awakening. By using the word "and" (ca), he indicates that this matter is established without effort, while simultaneously including the object of knowledge (*prameya*). For sovereignty is the full form of consciousness;
thus, its non-manifestation is indeed impurity. He states this with the words, "but not pure. He demonstrates equality [between the two].
And by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "by those and," it indicates a reason;
[the ego-sense] is said to be "refuted" because its existence is accepted as being a function of the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*). The word "of this" refers to the person (*puruṣa*).

The connection is with "it was said by those Sāṅkhyas. Now, one might object: "But since the form found in the Sūtras and their commentaries also belongs to the Vidyeśvaras, from what [source] does this distinction arise? He replies: "Of them," meaning "of those who possess some degree of independence."

This means [it refers to those] who are endowed with subordinate autonomy (aparasvātantrya) that is favored by a portion of the autonomy consisting of both the supreme and the non-supreme (parāpararūpa).

The intended meaning is that the attainment of distinction occurs through the "principles of the Tantra" (tantrayukti), namely through the prior and subsequent deliberation characterized by looking ahead to what is yet to come. Now, one might object: if the state of belonging to that same class is equal, then by the word *prāya*...
Anticipating the objection, "How can it be called an analogy?", he says: "Because of worldly renown.

This is because the supreme teaching of the Lord—which transcends the world of illusion—is prior to the world; for when the experience [of that teaching] is correctly attained, there is the attainment of both supreme and non-supreme accomplishments (*siddhi*), even if it is not correctly [attained].

The diversity of the Gāṇapatyas [is such that], though they are not in any way of the nature of the *pāśva* (the tethered animal), when one wishes to explain that [diversity] to them, it must be explained by means of what is well-known to them;
thus, because it is well-known, that which belongs to the same class is used as an illustration, just as: "This cow of mine is mostly tamed."

"Thus. Here, the scripture is indeed that of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara). Now, precluding its belonging to the same category [as other systems], he clarifies its similarity [to them] with the words "and by the Sāṅkhyas. As for the phrase "these [others]," it refers to those who possess the state of being a *vijñānakevalin* solely through a specific initiation (*dīkṣā*)—distinct from that which effects the supreme unification—which consists merely in crossing over the path of Māyā.

It is attained through the power of contemplating the true nature of the pure *puruṣa*, which is devoid of the bondage of karma as described in the *Gītā* and other texts, and through the power of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* directed toward that ultimate goal. And its attainment is indeed a specific kind of experience (*bhoga*). For this very reason, it has been said:
Whoever should desire enjoyments in whatever place, he is directed to that very place;
he becomes a possessor of accomplishment through the power of the mantra.

And so forth. Therefore, the similarity that exists between [the soul] and the Sāṅkhya *puruṣas* is not absolute—that is, it does not extend to the point of being of the same genus; thus, a similarity that is merely general (*prāyika*) is appropriate. || 7 ||
Thus,
there is a loss of autonomy for consciousness.
Having thus described this portion regarding the *vijñānākala*s,
[the author] states the subject matter of the aphorism: "The lack of awareness even of one's own sovereignty" (3.2.4).
The Pralayākalas, whose nature is the non-recognition of [the categories] beginning with Śūnya, are agents;
they possess both the karma-mala and the māyīya-mala, which is conceptualized. (8)

He introduces this by establishing the connection with the words "In this way," and so forth. "One" means a single mass of atoms. Because its nature is consciousness (*bodha*), since this *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (I-consciousness) is the very soul and essence of consciousness, therefore, when [the object] is superimposed there, the superimposition of the [object's] own inherent nature also necessarily occurs.
And stating that this alone is logical, he provides a further supporting reason: "Being distinct," etc.

As long as something external to consciousness is the object of the reflective awareness of "I," so long, being itself non-luminous, how could it be reflected upon as "I"? For this [awareness] is a self-luminous reflection; therefore...
Self-luminosity must indeed exist even as something superimposed; he refutes this with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
Self-luminosity may well be superimposed, yet it remains real; it does not exist as if it were withdrawn, but rather persists with its own nature intact, despite the presence of other-luminosity.
This is because the nature of that which is to be known as "this" remains in its original state. Thus he says, "by the concealment of the state of consciousness.

Since the state of consciousness (*bodhatā*) has been concealed, for that very reason the word *abodha* (non-consciousness) from the Sūtra was mentioned in the Vṛtti in order to explain it; however, the "I-ness" (*ahantā*), whose nature is pure sovereignty, is clearly present when it is being superimposed.

For there is no manifestation of separateness— characterized by disjunction— nor of dependence in the form of "he enjoys" or "he acts," which is contrary to autonomy and characterized by the thought "I act thus only through the favor of another. Indeed, this is for the sake of attaining the descent of the knowledge of reality.

When such a manifestation, though being raised up with effort, does not arise, then that self-luminosity which belongs to the "I" aspect has its very nature discarded by the state of being an object (*vedyatā*), which consists in being illuminated by another— a contradictory condition— and thus it is called non-awareness (*abodhatā*).
However, that very continuity and autonomy which exist in that same aspect are rendered "other-made" by the manifestation of discontinuity and dependence, which are opposed to them.
(Page 324)

The agency of the void (śūnya) and the others has been stated. With the intention that the meaning of the sūtra beginning with "of them" (*teṣām*) and so forth is worthy of explanation precisely through the power of the explanation of the meaning of the *pralayākala*, he says "dissolution" (*pralaya*) and so forth.
The "impression of creation" (*sargasaṃskāra*) is the impression that brings about creation. [This is] according to the principle that will be stated.

Regarding the passage: "Both that which is to be known (*savedya*) and that which is not to be known (*apavedya*)" (3.2.15), this is an *vyavasthitavikalpa* (a restricted option). For instance, some possess the state of dreamless sleep (*suṣupta*) characterized by the unmanifested (*apavedya*), consisting of consciousness (*saṃvit*) contracted by portions such as the void (*śūnya*); others are obstructed by portions such as the intellect (*buddhi*).

Those consisting of consciousness (dhacinmaya) are those who, through their connection with the remaining common objects of cognition such as pleasure and so forth, experience the state of dreamless sleep (savedyasuṣuptapada); however, their nature as being dissociated from gross effects and instruments is one and the same as that of the Pralayākala. || 8 ||
In this way,

by the context of explaining the subject matter of this portion— namely, "the lack of awareness even regarding one's own freedom" (3.2.4)— the domain of the *kārmamala* (the impurity of action) has also been shown.

The stain of *māyā* is also occasional (*pākṣika*). Now, it is established by the aphorism that even in the absence of the two stains of *āṇava* and *kārmika*, there remains an exclusive domain for the stain called *māyā*:
"Even for those who possess consciousness and enjoy agency, when the *kārmika* stain has perished..."
Those who possess different Vedas and sacrificial formulas have the impurity of Māyā; they are the Vidyeśvaras.

Those who perceive pure consciousness alone as the Self, with the wonder "I am," possess from that very state unimpeded knowledge and action; from that very state they are free from the *āṇava* impurity and devoid of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of karma, because they have transcended transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). For them, there is no object of knowledge (*vedya*) external [to themselves].

And seeing that there is an effect to be accomplished, those who accept the vision of duality—such as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyā) and the Lords of Mantras (Mantra-īśvara)—are like the Lord [Śiva] himself, though they are joined with the impurity called *māyā*; such is the meaning of the sūtra.
He introduces this with the words "in [the state of] sovereignty" (*svātantrye*) and so forth. This refers to the differentiation of agency.

"Variety" (*vaicitryam*) refers to distinctness (*vailakṣaṇyam*) due to being the supreme agent. "Another mode" (*prakārāntaram*) means that which is other than the mode described as belonging to the *pralayākala* through conceptualization; this is what he [the author] states. [This refers to the state] of the *sakala*, as distinguished from the *pralayākala*, by means of *niyati* and the other [categories].
By stating this with the words "kartṛtā" and so forth on page 325, the distinction from the *vijñānākala* is expressed;
for through the yoga of awakening there is contact with *vidyā*, and through agency (*kartṛtā*) there is the state of *īśvara*— thus [the distinction applies] even to the states of *vidyeśvara*.

This has been shown here in the commentary (*vṛtti*). By that [means], namely by the impurity called *māyā*, the state of non-separateness from the object of knowledge—which is appropriate for Sadāśiva and Īśvara—is concealed; the meaning is that it manifests precisely as a state of separateness. Is fullness (*pūrṇatā*) not present here even in the supreme state (*parā*)? As before.

He explains the commentary [on the sūtra]: "And from Īśvara"; by the word "and" (ca), he implies that it is also from the Blessed Lord. He elucidates the word "therefore" (ataḥ) with the introductory phrase beginning with "full" (pūrṇa).
Demonstrating that the word "also" (api) has a displaced position in the sequence, he shows that while their atomicity is indeed inconceivable, it nevertheless follows by the force of logic.
This indicates that [the objection] might indeed be so. || 9 ||

Now, in order to state the scope of the three impurities (mala) simultaneously, the aphorism [states]: "For all transmigrating beings, including the gods and others, there are three kinds of impurity;
even among those, the karmic impurity alone is the primary cause of saṃsāra."
In brief, the meaning of the sūtra is clear; however, it has been explained in detail only in the commentary (*ṭīkā*).

Regarding the phrase "the cause of saṃsāra," the meaning is that all three impurities (*mala*), by virtue of being a collective totality (*sāmagrī*), are causes of saṃsāra, yet through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the karmic impurity (*kārmamala*) is the primary one.

"Performing various functions" means that the fourteen-fold creation of beings arises precisely from the diversity of the powers (śakti) consisting of the body and the senses; he clarifies this by stating "fourteen. He connects this with "therein" and "threefold.
With the words beginning "of these," such as "the Lords of Knowledge" (vidyeśvara), he explains the preeminence of even these fourteen.

Only when the *kārmamala* (the impurity of karma) is absent is the binding of the steps upon the ladder of non-transmigration (*asaṃsaraṇa*) granted; for this very reason, the removal of the *kārmamala* alone is taught with great effort in the Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Purāṇas, Mahābhārata, Upaniṣads, and other scriptures. "Distinction" (*vyatireka*) refers to the *kārmamala* as distinct from those two [the *āṇavamala* and *māyīyamala*].

It is not observed as distinct from or unmixed with that [cause]; nor does it perform its own effect by deviating from or disregarding those two, since the effect of that [cause] is also observed. Or rather, this is the very same meaning (page 326).
This has been stated by way of a different formulation. What is the basis for asserting primacy? He says: "It is due to karma.
For those two impurities do not exist when impelled by that single motivating factor called *saṃsāra*;
rather, they exist when impelled even by one who has transcended *saṃsāra*, characterized as a *vijñānākala*, a *mantreśvara*, and so forth.

Regarding those two, [the statement] "it exists through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth" means that there is another [process], namely the drying up of the preceding "vine of karma" (*pūrvakṛtakarmavallī*), which consists of the pacification of karmas that obstruct further ascent;
for indeed, there is nothing equal to initiation.
Thus it is said in the *Śrīlalitā*. The venerable Gurus have also stated:

"Even that which has been performed would not lead to fruit—like a seed sown in barren soil after initiation—if one does not abandon that single [practice] born from the conflict with a more powerful specific scripture."
"Thus, O Blessed One, for one who is unimpeded...
and so forth. Or, just as mantras perform acts such as subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), there is no passion or hatred involved therein.
Is it the removal of [impurities] such as the form of giving (*dāna*)? For even without that, [the mantra] acts like medicine for one afflicted by disease.
Likewise, is it the lack of desire for passion, ignorance, and so forth? Even so, the power of bondage is removed by means of the mantra; therefore—

"The defects, being a continuous stream from their own seeds, are not prevented even in one who has been initiated"—this [objection] is not a refutation. Thus, there are seven conceptualizations of the subject (*pramātṛ*) through three groups of three, one group of two, and one group of three; and of these, there are also innumerable [variations] due to the combination of conceptualizations and the relationship of primary and subordinate members (*aṅgāṅgitā*).
"Differentiation" is thus aphorized. || 10 ||

In order to reveal the twofold nature— through the distinction between manifestation and concealment— of that very state of totality (sakalāvasthā) which consists of the potentiality characterized by the simultaneity of the three impurities (malatraya), the author first declares its state of manifestation by means of a sūtra.

And this very principle of consciousness (cittattva), consisting of agency and impelled by *kalā*, exists as a limited quality subordinate to that which is insentient in nature, such as the void (*śūnya*). 11.

The reality of consciousness (cit-tattva), which consists of autonomy because its nature as awareness has its impurity removed by the predominance of the aspect of agency in gods and others, is empowered by the Lord through the power of *kalā* and [concealed] by impurity (*mala*).
(327) Even though it has been suppressed, the power arising from everything beginning with emptiness and ending with the body has been established; for it remains as something subordinate.

Because it is submerged within the objects of cognition—such as the body and so forth—which fall under the category of "this-ness" (*idantā*), the object of cognition is also contracted. For those who exist in the world, it is precisely this "this-ness"—expressed as "I am he who is fair-complexioned," "I am he who is happy," "I am he who is thirsty," or "I am he who is empty of all forms"—that flashes forth as the qualifier of the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*). This is that [very thing].

"The state of transmigratory existence consists of the triad beginning with waking"—this is the meaning of the aphorism. He provides an introduction to this by saying "of the transmigrator alone," which refers to the *sakala* (the conditioned soul). He begins [his exposition] regarding the self and the non-self, corresponding to the portions of "I" and "this."

First, it assumes the predominance of non-self (*anātma*) to this extent: "of one who possesses *prasaṅkhyāna*" means of one whose mind is concentrated; "of the dull-witted" means of the worldly person; or "if so" refers to the Vaiśeṣika conception of the self.
For they [the Vaiśeṣikas] hold that passion and the like, which are of the nature of attributes (*dharma*), are subordinate, inherent, and conjoined [with the self].

They maintain that the self possesses an eternal and all-pervading nature. Furthermore, the distinctness of the created [body] should be understood as being implied by the context, even though it is not explicitly touched upon by the words. The remainder here is clear. || 11 ||
Having thus described the process of emergence, the Sūtra states the state of subsidence,
as well as the primacy of agency and consciousness within the conscious self (cidātman):
"In the void and so forth, which possess those qualities, knowledge is characterized by absorption into that."

Furthermore, when agency is primary, the objective aspect consisting of the void and so forth necessarily becomes secondary; and when that non-conscious aspect has become secondary, there is likewise a lack of awareness regarding autonomy. (3.2.4)
Thus, by the casting aside of that activity of impurity, even for consciousness—

the conscious self whose primary nature is the essence of cognition— there arises primacy within its own essential form as pure consciousness; at that time, this [state], characterized by total immersion (*samāveśa*), exists as the true nature through its opposition to the impurity consisting of ignorance.
It is the knowledge characterized by correct and complete penetration; by the attainment of which one is a *jñānin*,

and through the practice of which one becomes a *yogin* by acquiring the sovereign power (*vibhava*) whose nature consists of the infinite attributes of consciousness within the body, vital breath, and so forth.

It occurs as follows: this is what is meant— that when the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) [is established] precisely through the direction of autonomy by the power of the reflective awareness of pervasiveness, eternity, and so forth.

When [the subject] remains as if emerging from the void and other states that have been made objects of cognition, that is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta); yet even then, the latent impression (saṃskāra) of the void and so forth still exists—thus, it is indeed the equality of the non-distinct state beyond the fourth. But when [the subject exists] as the self whose essence is dense sovereignty, characterized by such qualities as eternality and pervasiveness that have been fully realized through the sense of "I" (ahambhāva)—

When the body—from the void (*śūnya*) to the final element—is pierced by the *siddharasa* (the perfected elixir) because it is an object of cognition, such that it seems to fall away, that is the state of the Fourth (*turya*). Furthermore, when this element of the vital breath, the body, and so forth, is pierced and thoroughly permeated by the *saṃvidrasa* (the elixir of consciousness), it is made to decay like the element of gold [is transmuted]. That [by which this occurs]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. This translation reflects the full syntactic structure as it stands.)
When only its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) appears like a swift flow of rasa, even then that state is the stage beyond the fourth (*turyātītadaśā*).
Both of these states are *samāveśa* (total immersion), for the sake of attaining which other [teachings] are instructed. As it is sung:
Having begun with the words, "Those who, having fixed their minds on me...
(12.2), [the Lord] continues with, "Now, in order to fix the mind... (12.9).
Thus, the praise, prostration, meditation, worship, and so forth of the Supreme Lord are merely its offshoots;
for their true essence consists in becoming humble, making one's own self a subordinate quality, and bringing about the predominance of the nature of the Supreme Lord.
"If you are unable even to practice [meditation], be intent on my work" (Gītā 12.10),
and so forth; however, upon the fall of the body, there is only the state of Śiva as a single mass, and at that time, no such conventional usage as "absorption" (*samāveśa*) exists.

"Someone" (kaścit) is the summary meaning of the aphorism. He introduces it with the words "of that very [self]. He establishes the correspondence between the aphorism and its commentary with the words "in the previous aphorism," and so forth. In the previous aphorism, agency was stated;
that very [agency] was merely attributed to the body, and its subordinate status was previously explained; however, here—

Because the state of being the primary [factor] exists therein as its counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), that which was stated in the Sūtra by means of the genitive case has been explained in the Commentary (*vṛtti*) by demonstrating the subordinate nature (*paścādgurutva*) of emptiness and so forth, even though they were indicated there by the nominative case; however, it was not stated directly. For [it is not the case that] the state of being the agent...
There is a commentary stating, "This refers to predominance. Now, if it is argued that emptiness and so forth are made subordinate later on, [it is said]:
"For indeed, before washing away the mud..."

By this rule, is primacy indicated by the mention of the first [term]? He says: "The state of being under investigation. That is to say, that which is the subject at hand here and must be investigated is the primary or principal [element]. "The state of being a subordinate quality" means that it constitutes the body of the investigation following upon that [principal element]. But is this not clear?

Why was the predominance of agency (*kartṛtva*) not shown directly in the commentary? Why this indirect manner (*bhaṅgī*)? He replies: "In the case of agency" means that if agency were primary, then [the object such as] emptiness would necessarily be secondary; but if that [emptiness] were primary, then agency would be secondary. When this is established by the commentary, it follows the logic of the scale's depression and elevation (*tulānatyunnatinyāya*).

It is obtainable. For this application—that this mode of conduct must necessarily be performed in accordance with the meaning of the Sūtra—is understood through such a principle (*nyāya*). If it is asked, "What is gained by this understanding?", it is said:
"Otherwise. If this principle were not understood, then in the preceding Sūtra...

In the passage "kalodbalitam" (3.2.11), although emptiness (*śūnya*) and the others are subordinate (*guṇa*), their status as primary (*pradhāna*) is implied by the mention of their correlative relationship; however, that implication would not have been made explicit in the commentary (*vṛtti*) were it not for this principle.

By being shown, it becomes manifest. In the commentary on the preceding sūtra, the subordination (*upasarjanatva*) of agency was indeed stated explicitly; and by the principle that "the predominance of emptiness and so forth is understood through its necessary concomitance," that predominance which must be predicated of emptiness and so forth [is here established].

In the previous sūtra, that meaning was implied; however, the fact that "the quality of being a subordinate element" (*guṇatva*) must be stated is here explicitly mentioned by its own name in this sūtra—this is what the word *tu* ("however") indicates in the phrase "here, however" (*iha tu*). That quality of being a subordinate element, having been stated in the sūtra, is explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of its nominative case designation. Now, for what purpose [is this]?

This has been explained by the first [verse]. He says: "By way of being primary. The nature of independent consciousness (*svatantra-bodha*) remains eternally primary; however, that [primacy] was eclipsed in the preceding verse by the manifestation of the primacy of Śūnya and the others, which was implicitly established there. Therefore, if it experiences a state of non-primacy...

For she indeed "emerges," which refers to the first designation. It is he—emptiness and so forth—who acts in this way by assuming both the predominance and non-predominance of the self; for his predominance exists upon the plane of saṃsāra.

(Page 330) By stating "when indeed," he recalls the very principle previously explained, namely that [the state of being] an animal and [the state of being] a fallen one have been demonstrated. Regarding "independent": who is this one who is celebrated as the independent consciousness, the subject in the form of "I"?

When, in the process of reflection, that form is filled out by means of the body and so forth— as in "I am he who is fair-complexioned," or "I am he who is hungry," and so on— then the body and such alone become primary, and the nature of consciousness becomes suppressed; thus, only the object of knowledge (vedya) becomes primary, not the nature of the knower (vedaka).

But when one begins to inquire into the true nature of the body and so forth, [realizing] that it is indeed the dense light of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*), then— having been made of the very essence of awareness— that [body] appears as permeated by its flavor (*rasa*) throughout, from the void (*śūnya*) up to the physical body; thus, through practice, the attributes of consciousness belong to it.
The specific powers, entering correctly, bring forth the supernatural manifestations (*vibhūtis*); even in the absence of prior practice,
there occurs at that very moment an immersion characterized by the sequence of the emergence of bliss, trembling, sleep, pervasion, and whirling.
The attainment of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). As it has been said:
"Even when [the goal] is attained, they succeed; there is no dispute about this," and so forth.
"This very [initiation] is the initiation for piercing the ultimate reality"—thus it has been said;
and this is the initiation of liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā). (Svacchandatantra-kalpa 32)
Thus say the Gurus; and the Blessed One has also said:
"For one who knows this according to reality, initiation leading to nirvāṇa occurs without doubt, even if it is devoid of oblations of sesame and clarified butter" (Pārameśvaratantra 25).

Thus [it is said]. Enough of this for now. Therefore he says: "Cognition is superimposed upon the void and so forth. He shows that this is not a superimposition like that of grains within a granary. By that agency, the void and so forth—which had remained as one with it through the force of effortless [identification]—is [perceived] by that very [agency].
By means of agency,
the nature of consciousness— which is unconditioned by space, time, attributes, or forms— is directed toward and fixed upon that which is intended to be defined by its characteristics.
Or, it is a transitive verb (*dvikarmaka*) because [the state] is attained preceded by intense attachment;
thus, that which is being intensely attached to is the nature of the universal self (*viśvātmakatva*).
(Page 331)

Since it belongs to consciousness, it too accepts that [consciousness]. Thus, "of the atom" (*aṇoḥ*) means that the relationship between the one who enters and the object entered is logical upon the cessation of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding the self; this is the sense. "In the visions of the particular" (*viśeṣadarśaneṣu*) refers to those systems where Śākta non-duality is primary;
for in these, the "particular"—characterized as *śakti*—is shown, that is, directly realized, by the self.
In these [states], one is led. Regarding "the radiance of knowledge" (*jñānollāsa*):
it is called "radiance" because of the departure of ignorance and the expansion of non-dual awakening; thus, it is established as "knowledge.
As for "the fourth" (*turya*): even the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), which consists of the ultimate consummation of the attainment of this very stage, is described in that same [text].

However, he indicates that by establishing emptiness (*śūnya*) and so forth through exclusion (*vyatireka*), the state beyond the fourth (*turyātītatā*)—described therein as "the state of the pure self," "partlessness" (*niṣkalatā*), and "pure consciousness" (*śuddhacaitanya*)—is shown in the general philosophical systems (*sāmānyadarśana*) which perceive that single form transcending all else. Now, [one might ask: was this not already mentioned in the preceding aphorism? Here...
Since the beginning was made to explain the subordinate and primary status of agency itself,

how is it that the portion of the sūtra "and of consciousness" (bodhasya ca) is not suspected [to refer to that], and when the commentary (vṛtti) appropriately states "having attained the nature of agency" (kartṛmayatām āpannasya), why does it say "the nature of consciousness" (bodhamayatām)? Anticipating this doubt, it has already been stated:
This object of knowledge (prameya), having been briefly reflected upon again for the sake of its resolution, is made the reason [for what follows].
The connection is as follows: because of that very reason which was just stated, this was said in the Sūtra; and that very point has been explained in this manner. || 12 ||
Now, one might object: "In this way, let the fourth state (turya) or that which transcends it belong to the Lord (pati);

however, the forms of the states of deep sleep, dreaming, and waking—which are shown in the scriptures according to the varying degrees of descent into consciousness for the bound soul (paśu)—must be explained. Keeping this in mind:

Establishing the true nature of deep sleep— which occurs immediately after the descent from the fourth state— through three verses, he first provides the foundational context for that initial deep sleep with one verse:
"In the void, which is the locus of the 'I'-sense and agency where the intellect and other faculties are absent..."
The emptiness of the object of knowledge consists in that which possesses only unmanifest formative predispositions. || 13 ||

The commentator will demonstrate this very "binding of the seat" (pīṭhabandha) with the words "the state of deep sleep is of both natures," and so forth. This [section] serves as the foundational platform for that which will be described in the third verse as being "of the nature of both. Here, the principle of consciousness (saṃvittattva) is...

Veiling its own true nature, it appears as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)— in the form of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth up to the body, and as jars and other external objects. And yet, this is all one and the same.

This is the unfolding of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*); yet here, neither succession nor differentiation exists in reality, for both appear solely through that freedom. Such being the case, that which is the aspect of the obscuration of the essential nature of the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*) is precisely this.
By virtue of disregarding the arising and destruction of subsequent parts,

it shines forth and comes to rest as an unmixed manifestation— just as in states such as dissolution, meditative absorption, sleep, or fainting— and therein alone it finds its footing as the "I" within the state of agency.
When that state occurs— due to the absence of clarity in reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), being characterized by a slight degree of impurity, having the nature of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*),
lacking the form well-known in the world, or being an insentient object of cognition (*avedya*) consisting of a negandum— then that state remains as nothing but the residual awareness of "it is not."

Just as the realization "I am nothing" implies a general state of being, so too that which has become the remainderless object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is called "empty" (*śūnya*). For this very reason, the scripture states:
"That which is non-empty is said to be empty, and emptiness is called non-existence."
That should be known as non-existence where all things have come to an end.

This very state of being a residual impression (*saṃskāraśeṣatā*) is everywhere described as the non-existence of one entity within another entity; it is not, however, the destruction of things that exist in their entirety, as has been stated more than once.

He introduces the meaning of the Sūtra by establishing its connection with what precedes it through the words "Thus," and so forth. The intention is that he will elaborate on this introduction in the third chapter. It has been stated that due to the absence of the effects—the elements (*bhūta*) and subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—as well as the thirteen instruments (*karaṇa*), there is the non-existence of everything.

By stating "in the self which is devoid of intellect and so forth" and "the emptiness of the knowable," he refutes the objection by repeating the opponent's doubt with the words "even though," and so on. Indeed, even if that [Self] exists, one might raise the doubt that it becomes an object of cognition, just like the reality of consciousness such as Paramaśiva. To this [he replies]:

The other objection has indeed been refuted by the passage beginning with "nanu" and ending with "tadātmatayā. And the reason for that is stated as "by way of being a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). The phrase "without distinction" means that even though there is a difference, it does not manifest. For this is precisely what constitutes being a latent impression; this has now been made clear.
Having thus restated the objection that [recollection occurs] by the power of what was previously experienced, he refutes it with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
Consciousness itself is contracted.
(Page 333)

Since its nature is consciousness, how can there be any objectivity in that which is empty? Now, it may be argued that objectivity belongs to consciousness itself when it comes into contact with the shadows of various appearances; however, there is no other object whatsoever, nor even another appearance of a body.

Thus [it is said]. He refutes this by raising an objection with the words "śūnyarūpa" and so forth. The sense is that whatever is known through worldly consensus must also be something additional [to the object]; however, that is not present there, and on the contrary, its negation is perceived.
This is intended to explain the particle *eva* found in the commentary (vṛtti) by the phrase "tāvataiva."

He shows the similarity [of this state] with the Sāṅkhya puruṣas by saying "and of the Sāṅkhya puruṣas. However, he states the distinction by saying "only" (kevalam). By the phrase "due to being free from obscuration" (nirāvaraṇāt), he accepts that the nature of reflective awareness (vimarśarūpatā) is innate; yet that [innate nature] does not exist in the state of the Vijñānakevalin. This is because it belongs to the realm of Māyā.

[This refers to] that which is produced by the arts and sciences. "Because of the absence of a substratum" means that the state of being a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) exists only on the level of the objective portion (*vedyabhāga*), but not in consciousness (*saṃvit*), because there [in consciousness], the entire mass of the knowable has attained identity with it in its totality; for this very reason, there is an absence of latent impressions.

Furthermore, the intention here is this: in the worldly states such as waking and so forth, that state [of deep sleep] does not exist as their "creation" (sṛṣṭi), meaning it does not function as their seed.
Thus, the nature of the "witnessed" form of deep sleep—which is characterized by being a seed—does not exist here; however, it certainly exists elsewhere. This is the underlying thought.

He corroborates this very point with another scriptural authority by saying "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). Since it is taught that the void (*śūnya*) is merely contracted consciousness (*bodhamātra*), its nature as a void is not of the form of a clearly manifest object of knowledge;
therefore, [the Lord] is endowed with the supreme power (*parā śakti*) whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
"In the two states, the All-pervasive One shines... (Spanda-kārikā 2.2).

Thus, the existence of an object of knowledge (*vedya*) is clearly stated for the states of waking and dreaming. However, because that [object] is absent in deep sleep and the fourth state (*turya*), they consist of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*). Due to the absence of that [object], this distinction exists here within the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*).

Within the Lord, whose defining characteristic is pure consciousness, that which flashes forth as "I am this"— therein, it is precisely the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā) that first implies a negation consisting of the mutual differentiation between consciousness and objective entities. In that context, since negation is subordinate, consciousness remains predominant.
Within the state of being the subject, there is the status of the Great Lords of Mantra and the state of the Vijñānākala,
depending on whether there is union with or separation from reflective awareness.
When negation is predominant, there is the state of the subject as emptiness; when existence is predominant, there is the state of being "with parts" (sakala).
Anticipating the objection that there may be another distinction between this [subject] and the Sāṅkhya Puruṣa, he refutes it with the verse beginning "sauṣupta" (13).
Explaining the remaining portion of what must be said regarding the empty cognizer alone, [the author] establishes the stage of the second deep sleep with a sūtra:
"The internal function of the senses is considered to be the impeller of the vital breaths and so forth."
Or rather, within the vital breath called *jīvana*, there is the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) consisting of the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*).

This empty subject is consecrated by the agency consisting of the form of "I-ness" [the *ahaṃtā*] over the group of the organs of cognition and action— which is the manifestation of the power of *vidyā* and *kalā*—
by virtue of its external function characterized by the perception of external objects and the creation of objective domains.
That internal function, which is distinct and unique to each [organ], by which the single air— expanded through the fivefold activities such as breathing—
attains a fivefold nature; that function, characterized as life, belongs to that group of senses.
According to the principle stated in *Svacchandatantra* 1.6, "Since this group of instruments belongs to the insentient," that [power] which,
by virtue of its own immersion (*svāveśa*), causes [the insentient] to arise is called the *jīva*. That is of such a nature...

The activity that arouses that void is its "life-function" (*jīvanakriyā*); or rather, it is that internal, common form of activity which arouses the functions of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth within the powers of the senses. In the ultimate sense, this activity belongs only to the agent, not to insentient things; therefore, that alone is life. When, however—

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself is the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*); even then it is thus. But at that time, the vital breath itself is the individual soul (*jīva*), because the penetration of the ego-sense occurs therein. Furthermore, this [entity] which migrates to other wombs is denoted by the term "the group of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), since it consists here of the pentad beginning with the vital breath, the two groups of sense organs, and the faculty of determination (*niścaya*).

The third [verse] reveals the intellect (*dhī*) which has accepted another internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). He introduces the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) with the words "another," and so forth. The word "own" (*sva*) refers to those things connected to the nature of the agent of emptiness; because they possess the very nature of instruments (*karaṇa*), it is due to their impelling that [the intellect acts]. The word "that" (*sā*) [in the aphorism] is used through the metaphorical identification of cause and effect.

Because it brings about the functioning of the senses in the form of the vital breath (*jīvana*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) itself is called "the functioning of the senses" (*akṣavṛtti*). Furthermore, the purpose for this metaphorical designation is stated to be [to show] that the senses are derived from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkārika*).
This is the indication that [this] alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). "Internal" means consisting of the impetus of the notion of "I.

By this, following the recurrence of the term "in the void" (*śūnye*) from the preceding sūtra, that "I-ness" (*ahantā*) which exists in the void—being the cause of the functioning of the senses and other internal organs such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—is what constitutes life, since the functioning of the senses takes that form.

The meaning of the sūtra has been indicated as follows: that which is the cause of the soul (jīva) is characterized by the act of living. Having thus explained it through figurative usage (upacāra), [the author] intends to show that, in the ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ), because the instrument (karaṇa) possesses the nature of an agent (kartṛ) through its involvement [with the agent], it possesses activity precisely through that action—just like a sword—and with this intention, he states it according to its primary sense in the sūtra.

Applying the term *vṛtti* in another way, he explains it with the words "or else" (*athavā*). In the previous explanation, the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound within the *vṛtti* was as follows: that which is called "living" (*jīvana*), common to the capacities of all the senses, consisting of the fivefold activities such as breathing (*prāṇana*) and so forth, and which serves as the cause for the differentiation into [the specific vital breaths] such as *prāṇa*.

That void (*śūnya*) whose activity consists of the fivefold operation characterized by the impulse of "I-am-ness" (*ahamiti-saṃrambha*) is described as such. Now, however, the analysis of the compound is as follows: it is the common impelling force of the vital airs (*prāṇa* etc. denoted by the term "life-force" (*jīvana*), which is shared by all the powers of the senses.

The "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which is denoted by the term "internal operation" (*antarvṛtti*); [the compound means] "that of which this is the characteristic. For that [characteristic] belongs to him alone because he is its agent, and not because they (the senses) are its cause—this is the intended meaning. He states this with the words "because it is inherent in that" (*tatsamavetatvāt*), which means "because it is present in the form of the agent. The word "iti" indicates a reason; for since...

In this way, their action is also related to him; for this reason, in this position, that living being (jīva) is made the referent of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as the external object of the compound. Otherwise, how could the action of one thing be related to another? This is the underlying intention. The phrase "of those not distinct from this" refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which were previously raised as objections.

The meaning is: "of those that have attained identity with the fivefold functioning. By this, it is meant that through that which arouses the fivefold [winds] beginning with *prāṇa* in all the sense organs, and by way of being the cause of other transformations such as *nāga* and so forth, and further, by way of the wheel of the vital breath (*prāṇacakra*) consisting of the modified and unmodified [winds], [the breath pervades] the pores of the skin.

The internal, common group of five powers (*śakti*) consists of the body composed of the wheels of the channels of the *yantra* and the movement of the *yantra*; it impels the group of vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth which are to be impelled,
