as well as the group of senses which are the impellers, and the void-I-consciousness (*śūnyāhaṃtā*) which presides over them.

(Page 336) It has been stated that the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) is the present [state]. In this regard as well—according to the view that the egoity of the vital breath (*prāṇāhaṃtā*) [is the subject]—the abiding of the eightfold city is accepted by everyone. However, some scriptures...
They have said this even regarding the state of "void egoity" (śūnyāhaṃtā). As they have said:
"Even in the absorption of the dissolved void (līnaśūnya-samādhi), the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) persists.
And thus, since it is so, the construction [of the sentence] is as follows: that egoity in the void [consists of] the vital breath and so forth—

The impeller (*prerikā*) consists of the activity of the senses and is of the nature of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*). Alternatively, he explains the sūtra beginning with "When," etc.; that is to say, the word *prāṇa* in the sūtra is a general term.
By the words "Then," etc., he shows that these two sūtras serve as the introduction to the subsequent sūtra. And then:

The pentad beginning with *prāṇa*, being impelled by the *ahaṅkāra* and the *paramāhaṅkāra*, is not to be counted as equal to them; rather, the meaning is that it is presided over by them. To explain what kind [of pentad] it is, he says "projected," and so forth. The pentad, together with the triad of categories in their causal form, is the substrate for consciousness (*saṃvedana*).

By its very nature, that which is to be presided over—namely, the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body) consisting of the vital breaths and so forth—is presided over by the state of the subject as "I. Previously, however, because the *liṅga* (the subtle body) is most subtle, the implication of the *tanmātras* was not explicitly shown; and for that very reason of subtlety, it was not mentioned earlier.

The ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and the mind (*manas*) projected by it are not counted as being on the same level; rather, they are said to be presided over by the ego. He demonstrates their grossness through the term "possessing power" (*śaktimat*), whereas previously, by saying "of the powers alone," their state of being most subtle was shown. For [the powers] belong to one whose body is delicate.
That [subtle body] is merely a preliminary sketch; however, the most gross body is what completes it from above.

That very [gross body], moving primarily through the intermediate places of birth, is called the "transmigrating being" (saṃsārī). For that very reason, its loosening must be brought about through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and initiation (dīkṣā), and so forth.

And by means of karma, through the surrender of the components of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) to the Lord of Causes, [the process occurs] in the form of the emergence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), abiding within the mind, ego, and intellect—as stated in the verse: "Thus, some [hold that] the five subtle elements and the internal organ [arise]" (Svacchandatantra 4.19). For this reason, some maintain that the pentad of subtle elements constitutes the internal organ.

They call it the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka) because it appropriates the vital breaths and so forth through the subtle element of touch; therefore, despite this variety of views regarding its constituents, there is no difference in the underlying reality. || 14 ||

(337) Regarding that for which two sūtras serve as the foundation, the sūtra is stated in order to characterize the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*): "The state of deep sleep, which consists of merely that much [remaining], is like cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*)."
It is both perceivable and imperceptible, and it is joined with or free from the impurity of māyā.

When there is a state of rest in the pure void that is mere emptiness, which is the repose of the ego-sense, and when it is likewise in the vital breath (prāṇa), then consciousness is rendered as if asleep by Māyā, which manifests the descent of impurity; and since it has not been awakened even by Kalā and Vidya, he is truly and profoundly asleep.

Being (*bhāva*) is, for its part, the manifestation whose essence is the cause of activity; and action (*karman*), being of the nature of an act, is for its part the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*) whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). However, the author of the *Vivṛti*, considering the word "pada" (state/foot) to be obtainable from the context according to the subsequent sūtra, [interprets it] as referring to this [state] of deep sleep as "this" (*idam*).
He conceives of [this] as a thorough understanding (*vyutpatti*). For this very reason, the first [state] is beyond the range of cognition (*apavedya*) and free from the impurity called *māyā*;

the second, however, is the opposite of that. The nature of dissolution (*pralaya*) is entirely of this same form; yet, in that case, there is the destruction and non-reappearance of the body and its duration for an extremely long time, whereas here, it is of that [body].
There is non-performance and lack of proficiency. Furthermore, if it is due to exhaustion, there is sleep;

if due to injury, imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and so forth, there is fainting (*mūrchā*); if due to the consumption of intoxicants and the like, there is intoxication, insanity, and so forth; and if [the action] arises from the force of an effort instigated by independence...

"Samādhi" and so forth are the intermediate subdivisions of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*). Because it has all things as its object, it was previously described as "accompanied by cognition" (*savedya*); such is the meaning of the aphorism. Having now established the introductory framework (*pīṭhabandha*), he concludes with two verses. By this, he reminds us that he will conclude what preceded.
He declares that these three sūtras constitute a single great sentence (mahāvākya) because they have as their meaning the definition of the state of deep sleep (sauṣupta).

Since there is an absence of any manifest object of knowledge possessing form, even though the two powers of limited knowledge (vidyā) and action (kalā) project a separate, constructed object of knowledge, they indeed conceal the very nature of the principle of consciousness (saṃvittattva).

With the intention that these two possess the nature of the impurity called *māyā* by virtue of their aspect as obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), he says, "in the form of *vidyā* and *kalā*. The connection is that in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), there is also consciousness (*saṃvedana*).

Furthermore, in the Sūtra, the two ablative cases in "due to the absence of the object of knowledge" (*vedyābhāvāt*) and "due to the presence of the object of knowledge" (*vedyasadbhāvāt*) [indicate this].
This indicates the relationship between cause and effect. By the phrase "the limbs of the previous octad," scripture (*āgama*) is indicated;

for that [state] arises from sleep due to the lack of attention to the respective objects of knowledge, the respective sense organs, and so forth, by virtue of the variety of such things as awakening from that dream.
(Page 338) "When consciousness sleeps in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is predominant in this or that particular aspect"—

such is the traditional scripture (*āgama*). [This refers to] the previous [statement] regarding the state of being situated in the functions (*vṛtti*) such as the vital breath, which was [expressed] with a different grammatical case (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

That must be considered in relation to the forest-dweller. By the phrase "by them," it is intended that there should be no difference from the waking state or from a dream by means of [objects] such as form and so forth. As for the connection with time, its nature as duration and so on is indeed remembered therein.

Now, one might object: "Let there be another state of deep sleep (suṣupti) that is devoid of clearly perceived objects; yet, even though there is no difference in its lack of connection with clearly perceived objects, what is the distinction between the states of dreaming and waking? Anticipating this doubt, he first defines the state of dreaming.
Even on the path of the mind alone, because of the delusion that things are objects of the senses, the vivid manifestation of entities is considered the state of dream. (16)
The mention of the "senses" (*akṣa*) is an indication for all the external sense-faculties. This is the meaning:

the physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*), such as the eyeballs and the five fingers, are perceived as motionless even while one is asleep. Then [one thinks], "I see a beloved woman with my eye," or "I beckon her with my hand."
In a dream, there exists a cognition characterized by a vivid manifestation, primarily consisting of a creation produced by the Lord at that very moment;

and in that state, the mind alone is active. However, when [the dream] has arisen as something previously created, it depends on that very [previous creation] to such an extent, while regarding the aspect of the objects of the senses, it shares a commonality with the creation of the Supreme Lord.

The summary of the meaning is as follows: in the waking state, because reflective awareness persists with stability amidst the appearance of other [objects] such as stability, there is no sublation; therefore, it does not possess the nature of an error. He introduces the meaning of the aphorism with the words "the seed of the universe," [referring to] how, in dissolution and deep sleep respectively, all the previously mentioned [elements] without exception—

The word "universe" (viśva) generally refers to this. Here, even that which is merely mind (manomātra) should be understood as being permeated by the seeds of the senses and their objects, which are established as parts of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka). It is described thus primarily with respect to its state as a creator; however, its state as an enjoyer exists even in the waking state. Thus [is meant] "that which."
The connection [is as follows]: by the phrase "the eye, etc. and so forth, he explains the meaning of the word *mātra* (only/merely) as referring to delusion (*vibhramatā*).
The intention is that this is because such a thing is observed even in the case of Īśvara, despite his lack of desire [to act].
(Page 339)

As for what was said [in the verse], "Otherwise, however, creation would proceed from independence," and so forth—it has been elucidated that the meaning here is: by that power of the Supreme Lord, which consists of action and assumes the form of the mind (*manas*) with respect to the object. [The phrase] "touched by the ointment of accomplishment" (*siddhāñjana*) and so forth refers to this.
"Dependent upon. "In another way as well" means: let it not be thus; it will exist in a different manner. "That" refers to that other manner. "And it is not so here" means:
even by those [objects] which are apprehended as continuous during the waking state, they are not seen [to exist] even by those who are authoritative (āpta).
Because of the non-occurrence of the *vāgbhava* [syllable]. He explains the commentary beginning with "at another time" (*kālāntare*) with the words "if, however" (*yadi ca*).

"It has been stated" means that what you yourself have stated illuminates my position while simultaneously contradicting your own statement; such is the intention of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). "In this way, this [is so]" refers to our own view; this is the underlying thought (*ākūtam*).
The meaning is that it appears in the mind (*manasi*) as such, and this is not an error; rather, it is an appearance within a conceptualized other-appearance (*vikalpite 'vabhāsāntare*).

"Previously" refers to the manyfold investigation into the nature of being either erroneous or non-erroneous. "Nevertheless," even though they do not perceive [the object] in that way, it is indeed non-apprehension (*akhyāti*)—insofar as it consists in incomplete apprehension—that constitutes error.

He reminds us of the truth (*tattva*). The phrase "even from that" means that it is not only appropriate to explain this according to the view of non-existent manifestation (*asatkhyāti*) as previously done, but that its being the root [of error] is also established by the view of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) which we have accepted. By that... [the sense is concluded].

[The connection is] "by the subtle [body]" and "because of perfect awareness and vision. Here too, there is the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*) as in the waking state, and therein also exists the state of being a creator (*sraṣṭṛtā*) as in the dream state; nevertheless, he shows that the systematic arrangement is determined by predominance with the words "but in the waking state," etc., [and] "even for the Lord."

Even the state of being an enjoyer that belongs to the sacrificial animal actually belongs to the Lord alone, according to the principle stated in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*: "For such is the nature of reality" (AP 20). In this context, the word "there" (*tatra*) refers to the waking state; here, there is an internal syntactic break. The word "here" (*atra*) likewise refers to the waking state.
"Stated" refers to the scriptures (*āgama*) and so forth. "Because it is included within that" means that it indeed becomes the very nature of the creator. For this very reason, (page 340)
"Having divided himself by himself"—
in this context,
[it means] "having created various kinds of entities."
Thus, having stated that the power of creation (*sarga-śakti*) is the root cause, he subsequently stated its inseparable concomitant,
the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*):
"The Lord of All, consisting of all things, is the enjoyer and the instigator within the dream."
Thus [ends section] 16.

Having thus described that creation as the state [of consciousness] in a dream, its objects as the domain, and the subjectivity directed toward those objects as the dream-state, he defines the waking state as the subjectivity whose objects are clearly perceived things, which is the opposite of that [dream-state].
That common creation which, by being the object of all the senses, exists externally as something stable, belongs to all subjects; that is the waking state. || 17 ||

"Emanation is waking"— because it is said that the subject (*pramātṛ*) whose object is that emanation "wakes" by virtue of being joined with the destruction of sleep, which is the cause of delusion, one should therefore understand that the state of waking is the state of subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*). For these five [states] belong to subjectivity as produced by the differentiation of objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

The states (avasthās) have been described in the Āgamas. He explains that, as in the previous case, the nature of dreaming is extended by way of analogy to the waking state with the words "even in waking" (jāgare 'pi). For this very reason, the mutual interpenetration of the states is said in the Āgamas to have many branches. || 17 ||
To state that what is to be adopted lies above [this], he declares these three to be objects of abandonment:

"This triad is to be abandoned because of the predominance of the agency of the vital breaths and so forth, due to their connection with pleasure, pain, and the like, which primarily consist in the loss or increase of that [agency]. (18)
When the self as agent is rendered secondary, then— on account of the primacy of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth relative to that [agent]—

the seeker of liberation regards even the three states of that [self], which has lost its independence, as fit for rejection, due to the various labors of abandoning or acquiring objects of pleasure and pain arising from the increase of its power.
The meaning of the sūtra is "one conceives [them]. He introduces that [sūtra] with the words "of these too," meaning "of all five" (page 341).
By the general statement "as far as it introduces," he indicates that [the text] is to be accepted, even though this is already understood;

for he will say later, "by implication, it is not excluded. In the phrase "or indeed the vital breath," the word "or" (vā) is used in relation to the alternative "or the void" (śūnya). Now, if there is indeed independence through the Self, and that very...
If [the Self] is thus transcendent, then what quality does It possess such that it is stated in the Sūtra that [agency] is a quality?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "That which is pure. By the word "that" (tat), he now indicates that for transmigrating beings, [agency] is not its object at all, even though it is being superimposed.
The sense is that even in play, among children, he is like a king; "by that much" means by that measure. For this very reason, the venerable Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa said:
"Whatever joy whatsoever is seen here, even throughout the three worlds..."
"That [is] the drop (*bindu*) of which... (Sta. Ci. 61).

And in the *Pratipattiviveka*, it is shown that in every case regarding worldly and scriptural duties, there is an underlying permeation of inner devotion, bliss, and faith; otherwise, the duties such as cognition (*bodha*) and so forth as stated by the Naiyāyikas—

"It would not even ascend into the state of form; thus, for men, the scripture would become a mere teaching, empty of that [reality]. By this, he explains the sūtra passage beginning with "the abandonment of that," and the word "etc. (ādi) refers to [the following]: "but in every way..."
By this [it is meant]. It will be stated in the sūtra: "The bliss of existence... (4.1.6).
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "the fourth and so forth" (*turyādi*), he also accepts that which transcends it (*tadatītatā*). Thus it has been said.

In the Sūtra and its Commentary: "For when there is a complete immersion [of consciousness], since the body, vital breath, and so forth lack predominance, and thus sufferings such as hunger and fatigue—brought about by their own power—do not arise, one should cover over hunger. (Svacchandatantra 4.8)

By this logic, there is also the happiness consisting of the satisfaction and repose born from that [cessation], which takes the form of even a slight drop of the bliss of sovereignty, indifference, and non-agency; thus, there is indeed nothing but the nature of supreme bliss.
And furthermore, as follows:
"In the section [beginning with] '(page 342) sādhāraṇo'nyathā caiśaḥ sargaḥ (4|1|11)'... || 18 ||

Now, one might object: "The state of being subordinate to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth is the cause of what is to be abandoned (*heya*); and that [subordination] has been stated to exist only in the three [lower centers], not above them. Therefore, it would follow that for one who has entered [the higher state], there is only the falling away of the body, and no emergence [from it]. With this concern in mind, [the author] proceeds to effect the division of the vital breaths and so forth.
There are two verses; first, then, he states the narrative concerning the three Vedas: "The breath consisting of prāṇa and apāna exists individually during both sleep and waking;
that which consists of their cessation is called samāna, as in the state of deep sleep and during the equinoxes. (19)

"Prāṇa" refers to that function of consciousness (cid-vṛtti) known as "breathing," which moves within the internal vital air and is called "life. Having the nature of a general vibration, it bestows non-inertness upon the inert body and so forth;
it consists of the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) in the form of conceptualization (vikalpa), characterized by the superimposition of the freedom of the "I" (ahaṃ). That very [function]...

Through the specific vibration of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, she becomes fivefold. Therein, abandoning [the external] in one place and falling [into it] in another, she gradually assumes the form of *prāṇa* and *apāna* as exhalation and inhalation.
Both of these are clearly manifest during the waking state, [moving] from the body toward the object, and from there...

Because one rests within the internal object of cognition itself, such as the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛti*) and so forth, that [mindfulness] exists even during sleep and dream; for while another person perceives the entry and exit of the breath of one who is sleeping, one also personally experiences the impact of the objects of cognition. Therefore, it is primarily characterized by the two specific states of inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*).

The state of *prāṇana* (vitality) exists in both waking and dreaming; however, as for that state of the subject who is in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), even though both *prāṇa* and *apāna* are present there in two ways, the primary form of deep sleep is simply rest in the heart-region, free from the senses. In that state, whatever slight distinction exists between *prāṇa* and *apāna* for a certain time...
He is the repose of the entire range of aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and so forth; by means of the activity of equalizing [all things] throughout the upper, lower, and horizontal directions,
he thereby causes the heart-lotus to blossom and performs the digestion of what is eaten and drunk.

Because it consists of the uninterrupted equilibrium of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, which take the form of day and night, there is a specific state called *samāna* that is equal to the equinox (*viṣuvat*); the category of bound souls (*paśu*) up to the *pralayākala*s consists of that [equilibrium], and it is within that *samāna*, whose nature is the cessation of that [equilibrium], [that they reside].

The connection is as follows: that state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*) belongs to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which, at that time, has as its name the "manifestation" (*prakhyā*)— that is, the complete and preeminent manifestation (*prakhyāna*) in a specific form.

The suffix *vati* is applied according to the rule *tadarham* (Pāṇini 5.1.117), meaning "that which deserves [the action]. Furthermore, the indeclinability (*avyayatva*) of *vati* when used in the sense of comparison is inherent.
These worlds of yours—the intermediate directions, the cardinal directions, the distant realms, the downward slopes, and the upward heights—[are all yours].
Some maintain this is because of the scriptural vision [found in] *Tai. Brā.* 2.8.1.3; as Parāśara said:
"Indeed, when there is the conjunction of pervasion (*vyāpti-yoga*) within a portion of time, through that conjunction, it is the day of the equinox (*viṣuvad-dina*)."
"Thus, equanimity (sāmya) is known as the Viṣuvat, which generates imbalance and is continuous.
This is stated in the *Śrīkālapādā*. In the Sūtra, it is said repeatedly in the present participle (*śatṛ*) form that "it is thus."

The *viṣuvat* (equinox) is so called because it continuously impels (*suvati*) or brings about the distinction (*viśeṣa*) characterized by the inequality of day and night, as well as their decrease and increase; it also refers to the twilights (*sandhyā*). That which constitutes an equal interval within the intervals of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), this alone is [the state] primarily.

The meaning of the aphorism is that [the state] is of the nature of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), as if it were trampling underfoot even the existing state of being characterized by *prāṇa* and *apāna*. He introduces it with the words "Now," and so forth. By "dividing" (*vibhajan*), he demonstrates its uninterrupted activity and also touches upon the function of the second verse. And that—
Thus, where it was previously stated—“In the vital breath, the sense of ‘I’...
(3.2.14)—the nature of being the living self (*jīvana-rūpatā*) was described; [and] in the commentary (*vṛtti*), [it is said] “become the self” means “having the vital breath as one's self.”

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound; that is to say, the word "nanu" (indeed) indicates what is to be excluded by each [term]. The phrase "coexisting with that" is used because otherwise life would be severed.
By the words "of these two," [it means] the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while emptying the body and so forth through its manifestation, [engages] the object.

The sun, by its illumination, is the day at that time; the apāna, by means of reflective awareness (vimarśana) and internal repose, bestows bliss and nourishes the state of the subject consisting of the body and so forth—thus the moon is the night at that time. In this way, it is manifested as such through the predominance of dependence upon the subject.

(344) Also by way of the reverse, with respect to the object of cognition (*prameya*). For this very reason he says: "Even upon the creation of objects, this activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the dissolution of the cognizer. This is the state of external quiescence.

The object is the "twelve-finger space" (dvādaśānta), while the "end" (anta) is the heart-abode as the "I. The connection is that for the knower, it is indeed a creation by virtue of having the nature of being (bhāva). The phrase "by this much alone" means merely by the requirement of the aspect of having the nature of being. He says "nanu" [to address this]: "of one who is waking..."

Having explained the dream state, [the author] explains it later by way of distinction with the words "bhedena" (by way of distinction), with the intention that although it was mentioned first because it is to be established with effort in the Sūtra, this [dream state] must be explained as being identical to the waking vision.

Now, intending to explain the phrase "atha tacchedātmā" (then, its cessation is the self), [he shows] that it is not the case that [this state] does not exist equally even at the beginning of the waking state.
Speaking thus, he explains that even though everything is possible everywhere, the distinction is made on the basis of predominance, by saying "externally" (*bahiḥ*).

The particle *tu* indicates a distinction from what preceded. This very point—that it pertains to "both"—is clarified as "externally and internally," referring to those two [states] which exist respectively in the object located at the *dvādaśānta* (the twelve-finger space) and in the subject situated in the ground of the heart (*hṛdayabhūmi*).

The two moments consist of the nature of rest; regarding them, it will be explained that at that very time they possess the state of dissolution (*pralaya*). The phrase "of both the grasped and the grasper" means that this is the dissolution of everything.
Now he explains the passage beginning with "the essence of its cutting off," starting with "but when. [This occurs] by way of deficiency or excess.

"That which is not inseparable (*nāntarīyaka*)—that which does not exist without it—must necessarily be absent wherever there is the sequence of engagement and withdrawal; by this, he indicates its nature as the equinox (*viṣuvad-rūpatā*). He establishes the logical justification for the statement "the division is explained through equality" with the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*).

In the interval between waking and sleeping, which consists of a mere moment, the phrase "at other times" refers to states such as fainting and deep sleep, where for a long duration neither of those two manifests; thus,
their commonality lies precisely in the cessation of both, which constitutes the attainment of the state of the seed (bījatā).

This means the cessation of the manifestation whose nature is disequilibrium (*vaiṣamya*). It is "significant" (*anvartha*) because, having made [everything] equal, it breathes—that is, it vitalizes—up to the sphere of its own activity; for this reason it is called *samāna*. Furthermore, that vitalization exists there in a subtle mode of operation, like the glowing of extinguished embers.
The movement (*cāra*) is thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)—
in this manner, that which constitutes the nature of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* through its long extension is [as follows].

It is said that [the breath] is interrupted; however, it indeed exists in a subtle state. [The author], seeing that "interruption" (cheda) implies "equality" (sāmya), as if it were jagged, explains it otherwise with the words "or else" (athavā). [An objection: But surely deficiency and so forth are not even mentioned in the Sūtra; how then can they be referred to by means of the pronoun (sarvanāman)? To this, he says: "day and night," and so forth.
In that context, the *sūtra* specifies *prāṇa* and *apāna* as being of the nature of day and night;

these two consist of activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*), and they do not exist in a state of perfect equilibrium. Rather, there must necessarily be a varied state of deficiency or excess therein; therefore, that [balance] is non-deviant (*avyabhicārī*).

The meaning is that *dharma* is included therein and is indicated by the pronoun *tat*. And it has been explained that the synonymy between *nirodha* (cessation) and *viccheda* (severance) is appropriate. For this very reason, because of the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), some say the reading should be "from its severance, it is called 'equal'. Regarding this, [the author] also provides a commentary (*vṛtti*).

"He calls her the witness. Now, in the previous explanation, "in equilibrium" (*sāmye*) was stated as the basis for the designation, while "because of cessation" (*nirodhāt*) was given as the reason for that equilibrium; but now, this very [cessation] has been made the reason for the designation. How, then, is "in equilibrium" (*sāmye*) not to be understood? To this he says: "In that regard... (*tatra*).

And the word "ca" (and) [indicates that] the equilibrium of the prāṇa and apāna breaths on the level of the seed (bījabhūmi)— which is like the equilibrium of the external night and day well-known in the world— is,
even when no other cause is mentioned, regarded as the instrumental cause for that restraint (nirodha) by relying upon worldly convention itself.

It is supported by what is indicated by the locative case (saptamī). This is logical because that which was previously designated is the cause (nimitta), whereas cessation (nirodha) is designated later; and a designation is made on account of its cause, just as one says, "I am Gārgya by lineage. Thus, it refers to the cessation of deficiency and excess produced by the equalization of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.

The designation "equinox" (*viṣuvat*) is well-known through the scriptures concerning the authority of time. By means of its similarity to that worldly form, he demonstrates this very point with the words "even then": even then, the state of deficiency or excess well-known in the two worldly equinoxes of Aries and Libra will spread. [Objection: But is not the entire day or night [equal]?

It is well known in the world as "the equinox" (*viṣuvat*), not merely for a single moment. True; however, he shows that this common usage is metaphorical (*upacāra*), because it is sustained by that [moment] and falls within its continuum, by saying "but at that time, not... and so forth.
(Page 346) It is not only at the equinox that this occurs; he says "and at the transition" (*saṅkrāntau*) to show that it is observed elsewhere as well.
That which is the movement of the Sun from one zodiac sign (*rāśi*) to another zodiac sign is [the movement] of the light whose nature is consciousness (*bodha*).
"Just as when moving from one object of knowledge to another,
for one who is intent upon a single thought... (Spandakārikā 41).
"Having known the knowledge of both states, [one attains] the Middle Way... (Vi.bhai. 61);
"When the state has been abandoned, consciousness is restrained... (Vi.bhai. 62).
Thus, according to the principle stated in the scriptures, the supreme merit consists in resting within one's own self. As it is said:
"This is that supreme dharma: the vision of the Self through yoga.
In this regard, even though it lasts for only a single moment—
According to the principle, "ten ancestors and ten descendants," some maintain that the meritorious time (*puṇyakāla*) consists of thirty-two *ghaṭikās* on both sides [of the sun's transit],
while others hold it to be sixty *ghaṭikās* on both sides; the same applies to the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) as well.

The intended meaning is as follows: Now, one might object: "In deep sleep (*suṣupta*), which is devoid of objects of cognition (*apavedya*), let there be a state of uniformity because of the absence of grasped objects and, consequently, the absence of mental expansion and so forth; but how can that [uniformity] exist when there is an object of cognition (*savedya*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says "in deep sleep," etc. He states the reason for what has been asserted here.

By the words "the eye and so forth," etc., this is what is meant: that which appears as separated from the subject (*grāhaka*) must necessarily involve the expansion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), but not in the case of every mere object of cognition (*vedya*). Furthermore, pleasure and the like appear as if inseparable from the subject; for [it is] of the subject...

However, by the principle stated in the *Svacchanda-kārikā* (8), "But [it is] from the touch of one's own power," there is only self-luminosity; what room is there for any outward expansion therein? Now, one might object that in a dream, the operation of the eyes and other senses is simply absent. To this, he says: "Even in a dream. Although [the senses are absent], by means of the mind—

The perception of that object occurs by means of the mind alone; nevertheless, it is established as being produced by the eye and other [senses] as well, because it is indeed aroused by the mind through the power of the mind.
Thus, it is aroused by the mind even when [perceived] by the eye.
(Page 347)

"I see [the object] even when there is mental activity"—this is a delusion; however, this is another matter. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) himself states "the grasper also," and so forth, expressing that which was situated in the heart of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), with the intention:
"From the perspective of reality (*vastu-dṛṣṭyā*), this does not invalidate my position. He says that very thing...

He demonstrates this with the words "And if... and so forth. The phrase "even in the illusory grasper" means while that which has become the grasper of the object is appearing. "And not thus" means that here the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not perceived, because such an operation completely dissolves in the states of the fourth (*turya*) and beyond. As it was said:
Wherein the vital breath comes to rest by its own nature, without being forcibly restrained— that is the state of steadfastness in Brahman, the Fourth Self (turyātman).
Thus [it is said]. Now, having raised the objection that in that [state] there exists a māyic subject, he says "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
In the absence of a māyic subject, there is a unity within the reality of supreme consciousness;
the state of existing together with that [unity] is *sāyujya*. This is because even the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the void (*śūnya*), and so forth, lack the status of being a subject.

Because [the self] is manifest as the supreme reality whose nature is consciousness, it is in a state of union (sāyujya) with wind, space, and so forth, which possess the single flavor of the absence of any object of perception; therefore, for one who has attained that state, this manifold arising— extending even to bodily movements— would not exist.

If for the yogin there were no illusory [subject], then the grasper would not exist; yet this [grasper] does exist, therefore that [illusory subject] also exists. Furthermore, since the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*) is impossible therein, its manifestation is perceived as being in something distinct, and not in mere objectivity (*vedyamātra*). And pleasure and so forth are not distinct [from the subject]. Thus he says: "And pleasure and so forth," etc. And...
He shows that it is not merely by way of externality, but rather through identity with the grasper (*grāhaka*), by saying "for instance" (*tathā hi*).
Now, even then, pleasure and so forth, when being remembered, ought to be remembered as designated by the grasper exactly as they were experienced; and yet, [they are not] in the grasper.
Anticipating the objection that [the self] depends upon the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, he says: "For the Self also... This is what is meant:
the aspect consisting of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is indeed eternally non-setting;
however, it does not possess the state of being remembered in this manner. (Spandakārikā 1.13)
According to this principle, that which is being remembered would be [the object], but if it were conceptualized, it would be so;
for [conceptualization] is preceded by conceptual construction itself.
(Page 348)
He will explain right now that recollection is to be expressed as "the remembered when it is being conceptualized.

And in the act of conceptualization, even the Self—having fallen onto the ground of the intellect—is indeed perceived as something separately created, and likewise pleasure and so forth; thus, there is a separate recollection of this [Self].

"Because it is preceded by conceptualization, it occurs exactly according to experience. Thus, when there is the manifestation of the self as the object (*grāhya*), the employment of the expansion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) certainly takes place; however, in the case of the subjectivity (*grāhakatā*) which is a single, solid mass, this sequence does not apply. He says "therefore," meaning that although [the process] proceeds from the emergence of the vital-breath layer (*prāṇamaya*).
Although the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is [established] in reality, it is not so when it has ascended to the plane of being the subject (*grāhaka*);

for if that were the case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because for each distinct object of knowledge, another subject would require yet another subject, and so forth. "For this very reason" means that there is no dependence upon a subject.

Regarding the state of being a subject (*grāhakatā*), [the text says] "then"; the word "also" (*api*) implies that even the body has a manifest state of being an object of cognition (*vedyabhāva*). It is said to be "of the nature of internal touch" because even when the eyes are closed and so forth, there arises the cognition "I am stout" and so on. The word "this" (*ayam*) refers to it in relation to other subjects.

"Since this group of instruments [is such that] by reciting the Spanda text without interruption... (Kārikā 6), and so forth; this recalls the entire purpose of the instruments. Now, if this is so, regarding the body...
If there is an immersion into the form of volition (*cetanā*), then why does the attainment of full sovereignty (*svātantrya*) not occur?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "of the forms and so forth residing in the body. The word "idantāyāḥ" is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of a cause. However, when the "this-ness" (*idantā*) is covered by the single-flavored penetration of "I-ness" (*aham*), [sovereignty is attained].

Through the habituation of cultivation (*bhāvanāsātmya*), it becomes like the consciousness of Īśvara or Sadāśiva in the fourth state (*turyadaśā*), according to the analogy of copper transmuted by mercury into gold; or else, when it is entirely destroyed or dissolved,
it becomes like the Śākta consciousness in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātītadaśā*).

By the analogy of the liquefied essence that remains as a yellow vine, brought about by the power of its refinement through the complete digestion of gold once it has been properly pierced by its own innate nature; at that time, even while the body still exists, there is the manifestation of full sovereignty due to the attainment of all-encompassing glory, just like the bodies of Sadāśiva and others. Thus...

Having spoken incidentally, he now returns to the subject at hand—the fact that even pleasure and other objects of cognition do not depend on an outward expansion at the time of self-awareness—and states: "And [this applies] to the minds as well. Thus, it is of a nature characterized by gross expansion.
It has been stated that the expansion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) preceded by conscious perception does not exist even in the case of what is perceived; however,
that which is not preceded by cognition, produced by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*), and comparable to the inflation of a bellows, occurs even in the case of what is not perceived.

It exists. However, if one considers that even within [the heart] there is a subtle vibration according to the analogy of a firebrand glowing with extinguished embers, then let the conjunction of prāṇa and apāna be subtle; yet it is firmly established that this very [subtle vibration] is the *samānā*.
He shows this same point from another perspective with the words "Or else" (*athavā*). || 19 ||
Thus, in every case regarding the subject (*pramātṛ*) throughout the three states, the predominance of the triad beginning with *prāṇa* has been stated; indeed, by virtue of its firmness,
even while there is a multiplicity of cognizable bodies at every moment, the division of the body as a real entity (*bhāvabhūta*) [is established].
In the *Śiva-sūtra*, by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Kallaṭa and others,

it was stated in the passage beginning with "the firmness of the cause called breath" (*prāṇākhya-nimitta-dārḍhyam*) that [this occurs] there. Now, regarding the two states in the case of the supramundane subject (*lokottara-pramātṛ*):

The Sūtra demonstrates the predominance of *udāna* and *vyāna*: "That which moves through the middle and upwards is called *udāna*; it is the fourth state (*turyaga*), consisting of fire (*hutabhujmaya*).
*Vyāna*, the Lord of Mantras (*mantreśa*), is the *vijñānākala*, the supreme, whose nature is the universe (*viśvātmaka*). (20)

When the *prāṇa* itself, having come to rest in the central place within the region of the heart and attained a state of equilibrium (*samānatā*), flows upward through the hollow channel by that very path due to the cessation of lateral flow, then it is called *udāna*, because it breathes (*aniti*) upward and all around (*samantāt*). And that—
Burning away all differentiation like fire, he [the Self] exists in that very state on the fourth plane (*turyabhūmi*). At that time, he alone is the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Starting from the form of the *vijñānākala*, who dwells above *māyā*, up to the subject of Sadāśiva, all that belongs to him alone; thus, he is both the *vijñānākala* and the *mantra*.

"Vividha" (the manifold) and "Īśa" (the Lord), whose nature is Sadāśiva—this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. When he alone, having pervaded (*vyāpya*) everything that exists within the body—the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth—breathes (*aniti*) from all sides (*samantāt*), then, by virtue of being the nature of Paramaśiva in the form of the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), he is the supreme, full *vyāna*. This is the extent [of the definition].
It has been stated that the two-fold form, which is the object of the knowing subject (pramātṛ) who is a yogi, is to be accepted; for even for the knower (jñānin),

it consists solely of absorption (āveśa) characterized by the direct experience of that [form], whereas for the yogi, it pertains to the Lord’s manifestations both externally and within the body, because all [forms] are capable of both expansion and repose.
The dyad consisting of prāṇa and apāna is the samāna [vital breath] of the pralayākalas and vijñānākalas; the mantras and so forth are the udāna [vital breath], which is the state of Śiva.
The meaning of the sūtra is that "vyāna" has also been shown [in this way]. He introduces it with the words "udāna," etc.

The illustration is the example; the distinction is that the objects such as the *vijñānākala* and so forth possess the characteristics of the fourth state (*turya*) and so on, because they belong to the upward-moving [state], preceded by the state of *samāna*.

By the passage beginning with "this is the tenfold" (*iyaṃ daśa*) and ending with "he attains" (*labhate*), [the author] shows that what precedes assumes the form of what follows, thereby indicating that although those two currents have indeed perished, how could the prāṇa and apāna [then] exist in the middle as an upward flow?

It is stated in the *Vṛtti*: "Having attained unity, they flow. The intention [of this statement] is that movement itself does not become stillness, and how it is that the transverse flow of the prāṇa and apāna is described as being distinct [from their vertical movement].
He answers this with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). [The phrase] "by way of having five forms" means that [the breath] is indeed one.

It is specified here that the subject (dharmin), air, attains five forms; therefore, it is established that by the terms "prāṇa" and "apāna," that very air is meant, and thus its state as "udāna" is logical. Regarding this, he says: "for a long time," meaning that the flow is endowed with that property (dharma); thus, there is an indication of distinction.

It is faultless. Thus he says: "The relation of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) also... By "it has been stated," he means their identical nature; "to that extent" means precisely that much. "Duality" (*dvandva*) is the perception of duality (*dvaitadṛṣṭi*). Just as the third eye has fire as its nature due to three causes, so too does this [relation]—this is the connection. That which...
I have described the infinite range of the three worlds, from Brahmā down to the smallest insect;
by means of this very vision of non-duality, my own nature thus reveals his pair of eyes.
Having reflected thus, my mind resting in the Infinite Power and desiring to abandon the perception of duality,
I have cultivated abundant devotion through the pure path revealed by your grace.

O Śiva, I have taken refuge in You, who are equal [to all], who shine with eyes fixed upon the point known as the "arisen-from-all" (samagrodaya) sensation, who have internalized the manifold forms of the universe, and whose vision is non-dual.
"That which is the supreme abode, which effects the destruction of other abodes"—
and so forth. He corroborates this very point with the words "And it has been said," referring to existence and non-existence in the form of creation and withdrawal (page 351).

When the state of duality— consisting of inhalation and exhalation, day and night, birth and death, attachment and aversion, and so forth— which are mutually inseparable, enters the center through the conjunction of their friction,
then the sun of prāṇa and the moon of apāna exist in the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed.

From the union characterized by mutual friction, the fire that has suddenly arisen and flows upward is the devourer of the entire sacrificial offering—that which has fallen into the state of "this-ness" (idantā) and constitutes the peak of all objects of enjoyment. As the scripture says:
"The fire named Śuci has arisen from the friction of the Moon and the Sun."
By means of the three-colored thread of the bindu situated in the center of the central channel?

Thus, the Brahmins— who find rest in the *vyāna* that will be described later— know this to be the supreme and primary form of *udāna*, because ascending to that [state] is like climbing a staircase consisting of the stages of *udāna*. For this very reason:
When non-duality (advaita) predominates due to the primary focus on burning away the impurity of illusion (māyā-mala),
there occurs an expansion of distinct objects of knowledge even within the Viṣṇu, Viriñca, and other Āgamas, during the emergence of Viṣṇu, Viriñca, and so forth as Vīreśvara.
Thus, by the refutation of the previously mentioned form, the opening of the third eye has indeed been demonstrated;
enough said. In this state, those established as *vijñānākalas*—this is the connection.
And they have already been described. Now, this is a stainless state; in that [state], they...

Anticipating the question "How so?", he says: because in this state there is purity, since the two impurities are absent from the very root; for even the *āṇava-mala*—which consists in the conceit of identifying with the self that which is not the self, such as the insentient *puryaṣṭaka* and so forth—is nothing other than the cessation of such [conceit], which is itself pure awareness.

This is due to the conceit of selfhood (*ātmatvābhimāna*); it is not, however, a misconception (*viparyaya*) consisting of impurity (*aśuddhi*). Since this is the nature of the *vijñānākalas*, for that reason they abide in this state. But if this is so, does it not follow from the scriptures that their connection with the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*) has many branches? As it has been said:
"The two *akalas* are to be correctly understood as being in the states of dream and deep sleep" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.28);
thus,
within the thirteenfold division, both *akalas* constitute the essential nature.
[The objection: "Even in the division of the *pralayākala*, both [the *pralayākala* and the *vijñānākala*] are their own [distinct categories]" (*Mālinīvijayottara* 2.30, p.
thus, that [statement] would be contradicted. [To this] he says: "And of those... Here, however, for one who desires to cross over from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), that...

Thus, this first state is to be accepted as that which is most to be abandoned from the perspective of the Lord's true nature; it is like the condition of one of the lowest sort who, just as he begins to awaken,
encounters a situation similar to the protection afforded by a general, and is therefore designated as the fourth.
The intention is that this is a calculation. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and also the Mantreśvaras," the term *mantreśa* is being explained.

Regarding the phrase "in this very [state]," it refers to the fourth state (*turyā*). As for the phrase "even though," it means that because one attains the full form from that [state], it is logical that it is the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*). Thus, the word *īśa* is indeed distinct from the word *mantra*.

He explains with the words "or rather" (*yadivā*). The phrase "those whose reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) has not blossomed" is restated here with the intention of providing an illustration within the context of the mantras. "In that very state" (*tatraiva*) refers to the fourth state (*turyadaśā*).
Thus, the connection is that Īśvara also is one whose station is in the fourth; he is simply "one in the fourth state" (*turyāvastha*). Now, [an objection]:

Many [objections] have been stated against this. He says: "At that time, he does not know. The point here is that his being the Lord (*īśvara*) is beyond dispute in terms of his oneness (*ekatva*). He supports the *karmadhāraya* compound by intending to show the identity between the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), beginning with the words "and of that," and so forth. Now, in this regard—

In the commentary, he shows by means of the word "or" (*athavā*) how the Lords of Mantras (*mantreśvarāḥ*) are subsumed under the term "mantra" because they belong to that same class, and under the term "Lord" (*īśa*) because they share the same denotation according to the principle of the Tantras. The phrase "those various [impurities]" refers to the attenuation of impurity (*malatānava*) in its forms as having an object of knowledge (*savedya*) or being without an object of knowledge (*apavedya*), and so forth.

As it is being drawn forth, it brings about the manifestation of various stages; likewise, the state of agency (*kartṛtā*) is also gradually drawn forth—this is the meaning. "Through the immersion into the power of Īśvara" means through the immersion into the power of the subject as "I"; this consists in the nature of a particular subject, which may be either impure or pure.

And it is logical that the excellence of agency belongs to that very one alone; such is the meaning. "Vyāna also" means that Vyāna is the supreme, whose nature is the universe; this is explained in the *Vṛtti* [on the verse] "herein. "Previously" refers to what was stated in both the *Sūtra* and the *Vṛtti*. He explains "Vyāna" in the passage beginning with "but in the state beyond the fourth."
The reason for not touching upon the operation of movement (*pravahaṇa*) is as follows: movement is a process of going that depends on distinctions of place and time;
however, in this case, both place and time consist solely of the essence of non-duality (*advaita*), and not in any other way.
(Page 353)

Regarding the phrase "the two are distinct": by the word "consisting of the universe" (*viśvātmaka*), the Lord (*īśvara*) is mentioned in some places, but here he shows that it is Śiva himself, as indicated by the words "even though. Keeping in mind that in the first explanation the term *mantreśa* constitutes a single word, he says "or else. The word "first" refers to this [state] of fullness.

The initial stage [of the descent of power] is like that of the *vijñānākala*, characterized by purity (*nirmalatā*). Although the *pralayākala* lacks the impurity known as *māyā*, it does not possess purity because its absence of impurity is not absolute due to the presence of the *kārmamala*. "Of this" refers to the Lord (*īśvara*), by virtue of his having abandoned the nature of being an object of knowledge (*vedyarūpatā*).
Consciousness, gradually assuming the form of the object of cognition by prioritizing its manifestation,
reaches the stages of the *bindu* and the half-moon due to the subtlety of that form; then,
because it is suppressed by the nature of darkness (*tamas*) resulting from the destruction of that [form], the aspect of manifestation is eclipsed.

Upon the acceptance of the reflective portion (*vimarśa-bhāga*), through resting in the non-verbal portion (*śabdana-abhāga*), it ascends to the nature of sound and its end (*nāda-nādānta-rūpatā*) due to the subtlety of the process supported by the path of vital breath (*prāṇa-patha*);
thereafter, upon the exhaustion of the nature of the wind consisting of the flow, [it proceeds] according to the degree of abandonment of contraction.

One attains the state of Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā; subsequently, upon the unfolding of one's own pure nature, one reaches the state of Supreme Śiva by virtue of being the Pure Self. Let this suffice for now. He says the same thing in the passage beginning with "the vital energy" (prāṇaśakti), [which is] presided over by the Supreme Lord.

The meaning is that [the world] consists merely of the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the Supreme Lord. By the word *kalpa*, as used in the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is meant that the word *kalpa* denotes "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). For it is said: this entire aggregate of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and subjects of knowledge (*pramātṛ*) is the very breath of the Supreme Lord. In that regard, it has been stated:
That which is to be presided over by the designations of the reality of the elements is called *piṇḍastha*; they know the other to be *padastha*.
The mantras, their lords, and Śiva are proclaimed as "abiding in form" (rūpastha);
the supreme power (parā śakti), though engaged in activity, is beyond form (rūpātītā) and free from affliction.
Free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, pure, and established in its own self;
Śiva is to be known as that which transcends all, by knowing whom one is liberated. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 2.42) (p. 354)

Thus, having explained it according to the intention of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), he explains it according to the intention of those such as ourselves with the words "but for the yogins. The phrase "with respect to that" means with respect to the perceivers of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; "reasoning" (*yukti*) is the reflective awareness of thousands of appearances consisting of the methods of joining and separating appearances. By that [reasoning]...
This, the essence of the meaning of the scriptures, has been set forth; "having expanded" means it has not been composed in an excessively elaborate manner—thus all is auspicious. || 20 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, the Investigation of the Nature of the Subject (*pramātṛtattvavimarśa*), in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, a devotee of Maheśvara. 2.
And this chapter on the summary of the meaning of the scriptures is completed. || 3 ||
The *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*,
composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the Great Mahāmaheśvara.
The Chapter on the Compendium of Principles (*Tattvasaṅgrahādhikāra*).
Now begins the first chapter: I bow to that Amṛteśa, who, within his own supreme abode, causes the bindu— the object of knowledge consisting of the essence of nectar— to become completely full.

Thus, the reality of the Self, which is self-luminous and of the nature of Maheśvara due to the unimpeded power consisting of knowledge and action, has been explained at length through the threefold qualification, supported by reasoning and scripture;
that very same [reality] is now stated in brief for the sake of attaining the state of one who has well-practiced knowledge, the state of a knower, and the state of a yogi.
In order to instill in the minds of disciples that which is useful for cultivation and so forth, he demonstrates the compendium of reality (*tattvārthasaṅgraha*) in fifteen verses, beginning with:
"The very self of all living beings..."
By these [verses] beginning with "ityādibhiḥ" and ending with "jānāti ca karoti ca," the ultimate nature (*pāramārthika-svarūpa*) is stated in that verse; thereafter—

The purport of this reflection is that the reality of bondage consists of nine principles according to the perspective of the knower, the known, and the true nature of reality, while the reality of liberation consists of five principles consisting of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Now,
the meaning of the text is being elucidated.
One's own self alone is the one Great Lord of all living beings; I am the universal form, "this," nourished by the undivided awareness [of "I"]. (1)
There, he introduces the Sūtra with the words "Now," and so forth.

Immediately after the extensive exposition, those for whom the full extent [of the subject] has not yet been unfolded are favored by this introduction; whereas those for whom the full extent has already been unfolded—

Furthermore, he shows that there is no redundancy by means of this [verse], for even those who desire a concise statement of the essential meaning and fear excessive prolixity may still desire a moderate degree of elaboration:
"In this world, the learned desire both summary and detailed exposition. (YS 1.25)
Thus, with the words "here," etc., he demonstrates the burden [of existence] upon the state of being a living creature (*jantu*). By that, this is taught without distinction:
"The Puruṣa alone is all this," and so forth. Therefore, the great distinction of this teaching has been stated. For this very reason, by the venerable Parameṣṭhipāda in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:

The view that "all things are Śiva" or "Śiva is the self of all things" is not what is meant by the *śivadṛṣṭi*; rather, it is this self that shines forth within those [things] which themselves possess the property of non-manifestation—that is Śiva. And this has already been stated at the very beginning. This is indicated by the word "apitu."
The Lord is one's very own self, not a Lord existing separately like a king.

To the question "In what manner is He the Lord?", it is thus stated; or to the question "By what kinship is the Lord related to living beings, such that He is their Lord?", [the answer is: He is indeed one's own self.

It occurs to them that "these are not some other [entities]. To this he says, "Or rather" (*yadivā*). "The previously mentioned" refers to the one whose body is the universe (*viśvaśarīra*). "Who" means by what relationship is He connected to living beings;

that is to say, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is grounded in the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and since the object of knowledge is the universe, [the question arises] following upon that.
With the intention that there is an occasion for the instruction on reality (tattva), he asks: "Of what is the nature of the states?
For immediately thereafter, because it has descended into the form of the Fourth (turya), the principle of consciousness (saṃvittattva) directly assumes the differentiation of the universe.

Having ascended to the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), while resting in the middle [state] of the fourth (*turya*), one should embrace the manifoldness of the universe (*viśvabheda*). By that [state], his engagement with the events of the universe is mediated. Now, one might object: "In this way, the state beyond the fourth should not be described at all within the context of the universe's activities. It is not that it is not to be described; rather, it is [described] as being mediated by that [fourth state].
He says "it is to be described" regarding that [state] as well. Or else, according to this interpretation (on page 357),
by one who touches even the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*)— which is its first stage, the final stage of the fourth (*turyāntyabhūmikā*)— [the following occurs].

It is clearly "touched" (spṛṣṭam) indeed. As for the statement "in the initial stage," this refers to its being the first thing to be adopted, because from that point on the process of shedding impurities begins. He explains the great term from the commentary beginning with "the unbroken grāhaka" as "that which... By this, the word *grāhaka* [is explained].

It has been explained. He explains the term *akhaṇḍitapada* with the passage beginning with "where" (*yatra*) and ending with "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍita*). He explains the term *grāhyapada* with the passage beginning with "thus" (*tathā*). He explains its qualifier, "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍita*), with the passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*). He explains the term *melanāpada* with the passage beginning with "of those two" (*tayor*). Regarding the phrase "of those two":

Regarding the apprehender and the apprehended: the phrase "mutually" (*parasparam*) indicates—by means of the term "undivided" (*akhaṇḍita*)—that there is no separation of the apprehender from another apprehender, nor of the apprehended from another apprehended; however, by this [term "mutually"], it is shown that there is also [no separation] from each other. He explains the word "augmented" (*upabṛṃhita*) with the words ending in "free from expectancy" (*nirākāṅkṣa*).
The term "having made internal" (antaḥkṛta) summarizes all these meanings. || 1 ||
Now, one might object: "In that case, who is bound by what, such that this effort is made for the sake of liberation?
Anticipating this doubt, the Sūtra says:
"Therein, within the portion of 'this' created by Himself, [the Self exists] as the subject consisting of the intellect and so forth."
By this [means], that has been brought to the state of being grasped as the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). || 2 ||

Thus, while Maheśvara abides within his own self, that portion of "this-ness" (idambhāga) which is created by him— through his very sovereignty— within that very mirror of his own self, preceded by contraction; and within that [portion],
that which is knowable as "this" in the form of intellect, vital breath, body, and so forth, [is distinct] from the knowable that is different from it.

For its reflective awareness appears as an incomplete, artificial *ahambhāva* (I-consciousness), which is of the nature of a subject and is incapable of overcoming the "this-ness" (*idantā*) associated with the state of being a grasper. That [subject] is thus created as a grasper, such as "I am happy," and so forth; and that...
"The liberation of that which is bound" is the meaning of the aphorism. He states the introduction with the words "now," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in its non-difference": even though there is identity (*aikya*) between that [liberation] and the Self (*ātman*), and even though there is no distinction from that Self within the aggregate of the subject and the object; the reason for this logical possibility is the power of *māyā*.

"By implication" (*sāmarthyāt*): the intention is that such is the purport of the nine verses beginning with "he proceeds" (*prakramate*). Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*), it has been explained by way of grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇyena*).

He explains by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "in that [world] indeed" (*tasmin vā*); and the non-coreferential construction (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) has already been applied in both ways during the occasion of explaining the Sūtra. The meaning of "that which exists" is that it is situated within that very [world]. "By that alone" means by the Lord (*īśvara*). "Renowned" (*prathita*) is derived from the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
The meaning is "made manifest. "Even as 'this'" means "as a clearly perceptible object of knowledge.

"Exactly as stated" refers to the inquiry regarding the subject (*pramātṛ*)—namely, "to whom does transmigration belong?"—in order to state that "the true meaning" (tattvārtha) is the sequence of instruction on the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Thus, [it was] previously...

The connection is: "the exposition of the nature of consciousness. In that very [nature], i.e., in the nature of consciousness, whatever is the Spanda-śāstra—that reality should be examined with effort. (1.7)
Thus, in the introduction [it was said]:
"For thus, for those who have become inert... (1.1.4).
That description which begins with the inert is intended for those who are extremely dull-witted; but this, however—

The distinction here is shown as being "with respect to those who are awakened. This was previously indicated by the statement, "Not only one's own self [is the object], but [the self] of all living beings... (4.1.1), and this very same point is also found in another aphorism.

He says "it has been followed" with the words "for thus. By the term "one's own," the very nature of the full consciousness (*pūrṇa-cit*), which consists of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), is indicated. "Having manifested"—in this way, [the unity] of those things which are mutually distinct... (1.3.6)
By the phrase "ityādinā" (and so forth), [it is meant] by these two previously mentioned sūtras. The word "tadapi vā" (or even that) refers to knowledge (*jñāna*).

The connection with the preceding [sūtra] is through the word "na" (not) as the agent. The phrase "tirodhatte ca" (and it conceals) means that it veils itself during states such as sleep; this is because the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*), and thus there is no passive suffix (*yag*). [The word] "ātmane"—
The word *pada*, however, [is used] precisely because of its status as a *ñit* suffix. By the term *tamaḥ*, it is explained that [the self] "conceals itself. || 2 ||

Granted that this may be so, even then there exists nothing distinct from the Lord for whom bondage could occur; moreover, the nature of the intellect and the rest is simply their own essence as the sense of "I."
Because its ultimate reality consists of the reflective awareness of manifestation (*prakāśaparāmarśa*), even that [intellect] does not bring about bondage for this [Self].

As for the commentary on the descent [of the power], beginning with "even in a single portion of the object of knowledge" (*vedyaikadeśe’pi*) and so forth, by this very [passage], it is indeed established that even the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, when consecrated by the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*), do not possess the nature of bondage.
It has been stated that [bondage] must exist; therefore, he says that bondage must be established:
"That person is considered manifold, consisting of the non-recognition of his own true nature.
In that regard, within creation, there is activity and bliss, and experience consisting of pain and pleasure. (3)
True, in reality there is no such thing as bondage for anyone;

in fact, the one Śiva is independent and of the nature of consciousness alone. However, when that very consciousness appears in a contracted state due to His own unsurpassed sovereignty, then there arises a lack of recognition of His own full nature.

For everyone, due to the longing for full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*), there is the appearance of that which is to be abandoned; its very nature is rooted in that [longing], and by that alone it is woven warp and woof as the ultimate reality of non-recognition (*akhyāti*). Variegated by the diversity of contractions such as the vital breath, the void, and the body, it is therefore regarded in the world and in the Sāṅkhya and other scriptures as the manifold person (*puruṣa*). And he—

The enjoyer is bound, and as for that which is called enjoyment—within that [bound soul], in those many individual subjects (*puṃs*), there are two things projected and imagined: activity and bliss, which are the powers of action and knowledge, consisting respectively of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and luminosity (*prakāśa*).
These two alone are, in their respective order, pleasure and pain; while in the middle [between them] is *tamas*, whose nature is rest.

"That which consists of *māyā*" refers to that very experience (*bhoga*). He introduces the aphorism with the intent of resolving a doubt, beginning with "even in a single portion of the object of knowledge" (*vedyaikadeśe 'pi*) and ending with "also" (*api*). By this, the doubt is indicated; by the remainder [of the commentary], its resolution is provided. Regarding the word "masculinity" (*puṃstva*) from the aphorism, [it is explained as] "the male" (*pumān*).
The commentary on the "follower of the words" (*padānusārin*) is that "subtlety" (*aṇutva*) means "being bound" (*baddhatva*).

"Mutual differentiation" (*anyonyabheda*) refers to the multiple words in the Sūtra; "its experience" (*tasya bhogaḥ*) is the final half of the Sūtra. "This" (*etat*) refers to the form consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. And "non-comprehension is likewise" (*aparijñānaṃ ca tathā*).

Because they are limited, they also possess each other's forms. Therefore, that which is well-known to one [tradition] should be explained by means of that which is well-known to the other, because the nature of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is always of this kind; this is the intended meaning.
[The term] *āṇava* [is used].

Because of the arousal of [the notion of] atomicity. "This" refers to the non-recognition of the nature of the Other. "For this very reason" means that limitation is indeed non-recognition; therefore, even its opposite is merely the opposite of the second [non-recognition].

Alternatively, the word "or" (*yadvā*) indicates that the various mental states— such as "I am happy," "I am suffering," or "I [possess] wealth, learning, enjoyment," and so forth— are themselves manifold; however, because there is again a continuous connection with a single sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) within those states, the impossibility of their being truly multiple is signified by the word "or."

"By this" refers to the text of the commentary (*vṛtti*). By the word "fragment" (*khaṇḍa*), it is meant that when there is a single living being (*jīva*) residing in the body of a very long ox-nose, if that body is cut into pieces, each fragment possesses its own separate living being; yet, upon their reintegration, they attain the state of a single living being once more.

By the word "resounding" (*dhvanatā*), subtlety (*aṇutva*) is shown; and by the phrase "successive words," limitation (*parimitatva*) is indicated. However, if multiplicity were not fully understood, it would have been stated by its own specific term alone. By saying "it conceals itself" (*tirodhatte*), he demonstrates non-apprehension (*akhyāti*). Right here, he recalls the logical proof: "for in the case of error... as was previously stated.

Having summarized that very point, he says again, "as far as... and so forth. Having set aside the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), he establishes the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) with the word "merely" (*kevalam*). The word "of them" (*teṣām*) refers to other cognizers;
"by them" (*taiḥ*) refers to those other cognizers; and "that" (*tacca*) refers to the absence of such a perception on the part of those other cognizers.

It has the nature of the meaning of a sentence. Now, what is the purpose of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) such that it was said that one who wishes to engage in transaction must necessarily know [this]? To this he says: "on the path of worldly transaction.
"Even here" refers to the investigation into the nature of the person. "And that" refers to the substratum. By means of the full sense of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*).

"That which is not recognized" refers to that which is non-existent (*asaḥ*). "Otherwise" means in the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the full *I*-consciousness of the universe. Having explained the first half-verse, he explains the second with the words beginning with "And those who... and so forth. Regarding the term "in creation" (*nirmitau*), [the rule] is *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini Sūtra...).

The term *ekaśeṣa* [is applied] according to [Pāṇini 1.2.64]: "When [words] of the same form are repeated, one may remain. It will be explained that "existence, bliss, and action" belong to the Lord (*pati*) in the passage [Tantrāloka 4.1.6].
And as for the word "created," this is expressed by the verb "to do" (*karoti*) in the sūtra as "egoity" (*ahaṅkāra*). In that regard:

He explains this portion with the words "pertaining to the form of the apprehender" (*grāhakākāragata*). He shows what is to be excluded from that very [form] with the words "belonging to another," and so forth. "[Of the] yogin" (p.

The term *yogī* is intended to mean that even when that [object] is divided, experience (*bhoga*) is possible for him through the connection with various states of pleasure and pain residing in the form of the subject (*grāhakākāra*), just as in the case of a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*); it does not mean that for non-yogins (*ayogin*) alone, the mere cognition of another's pleasure and so forth constitutes experience. And the phrase "in the intellect" (*buddhau ca*) refers to [the intellect] as the subject (*grāhakatvena*).

The sense is: "while [the object] is being identified as such. The intellect (*buddhi*), for its part, even when made into the subject (*grāhikā*), has a limited appearance; therefore, the bliss (*ānanda*) and activity (*kriyā*) residing within it must necessarily be of the same nature, either as having a limited appearance because they have a limited appearance as their object, or simply as having a limited appearance themselves. "Then" means "consequently" from that.
The meaning is "because of being limited. || 3 ||
In order to demonstrate the distinction between what is to be included and what is to be excluded from the category of "creation," the Sūtra states:

"In the case of the Lord, with respect to the entities that are His own limbs, there are knowledge and action, with Māyā as the third; these same [three] are the sattva, rajas, and tamas of the bound soul (paśu). (4)

Throughout the universe, which is non-different from His own essential nature, the Lord possesses the powers of light (*prakāśa*) and self-awareness (*vimarśa*), which are His powers of knowledge and action.

Within the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, the power of Māyā—which consists of the unfolding of the power of action itself—acts as the concealer that grants the emergence of the "I" (*ahantā*). These innate powers of the Lord have been observed [by the masters].

But when there is non-recognition of one's own true nature (svarūpa), cognition regarding entities is merely action; it is pure differentiation, ungraced by light (prakāśa) and self-reflexive awareness (vimarśa).

From the perspective of the bound soul (paśu), light is the state of being both manifest and unmanifest, while non-light is the absence of manifestation; thus, the qualities of sattva and the rest consist in the regulation of the activity of light.
"Consisting of that" means consisting of pleasure and so forth. And by the phrase "by the power of *māyā*," he says this:

in the Blessed One, whose nature is pure consciousness, it is precisely the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)—consisting of freedom and composed of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—that exists, and there is no quality of *māyā* whatsoever therein; however, [the appearance of such] is with respect to the differences of the objects to be created.

The word "that" (*tat*) refers precisely to Māyā, which is inherently bound to the form of the limited subject (*paśu*). For this very reason, Jñāna, Kriyā, and Māyā are not mentioned as being on an equal footing in the Sūtra. This is stated in the *Sattānanda-sūtra* (4.1.6) with the phrase "before long.
It is for this reason that it was said in the introduction: "it proceeds from here," meaning that the state of being identical with that [Māyā] does not exist right here [in the initial stage].
He makes it clear. || 4 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Why are the qualities such as *sattva* not described in the scriptures as being powers (*śakti*) of the bound soul (*paśu*), just as knowledge and other attributes are powers of the Lord (*īśvara*)? To this, the Sūtra states:
"The state of being a power is not predicated of that which possesses power, because of the distinction [between them]."
Of these qualities, which undergo transformation as both instruments and effects. || 5 ||

(Page 362) This conventional usage of difference is now being examined. In that regard, the *puruṣa* has as its essential nature pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone; it does not possess, by its own inherent nature, a manifestation directed toward objects that exists at all times.

Because of that connection; therefore, that [state] is produced by a relation with something other than that. And because the qualities such as *sattva* exist as distinct from the animal—which is suspected of possessing power—therefore they cannot be designated as "powers. Furthermore, since those [qualities] exist as distinct from the Self, which is the Puruṣa in the form of the enjoyer.
One thinks [them to be so], and thus, by the power of that conceit (*abhimāna*), they appear as distinct even from the Supreme Enjoyer who possesses all powers;

yet in reality, these [principles] ending with Earth, though they are of the nature of power (*śakti*), are not so [distinct]. Now, why are they maintained to exist as distinct from the *puruṣa*? It is said: because here, that which consists of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and their effects (*kārya*)—if indeed...

If pleasure and the rest were not distinct from the Puruṣa, then the Puruṣa alone would consist of the instruments; yet this is not so, because that [position] is refuted by the doctrine of transformation (pariṇāma). Therefore, the Puruṣa is independently the essence of the universe.
