And thus, this is indeed Īśvara, not some [ordinary] Puruṣa. Consequently, there is no non-recognition—

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: when the nature of the Puruṣa is being contemplated, since the qualities beginning with *sattva* and ending with earth consist of transformations (*pariṇāma*), they are indeed distinct from Him; therefore, it is logical that they are enumerated separately in the scriptures (*āgama*).
He introduces this [point] with the words "knowledge and action," etc. The phrase "not so" means [they are not distinct] in their capacity as powers (*śakti*). The reason for this is as follows:

The manifestation [of these categories] as distinct from one another occurs both in relation to the bound soul (*paśu*)—due to its sense of egoity—and in relation to the Supreme Lord, according to the principle that "these are distinct from everything that exists for the enjoyer.
Therefore, their being powers (*śaktitva*) in relation to Him is contradictory; for it has been stated more than once that power is not a separate entity from the possessor of power.
The term *bhoktāram* refers to the Supreme [Lord] and the bound soul (*paśu*). The term *bhoktum* refers to [the purpose] of the Supreme and of the bound soul.

Anticipating the question of where the bound soul is employed, he says *tato'pi ca*, referring to that which is intended as the causal state of the power of *māyā*. The phrase *tadupapattaye* means for the sake of establishing the manifestation of distinctness. He who, by means of *māyā*...

The connection is as follows: that cognizer (pramātā), having constructed [the object], considers that [object]—beginning with the sentient being (sattva) and ending with the earth—to be within the sphere of the "I-sense" (ahambhāva). Now, one might ask: let this distinction belong to the bound soul (paśu), but how can it belong to the supreme enjoyer (paramabhoktṛ)? To this he says: "even by a slight degree of being an enjoyer. And thus, his conceit (abhimāna) is as follows: [...text missing... ...that which is [the object]. Thus, even though the supreme enjoyer is essentially free from all objects, he nevertheless possesses a slight degree of enjoyment through the manifestation of the object; and it is precisely by virtue of that slight degree of enjoyment that he maintains the conceit of being the enjoyer. The enjoyer;
therefore, the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, which take the form of pleasure and the like, are indeed distinct from him. Now, if this [notion] is not a mere conceit—
If [one] attends [to this], then there are no such things as pleasure and so forth, nor goodness (*sattva*) and so forth, nor jars and the like;

rather, there are only powers (*śakti*) such as cognition and so forth. Thus he says: "But the power... The intention is that the very nature of goodness and so forth, when emerging, emerges through the subordination of its status as a power. Such is the state of being.

The contingency of having the nature of being a knower and an agent is inferred from power alone, because otherwise the restatement would be inexplicable. "Anvartha" means a quality that is subordinate or an instrument; this is the meaning. "Of them"—the word "in their opinion" is to be supplied as the remainder. "In the scripture"—this is the context.
In the Śrīmaṅgalāśāstra, verse 5.

It is established that for the bound soul (paśu), the powers of knowledge and so forth take the form of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest; for the Lord (pati), these are existence (*sattā*), bliss (*ānanda*), and action (*kriyā*), whereas for the bound soul, they are even the absence thereof.
That passion (rajas) consists of a dual nature; it is suffering, composed of both attachment (sattva) and darkness (tamas).

The existence of the Lord, the Master of the Universe, is His very manifestation; in the world, it is His agency alone, whose nature is pure self-reflection, which constitutes His power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

And because He is devoid of dependence on anything else, this same state, by virtue of being the form of repose, is His power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*). Thus, this [divine] nature of consciousness itself extends to this extent. But for the bound soul (*paśu*), existence is his bliss.

Its absence consists of two natures. Among these, the first is that portion which is existence and bliss; "it" refers to *sattva*, which is being (*sattva*), meaning it consists of light and pleasure. That which is its absence—the absence of light and bliss—is the absence of *sattva*, namely *tamas*, which is of the nature of obscuration. This is the nature of the pair.
Existing by the power of a single unifying awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*), according to the analogy of the blue and non-blue colors found in a variegated butterfly wing,

it is of a mixed nature. Therefore, that *rajas*— whose form consists of the *sattva* and *tamas* which are joined and mutually intermingled— is of the nature of both light and non-light, and is essentially suffering.

For when light and darkness are of a single, solid mass, there is merely pleasure and delusion; however, for a son who is ill, the manifestation [of his condition] is pain, while its non-manifestation is well-being. This very state, fluctuating in form through successive stages, is action (*kriyā*); indeed, there is no such thing as that which is neither of these two forms, just as [there is no such thing as a color that is neither light nor dark].

A blue object appears as blue in the cognition [of it]; that which is both blue and non-blue would appear in the cognition that synthesizes those two; but a fourth [type] cannot possibly manifest in either a constructed (*kalpitā*) or an unconstructed (*akalpitā*) cognition. [This applies to] the non-blue and the blue.
"For indeed, at that time, there would be only these three qualities"—thus [it is said]. The word *api* has the sense of "also. The term *sattā* (existence) is repeated.

He introduces this meaning of the sūtra with the words beginning "of sattva and the others," and concludes with the passage from "in the ultimate sense" up to "is already established," [showing] that the nature of consciousness itself extends this far.
He recalls that which was stated in the passage beginning with "that vibration... (1.5.14): by the phrase "by the counter-correlate," he means by non-existence;
for it has been stated that she pervades even that, because even that is animated by light and reflective awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*).

Regarding the phrase "the counter-correlative of non-existence," for the bound soul (*paśu*), it is the counter-correlative of the non-existence of its own self. The reason for this is its limitation (*pārimitya*), and therein lies the induction of the state of being an object of cognition (*grāhyatā*).

He explains the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of [the term] "from coloring" (*uparañjanāt*) with the words beginning with "mutually" (*anyonya-*), and so forth. Now, one might object that even the fourth quality is of neither form.

Why was it not stated? He says: "But because it has the nature of neither. That which is not perceived in any way is of the nature of non-perception. For that would be something only if there were such a thing as "both" apart from blue and non-blue; even then, both would be unconstructed and their absence likewise.

The "neither" (anubhaya) is made an object by a conceptualizing intellect (*kalpanābuddhi*). Nor is it possible for there to be such a thing apart from those two. In the case of a variegated butterfly, both the blue color being apprehended as "blue" and its non-blue aspect constitute the "both"; however, there is no third state of "both-ness" apart from those two. Thus he says: "the third."

And so forth. He consolidates this very point with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). By the passage beginning with "and non-blue" (*anīlaṃ ca*), he establishes that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a real entity (*vastu*) because its essence is manifestation (*avabhāsa*). And with the words "in this way" (*evaṃ ca*), he demonstrates the contradiction regarding its being a real entity. The word "that which" (*yat*) refers to both [blue and non-blue]. A third category other than blue and non-blue—
"It is thus" (*tathā ca*) confirms that "it is nothing at all. [Objection: But in this case, how can there be a third quality? [Response:

He says, "by the force of the connection" (*anusandhibalāt*). Furthermore, he clarifies what was stated as being "of the nature of non-apprehension" (*apratītirūpam*) with the words "as for that which... (*yat punar*). For indeed, it is precisely because we accept a third quality in this manner that...
It was stated that it has a dual nature (*dvayātmā*);
namely, "the duality" (*dvaya*) and "that which has that as its nature" (*tadātmā*), or "the nature of the duality" (*dvayasya ātmā*). This applies in both ways.

Thus, in the case of the single cognition as "blue," which consists of a synthesis (*anusandhi*); having thus established the third [alternative], he concludes that there is nothing else besides these four by saying "yat punaḥ" (as for what again...). "Tat" means blue; "atat" means non-blue; in the cognition of an object, there is "na kiñcit" (nothing at all)—this is merely words.

[This continues] until the word "meva" (indeed). He shows that for the third [moment], however, there is no state of being non-manifest (*apratītirūpatva*) by saying "but the action" (*kriyā tu*). He provides the justification for this very point with "for not" (*na hi*). "Then" (*tadā*) refers to the manifestation of the action. Now, if action is suffering, then since it is admitted in the Blessed One, he would be subject to suffering. He says "no," beginning with "previously" (*pūrvam*).
In the verse "consisting of the non-recognition of one's own nature" (4.1.3), there is the existence of the bound soul (paśu) who was indicated in general terms [in the preceding verse] (4.1.4).
In passages such as "its absence also [is] that of the bound soul" (4.1.6),
and so forth, this meaning is based on the specific term *paśu* (bound soul) which has been employed as a qualifier.
It is understood that the fact that action consists of the nature of passion (*rajas*) and suffering is a modality of *māyā*.

And from that, this [distinction] arises; thus he says: "on the further shore of *māyā*. "From this" refers to action consisting of consciousness (*cinmayī kriyā*). This very mutual distinction exists between the pure state and the state of *māyā*.

He clarifies this with the words "of a contrary nature" and "surely not. Therefore, that which is contrary to the non-sequential—the sequential—is indeed the *māyīya* impurity (*mala*) within the state of limited subjectivity (*paśutva*), even though it is not actually additional to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the state of pure consciousness; for there, in the state of Cit, there is no appearance of that which is contrary [to consciousness], namely the cause of time.

Because of its non-existence. The reason for this is stated as "then" (*tadā*). Now, if knowledge does not differ from that action consisting of consciousness (*cinmayī kriyā*), then how can knowledge and action be spoken of as distinct with respect to the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)?
(Page 366)

In the context of [the rule] *svāṅgarūpeṣu... patyuḥ...* (Pāṇini 4.1.4), he addresses this [objection] with the words "Raudrī," and so forth. The earthly sphere (*pārthivamaṇḍa*), which is characterized by manifold creation, is presided over by Brahmā; however, the primordial nature (*prākṛta*) remains as a residue of manifest latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

The egg of Māyā (*māyāṇḍa*) is presided over by Viṣṇu as its primary function of maintenance (*sthiti*); however, because it is the unfolding of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of *nīla* (the blue), it is the locus of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) where the cognition of "I" (*pratyaya*) is primary, and thus it is presided over by Rudra. That power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of the Blessed Lord, which consists of withdrawal, belongs to the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), whose primary function is manifestation (*avabhāsana*).
That [power] which consists of the mutual exclusion of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the object (*prameya*),

characterized primarily by emptiness (*śūnyatā*), is called the power of *māyā*. And that power, which is of the nature of negation and presided over by Rudra, takes the form of the initial sketching of the subordinate state within the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara.
It also exists there; for in that state, this "thisness" (idaṃbhāva), which is of a different nature and is to be concealed by the form of "I," must be raised up by that power belonging to Rudra.
And because it takes the form of withdrawal, the nature of consciousness (cidrūpatā) is appropriate for that power in that state.

Even in the subsequent stage (*parabhāga*), the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara is not unsuitable; for, due to the absence of distinctions such as space and time, it does not differ from the Supreme State (*paramapada*). Thus, Śivanātha is precisely that much [in extent]. Consequently, the levels of Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva consist of the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvarapada*); therefore, [this applies] to those situated below that.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others possess the status of both *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) and *paśu* (the bound soul). As it has been stated:
"In the expansion of diverse objects of knowledge, Brahmā and Viṣṇu... (3.2.1), so too [is it stated] in the *Nareśvaraviveka*.
And that state has Rudra as its presiding deity;
although it is of the nature of negation, in the northeastern quarter (Īśāna) I am indeed all.

And so forth. Consequently, it is conceivable that within the state of Rudra, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is established as a differentiation by merging both aspects characterized by manifestation and non-manifestation;
for when that [power] exists, there is the state of being indefinable as "this-ness" (*idantā*), which is of a different nature yet non-different from it.

The supreme consciousness also exists as the full "I" (aham); for this very reason, it is of the nature of both the supreme and the non-supreme, and is characterized primarily by the power of action (kriyā-śakti).

In the Āgamas, the state of the Lord (īśvarāvasthā) is described; and that [state] does not differ from the Blessed One (bhagavat), because it is of the same nature as consciousness (*saṃvid*). Thus, what was previously stated regarding the knowledge and action of the Lord (*pati*) being distinct is not incorrect.
In this way, the principle of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*) has been described through its differentiation from the bound soul (*paśu*), as well as enjoyment (*bhoga*) consisting of pleasure—

The nature of the subject (*ātman*) has been described according to its application; now, the reality of the object of cognition (*prameya*), which consists of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the enjoyed (*bhogya*), must be stated. Furthermore, this investigation into the principles of the enjoyer, the enjoyment, and the enjoyed must be carried out as a single, unified whole so that there may be no interruption in the contemplation; thus, it constitutes a single treatise.

This has been explained. In that regard, he first determines the established nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) with respect to the Lord (*pati*), stating: "Even those [objects] which arise from the Lord’s non-conventional awareness of 'this-ness' (*idantā*)," and so forth.
These appear as mixed, as distinct, and likewise as variegated.

In this context, objects are first of all merely manifestations (*ābhāsa*). These are sometimes mixed together through a single act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), wherein there is the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇatā*). However, they are sometimes reflected upon precisely as unmixed, wherein there is the nature of a universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇatā*). This applies even to those things that possess both natures when not subject to conventional linguistic usage.

By means of that which is uncreated— an "thisness" (idambhāva) similar to what is pointed out by a finger or the like, consisting of the innate discernment of difference— even the Lord, even Īśvara himself, is made an object of experience, not merely infants and the like;
having thus created a manifold [world] through that mode of universal and particular, [he establishes] simultaneously a single I-consciousness (ahantā).

They are characterized by manifestation through rest. Indeed, in the state of Īśvara, because it is inseparable from the efflorescence of existence (*bhāva*), the void— which consists merely of the meaning of negation uncolored by any object of negation and which takes the form of the contraction of consciousness— is manifested by the light of consciousness itself, presided over by Rudra.

It brings forth this non-conventional "thisness" (idantā), which consists in the negation of the greatness of the ego-sense (māna-mahantā). This has been determined immediately below. Thus is the account regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) in relation to the Lord (*pati*);

however, the intention of the Sūtra is that in the case of the Supreme Lord (*paramapati*), the Blessed One, there is no discourse whatsoever concerning an object of knowledge. [The text continues with] the preceding and following...
Connecting [the context] to the introduction of the treatise, he introduces the sūtra with the words "Thus," and so forth.

Although [it applies to] children, infants, and the like; by the phrase "not only," it is shown that the word "also" (*api*) in the sūtra is to be explained as immediately following the word "Lord" (*prabhoḥ*).

(368) But surely, even in the case of an infant, the state of being referred to by the word "this" (*idantā*) outside of a linguistic convention is not perceived; so how can that be used as an example in the commentary? He shows that it is indeed perceived by means of inference, with the words beginning "of that" (*tasya*).
[This is] up to this point. He connects this very point with the words "yadi hi" (for if). "Sa tu" refers to the fool (*bāla*). "Tasya" refers to that fool.

"Prāk" [refers to] the Sūtra on Direct Realization (*sākṣātkāra-sūtra*). Having thus clearly elucidated in the Commentary (*vṛtti*) the example indicated by the word "api" in the Sūtra, he joins it to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "te ca," meaning "those many..."

By the phrase "and so forth," those whose nature is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) are indicated, while by the phrase "separately" and so forth, those whose form is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are pointed out. Now, one might raise this objection: previously, the operation of cognition was discussed with respect to each individual manifestation, and consequently, at all times, manifestations appear separately and not in a mixed state. Anticipating this doubt:

Having grasped in his heart that even a single manifestation—provided it carries within it a group of manifestations necessarily connected with it—is not unfit for the reflective awareness of a sentence, he says: "And therein, 'the jar', etc.
The word "likewise" refers to the single manifestation "jar. And it is not [unfit] merely because of its state as a manifold manifestation.

He says that "specific individuality" (svālakṣaṇya) consists of place, time, and so forth. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), he indicates [the inclusion of] being perceivable by another subject and so on. He shows that when there is no non-mixture with other manifestations such as place and so on, there is only the nature of a universal (sāmānyarūpatā), and not specific individuality; thus, it is a manifold manifestation.

By the words "ityādi" (and so forth): "in front" refers to the manifestation of space; "situated" refers to the manifestation of present time. Having thus examined the mixed manifestation of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), he examines the manifestation of the universal (*sāmānya*) with the words "manifesting as situated in front. This is because of the word "api" (also).

Although being conceptualized independently does not exist from the perspective of the Lord (Īśvara), nevertheless, even direct perception (sākṣātkāra) is possible for the Lord, because the manifestation of the general appearance (sāmānyābhāsa) likewise appears within the Lord as the objects of direct perception; this is what is implied. For this very reason, it says "even for the Lord."

He will read the word *api* [in the sūtra]. Now, it was established in the *Pṛthagdīpa-sūtra* (2.3.7) that the conjunction of appearances that are not contradictory is possible; and both contradiction and non-contradiction depend upon the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) with respect to limited subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*), but there is no rule of contradiction or non-contradiction whatsoever regarding the Blessed Lord. Therefore—

In the absence of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), why would the appearance of "hornedness" not also be mixed with the appearance of the shape of a broad base and belly? And consequently, how could these [appearances] be our own particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) within the Blessed Lord?
Showing the doubt that [the world] is a mere appearance (*bhāsa*), he dispels it with the word "tathā" (thus). In the manner stated by that [word],
although the variegated nature (*vaicitryavattva*) of appearances— which consists in their mutual blending—
is not fixed within the Blessed Lord, for that very reason, even a jar is "horned" from the perspective of Īśvara.
Even Maṇḍūka, radiant with a mass of matted locks, appears as the very embodiment of direct realization;

nevertheless, with respect to those beings who are to be graced by creation, the restriction of possessing horns and a dewlap does not fail to manifest through the power of the principle of necessity (niyati-śakti). Therefore, let there be a manifestation of that [restriction] therein.

"But is it not the case that there is no manifestation there appropriate for us? "Are those entities not simply some things that remained from a previous creation? "No," he says, "and they... "They not" means "they certainly not. For objects perceived by beings such as ourselves are created by that very Lord alone—by Prajāpati, by mother and father, or by the potter.
As for the conceit of being a creator, it has been stated more than once that even that is the creation of that very [Lord]. || 7 ||
Thus, the account regarding the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) has been described in relation to the state of Sadāśiva-Īśvara;

however, for Paramaśiva, this alone constitutes his connection with objects of knowledge, and there is nothing separate from it. Hereafter, the account regarding the objects of knowledge in relation to the bound soul (*paśu*) is stated in three verses. Of these, by the first:
They indeed establish the foundation for the internal Self;
those objects, which appear as distinct, are to be conceptualized through their respective diverse designations within the sphere of memory, imagination, and so forth.

The term "viśeṣadyotaka" (indicating particularity) distinguishes [the objects] from the objects of knowledge belonging to the Lord of Turī (turīśvara). For all objects are the domain of the Lord’s pure reflective awareness (*śuddhavimarśa*), and not conceptual constructs as they are for the bound soul (*paśu*); thus, by virtue of being both particular and universal, they appear as distinct in the relationship of substrate (*dharmin*) and attribute (*dharma*). This is likewise the case for every living being and in every state.

And according to one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), these [objects] are to be conceptualized— that is, they are to be mentally constructed— as having diverse appearances through various designations established by oneself, such as "this is a friend" or "this is an enemy. For this very reason, even when the flash of the light of consciousness (*vidyā*), which consists of relation, arises...
Because they consist essentially in the negation of the *pradhāna* manifested as illusion,
objects become the targets of acceptance, rejection, and so forth, such that [one thinks], "this is blue," or "I am fair."
"I am happy"—this is because the manifestation [of consciousness] is, in every respect, the locus of rest. Of whom, and where? He says:

of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which, by virtue of being of the nature of an unmixed self-awareness and realization for each individual person, consists of the light of the "I" as it is unconfused with the limitations of the body and so forth.

[The subject] is characterized by various distinct designations such as "I am emaciated" and so forth, [appearing] as the object within memory, imagination, volition, and other forms of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). And it is precisely because this conceptualization is predominant that the bound soul (*paśu*) is always [in that state]; such is the meaning of the aphorism. Having summarized that, he says:
"In this way" means that not only is there the manifestation of existence for bound souls (*paśu*), but even for the Lord (*īśvara*) it is so;
however, the distinction is that for him it is "in this way" by virtue of being beyond conceptual construction (*avikalpyatayā*). Alternatively, by the word "Lord," *paramaśiva* is meant;

for him too, there is indeed the manifestation of existence "in this way" through the medium of lordship (*īśvaratā*). By the particle "eva" (only/indeed), the sense of "tu" (but/however) is conveyed.
It has been explained. The meaning is that he will carry it through in the third verse with the words "he undertakes.

In order to explain the sense of the word "but" (*tu*), and to demonstrate the non-separation of each preceding level of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*) within the successive stages of subjects, he restates what was previously said as follows: "Thus..."
From the words "by such [means]" up to "are established," [it is shown that] they have a universal nature (*sāmānyātmānaḥ*).

Although they consist of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it has already been stated more than once that, because they are made the objects of words, they possess only a universal nature. Through the proliferation of various designations (*saṃjñāprapañca*), they...

The connection is that "they are brought into the path of conventional usage. By the phrase "even by oneself through various designations," he applies the sūtraic expression "that and that" and so forth to both objects. "Immediately thereafter" [is the meaning].

Regarding the phrase "tasyāsādhāraṇī" (4.1.9), he states that by these three verses, the subject matter under discussion is concluded through the syntactic unity of the sentences (*vākyaikavākyatayā*), beginning with the words "tattadvibhinna" and so forth; furthermore, this applies in both ways even within the commentary on the Sūtra.

He shows that [this] is applied even to the subjects (*pramātṛ*) by saying "of the subjects as well. He establishes this very point with the words beginning "belonging to Māyā" (*māyīya*). For when there is a differentiation of objects of knowledge (*prameya-bheda*), there is the state of the subjects of Māyā; and when that exists, there is the differentiation of objects of knowledge. Thus, the creation of the pair belongs to the Blessed Lord.

(371) The arousal of saṃsāra. He expresses this very point by way of its opposite: "Even in the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), those two" means that which consists of the object of cognition (*vedya*) and the cognizer (*vedaka*) is indeed non-different. And this has been stated by me.

"That is seen by me, having been seen"—this is stated in the sūtra [1.4.8]. Now, if everything is non-different within the ultimate subject (*paramārthapramātṛ*), then let the body be an object of knowledge (*vedya*) in relation to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth; but in relation to what is the vital breath and so forth [an object]?
The object of knowledge (*vedya*) is being discussed. Here he says: "But with respect to the void subject (*śūnyapramātṛ*).
Now, one might ask: "Is not the void itself also an object of knowledge? With respect to what, then, is it [the subject]? It is replied: "Even of the void...
By "knower" (*vedaka*), one means "the conceptualizer" (*vikalpaka*). For to those of limited vision (*arvāgdṛśām*), the void is not [an object].

The "ground of direct realization" (sākṣātkārabhūmi) is not [perceived] through a state of vivid manifestation; rather, it shines forth within conceptual cognition—arising from reasoning, scripture, and so forth—as that which has been postulated by the proponents of Brahman as being free from all objects of knowledge such as sound and the like, and as being "not this, not this" (neti neti). Now, [the question arises:]...

In this regard, one might ask: is direct experiential awareness (*saṃvedana*) consisting of realization not possible at all for the subject who is empty? He says that it is indeed possible, referring to "yogis"—those who, following the direct realization of the vital breath, the intellect, and so forth, possess knowledge produced by the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Even when intent on making emptiness an object, they become established as subjects who have extended their state of being bound within another emptiness, in relation to the emptiness that was previously cognized. For instance, the emptiness consisting of the absence of the body is made an object by means of the state of being a subject within the emptiness above the *brahmarandhra*, which transcends the body.

Furthermore, in the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the *mahāvideha-dhāraṇā*, beyond that, there is the void (*śūnya*) consisting of the absence of vital breath (*prāṇa*), characterized by the void at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*); and even that is [transcended] by what is further beyond it—
thus, through such gradations of difference, there is indeed no finality within the sphere of *māyā*.

Because no limit can be found for those [subjects] being produced as empty, this infinite regress does not cause any harm whatsoever. For if an imagined grasper were grasped by another grasper, it would,
while making its own state of being an object (vedyatā) predominant, employ that very state as the instrumental cause for its status as a knower (vedakatā), thereby becoming an object.
If it were accepted that [consciousness] knows [itself], then, due to infinite regress, there would be no cognition of the object of knowledge at all;

rather, since the subject—whose sense of "I" is permeated by consciousness—possesses autonomy, that very subjectivity is the cause of the state of being a grasper. Thus, in reality, pure consciousness alone is present everywhere.
Although the apprehension of an object is [the nature of] the grasping [cognition]— (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 20).

This follows from that logic. However, the state of being an object (*vedyatā*) therein belongs to the realm of *māyā*; in that case, the mere non-termination of another subject (*grāhaka*) is not a fault, because in reality, such a refutation is impossible. And at the occasion of its status as a subject (*pramātṛtā*), even though that void (*śūnya*) is permeated by consciousness (*saṃvit*), [it remains so].

It means that, in relation to other omniscient subjects such as the Vidyēśvaras whose nature is distinct consciousness, the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is distinct. Thus he says "and not" (*na ca*), meaning that in this case, infinite regress (*anavasthā*) does not bring about a fault. Now, even if there be no fault here due to infinite regress, what of that which is the Void (*śūnya*) in the state of the Lord (*īśvara*), in relation to which...
The manifestation of this state of being concealed—by what could that be known?

If you say it is by another void (*śūnya*), then by what is that [second void] known? This leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, if it were unknowable, that void would not manifest as "this" (*idantayā*); thus, being of the nature of non-manifestation, it would be non-existent. And if that non-existence were the case, what...?

The fault [in your position] is that "this-ness" (*idantā*) [would have to be admitted]. This fault would indeed arise if, in this case, another void (*śūnyāntara*) were the object of knowledge and thus the grasper; but it is not so. Nor is it the full nature of consciousness (*pūrṇacidrūpa*), because in relation to that [void], the manifestation of duality consisting in the emergence of "this-ness" would be impossible. Rather, it is that which exists within that full nature of consciousness...

Contraction, which is the very nature of the non-existence of the universe and seems to flee from all sides, is consciousness— self-luminous, untouched by time, and full— which, though in ultimate reality non-different from the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*),
appears as if different due to the sovereignty of that very nature of consciousness.

Since it brings about the manifestation of both the higher (parā) and lower (apara) natures, the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā) with respect to that is entirely appropriate; there is no infinite regress whatsoever. He explains this point at length, beginning with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). The phrase "pure consciousness alone" (*cinmātra*) means with reference to the nature of pure, perfect consciousness. The phrase "the impossibility of non-duality" (*advayānupapatti*) [is used].

And it has been established that, from the perspective of pure consciousness (*śuddhacid*), everything is non-dual because it is not distinct [from it]; this is the intended meaning. Neither from the perspective of consciousness itself, nor through mutual dependence, is a difference between entities tenable; yet, such difference does exist. Therefore, for this reason, the following must be accepted. What is that? He says: "Of that..."

By such statements as these: Īśvara is the self of both the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā) states; that which is his nature as pure consciousness is the portion consisting of the supreme state. "There too" means resting in that very [state]. "Again," he states its distinction from that portion of the supreme state: "precisely because it is of the nature of non-existence."
The nature of consciousness (cidrūpatā),
full of the reflective awareness of luminosity, vibrates; however, the non-existence of the universe does not belong to the universe itself.

The meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) here is "illumination, not reflective awareness. However, even that [negation] necessarily rests upon both illumination and reflective awareness; thus he says, "And in the reflective awareness of its absence," because the state of being reflected upon as illumination also flashes forth. [Objection: But in that case, let it simply be insentient (*jaḍa*).

He says that even this is not so, because words and the like do not manifest in the form they have when separate from the cognizer—namely, as "this is something"—since they do not flash forth in that manner. [Objection: But surely non-existence, being of the nature of the property to be negated, manifests even externally as a property of the verbal designation (ākhyāti) of that which is to be negated, such as "the absence of sound."

"An absence of contact"—thus [it is said]. True, this is so where the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) manifests; but here it is not so, as he says with "not indeed. "[There would be] a manifestation"—this is the intended meaning: that very manifestation of the universe has begun to be contemplated as "this-ness" (*idantā*). How then is there this reflective awareness of non-existence? He says:
"But [it is] indeed without qualification. Now, what is the nature even of such a thing here?
And how is there no infinite regress in that case? To this, he says the passage beginning with "the object of knowledge" (*vedyam*) and ending with "is urged" (*codyate*).
Here, in the word "Lord" (*īśvara*), regarding the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) that manifests, no other cognizer is required.

The connection [is as follows]: since that which is merely the object of knowledge (*vedyamātra*)— insofar as it is characterized by the absence of an object of knowledge— is itself undifferentiated precisely because it is not qualified by an object of knowledge,
for that reason, it belongs to the nature of the individual subjects (*kṣetrajña*), the principles of consciousness (*cittattva*), and even the subjects under the influence of *māyā*.

The meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is negation. The sense is that "the universe"—meaning everything consisting of subject and object belonging to the realm of *māyā*—is negated by the word "not. He then states another aspect of that negative meaning: "And it is devoid of a manifest form through the expansion of time. The reason for this is as follows.

Because it is being directly realized as "that," and because it is being remembered as such, and because it is synthesized precisely by these two acting in conjunction, it does not fall within the domain of objective manifestation (*ābhāsa*). Therefore, the time that is fixed within the "this" portion of a manifestation is not a qualifier of that [consciousness]. For this very reason, that [time] is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) for the Lord.
It is like a second form of Śivanātha; for it will be said (on page 374):
"And that state of Rudra is another condition of the Śiva-tattva."

Thus [he says]. He clarifies this very state of being "second" with the words "contraction of one's own self": for those who maintain the doctrine of duality, the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) is eternally as if contracted from the entire mass of the universe. Precisely because of this contraction, it is denoted by the word "void" (*śūnya*), characterized by the darkness of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-tamas*), and devoid of the manifestation of the universe.
The state of *māyā* is presided over by Rudranātha. He clarifies the meaning of the word "as it were" (*iva*) with the phrase "it is indeed full" (*pūrṇameva*);

in reality, that nature of consciousness is indeed full, yet it manifests as such through contraction—this is the meaning. Or, [it refers] to the Lord (*īśvara*), whose nature consists of the intermediate state between the supreme and the non-supreme.
The second nature, consisting of the "other" (apara-daśā), is the meaning of the negative particle;
and the word "as if" (*iva*) indicates that this [nature] is submerged within the form of the other. He clarifies this very point with the words "And he too...
Although the universe is indeed included within the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) of the Lord’s consciousness, nevertheless, that "I-ness"...

Even though [the senses] are contracted on all sides, they flash forth there and become essentially characterized by light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). How so? By virtue of being a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), that is, through being immersed in the supreme state (*paradaśā*). Now, one might object: as long as the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) is not contracted, there can be no manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā*); and as long as that [manifestation of "this-ness"] does not exist, how can there be "I-ness"?
"To contract" would involve a circular dependency;

he shows that this is not the case by stating "and it is one alone. This is what is meant: due to the sovereignty of consciousness, even this most difficult-to-accomplish [distinction]—namely, "I am this"—shines forth equally from the Absolute (Anuttara).
In that context, "I" is the full form of consciousness itself, whereas "this" is that which is projected [by it] and is therefore contracted.

Regarding that which has the form of "I," the aspect of "I" manifests as nothing other than non-different from the state of "I" which is the full form of consciousness; however, the aspect of contraction...

That which has transcended "this-ness" (*idantā*) shines forth within that very form of "I-ness" (*aham*) like a reflection; yet it is neither manifest through the state of "this-ness," nor is it indistinct. Rather, it exists as a second, stainless mirror that assists in apprehending another "this-ness. Such is this single-flavored [consciousness].

The sovereignty of consciousness. This form exists not only in the state of the Lord (*īśvara*), where *māyā* has not yet fully unfolded, but even in the state of *māyā* where contraction is firmly established; he demonstrates this very path [of manifestation] with the words beginning "in the state of *māyā*. The phrase "due to being formless" is separate.
The meaning is that no form whatsoever of that consciousness appears from the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*). "Those two" refers to the absence of the jar and the absence of the cloth.

He clarifies the very nature of the state of *māyā* with the words "and contraction. He explains this same point with the phrase "by the reflective awareness of 'I' (*ahaṃvimarśa*)," where "removal" means separation. "Primarily" refers to that which has the form of the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*). "Of consciousness alone" refers to the stage of Raudrī, which has the form of the Great Withdrawal (*mahāsaṃhāra*); and this...
He says this by using the term "vāk" (speech), implying that it ultimately rests in the self-awareness of the Lord (*īśvara-saṃvedana*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);
otherwise, he would have designated it separately with the expression "this other one.
Now, even in the Great Dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*), [it exists] in the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*.

Anticipating the objection that "if individual souls (aṇus) remain possessed of the diversity of future dissolution, how can there be for the conscious subject the state of being devoid of the universe?", he says: "The dissolution of the *puryaṣṭaka* as well.
This means that at the time of the dissolution into the non-objective (*apavedya*), even the *puryaṣṭaka* reaches the state of being a seed.

Regarding the state of being empty in form: that very emptiness of form, through the diversity of its seeds, consists of the differentiation of subjects; it remains there in the fierce Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnya*) in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) until the onset of emanation, after which, once again, due to the awakening of the seeds.

In the creation of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), there is a variety of conditions such as the formation of the body, according to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma contained within the previous [state]. "The other" refers to the state of waking and dreaming on the ground of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, the *puryaṣṭaka* is also an elliptical designation for the intellect (*buddhi*) and the body.
Regarding what was said concerning "where":

that is a certain non-recognition (*akhyāti*) rooted in the state of others within the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), which consists solely in the manifestation of the pure *puryaṣṭaka*, occurring in a dissolution other than the previously mentioned dissolution rooted in *māyā* and occurring prior to the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

In the intermediate dissolution (*avāntara-pralaya*), which consists of the resting of the primary matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth, this also serves as an illustration for deep sleep (*suṣupta*) characterized by consciousness (*savedya*); however, that which is devoid of consciousness (*apavedya*) is illustrated by the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Thus, the separation from the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is one and the same for the pure subject (*vedaka*) and the imagined subject; or rather, it is the same for the object of knowledge itself.

"Teneti" (by that) means mutual separation; whether that [separation] also rests in non-separation or not—these are the distinctions according to the appropriate application. Now, he demonstrates that there is a separation of one object of knowledge from another object of knowledge, or that there is a mutual [separation] between those two: "anya" (other), because it resides within the object of knowledge, [denotes] a specific distinction consisting of mutual non-existence.
Without a separate introductory statement,
he says "all indeed," meaning that from the state of the Lord down to the mere object of knowledge, within the manifestation of non-existence,
this alone is the reality of the other.
In that context, "non-manifestation" (*aprathana*) refers to that which, even while possessing the nature of another, remains as such; it is of the nature of delusion (*bhrama*),
denoted by terms such as "dissolution," "void," and "non-existence," and presided over by Rudra.

When [the Lord], through His primordial sovereignty whose nature is will, projects that which is called the impure state of "this-ness" (*idambhāva*) within pure consciousness, the seed [of manifestation] unfolds.
Thus he says, "pure," and so forth. He corroborates this very point with scripture: "And that..."

He establishes the equality of both states with the words "he joins them there," and so forth. Even in that state of equality, he explains the specific distinction by which there remains a difference and the connection with priority and posteriority, using the word "merely" (*kevalam*). By the phrase "even though they possess seeds," it is meant that even the seed has dissolved and becomes nothing more than the residual power of the Supreme Lord’s sovereignty; thus, all things remain as having their seeds intact.
The connection is that "entities" (*bhāvāḥ*) on the plane of Rudra are denoted by terms such as "fitness" (*yogyatā*).
He states that even in the form of fitness, there is a partial similarity between the two states of Śiva and Rudra with the words "at that time.
Those differentiated objects belonging to Māyā which, through the application of the sowing of seeds (*bījapāta*), exist on the plane of Rudra, [reside] within the self of Śiva.

They are manifested as being established in a state of knowability (*vedyatā*), such that they can be designated [as such]. But surely, capacity (*yogyatā*) is the state of being a seed (*bījarūpatā*); has even that dissolved there? True. That incapacity which exists in the form of duality (*bhedarūpatva*) has dissolved into the state of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābhedarūpatva*), by way of being both supreme and non-supreme (*parāparatā*). However, by that [capacity], [it persists] within the consciousness of Īśvara.

Manifestation (*prathā*) is evident; its necessary seed-state (*bījabhāva*) is precisely that which is the Lord’s sovereignty—this is indeed a specific form of fitness (*yogyatā*). Anticipating and resolving the objection—"Surely the effect is appropriate to the cause by way of fitness, but Śiva and Īśvara do not stand in a relationship of cause and effect"—he says:
Even so, because those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*), by means of the practice of knowledge and yoga, gradually ascend to that ultimate state and thereby perceive and accept it,
there may be a sequence of the created world in relation to its appearances; and of that...
"Because it is bound to the ultimate form,
it is not liberated from its autonomy"—
according to this stated principle, even in the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is an establishment of such a state because [it] has been created, but not by itself.
Or rather, let the relationship of cause and effect be inherent by its own nature, as it has been stated:
"O virtuous lady, [this applies] to everything from the earthly element up to Sadāśiva."
All that should be known as *prākṛta* (derived from primordial nature), being subject to both destruction and origination.

Thus, because even the Sakala, Pralayākala, Vijñānākala, Mantra, Mantreśvara, and Maheśvara are permeated by the aspect of "this-ness" (idambhāva)—which is characterized by limitation—they are said to be "created" in relation to that [aspect]. The same applies to Sadāśiva and Īśvara. For this very reason, it was previously stated that they are "natural" (prākṛta).
He states this very point with the words "this portion," and so forth. He clarifies this through a summary with the words "thus, therefore.
If the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*) were clearly manifest there, then that would be the universe itself;
however, the appropriate term is "the seed of the universe" (*viśvabīja*). And [it is] in the form of a power consisting of the fitness for the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the seed.

Even that which is eternally inferable for those such as us is indeed fit for clear manifestation within the state of the Omniscient One; thus, it comes to rest in *ahantā* (the I-sense) alone, yet this *ahantā* is not merely pure, because it possesses the nature of being the seed of the universe.

It is like the manifestation of the specific tasks to be performed by world-ruling monarchs, scholars, poets, artisans, and others, which remains unmanifest [prior to their activity]. For this very reason, the conventional usage here is expressed through the term "power" (*śakti*).
Therefore, it is said: "which does not depend on another grasper. Thus is this [nature of cognition].
The ground of the seed, whose nature is emptiness (*śūnya*), is eternally attached to the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvara-saṃvit*);

therefore, how could there be for that emptiness a separate subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) or objectivity (*prameyatā*)? To this, he replies: "And that," meaning the emptiness which is the agent, having abandoned the non-difference from the consciousness of the Lord by means of the veiling of the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā-ācchādana*).

"By the power of *māyā*," meaning by virtue of its manifestation characterized as such; "in that very way," meaning in that same pure form, devoid of the penetration (*anuvedha*) of supreme consciousness. He shows both that [state], which is void and consists of pure consciousness alone, and that which is characterized by contraction, by saying "And that."

"Empty. "Then" refers to states such as deep sleep, fainting, or meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Now, one might object: "The consciousness itself will remember [the experience] in that way; what is the use of this additional 'emptiness' that is distinct from consciousness? To this he says "Not so," with the word "nahi" (for it is not).
As for the memory—whether regarding the state of being the creator of creation or the presence of contraction—that [memory] occurs by itself.
It pertains precisely to the aspect of the object of knowledge (*vedyāṃśa*). As it has been said:
"But that reality does not attain the state of being remembered in this way" (*Svacchanda-kārikā* 1.13).
(Page 378)

Thus [it is said]. And "that" refers to the resting within the subject of vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of touch and the other [sensations]. "That being so" means while the subject remains in the state of vital breath and so forth. Here, the phrase "remaining" should be explained with the intended meaning that it is because one is established precisely in the subject of the void (*śūnya*). "Has not ceased" means [not ceased] upon the cessation of that [state].

Because, like a *pralayākala*, there is no possibility of the body being vitalized by it, nor of its arising from that body and so forth. "The absence of such states" means the absence of passion, hatred, hunger, thirst, and the like. "Only limited" means that a rice seed, for instance, is filled only with husk and a grain of rice.

Just as from a great seed such as that of the *nyagrodha* tree, which contains within it infinite branches, shoots, and trunks, only a limited [form] emerges; so too is there a gradual expansion within the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*), up to the degree of expansion found among the omniscient ones. The supreme expansion of the Void (*śūnya*) occurs on the plane of Rudra. Thus it is said:

"Of all existents" (*sarvabhāva*); "that" (*tat*) refers to the true nature of consciousness (*cittattva*). By the word "as if" (*iva*), he shows that there is no real limitation whatsoever, other than its mere appearance as such; yet even so (*tathāpi*), despite such limitation, [there is] this [state] of the void (*śūnya*) caused by the deficiency or excess of various objects contained within it.

Having stated that there is a gradation of contraction and expansion, it follows that when all veils are removed, because that knowledge is infinite, the object of knowledge becomes small; from this perspective,
through the progressive severance of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the objects of knowledge, there occurs an expansion of the portion of consciousness.

He shows that the gradation of expansion (vikāsa-tāratamya) is what gives rise to the state of the grasped and the grasper by saying "and for the yogins," and he reminds us of the absence of that [graduation] by saying "but not for the non-yogin" and "for him, however. He states the distinction of this [yogic void] from the other voids which are objects of cognition by using the word "tu" (but). Thus, for those who lack instruction in immersion (samāveśa)—

It has been stated that for those who perceive only negation conjoined with its counter-positive, as well as for the ignorant and for yogis, there is a union with the infinite void being created. However, those who are experts in immersion (*samāveśa*) and knowers of reality, although [they may perceive] the body and so forth...
Although they consider [the self] to be permeated by the nature of consciousness, nevertheless,
there must necessarily be an internal void that serves as the medium for the manifestation of the distinctions of body, vital breath, and so forth;
he demonstrates that nothing else exists there besides that void.
"Or else, by adopting another ultimate position," meaning "because there is no difference.

This refers to the emptiness that appears as not being [present] in a jar, and that which [appears] in both a jar and a cloth; regarding these, there is a distinction of the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).

(Page 379) Since no difference appears to those possessed of discernment (*vivekin*) as anything other than the relinquishing of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is no further void whatsoever. But one might ask: "In that case, by what means does the experience of the void arise for transmigrating beings on the ground of yoga?"

For they do not possess sovereign consciousness (*aiśvarī saṃvit*). Who says this? [The author replies: "It certainly exists. Thus he says, "And all this... It has been established that each preceding [position] deviates from each succeeding one, but the succeeding one does not deviate from the preceding; this is what was stated. In that regard—meaning, within that succession of subjects (*pramātṛ-paramparā*).

In the middle is the "fierce" (raudra) state; that too is to be abandoned because it belongs to the realm of Māyā. Nevertheless, he says "but that" to indicate that it is not to be abandoned. Having thus demonstrated the nature of the subject as void (śūnya-pramātṛ-svarūpa), he explains the commentary with the word "here" (atra).
By using the word "field" (kṣetra) to denote the body, he implies that those who are void of it lack the power of conceptualization (vikalpana-śakti).

It has been stated: that power of conceptualization which, with respect to consciousness (*saṃvit*), is engaged in the process of excluding (*apohyamāna*), attains the nature of reality through the perception of difference; this is the mind (*manas*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). And its function consists in the reflective awareness of an object accompanied by the exclusion of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*); it is precisely in this [function] that it is established.

The state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritā*) arises from that very [source]; subsequently, there is the section on exclusion (*apoha*), while the connection consists in the contact with power (*śakti*). Thus, the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), whose nature consists of both consciousness and non-consciousness, finds rest in the ultimate cognizer—the non-inert, whose essence is the self-awareness of consciousness (*cidvimarśa*). It is for this reason that [the text] extends up to the end of exclusion; such is the fivefold sequence of sections.
The intent lies in the cultivation [of the sequence] both in reverse and in direct order. In its removal, the supreme is the primary factor.

He clarifies this very point with the words "for the mind" (*mano hi*). And that—namely, the power of conceptualization (*vikalpana-śakti*)—[arises] from the mass of sounds... (Svacchanda Tantra 3.17).
Thus,

according to the principle stated in [Svacchanda Tantra 3.15], "and regarding this concealment of its own nature," it is precisely the powers of manifestation (*śabdana-śaktayaḥ*) that appear in diverse forms for every living being at every stage.

Arising as a manifold activity of conceptualization bound to worldly treatises and conventions, and having the subject-object duality as its object, they sustain the three impurities. As it has been stated:
"The powerful mistresses of the sacred seats (pīṭheśvarīs), who are most terrible, delude [beings] again and again."
Thus,
[the senses] are completely absorbed in the objects themselves— (Mālavikāgnimitra 3.31).
And thus it is said: "Those very [powers], leading even conceptual thought to a state where only pure reflective awareness remains, bestow liberation; as it has been taught:
'They grant the fruit of the abode of Śiva to the entire circle of living beings.'"
"The supreme, non-terrible powers of Śiva have been described by those who know that [reality]" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.33).
"My own Māyā alone exists, divided into sixty-four [forms];
thus, when known as abiding on its own path, it brings about accomplishment. (Svacchanda Tantra 3.16)
Thus it is said: "In the conceptualization of designations" (*saṃjñāvikalpe*).
This very designation of transmigrating beings operates both externally and internally. (Vākya-pada 1.127).
Thus, due to the diversity of each individual cognizer, there is the *śabdabhāvanā*, which consists of the power of verbalization; [it is] caused by that.

Regarding the manifold variety of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*): [the text states that] it does not touch the ground of the fundamental awareness (*mūlaparāmarśa*) that [this variety] is limited to just this much; for if it were to touch that, even conceptual construction would lack the nature of bondage. This will be explained later: "Transmigration has come to rest;
it says that transmigration is of the nature of bondage because it is to be abandoned. However, [the text] speaks of its life as its own essential nature (*svarūpajīvita*).
"Regarding the three impurities," and so forth. It has been stated that all three belong to Māyā:
"That triad [of impurities] exists solely through the power of Māyā" (3.2.5). By this much, the function consisting of sound has been explained. And this is the supreme reality of the teaching.

He says: "Right here. This refers either to the pacification of conceptual construction through focused attention (*avadhāna*), or—as will be explained according to the forthcoming method [in 4.1.11]—to the reduction of conceptual construction until only pure reflective awareness remains.
"According to the principle stated in [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.112cd]: 'All this wealth is mine,' the duty [must be performed]. (4.1.12) || 8 ||
(381) But surely it has been stated that an object is a cause of bondage only when it is being conceptualized; and that is incorrect.
For whether it is conceptualized—be it to whatever extent or in whatever manner—or even when not conceptualized, the object remains exactly the same. So what [is the difference]?

The distinction of the object of knowledge lies in its state as the Lord, the bound soul, and the knower. For this [distinction], namely "this [is it]," is its unique creation, subsisting upon the creation of the Lord.
Even this [creation] is truly real through the power of the Lord, by virtue of its being identical with Him, despite its state of ignorance.
By means of the fluctuating activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of the diversity of various phonemes and which obstructs its own repose; || 10 ||

The phrase "of that" [refers to] the creation performed by a limited subject (*paśu*), which, because it follows upon the creation of the Lord (*īśvara*), depends upon it; yet it is unique to each individual subject and occurs at each specific moment, devoid of any continuity with the states or other moments belonging to different subjects. For instance, when something is created by a particular person at a particular time with the thought, "This is pleasing to my heart," that [creation]...

At that very time, for him alone. Now, if the bound soul (*paśu*) possesses the power of creation, then he is indeed the Lord; in that case, why would his creation not be common to all? If that [power] were known to him as his own, it would be so; however, for one who is ignorant and dependent on another, the power of conceptualization (*vikalpana-śakti*) arises. By whom is that [power] his?

If it is argued that [the soul] is awakened, it is so only by virtue of being the Lord (*īśa*). For bondage and liberation consist merely in the non-recognition or recognition of that [Lord]. To explain: the power called *māyā*—which belongs to the Lord, whose body is the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) and whose nature is the reflective awareness of the universe—is the supreme state consisting in the repose within one's own essential nature.
It has as its purpose the obstruction of [ordinary] sovereignty; it consists of the eight groups presided over by the circle of deities beginning with Brahmā.

Precisely for that reason, it is variegated by the thousandfold variety of the divisions of the eight-times-eight [groups], being pregnant with hundreds of thousands of diversities of expansion and contraction inherent in the phonemes beginning with *ka*. For that very reason, [it comprises] the prāṇa, apāna, and so forth—
Fickle in its swinging, unable to find stability even for a moment in one place,
it is by this [power] that conceptualizations such as "this is a friend" or "this is an enemy" are produced;
thus, even the unique creation of the bound soul (*paśu*), whose nature is that of the Lord (*īśvara*), such as "the ten-faced one" or "the tusked one," is likewise [produced].
The meaning of the sūtra is that [the soul] subsists upon those very appearances which appear as distinct and are created by the Lord.
He states this intended meaning with the words beginning "And this," etc.
(page 382).

"From which" (*yataḥ*) means that [the universe] has arisen from the power of sovereignty (*aiśvarya-śakti*) itself. "And just as" (*yathā ca*) implies by the mere fact of not fully understanding it in that way. With the great sentence, "He creates without any material cause" (*nirupādānān eva sṛjati*), the entire meaning of the Sūtra has been explained in brief. This is shown by the section beginning with "those respective [objects]" (*tattat*) and ending with "refined" (*saṃskṛta*).

The compound word has been explained as "subsisting upon the creation of Īśvara. Now, an objection is raised: even in the case of independent conceptual construction (*svatantra-vikalpa*), objects appear precisely with restricted space and time; so how is it stated in the commentary that they are "in a general form" (*sāmānyarūpān*)? He resolves this by saying, "by way of having a general form" (*sāmānyarūpatvena*).

Even when the object of memory is being conceptualized, it does not possess the space and time produced by itself; rather, it possesses only the well-established space and time. Therefore, within the power of autonomous conceptualization, objects consist solely of the fusion of the appearances of space and time created by that [power], and not otherwise.
The intended meaning is that there are certain appearances of place and time that have become firmly established [as real].

Furthermore, the word "only" (*kevalam*) is to be connected specifically with the phrase "of the narrative text in its general form" (*sāmānyarūpāt itivṛttigranthasya*). In that context, one must avoid the misconception that the second instance of perception is a "re-perception" (*punarupalambha*).

[The author] explains [the point] from the words "the previous experience pierces" (*bhinatti pūrvānubhava*) up to "it shines forth" (*sphurati*). The meaning is that the very same prior perception exists merely as a re-emergence. He clarifies precisely what was stated by the word "only" (*kevalam*) with the passage beginning "now" (*nanu*). Now, it is indeed one who is about to die who remembers; therefore...
How was it stated [that it is] "due to a lack of power"? To this he replies: "by way of neither deficiency nor excess.

The sense is that just as, even when one desires to see, the desire for that object does not prevail over the objective aspect [of the act of seeing], so it is here as well. But surely, previously it was manifest, whereas now it is not so?
[The objection regarding] deficiency or excess [of the senses]. To this also, he says: "lack of clarity.
For people employ the convention of "clarity" (*sphuṭatva*) when something is made an object of the functioning of the senses at that moment;
and that [clarity] does not exist here—this is the meaning. [Objection: But in this way, it would not exist at all within the range of experience of an animal.

The power of creation does not not exist; however, he says "being experienced" to show that it possesses a substrate (*sabhitti*) and is thus distinct from that which is without a substrate (*nirbhitti*). For the state of being an object of passion and so forth, consisting of the appearance of the heart and the like, is indeed the construction of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field).

(383) The connection [of the argument] is as follows. Here, the reason is "clear" (*svaccha*), and so forth. By the phrase "for every cognizer" (*pratipramātṛ*), its non-commonality (*asādhāraṇatva*) is stated.
Furthermore, whatever object appears, that is indeed the creation of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field). Now, as for that state...
He states the seed of doubt with the words "previously," and so forth. For loveliness (*hṛdyatā*) is not some external form that has been experienced;

however, in this case, the appearance of the water in the well, the appearance of the thread, and so on, have indeed been experienced. Thus, the seed of doubt is: "In what respect is the bound soul (*paśu*) consecrated as the creator? One might object: "Let this be so; but what of creation (*sṛṣṭi*)?"

Whence does that [bondage] of his arise? He says: "In that well," and so forth, up to the end of the word "liberation" (*mokṣa*). By this explanation of the first verse, there is no redundancy with the phrase "with respect to the bound soul" (*paśuṃ prati*). Within this very power of *māyā*, he includes the three impurities (*malatraya*) and transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
"This very power, whose nature is action, belonging to Śiva and residing in the bound soul (paśu), is the binder... (Spanda Kārikā 3.16).
Thus, following the traditional scripture (*āmnāya*), [the text] begins with "merely a negation" (*niṣedhamātra*) and so forth, introducing the appearance of insubstantiality (*tucchatā*).

The meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is the appearance of contrariety. The intended sense is that this *māyā*—consisting of three components, namely, the object of contrariety, the cognition of contrariety, and the action [of contrariety]—proceeds by means of the three impurities (*mala*). He clarifies that this is "illogical" by stating it is "divided and limited. That which is to be known is what is to be manifested; that which is to be produced is what is to be reflected upon.

And that [object], being non-different from consciousness—which consists of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and which is itself immeasurable due to its lack of spatial and other limitations—is established as being both non-distinct and immeasurable; it is logically untenable for it to appear otherwise.
"Of her who causes to appear" means of her who makes [the object] known as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*); and "of her who performs an action" means...

The meaning is: "by one who is making [it] an object of investigation. He states, beginning with the words "kāryakāraṇa," that the persistence of the *kārma-mala* (the impurity of action) resides within the expanded self (*vitatātman*) which is merely the appearance of activity (*kriyābhāsa*). Regarding the phrase "beginning with the letter *ka*":
[this refers to those things] possessing variety through the states of being clear, unclear, and unmanifest, and through the diversity of *vaikharī* and the other stages of speech.

Through the differentiation of the combined, the individual, and their permutations, by means of the activity of manifesting conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), the phonemes (*vyañjana*)— possessing the power to project the manifold variety of emanation, maintenance, and so forth through their association with the deities of the consonant classes (*varga*)— [constitute] the multitude of infinite subjects such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, along with the aggregate of their effects.

And by means of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the splendor of enjoying those [objects], and so forth, it is being raised up by the infinite names well-known in various respective scriptures that have been acquired.

By means of the phonemes beginning with *a*, which— through their nature as sound that serves as the seed-breath (*bīja*) animating the form of the Supreme Lord— are characterized by the states of being established, ceasing, being joined, being separated, and so forth, and by virtue of both compressing the internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of bliss and the like, and by encompassing everything, [the phonemes] themselves...

Since the variety of the phonemes beginning with *ka*, which are vitalized by the three queens through their own essential forms, is beyond counting, their infinity is likewise demonstrated in the Āgamas. The phrase "perceived by themselves" means that they consist of the various modifications of the mind (*cittavṛtti*).
By the phrase "each proceeding toward its own person," their uniqueness is stated, as well as the fact that they consist essentially in internal perception alone.

By the phrase "for only a moment," their flickering nature is stated in another manner as well, namely, that they proceed at every moment. For this very reason, a temporal distinction is found among the phonemes (*varṇa*) in the scriptures (*āgama*).

It is stated as "the short [vowel]," etc. Regarding the phrase "the internal cognitions known as *pratyaya*": in the *Āgama*, the emission of existence (*bhāvasarga*) which rests upon the principles (*tattva*), elements (*bhūta*), and worlds (*bhuvana*) is called the emission of cognition (*pratyayasarga*). And therein, the presiding deities of the phonemes (*varṇa*) belonging to the portion of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) have been described.
"And its powers for veiling its own nature are perpetually active, because the arising of cognition does not occur without the interpenetration of sound (*śabda*). (Svacchandatantra 3.15).
Thus it is stated in the *Śrī-māyāvaibhavāgama*.
"My own single *māyā* stands as that which divides the sixty-four [powers]," and so forth.
Also, in the *Śrīsarvavīra*:
"Without those, there would be neither word, nor meaning, nor even consciousness."

Thus: "Kādi" refers to those letters by which they are presided over; their enumeration is infinite. And these are merely the manifestations of the power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*). As it has been said:
"We praise Śaṅkara, who is the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers" (*Svacchanda Tantra* 1.1).

Thus; "in that way" means by the *bahuvrīhi* compound contained within the commentary, namely "the infinite enumeration of hundreds of different classes of phonemes. "He" refers to the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field). "Pot-maker" means one whose nature consists of the creation of pots.
"He" refers to the aforementioned *pratyayasarga* (the creation of mental impressions), which is like a pot.

(Page 385) Its body appears as something fashioned by a potter; for we have stated many times that even though this diversity of manifestation is created solely by the Supreme Lord, it is like the variety seen in dreams, mental constructs, and the like.

"Both": by this, that which was stated in the introduction—that from what this appearance of difference arises, and how it assumes the form of limitation—is now determined. It has arisen from the very power of Īśvara having attained the state of *māyā*, and by means of those [powers] which effect the concealment of one's own nature.

Since this manifestation of difference is led to a state of conceptualization by the deities of the phonemes (varṇadevatās), it therefore assumes the nature of bondage. The phrase "to be explained" refers to the immediately following sūtra. It was stated above that [this manifestation] possesses a foundation because it subsists upon that [foundation]. Now, one might object: what of that which is seen suddenly from afar?

When this [person] becomes attached or detached, his creation—consisting of passion and hatred—is produced through dependence on another, even though it is self-made; for even against his will, desire, anger, fear, terror, and so forth arise. Consequently, the lack of recognition of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) therein serves as the cause of bondage.
May that which is raised by the wheel of powers (śakticakra) that deludes the presiding deities of the [five] elements be present—

wherein, however, through the mere force of one's own volitional effort arising from mental fantasies such as "I am this king" or "this enemy has been slain by me," one mounts a vehicle that brings about one's own destruction, impelled by passion, hatred, and the like.
He creates an elephant within his enemy; since his sovereignty (*svātantrya*) in that act is manifest, one might raise the objection:

"In that case, because there is no obscuration of one's own nature (*svarūpāvaraṇa*), how can it be of the nature of bondage? Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "or even that which... (*yāpi vā*). The word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). The mention of "attachment, aversion, and so forth" (*rāgadveṣādi*)...

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he shows by the sentence beginning with "by force" (*balāt*) that what is intended as the instigator (*uddīpaka*)— namely, independence (*svātantrya*)— is precisely the cause that provides the occasion for the opponent’s rebuttal; for this *kṣetrajña*, having been overcome by force, becomes as if unwilling while being enveloped by passion (*rāga*) and the like.

It is produced by conceptual cognitions, which are manifested by delusive powers (*śakti*) having the form of phonemes such as *ka* and so forth; and once thus produced, that creation is forcibly seized by those [powers] presided over by deities and made to function, even during the arising of his mental kingdom (*manorājya*).
Because of dependence on others, even when there is a desire to give rise to wishes that bring about mental joy,

other mental constructions— which serve as the primary causes for fear, dejection, and so forth— arise from the destruction of food and the like; therefore, [this is not possible] through self-mastery.
The connection is that even though that creation appears in the forefront [of consciousness], it is entirely dependent on another; this very point—

It confirms that this belongs to the state of the *kṣetrajña* alone. For when his sovereignty has blossomed, he is no longer merely the *kṣetrajña*, but rather the Lord (*bhagavān*) himself. Regarding the expression "by the activity called conceptualization" (*vikalpākhyavyāpāreṇa*) in the sūtra, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "by the act of conceptualizing," which qualifies the power (*śakti*); thus he says. || 10 ||
If the bondage of the bound souls (*paśu*) is of the nature of a fetter (*pāśa*), then one might ask: what is the creation of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*)?
In response to this doubt, the Sūtra states:
"The creation of the Lord is both common and otherwise, because it is clearly manifest."
Through the abandonment of conceptual construction and one-pointedness, one gradually attains the state of lordship.
The form [of the divine creation] is its state of clear manifestation, and for that very reason, its non-conceptual nature.

And that [object], such as a jar and so forth, being common to all—or by the word "or," even if it is uncommon, such as the double moon and the like—is in both cases other than the creation of bound souls (*paśu*); furthermore, as for the common [creation]:
Or otherwise, it is the uncommon [cause]. When this very creation, through the process of abandoning conceptualization (*vikalpa*),

attains the state of the reflective awareness of sovereignty— namely, "I am this"— by relying on one-pointedness toward the object of a clear thing grasped by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), then [there occurs] the closing and opening of the inner objective and the outer gaze.

Through the perspective of withdrawal (*parihāra*), at the culmination of the gradations of practice, it destroys the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) for the animal-like individual (*paśu*) and reveals his true lordship (*īśvaratā*). As it has been said:
"Liberation (*kaivalya*) arises immediately when the eyes are merely fixed. (Vi.bhai. 113)

Thus it is said. Furthermore, even the animal creation (*pāśava-sarga*) becomes otherwise for one who has realized identity with the Lord through the power of the Lord known as *parijñā* (perfect knowledge); if a clear manifestation occurs, then that [creation], becoming common to all, bestows lordship upon him, just like the ritual options of nourishment (*āpyāyana*) or malevolent rites (*abhicāraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "of one whose mantra has been deposited and whose internal organ is purified": this [emanation] is also always of the nature of the Lord (aiśvara).

With this intention, no alternative interpretation was adopted in the Vivṛti or the Vṛtti; however, we have distinguished [the matter] in this way because we wish to state our intended meaning more clearly.
(Page 387) He introduces the meaning of the sūtra with the words "evam" and so forth. The connection is that [the author] intends to say "iti ca" (and thus).
Since the divine creation (*aiśvara-sarga*) is common [to all], it is therefore different from the animal creation (*pāśava-sarga*).
