[The word] "taḥ" [is used]; and by the force of the word "ca" (and), that which is also uncommon—such as the manifestation of two moons and so forth—is also other than that [ordinary creation], because it appears with extreme clarity and is non-conceptual. Thus he explains the Sūtra with the passage beginning with "aiśvara" and ending with "anyathātvam eva" regarding the creation.

If it is asked, "What is the use of considering the commonality [of the object] among subjects? [the author] shows by means of the words beginning with *saha* that the creation of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) occurs through association with the subject (*pramātṛ*), and not otherwise; for without that which serves as the locus for the manifestation of difference, such [creation] would be impossible. The word *uktyā* refers to what is contained in the commentary (*vṛtti*). By this much—

Thus, according to the commentary (*vṛtti*). For this very reason—namely, because the divine creation (*aiśvarasarga*) pertains even to a single cognizer (*pramātṛ*)—the meaning of the sūtra must also be stated as follows:
"In this sūtra, by the words 'common' (*sādhāraṇa*) and 'otherwise' (*anyathā*), the divine creation is twofold, namely common and uncommon. Now, if...

The distinction between the creation of the Lord (aiśa) and that of the fettered (pāśava) lies in their being manifest or unmanifest; however, that [distinction] exists even in dreams. True; for that very reason, in all cases, both kinds of creation remain established.
Thus he says, "even in a dream. Regarding the word "there" (tatra): for even in a dream, volition and so forth are indeed experienced.

Regarding the phrase "touch, taste, and so forth": by the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), certain specific odors, forms, and sounds are also exclusively uncommon [to a particular sense]. For this very reason:
"Whatever may be visible or audible..."

Thus, the sage has also shown that this [consciousness] is common to all subjects (*pramātṛ*). And that [consciousness] is recited as being merely "I am this" (*ahamidam*), which is a single part of its function (*vṛtti*). Regarding the phrase "of its manifestation":
the manifestation of the *kṣetrajña* belonging to Māyā is such because of its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
It is accompanied by that which is being excluded; therefore, the previously stated definition of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is applicable here:

"For it has been said that a definitive cognition (*viniścaya*) implies both [the affirmation and the negation]. And this [cognition], accompanied by the emergence of differentiation, possesses a clear manifestation.
It occurs by virtue of being common to all living beings, even to one who is unwilling, such as an animal; nor does it depend upon practice like passion and other such afflictions.

It is said to be presided over by Brahmā. Thus [it is said]. "Because there is no arising of differentiation"—by this, the distinction of the Lord's creation from the fettered (pāśava) creation is shown. Since it is so, therefore that [creation]—namely, the creation of the Lord—is not a cause of bondage; rather, it is the fettered creation following upon it [that might be so], yet even that is not [a cause of bondage].

Established in Brahman, its essence consists solely in the emergence of differentiation; it is of the nature of the manifestation of the *māyīya* and *āṇava* impurities. Moreover, it is precisely the creation of objective cognitions (*pratyaya-sṛṣṭi*) that nourishes the *kārmamala*; this very [creation] is the supreme nectar-essence, a mass of bliss through its own repose. Therefore, this alone is the "descent" (*apāya*), which is the emergence of the creation of objective cognitions.
For by means of that [intellect], this knower of the field (kṣetrajña) attains a state of non-sovereignty.
And that arising of cognition, which consists of passion, aversion, and so forth, emerges only following upon objects such as sound created by the Supreme Lord.
As it has been said:
"Therefore, it attains a state of non-independence, and that [consciousness] has only those [objects] as its domain" (Spandakārikā 3.14).

Thus, half of the verse has been explained. Now, he begins to explain the commentary on the aphorism beginning with "by the abandonment of conceptual construction," starting with the words "tatrāntara" and so forth.

And regarding the phrase "of that," it refers to the attainment of attenuation of this very creation of mental constructs (*pratyaya*). The cause for this is "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*), and so forth.

If one asks, "Why is there such practice? he says, "bondage," and so forth. "In this very world" means even while not having abandoned the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) with respect to the body. As Bhaṭṭa Divākaravatsa has said:
When the island of bodily perception has dissolved and you have attained oneness in the stainless ocean of consciousness,
you, the universal self, shine eternally as the one within, having withdrawn the entire collection of the senses so that they never turn back again.

Thus, by this [statement], it is said that at the very stage of the direct realization of all the senses, when the production of cognitions appropriate to the body and so forth has ceased, there remains only the manifestation of jars and other objects as the residual eternal consciousness contracted by all subjects— a state whose essence is non-extraneousness and which is marvelous. "Even though" (yadyapi)— and in the case of coexistence (sahabhāve).

The sense is that "at intervals" is the appropriate reading. Nevertheless, it is not here stated that the emergence of the creation of conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*) occurs at intervals; rather, it is their diminution (*nirhrāsa*) that is meant. And the diminution of conceptual construction is observed in the interim.
Having withdrawn all thought from every direction—
thus.
"In states such as those described in the verse: 'Even while conceptualizing one object, one perceives another as well' (Pātañjala-vārttika 3.207),
if one cultivates that very reduction of conceptualization, then—
with a heart adorned by the jewel-garland of incessant non-conceptual awareness— one attains the state of the Supreme Lord."

Having thus explained [the meaning of] "it is possible" according to the Sūtra and its Commentary, the compassionate Teacher, demonstrating that one should not succumb to despondency here on account of its difficulty, shows that this ground is not beyond the reach even of worldly beings; it is simply that they must attain it by means of the sequence of the ladder consisting of instruction, attentiveness, and practice.

By saying "one should cause [them] to ascend," he encourages [the reader] and unifies the aforementioned objects of knowledge (prameya) with the words beginning "of those in saṃsāra. And here, in this treatise on the compendium of the true meaning (tattvārthasaṅgraha), the jewels of the objects of knowledge mentioned previously are extracted from among other intermediate objects of knowledge and presented as the essential core.

By establishing [the reality] within the treasury of the heart (*hṛdayagañja*), it serves to achieve the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratā*); therefore, it is indeed an ornament, and one should not fall into the error of thinking it a defect due to the suspicion of redundancy. With the intention that everything therein may be determined by this very [text] as being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*), [it is stated]: "all..."
To demonstrate that non-conceptual self-awareness (*nirvikalpa-saṃvedana*) is the abundance of the Lord (*īśvara-bhū*), he says: "The universal" (*sāmānya*).

Those internal and external organs which are related to the unfolding (*vijṛmbhā*) of the two powers of knowledge (*vidyā*) and action (*kalā*), whose nature consists in the universalizing instruments (*sāmānya-karaṇa*)—among those [organs], whatever...

The specific forms such as the manifestation of sound, reflection, and creative emanation (nirmāṇa) are those by which a fragment of the powers of knowledge and action is manifested according to their respective capacities; yet these remain incomplete,
and thus [the term] is merely a linguistic construction applied [to them], since the object of cognition has already been determined in detail.

At the conclusion of the commentary on this sūtra, "This is a jar" (*ghaṭo'yam*), as well as in the *Ādisiddhasūtra* and elsewhere; having thus described the process regarding the indeterminate [perception], he states that this same process applies even when one who perceives many things forms a single conceptual construction (*ekavikalpana*).

"Many," and so forth. To establish these two very objects of cognition (*prameya*), he first establishes the object of cognition with the passage beginning with "since" and ending with "only"; then he applies this to the subject at hand with the passage beginning with "therefore" and ending with "even that which resides in a jar, etc."

And here, the connection with what precedes is that there is the cognition "I am this. He states the fruit of this object of knowledge (*prameya*) with the words "in that much" (*tāvati*). Now, having raised the doubt as to how transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritā*) could exist in such a case, [the author] points to the threefold impurity (*malatraya*) itself.

Is it by stating that "examining this very practice of the ten stages, being the cause for the removal of impurity, brings about liberation," and so forth, up to the passage beginning with "only" and ending with "the devotee"?
Regarding the phrase "they are told": at this point, no realization whatsoever has arisen because the innate state (*sahaja*) is obscured.
Because that which is produced has been conquered; this was stated in the *Ādisiddha-sūtra*.

"That" refers to what was called *rajas*—consisting of both manifestation (*prakāśa*) and non-manifestation—in the *Sattānanda-sūtra* (4.1.6). "Then" means at the time of the manifestation of the subject and object belonging to Māyā. And the cultivation of this state is as follows:

He states that it is the cause of liberation with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*). The very removal of those two impurities is the attainment of what lies above *māyā*; thus, due to the absence of transmigratory existence, liberation in the form of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) has arisen.
Furthermore, if one effects the shattering of the *āṇava* impurity through non-attachment, one also attains immersion into the state of Śiva.

Thus he says, "even there," meaning "the devotee. This refers to one whose worldly tendencies—which normally obscure such firm and stable [divine] impressions due to the descent of the Lord's power (*śaktipāta*)—have been set aside; yet, his own inherent glory is not something to be obscured. Therefore, the sense is that this [attainment] is indeed not difficult to obtain. And this much...

He states that "everything is indeed self-luminous" with the words beginning "sarvaṃ ca" and so forth. "Tat" refers to this innate awareness of "this-ness" (idantā). Now, one might object: if this is an awareness of "this," how can there be non-conceptuality? To this he replies: "And not... because here, due to the veiling of the "I-ness" (ahantā), there is no appearance of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin).

The intention [of the author] is as follows: "internal" means that because there is identification with the body even in total darkness; "all indeed" means that at that time, like a reflection in a mirror, the touch of the body and so forth, or external objects such as a jar, appear; "this" refers to everything from internal touch and so on up to the jar and so forth.

As for the doubt that "manifestation is not possible without a distinction between the grasped and the grasper," that is not so. He recalls the reason for this with the words "since" (*yataḥ*) and so forth. [An objection: "But if this is so, what is the use of the effort involved in the instruction of the scriptures and the like? To this he says: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*), even in the case of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśe*).
When [the Self] is concealed by the delusion of conceptual construction, one might ask: "If there is no difference from the Light, how can there be the form of blue and so forth?
He replies: "And also of the *cittattva*... by itself. This means that blue and so forth appear in the proximity of pure consciousness (*saṃvedana*).

Thus, indeed, it shines forth through perception when there is no internal deception. The term "popular saying" (*pravāda*) refers to that which is constructed by the world and its scriptures based on illusion (*māyīya*). Now, whether it be the blue and so forth that appears, or that which is perceived even more intensely by a yogi possessing superior attentiveness—the nature of the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) consists precisely in this manifestation.

Granted that this is established by consciousness; however, from what [source] does its nature as the manifestation of the universe follow, which is to say its nature as the Supreme Lord? If it is argued that even though it appears as such, it possesses the capacity for this because we observe ever-increasing levels of consciousness, then from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that capacity known? It is known through perception itself, by virtue of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).

He demonstrates this: even within the supreme sovereignty of the Lord, which consists in the manifestation of the non-difference of all things, that capacity exists—not merely as the essential nature alone—but it is indeed self-established. How so? He says:
because, according to the principle already stated, there is a continuous contemplation of the very nature of consciousness.

"Reality is to be examined with effort"—according to this principle, there is thorough cultivation; one whose mental disposition (*āśaya*) or conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is refined and perfumed by that [cultivation] is [the subject].
Now, one might object: "Capability (*yogyatā*) must be inferred from its effects; it is not established through direct perception. Anticipating this doubt regarding consciousness...

For one who states a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason) regarding that object, that [reason] is indeed established by perception; because it has been determined that every *svabhāvahetu* has as its fruit the establishment of mere conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
he explains the introduction of the example with the words "fire, fuel, and so forth."
The inclusion of both [the efficient cause and the material cause] is due to the arising of the effect, which is qualified by whether or not it depends on the passage of time (*kālaparivāsa*).

By the mention of "etc. (*ādi*), deficiency is also included. [Objection: But surely causality (*kāraṇatā*) is a property (*dharma*) consisting of power (*śakti*), and thus it is imperceptible (*parokṣa*). [Response: No; he says this with the passage beginning with "in the effect" and ending with "is observed. Therefore, in this case:

When the nature of a complete cause is established through direct perception, one employs an illustration regarding the nature of a possible cause, saying "just as. For if a person seeking smoke did not conceive of fire's causality with respect to smoke, then even when that fire is seen, it would be like a clod of earth, lacking any cooperative efficacy.

One should maintain [this]. He applies this to the subject at hand (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). For just as fullness is directly perceived because no effort is seen toward accumulating anything beyond it, so too is the state of being a complete cause (*pūrṇakāraṇatā*).
(Page 392) Up to this point: But surely, the perception of the mere nature of fire is not the perception of its causality;
rather, it must be perceived in this way: that smoke invariably follows after fire.

[The opponent claims: "It is the observation of its being the cause. Let this also be granted; nevertheless, that very observation of fire occurred in such a way that one who, at a later time, sees smoke and desires smoke, procures fire.

This is what [the author] says with the words "in the effect," and so forth. Even if this is said, it is not tenable because, by what has been stated, that [observation] does not [establish the causal relationship].

It has been transgressed by us when we stated that perceptibility is established within the domain of causality. How is it not transgressed? He says: "In such a manner," meaning for a person whose mind is thus conditioned by the cognition of smoke immediately following fire.

Likewise, there exists an appearance of the cause that culminates in the mere perception of fire, just as there is a concomitance when observing the subsequent existence of smoke. In this case, it is precisely the necessity of a fixed temporal sequence, dependent upon certainty, that must be made the object of perception and non-perception.
It must be reflected upon. Having thus considered the analogy, he applies it to the subject at hand with the word "evam" (thus).

And this aforementioned capacity for the manifestation of all objects—though it exists from the state of Īśvara up to the attainment of Śivatva—is present even in the case of those who are knowers, yogis, and the initiated, despite their having removed their impurities (*nivṛttamalatva*).

Because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of impurity (*mala*) exists, [Śiva-nature] remains unmanifest; upon its destruction, it becomes manifest, whereby one is liberated at the dissolution of the body. Alternatively, while the latent impression of impurity—which consists of the veils of the body and so forth—still exists, when one enters into Śiva-nature through practice (*abhyāsa*), that Śiva-nature is not yet full.

Or rather, lordship (*īśvaratā*) becomes manifest; for it is precisely the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the body and so forth that is thus dissolved. Therefore, this is not the supreme accomplishment (*parā siddhi*), but rather the intermediate (*aparā*) or the supreme-intermediate (*parāparā*). In this regard as well, it was previously stated that "some portion of the sovereign powers (*vibhūti*) [is attained]. Thus...

The manifestation of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) as non-conceptual form, consisting of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), is established through self-awareness; having thus established its sovereignty, [the text] now establishes that it also consists of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) by means of the passage beginning with "even the reflective awareness of duality" (*bhedaparāmarśo’pi*). And although previously...

Although the application of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been strenuously set aside in the *Ādisiddhasūtra* on the grounds that [the Self] has the single form of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), nevertheless, if it is by these verbal maneuvers that the very nature of the established reality is said to be self-luminous (*svaprakāśatā*)—
just as the Buddhists use the term "Self" (*ātman*) for a mere series of cognitions (*jñānamālā*)— then [that is so].

With the intention that there would be no harm to the [established] entity (*vastu*), [the author] employs the discourse of perception and so forth, which serves as a ground for the confidence of all people. (Page 393)
Therefore, this usage is also entirely faultless. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), scripture (*āgama*) and so forth are included.
Thus, by establishing its proximity (*adūratā*), [it is said]:
"And that is near" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.15).
Thus, having encouraged the disciples by means of this reminder, he concludes the subject matter of the sūtra with the words "tadevam" and so forth. || 11 ||

Having thus attenuated conceptualization, liberation is shown to be one's own self-cognition (*svapratyaya*), which, through the internalization of non-conceptuality, is characterized by the direct realization of the Self of the universe due to its self-luminosity;
however, [the author] shows by means of a sūtra how that [liberation] occurs in the absence of the reduction of conceptualization.
For one who fully understands, "All this is my own manifestation," there is the state of the Great Lord even amidst the proliferation of mental constructs regarding the universal self.

There is no such thing as a "reflexive self" (pratyagātman) other than myself; rather, I am that Supreme Lord who is a mass of light consisting of the grasped, the grasper, and the act of illumination. And He is none other than I; there is nothing else whatsoever.
Therefore, even the creation of conceptual constructs is my own sovereign power, which is essentially freedom—such is the reflective awareness.
When [the state] has become firm, even his conceptual constructions, having fallen into the great reflective awareness (*mahāvimarśa*), become non-conceptual. As it is said in the *Śrīpāradarśana*:
"Even doubt should not be doubted; this is clearly the state of being free from doubt."

Thus, having demonstrated the ignorance that consists of bondage by means of the words "merely," etc., he shows the other [type of ignorance] with the words "but thorough knowledge. He addresses the doubt: "Where is such a manifestation seen, which has its own obscuration as its nature?"
Just as a universal monarch, permeated by the fragrance of his sovereign power,
while sporting may adopt the behaviors of foot-soldiers through his association with those duties.
"Likewise, the Lord, whose nature is joy... (Śivadṛṣṭi 1.38).

With this intention from the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, he pacifies [the objection] by means of another illustration: "Just as he, having attained the state of being Nature (*prakṛti*), brings about the modifications (*vikāra*)."

That very nature of Brahman, its own essential being, brings about modifications— which consist of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and the like— by scattering and breaking apart their respective forms; it manifests them as the agitation of its own powers.

And those transformations, having attained the state of being the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the seed of all worldly activity, are like the sun, known as *ṛtudhāmā* (the sustainer of the seasons), who, at the end of the summer heat (*dharmānta*), through the specific movement [of the breath] occurring during the conjunction of the signs of Cancer, Leo, and Gemini— well-known as the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*)— [manifests] the infinite internal bliss that constitutes his own respective glory.

He beheld the gathering clouds, which are the primordial source of the juices of all medicinal herbs and fruits; these clouds manifest the dispersion and the return of his own luminous nature— which consists of the accumulation of the universal essence of the yogi who has begun the initial expansion attained through identity with the auspicious *ṣumna* channel— and they serve as the great substratum for the juices of the world.
The agreement with the scriptural text recited by Bhartṛhari is thus shown:

"They return" (*pratyāpadyante*) means that their essential nature consists solely of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); and since that very nature has returned again due to the cessation of the appearance of particularities projected by the subject under the influence of *māyā*, this is called "return" (*pratyāpatti*).
He explains the commentary on the phrase "the state of being Maheśvara" with the words beginning "recognition," and so forth. || 12 ||
Now, one might raise the objection: "In that case, what is the difference between the bound and the liberated with respect to the object of knowledge? To this, the Sūtra states:
"The object of knowledge is common [to both], but the liberated one perceives it as non-different from his own self."
Just as Maheśvara is bound, so too [is he] characterized by absolute difference once again. || 13 ||

From the venerable state of Sādākhya down to the level of a worm, whatever constitutes the group of subjects (*mātṛvarga*) and its presiding form of "I-consciousness" (*ahamiti*), the liberated one identifies with that very thing as his own self. Consequently, whatever is an object of knowledge (*prameya*) for the universe is also mine;
and whatever is mine is also another's. And this is the object of knowledge.

"Since it is a limb of my very own self, and other objects of knowledge (*meyāntara*) are likewise so, the object of knowledge (*meya*) is thus not excluded from one another nor from the group of subjects (*mātṛvarga*); therefore, everything reaches the state of being an object of reflective awareness (*parāmarśapada*), which is the reality of resting in the non-dual single flavor. This is what was established in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*.
"The jar knows through my self, and I know through the jar's self;
I know through the self of Sadāśiva, or he knows through my self. (5.106) "In this form there is nothing that belongs to me which does not exist for me in another form. (7.91)

"In this form there is no worship for me, and that [worship] is within the Self of Sadāśiva," and so forth. But for the bound soul (*baddha*), all of this is the reverse; thus, he rests solely in the repose of undivided unity.

Such is the meaning of the sūtra. "Equally" (*tulyam*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Its meaning is "by way of concomitance and without distinction. He states "that" (*tat*) with a sense of distinction: not only does the object of cognition appear as having the sole essence of difference, but the subject of cognition (*grāhaka*) likewise appears so; thus, he has explained this excellence of difference.

With the words "Alternatively," he explains, by way of adopting another position, the fully developed characteristic—the excellence—of the very distinction residing in the object of apprehension. The phrase "Even so" means: let alone the supreme non-difference; even in the form of the higher and the lower, that [distinction] does not exist.

Regarding the phrase "of suchness" (tathātvasya), it should be applied according to the circumstances to both thorough knowledge and lack of thorough knowledge, distinguished by the states of being bound and liberated; however, it is not to be applied according to the literal order [of the words]. || 13 ||

Now, it may be asked: has the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) been examined in the stages of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, as well as in the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) which pertains to the subject as a bound soul (*paśu*); but how is it in the case of Paramaśiva? Furthermore, the sequence of objects of knowledge has been described for the yogin whose senses are fully expanded in the realm of both conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*), yet [what of the one] whose [senses] are entirely closed?
But what is this [nature] of the instrument? To that, the Sūtra says: "In that regard, it is nothing at all";
rather, it is entirely filled with the flood of infinite categories absorbed within it:
Śiva, a mass of consciousness and bliss, whose form is the supreme syllable. (14)
He explains what is to be excluded by the term "sarvathā" (in every way) with the words beginning with "sarvam" (all), etc.

The intention is that the phrase "only an appearance" (*avabhāsa eva*) means that it has not reached full development (*prarūḍhi*); this is a different matter. While explaining the word "nirbhara" (intense/abundant), he shows that "paratvam" (supremacy) here is literal, stating: "it is simply the cognition of 'I'."

The phrase "it is filled" clarifies its purity by stating "even in that which has become its own limb. The word "api" (even) indicates that the desire for a separate object of cognition is utterly remote, as is the state of a subject characterized by wretchedness. The expression "a mass of consciousness and bliss" is from the Sūtra; [this is understood] by the extent of the statement "when the self-awareness is full."
The phrase "it has been explained" is clarified by the passage beginning with "or in the Full" and ending with "is said.
By this very same explanation, the term "the Supreme Syllable" (paramākṣara) is also explained. || 14 ||
(Page 396) Regarding the reality thus described in the fourfold section, the Sūtra states its fruit: "In this way, his self, as well as right knowledge and action," [are perfected].
Knowing and seeing according to his desire, he both knows and acts. || 15 ||

"In this way" means perceiving the Self as having the form of the Lord (Īśvara), and seeing His powers of knowledge and action in their essential nature, rather than concealing them according to the systems of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others. Whatever one desires,
that very thing one knows and accomplishes with this very body through being intent on the practice of immersion (samāveśa), even when not so intent.

One whose heart is firmly established in the vision of the Supreme Lord as the subject within the body is liberated while living; upon the fall of that body, he is the Supreme Lord himself. Thus, the entire meaning previously stated is here presented in a concise form, joined with the commentary on the sūtras and free from even a trace of any obstacle, being truly "fly-free" (nirmakṣika).

Out of supreme compassion, [the author], turning back in order to instill this in the minds of his disciples, explains the Sūtra beginning with "here" (*iha*) by saying "thus" (*evam*). Even in the state of *māyā*, the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) is of such a nature. Furthermore, it is untouched by space and time; therefore, it is full and designated as Śiva—thus [he explains].
The state of Supreme Śiva (paramaśivatva) has been shown. He also describes the nature of Sadāśiva and Īśvara with the words beginning with "And he" (sa ca).

Thus, he states with the words beginning with "In that manner" (tathā) that this ground of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), consisting of Māyā, is indeed fallen within the sphere of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, who are the forms of His power residing within the Supreme Lord and Supreme Śiva.

And he shows that this [power] does not fragment the nature of consciousness with the words "and here too. The connection is with the word "any" (kācit), followed by "not" (na). By this, it is stated that there is no fragmentation whatsoever of the power in its own essential nature.
The reason for this is given as "even in the slightest" (manāgapi); the manifestation of blue and so forth is diverse and distinct, whereas the pure [consciousness]—

And since the nature of space is untouched by time, [the author] establishes through an illustration that this much constitutes the body of a single consciousness alone, as is the case for the Buddhists. "Because of its absence" means because of the absence of any other cause;
even that [cause], if it were not luminous, would be nothing at all, whereas if it is luminous, it is simply consciousness itself—this much. From the very beginning.

Thus he states that [the Self] is established without effort by virtue of being self-luminous. Nevertheless, he states its utility for instruction with the word "merely" (*kevalam*). He also briefly recalls the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "as for what [was said] here," which connects with the phrase "they dispute. Of these...

Thus, the connection is as follows: the cognition of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), who is the substratum of these diverse appearances, is not an object at all. The reason for this is that [the cognizer] has no object distinct [from itself], namely, "I" (*aham*).

A cognition in the form of conceptual construction has as its object its own self which is non-different from it; for a conceptual construction such as "this" is indeed distinct [from the subject]. In that case, to claim that it has its own self as its object while still being a conceptual construction is inconsistent, because it is impossible for one's own self to be an object of conceptual construction. And here:

"One must follow the traditional teaching (āgama) that 'the self is indeed incapable of being designated by convention' (Pāṇini-vārttika 3.2.49). Now, if this [notion of the self] is inconsistent, what then is it?
It is merely an error consisting of the manifestation of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), insofar as this grasping at a self is ignorance."
That entity has arisen with precisely such a nature of existing for only a moment; so what room is there for considering a contradiction?

Since it was said that "there is no contradiction regarding what is non-existent," by thus explaining [the matter], the Buddhist has indeed abandoned the supreme weapon of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). Even so, it can be argued as follows:
It has arisen such that it remains until the blow of the hammer falls—to say this, he says "And not... and so forth.

Now, if an entity is non-existent at the very same time that it is existent, then there is a contradiction. But if it is non-existent only at a subsequent moment, then because of the difference in time, what contradiction is there? He says this with the words "Even in the second [moment]... and so forth.

As for what is also said—that there is no contradiction with destruction in the second moment—that too is not [correct], because the very state of being in the second moment is itself subject to inquiry due to its being produced by destruction; this is done through the consideration of contradiction. Thus he says: "True. In this way, the restriction of time—

Having set aside the basis for momentariness, one will also discard the spatial contraction based on atomism, even when there is a difference in location. We have questioned how that which has manifestation as its very nature could be of a non-manifest form; how then can this [be explained]?
The underlying intention is that it is proper to "make [it] an upper garment" (*uttarīkartum*).

By this much—namely, by grasping [reality] as being merely a moment or a mere atom—they compose a nature of existence that is corrupted by contraction and their own inherent luster; thus, they are cast into this category along with the outbursts of the dull-witted. Therefore...
It has been stated (on page 398) that the ultimate expansion of entities alone is the reality;
whether it be the case for insentient things or whatever else exists, let it be so, but for consciousness, there is no contraction by time and the like.

He says that [consciousness] is not tenable in any way with the words "nor is [it] of consciousness" (*naca citaḥ*). Now, one might object: "Awareness (*saṃvit*) is said to be the locus for the establishment of blue and other objects, and it is necessarily accompanied by manifestation (*sābhāsa*). To this he replies: "without manifestation" (*niravabhāsā*). As it has been said: "Even though the stability of the object... (*yadyapyarthasthitiḥ*, *Āgama-prāmāṇya-siddhi* 20).
Thus [it is said]. "In connection with that" means: this very point has been clarified by the words "action and agent.

"Even by way of a difference in object" refers to the connection with the preceding phrase "the nature of being one or many. "Of those two as well" refers to space and time. Now, just as in the case of the appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell...
When the persistence of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is broken, there is instability; when the persistence of the reflective awareness of the mother-of-pearl is dense, there is stability.
Thus, the state of being an error—namely, "this is indeed mother-of-pearl, not silver"—is established.

This will likewise occur in the case of the subject (*pramātṛ*). [The author] negates this by saying "not appearing," meaning that [the distinction between truth and error] exists only within appearances (*ābhāsa*).

The intention of that suffix (*taddhita*) is this: it is appropriate to speak thus regarding those things in which reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is distinct [from consciousness], but not regarding consciousness itself, in which reflective awareness is non-distinct. And while this may be logical when an external sublater (*bādhaka*) exists, here there is none; thus he says, "Nor even... On the contrary, he states that in the perspective of the Supreme (*paradṛśi*), there actually exists a sublater.

"Now, regarding 'airyā' and so forth: [an objection]—surely all this is inconsistent, lacking the essence of beauty when unexamined, and is subverted; let us set aside for now the refutation of even this. Furthermore, refutation occurs only when there is a stable cognizer," he says with the words "of inconsistency" (*āsamañjasya*). "In this very [context]" means that in his own liberation, because of the absence of a third category, by others...

The intended meaning is that [this] has been established. The connection is that "it would thus be satisfied. As for the phrase "even that": otherness exists from the perspective of cognition, yet cognition itself certainly exists as having a single universal as its object;
thus, there is multiplicity by way of its specific form and unity by way of its universal aspect.

[This refers to] the perception of a single and manifold nature. Now, one might object: "If the 'I' is to be apprehended as a qualification of the King (the subject), its own essential nature would be lost; thus, the person would remain indistinct.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "in the reflective awareness of 'this-ness' (*idantā*," [meaning] "by means of 'this-ness'" in a firmly established manner.
The remainder: having thus explained the meaning of the word *evaṃ*,
he explains [the term] *ātmānam* as being in syntactic agreement with this very [passage], starting from "Thus, one who consists of consciousness" (*evamekaścinmayaḥ*), and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Is not the state of Lordship (*īśvaratā*) a single form of consciousness through its identity with the One, and is that itself not the state of Śiva (*śivatā*) at the time of worldly transaction? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with the words "And of those two. Consequently, even Lordship flashes forth only as merged within the nature of Paramaśiva; for this very reason, it is so stated.
"Wherein all this effect is situated... (Spandakārikā 1.2), and so forth—thus all is auspicious. 15.

Thus ends the third chapter, the investigation into the reality of the subject, the object, bondage, and liberation, within the section on the Compendium of the Meaning of the Principles (*Tattvārthasaṅgraha*), in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara, the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. || 3 ||

Now begins the fourth reflection: I pay homage to Him who, having emanated this entire universe from His supreme form through the sequence beginning with bliss (ānanda), pours it forth both internally and externally while sustaining all nectar.

By means of the pair of chapters on Knowledge and Action, together with the *Tattvārthasaṅgraha*, the aspect "by itself" (*svataḥ*) has been fulfilled once the reality (*tattva*), though self-luminous, has been established through reasoning;
by means of the chapter on Scripture (*āgama*), the aspect "from scripture" (*śāstrataḥ*) has been fulfilled, thereby corroborating that very same meaning.

Even the perspective of the scriptures (*śāstradṛṣṭi*) must be correctly understood as being based on scripture through the instruction of the well-known lineage of gurus, as was previously stated regarding the *śāmbhava* method and so forth. For that very reason,
one should disregard the connection between the supreme, the great, the intermediate, and the divine, semi-divine, and non-divine levels.
With the intention that they are mere mockeries who take refuge only in their own intellects and books,
those who have studied knowledge from books while being devoid of the lineage of gurus,
and who both practice and teach [such things], are cooked in hell for a long time.
Those who revile [the lineage] shall be the consumers of the torments of the kings of hell;
therefore, by imparting that which has come down through the succession of gurus, one attains supreme Śiva.
Thus it has been said. Therefore, this third component, "from the guru," must be completed. For it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"From the guru, from the scripture, and from oneself."
Thus [it is said]. To complete that portion, he states another method by means of three verses.

Therein, by means of the first verse, while stating the lineage of his own gurus, he demonstrates the origin of this [teaching] from the primordial Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, because the instruction is unprecedented and brings about its results without effort.

And [the necessity of] its being taught is shown: by the second [verse], through the manifestation of the sign of recognition (*abhijñāna*), it is demonstrated that the teaching—though existing, yet appearing as if non-existent—is the vitalizing breath [of the lineage], and thus one must show respect toward it;
by the third [verse], for the sake of achieving the fruitfulness of explaining, hearing, reflecting upon, and practicing [the teachings].

In order to favor the disciples who have been engaged by the instruction that "one must necessarily perform the salutation to one's own former guru," and to state the fitness for the status of being a guru oneself,
[the author says] on page 401:
The group of teachers is to be praised for the successful realization of the meaning of the scriptures;

in order to uphold this principle, people proceed toward their goals when they are directed by a father who is renowned for his ability to explain supramundane matters, thereby providing assistance through such renown.

Thus, the meaning of this treatise is the conclusion regarding the designation of the authority, purpose, relationship, and subject matter, preceded by the manifestation of his own name and the display of his lineage, for the sake of initiating those who have not yet entered upon the path and for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world.

The meaning of each verse must be examined; and that is indeed clear, having been established in both the commentary (*vṛtti*) and the sub-commentary (*vivṛti*). However, whatever little remains somewhat unclear here, that alone is being deliberated upon.
Thus, this new path has been made manifest by me as easily traversable.
As it was stated by the Great Teachers in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise:
"One who places his foot here [in this system], perceiving his own nature as the creator of the universe, and constantly entering into that which consists of Śiva-nature, attains perfection. (1)
"For this very reason" means that since liberation arises from recognition alone,

the practice of the "afflictions" (kleśas) such as the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) is simply of no use here. "Because of its lack of clarity" refers to [the fact that other paths] have clear means, are effortless, require no exertion, yet yield great results.
O Lord of Gods, best among those who know yoga, I desire to hear about yoga.
Since yogas consisting of parts such as breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth are artificial,
they do not equal even a sixteenth part of this uncreated [yoga].

And as for that which has been described in the secret scriptures (*rahasyāgama*) by such statements as these, although it was not stated with explicit clarity, it was nonetheless described by way of implication; furthermore,
this is not taught by Śaṅkara unless he is [himself] pleased.
Even when something is perceived in some way, no latent impression (vāsanā) is produced.
Even when one has attained the mere state of latent impressions (vāsanā), if one does not remain vigilant,
the dispensers of justice consign such a person to impermanent enjoyments.
(Page 402) Thus [it is said]:

"If I am Paramaśiva because of being omniscient and the agent of all, then why do I not instantly devour all my enemies? and so forth—[this arises] from a lack of practice regarding the body and other such things belonging to *māyā*.

For the supreme obstacle consists of the desire for worldly existence; that is removed by the thorough cultivation of the meaning of this treatise. Regarding the phrase "by those [means] well-known in the world," the explanation is as follows: they are not recognized in the world as means to liberation; however, in the absence of the negative particle (*nañ*), it refers to those things such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) which are well-known in the world. Having thus explained the first quarter-verse:

He explains the second [verse] with the passage beginning with "And this" and ending with "unentered," stating that at the point where it says "by the abandonment of conceptual construction, through one-pointedness" (4.1.11),
"constant entry" and so forth have been taught.
In the passage "All [is] mine...

(4.1.12), by means of the words beginning with "the state of Śiva," there is the fulfillment of all duties through the vision of the true reality, characterized by non-attachment to the appropriate manifestations desired by the class of practitioners who are defiled by the latent impressions of delusion caused by Māyā within their own selves.

Because knowledge and action are distinguished by their residual nature, they depend upon the grace of another. Having attained the state of being the eye for the entire world, the culmination of one’s renown is indeed the previously mentioned characteristic of a Guru. This is called the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, which proceeds from the Lord Āśrīkaṇṭha.

This indicates the succession of the lineage of gurus (*guruparvakrama*). For in that tradition, when the teaching had declined, the venerable Śrīkaṇṭhanātha commanded the sage Śrī Durvāsas to restore it;
he, in turn, [instructed] Śrī Tryambakāditya at the place known as Traiyambaka, popularly called Tairimbā.
"He created the mind as the initiator within the lineage of the Gurus"—this and more has been stated at length.

Furthermore, that Lord Śrīkaṇṭha attained the reality from the venerable Lord Ananta, and he [Ananta] likewise [attained it] from the power of the Blessed Lord; this and other such matters have been described in the Āgamas. Thus, it is complete.

The succession of gurus has been stated. "Samūḍha" means awakened; it also refers to one whose fragrance has been stabilized by the refinement of mature sandalwood and other substances. "Ghanasāra" is camphor.
Even now, this man is merely a boaster, deluded by the false perception that he has directly realized the form of the eighteen-armed deity and others.

With the intention that there should not arise the notion, "This person does not know reality" or "This person delights in useless descriptions," he says: "having internalized [the world within himself]. One might ask: what is the use of the art of painting in the present context?
He replies: it is for the sake of the knowledge thereof.
(Page 403) Thus,

when there is the attainment of extraordinary worldly objects through the knowledge of sovereignty (*aiśvaryajñāna*), a firm conviction arises among the deluded. He explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "the Lord" (*īśvara*) and so forth.

By this word ending in the instrumental case expressing the reason (*hetutṛtīyānta*), he has explained the meaning of the sūtra phrase *tat* as being equivalent to *tasmāt*. Regarding the particle *eva* used in the commentary (*vṛtti*) for the purpose of providing a restrictive interpretation in such scriptural passages (*āgamasthāna*) as "he is liberated while living, there is no doubt," etc.:

He explains this with the words "from the falling of the body" and so forth. Furthermore, the quality of being most wonderful is indicated by the particle *eva* (only) in this teaching; for it is indeed a marvel that liberation occurs in a single lifetime simply from the falling of the body.
Let liberation in a single lifetime be examined first;
liberation over many lifetimes will be addressed later.
Thus, indeed, the Blessed One, out of supreme compassion, has established this wonder in his scriptural treatises;
yet this is the most wonderful of all wonders: that one is liberated even while still living. (1)

Just as the beloved of a slender woman, though standing near her, cannot provide pleasure because he remains unrecognized as such due to all those various entreaties she makes— being perceived by the world as merely an ordinary person—
so too is this Lord of the Universe, whose virtues go unnoticed by the world, even his own Self.
That [recognition] alone is not sufficient for its own manifestation; therefore, this recognition has been set forth. (2)

"By means of vows" (upayācitaiḥ) refers to prayers to the deities, sending female messengers, and reporting on one's own condition. "Of the slender one" (tanvyāḥ) refers to her who has become emaciated by separation; the connection is that she is "not able to enjoy love-making."

The attainment of bliss from mere recognition and the acquisition of a thousandfold enjoyment through repeated cultivation are equal in both cases. "A particular object" (*vastuviśeṣa*) refers to the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) regarding an object; and "in the beloved" (*kānte*) means that even though she was previously seen, she was not recognized before due to delusion.

This is the state of being (*bhāva*). Or rather, even when something has manifested, there is a state of appearing as if it were not yet manifested; therefore, the conceit that "it is thus" arises upon firm conviction—this is the same in both cases. Unity is the essence of manifestation;
for even here, in the thought "this is that," the unification of "that-ness" (*tattva*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) is what constitutes manifestation, and it is the same here as well.
The meaning is "of lordship and of the ego-sense.
Regarding the phrase "appropriateness of the substratum": the two substrata consist of the form of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).
In that case, the distinction brought about by the force of propriety itself is the ornament; otherwise, there would be mere identity, not similarity. || 2 ||
For the sake of the effortless accomplishment [of liberation] for people, this Recognition of the Lord (Īśvarapratyabhijñā) has been established by Utpaladeva, the son of Udayākara. (3)

Whoever possesses the nature of being born, for him there is accomplishment from this [source]; however, there is no emphasis here on caste, conduct, and so forth—thus its quality of being beneficial to all has been stated. And this has already been explained by us at the very beginning. "From that too" means through the connection with the father’s fruit appropriate to his fame. "Of this" refers to...
[This refers to] the agent. By this, the state of having accomplished all that was to be done by him is demonstrated—may there be auspiciousness! || 3 ||
The author of the commentary summarizes everything with the verses beginning with "ittham" (thus) and so forth.

By this means—by the manner of lordship described by us—he refers to that well-established *susaṃvitti* (perfect consciousness). With the words "lāṭa" and so forth, he refers to [the author] who was previously born into a pure lineage and was subsequently born from the womb of Vāgīśvarī.

"When [the initiation] is performed, the status of being twice-born (dvijatva) becomes complete. "The internal nature" refers to those consisting primarily of ministers and friends. "Named Karka" refers to this treatise such as the *Karkasaṃgraha*. By saying "Tryambaka," he shows that there is pride only in the final [birth], which is birth alone.

When the three goddesses [unite] with him... thus, through the union with the glory of being a servant of Tryambaka, who is complete with the three powers (śaktis), he becomes his servant by virtue of the immersion (*samāveśa*) that consists in subordinating the previously mentioned limited selfhood and emerging in His very nature.

I am possessed of self-conceit because I have accomplished what was to be done. The words "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) and so forth are qualifiers of the *Viśveśvara* and the *Pratyabhijñāmṛta*. He states its worthiness of acceptance with the words beginning "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*).
Teachers such as Kheṭapāla and others relied primarily upon duality.

Others who follow that [view] are likewise [in error]. "By ignorance" means by that which is of an indeterminable nature (*anirvācya-rūpa*). This doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*) is not a monistic doctrine (*ekāntavāda*), nor is it a definitive doctrine of non-duality (*niścita-advayavāda*). The connection is that their view is not clear. For them, there is no Self (*ātman*) or Lord (*īśvara*) that exists in reality.

And there exists another continuum which does not exist in reality—thus [it is said]. "Frustrated" means due to the absence of obtaining the means. But this being the case, one should discard the dualistic interpretation found in the scriptures.

In this discourse on Brahman (*brahmavāda*), having treated ignorance (*avidyā*) as the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) and having defined it with the intention that the Self is the non-dual Lord of Consciousness (*vijñānādvaya-ātmeśvara*), he shows that the person indeed attains success just as previously stated, by saying "in this [system] thus. This applies first to the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-āgama*).

This very point we have stated is clearly expressed in the secret teachings of the Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas, as well as in the Vedāntas; it was precisely in accordance with that [teaching] that the Sugata declared:
"All this, namely the triple world, is mind-only."

Thus [it is said]. In this matter, people have been misled by the Vivaraṇakāras due to their persistent attachment to a wrong view; however, the intended meaning is simply that "this alone is the truth. For this very reason, by using the term "entirety" (*akhila*) at the beginning, he says this:
"Even though the whole world and the entire scripture are not perceived by us, nevertheless, whatever [is perceived]..."
Whether it be an objective reality (*vastu*) or a conceptual construction (*vikalpita*), all that exists only as manifestation.
And this state of manifestation is not distinct from the Lord Paramaśiva, whose very nature is manifestation;
thus, that very Paramaśiva, who is to be worshipped as the ultimate goal, when worshipped, is fit for becoming Paramaśiva himself.
Auspiciousness.
Born from Varāhagupta, who was descended from the family of Bhaṭṭātrigupta, there was Cukhulaka, who was firmly established in the path of Śiva;
[he was one] for whom the teachings of Śambhu were proclaimed by the mouth of the illustrious Bhūtirāja.
He who has completely dispelled the darkness of worldly existence with the rays of reality. || 1 ||

One who, through the power of the Supreme Lord’s energy, possesses an intellect refined by the study of words, sentences, measures, and grammatical refinements pertaining to that birth, body, and station,
becomes a partaker of devotion for the lotus feet of Śiva.
He has no concern for talk of kinsmen, such as wife, son, and the like. || 2 ||
The glory [of realization] was established by the blossoming of the lotus of consciousness, produced through prostrating at the feet of various eminent gurus.
He is proud of his exposition of the non-dual doctrine of Śiva, as demonstrated by the truth revealed by the venerable Lakṣmaṇagupta, the author of the illustrious Śāstra. || 3 ||
While here, amidst the essence of the scriptures, he renders all other non-Buddhist discourses as mere playthings of the kalaviṅka bird,
[he honors] the command of the feet of his venerable master, which yields unfailing fruit.
Having attained [this] through the practice of yoga consisting of constant worship and remembrance.
In order to establish the people in the non-dual state of the illustrious Śāmbhava, which abounds in the noble conduct of all perfections,
he composed this commentary and investigation by means of a concise method.
And clearly established in the state of Abhinavagupta. || 5 ||
When people, reasoning that "this is neither easy to take nor to give— what is to be done with so much?", break it into pieces and then take it away,
O Mountain of Rubies, that fame of yours, as white as the moon, remains unshakable and pervades the entire world.
But this refutation is intended for the world itself, which delights in limited utility.
Having contracted whatever here is indeterminate, then having expanded it, having cast away something as if it were something else, and even having discarded [the rest],
let the wise person now become a composer of the Śāstra.
The method of correct practice is his true birth. || 7 ||
Even the vast ocean at the end of an eon, with its mountain ranges perishing as its waves collide with the mass of flames from the Aurva fire agitated by fierce winds—
this could not suffice for immersion unless one possesses the realization of the Lord.
No one other than Śaṅkara is capable of subjecting an established rule to further investigation.
May it flash forth first in the *paśyantī* state, attain expansion in the *madhyamā*,
and reach the manifest path of the auditory faculty in the *vaikharī*.
(page 407)
If the fresh intellect has come to rest, then, by reflecting upon that [rest], the recognition of the Lord attains its ultimate fulfillment. 9.
Who can speak to stones? Listen, O mobile beings, I speak to you:
what is this futile effort toward the path of worldly gain, which results only in rising from one's bed to face misfortune?
If you would enter the abode of consciousness within the nature of Śiva, then [you will find] but a single moment of the Kali age.
What indeed will you truly know for yourselves by means of these various descriptions?
Understand this *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* (Recognition of the Lord);
burn away the entire circle of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that has settled within your hearts.
Is a heap of seeds, having long been accustomed to the steady state of being licked by the flames within a blazing fire, fit for production? 11.
Indeed, the meanings of sentences, means of valid cognition, words, reality, and the true scriptures lead to one's own spiritual benefit through this treatise;
yet the juices of the earth and those consisting of water do not suffice for the nourishment of crops.
Who else here is capable of joining [the sun] except for the one Sun alone? || 12 ||
What can be said of that deluded person who, without knowing the self, desires to discern something else?
Regarding this question, "Who are you?", what indeed can he say? || 13 ||
Whatever conceptual construction is capable of concealing the Self,
that very same construction has been employed for the purpose of revealing the Self;
by which [revelation], it is clearly [shown] to the Supreme Guru, who is filled with intense compassion—
Salutations to him who is constantly possessed by Śrī Śarvāṇī’s beloved. || 14 ||
Thus, in this ninetieth year, during its final quarter,
when the moon [one] was situated in the ocean [four] of lunar days at the end of Mārgaśīrṣa,
he composed the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, which bestows awakening upon the world.
Impelled by the feet of Śambhu, he revealed it in its entirety.
O Supreme Śiva, there is nowhere such a place, whether within or without, that could be devoid of the manifestation of Your power.
Thus, by one who is immersed in a most firm discernment, this hymn has been composed in order to place you directly before me. 16.
But through reflective awareness, the recognition of the Lord [is achieved]; by that, one should perform the action characterized by the exertion of the reflective awareness of the Self. 17.
Thus ends the fourth reflection, the general conclusion, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* composed by the illustrious teacher Abhinavagupta, the great devotee of Maheśvara. 4.
And this *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* is completed.
This is the work of the venerable Abhinavagupta, whose renown was attained through contemplation of the feet of the illustrious Three-Eyed One (Śiva).
